Glossary

Zig from Zero to IRON LEDGER

A patient, exercise-driven course in the Zig programming language (version 0.16), starting from the first line you type and ending inside the source of IRON LEDGER, a 31,000-line BattleTech mercenary-company simulator written in pure Zig with no libraries.

This book grew out of a short guide, Learning Zig through IRON LEDGER, which taught the language in seventeen brisk sections and then toured the program's architecture. That guide assumed you already knew a systems language. This book does not. It takes the same destination and walks there slowly, the way a traditional programming book does: one idea per chapter, a complete runnable program for every idea, its real output, the trap that catches beginners, and a set of exercises with solutions you can reveal when you are ready. The original guide's architecture tour survives, expanded, as Part 5, and it is where you will find yourself reading real production code with confidence.

Every program in this book was compiled and run with Zig 0.16 on the day it was written. Zig changes between versions, and 0.16 changed how programs talk to the outside world (the std.Io interface) and how the standard containers are used (lists and maps no longer remember their allocator). Tutorials found on the web will often show older forms that no longer compile. When this book and a web page disagree, trust this book and the compiler, and see Appendix A3 for the translation table.

How to read. Chapters build on each other, so read in order the first time. Every chapter ends with exercises and a short quiz. The exercise files live in the exercises/ folder beside this page, with solutions in each chapter's solutions/ subfolder; type the solutions in yourself rather than copying, and run them. Chapter 0 explains the mechanics. Use the sidebar to jump around later; the buttons at the top of it reveal every answer at once or every subsection heading.

0. How to use this book

In this chapter you will learn how the book is laid out, how to run the examples and exercises with the zig command, how to check your answers, and what IRON LEDGER is and why every chapter keeps pointing at it.

0.1 What this book is

This is a slow book. It teaches the Zig programming language, version 0.16, from the very first line you type to the point where you can open a real 31,000-line program and read it with understanding. It assumes you have written a little code in some language, enough to know what a loop and a function are, and nothing else. If you have never used C, never thought about where a variable lives in memory, and never seen a compiler refuse to build your program because of an unused variable, you are exactly the reader it was written for.

Zig is a small language with strong opinions. It has no hidden memory allocation, no hidden control flow, no exceptions, and no garbage collector. Every one of those absences is a design choice, and the book explains the reason each time one of them shows up. Learning Zig is largely learning to like those reasons.

0.2 How the book is organised

The book has six parts and a set of appendices.

Every chapter from 1 onward follows the same shape. It opens with a short statement of goals, works through its topic in numbered subsections, and ends with three fixed pieces: a blue In IRON LEDGER box that shows where the chapter's idea appears in the game's source, a set of exercises with hidden solutions, and a short quiz with hidden answers. A summary box closes the chapter.

Inside a chapter you will see callouts. An amber note adds context. A green Try it box asks you to change something and run it again. A red warning marks a trap that catches beginners. Read the warnings twice.

The book is meant to be read in order through Part 2 at least. Later parts lean on earlier ones, and the exercises assume you did the previous chapter's exercises. Part 5 can be read on its own by someone who already knows Zig.

0.3 Running the examples

You need a terminal and the Zig compiler. Chapter 1 walks through installing it. Once zig version prints 0.16.0, you can run any single-file example in this book with one command:

$ zig run hello.zig
Hello, world!

zig run compiles the file to a temporary executable and runs it. There is no project to set up and no build file to write. Every example in Parts 0 to 3 is a complete file you can copy into an editor, save, and run this way. Programs whose output goes to the terminal print it through std.debug.print, which writes to the standard error stream; you will see the output either way, and Chapter 2 explains the difference.

Examples that contain tests are run with a different command:

$ zig test ex2_overflow.zig
All 4 tests passed.

zig test compiles the file, runs every test "..." { } block in it, and reports how many passed. A test that fails prints where and why. This is the main way you will check your own work.

All output shown in the book in a dark terminal block was produced by actually running the code with Zig 0.16.0. Where a program is meant to fail, the book shows the real compiler error or the real panic message, trimmed of a few lines of internal stack trace, so you learn what those messages look like before you meet them alone.

0.4 Doing the exercises

Each chapter has three to six exercises, marked warm-up, practice, or challenge. They live in the exercises/ folder next to the chapters, one folder per chapter, and every exercise is a single .zig file with a header comment that tells you three things: what to do, which command runs it, and how you will know you are done.

//! Chapter 04, exercise 2: overflow arithmetic.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_overflow.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.

There are two kinds. A zig test exercise has tests at the bottom of the file; you fill in the function bodies marked // TODO until every test passes. A zig run exercise asks you to make the program print exactly the output listed in the header. Some starters do not compile until you finish them, and the header says so when that is the case.

Every exercise has a complete solution in a solutions/ subfolder and, in the book, behind a Solution disclosure under the exercise text. Try before you look. When you do look, read the explanation under the code, because the point of most exercises is a rule, not a program.

Try it. Before going on, make a folder for your work, such as ~/zig-book. You will keep every program you write in it, and by the end of Part 0 it will hold a few dozen small files you can look back on.

0.5 What IRON LEDGER is, and why it anchors the book

IRON LEDGER is a mercenary-company simulator set in the BattleTech universe. You command a small band of BattleMech pilots in the year 3025, take contracts, fight battles, repair machines, pay salaries, and try to end each month with more C-bills than you started with. It runs in a terminal, saves to a SQLite database, and is written entirely in Zig with no third-party libraries. Its source lives in the game/ folder next to this course and is about 31,000 lines long.

It is here for a reason that has nothing to do with giant robots. A book that teaches a language with toy examples leaves you unable to read a real program, because real programs are where the toy pieces meet: a struct holds a list that was made by an allocator that belongs to a game state that a command mutates that a query reads that a screen draws. IRON LEDGER is big enough to have all of that, small enough to read in full, and, because it was written in Zig 0.16 with no libraries, every idiom it uses is one this book can teach you.

So each chapter ends by pointing at the game. In Chapter 4 you learn integer arithmetic, then see that the game stores money as a 64-bit integer and never uses a float for it. In Chapter 6 you learn switch, then see the calendar's days-in-month function. By the time you reach Part 5, the tour of the game's architecture, you have already met most of its code in small pieces. The last chapters put the pieces together and follow one keypress from the terminal all the way through the simulation and back.

You do not need to know BattleTech. A BattleMech is a walking tank measured in tons; a lance is four of them; a C-bill is money; a contract is a job. That is the whole glossary you need, and the appendix has the rest.

0.6 A word about compile errors

Zig's compiler is strict in ways that surprise people who come from Python or JavaScript. An unused variable is an error. A variable declared changeable but never changed is an error. Reusing a name from an outer scope is an error. None of these stop a Python program. In Zig they stop the build, and the book shows you each one deliberately, with the exact text the compiler prints, so that the first time it happens on your own code you recognise it and know the one-line fix.

Treat the compiler as a patient reviewer rather than an obstacle. Almost every message it prints names the file, the line, the column, and often what to do about it. Learning to read those messages is a skill this book teaches on purpose, and Appendix A4 collects the common ones in one place.

What you learned.
  • The book has six parts; Parts 0 to 2 should be read in order.
  • zig run file.zig runs a program; zig test file.zig runs its tests.
  • Exercises are single files with a header that names the command and the goal; solutions are in solutions/ and behind the Solution disclosure.
  • IRON LEDGER is a real 31,000-line Zig program; each chapter ends by pointing at where its idea appears there, and Part 5 reads the game end to end.
  • Compile errors are the compiler helping; the book shows real ones on purpose.

1. Installing Zig and your first program

In this chapter you will install the Zig 0.16 compiler, write a hello-world program by hand, run it three different ways, and read it line by line until every character in it makes sense. You will also meet the three shapes a Zig main function can take and learn why they differ.

1.1 What Zig is

Zig is a general-purpose programming language in the C tradition. Programs compile to native machine code, run without a virtual machine or a runtime, and manage their own memory. If you have used Python or JavaScript, the biggest change is that there is nothing between your code and the machine: no interpreter, no garbage collector, no exception system. If you have used C, the biggest change is that Zig removes the parts of C that cause most bugs (undefined behaviour is caught in debug builds, integer overflow panics rather than silently wrapping, and the preprocessor is gone) and adds compile-time code execution, a proper module system, built-in tests, and a cross-compiler that can build for any target from any machine.

Three of Zig's slogans will come up again and again in this book, so here they are once:

  • No hidden control flow. When you read a line of Zig, what it does is what it says. A function call is written as a call. Nothing runs behind your back, so there are no exceptions that unwind through your code and no destructors that fire when a scope ends. Cleanup is written explicitly with defer (Chapter 17).
  • No hidden memory allocation. Nothing in the language or the standard library allocates memory unless you hand it an allocator. This is why Zig programs can run on tiny devices and why IRON LEDGER can free its entire campaign with one call.
  • Errors are values. A function that can fail says so in its return type, and the caller must do something about it. The compiler makes forgetting impossible.

Zig is still a young language and its standard library changes between releases. This book is written for version 0.16. Tutorials on the web written for 0.11, 0.13, or 0.14 will show you functions that no longer exist. When in doubt, trust the compiler in front of you, not a blog post.

1.2 Installing the compiler

Zig ships as a single folder containing one executable, zig, and its standard library. There is nothing to configure.

macOS. If you use Homebrew, one command does it:

$ brew install zig

Linux and Windows. Go to https://ziglang.org/download/, download the archive for your platform (for example zig-x86_64-linux-0.16.0.tar.xz or zig-x86_64-windows-0.16.0.zip), unpack it somewhere permanent such as your home folder, and add that folder to your PATH. On Linux that usually means one line in ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc:

export PATH="$HOME/zig-x86_64-linux-0.16.0:$PATH"

On Windows, open Edit environment variables for your account and add the unpacked folder to Path. Many Linux distributions also package Zig, but the packaged version is often old; the download from ziglang.org is the reliable route.

Check it. Open a new terminal and ask the compiler for its version:

$ zig version
0.16.0

If you see 0.16.0 (a suffix such as 0.16.0-dev.123 is fine too), you are ready. If you see an older number, you have an old install somewhere on your PATH; find it with which zig on macOS and Linux or where zig on Windows and remove it.

An editor. Any text editor works. VS Code with the Zig Language extension, or any editor that speaks the language server zls, gives you error underlines as you type. The book never depends on an editor feature, so use what you like.

1.3 A folder and a file

Make a folder for the book's programs and go into it. Every command in Part 0 assumes you are inside this folder.

$ mkdir ~/zig-book
$ cd ~/zig-book

Now create a file called hello.zig in that folder and type the following into it. Type it rather than pasting: five lines is short enough, and your fingers will learn the shape of a Zig file.

hello.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("Hello, world!\n", .{});
}

Save the file. The extension .zig matters; the compiler will not look at anything else.

1.4 Running it: zig run

The quickest way to run a single file is zig run:

$ zig run hello.zig
Hello, world!

The first run takes a few seconds while the compiler builds the standard library's pieces that your program uses; later runs are cached and fast. zig run compiles your file into an executable in a cache folder, runs it, and shows you the output. It is the command you will use most in Part 0.

If you mistype something, the compiler tells you where. Delete the second argument to print so the line reads std.debug.print("Hello, world!\n"); and run again:

$ zig run hello.zig
hello.zig:4:14: error: expected 2 argument(s), found 1
    std.debug.print("Hello, world!\n");
    ~~~~~~~~~^~~~~~
<zig>/lib/std/debug.zig:307:5: note: function declared here
pub fn print(comptime fmt: []const u8, args: anytype) void {
~~~~^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Read that from the top. hello.zig:4:14 is the file, the line, and the column. Then the word error: and a sentence. Then the offending line with a marker under the spot. Then a note: showing the declaration of the function you called wrongly, in this case in the standard library's debug.zig. Nearly every Zig error has this shape: location, message, source line, and notes. Put the argument back before going on.

1.5 Building an executable: zig build-exe

zig run hides the executable. When you want a file you can copy somewhere and run later, use zig build-exe:

$ zig build-exe hello.zig
$ ls -la hello
-rwxr-xr-x  1 john  staff  1873176 Sep  9 10:29 hello
$ ./hello
Hello, world!

The compiler wrote a native executable called hello (hello.exe on Windows) into the current folder, and running it prints the same line. It is 1.8 megabytes because a debug build carries symbol tables and safety checks; a release build (zig build-exe -O ReleaseSmall hello.zig) is a few kilobytes. You do not need release builds until much later; the debug build is the one that catches your mistakes.

Real projects with many files use a third command, zig build, driven by a script called build.zig. That is Chapter 31. For now, one file and zig run is all you need.

1.6 One formatter: zig fmt

Zig has exactly one code style, and the compiler ships the tool that enforces it. Write the hello program badly on purpose:

ugly.zig
const std=@import("std");
pub fn main() void{
std.debug.print("Hello, world!\n",.{}); }

It runs fine, because the compiler does not care about whitespace. Now ask zig fmt to fix it in place:

$ zig fmt ugly.zig
ugly.zig
$ cat ugly.zig
const std = @import("std");
pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("Hello, world!\n", .{});
}

zig fmt prints the name of each file it changed and rewrites it: four-space indentation, spaces around =, one statement per line, the closing brace on its own line. It will also add a trailing comma to a multi-line list and reflow the list one item per line, which is how the long argument lists in this book got their shape. There is no configuration, so every Zig codebase in the world looks the same, and code review never argues about style.

Two habits worth forming now: run zig fmt . (with a dot, meaning the current folder) before you consider any file finished, and run zig fmt --check . to list files that need formatting without changing them. IRON LEDGER's test suite refuses to pass if zig fmt --check src/ finds anything.

1.7 The anatomy of hello world

Here is the program again, and then one paragraph per line.

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("Hello, world!\n", .{});
}

const std = @import("std"); brings the standard library into the file under the name std. Three things are happening. @import is a builtin function: anything starting with @ is part of the language rather than something defined in a library, and there are about a hundred of them (Appendix A1 lists them). @import("std") returns a value, the whole standard library as one big struct. And const std = … binds that value to a name that cannot be reassigned. You could call it anything, but every Zig file on Earth calls it std, so do that. A file that does not print, read files, or use any library code does not need this line.

pub fn main() void { declares a function. fn introduces it, main is its name, the empty parentheses say it takes no parameters, and void is its return type: it gives nothing back. pub makes the function visible outside this file. The program's entry point must be pub, because the code that starts your program lives in the standard library and has to be able to see main from there. Leave pub off and the compiler says so:

$ zig run hello.zig
<zig>/lib/std/start.zig:697:43: error: 'main' is not marked 'pub'
    const fn_info = @typeInfo(@TypeOf(root.main)).@"fn";
                                      ~~~~^~~~~
hello.zig:3:1: note: declared here
fn main() void {
^~~~~~~~~~~~~~
<zig>/lib/std/start.zig:638:20: note: called inline here
    return callMain(argv[0..argc], env_block);
           ~~~~~~~~^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
<zig>/lib/std/start.zig:590:38: note: called inline here
    std.process.exit(callMainWithArgs(argc, argv, envp));
                     ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Notice where the error is reported: inside the standard library's start.zig, the file that calls your main, with a note pointing back at your declaration. You will occasionally see errors located in library code like this; the note is the part to read.

std.debug.print("Hello, world!\n", .{}); is a function call. std.debug is a namespace inside the standard library, print is a function in it, and it takes two arguments: a format string and a list of values to substitute into it. The format string here has no placeholders, so the list is empty. The \n at the end is an escape sequence meaning a newline; without it the next thing printed would land on the same line. The semicolon ends the statement, as in C or JavaScript, and it is not optional.

.{} is the piece that puzzles everyone. It is an empty anonymous struct literal, which is Zig's way of writing "a bundle of values whose type the callee will figure out". Because print may be given any number of values of any type, it cannot declare a fixed parameter list, so it takes one parameter that is a bundle. With no values the bundle is .{}; with one value it is .{name}; with two, .{ a, b }. You will write .{} thousands of times, and Chapter 2 is entirely about what goes inside it.

Finally the closing brace ends the function body. Zig uses braces for blocks and does not care about indentation; zig fmt cares for you.

Try it. Add a second line to main that prints your name using a placeholder: std.debug.print("Welcome, {s}. The company is yours.\n", .{"Commander"});. Run it. Then remove the \n from the first line and run it again to see the two lines collide.
name.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const name = "Commander";
    std.debug.print("Welcome, {s}. The company is yours.\n", .{name});
}
$ zig run name.zig
Welcome, Commander. The company is yours.

1.8 Three shapes of main

The main you wrote returns void and takes nothing. That is the simplest form, and it is enough for every program in Part 0. But you will see two other forms in real code, including in IRON LEDGER, so here they are.

Form 1: pub fn main() void. No parameters, cannot fail. The program exits with status 0 when main returns. Use it for small programs that only compute and print.

Form 2: pub fn main() !void. The exclamation mark makes the return type an error union: the function returns either nothing or an error. This lets you write try inside main to propagate failures, which Chapter 16 covers properly. If an error escapes from main, the program prints it and exits with status 1:

hello_err.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() !void {
    std.debug.print("about to fail\n", .{});
    return error.SomethingWentWrong;
}
$ zig run hello_err.zig
about to fail
error: SomethingWentWrong
hello_err.zig:5:5: 0x10000abcd in main (hello_err)
    return error.SomethingWentWrong;
    ^

The first line is your print. Then the runtime reports the error by name and shows where it was returned. The last line of the transcript, cut here, is a stack trace into the standard library. Try it and check the exit status: echo $? prints 1.

Form 3: pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void. This is new in 0.16 and it is the form every real program uses. The single parameter, conventionally called init, is a struct that the runtime fills in before calling you. It carries an allocator (init.gpa), an I/O context (init.io), the command-line arguments, and the environment. Anything that touches the outside world, which means writing to standard output, reading a file, or asking the time, needs the init.io value. Here is the standard-output version of hello world:

hello_stdout.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var w = std.Io.File.stdout().writer(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &w.interface;
    try out.print("Hello from stdout, {d}\n", .{42});
    try out.flush();
}
$ zig run hello_stdout.zig
Hello from stdout, 42

Do not worry about the middle four lines yet. Chapter 2 takes them apart, and Part 4 explains the design behind std.Io. What matters now is the pattern: a program that only needs to show you something uses std.debug.print and Form 1; a program that produces output meant to be captured, piped, or saved uses a real writer and Form 3. IRON LEDGER's main is Form 3.

Trap: old tutorials. Code written for Zig 0.13 or 0.14 obtains standard output with std.io.getStdOut().writer(). That function does not exist in 0.16 and the compiler will tell you no field named 'getStdOut'. When a snippet from the web will not build, check its Zig version before you check your typing. Appendix A3 lists the old and new forms side by side.

1.9 What just happened, in order

It helps to have a picture of the pipeline, because the error messages refer to its stages. When you type zig run hello.zig:

  1. The compiler parses hello.zig into a tree. Syntax errors (a missing semicolon, an unbalanced brace) stop it here.
  2. It analyses the tree, starting from main and following every reference. Only code that is reachable from main gets checked, which is why a typo in a function you never call can go unnoticed until you call it. Type errors, unused variables, and missing arguments stop it here.
  3. It generates machine code for your target, links it with the pieces of the standard library you used, and writes an executable to its cache.
  4. It runs that executable, passing through any arguments you gave after the file name, and shows you its output.

When something goes wrong at stage 1 or 2, you get a compile error and no program runs. When it goes wrong at stage 4, you get a runtime panic with a stack trace, which you will see for the first time in Chapter 4. Keeping the two apart is the beginning of reading Zig's messages well.

In IRON LEDGER. The game's entry point is game/src/main.zig, and its main is Form 3: pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void. The first thing it does is build the game state from the allocator the runtime handed it, then it walks the command-line arguments looking for flags such as --tui and --repl: 
pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var gs = game.state.GameState.init(init.gpa, .{ .seed = 3025 });
    defer gs.deinit();

    var args = std.process.Args.Iterator.init(init.minimal.args);
    _ = args.next(); // exe name
    var repl = false;
    var tui = false;
    while (args.next()) |arg| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "--repl")) repl = true;
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "--tui")) tui = true;
        // …
    }
Every piece of that will be familiar by the end of Part 1: defer in Chapter 17, the while … |arg| capture in Chapter 15, std.mem.eql in Chapter 11. The file also starts with a //! comment, a doc comment for the whole file; the game's house rule is that every file opens with one.

Exercises

Exercise 1.1 · Hello, by hand warm-up

Without looking at the chapter, write a complete program that prints Hello, world! and a newline, then run it with zig run and format it with zig fmt. The starter file contains only the import line. Name the file: exercises/01-first-program/ex1_hello.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 01, exercise 1: hello, world by hand.
//! Run with:  zig run ex1_hello.zig
//! Expected output (on stderr):
//!   Hello, world!
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("Hello, world!\n", .{});
}

Four things must be present: the pub, the name main, a return type, and the empty argument bundle .{}. Forget any one of them and the compiler names the problem; the missing-pub and missing-argument errors are both shown in this chapter.

Exercise 1.2 · Three lines, three values warm-up

The starter declares a company name, a commander name, and a unit count. Print them on three lines exactly as the header comment shows, using {s} for text and {d} for the number. The file does not compile until every constant is used. Name the file: exercises/01-first-program/ex2_roster.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 01, exercise 2: three lines, one placeholder each.
//! Run with:  zig run ex2_roster.zig
//! Expected output (on stderr):
//!   Company: Grey Death Legion
//!   Commander: Carlyle
//!   Units: 4
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const company = "Grey Death Legion";
    const commander = "Carlyle";
    const units: u32 = 4;
    std.debug.print("Company: {s}\n", .{company});
    std.debug.print("Commander: {s}\n", .{commander});
    std.debug.print("Units: {d}\n", .{units});
}

Each print call takes one placeholder and a one-element bundle .{value}. The reason the starter refuses to compile is Zig's unused-constant rule, which Chapter 3 explains: declaring a value and never using it is an error, not a warning.

Exercise 1.3 · The stdout version practice

The starter is a Form 3 program that writes to standard output, but when you run it nothing appears. Work out why (the chapter mentions it), fix it, and add a second line that prints The answer is 42. using a {d} placeholder. Confirm the output really goes to stdout by running zig run ex3_stdout.zig 2>/dev/null, which hides stderr. Name the file: exercises/01-first-program/ex3_stdout.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 01, exercise 3: the same greeting, written to stdout.
//! Run with:  zig run ex3_stdout.zig
//! Expected output (on stdout, so `zig run ex3_stdout.zig 2>/dev/null` still shows it):
//!   Hello from stdout!
//!   The answer is 42.
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var w = std.Io.File.stdout().writer(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &w.interface;
    try out.print("Hello from stdout!\n", .{});
    try out.print("The answer is {d}.\n", .{42});
    try out.flush();
}

The missing piece is try out.flush();. The writer collects text in the 1024-byte buffer you gave it and only hands it to the operating system when the buffer fills or when you flush. A program that returns from main without flushing throws away whatever is still in the buffer. std.debug.print has no buffer, which is why it never needs a flush; Chapter 2 goes into the trade-off.

Check your understanding

  1. What does zig run hello.zig do that zig build-exe hello.zig does not?
    AnswerIt runs the program after compiling it, and it keeps the executable in a cache folder instead of writing it next to your source file. build-exe only compiles, and leaves the executable in the current folder.
  2. Why must main be marked pub?
    AnswerThe code that starts your program lives in the standard library (start.zig) and calls main from outside your file. Without pub the function is private to the file and the library cannot see it.
  3. What is .{} in std.debug.print("hi\n", .{});?
    AnswerAn empty anonymous struct literal: the bundle of values to substitute into the format string. It is empty because the string has no placeholders.
  4. What does the ! in pub fn main() !void mean?
    AnswerThe return type is an error union: main returns either nothing or an error. If an error escapes, the runtime prints its name and exits with status 1.
  5. Which form of main does a program need if it wants to write to standard output, and why?
    Answerpub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void. Writing to stdout in 0.16 needs the I/O context init.io, which only arrives through that parameter, and the try on the write and flush needs the ! return type.
  6. What does zig fmt --check . do?
    AnswerIt lists every file in the current folder that is not formatted the standard way and exits with an error if there are any, without modifying anything. Without --check, zig fmt rewrites the files.
What you learned.
  • Zig is a compiled systems language with no hidden control flow, no hidden allocation, and errors as values; this book is for version 0.16.
  • Install with brew install zig on macOS or the archive from ziglang.org elsewhere; confirm with zig version.
  • zig run compiles and runs one file; zig build-exe writes an executable; zig fmt is the single formatter.
  • Hello world is an import, a pub fn main, and one std.debug.print call whose second argument is the value bundle .{}.
  • main comes in three shapes: void, !void, and (init: std.process.Init) !void; the last one is what real programs use.
  • A compile error names file, line, column, message, and notes; learn to read it top to bottom.

2. Printing to the screen

In this chapter you will learn the two ways a Zig program writes text to the terminal and when to use each, how format strings and their placeholders work, how to line values up in columns, and how to write strings that contain quotes, braces, and line breaks.

2.1 Two streams

Every program started from a terminal has two output channels. Standard output (stdout) is for the program's real product: the thing a user would save to a file or pipe into another program. Standard error (stderr) is for messages about the program: progress, diagnostics, complaints. Both appear on your screen by default, which is why beginners rarely notice the difference, but the shell can redirect them separately, and tools that consume output only read stdout.

Zig gives you a different function for each, and they look very different.

two_streams.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    std.debug.print("this goes to stderr\n", .{});

    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var w = std.Io.File.stdout().writer(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &w.interface;
    try out.print("this goes to stdout\n", .{});
    try out.flush();
}
$ zig run two_streams.zig
this goes to stdout

On screen the two lines look the same. Ask the shell to hide stderr and only one survives:

$ zig run two_streams.zig 2>/dev/null
this goes to stdout
$ zig run two_streams.zig >out.txt
this goes to stderr
$ cat out.txt
this goes to stdout

2>/dev/null throws away stderr; >out.txt sends stdout to a file. This is how you will confirm, in the exercises, that your program is writing where you think it is.

2.2 std.debug.print

std.debug.print(fmt, args) writes to stderr, immediately, with no buffer and no possibility of failure. It needs no setup and no init parameter, which is why it works from a main() void. Its name says what it is for: debugging, progress messages, and, in this book, every example whose output is meant for your eyes rather than for another program. Its cost is that each call is a separate write to the operating system, which is slow if you print ten thousand lines, and that its output is on the wrong stream for a tool whose text someone wants to capture.

2.3 The stdout writer, and flush

Writing to stdout takes four lines, and each one is there for a reason.

    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var w = std.Io.File.stdout().writer(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &w.interface;
    try out.print("this goes to stdout\n", .{});
    try out.flush();

var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined; declares an array of 1024 bytes and leaves its contents unset. This is the buffer: text you print is collected here and sent to the operating system in one piece instead of one call per line. You choose the size; 1024 is fine for a few lines and 4096 is common.

std.Io.File.stdout() is the file handle for standard output. Calling .writer(init.io, &buf) on it makes a writer, an object that knows how to push bytes into that file, using your buffer and the I/O context that came in through init. The & means "the address of": the writer keeps a pointer to your buffer rather than a copy. Pointers are Chapter 18; for now, &buf is simply how you lend the buffer out.

const out = &w.interface; takes the generic writer interface out of the file-specific writer. It is the interface field that has the print method, and taking its address once saves writing w.interface.print every time.

try out.print(…) formats into the buffer. It can fail (the disk could be full, the pipe could be closed), so it returns an error union and you must try it, which is why this main returns !void.

try out.flush(); pushes whatever is in the buffer to the file. Forget it and your program prints nothing:

noflush.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var w = std.Io.File.stdout().writer(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &w.interface;
    try out.print("you will never see this\n", .{});
    // no flush!
}
$ zig run noflush.zig

The transcript is empty on purpose. The text went into buf, main returned, and the buffer was discarded with the rest of the stack frame. Nothing in Zig runs at scope exit unless you write it, so nothing flushed. This is the "no hidden control flow" rule in action, and it is the single most common mistake in Zig printing.

Why so much ceremony? Python's print hides a buffer, a stream, an encoding, and an implicit flush at exit. Zig shows you all of them because each is a decision: the buffer is memory you own, the stream is chosen explicitly, and flushing is a moment you pick. When a program writes a million lines, the buffer size and flush points are where its speed lives. Until then, the recipe above is fixed and you can copy it.

For the rest of Part 0 the examples use std.debug.print, because it is shorter and the output is for you. Everything said below about format strings applies identically to out.print.

2.4 Placeholders

The first argument to print is a format string. Inside it, each pair of braces is a placeholder that will be replaced by the next value from the bundle. The letter inside the braces says how to render the value.

placeholders.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const name = "Atlas";
    const tonnage: u32 = 100;
    const grade: u8 = 'A';
    const price: i64 = 9_626_000;

    std.debug.print("{s} weighs {d} tons\n", .{ name, tonnage });
    std.debug.print("rating {c}\n", .{grade});
    std.debug.print("price {d} C-bills\n", .{price});
    std.debug.print("hex {x}, HEX {X}, binary {b}\n", .{ tonnage, tonnage, tonnage });
    std.debug.print("octal {o}\n", .{tonnage});
}
$ zig run placeholders.zig
Atlas weighs 100 tons
rating A
price 9626000 C-bills
hex 64, HEX 64, binary 1100100
octal 144
PlaceholderRendersWorks on
{s}textstrings (byte slices and string literals)
{d}decimal numberintegers and floats
{c}a single charactera u8
{x} / {X}hexadecimal, lower / upper caseintegers
{b}binaryintegers
{o}octalintegers
{e}scientific notationfloats
{any}whatever the type's default looks likeanything
{}the default for simple typesnumbers, booleans

The values come from the bundle in order. .{ name, tonnage } feeds name to the first placeholder and tonnage to the second. When there is one value you can write .{grade} without spaces; zig fmt adds the spaces inside the braces when there are two or more.

{any} is the escape hatch. It prints any value in a debugging-friendly form and is what you reach for when you do not know or care about the exact type, such as an array or a struct:

any.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const tonnage: u32 = 100;
    const ratio: f64 = 2.5;
    const flag = true;
    const point = .{ 3, 4 };
    std.debug.print("{any} {any} {any} {any}\n", .{ tonnage, ratio, flag, point });
    std.debug.print("{d} {d} {}\n", .{ tonnage, ratio, flag });
}
$ zig run any.zig
100 2.5 true .{ 3, 4 }
100 2.5 true

The second line shows that {d} also works on floats, and that a bare {} is fine for a boolean. You will see {} used for numbers in other people's code; it means the same as {d} for integers. This book prefers the explicit letter.

The compiler checks the format string against the bundle at compile time. Use the wrong letter for a type and the program does not build:

wrongspec.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const tonnage: u32 = 100;
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{tonnage});
}
$ zig run wrongspec.zig
<zig>/lib/std/Io/Writer.zig:1803:5: error: invalid format string 's' for type 'u32'
    @compileError("invalid format string '" ++ fmt ++ "' for type '" ++ @typeName(@TypeOf(value)) ++ "'");
    ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

The error is reported inside the standard library's Writer.zig, because that is where the check runs, but the message names your mistake exactly: {s} on a u32. Give it too few values and you get a similarly blunt message:

$ zig run toomany.zig
<zig>/lib/std/Io/Writer.zig:717:13: error: too few arguments
            @compileError("too few arguments");
            ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This is worth pausing on. In C, a wrong printf specifier is a runtime crash or silent garbage. In Python it is a runtime exception. In Zig it is a compile error, because the format string is a compile-time constant and print is checked against it while the program is built. Your first encounter with comptime is a printf that cannot be wrong.

2.5 Width, alignment and precision

After the letter, a colon introduces options. The most useful three are a fill-and-alignment, a width, and a precision.

width.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const pi: f64 = 3.14159265;
    std.debug.print("[{d:.2}]\n", .{pi});
    std.debug.print("[{d:8.3}]\n", .{pi});
    std.debug.print("[{d:>6}]\n", .{42});
    std.debug.print("[{d:<6}]\n", .{42});
    std.debug.print("[{d:^6}]\n", .{42});
    std.debug.print("[{d:0>6}]\n", .{42});
    std.debug.print("[{s:<10}]|\n", .{"Atlas"});
    std.debug.print("[{s:>10}]|\n", .{"Atlas"});
    std.debug.print("[{x:0>4}]\n", .{255});
}
$ zig run width.zig
[3.14]
[   3.142]
[    42]
[42    ]
[  42  ]
[000042]
[Atlas     ]|
[     Atlas]|
[00ff]

Read {d:0>6} from left to right: render as decimal, then pad with 0, aligned to the right (>), in a field 6 wide. The alignment characters are < for left, > for right, and ^ for centred. If you give a width without an alignment, numbers align right and strings align left. The fill character goes just before the alignment character and defaults to a space.

A precision comes after a dot: {d:.2} shows two digits after the decimal point, rounding. Width and precision combine as {d:8.3}, meaning width 8, three decimals. Chapter 23 and Appendix A2 have the complete grammar; these five forms cover nearly all real use.

Put together, they make tables:

table.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{s:<12}{s:>6}{s:>12}\n", .{ "Unit", "Tons", "Price" });
    std.debug.print("{s:<12}{d:>6}{d:>12}\n", .{ "Locust", 20, 1_512_000 });
    std.debug.print("{s:<12}{d:>6}{d:>12}\n", .{ "Shadow Hawk", 55, 4_701_000 });
    std.debug.print("{s:<12}{d:>6}{d:>12}\n", .{ "Atlas", 100, 9_626_000 });
}
$ zig run table.zig
Unit          Tons       Price
Locust          20     1512000
Shadow Hawk     55     4701000
Atlas          100     9626000
Trap: a plus sign appears. When you give a width to a signed integer, 0.16 prints positive values with a leading +: {d:8} on an i64 holding 75000 gives   +75000. Unsigned types never do this, and a signed value with no width does not either. If you want a padded column of signed numbers without the sign, cast to an unsigned type when you know the value is not negative, or format into a buffer first (Chapter 23).

2.6 Escapes and literal braces

A string literal is written between double quotes. Some characters cannot be typed directly inside it, so a backslash introduces an escape:

EscapeMeaning
\nnewline
\ttab
\"a double quote
\\one backslash
\rcarriage return (Windows line endings are \r\n)
\x41the byte with hex value 41 (the letter A)
\u{2588}the Unicode character with that code point, encoded as UTF-8

Braces are special in a format string, so to print one you double it: {{ and }}.

escapes.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("tab:\there\n", .{});
    std.debug.print("quote: \"IRON LEDGER\"\n", .{});
    std.debug.print("backslash: C:\\games\\ledger\n", .{});
    std.debug.print("unicode: \u{2588}\u{2588} 100%\n", .{});
    std.debug.print("braces: {{d}} prints literally, {d} does not\n", .{7});
}
$ zig run escapes.zig
tab:	here
quote: "IRON LEDGER"
backslash: C:\games\ledger
unicode: ██ 100%
braces: {d} prints literally, 7 does not

Strings in Zig are sequences of bytes, not characters, and the source file is UTF-8, so you can also type █ directly into the literal and it prints correctly. The \u{…} form is for when you want the code to be readable on any keyboard. Chapter 11 goes into what a string really is.

2.7 Multi-line strings

For text with several lines, escapes get tiresome. Zig has a second string syntax: each line starts with \\, and the string is everything after the two backslashes on each line, joined with newlines. Nothing inside is escaped, so quotes and backslashes are literal.

multiline.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const banner =
        \\==============================
        \\   IRON LEDGER   day {d}
        \\   "no plan survives contact"
        \\==============================
        \\
    ;
    std.debug.print(banner, .{1});
}
$ zig run multiline.zig
==============================
   IRON LEDGER   day 1
   "no plan survives contact"
==============================

Three details. There is no newline after the last line unless you add an empty \\ line, which the example does. The string is still a format string when you pass it to print, so {d} inside it is a placeholder and braces must still be doubled. And the closing semicolon goes on its own line after the last \\, because anything on a \\ line is part of the string.

Try it. Remove the final empty \\ line and run the program; the shell prompt lands on the same line as the bottom border. Then change {d} to {d:0>3} to get day 001.
In IRON LEDGER. The game uses both streams for exactly the reasons above. Diagnostic messages and the scripted demo go through std.debug.print, as in game/src/main.zig where the saved-campaign list is reported (three of the messages, trimmed): 
std.debug.print("could not read the campaign registry\n", .{});
// …
std.debug.print("no saved campaigns.\n", .{});
// …
std.debug.print("campaigns (most recently saved first):\n", .{});
The terminal client, on the other hand, draws the whole screen into a large buffer and writes it to stdout in one flush per frame, because a screen redraw is one product, not a series of messages (see game/src/tui/term.zig and Chapter 48). Every {s}, {d} and column width you learn here is used there, many thousands of times.

Exercises

Exercise 2.1 · Five placeholders warm-up

The starter declares a name, a grade character, and a tonnage. Produce the single line shown in its header with one print call, using {s}, {c}, {d}, {x} and {b}. The tonnage appears three times, in three bases. Name the file: exercises/02-printing/ex1_placeholders.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 02, exercise 1: one line, five placeholders.
//! Run with:  zig run ex1_placeholders.zig
//! Expected output (on stderr):
//!   Atlas (grade A) weighs 100 tons, hex 64, binary 1100100
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const name = "Atlas";
    const grade: u8 = 'A';
    const tonnage: u32 = 100;
    std.debug.print("{s} (grade {c}) weighs {d} tons, hex {x}, binary {b}\n", .{
        name, grade, tonnage, tonnage, tonnage,
    });
}

A value can be passed more than once; the bundle just lists it again. When the bundle gets long, zig fmt breaks it one item per line if you leave a trailing comma after the last item, which is what the solution does.

Exercise 2.2 · An aligned table practice

Print the four-row unit table shown in the starter's header. The name column is 12 wide and left-aligned, tons is 4 wide and right-aligned, price is 7 wide and right-aligned, with one space between columns. The header row is strings; the others mix strings and numbers. Name the file: exercises/02-printing/ex2_table.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 02, exercise 2: an aligned table.
//! Run with:  zig run ex2_table.zig
//! Expected output (on stderr):
//!   Unit         Tons   Price
//!   Locust         20 1512000
//!   Shadow Hawk    55 4701000
//!   Atlas         100 9626000
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{s:<12} {s:>4} {s:>7}\n", .{ "Unit", "Tons", "Price" });
    std.debug.print("{s:<12} {d:>4} {d:>7}\n", .{ "Locust", 20, 1_512_000 });
    std.debug.print("{s:<12} {d:>4} {d:>7}\n", .{ "Shadow Hawk", 55, 4_701_000 });
    std.debug.print("{s:<12} {d:>4} {d:>7}\n", .{ "Atlas", 100, 9_626_000 });
}

The header row uses {s:>4} to right-align the word Tons over a numeric column; the same width spec works for strings and numbers. The number literals with underscores are just readable integers; underscores are ignored by the compiler.

Exercise 2.3 · A banner practice

Build the five-line box in the starter's header as one multi-line string literal, with the day number substituted through a {d} placeholder, then print it. The third line contains braces that must print literally and the fourth contains double quotes. Name the file: exercises/02-printing/ex3_banner.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 02, exercise 3: a multi-line banner with a placeholder inside.
//! Run with:  zig run ex3_banner.zig
//! Expected output (on stderr):
//!   +----------------------+
//!   | IRON LEDGER   day 12 |
//!   | funds: {not a hole}  |
//!   | "trust the ledger"   |
//!   +----------------------+
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const day: u32 = 12;
    const banner =
        \\+----------------------+
        \\| IRON LEDGER   day {d} |
        \\| funds: {{not a hole}}  |
        \\| "trust the ledger"   |
        \\+----------------------+
        \\
    ;
    std.debug.print(banner, .{day});
}

Inside a \\ string nothing is escaped, so the quotes are typed as they are. But the string is still a format string when handed to print, so the literal braces are doubled. Note the trailing empty \\ line for the final newline.

Exercise 2.4 · One number, six ways warm-up

Print the value 255 as plain decimal, zero-padded to five places, space-padded to five places, lowercase hex, uppercase hex with a 0x prefix, and binary, each in square brackets, all on one line. Name the file: exercises/02-printing/ex4_padding.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 02, exercise 4: the same number, five ways.
//! Run with:  zig run ex4_padding.zig
//! Expected output (on stderr):
//!   [255] [00255] [  255] [ff] [0xFF] [11111111]
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const n: u8 = 255;
    std.debug.print("[{d}] [{d:0>5}] [{d:>5}] [{x}] [0x{X}] [{b}]\n", .{ n, n, n, n, n, n });
}

The 0x is ordinary text in the format string, not part of the specifier. {d:0>5} reads: decimal, fill with zeros, right-aligned, width five.

Check your understanding

  1. Which stream does std.debug.print write to, and does it buffer?
    AnswerStandard error, and no: each call writes immediately and cannot fail.
  2. A stdout program prints nothing at all. What is the most likely cause?
    AnswerA missing try out.flush(); before main returns. The text is still in the buffer when the program exits.
  3. What happens if you write {s} for an integer?
    AnswerA compile error: invalid format string 's' for type 'u32'. Format strings are checked at compile time.
  4. What does {d:0>6} mean, piece by piece?
    AnswerDecimal; fill character 0; right-aligned; width 6.
  5. How do you print a literal { in a format string?
    AnswerDouble it: {{. Likewise }} for a closing brace.
  6. In a multi-line string, how do you get a newline after the last line?
    AnswerAdd an empty \\ line at the end. Without it the string ends right after the last character.
  7. Why does {d:8} on a positive i64 show a plus sign?
    AnswerIn 0.16 a width on a signed integer renders an explicit sign for positive values. Unsigned types and unpadded signed values do not show it.
What you learned.
  • stderr is for messages, stdout is for output; std.debug.print writes to stderr with no setup, the stdout writer needs a buffer, init.io, and a flush.
  • Placeholders: {s} text, {d} number, {c} character, {x}/{X} hex, {b} binary, {any} anything.
  • Options after a colon: fill, alignment (< > ^), width, and .precision.
  • Format strings are checked at compile time; a wrong specifier or a missing value is a compile error.
  • Escapes use a backslash; literal braces are doubled; multi-line strings start each line with \\.

3. Variables, constants and types

In this chapter you will learn how Zig names values with const and var, when you must write a type and when the compiler works it out, and what undefined means. You will meet four compile errors that every Zig beginner hits in their first hour, with the exact text the compiler prints, and learn the one-line fix for each.

3.1 const and var

A name is introduced with one of two keywords. const binds a name to a value that will never change. var declares a variable that can be assigned again later.

constvar.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const company_name = "Grey Death Legion";
    var funds: i64 = 1_000_000;
    funds -= 250_000;
    std.debug.print("{s} has {d} C-bills\n", .{ company_name, funds });
}
$ zig run constvar.zig
Grey Death Legion has 750000 C-bills

The company name never changes, so it is a const. The funds go down, so they are a var. funds -= 250_000 is short for funds = funds - 250_000, and the same shorthand exists for +=, *=, and the other operators.

Try to change a const and the compiler refuses:

assign_const.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const funds: i64 = 1_000_000;
    funds -= 250_000;
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{funds});
}
$ zig run assign_const.zig
assign_const.zig:5:5: error: cannot assign to constant
    funds -= 250_000;
    ^~~~~

The habit to build is the reverse of what most languages teach: start with const, and only write var when you have a line that assigns to the name a second time. This is not a matter of style. The compiler enforces it, as you will see in section 3.5, and it makes code easier to read, because every var is a promise that the value changes somewhere below.

3.2 Type annotations and inference

Every value in Zig has a type, and the type is fixed for the life of the name. You can write the type after a colon, or you can leave it out and let the compiler infer it from the value.

annot.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const a: u8 = 200; // annotated
    const b = a; // inferred: b is also u8
    const c: i64 = a; // u8 fits inside i64, so this is allowed
    const d: f64 = 2.5; // a float literal needs a home too
    std.debug.print("{d} {d} {d} {d}\n", .{ a, b, c, d });
    std.debug.print("{s} {s} {s} {s}\n", .{
        @typeName(@TypeOf(a)), @typeName(@TypeOf(b)),
        @typeName(@TypeOf(c)), @typeName(@TypeOf(d)),
    });
}
$ zig run annot.zig
200 200 200 2.5
u8 u8 i64 f64

@TypeOf(x) is a builtin that gives the type of an expression, and @typeName turns a type into a printable string; together they let a program report what the compiler decided. Here b was declared with no annotation and got u8 because it was initialised from a u8. c was annotated i64 and the u8 value was coerced to the wider type, which is allowed because every u8 value fits in an i64. The reverse, putting an i64 into a u8, is refused, and Chapter 4 covers the rules.

So when do you need the annotation? Inference works whenever the right-hand side already has a concrete type: another variable, a function's return value, an expression of typed values. It does not work, or works differently from what you meant, in two common cases.

3.3 Number literals are comptime_int

Write const x = 42; and ask for its type.

comptime_int.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const x = 42;
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{@typeName(@TypeOf(x))});
    const big = 1_000_000_000_000_000_000_000; // does not fit in u64
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{big});
    const y: u8 = x; // fine: 42 fits in a u8
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{y});
}
$ zig run comptime_int.zig
comptime_int
1000000000000000000000
42

The type is comptime_int: an integer known at compile time, with no fixed width. It can be as large as you like, which is why the thousand-billion-billion literal printed without complaint, and it silently becomes whatever concrete type it is used as, which is why const y: u8 = x worked. A comptime_int is more like a number written on paper than a number stored in memory. Float literals are the same: 2.5 has type comptime_float.

This is convenient right up until you try to change one at runtime:

var_needs_type.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var count = 0;
    count += 1;
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{count});
}
$ zig run var_needs_type.zig
var_needs_type.zig:4:9: error: variable of type 'comptime_int' must be const or comptime
    var count = 0;
        ^~~~~
var_needs_type.zig:4:9: note: to modify this variable at runtime, it must be given an explicit fixed-size number type

The note tells you the fix. A var lives in memory and memory has a fixed size, so the compiler needs to know how many bytes to set aside. Write var count: u32 = 0; and the program builds. Rule: a var initialised from a bare number literal always needs a type annotation. A const initialised from a literal does not, and stays a comptime_int until it is used somewhere with a concrete type.

Why not just default to i32 or i64? C does, and the result is that 1 << 40 is silently zero on many compilers because the literal was an int. Zig's literal type is exact and unbounded; only when it meets a concrete type does it get a width, and if it does not fit you get an error at that spot rather than wrong bits.

3.4 Four errors you will hit today

Zig refuses to build code that contains things which are almost always mistakes. Other languages emit warnings for these; Zig emits errors, on the grounds that a warning everyone ignores is worth nothing. Here are the four you will meet first, each with its real message and its fix.

Unused local. Declare something and never use it:

unused.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const tonnage: u32 = 100;
    std.debug.print("ready\n", .{});
}
$ zig run unused.zig
unused.zig:4:11: error: unused local constant
    const tonnage: u32 = 100;
          ^~~~~~~

Usually the fix is to delete the declaration or to use it. Sometimes you genuinely want a name you do not use yet, for example while writing a function one piece at a time; then you discard it by assigning it to the underscore:

discard.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const tonnage: u32 = 100;
    _ = tonnage;
    std.debug.print("ready\n", .{});
}
$ zig run discard.zig
ready

_ = tonnage; tells the compiler "I know, and I mean it." The same applies to function parameters (Chapter 7) and to return values you choose to ignore. The exercise starters in this book use it constantly, so that a half-finished function still compiles. Using a name after discarding it is itself an error ("pointless discard"), so remove the underscore line when you fill the function in.

Never-mutated var. Declare a var and never assign to it again:

never_mutated.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var tonnage: u32 = 100;
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{tonnage});
}
$ zig run never_mutated.zig
never_mutated.zig:4:9: error: local variable is never mutated
    var tonnage: u32 = 100;
        ^~~~~~~
never_mutated.zig:4:9: note: consider using 'const'

The fix is in the note: change var to const. This is the rule that makes the "start with const" habit mandatory rather than optional.

Shadowing. Reuse a name that is already visible:

shadow.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const count: u32 = 1;
    {
        const count: u32 = 2;
        std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{count});
    }
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{count});
}
$ zig run shadow.zig
shadow.zig:6:15: error: local constant 'count' shadows local constant from outer scope
        const count: u32 = 2;
              ^~~~~
shadow.zig:4:11: note: previous declaration here
    const count: u32 = 1;
          ^~~~~

In most languages the inner count would quietly hide the outer one inside the braces. Zig forbids it, because a reader scanning the function sees one name and expects one meaning. The fix is a different name. The rule applies to every kind of declaration, including the standard-library import at the top of the file:

shadow_std.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const std = 5;
    _ = std;
}
$ zig run shadow_std.zig
shadow_std.zig:4:11: error: local constant shadows declaration of 'std'
    const std = 5;
          ^~~
shadow_std.zig:1:1: note: declared here
const std = @import("std");
^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Assigning to a const you met in section 3.1: error: cannot assign to constant. The fix is var, if the value really changes.

Trap: the errors come one at a time. When a file has several problems the compiler often reports only the first, because it stops analysing a function at its first error. Fix it, run again, and the next one appears. This is normal and not a sign that you have made things worse.

3.5 undefined

Every declaration needs an initial value. When you have nothing meaningful to put there yet, because the value will be filled in before it is read, you write undefined:

undef.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var total: u32 = undefined;
    total = 10;
    total += 5;
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{total});
}
$ zig run undef.zig
15

undefined is a promise: "I will assign this before I read it." The compiler reserves the memory and does not initialise it. You saw var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined; in Chapter 2, where a 1024-byte buffer was declared for a writer to fill; zeroing it first would be wasted work.

Break the promise and you get garbage, not an error:

undef_read.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var total: u32 = undefined;
    total += 5;
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{total});
}
$ zig run undef_read.zig
2863311535

In a debug build Zig fills undefined memory with the byte 0xAA, which is why the number is 2863311535 (0xAAAAAAAA) plus five. That pattern is a deliberate tell: if you ever see 43690, 2863311535, or a string of AA bytes in a value, you read something you never set. In a release build the memory holds whatever was there before, and the bug is silent. Use undefined only when the assignment is a line or two away, and prefer a real initial value whenever one makes sense.

3.6 Block scope

A pair of braces is a block, and a name declared inside a block exists only until the closing brace.

block.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const outer: u32 = 1;
    {
        const inner: u32 = 2;
        std.debug.print("inside: {d} {d}\n", .{ outer, inner });
    }
    std.debug.print("outside: {d}\n", .{outer});
    std.debug.print("outside: {d}\n", .{inner});
}
$ zig run block.zig
block.zig:10:41: error: use of undeclared identifier 'inner'
    std.debug.print("outside: {d}\n", .{inner});
                                        ^~~~~

The outer name is visible inside the block; the inner name is gone after it. Function bodies, loop bodies, and the branches of an if are all blocks. You can also open a bare block anywhere just to limit how long a name lives, which the first example did.

A block can also produce a value. Give it a label, and break :label value leaves the block with that value as its result:

block_value.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const tonnage: u32 = 55;
    const weight_class = blk: {
        if (tonnage <= 35) break :blk "light";
        if (tonnage <= 55) break :blk "medium";
        if (tonnage <= 75) break :blk "heavy";
        break :blk "assault";
    };
    std.debug.print("{d} tons is {s}\n", .{ tonnage, weight_class });
}
$ zig run block_value.zig
55 tons is medium

The label blk: goes before the opening brace; the name is yours to choose. Each break :blk ends the block and supplies the value for weight_class. This is how Zig writes "compute a value in several steps, right here" without a helper function or a mutable temporary, and IRON LEDGER uses it often. Chapter 6 shows that if and loops can produce values in the same spirit.

3.7 Top-level declarations

So far every name was declared inside main. Names can also be declared at the top of the file, outside any function, where they are visible to every function in the file.

globals.zig
const std = @import("std");

const max_lance_size = 4;
var battles_fought: u32 = 0;

pub fn main() void {
    battles_fought += 1;
    battles_fought += 1;
    std.debug.print("lance size {d}, battles {d}\n", .{ max_lance_size, battles_fought });
}
$ zig run globals.zig
lance size 4, battles 2

Top-level const is common and good: it is how a file names its constants, imports, and types. Top-level var is a global variable, which every function can change from anywhere; it is legal, occasionally useful, and generally avoided for the same reasons as in any language. IRON LEDGER's simulation core has no global variables at all, by design, and Chapter 41 explains why that matters for a game that must replay identically from a seed.

One difference from local declarations: the order of top-level declarations does not matter. main can use max_lance_size even if it were declared below it, and a function can call another declared further down the file.

3.8 Naming

zig fmt does not police names, but the standard library and nearly all Zig code follow one convention, and this book does too:

  • snake_case for variables, constants, and struct fields: company_name, max_lance_size.
  • camelCase for functions: applyBp, daysInMonth.
  • TitleCase for types: GameState, Date. A function that returns a type is also TitleCase (Chapter 26).

Constants are not shouted in capitals; max_lance_size, not MAX_LANCE_SIZE. Names can contain digits and underscores but not start with a digit. If you truly need a name that is a keyword or contains odd characters, @"…" quoting exists, and you will see it in Chapter 27.

In IRON LEDGER. The game's main opens with a run of var declarations for its command-line flags, each with an explicit initial value, followed by a loop that sets them (game/src/main.zig): 
var repl = false;
var tui = false;
var ascii = false;
var no_splash = false;
var no_music = false;
var data_dir: ?[]const u8 = null;
The first five need no annotation because false has a concrete type, bool. The last one must be annotated because null alone does not say what kind of thing might be there; ?[]const u8 means "either a string or nothing" (Chapter 15). Each of these is a var because the loop below assigns to it; if the loop stopped assigning to one, the build would fail with "local variable is never mutated". And further down game/src/main.zig you will find var stdin_buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;, a buffer declared exactly the way Chapter 2's output buffer was.

Exercises

Exercise 3.1 · Make the compiler happy warm-up

The starter contains four compile errors of the kinds shown in this chapter: an unused local, a never-mutated var, a shadowed name, and an assignment to a const. Fix each in the smallest way that keeps the program's meaning, running zig run after each fix to see the next error. Do not delete the print at the bottom. Name the file: exercises/03-variables/ex1_fix_errors.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 03, exercise 1: make the compiler happy.
//! Run with:  zig run ex1_fix_errors.zig
//! Expected output (on stderr):
//!   4 units, 250 tons, avg 62
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const units: u32 = 4;
    const total: u32 = 250; // was var, never mutated
    const commander = "Carlyle";
    _ = commander; // was unused
    const average = total / units;
    {
        const inner_average = 0; // was shadowing `average`
        _ = inner_average;
    }
    // `units = 4;` removed: you cannot assign to a const
    std.debug.print("{d} units, {d} tons, avg {d}\n", .{ units, total, average });
}

The compiler reports the shadowing first and the others one at a time as you fix them. Notice that the unused name is fixed with a discard rather than a deletion, which is what you do when the name is part of a design you have not finished.

Exercise 3.2 · Name the types warm-up

Four top-level constants are declared without types. The tests below them check the type of each with @TypeOf. Add the annotation each test asks for, and nothing else. Run with zig test. Name the file: exercises/03-variables/ex2_types.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 03, exercise 2: give each value the type the tests expect.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_types.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass by changing only the declarations marked TODO.
const std = @import("std");

const seats: u8 = 4;
const tonnage: u32 = 55;
const ratio: f64 = 0.5;
const funds: i64 = 1_000_000;

test "seats is a u8" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(u8, @TypeOf(seats));
}

test "tonnage is a u32" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(u32, @TypeOf(tonnage));
}

test "ratio is an f64" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(f64, @TypeOf(ratio));
}

test "funds is an i64 and can go negative" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(i64, @TypeOf(funds));
    const after: i64 = funds - 2_000_000;
    try std.testing.expect(after < 0);
}

Without annotations the four constants are comptime_int and comptime_float, and expectEqual(u8, @TypeOf(seats)) fails because the types differ. Types are values in Zig, so a test can compare them like numbers; Chapter 26 makes much of this.

Exercise 3.3 · A value from a block practice

Write weightClass so that it computes its result with a labeled block and break :blk, without early returns, then returns that value. The tests define the boundaries. Name the file: exercises/03-variables/ex3_block_value.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 03, exercise 3: compute a value with a labeled block.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_block_value.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Return the weight class name for a BattleMech tonnage:
/// up to 35 "light", up to 55 "medium", up to 75 "heavy", otherwise "assault".
fn weightClass(tonnage: u32) []const u8 {
    const class = blk: {
        if (tonnage <= 35) break :blk "light";
        if (tonnage <= 55) break :blk "medium";
        if (tonnage <= 75) break :blk "heavy";
        break :blk "assault";
    };
    return class;
}

test "light" {
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("light", weightClass(20));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("light", weightClass(35));
}

test "medium" {
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("medium", weightClass(36));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("medium", weightClass(55));
}

test "heavy and assault" {
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("heavy", weightClass(75));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("assault", weightClass(100));
}

Every path through the block must reach a break :blk; the final one has no condition so that the block always produces something. If you forget it the compiler complains that the block's value is void where a string was expected.

Exercise 3.4 · Swap practice

The starter declares a, b and swaps as constants and then tries to swap the first two and count the swap. Change the declarations that must change, and only those, then write the swap with a single temporary. Name the file: exercises/03-variables/ex4_swap.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 03, exercise 4: swap two variables and count mutations.
//! Run with:  zig run ex4_swap.zig
//! Expected output (on stderr):
//!   before: a=3 b=7
//!   after:  a=7 b=3
//!   swaps: 1
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var a: u32 = 3;
    var b: u32 = 7;
    var swaps: u32 = 0;
    std.debug.print("before: a={d} b={d}\n", .{ a, b });
    const tmp = a;
    a = b;
    b = tmp;
    swaps += 1;
    std.debug.print("after:  a={d} b={d}\n", .{ a, b });
    std.debug.print("swaps: {d}\n", .{swaps});
}

All three become var because all three are assigned again. The temporary is a const because it is set once. If you had made tmp a var, the compiler would have told you it is never mutated.

Check your understanding

  1. What is the type of x in const x = 42;?
    Answercomptime_int: an exact compile-time integer with no fixed width. It becomes a concrete type when used as one.
  2. Why does var count = 0; fail to compile?
    AnswerA runtime variable needs a fixed size, and a comptime_int has none. Write var count: u32 = 0; (or another concrete type).
  3. You declared var total: u32 = 5; and the compiler says "local variable is never mutated". What is the fix?
    AnswerChange var to const. Nothing assigns to total after its declaration.
  4. How do you keep an unused variable without deleting it?
    AnswerDiscard it: _ = name;. Remove the discard once you start using the name, or you get a "pointless discard" error.
  5. Is it legal to declare const i inside a loop body when a const i exists outside the loop?
    AnswerNo. Shadowing is a compile error in Zig; pick a different name.
  6. What value does a var x: u32 = undefined; hold if you read it before assigning?
    AnswerIn a debug build, the byte pattern 0xAA repeated (2863311535 for a u32); in a release build, whatever was in that memory. Either way it is a bug.
  7. How does a block produce a value?
    AnswerLabel it, blk: { … }, and leave it with break :blk value;. The block expression evaluates to that value.
What you learned.
  • const never changes; var can be reassigned. Start with const; the compiler rejects a var that is never mutated.
  • Types come after a colon and are usually inferred, but a var initialised from a bare literal must be annotated because literals are comptime_int / comptime_float.
  • Unused locals, never-mutated vars, shadowing, and assigning to a const are compile errors; the fixes are delete or _ =, const, rename, and var.
  • undefined reserves memory without initialising it; read it only after assigning.
  • Braces make a scope; a labeled block can yield a value with break :label value.
  • Top-level declarations are visible file-wide in any order; names are snake_case, camelCase for functions, TitleCase for types.

4. Integers and arithmetic

In this chapter you will learn Zig's integer types and how to choose one, what happens when arithmetic overflows and the three operators Zig gives you for it, why signed division needs a builtin, how to convert between integer types on purpose, and how bit operators and shifts work. Along the way you will see your first runtime panic.

4.1 Widths and signedness

An integer type in Zig is a letter and a number: u for unsigned or i for signed, then the number of bits. u8 holds 0 to 255. i8 holds -128 to 127. u32 holds 0 to about four billion; i64 holds plus or minus about nine quintillion. The number can be anything from 1 to 65535, so u3 and i7 are real types, though in practice you use 8, 16, 32 and 64.

widths.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const a: u8 = 255;
    const b: i8 = -128;
    const c: u16 = 65_535;
    const d: i32 = -2_147_483_648;
    const e: u64 = 18_446_744_073_709_551_615;
    const f: u3 = 7; // three bits: 0..7
    const g: usize = 42;
    std.debug.print("{d} {d} {d} {d} {d} {d} {d}\n", .{ a, b, c, d, e, f, g });
    std.debug.print("usize is {d} bits on this machine\n", .{@bitSizeOf(usize)});
    std.debug.print("u8 max {d}, i8 min {d}, i8 max {d}\n", .{
        std.math.maxInt(u8), std.math.minInt(i8), std.math.maxInt(i8),
    });
}
$ zig run widths.zig
255 -128 65535 -2147483648 18446744073709551615 7 42
usize is 64 bits on this machine
u8 max 255, i8 min -128, i8 max 127

Two types stand apart. usize is an unsigned integer as wide as a memory address on the machine you compile for: 64 bits on any modern computer. It is the type of every array index, length, and count in the standard library, and you will use it constantly from Chapter 9 on. Its signed twin isize is rarer. std.math.maxInt(T) and minInt(T) give the limits of any integer type.

Choosing a width is part of design. A tonnage that is never above 100 fits a u8; a day count fits a u32; money that can be negative and large is an i64. Smaller types save memory in arrays and make invalid values impossible to store. Larger types avoid overflow. When unsure, u32 or i64 is a reasonable default, and usize for anything that indexes memory.

4.2 Literals

An integer literal can be written in four bases, and underscores can be placed anywhere inside it for readability.

literals.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const decimal = 9_626_000;
    const hex = 0xFF;
    const binary = 0b1010_1010;
    const octal = 0o755;
    const char = 'A'; // a character literal is a comptime_int too
    std.debug.print("{d} {d} {d} {d} {d}\n", .{ decimal, hex, binary, octal, char });
    std.debug.print("{x} {b} {o} {c}\n", .{ hex, binary, octal, char });
}
$ zig run literals.zig
9626000 255 170 493 65
ff 10101010 755 A

0x is hexadecimal, 0b binary, 0o octal. A character in single quotes, 'A', is also an integer literal whose value is the character's code (65 for A), which is why it can be printed with {d} or with {c}. As Chapter 3 explained, all of these are comptime_int until they meet a concrete type, and they must fit that type:

toobig.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const a: u8 = 256;
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{a});
}
$ zig run toobig.zig
toobig.zig:4:19: error: type 'u8' cannot represent integer value '256'
    const a: u8 = 256;
                  ^~~

The same message appears if you put a negative literal into an unsigned type: type 'u8' cannot represent integer value '-1'. Both are caught before the program runs.

4.3 Overflow, and your first panic

A u8 holds at most 255. What happens when you add 10 to 250?

overflow.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var armor: u8 = 250;
    armor += 10;
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{armor});
}
$ zig run overflow.zig
thread 12345 panic: integer overflow
overflow.zig:5:11: 0x10000abcd in main (overflow)
    armor += 10;
          ^

The program stops with a panic. This is the runtime, not the compiler: the program built and started, and then the addition on line 5 produced a value that does not fit, and Zig's safety check caught it. A panic prints a message, the source location, and a stack trace, then exits with a failure status. The full trace continues into the standard library's start.zig; the transcript cuts it there, and you can too when reading one.

Compare this with C, where the same addition silently gives 4, and with Python, where integers grow without bound. Zig's position is that overflow in ordinary arithmetic is nearly always a bug, so in Debug and ReleaseSafe builds it is checked and stops the program. In ReleaseFast builds the check is removed and the result is undefined, which is why you test in Debug.

When the operands are known at compile time, the same overflow is reported even earlier:

overflow_comptime.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const armor: u8 = 250;
    const more = armor + 10;
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{more});
}
$ zig run overflow_comptime.zig
overflow_comptime.zig:5:24: error: overflow of integer type 'u8' with value '260'
    const more = armor + 10;
                 ~~~~~~^~~~

That is why the first example used a var and a separate +=: to make the value a runtime one, so you could see the runtime check. The compiler folds constant arithmetic whenever it can, and reports what it finds.

4.4 Wrapping and saturating operators

Sometimes overflow is what you want. A hash function multiplies numbers expecting the high bits to fall off. An 8-bit counter is meant to roll over. A count that must never go below zero should stop at zero rather than crash. Zig has separate operators for these cases, so the intent is visible in the source.

wrapsat.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var armor: u8 = 250;
    const wrapped = armor +% 10;
    const saturated = armor +| 10;
    std.debug.print("wrapped {d}, saturated {d}\n", .{ wrapped, saturated });

    armor = 3;
    std.debug.print("3 -% 5 = {d}, 3 -| 5 = {d}\n", .{ armor -% 5, armor -| 5 });
    std.debug.print("200 *% 2 = {d}, 200 *| 2 = {d}\n", .{ @as(u8, 200) *% 2, @as(u8, 200) *| 2 });
    var i: i8 = 127;
    i +%= 1;
    std.debug.print("i8 127 +%= 1 -> {d}\n", .{i});
}
$ zig run wrapsat.zig
wrapped 4, saturated 255
3 -% 5 = 254, 3 -| 5 = 0
200 *% 2 = 144, 200 *| 2 = 255
i8 127 +%= 1 -> -128
OperatorNameOn overflow
+ - *plainpanic in Debug and ReleaseSafe; undefined in ReleaseFast
