+% -% *%wrappingwraps around modulo 2bits: 250 +% 10 is 4
+| -| *|saturatingclamps to the type's minimum or maximum: 250 +| 10 is 255

All three have assignment forms: +=, +%=, +|=. The saturating subtraction -| is the one you will use most, because "how many more do we need" is naturally need -| have, zero when there is already enough, and never a negative number stored in an unsigned type. Read the wrapping example for signed types too: i8 127 +% 1 is -128, the way the bits work in hardware.

Try it. Change +% and +| in wrapsat.zig to plain + and run it. Then make the type u16 and run it again; the panic disappears because 260 fits. Choosing the width is the first line of defence against overflow, and the operators are the second.

4.5 Division: four builtins

For unsigned integers, / divides and % gives the remainder, both rounding toward zero, and there is nothing to decide. For signed integers there is a genuine choice: -17 divided by 5 is -3 remainder -2 if you round toward zero, or -4 remainder 3 if you round toward negative infinity. Languages disagree (C does the first, Python the second), and each answer is right for some problems. Zig refuses to guess:

signed_slash_rt.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var n: i32 = -17;
    n -= 0;
    const d: i32 = 5;
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{n / d});
}
$ zig run signed_slash_rt.zig
signed_slash_rt.zig:7:34: error: division with 'i32' and 'i32': signed integers must use @divTrunc, @divFloor, or @divExact
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{n / d});
                               ~~^~~

So you say which you mean:

division.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const a: u32 = 17;
    const b: u32 = 5;
    std.debug.print("unsigned: {d} / {d} = {d}, remainder {d}\n", .{ a, b, a / b, a % b });

    const n: i32 = -17;
    const d: i32 = 5;
    std.debug.print("@divTrunc(-17, 5) = {d}\n", .{@divTrunc(n, d)});
    std.debug.print("@divFloor(-17, 5) = {d}\n", .{@divFloor(n, d)});
    std.debug.print("@rem(-17, 5) = {d}\n", .{@rem(n, d)});
    std.debug.print("@mod(-17, 5) = {d}\n", .{@mod(n, d)});
    std.debug.print("@divExact(20, 5) = {d}\n", .{@divExact(@as(i32, 20), 5)});
}
$ zig run division.zig
unsigned: 17 / 5 = 3, remainder 2
@divTrunc(-17, 5) = -3
@divFloor(-17, 5) = -4
@rem(-17, 5) = -2
@mod(-17, 5) = 3
@divExact(20, 5) = 4
  • @divTrunc(a, b) rounds toward zero. Its matching remainder is @rem, which has the sign of a.
  • @divFloor(a, b) rounds toward negative infinity. Its matching remainder is @mod, which has the sign of b and is therefore never negative for a positive divisor. Use @mod for "day of the week" style wrap-around on values that can go negative.
  • @divExact(a, b) asserts that the division has no remainder and panics if it does. Use it when a remainder would mean a bug.

If the operands happen to be compile-time constants, the compiler lets / through, because there is no ambiguity about a number it can see. With runtime signed values you must use a builtin, and the error message lists them. The same holds for % on signed values: "signed integers and floats must use @rem or @mod".

Division by zero is a panic in the same family as overflow:

$ zig run divzero.zig
thread 12345 panic: division by zero
divzero.zig:6:35: 0x10000abcd in main (divzero)
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{10 / d});
                                  ^

4.6 Mixing types: peer type resolution

Arithmetic between two different integer types is allowed when one can hold every value of the other; the result takes the wider type. This is called peer type resolution, and it also explains what happens when a literal meets a typed value.

mixed.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const a: u8 = 200;
    const b: u32 = 100_000;
    const sum = a + b; // peer type resolution: u8 + u32 -> u32
    std.debug.print("{d} is a {s}\n", .{ sum, @typeName(@TypeOf(sum)) });

    const c: i32 = -5;
    const d: u8 = 3;
    const e = c + d; // i32 + u8 -> i32
    std.debug.print("{d} is a {s}\n", .{ e, @typeName(@TypeOf(e)) });

    const lit = a + 1; // u8 + comptime_int -> u8
    std.debug.print("{d} is a {s}\n", .{ lit, @typeName(@TypeOf(lit)) });
}
$ zig run mixed.zig
100200 is a u32
-2 is a i32
201 is a u8

A u8 plus a u32 is a u32. An i32 plus a u8 is an i32, because every u8 value fits in an i32. A u8 plus a literal stays a u8, because the literal takes on the concrete type next to it, and it would be an error if the literal did not fit.

When neither type contains the other, there is no safe answer and the compiler stops:

mixed_bad.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const a: u32 = 5;
    const b: i32 = -3;
    const c = a + b;
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{c});
}
$ zig run mixed_bad.zig
mixed_bad.zig:6:19: error: type 'u32' cannot represent integer value '-3'
    const c = a + b;
                  ^

A u32 cannot hold -3 and an i32 cannot hold 4 billion, so u32 + i32 has no type both sides fit. The message here names the literal because b was compile-time known; with runtime values the message is "incompatible types". Either way the fix is the same: convert one side explicitly, which is the next section.

The same rule governs plain assignment. Widening is free; narrowing is refused:

narrowing.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const big: u32 = 300;
    const small: u8 = big;
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{small});
}
$ zig run narrowing.zig
narrowing.zig:5:23: error: type 'u8' cannot represent integer value '300'
    const small: u8 = big;
                      ^~~

4.7 Casts that say what they mean

Zig has no single "cast" operator. It has several builtins, each doing one specific thing to the bits, so a reader can see which one you chose and why.

casts.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const wide: u32 = 200;
    const narrow: u8 = @intCast(wide); // fits, ok
    std.debug.print("intCast: {d}\n", .{narrow});

    const big: u32 = 0x1234_5678;
    const low: u8 = @truncate(big); // keeps the low 8 bits
    std.debug.print("truncate: 0x{x}\n", .{low});

    const signed: i8 = -1;
    const bits: u8 = @bitCast(signed); // same 8 bits, read as unsigned
    std.debug.print("bitCast: {d}\n", .{bits});

    const small: u8 = 7;
    const widened = @as(u32, small) * 1_000_000; // widen before multiplying
    std.debug.print("as: {d}\n", .{widened});
}
$ zig run casts.zig
intCast: 200
truncate: 0x78
bitCast: 255
as: 7000000
BuiltinWhat it doesIf the value does not fit
@as(T, x)gives x the type T using the normal coercion rules (widening, literals)compile error
@intCast(x)converts to the target type, keeping the numeric valuepanic in Debug
@truncate(x)keeps only the low bits that fit the targethigh bits are dropped, silently and on purpose
@bitCast(x)reinterprets the same bits as another type of the same sizesizes must match, else compile error

Notice that @intCast, @truncate and @bitCast do not take the target type as an argument. They get it from context: the declared type of the variable they are assigned to, or the parameter type they are passed as. When there is no context, wrap them in @as: @as(u8, @intCast(x)). This looks odd for a week and then becomes natural.

@as(u32, small) * 1_000_000 in the example is the idiom for "widen before multiplying". Written as small * 1_000_000 it would try to compute in u8 and fail at compile time because the literal does not fit. Widening first makes the multiplication happen in u32.

And @intCast is a checked cast: it promises the value fits, and in Debug builds the promise is verified.

intcast_fail.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var wide: u32 = 200;
    wide += 100;
    const narrow: u8 = @intCast(wide);
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{narrow});
}
$ zig run intcast_fail.zig
thread 12345 panic: integer does not fit in destination type
intcast_fail.zig:6:24: 0x10000abcd in main (intcast_fail)
    const narrow: u8 = @intCast(wide);
                       ^
Which one? If you want the same number in a different width, @intCast. If you want the low byte of a bigger number, @truncate. If you want to look at the bits of a signed number as unsigned, or a float as an integer, @bitCast. If the compiler would already allow the conversion and you only need to pin the type, @as. If you are casting to make an error go away and cannot say which of these you mean, stop and work out where the types should have matched.

4.8 Bit operators and shifts

Integers are bits, and Zig has the usual operators for working on them directly: & and, | or, ^ exclusive or, ~ not, << shift left, >> shift right.

bits.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const a: u8 = 0b1100_1010;
    const b: u8 = 0b1010_0101;
    std.debug.print("a     = {b:0>8}\n", .{a});
    std.debug.print("b     = {b:0>8}\n", .{b});
    std.debug.print("a & b = {b:0>8}\n", .{a & b});
    std.debug.print("a | b = {b:0>8}\n", .{a | b});
    std.debug.print("a ^ b = {b:0>8}\n", .{a ^ b});
    std.debug.print("~a    = {b:0>8}\n", .{~a});
    std.debug.print("a << 1 = {b:0>8}\n", .{a << 1});
    std.debug.print("a >> 2 = {b:0>8}\n", .{a >> 2});

    const flags: u8 = 0;
    const with_bit_3 = flags | (1 << 3);
    std.debug.print("set bit 3: {b:0>8}, is set? {}\n", .{ with_bit_3, (with_bit_3 & (1 << 3)) != 0 });
}
$ zig run bits.zig
a     = 11001010
b     = 10100101
a & b = 10000000
a | b = 11101111
a ^ b = 01101111
~a    = 00110101
a << 1 = 10010100
a >> 2 = 00110010
set bit 3: 00001000, is set? true

The {b:0>8} format from Chapter 2 prints all eight bits so the columns line up. Shifting left by one doubles a number and drops the top bit; shifting right by one halves it. The last two lines show the classic flag idiom: flags | (1 << n) turns bit n on, flags & ~(1 << n) turns it off, and (flags & (1 << n)) != 0 tests it.

Shifts have a rule that surprises everyone once. The shift amount must be a type just wide enough to express every valid shift for the value's width. A u8 can be shifted by 0 to 7, which needs 3 bits, so the amount must be a u3:

shift_amount.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const value: u8 = 1;
    var amount: u8 = 3;
    amount += 1;
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{value << amount});
}
$ zig run shift_amount.zig
shift_amount.zig:7:41: error: expected type 'u3', found 'u8'
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{value << amount});
                                        ^~~~~~
shift_amount.zig:7:41: note: unsigned 3-bit int cannot represent all possible unsigned 8-bit values

The reason is that shifting a u8 by 8 or more is undefined in hardware, and the type of the amount makes that impossible to write. Literal amounts are fine because the compiler can see them fit; a runtime amount has to be narrowed:

shift_amount_ok.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const value: u8 = 1;
    var amount: u8 = 3;
    amount += 1;
    const shifted = value << @intCast(amount); // amount becomes a u3
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{shifted});
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{@typeName(std.math.Log2Int(u8))});
}
$ zig run shift_amount_ok.zig
16
u3

std.math.Log2Int(T) names the correct shift type for any integer type T, which is handy in generic code. For a u32 it is u5, for a u64 it is u6.

4.9 Small helpers

Three builtins and one library function cover most of the remaining integer chores:

minmax.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const fatigue: u8 = 95;
    const add: u8 = 20;
    const capped = @min(100, fatigue + add);
    std.debug.print("capped {d}\n", .{capped});
    const clamped = std.math.clamp(@as(i32, -7), 0, 10);
    std.debug.print("clamped {d}\n", .{clamped});
    std.debug.print("abs {d}\n", .{@abs(@as(i32, -42))});
}
$ zig run minmax.zig
capped 100
clamped 0
abs 42

@min and @max take any number of arguments of any numeric type and use peer type resolution on them. std.math.clamp(x, lo, hi) pins a value into a range. @abs gives the absolute value; note that its result for a signed type is the matching unsigned type, because the absolute value of the most negative i32 does not fit in an i32.

In IRON LEDGER. The game never stores money in a float. Every amount is a CBills = i64, and every multiplier is an integer number of basis points, so that the same campaign replays to the C-bill on any machine (game/src/domain/types.zig): 
/// Integer C-bills. Never floats in financial or rules math.
pub const CBills = i64;
/// Basis points: 10_000 = ×1.
pub const Bp = i64;

pub fn applyBp(amount: CBills, bp: Bp) CBills {
    return @divTrunc(amount * bp, 10_000);
}
A 10 percent markup is applyBp(cost, 11_000), and the rounding direction is written down in the source as @divTrunc. The other two operators from this chapter are all over the code as well. The random number generator seeds its streams with a wrapping multiply that is meant to overflow (game/src/sim/rng.zig): seed ^ (0x9E3779B97F4A7C15 *% (i + 1)). And every "how many are still needed" is a saturating subtraction, such as const gap = n.need -| personnel.manningHave(gs, f.id, n.role); in game/src/econ/contract_market.zig, which is zero when the slot is filled and never a negative count. Chapter 45 follows the money through the whole program.

Exercises

Exercise 4.1 · Pick a width warm-up

Five constants are declared without types, each with a comment describing its range. Add the smallest integer type that fits each one, choosing signed or unsigned correctly. The tests check bit widths and signedness. Name the file: exercises/04-integers/ex1_widths.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 04, exercise 1: pick the smallest integer type that fits.
//! Run with:  zig test ex1_widths.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass by changing only the type annotations.
const std = @import("std");

const armor_points: u8 = 255; // 0..255, never negative
const temperature: i8 = -40; // -40..40
const day_index: u16 = 40_000; // 0..65535
const funds: i64 = -3_000_000_000; // can be hugely negative
const bit_flags: u3 = 0b101; // exactly three flags

test "each value fits and the width is minimal" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(8, @bitSizeOf(@TypeOf(armor_points)));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(8, @bitSizeOf(@TypeOf(temperature)));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(16, @bitSizeOf(@TypeOf(day_index)));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(64, @bitSizeOf(@TypeOf(funds)));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(3, @bitSizeOf(@TypeOf(bit_flags)));
}

test "signedness" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(.unsigned, @typeInfo(@TypeOf(armor_points)).int.signedness);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(.signed, @typeInfo(@TypeOf(temperature)).int.signedness);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(.signed, @typeInfo(@TypeOf(funds)).int.signedness);
}

@bitSizeOf and @typeInfo(...).int.signedness are reflection builtins from Chapter 27; here they simply let the tests look at the types you chose. The tests compare against bare literals like 8, which works because @bitSizeOf returns a comptime_int.

Exercise 4.2 · Overflow arithmetic practice

Four small functions use plain operators and the tests make them overflow, so running the file panics. Replace each operator with the wrapping or saturating form that the function's comment calls for. Name the file: exercises/04-integers/ex2_overflow.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 04, exercise 2: overflow arithmetic.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_overflow.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Add `heal` armor points but never exceed 255.
fn repair(armor: u8, heal: u8) u8 {
    return armor +| heal;
}

/// Take `hit` points of damage but never go below zero.
fn damage(armor: u8, hit: u8) u8 {
    return armor -| hit;
}

/// An 8-bit counter that is meant to roll over from 255 back to 0.
fn tick(counter: u8) u8 {
    return counter +% 1;
}

/// Mix a seed the way a hash would: the multiplication is meant to overflow.
fn mix(seed: u64, i: u64) u64 {
    return seed ^ (0x9E3779B97F4A7C15 *% (i + 1));
}

test "repair saturates at 255" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 255), repair(250, 10));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 60), repair(50, 10));
}

test "damage saturates at 0" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 0), damage(3, 5));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 40), damage(50, 10));
}

test "tick wraps" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 0), tick(255));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 8), tick(7));
}

test "mix does not panic and differs per index" {
    const a = mix(3025, 0);
    const b = mix(3025, 1_000_000_000);
    try std.testing.expect(a != b);
}

Armor repair and damage saturate; a rollover counter and a hash mix wrap. The point of having three operators is that the choice is written in the code where a reader can see it, rather than living in your head.

Exercise 4.3 · Basis points and signed division practice

Implement applyBp (scale by basis points, rounding toward zero), weekOf (which week a day index falls in, correct for negative days), and dayOfWeek (0 to 6, never negative). Each needs a different division builtin. Name the file: exercises/04-integers/ex3_division.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 04, exercise 3: basis points and signed division.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_division.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const CBills = i64;
const Bp = i64;

/// Scale `amount` by `bp` basis points (10_000 = x1), rounding toward zero.
fn applyBp(amount: CBills, bp: Bp) CBills {
    return @divTrunc(amount * bp, 10_000);
}

/// Which week (starting at 0) a day index falls in, for negative days too.
/// Day -1 is the last day of week -1, not week 0.
fn weekOf(day: i32) i32 {
    return @divFloor(day, 7);
}

/// Day of the week, 0..6, for negative days too.
fn dayOfWeek(day: i32) i32 {
    return @mod(day, 7);
}

test "applyBp" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(CBills, 1_100), applyBp(1_000, 11_000));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(CBills, 500), applyBp(1_000, 5_000));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(CBills, -33), applyBp(-100, 3_333));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(CBills, 33), applyBp(100, 3_333));
}

test "weekOf" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, 0), weekOf(6));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, 1), weekOf(7));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, -1), weekOf(-1));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, -1), weekOf(-7));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, -2), weekOf(-8));
}

test "dayOfWeek" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, 6), dayOfWeek(6));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, 0), dayOfWeek(7));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, 6), dayOfWeek(-1));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, 0), dayOfWeek(-7));
}

applyBp is the game's own function and uses @divTrunc, so a negative amount rounds toward zero just as a positive one does. weekOf needs @divFloor so that day -1 lands in week -1, and dayOfWeek needs @mod so the result is never negative. Try swapping them and watch which tests fail.

Exercise 4.4 · A flag set practice

Write set, clear, isSet and count for an 8-bit flag set using only bit operators. The bit index parameter is a u3; think about why. Name the file: exercises/04-integers/ex4_bits.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 04, exercise 4: a bit-flag set for unit status.
//! Run with:  zig test ex4_bits.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const damaged: u3 = 0;
const low_ammo: u3 = 1;
const pilot_injured: u3 = 2;

/// Return `flags` with bit `bit` turned on.
fn set(flags: u8, bit: u3) u8 {
    return flags | (@as(u8, 1) << bit);
}

/// Return `flags` with bit `bit` turned off.
fn clear(flags: u8, bit: u3) u8 {
    return flags & ~(@as(u8, 1) << bit);
}

/// Is bit `bit` on in `flags`?
fn isSet(flags: u8, bit: u3) bool {
    return (flags >> bit) & 1 == 1;
}

/// How many bits are on?
fn count(flags: u8) u8 {
    return @popCount(flags);
}

test "set and test" {
    var f: u8 = 0;
    f = set(f, low_ammo);
    try std.testing.expect(isSet(f, low_ammo));
    try std.testing.expect(!isSet(f, damaged));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 0b010), f);
}

test "clear" {
    var f: u8 = 0b111;
    f = clear(f, pilot_injured);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 0b011), f);
    f = clear(f, pilot_injured); // clearing twice is harmless
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 0b011), f);
}

test "count" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 0), count(0));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 3), count(0b111));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 8), count(0xFF));
}

The u3 parameter is exactly the shift-amount type for a u8, so 1 << bit compiles without a cast. The @as(u8, 1) is needed because a bare literal shifted by a runtime amount has no width to shift within. @popCount counts set bits directly; a loop that tests each bit is the other valid answer.

Exercise 4.5 · Four casts challenge

Four functions each need exactly one cast builtin: widen two u8 values before multiplying, take the low byte of a u32, reinterpret an i8 as a u8, and narrow a usize to a u16. Pick @as, @truncate, @bitCast or @intCast for each based on what the doc comment says. Name the file: exercises/04-integers/ex5_casts.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 04, exercise 5: casts that mean what they say.
//! Run with:  zig test ex5_casts.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Total tonnage of a lance of `count` units at `each` tons, as a u32.
/// Both inputs are u8, so the product must be widened before multiplying.
fn lanceTonnage(count: u8, each: u8) u32 {
    return @as(u32, count) * @as(u32, each);
}

/// The low byte of a 32-bit colour value (the blue channel of 0xRRGGBB).
fn blue(rgb: u32) u8 {
    return @truncate(rgb);
}

/// Reinterpret the bits of a signed byte as unsigned, without changing them.
fn rawByte(x: i8) u8 {
    return @bitCast(x);
}

/// Convert an index (usize) into a u16 row number. Callers promise it fits.
fn rowNumber(index: usize) u16 {
    return @intCast(index);
}

test "lanceTonnage does not overflow" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 400), lanceTonnage(4, 100));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 65_025), lanceTonnage(255, 255));
}

test "blue keeps the low byte" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 0x56), blue(0x123456));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 0xFF), blue(0x0000FF));
}

test "rawByte keeps the bits" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 255), rawByte(-1));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 128), rawByte(-128));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 5), rawByte(5));
}

test "rowNumber narrows" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u16, 12), rowNumber(12));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u16, 65_535), rowNumber(65_535));
}

Each cast leaves a different mark. @truncate says "I only want the low bits", @bitCast says "same bits, different label", @intCast says "this fits, check me". Use the wrong one and either the compiler objects (@bitCast between sizes) or a test fails (@intCast where truncation was wanted panics on 0x123456).

Check your understanding

  1. What range does an i8 hold, and a u8?
    Answeri8: -128 to 127. u8: 0 to 255.
  2. What happens when var a: u8 = 250; a += 10; runs in a Debug build?
    AnswerA runtime panic, "integer overflow", with the file and line. In ReleaseFast the result would be undefined.
  3. What do 250 +% 10 and 250 +| 10 give for u8?
    Answer4 (wrapping) and 255 (saturating).
  4. Why is a / b an error for runtime signed integers?
    AnswerRounding toward zero and rounding toward negative infinity give different answers for negatives, so Zig makes you choose @divTrunc, @divFloor, or @divExact.
  5. What is the type of x + y when x: u8 and y: u32? And when x: u32 and y: i32?
    Answeru32 in the first case. The second is a compile error: neither type can hold all values of the other.
  6. What is the difference between @intCast and @truncate?
    Answer@intCast keeps the numeric value and panics in Debug if it does not fit. @truncate keeps only the low bits and never panics.
  7. What type must the shift amount have in x << n when x is a u32?
    Answeru5, because valid shifts are 0 to 31. Use @intCast(n) on a wider runtime value.
  8. Why does IRON LEDGER store money as i64 rather than f64?
    AnswerInteger arithmetic is exact and identical on every machine, so a campaign replays to the C-bill; percentages are done with integer basis points and @divTrunc.
What you learned.
  • Integer types are u/i plus a bit width; usize is the index type; literals accept 0x, 0b, 0o, and underscores.
  • Plain arithmetic panics on overflow in Debug builds; +% wraps and +| saturates, with matching - and * forms.
  • Signed division and remainder need @divTrunc/@rem or @divFloor/@mod; division by zero panics.
  • Mixed types resolve to the wider one when it contains the other; otherwise you cast explicitly.
  • @as coerces, @intCast converts with a check, @truncate drops high bits, @bitCast reinterprets bits; the target type comes from context.
  • Bit operators are & | ^ ~ << >>; a shift amount must be the narrow type that fits every valid shift.

5. Floats, booleans and comparisons

In this chapter you will learn Zig's two floating-point types and why 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3, how to convert between integers and floats deliberately, how to print floats, what NaN and infinity are, and how comparisons and the boolean operators and, or and ! work. You will also see that Zig has no notion of a "truthy" value.

5.1 f32 and f64

A floating-point number stores a sign, a fraction, and an exponent, so it can hold 0.001 and 6.02e23 in the same type. Zig's two everyday float types are f32 (about 7 significant digits) and f64 (about 16). There are also f16, f80 and f128 for special purposes. Use f64 unless you have a reason not to; it is the natural type of most maths libraries and of the constants in std.math.

floats.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const a: f32 = 0.1;
    const b: f64 = 0.1;
    std.debug.print("f32: {d}\n", .{a});
    std.debug.print("f64: {d}\n", .{b});
    const widened: f64 = a; // f32 widens to f64 for free
    std.debug.print("the f32 0.1, seen as f64: {d}\n", .{widened});
    var sum: f64 = 0.0;
    sum += 0.1;
    sum += 0.1;
    sum += 0.1;
    std.debug.print("0.1 + 0.1 + 0.1 = {d}\n", .{sum});
    std.debug.print("equal to 0.3? {}\n", .{sum == 0.3});
}
$ zig run floats.zig
f32: 0.1
f64: 0.1
the f32 0.1, seen as f64: 0.10000000149011612
0.1 + 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.30000000000000004
equal to 0.3? false

The first two lines look identical because Zig prints the shortest decimal that reads back as the same float. The third line tells the truth: the f32 nearest to 0.1 is actually 0.100000001490116…, and widening it to f64 exposes the digits. The last two lines are the famous one. Three tenths added together is not three tenths, because none of them was exactly a tenth to begin with. Floats are binary fractions; 0.1 in binary repeats forever, the way 1/3 does in decimal, and gets cut off.

The rule that follows is: never compare floats for equality when they came from arithmetic, and never use floats for money. Section 5.5 shows the comparison technique; IRON LEDGER's answer to money is Chapter 4's integers.

5.2 Float literals

A literal with a decimal point or an exponent is a comptime_float, the float twin of comptime_int from Chapter 3. It becomes an f32 or f64 when it meets one.

float_literal.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const x = 2.5;
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{@typeName(@TypeOf(x))});
    const y: f64 = x;
    const z: f32 = 1.0e3;
    const w: f64 = 6.02e23;
    std.debug.print("{d} {d} {d} {e}\n", .{ y, z, w, w });
}
$ zig run float_literal.zig
comptime_float
2.5 1000 602000000000000000000000 6.02e23

1.0e3 is scientific notation for 1000; 6.02e23 is 6.02 times ten to the 23rd. A float literal must have a digit on both sides of the point: 1.0, not 1. and not .5. As with integers, a var initialised from a bare float literal needs a type annotation.

5.3 Converting between integers and floats

Integers and floats are different kinds of value, and Zig makes you say when you move between them.

float_conv.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const tons: u32 = 55;
    const as_float: f64 = @floatFromInt(tons);
    const half = as_float / 2.0;
    std.debug.print("half of {d} tons is {d}\n", .{ tons, half });

    const price: f64 = 4_701_000.75;
    const whole: i64 = @intFromFloat(price); // truncates toward zero
    std.debug.print("truncated: {d}\n", .{whole});

    const rounded: i64 = @intFromFloat(@round(price));
    const floored: i64 = @intFromFloat(@floor(-2.5));
    const ceiled: i64 = @intFromFloat(@ceil(-2.5));
    std.debug.print("round {d}, floor(-2.5) {d}, ceil(-2.5) {d}\n", .{ rounded, floored, ceiled });

    const narrow: f32 = @floatCast(price); // f64 -> f32 loses precision
    std.debug.print("as f32: {d}\n", .{narrow});
}
$ zig run float_conv.zig
half of 55 tons is 27.5
truncated: 4701000
round 4701001, floor(-2.5) -3, ceil(-2.5) -2
as f32: 4701001
  • @floatFromInt(x) makes a float from an integer. The target type comes from context, as with the casts in Chapter 4, so you write it on a line with a type annotation or wrap it in @as(f64, …).
  • @intFromFloat(x) makes an integer from a float, dropping the fraction (rounding toward zero). Combine it with @round, @floor, or @ceil to choose a different rounding first.
  • @floatCast(x) changes float width. Going from f64 to f32 rounds to fewer digits, as the last line shows.

Two shortcuts exist, and you should know them so you are not surprised, but you should not lean on them. First, an integer type coerces to a float type without a builtin when every value of the integer type is exactly representable in the float: a u32 becomes an f64 silently, because f64 has 53 bits of fraction and can hold any 32-bit integer. The same applies inside arithmetic, so tons * ratio with a u32 and an f64 compiles and gives an f64:

mix_bad2.zig
const std = @import("std");

fn scale(tons: u32, ratio: f64) f64 {
    return tons * ratio;
}

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{scale(55, 0.5)});
}
$ zig run mix_bad2.zig
27.5

But a u64 does not fit exactly in an f64, nor an i32 in an f32, and those are refused:

coerce7.zig
const std = @import("std");
fn a(x: u64) f64 {
    return x; // u64 -> f64 is lossy above 2^53
}
pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{a(55)});
}
$ zig run coerce7.zig
coerce7.zig:3:12: error: expected type 'f64', found 'u64'
    return x; // u64 -> f64 is lossy above 2^53
           ^
coerce7.zig:2:14: note: function return type declared here
fn a(x: u64) f64 {
             ^~~

Second, a runtime integer and a float literal do not mix at all, because the literal has no concrete type to resolve against:

coerce2.zig
const std = @import("std");
fn f(tons: u32) f64 {
    return tons + 0.5; // int + float literal
}
pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{f(55)});
}
$ zig run coerce2.zig
coerce2.zig:3:17: error: incompatible types: 'u32' and 'comptime_float'
    return tons + 0.5; // int + float literal
           ~~~~~^~~~~
coerce2.zig:3:12: note: type 'u32' here
    return tons + 0.5; // int + float literal
           ^~~~
coerce2.zig:3:19: note: type 'comptime_float' here
    return tons + 0.5; // int + float literal
                  ^~~

And a float never becomes an integer by itself, whatever its value:

$ zig run coerce3.zig
coerce3.zig:3:12: error: expected type 'u32', found 'f64'
    return x; // float -> int should never coerce
           ^
coerce3.zig:2:14: note: function return type declared here
fn f(x: f64) u32 {
             ^~~

The habit that avoids all of this is to write @floatFromInt whenever an integer enters a float calculation. It always works, it is explicit about where precision might be lost, and a reader does not have to remember the exact-representability table.

Trap: integer division happens first. const half: f64 = tons / 2; with tons: u32 = 55 gives 27, not 27.5. The division is done between integers, truncating, and the result is only then widened to a float. Convert before dividing: @as(f64, @floatFromInt(tons)) / 2.0.

Converting the other way is also checked. @intFromFloat panics in Debug builds if the float's integer part does not fit the target type:

intfromfloat_fail.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var big: f64 = 300.0;
    big += 1.0;
    const small: u8 = @intFromFloat(big);
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{small});
}
$ zig run intfromfloat_fail.zig
thread 12345 panic: integer part of floating point value out of bounds
intfromfloat_fail.zig:6:23: 0x10000abcd in main (intfromfloat_fail)
    const small: u8 = @intFromFloat(big);
                      ^

5.4 Printing floats

The {d} placeholder prints a float in plain decimal, and the precision option controls how many digits follow the point:

fmt_floats.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const x: f64 = 1234.5678;
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{x});
    std.debug.print("{d:.1}\n", .{x});
    std.debug.print("{d:.0}\n", .{x});
    std.debug.print("{d:12.2}|\n", .{x});
    std.debug.print("{d:<12.2}|\n", .{x});
    std.debug.print("{e}\n", .{x});
    std.debug.print("{e:.3}\n", .{x});
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{x});
    std.debug.print("{}\n", .{x});
}
$ zig run fmt_floats.zig
1234.5678
1234.6
1235
     1234.57|
1234.57     |
1.2345678e3
1.235e3
1234.5678
1234.5678

{d} alone prints the shortest exact representation; {d:.1} rounds to one decimal and {d:.0} to none. Width and alignment work as for integers. {e} prints scientific notation, with its own precision. {any} and the bare {} both give the same shortest form as {d}. For a table of prices, {d:.2} is almost always what you want.

5.5 Arithmetic, NaN and infinity

The four operators work on floats as you would expect, and the remainder builtins from Chapter 4 apply to floats as well: % on a float is an error, @rem and @mod are not. std.math has the usual functions and constants.

float_ops.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const a: f64 = 7.0;
    const b: f64 = 2.0;
    std.debug.print("{d} {d} {d} {d}\n", .{ a + b, a - b, a * b, a / b });
    std.debug.print("rem {d}, mod {d}\n", .{ @rem(a, b), @mod(-a, b) });
    std.debug.print("sqrt {d}, pow {d}, pi {d:.4}\n", .{ @sqrt(a), std.math.pow(f64, a, b), std.math.pi });
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{1.0 / 3.0});
}
$ zig run float_ops.zig
9 5 14 3.5
rem 1, mod 1
sqrt 2.6457513110645907, pow 49, pi 3.1416
0.3333333333333333333333333333333333

Notice the last line: 1.0 / 3.0 printed with far more digits than an f64 has. Both operands were literals, so the division happened at compile time in comptime_float, which is exact, and only the printing rounded it. Give either side a runtime type and you get the sixteen-digit f64 answer.

Unlike integer division, float division by zero does not panic. It produces one of the special values that every float type carries:

naninf.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var zero: f64 = 0.0;
    zero += 0.0;
    const one: f64 = 1.0;
    const inf = one / zero;
    const neg_inf = -one / zero;
    const nan = zero / zero;
    std.debug.print("{d} {d} {d}\n", .{ inf, neg_inf, nan });
    std.debug.print("nan == nan? {}\n", .{nan == nan});
    std.debug.print("isNan {}, isInf {}\n", .{ std.math.isNan(nan), std.math.isInf(inf) });
    std.debug.print("constants: {d} {d}\n", .{ std.math.inf(f64), std.math.nan(f64) });
    std.debug.print("f64 max {e}, f32 max {e}\n", .{ std.math.floatMax(f64), std.math.floatMax(f32) });
}
$ zig run naninf.zig
inf -inf nan
nan == nan? false
isNan true, isInf true
constants: inf nan
f64 max 1.7976931348623157e308, f32 max 3.4028235e38

Dividing a nonzero number by zero gives infinity with the appropriate sign. Dividing zero by zero, or taking the square root of a negative, gives NaN, "not a number". NaN has one property that catches everyone: it is not equal to anything, including itself. nan == nan is false. To test for it, use std.math.isNan; for infinity, std.math.isInf. std.math.inf(T) and std.math.nan(T) construct them, and std.math.floatMax(T) is the largest finite value of the type.

A NaN spreads: any arithmetic with a NaN gives a NaN, so one bad division early in a calculation poisons everything after it. If a float result looks wrong, print it; nan in the output points straight at the problem.

5.6 Comparisons

Six operators compare two values of the same type and produce a bool:

compare.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const a: i32 = 5;
    const b: i32 = 7;
    std.debug.print("{} {} {} {} {} {}\n", .{ a == b, a != b, a < b, a <= b, a > b, a >= b });

    var x: f64 = 0.1;
    x += 0.2;
    std.debug.print("0.1 + 0.2 = {d}\n", .{x});
    std.debug.print("0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 ? {}\n", .{x == 0.3});
    const close = std.math.approxEqAbs(f64, x, 0.3, 1e-9);
    std.debug.print("close enough? {}\n", .{close});

    const result = a < b;
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{@typeName(@TypeOf(result))});
}
$ zig run compare.zig
false true true true false false
0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004
0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 ? false
close enough? true
bool

==, !=, <, <=, >, >=. They work on integers, floats, booleans (only == and !=), enums, and a few other types; they do not work on strings, which need std.mem.eql (Chapter 11). Comparison between different integer types follows peer type resolution; comparing an integer to a float needs a conversion.

The float lines demonstrate the fix for section 5.1's problem. Instead of asking whether two computed floats are equal, ask whether they are within a tolerance: std.math.approxEqAbs(f64, a, b, 1e-9) is true when the absolute difference is below the fourth argument. There is also approxEqRel for a relative tolerance, which suits very large or very small values. In tests, std.testing.expectApproxEqAbs does the same job.

One thing Zig does not allow that Python does: chaining. 1 < x < 10 is a compile error, "comparison operators cannot be chained". Write 1 < x and x < 10.

5.7 Booleans

bool has two values, true and false, and three operators, which are words rather than symbols:

bools.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const has_pilot = true;
    const has_mech = false;
    std.debug.print("and: {}\n", .{has_pilot and has_mech});
    std.debug.print("or:  {}\n", .{has_pilot or has_mech});
    std.debug.print("not: {}\n", .{!has_mech});
    std.debug.print("as int: {d}\n", .{@intFromBool(has_pilot)});
    const morale: u8 = 60;
    const fatigue: u8 = 30;
    const ready = has_pilot and morale >= 50 and fatigue < 40;
    std.debug.print("ready to deploy: {}\n", .{ready});
}
$ zig run bools.zig
and: false
or:  true
not: true
as int: 1
ready to deploy: true

and, or, and !. There is no && or ||; type a && b and the compiler says "ambiguous use of '&&'; use 'and' for logical AND". @intFromBool converts to 1 or 0 when you need to add a flag to a number. Comparisons bind tighter than and, and and binds tighter than or, so a and b >= 50 or c means (a and (b >= 50)) or c. When in doubt, add parentheses; zig fmt will not remove them.

and and or short-circuit: the right side is only evaluated when the left side has not already decided the answer.

shortcircuit.zig
const std = @import("std");

fn loud(name: []const u8, value: bool) bool {
    std.debug.print("  evaluating {s}\n", .{name});
    return value;
}

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("false and ...:\n", .{});
    _ = loud("left", false) and loud("right", true);
    std.debug.print("true or ...:\n", .{});
    _ = loud("left", true) or loud("right", false);
}
$ zig run shortcircuit.zig
false and ...:
  evaluating left
true or ...:
  evaluating left

This matters when the right side is expensive or would fail: i < items.len and items[i] == x is safe because the index is only read when it is in range. Chapter 15 leans on this with optionals.

5.8 No truthiness

In Python, JavaScript and C, a number can stand in for a boolean: zero is false, anything else is true. Zig does not do this. The condition of an if or a while must be a bool, and a number is not one:

truthy.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const count: u32 = 3;
    if (count) {
        std.debug.print("nonzero\n", .{});
    }
}
$ zig run truthy.zig
truthy.zig:5:9: error: expected type 'bool', found 'u32'
    if (count) {
        ^~~~~

Write the comparison out: if (count != 0) or if (count > 0). The same applies to pointers and everything else. It costs a few characters and removes a whole class of "is an empty list false?" questions. The only values that can appear in a condition besides bool are optionals and error unions, which have their own special if syntax that captures the inner value; those are Chapters 15 and 16.

In IRON LEDGER. Floats appear in exactly two places in the whole game, and both are geometry rather than accounting: the distance between two worlds in game/src/domain/planet.zig (const dx: f64 = @floatFromInt(a.x - b.x); and then @sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy)), and the star map, where light-year coordinates are scaled to terminal columns (game/src/tui/app.zig): 
const usable_w: f64 = @floatFromInt(@max(20, @as(i32, inner.w) - 16));
const usable_h: f64 = @floatFromInt(@max(6, @as(i32, inner.h) - 2));
var sx: f64 = @as(f64, @floatFromInt(max_x - min_x)) / usable_w;
var sy: f64 = @as(f64, @floatFromInt(max_y - min_y)) / usable_h;
// …
return .{ @intFromFloat(@floor(cx)), @intFromFloat(@floor(cy)) };
Every integer that enters the calculation goes through @floatFromInt, every result that becomes a screen position goes through @floor and then @intFromFloat, and there is no float anywhere in src/sim/ or src/econ/. Booleans, on the other hand, are everywhere; the calendar's leap-year test in game/src/sim/clock.zig is a one-line boolean expression: return (year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0) or year % 400 == 0;. You will write it yourself in Chapter 7.

Exercises

Exercise 5.1 · Integer in, float out warm-up

Write average3, which returns the mean of three u32 values as an f64, and percent, which returns part as a percentage of whole rounded to the nearest whole number. You will need @floatFromInt, @intFromFloat and @round. Name the file: exercises/05-floats-bools/ex1_average.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 05, exercise 1: integer in, float out.
//! Run with:  zig test ex1_average.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Average of three tonnages as an f64 (so 20, 55, 100 gives 58.333...).
fn average3(a: u32, b: u32, c: u32) f64 {
    const sum: f64 = @floatFromInt(a + b + c);
    return sum / 3.0;
}

/// Percentage of `part` out of `whole`, rounded to the nearest whole number.
/// 1 out of 3 is 33, 2 out of 3 is 67.
fn percent(part: u32, whole: u32) u32 {
    const p: f64 = @floatFromInt(part);
    const w: f64 = @floatFromInt(whole);
    return @intFromFloat(@round(p / w * 100.0));
}

test "average3" {
    try std.testing.expectApproxEqAbs(@as(f64, 58.3333), average3(20, 55, 100), 0.001);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(f64, 50), average3(50, 50, 50));
}

test "percent rounds" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 33), percent(1, 3));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 67), percent(2, 3));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 100), percent(7, 7));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 0), percent(0, 7));
}

The sum is computed in u32 and converted once, which is fine here; converting each value first would also work. In percent, the conversions happen before the division, avoiding the integer-division trap, and @round runs before @intFromFloat so that 66.67 becomes 67 rather than 66.

Exercise 5.2 · Comparing honestly practice

Write nearlyEqual(a, b, tolerance) without using std.math.approxEqAbs, and isUsable(x), which is true only for finite numbers. The first test adds 0.1 ten times and checks that the sum is not 1.0 but is nearly 1.0. Name the file: exercises/05-floats-bools/ex2_approx.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 05, exercise 2: comparing floats honestly.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_approx.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// True when a and b are within `tolerance` of each other.
fn nearlyEqual(a: f64, b: f64, tolerance: f64) bool {
    return @abs(a - b) <= tolerance;
}

/// True when x is a finite number (not NaN, not +/- infinity).
fn isUsable(x: f64) bool {
    return !std.math.isNan(x) and !std.math.isInf(x);
}

test "nearlyEqual" {
    var sum: f64 = 0.0;
    for (0..10) |_| sum += 0.1;
    try std.testing.expect(sum != 1.0); // the classic surprise
    try std.testing.expect(nearlyEqual(sum, 1.0, 1e-9));
    try std.testing.expect(!nearlyEqual(1.0, 1.1, 0.01));
}

test "isUsable" {
    try std.testing.expect(isUsable(3.5));
    try std.testing.expect(isUsable(0.0));
    try std.testing.expect(!isUsable(std.math.nan(f64)));
    try std.testing.expect(!isUsable(std.math.inf(f64)));
    try std.testing.expect(!isUsable(-std.math.inf(f64)));
}

@abs works on floats as well as integers. isUsable must reject NaN explicitly, because x == x is the only comparison that catches it and that reads as a trick; std.math.isNan says what it means.

Exercise 5.3 · Ready to deploy practice

Write canDeploy as a single boolean expression from four inputs, following the rule in its doc comment, and moraleLabel as an if expression with three outcomes. Name the file: exercises/05-floats-bools/ex3_ready.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 05, exercise 3: a readiness check with and/or/not.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_ready.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// A unit may deploy when it has a pilot, is not destroyed, and either has
/// at least 30 armor or is being sent on a milk run.
fn canDeploy(has_pilot: bool, destroyed: bool, armor: u8, milk_run: bool) bool {
    return has_pilot and !destroyed and (armor >= 30 or milk_run);
}

/// Morale label: "high" at 70 or more, "low" below 30, otherwise "steady".
fn moraleLabel(morale: u8) []const u8 {
    return if (morale >= 70) "high" else if (morale < 30) "low" else "steady";
}

test "canDeploy" {
    try std.testing.expect(canDeploy(true, false, 50, false));
    try std.testing.expect(canDeploy(true, false, 10, true));
    try std.testing.expect(!canDeploy(true, false, 10, false));
    try std.testing.expect(!canDeploy(false, false, 100, true));
    try std.testing.expect(!canDeploy(true, true, 100, true));
}

test "moraleLabel" {
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("high", moraleLabel(70));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("steady", moraleLabel(69));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("steady", moraleLabel(30));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("low", moraleLabel(29));
}

The parentheses around the or are required: without them, and would bind first and a milk run would let a pilotless, destroyed unit deploy. if … else if … else as an expression is previewed here and covered in Chapter 6.

Exercise 5.4 · Price per ton challenge

Write perTon and then print the three-row report in the starter's header: name 12 wide, tons 3 wide, price 9 wide, and price per ton 10 wide with two decimals, followed by the average per-ton price. The starter already loops over three arrays at once with for (names, tons, prices) |name, t, price|, a form Chapter 6 explains. Name the file: exercises/05-floats-bools/ex4_report.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 05, exercise 4: a formatted float report.
//! Run with:  zig run ex4_report.zig
//! Expected output (on stderr):
//!   Locust        20 t   1512000 C-bills   75600.00 per ton
//!   Shadow Hawk   55 t   4701000 C-bills   85472.73 per ton
//!   Atlas        100 t   9626000 C-bills   96260.00 per ton
//!   average price per ton: 85777.58
const std = @import("std");

fn perTon(price: u32, tons: u32) f64 {
    const p: f64 = @floatFromInt(price);
    const t: f64 = @floatFromInt(tons);
    return p / t;
}

pub fn main() void {
    const names = [_][]const u8{ "Locust", "Shadow Hawk", "Atlas" };
    const tons = [_]u32{ 20, 55, 100 };
    const prices = [_]u32{ 1_512_000, 4_701_000, 9_626_000 };
    var total: f64 = 0.0;
    for (names, tons, prices) |name, t, price| {
        const ratio = perTon(price, t);
        total += ratio;
        std.debug.print("{s:<12} {d:>3} t {d:>9} C-bills {d:>10.2} per ton\n", .{
            name, t, price, ratio,
        });
    }
    std.debug.print("average price per ton: {d:.2}\n", .{total / 3.0});
}

{d:>10.2} combines width, alignment and precision. The running total is an f64 so that the average keeps its fraction; dividing by 3.0 rather than 3 keeps the literal a float, although a comptime_int would also coerce here.

Check your understanding

  1. Why is 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 false for f64 values?
    AnswerNone of 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 is exactly representable in binary, and the rounding errors of the two operands do not cancel. Compare with a tolerance instead.
  2. How do you turn a u32 into an f64, and the reverse?
    Answer@floatFromInt(x) and @intFromFloat(x), with the target type given by context. The reverse drops the fraction and panics if the integer part does not fit.
  3. What does const h: f64 = n / 2; give when n: u32 = 7?
    Answer3, not 3.5. The integer division runs first, then the result is widened.
  4. What is nan == nan?
    Answerfalse. NaN is unequal to everything, itself included. Use std.math.isNan.
  5. Does 1.0 / 0.0 panic?
    AnswerNo. Float division by zero gives infinity (or NaN for 0/0); only integer division by zero panics.
  6. Why does if (count) fail when count is a u32?
    AnswerZig has no truthiness; a condition must be a bool. Write if (count != 0).
  7. What is wrong with a && b?
    AnswerZig's logical operators are the words and and or; && is a compile error that tells you so.
What you learned.
  • f64 is the default float; floats are approximate, so never test computed floats for equality and never use them for money.
  • @floatFromInt, @intFromFloat and @floatCast convert explicitly; some lossless int-to-float coercions are allowed, but write the builtin anyway, and convert before dividing.
  • {d:.2} prints a float with two decimals; {e} is scientific notation.
  • Float division by zero gives inf or NaN rather than panicking; NaN is never equal to anything; test with std.math.isNan.
  • Comparisons give bool, cannot be chained, and need std.math.approxEqAbs for floats.
  • Boolean operators are and, or, !; they short-circuit; there is no truthiness.

6. Control flow: if, while, for, switch

In this chapter you will learn Zig's four control-flow constructs and the ways they differ from what you know: if and switch are expressions that produce values, while has a continue expression, for walks ranges and arrays without an index variable, loops can be labeled and can produce values with else, and switch must be exhaustive. You will also meet unreachable.

6.1 if as a statement

An if tests a bool and runs a block. else if and else chain on as in C or JavaScript. The parentheses around the condition are required; the braces can be dropped when the body is a single statement.

if_stmt.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const funds: i64 = -25_000;
    if (funds < 0) {
        std.debug.print("the company is in debt\n", .{});
    } else if (funds == 0) {
        std.debug.print("the company is broke\n", .{});
    } else {
        std.debug.print("the company is solvent\n", .{});
    }
    if (funds < 0) std.debug.print("(one-line form works too)\n", .{});
}
$ zig run if_stmt.zig
the company is in debt
(one-line form works too)

As Chapter 5 said, the condition must be a bool. There is no truthiness, so if (funds) is an error and if (funds != 0) is what you write.

6.2 if as an expression

In Zig, if can also be a value. Each branch is an expression, and the whole thing evaluates to whichever branch ran. This replaces the cond ? a : b operator of C and JavaScript.

if_expr.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const tonnage: u32 = 75;
    const class = if (tonnage <= 35) "light" else if (tonnage <= 55) "medium" else "heavy";
    std.debug.print("{d} tons: {s}\n", .{ tonnage, class });
    const bonus: u32 = if (tonnage > 50) 10 else 0;
    std.debug.print("bonus {d}\n", .{bonus});
}
$ zig run if_expr.zig
75 tons: heavy
bonus 10

An if expression must have an else, because it has to produce a value on every path, and both branches must have compatible types (peer type resolution again). The bonus line shows that a literal in a branch takes the annotated type. This form is used constantly in real code for small decisions inline, and it pairs with const: instead of declaring a var and assigning it in each branch, you declare a const and let the if produce it.

6.3 while

while repeats a block as long as a condition holds.

while_basic.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var day: u32 = 1;
    while (day <= 3) {
        std.debug.print("day {d}\n", .{day});
        day += 1;
    }
    std.debug.print("after the loop, day = {d}\n", .{day});
}
$ zig run while_basic.zig
day 1
day 2
day 3
after the loop, day = 4

Zig has no do … while and, as you will see, no C-style three-part for. Instead while takes an optional continue expression after a colon, which runs at the end of every iteration, including after a continue:

while_cont.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var day: u32 = 1;
    while (day <= 3) : (day += 1) {
        std.debug.print("day {d}\n", .{day});
    }

    var i: u32 = 0;
    var total: u32 = 0;
    while (i < 10) : (i += 1) {
        if (i % 2 == 1) continue; // skip odd numbers; the continue expression still runs
        total += i;
    }
    std.debug.print("sum of even numbers below 10: {d}\n", .{total});
}
$ zig run while_cont.zig
day 1
day 2
day 3
sum of even numbers below 10: 20

while (day <= 3) : (day += 1) reads: while this holds, run the body, then do this. The increment lives in the loop header, where it cannot be forgotten and where a continue in the body cannot skip it. That second point is the reason the form exists: in the second loop, continue jumps past total += i but the i += 1 still runs, so the loop cannot get stuck.

break leaves the loop immediately. A while (true) with a break inside is the idiom for "loop until something happens in the middle":

while_break.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var funds: i64 = 100_000;
    var day: u32 = 0;
    while (true) {
        day += 1;
        funds -= 35_000;
        if (funds < 0) break;
    }
    std.debug.print("ran out of money on day {d}\n", .{day});
}
$ zig run while_break.zig
ran out of money on day 3

6.4 for over ranges and arrays

Zig's for does not count; it iterates. Give it something to walk, and a name in pipes for each element.

for_range.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    for (0..3) |i| {
        std.debug.print("i = {d}\n", .{i});
    }
    for (1..4) |n| std.debug.print("n = {d} ", .{n});
    std.debug.print("\n", .{});
    for (0..3) |_| std.debug.print("tick ", .{});
    std.debug.print("\n", .{});
}
$ zig run for_range.zig
i = 0
i = 1
i = 2
n = 1 n = 2 n = 3 
tick tick tick

0..3 is a range: 0, 1, 2. The end is exclusive, so 0..n runs n times and 1..4 gives 1, 2, 3. The name between the pipes, |i|, is the capture: a fresh const for each iteration. If you do not need the value, capture |_|, since an unused capture is an error like any unused name.

The type of a range capture is usize. That matters as soon as you try to store it somewhere narrower:

$ zig run for_index_type.zig
for_index_type.zig:6:23: error: expected type 'u8', found 'usize'
        const x: u8 = i;
                      ^
for_index_type.zig:6:23: note: unsigned 8-bit int cannot represent all possible unsigned 64-bit values

Use @intCast(i) when you need the index as a smaller type.

The same syntax walks an array. Arrays are Chapter 9, but you can read [_]u32{ 20, 55, 75, 100 } as "an array of four u32, count them for me":

for_array.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const tonnages = [_]u32{ 20, 55, 75, 100 };
    var total: u32 = 0;
    for (tonnages) |t| {
        total += t;
    }
    std.debug.print("total {d}\n", .{total});

    for (tonnages, 0..) |t, i| {
        std.debug.print("slot {d}: {d} tons\n", .{ i, t });
    }

    const names = [_][]const u8{ "Locust", "Shadow Hawk", "Marauder", "Atlas" };
    for (names, tonnages) |name, t| {
        std.debug.print("{s} ({d}t)\n", .{ name, t });
    }
}
$ zig run for_array.zig
total 250
slot 0: 20 tons
slot 1: 55 tons
slot 2: 75 tons
slot 3: 100 tons
Locust (20t)
Shadow Hawk (55t)
Marauder (75t)
Atlas (100t)

Three forms appear. for (tonnages) |t| gives each element. for (tonnages, 0..) |t, i| gives each element and its index, by iterating the array and an open-ended range together. for (names, tonnages) |name, t| walks two arrays in step; they must have the same length, and Zig checks that in Debug builds. There is no separate "enumerate" or "zip"; you just list more things to iterate.

The capture is a copy. To change the elements you iterate the array's address and capture a pointer, which is Chapter 18's topic, but the shape is worth seeing now:

for_mut.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var armor = [_]u8{ 10, 20, 30 };
    for (&armor) |*a| {
        a.* += 5;
    }
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{armor});
}
$ zig run for_mut.zig
{ 15, 25, 35 }

&armor lends the array itself, |*a| captures a pointer to each slot, and a.* is the value behind that pointer. Without the & and the *, a += 5 would be an error, because the capture is a const.

6.5 Labeled loops

A break or continue normally applies to the innermost loop. To reach an outer one, give it a label:

labeled.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const grid = [_][3]u8{
        .{ 1, 5, 3 },
        .{ 4, 9, 6 },
        .{ 7, 8, 9 },
    };
    outer: for (grid, 0..) |row, r| {
        for (row, 0..) |cell, c| {
            if (cell == 9) {
                std.debug.print("found 9 at row {d}, col {d}\n", .{ r, c });
                break :outer;
            }
        }
    }
    var lines: u32 = 0;
    rows: for (grid) |row| {
        for (row) |cell| {
            if (cell % 2 == 0) continue :rows; // skip rows with any even cell
        }
        lines += 1;
    }
    std.debug.print("rows with only odd cells: {d}\n", .{lines});
}
$ zig run labeled.zig
found 9 at row 1, col 1
rows with only odd cells: 1

outer: for … names the loop, and break :outer leaves it from inside the inner loop. continue :rows abandons the rest of the current row and moves to the next one. Without labels, the first search would need a flag variable checked after the inner loop, and the second would need to remember whether it had already seen an even cell. Labels are the same mechanism as the labeled blocks of Chapter 3; a loop is just a block that repeats.

6.6 Loops as expressions: else

Because loops are blocks, they can produce values too. A break can carry a value, and the loop can have an else clause that supplies the value when the loop finishes without breaking.

loop_else.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const roster = [_]u32{ 3, 8, 12, 27 };
    const wanted: u32 = 12;
    const found = for (roster, 0..) |id, i| {
        if (id == wanted) break i;
    } else null;
    std.debug.print("found at: {?}\n", .{found});

    var n: u32 = 91;
    var divisor: u32 = 2;
    const factor = while (divisor * divisor <= n) : (divisor += 1) {
        if (n % divisor == 0) break divisor;
    } else 0;
    n += 0;
    std.debug.print("smallest factor of 91: {d}\n", .{factor});
}
$ zig run loop_else.zig
found at: 2
smallest factor of 91: 7

The first loop is a search. If it finds the id, break i makes the loop's value the index; if it runs out of elements, the else null makes it null. The result type is ?usize, "an index or nothing", and {?} prints an optional; Chapter 15 is all about these. The second loop uses while … else the same way, with a continue expression, to find the smallest factor of a number.

The else of a loop runs only when the condition ends the loop naturally. It is the "not found" branch, and it removes the need for a "found" flag. This is a Zig habit worth acquiring early: compute the value with the loop, rather than declaring a variable and mutating it from inside the loop.

6.7 switch

switch compares one value against a list of cases and runs the matching arm. Unlike C's switch there is no fall-through and no break; exactly one arm runs. Like if, it is an expression.

switch_basic.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const month: u8 = 2;
    const days: u8 = switch (month) {
        1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12 => 31,
        4, 6, 9, 11 => 30,
        2 => 28,
        else => 0,
    };
    std.debug.print("month {d} has {d} days\n", .{ month, days });

    const roll: u8 = 9;
    const outcome = switch (roll) {
        2...4 => "disaster",
        5...8 => "setback",
        9...11 => "success",
        12 => "triumph",
        else => "impossible",
    };
    std.debug.print("rolled {d}: {s}\n", .{ roll, outcome });
}
$ zig run switch_basic.zig
month 2 has 28 days
rolled 9: success

Cases are written to the left of =>. A single value: 12. A list: 1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12. An inclusive range: 2...4, with three dots (a range in a for has two dots and an exclusive end; a range in a switch has three and an inclusive end; this is confusing for a week). else catches anything not listed. Arms are separated by commas, and each arm is an expression; when an arm needs several statements, make it a block:

switch_stmt.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const key: u8 = 'q';
    switch (key) {
        'q' => std.debug.print("quit\n", .{}),
        'h', '?' => std.debug.print("help\n", .{}),
        '0'...'9' => |digit| std.debug.print("digit {c}\n", .{digit}),
        else => {
            std.debug.print("unknown key ", .{});
            std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{key});
        },
    }
}
$ zig run switch_stmt.zig
quit

This one is a statement, so its arms produce nothing; the block arm ends with a comma after its closing brace. The '0'...'9' => |digit| arm shows that an arm can capture the matched value, which is useful when the case is a range.

Two rules make switch safer than its relatives in other languages. First, it must be exhaustive: every possible value of the type must match some arm, or there must be an else.

switch_missing.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const d: u2 = 3;
    const name = switch (d) {
        0 => "north",
        1 => "east",
        2 => "south",
    };
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{name});
}
$ zig run switch_missing.zig
switch_missing.zig:5:18: error: switch must handle all possibilities
    const name = switch (d) {
                 ^~~~~~

A u2 has four values and only three are handled, so the compiler refuses. Add the fourth arm and it builds; with a small type like u2 or bool you can list every case and leave out else entirely, which means that if the type ever grows, the compiler will find every switch that needs updating. This is a big part of why the game uses enums so heavily (Chapter 13).

$ zig run switch_full.zig
west
yes

Second, cases may not overlap. Two ranges that share a value are an error, so a value can never match two arms:

$ zig run switch_dup.zig
switch_dup.zig:7:10: error: duplicate switch value
        6...12 => "high",
        ~^~~~~
switch_dup.zig:6:10: note: previous value here
        1...6 => "low",
        ~^~~~

6.8 unreachable

Sometimes a case is impossible by construction, and you want to say so instead of inventing a default value. unreachable is a statement that asserts control never gets here.

unreach.zig
const std = @import("std");

fn daysInMonth(month: u8) u8 {
    return switch (month) {
        1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12 => 31,
        4, 6, 9, 11 => 30,
        2 => 28,
        else => unreachable, // months are always 1..12 here
    };
}

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{daysInMonth(4)});
    var bad: u8 = 12;
    bad += 1;
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{daysInMonth(bad)});
}
$ zig run unreach.zig
30
thread 12345 panic: reached unreachable code
unreach.zig:8:17: 0x10000abcd in daysInMonth (unreach)
        else => unreachable, // months are always 1..12 here
                ^
unreach.zig:16:43: 0x10000abcd in main (unreach)
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{daysInMonth(bad)});
                                          ^

The first call works. The second passes 13, hits the else, and panics with "reached unreachable code", naming the line. In a Debug build unreachable is a check; in ReleaseFast it is a promise the optimiser may rely on, and breaking it is undefined behaviour. So use it for cases that truly cannot happen given how the function is called, not for cases you have not thought about yet. unreachable also satisfies the exhaustiveness rule, because an arm that never returns has no type to disagree with the others.

6.9 Putting it together

Here is a small simulation of a month's cash flow using several constructs at once, so you can see them cooperate.

nested.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var day: u32 = 1;
    var funds: i64 = 120_000;
    const daily_cost: i64 = 45_000;
    while (day <= 30) : (day += 1) {
        funds -= daily_cost;
        if (day % 7 == 0) funds += 200_000; // weekly contract pay
        const status = if (funds < 0) "DEBT" else "ok";
        if (day <= 8) std.debug.print("day {d:>2}: {d:>8} {s}\n", .{ day, funds, status });
    }
    std.debug.print("month end: {d}\n", .{funds});
}
$ zig run nested.zig
day  1:   +75000 ok
day  2:   +30000 ok
day  3:   -15000 DEBT
day  4:   -60000 DEBT
day  5:  -105000 DEBT
day  6:  -150000 DEBT
day  7:    +5000 ok
day  8:   -40000 DEBT
month end: -430000

A while with a continue expression drives the days. An if statement adds the weekly pay. An if expression picks a status word into a const. Another one-line if limits the printing. The {d:>8} on the signed funds shows the plus sign that Chapter 2 warned about.

Try it. Make the loop stop on the first day the company goes into debt, using break, and print the day number after the loop. Then rewrite it so the loop itself produces the day number with break day and else 0.
In IRON LEDGER. The calendar in game/src/sim/clock.zig is a switch on the month with list cases, an if expression in one arm, and an unreachable for the months that do not exist: 
pub fn daysInMonth(year: u16, month: u8) u8 {
    return switch (month) {
        1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12 => 31,
        4, 6, 9, 11 => 30,
        2 => if (isLeapYear(year)) @as(u8, 29) else 28,
        else => unreachable,
    };
}
The @as(u8, 29) is there because both branches of the inner if are literals and the outer switch needs one of them to have a concrete type. In game/src/main.zig the demo's contract hunt is a while with a continue expression: while (pick == null and hunts < 8) : (hunts += 1) { … }. And the simulation's "is this person in this company" check walks up the force tree with a while … else expression that yields a bool, which you will read in Part 5.

Exercises

Exercise 6.1 · Countdown and fizzbuzz warm-up

Print a countdown from 5 with a while loop and a continue expression, then a fizzbuzz line for 1 to 15 with a for over a range, formatted exactly as the header shows. Name the file: exercises/06-control-flow/ex1_countdown.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 06, exercise 1: while, for and if together.
//! Run with:  zig run ex1_countdown.zig
//! Expected output (on stderr):
//!   T-5 T-4 T-3 T-2 T-1 launch
//!   1 2 fizz 4 buzz fizz 7 8 fizz buzz 11 fizz 13 14 fizzbuzz
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var t: u32 = 5;
    while (t > 0) : (t -= 1) {
        std.debug.print("T-{d} ", .{t});
    }
    std.debug.print("launch\n", .{});

    for (1..16) |n| {
        if (n % 15 == 0) {
            std.debug.print("fizzbuzz", .{});
        } else if (n % 3 == 0) {
            std.debug.print("fizz", .{});
        } else if (n % 5 == 0) {
            std.debug.print("buzz", .{});
        } else {
            std.debug.print("{d}", .{n});
        }
        if (n == 15) {
            std.debug.print("\n", .{});
        } else {
            std.debug.print(" ", .{});
        }
    }
}

The separator is printed by an if statement rather than an if expression inside print, because the format string must be known at compile time and the choice depends on a runtime n. That is a rule you will meet again in Chapter 23.

Exercise 6.2 · Dice, months and keys practice

Write three switch expressions: the outcome of a 2d6 roll from four ranges, the days in a month from two lists and a single case, and the action for a keypress including a character range. The last returns an enum value; write those as .quit, .help and so on. Name the file: exercises/06-control-flow/ex2_dice.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 06, exercise 2: switch on ranges and lists.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_dice.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Outcome of a 2d6 roll: 2..4 "disaster", 5..8 "setback", 9..11 "success",
/// 12 "triumph". Anything else cannot happen with two dice.
fn outcome(roll: u8) []const u8 {
    return switch (roll) {
        2...4 => "disaster",
        5...8 => "setback",
        9...11 => "success",
        12 => "triumph",
        else => unreachable,
    };
}

/// Days in a month of the year 3025 (not a leap year).
fn daysInMonth(month: u8) u8 {
    return switch (month) {
        1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12 => 31,
        4, 6, 9, 11 => 30,
        2 => 28,
        else => 0,
    };
}

/// A single keypress in the terminal client: 'q' quits, 'h' or '?' shows
/// help, a digit selects that slot (0..9), anything else is ignored.
const Action = enum { quit, help, select, ignore };

fn keyAction(key: u8) Action {
    return switch (key) {
        'q' => .quit,
        'h', '?' => .help,
        '0'...'9' => .select,
        else => .ignore,
    };
}

test "outcome" {
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("disaster", outcome(2));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("disaster", outcome(4));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("setback", outcome(5));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("success", outcome(11));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("triumph", outcome(12));
}

test "daysInMonth" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 31), daysInMonth(1));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 28), daysInMonth(2));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 30), daysInMonth(4));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 0), daysInMonth(13));
}

test "keyAction" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Action.quit, keyAction('q'));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Action.help, keyAction('?'));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Action.select, keyAction('7'));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Action.ignore, keyAction('x'));
}

In outcome, the else => unreachable documents that two dice cannot produce 1 or 13; if you preferred a safe default you could return a string instead, and both satisfy exhaustiveness. Character literals are integers, so '0'...'9' is an ordinary range.

Exercise 6.3 · Loops that produce values practice

Write indexOf with a for … else expression, everyRowHasZero with a labeled outer loop and continue :label, and smallestDivisor with a while … else and a continue expression. No flag variables in the first and third. Name the file: exercises/06-control-flow/ex3_search.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 06, exercise 3: loops that produce values, and labeled loops.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_search.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Index of the first element equal to `wanted`, or null if absent.
/// Use a `for ... else` expression, not a separate flag variable.
fn indexOf(items: []const u32, wanted: u32) ?usize {
    return for (items, 0..) |item, i| {
        if (item == wanted) break i;
    } else null;
}

/// True when every row of the grid contains at least one zero.
/// Use a labeled outer loop with `continue :label`.
fn everyRowHasZero(grid: []const [3]u8) bool {
    var rows_with_zero: usize = 0;
    rows: for (grid) |row| {
        for (row) |cell| {
            if (cell == 0) {
                rows_with_zero += 1;
                continue :rows;
            }
        }
    }
    return rows_with_zero == grid.len;
}

/// Smallest divisor of n greater than 1 (n itself when n is prime).
/// Use a `while ... else` expression with a continue expression.
fn smallestDivisor(n: u32) u32 {
    var d: u32 = 2;
    return while (d * d <= n) : (d += 1) {
        if (n % d == 0) break d;
    } else n;
}

test "indexOf" {
    const roster = [_]u32{ 3, 8, 12, 27 };
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?usize, 2), indexOf(&roster, 12));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?usize, 0), indexOf(&roster, 3));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?usize, null), indexOf(&roster, 99));
}

test "everyRowHasZero" {
    const yes = [_][3]u8{ .{ 1, 0, 2 }, .{ 0, 5, 5 }, .{ 7, 7, 0 } };
    const no = [_][3]u8{ .{ 1, 0, 2 }, .{ 4, 5, 5 } };
    try std.testing.expect(everyRowHasZero(&yes));
    try std.testing.expect(!everyRowHasZero(&no));
}

test "smallestDivisor" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 7), smallestDivisor(91));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 2), smallestDivisor(100));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 13), smallestDivisor(13));
}

The parameters are slices, []const u32, which Chapter 10 explains; for now they behave like arrays under for. Each function's shape matches one construct from this chapter, and the point of the exercise is to feel where each one is the natural fit.

Exercise 6.4 · A month of payroll challenge

Simulate thirty days of costs and weekly pay following the rules in the starter's header, printing a line each payday and stopping with a DEBT line the moment funds go negative. The expected output is given exactly. Name the file: exercises/06-control-flow/ex4_payroll.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 06, exercise 4: a month of payroll, day by day.
//! Run with:  zig run ex4_payroll.zig
//! Expected output (on stderr):
//!   day 7: paid 200000, funds 385000
//!   day 14: paid 200000, funds 270000
//!   day 21: paid 200000, funds 155000
//!   day 25: DEBT (-25000), stopping
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var funds: i64 = 500_000;
    const daily_cost: i64 = 45_000;
    const weekly_pay: i64 = 200_000;
    var day: u32 = 1;
    while (day <= 30) : (day += 1) {
        funds -= daily_cost;
        if (day % 7 == 0) {
            funds += weekly_pay;
            std.debug.print("day {d}: paid {d}, funds {d}\n", .{ day, weekly_pay, funds });
        }
        if (funds < 0) {
            std.debug.print("day {d}: DEBT ({d}), stopping\n", .{ day, funds });
            break;
        }
    }
}

Order matters: the day's cost is subtracted, then pay is added and printed if it is a payday, then the debt check runs. Getting day 25 rather than day 26 depends on doing the check after the cost on the same day. The break leaves the while even though the continue expression has not run, which is exactly right.

Check your understanding

  1. What is the difference between 0..n in a for and 0...n in a switch?
    AnswerTwo dots is an exclusive-end range for iteration (0 to n-1); three dots is an inclusive range for a switch case (0 to n).
  2. When does a while loop's continue expression run?
    AnswerAt the end of every iteration, including after a continue statement; it does not run after a break.
  3. What type does |i| have in for (0..10) |i|?
    Answerusize. Use @intCast to store it in a narrower type.
  4. How do you get both the element and its index from a for?
    AnswerIterate the array together with an open range: for (items, 0..) |item, i|.
  5. When does the else of a loop run?
    AnswerWhen the loop ends because its condition became false or its items ran out, not when it ends by break. It supplies the loop's value in that case.
  6. Why does switch (x) { 0 => "a", 1 => "b" } fail for x: u2?
    AnswerA u2 has values 0 to 3; the switch is not exhaustive. Add arms for 2 and 3 or an else.
  7. What happens if execution reaches unreachable in a Debug build? And in ReleaseFast?
    AnswerDebug: a panic, "reached unreachable code". ReleaseFast: undefined behaviour; the optimiser assumed it could not happen.
What you learned.
  • if takes a bool and can be an expression with a mandatory else.
  • while (cond) : (step) runs step after every iteration; break and continue work as expected.
  • for iterates ranges a..b and arrays, captures with |x|, gets an index from 0.., and walks several things in step.
  • Labels let break :outer and continue :outer reach an enclosing loop; loops can yield values with break v and else.
  • switch has values, lists, and inclusive a...b ranges, must be exhaustive, allows no overlap, and is an expression.
  • unreachable asserts a path cannot happen: a panic in Debug, a promise in release.

7. Functions

In this chapter you will learn how to declare and call functions, why parameters cannot be changed inside a function and what to do instead, how return types including void work, how early return keeps code flat, how recursion looks in Zig, what pub does, and how a function can be passed around as a value. You will also get a preview of functions living inside a struct, which is where methods come from.

7.1 Declaring and calling

A function is declared with fn, a name, a parameter list where every parameter has a type, a return type, and a body.

basic.zig
const std = @import("std");

fn add(a: i32, b: i32) i32 {
    return a + b;
}

fn greet(name: []const u8) void {
    std.debug.print("Welcome aboard, {s}.\n", .{name});
}

pub fn main() void {
    const total = add(2, 3);
    std.debug.print("2 + 3 = {d}\n", .{total});
    greet("Commander");
}
$ zig run basic.zig
2 + 3 = 5
Welcome aboard, Commander.

fn add(a: i32, b: i32) i32 reads: a function named add taking two i32 values and returning an i32. There is no arrow or colon before the return type; it simply follows the parentheses. return ends the function with a value. Calling it is add(2, 3), and the result can be bound to a const or used directly inside another expression.

greet takes a []const u8, which is the type of a string (Chapter 11 explains the name; read it as "text" for now), and returns void, meaning nothing. A void function has no return value; it just runs off the end of its body, or uses a bare return; to leave early.

Order does not matter. main can call a function declared below it, because all top-level declarations in a file are visible to each other, as Chapter 3 noted:

order.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{later(4)});
}

fn later(x: u32) u32 {
    return x + 1;
}
$ zig run order.zig
5

Zig has no default arguments, no keyword arguments, and no overloading (two functions with the same name and different parameters). Each of these has a Zig idiom that arrives later: an options struct with default fields for the first two (Chapter 12), and comptime or anytype parameters for the third (Chapter 26).

7.2 Types are checked, and unused parameters are errors

Arguments must match the parameter types under the same coercion rules as assignment. Widening is free; anything else is refused:

wrong_type.zig
const std = @import("std");
