The histogram indexes the array directly by the roll value, which is why it has 13 slots for values up to 12. mode starts at 2 and only moves on a strictly larger count, so ties go to the smaller total. bar takes a slice rather than an array so it works with any buffer size; the next chapter explains why that is the better signature.

Check your understanding

  1. Are [3]u8 and [4]u8 the same type?
    AnswerNo. The length is part of an array type, so they are different types and cannot be assigned to each other or passed where the other is expected.
  2. What does [_] mean in [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3 }?
    Answer"Count the elements for me." The type is still a fixed [3]u8; the underscore only saves you writing the number.
  3. What happens when you index past the end with a runtime index in a Debug build?
    AnswerThe program panics with index out of bounds: index N, len M and a stack trace. With a compile-time index it is a compile error instead.
  4. How do you modify each element in a for loop?
    AnswerLoop over &array and capture with |*item|, then assign through item.*. The array must be a var.
  5. What does var b = a; do when a is an array?
    AnswerCopies every element. b is an independent array; changing it does not affect a.
  6. Why does a == b not compile for arrays, and what do you use instead?
    AnswerZig reserves operators for cheap operations; element-wise comparison is a loop, so it is the function std.mem.eql(T, &a, &b). In tests, expectEqual also compares arrays element by element.
  7. When should a parameter be *[4]u8 instead of [4]u8?
    AnswerWhen the function must modify the caller's array, or when the array is large enough that copying it is wasteful. For read-only access to arrays of any length, a slice []const u8 is better still.
What you learned.
  • An array type [N]T includes its length; [_]T{...} lets the compiler count.
  • Indexes are usize, start at 0, and are bounds-checked: a compile error for constant indexes, a panic for runtime ones.
  • for (arr) |x| reads, for (arr, 0..) |x, i| adds the index, for (&arr) |*x| lets you write.
  • [N][M]T is an array of arrays; index with a[r][c].
  • ** repeats and ++ concatenates compile-time arrays; undefined reserves space you promise to fill.
  • Arrays are values: assignment and by-value parameters copy. Compare with std.mem.eql, not ==.
  • Pass *[N]T to modify in place; pass a slice to accept any length.

10. Slices

In this chapter you will learn the type you will use more than any other in Zig: the slice. A slice is a pointer plus a length, a window onto some array that lives elsewhere. You will make slices from arrays, read and write through them, learn why []const T and []T differ, see the bounds check that protects you, meet the sentinel-terminated and many-item cousins briefly, and understand why nearly every function you write from now on takes a slice instead of an array.

10.1 A window onto an array

The previous chapter ended on a wall: a function taking [4]u8 cannot accept a [3]u8. Slices are how Zig climbs that wall without losing safety. A slice does not own any elements. It says "start here, and there are this many". Make one by writing a range in square brackets after an array:

basics.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const roster = [_]u8{ 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 };
    const middle = roster[1..4]; // elements 1, 2, 3 (4 is excluded)
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{middle});
    std.debug.print("len {d}, first {d}\n", .{ middle.len, middle[0] });
    std.debug.print("type: {any}\n", .{@TypeOf(middle)});
}
{ 20, 30, 40 }
len 3, first 20
type: *const [3]u8

roster[1..4] means "from index 1 up to but not including index 4": elements 1, 2 and 3. The end is exclusive, exactly like Python's roster[1:4], so end - start is the length. The result knows its length, 3, and you index it from zero: middle[0] is roster[1].

Look at the printed type, though: *const [3]u8, a pointer to a three-element array, not a slice. That is a small 0.16 detail worth knowing. When both bounds are compile-time constants, Zig can work out the length and gives you the more precise pointer-to-array type. It coerces to a slice the moment you need one, so in practice you treat it as a slice. Use runtime bounds, or write the slice type explicitly, and you get a real slice:

forms.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var roster = [_]u8{ 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 };
    const tail = roster[2..]; // from index 2 to the end
    const head = roster[0..2]; // first two
    const all: []u8 = &roster; // &array coerces to a slice of the whole thing
    var n: usize = 1;
    n += 2;
    const runtime = roster[n..]; // the bounds can be runtime values
    std.debug.print("tail {any}\n", .{tail});
    std.debug.print("head {any}\n", .{head});
    std.debug.print("all  {any} (type {any})\n", .{ all, @TypeOf(all) });
    std.debug.print("runtime {any} (type {any})\n", .{ runtime, @TypeOf(runtime) });
}
tail { 30, 40, 50 }
head { 10, 20 }
all  { 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 } (type []u8)
runtime { 40, 50 } (type []u8)

Three forms to memorise:

  • arr[a..b]: from a to b exclusive.
  • arr[a..]: from a to the end.
  • &arr: the whole array. A pointer to an array coerces to a slice whenever a slice is expected, which is why you passed &a to std.mem.eql in the last chapter.

The type []u8 reads "slice of u8". No number in the brackets, because the length is not part of the type any more; it is a field of the value.

10.2 A slice is a view, not a copy

This is the fact that separates slices from arrays. Assigning an array copies it; making a slice copies nothing. The slice points into the original memory, and writing through it changes the original.

view.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var roster = [_]u8{ 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 };
    const window = roster[1..3];
    window[0] = 99; // writes through to roster[1]
    std.debug.print("roster: {any}\n", .{roster});
    std.debug.print("window: {any}\n", .{window});
    std.debug.print("same memory: {}\n", .{&window[0] == &roster[1]});
}
roster: { 10, 99, 30, 40, 50 }
window: { 99, 30 }
same memory: true

window[0] = 99 wrote into roster[1], because that is where the window starts. The last line proves it: the address of window[0] is the address of roster[1]. There are two names for one byte.

In memory a slice is two machine words: a pointer to the first element and a usize length. You can look at them as .ptr and .len. Copying a slice copies those two words, not the elements. That makes slices cheap to pass around and dangerous in exactly one way: the array they point at must outlive them. Zig catches the most common version of that mistake at compile time:

dangling.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn makeSlice() []const u8 {
    var local = [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3 };
    local[0] = 9;
    return &local; // points at a variable that is about to disappear
}

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{makeSlice()});
}
dangling.zig:6:13: error: returning address of expired local variable 'local'
    return &local; // points at a variable that is about to disappear
            ^~~~~
dangling.zig:4:9: note: declared runtime-known here
    var local = [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3 };
        ^~~~~

local lives on the stack frame of makeSlice, which is torn down when the function returns. A slice pointing into it would point at garbage. The compiler refuses. When you want a function to hand back text or data, either the caller provides the buffer (the pattern in 10.6 and in every bufPrint call) or the function allocates (Chapter 19).

10.3 []const T and []T

A slice type says whether you may write through it. []u8 allows writes; []const u8 does not. The rule for coercion is one-way: a mutable slice can become a const slice for free, never the reverse.

constness.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn sum(xs: []const u8) u32 {
    var t: u32 = 0;
    for (xs) |x| t += x;
    return t;
}

fn zero(xs: []u8) void {
    for (xs) |*x| x.* = 0;
}

pub fn main() void {
    var a = [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3 };
    const b = [_]u8{ 4, 5, 6 };
    std.debug.print("{d} {d}\n", .{ sum(&a), sum(&b) }); // []u8 coerces to []const u8
    zero(&a);
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{a});
}
6 15
{ 0, 0, 0 }

sum only reads, so it takes []const u8, and both the var array and the const array can be passed to it. zero writes, so it takes []u8, and only the var array works. Try the other way and the compiler says exactly what is wrong:

const std = @import("std");

fn zero(xs: []u8) void {
    for (xs) |*x| x.* = 0;
}

pub fn main() void {
    const b = [_]u8{ 4, 5, 6 };
    zero(&b);
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{b});
}
constness_err.zig:9:10: error: expected type '[]u8', found '*const [3]u8'
    zero(&b);
         ^~
constness_err.zig:9:10: note: cast discards const qualifier
constness_err.zig:3:13: note: parameter type declared here
fn zero(xs: []u8) void {
            ^~~~
referenced by:
    callMain [inlined]: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:698:59
    callMainWithArgs [inlined]: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:638:20
    main: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:663:28
    1 reference(s) hidden; use '-freference-trace=4' to see all references

cast discards const qualifier is the phrase to recognise. It means "you are trying to get write access to something that was declared read-only".

Rule of thumb. Declare a slice parameter []const T unless the function needs to modify the elements. It documents intent, it accepts more arguments, and the compiler holds you to it. Nearly every string parameter in IRON LEDGER is []const u8.

10.4 Bounds are checked here too

A slice knows its length, so indexing and re-slicing are checked just as with arrays. Because the bounds are usually runtime values, the check is usually at runtime:

bounds.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn firstN(xs: []const u8, n: usize) []const u8 {
    return xs[0..n];
}

pub fn main() void {
    const roster = [_]u8{ 10, 20, 30 };
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{firstN(&roster, 2)});
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{firstN(&roster, 5)});
}
{ 10, 20 }
thread 5972081 panic: index out of bounds: index 5, len 3
ch10/bounds.zig:4:14: in firstN (bounds)
    return xs[0..n];
             ^
ch10/bounds.zig:10:40: in main (bounds)
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{firstN(&roster, 5)});
                                       ^
<zig>/lib/std/start.zig:698:59: in callMain (bounds)
    if (fn_info.params.len == 0) return wrapMain(root.main());
                                                          ^
???:?:?: in start (/usr/lib/dyld)

The first trace line points at xs[0..n] inside firstN, the second at the call in main. You get to see both where the bad slice was made and who asked for it.

Note also what the check is guarding. Slicing does not copy, so the check is the only thing standing between your program and reading memory it has no business with. In C the equivalent call quietly returns a pointer past the end of the buffer.

10.5 Why functions take slices

The payoff comes now. Rewrite the average with a slice parameter and it works for four elements, twelve, a window of four in the middle of twelve, or none at all:

why.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn average(xs: []const u32) u32 {
    if (xs.len == 0) return 0;
    var t: u32 = 0;
    for (xs) |x| t += x;
    return t / @as(u32, @intCast(xs.len));
}

pub fn main() void {
    const lance = [_]u32{ 55, 65, 70, 50 };
    const company = [_]u32{ 55, 65, 70, 50, 80, 85, 75, 60, 35, 40, 30, 45 };
    std.debug.print("lance avg {d}\n", .{average(&lance)});
    std.debug.print("company avg {d}\n", .{average(&company)});
    std.debug.print("heavy lance avg {d}\n", .{average(company[4..8])});
    std.debug.print("nothing avg {d}\n", .{average(&[_]u32{})});
}
lance avg 60
company avg 57
heavy lance avg 75
nothing avg 0

One function, any length. company[4..8] hands it the middle of an array without copying anything. &[_]u32{} is an empty array's address, which coerces to an empty slice; the len == 0 guard handles it.

The @intCast is because xs.len is a usize and the arithmetic is in u32; Zig will not silently narrow a 64-bit value to 32 bits. You will write this cast often when mixing lengths with other integers.

This is why the standard library is written in terms of slices. std.mem.eql, std.mem.indexOf, std.fmt.bufPrint, the writer print methods: all of them take and return slices, so they compose with arrays of any size, with pieces of arrays, and, once you have an allocator, with memory from the heap.

10.6 Loops and mutation through a slice

Slices loop exactly like arrays. The pointer-capture form is how you modify elements in place, and it needs no & in front, because a slice is already a kind of pointer:

iter.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var hp = [_]u8{ 12, 7, 0, 3 };
    const wounded: []u8 = &hp;

    for (wounded, 0..) |h, i| {
        std.debug.print("pilot {d}: {d} hp\n", .{ i, h });
    }
    for (wounded) |*h| { // capture a pointer to mutate in place
        if (h.* > 0) h.* += 1;
    }
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{hp});

    // Two slices of equal length walked together.
    const names = [_][]const u8{ "Kai", "Nat", "Bo", "Ivy" };
    for (names, wounded) |n, h| {
        std.debug.print("{s}={d} ", .{ n, h });
    }
    std.debug.print("\n", .{});
}
pilot 0: 12 hp
pilot 1: 7 hp
pilot 2: 0 hp
pilot 3: 3 hp
{ 13, 8, 0, 4 }
Kai=13 Nat=8 Bo=0 Ivy=4

Three loops: (slice, 0..) |v, i| gives value and index; (slice) |*v| gives a pointer for writing; (a, b) |x, y| walks two slices in step. That last form requires equal lengths and panics otherwise, which is a feature: it turns a silent mismatch into a loud one.

For bulk copies and fills there are two builtins and two helpers:

copies.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var buf: [8]u8 = undefined;
    @memset(&buf, '.'); // fill every byte
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{&buf});

    const src = "mek";
    @memcpy(buf[0..src.len], src); // lengths must match exactly
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{&buf});

    // Overlapping copy: shift "mek" two places right.
    std.mem.copyForwards(u8, buf[2..5], buf[0..3]);
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{&buf});
    std.mem.copyBackwards(u8, buf[3..6], buf[1..4]);
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{&buf});
}
........
mek.....
memem...
mememe..

@memset fills every element with one value. @memcpy(dst, src) copies, and insists that the two lengths are exactly equal:

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var buf: [8]u8 = undefined;
    @memcpy(&buf, "mek");
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{&buf});
}
memcpy_len.zig:5:5: error: non-matching copy lengths
    @memcpy(&buf, "mek");
    ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
memcpy_len.zig:5:13: note: length 8 here
    @memcpy(&buf, "mek");
            ^~~~
memcpy_len.zig:5:19: note: length 3 here
    @memcpy(&buf, "mek");
                  ^~~~~
referenced by:
    callMain [inlined]: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:698:59
    callMainWithArgs [inlined]: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:638:20
    main: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:663:28
    1 reference(s) hidden; use '-freference-trace=4' to see all references

That is why the working version slices the destination first: buf[0..src.len]. @memcpy also requires that the regions do not overlap. When they might, as when shifting bytes inside one buffer, use std.mem.copyForwards (safe when the destination starts before the source) or std.mem.copyBackwards (safe when it starts after). The output above shows each one shifting mek along the buffer.

10.7 Sentinel-terminated slices

A string literal is not quite a plain array. Its type carries an extra promise: there is a zero byte just past the end.

sentinel.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const lit = "Alpha"; // *const [5:0]u8: five bytes plus a hidden 0
    const s: [:0]const u8 = lit; // sentinel-terminated slice
    const plain: []const u8 = lit; // ordinary slice, sentinel forgotten
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{@TypeOf(lit)});
    std.debug.print("{any} len {d}, byte after end: {d}\n", .{ @TypeOf(s), s.len, s[s.len] });
    std.debug.print("{any} len {d}\n", .{ @TypeOf(plain), plain.len });
}
*const [5:0]u8
[:0]const u8 len 5, byte after end: 0
[]const u8 len 5

*const [5:0]u8 reads "pointer to a constant array of 5 bytes, terminated by 0". The :0 is the sentinel. A slice can carry the same promise, [:0]const u8, and it is allowed to read the element at len, which a plain slice may not. The promise is what C needs (C strings find their end by looking for the zero), so you meet this type mostly at the edge where Zig calls C (Chapter 35) and in std.process arguments. The rest of the time you drop the sentinel by coercing to []const u8, as the third line shows, and nothing is lost: the length is still there.

10.8 Many-item pointers, briefly

The .ptr field of a slice has type [*]T, a many-item pointer. It is a pointer to some number of elements, with no idea how many. You can index it and it will not check anything.

many.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const roster = [_]u8{ 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 };
    const slice: []const u8 = &roster;
    const p: [*]const u8 = slice.ptr; // many-item pointer: no length
    std.debug.print("{d} {d}\n", .{ p[0], p[4] });
    // p[5] would compile and read garbage: nothing knows where the end is.
    const back: []const u8 = p[0..3]; // give it a length again
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{back});
}
10 50
{ 10, 20, 30 }

This is the C pointer, and Zig keeps it for talking to C and for the rare data structure that tracks its own lengths. In ordinary code you should almost never write [*]T; if you find yourself reaching for it, a slice is what you want. Knowing it exists helps you read error messages like expected '[]u8', found '[*]u8': something lost its length, and p[0..n] gives it back.

10.9 Slices of slices

The element type of a slice can be a slice. A list of names is the everyday example: []const []const u8, a slice of strings.

nested.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const names = [_][]const u8{ "1st Lance", "2nd Lance", "3rd Lance" };
    const some: []const []const u8 = names[1..];
    for (some, 0..) |name, i| {
        std.debug.print("{d}: {s} ({d} bytes)\n", .{ i, name, name.len });
    }
    const one = names[0];
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{one[0..3]}); // slicing a slice
}
0: 2nd Lance (9 bytes)
1: 3rd Lance (9 bytes)
1st

Read it inside out: []const u8 is one string; []const ([]const u8) is a slice of them. names[1..] takes the last two strings without copying any characters, and one[0..3] slices a string, which is what the next chapter is all about.

In IRON LEDGER. The command parser is built entirely on slices. Every function in src/sim/cli.zig takes a []const u8 and returns a slice or a parsed value, so the same code handles a keystroke buffer in the terminal and a line from a script file: 
// src/sim/cli.zig
pub fn parseSite(tok: []const u8) ParseError!types.Site { ... }
pub fn parseTreasury(tok: []const u8) ParseError!Treasury { ... }
pub fn need(tok: ?[]const u8) ParseError![]const u8 { ... }
pub fn usage(verb: []const u8) ?[]const u8 { ... }

Notice ?[]const u8: an optional slice, meaning "maybe a token, maybe nothing" (Chapter 15). The terminal reads keys into a fixed byte array and hands slices of it to the decoder, so no memory is allocated per keypress. And the guide's one-liner for a file's base name is pure slicing: if (std.mem.lastIndexOfScalar(u8, path, '/')) |k| path[k + 1 ..] else path.

Exercises

Exercise 10.1 · Slice basics warm-up

Write lastN, inner and halves, each returning slices of the input without copying. Name the file: exercises/10-slices/ex1_slice_basics.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 10, exercise 1: slice basics.
//! Run with:  zig test ex1_slice_basics.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// The last `n` elements of `xs`. If n is larger than xs.len, return all of xs.
fn lastN(xs: []const u8, n: usize) []const u8 {
    if (n >= xs.len) return xs;
    return xs[xs.len - n ..];
}

/// Everything except the first and last element. Empty if xs has fewer than 3.
fn inner(xs: []const u8) []const u8 {
    if (xs.len < 3) return xs[0..0];
    return xs[1 .. xs.len - 1];
}

/// Split `xs` in half. The first half gets the extra element when odd.
fn halves(xs: []const u8) [2][]const u8 {
    const mid = (xs.len + 1) / 2;
    return .{ xs[0..mid], xs[mid..] };
}

test "lastN" {
    const d = [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 };
    try std.testing.expectEqualSlices(u8, &[_]u8{ 4, 5 }, lastN(&d, 2));
    try std.testing.expectEqualSlices(u8, &d, lastN(&d, 9));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 0), lastN(&d, 0).len);
}

test "inner" {
    const d = [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 };
    try std.testing.expectEqualSlices(u8, &[_]u8{ 2, 3, 4 }, inner(&d));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 0), inner(d[0..2]).len);
}

test "halves" {
    const d = [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 };
    const h = halves(&d);
    try std.testing.expectEqualSlices(u8, &[_]u8{ 1, 2, 3 }, h[0]);
    try std.testing.expectEqualSlices(u8, &[_]u8{ 4, 5 }, h[1]);
    const e = halves(d[0..0]);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 0), e[0].len + e[1].len);
}

The empty slice xs[0..0] is a legitimate value: pointer to the start, length zero. halves returns an array of two slices; the array is copied out (two pointer-length pairs), the data is not.

Exercise 10.2 · Mutating through slices practice

Write heal (saturating add on every element), raiseFloor, and padCopy using @memcpy and @memset. Note that the tests pass sub-slices like xs[2..] and buf[4..]. Name the file: exercises/10-slices/ex2_mutate.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 10, exercise 2: mutating through slices.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_mutate.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Add `delta` to every element, saturating at 255.
fn heal(hp: []u8, delta: u8) void {
    for (hp) |*h| h.* +|= delta;
}

/// Set every element that is below `floor` to `floor`.
fn raiseFloor(xs: []i32, floor: i32) void {
    for (xs) |*x| {
        if (x.* < floor) x.* = floor;
    }
}

/// Copy `src` into the front of `dst` and fill the rest with `pad`.
/// Returns dst.len. Panics if src is longer than dst (that is a caller bug).
fn padCopy(dst: []u8, src: []const u8, pad: u8) usize {
    @memcpy(dst[0..src.len], src);
    @memset(dst[src.len..], pad);
    return dst.len;
}

test "heal saturates" {
    var hp = [_]u8{ 250, 10, 0 };
    heal(&hp, 10);
    try std.testing.expectEqual([3]u8{ 255, 20, 10 }, hp);
}

test "raiseFloor" {
    var xs = [_]i32{ -5, 0, 5 };
    raiseFloor(&xs, 0);
    try std.testing.expectEqual([3]i32{ 0, 0, 5 }, xs);
    raiseFloor(xs[2..], 100); // only the tail
    try std.testing.expectEqual([3]i32{ 0, 0, 100 }, xs);
}

test "padCopy" {
    var buf: [8]u8 = undefined;
    const n = padCopy(&buf, "mek", ' ');
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 8), n);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("mek     ", &buf);
    _ = padCopy(buf[4..], "ab", '-');
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("mek ab--", &buf);
}

+|= is saturating addition (Chapter 4). padCopy works on any buffer size because dst is a slice; the second call in the test fills only the last four bytes.

Exercise 10.3 · Searching and windows practice

Write argMax (returning an optional index), from (a suffix slice starting at the first element over a threshold), and bestWindow (the largest sum of w consecutive elements). Name the file: exercises/10-slices/ex3_search.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 10, exercise 3: searching and windows.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_search.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Index of the largest element, or null when the slice is empty.
fn argMax(xs: []const i32) ?usize {
    if (xs.len == 0) return null;
    var best: usize = 0;
    for (xs, 0..) |x, i| {
        if (x > xs[best]) best = i;
    }
    return best;
}

/// The slice of `xs` that starts at the first element >= `threshold`.
/// Empty slice at the end if nothing qualifies.
fn from(xs: []const i32, threshold: i32) []const i32 {
    for (xs, 0..) |x, i| {
        if (x >= threshold) return xs[i..];
    }
    return xs[xs.len..];
}

/// The largest sum of any `w` consecutive elements. Requires w <= xs.len and w > 0.
fn bestWindow(xs: []const i32, w: usize) i32 {
    var best: i32 = std.math.minInt(i32);
    var start: usize = 0;
    while (start + w <= xs.len) : (start += 1) {
        var s: i32 = 0;
        for (xs[start .. start + w]) |x| s += x;
        if (s > best) best = s;
    }
    return best;
}

test "argMax" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?usize, 2), argMax(&[_]i32{ 1, 5, 9, 3 }));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?usize, 0), argMax(&[_]i32{ 9, 9, 9 }));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?usize, null), argMax(&[_]i32{}));
}

test "from" {
    const d = [_]i32{ 1, 4, 2, 8, 3 };
    try std.testing.expectEqualSlices(i32, &[_]i32{ 4, 2, 8, 3 }, from(&d, 4));
    try std.testing.expectEqualSlices(i32, &[_]i32{ 8, 3 }, from(&d, 5));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 0), from(&d, 100).len);
}

test "bestWindow" {
    const d = [_]i32{ 1, 4, 2, 8, 3 };
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, 8), bestWindow(&d, 1));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, 11), bestWindow(&d, 2));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, 18), bestWindow(&d, 5));
}

bestWindow slides a sub-slice xs[start .. start + w] along the input; each window is a view, so the loop allocates nothing. xs[xs.len..] is the empty slice at the very end, a legal way to say "no elements qualified".

Exercise 10.4 · A fixed-size log challenge

A struct keeps the last four values pushed into a ring. Implement push, ordered (oldest first, written into a caller's buffer) and raw (a slice of the valid part of the internal array). This previews structs from Chapter 12; the method syntax is explained there. Name the file: exercises/10-slices/ex4_ring.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 10, exercise 4: a fixed-size log with a slice view (challenge).
//! Run with:  zig test ex4_ring.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Keeps the last `cap` values pushed. Older values are overwritten.
const Log = struct {
    buf: [4]u32 = undefined,
    len: usize = 0, // how many slots are valid (0..4)
    next: usize = 0, // where the next push goes

    fn push(self: *Log, v: u32) void {
        self.buf[self.next] = v;
        self.next = (self.next + 1) % self.buf.len;
        if (self.len < self.buf.len) self.len += 1;
    }

    /// Copy the valid values, oldest first, into `out` and return the filled part.
    fn ordered(self: Log, out: []u32) []u32 {
        const start = if (self.len < self.buf.len) 0 else self.next;
        var i: usize = 0;
        while (i < self.len) : (i += 1) {
            out[i] = self.buf[(start + i) % self.buf.len];
        }
        return out[0..self.len];
    }

    /// The valid part of the raw buffer (no reordering).
    fn raw(self: *const Log) []const u32 {
        return self.buf[0..self.len];
    }
};

test "fills up then wraps" {
    var log = Log{};
    var out: [4]u32 = undefined;
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 0), log.ordered(&out).len);
    log.push(1);
    log.push(2);
    try std.testing.expectEqualSlices(u32, &[_]u32{ 1, 2 }, log.ordered(&out));
    log.push(3);
    log.push(4);
    log.push(5); // overwrites 1
    try std.testing.expectEqualSlices(u32, &[_]u32{ 2, 3, 4, 5 }, log.ordered(&out));
    try std.testing.expectEqualSlices(u32, &[_]u32{ 5, 2, 3, 4 }, log.raw());
}

raw returns a slice into the struct's own array, so it takes self by pointer: a by-value self would be a copy that dies when the function returns, and the compiler would reject the slice, as in 10.2. ordered writes into the caller's buffer instead, so it can take self by value.

Check your understanding

  1. What two pieces of information make up a slice?
    AnswerA pointer to the first element (.ptr) and a length (.len).
  2. How many elements does arr[2..5] have, and which ones?
    AnswerThree: indexes 2, 3 and 4. The end bound is exclusive.
  3. Does writing through a slice change the original array?
    AnswerYes. A slice is a view; it does not copy the elements.
  4. Can you pass a []u8 where []const u8 is expected? The reverse?
    AnswerYes to the first, no to the second. Mutable coerces to const; going the other way is a compile error ("cast discards const qualifier").
  5. Why does return &local; fail to compile when local is an array inside the function?
    AnswerThe array lives in the function's stack frame and is gone after the return; a slice into it would be dangling. Have the caller supply a buffer instead.
  6. What does [:0]const u8 promise that []const u8 does not?
    AnswerThat the element just past len is a zero byte. C APIs rely on it.
  7. What is wrong with @memcpy(&buf, "mek") when buf is [8]u8?
    AnswerThe lengths differ (8 versus 3) and @memcpy requires them to match. Slice the destination: @memcpy(buf[0..3], "mek").
What you learned.
  • A slice []T is a pointer and a length: a window onto an array, not a copy.
  • Make one with arr[a..b], arr[a..], or &arr. Compile-time bounds give *const [N]T, which coerces to a slice.
  • []const T for reading, []T for writing; mutable coerces to const, never the reverse.
  • Indexing and slicing are bounds-checked; a slice must not outlive its array, and the compiler catches returning a local's address.
  • Functions take slices so one signature serves any length or sub-range.
  • for (s) |*v| mutates in place; @memset, @memcpy (equal lengths, no overlap) and std.mem.copyForwards/copyBackwards do bulk work.
  • [:0]T adds a sentinel for C; [*]T is a length-less many-item pointer you rarely need.

11. Strings

In this chapter you will learn that Zig has no string type, and why that turns out to be fine. A string is a slice of bytes, []const u8, and everything you want to do with one (compare, search, trim, split, change case, build, parse) is a function in std.mem, std.ascii or std.fmt. You will also learn where bytes and characters part ways, and how to build text into a buffer you own.

11.1 A string is a slice of bytes

Start with a literal and ask Zig what it is:

literal.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const name = "Kai Allard";
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{name});
    std.debug.print("type: {any}\n", .{@TypeOf(name)});
    std.debug.print("len: {d}\n", .{name.len});
    std.debug.print("first byte: {d} ('{c}')\n", .{ name[0], name[0] });
    const s: []const u8 = name; // the everyday string type
    std.debug.print("as slice: {any}\n", .{@TypeOf(s)});
}
Kai Allard
type: *const [10:0]u8
len: 10
first byte: 75 ('K')
as slice: []const u8

*const [10:0]u8: a pointer to a constant array of ten bytes with a zero after them (Chapter 10 covered the sentinel). Ten bytes, not ten characters; for plain ASCII text those are the same, and 11.8 covers when they are not. name[0] is the byte 75, which {c} shows as the letter K.

The literal's pointer-to-array type coerces to []const u8, and that is the type you will write on every string parameter and most string variables. When people say "a Zig string" they mean []const u8: a read-only slice of bytes, with a length, and no promise about what the bytes mean.

There is no String class with methods. Instead, there are free functions that take slices. Because every one of them takes the element type as its first argument, you will type u8 a lot: std.mem.eql(u8, a, b). Those functions also work on slices of u32 or of structs, which is the reason for the parameter; strings are just the common case.

11.2 Comparing

The first thing every newcomer tries is ==:

nostring.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var buf: [5]u8 = undefined;
    @memcpy(&buf, "lance");
    const typed: []const u8 = &buf;
    std.debug.print("{}\n", .{typed == "lance"});
}
nostring.zig:7:37: error: cannot compare strings with ==
    std.debug.print("{}\n", .{typed == "lance"});
                              ~~~~~~^~~~~~~~~~

The compiler has a special message for it. The reason is the same as for arrays in Chapter 9: comparing contents is a loop, and Zig does not hide loops behind operators. Use std.mem.eql:

compare.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn isQuit(cmd: []const u8) bool {
    return std.mem.eql(u8, cmd, "quit") or std.mem.eql(u8, cmd, "q");
}

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{} {} {}\n", .{ isQuit("quit"), isQuit("q"), isQuit("quit ") });
    std.debug.print("{}\n", .{std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase("QUIT", "quit")});
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{std.mem.order(u8, "alpha", "bravo")});
}
true true false
true
.lt

eql is exact: "quit " with a trailing space is not "quit". For a case-blind comparison use std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase. For ordering (sorting names, say) std.mem.order returns .lt, .eq or .gt, comparing byte by byte.

11.3 Searching

Prefixes, suffixes and substrings all live in std.mem. The functions that search for a position return an optional ?usize: an index, or null for not found. You will meet optionals properly in Chapter 15; for now, {?} prints one, and if (x) |k| ... else ... unwraps one.

search.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const path = "data/units/atlas.zon";
    std.debug.print("{}\n", .{std.mem.startsWith(u8, path, "data/")});
    std.debug.print("{}\n", .{std.mem.endsWith(u8, path, ".zon")});
    std.debug.print("{?}\n", .{std.mem.indexOf(u8, path, "units")});
    std.debug.print("{?}\n", .{std.mem.indexOf(u8, path, "mek")});
    std.debug.print("{?}\n", .{std.mem.indexOfScalar(u8, path, '/')});
    std.debug.print("{?}\n", .{std.mem.lastIndexOfScalar(u8, path, '/')});
    // The classic: the file name after the last slash.
    const base = if (std.mem.lastIndexOfScalar(u8, path, '/')) |k| path[k + 1 ..] else path;
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{base});
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{std.mem.count(u8, path, "/")});
}
true
true
5
null
4
10
atlas.zon
2

indexOf finds a substring; indexOfScalar and lastIndexOfScalar find a single byte from the front or from the back. The base line is the guide's own idiom for a file name: find the last slash, and slice from one past it. If there is no slash the whole path is the name. count tells you how many times a needle appears.

11.4 Trimming and splitting

User input arrives with spaces and newlines around it. std.mem.trim takes the set of bytes to strip as its third argument:

trim.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const raw = "   hire Kai mekwarrior  \n";
    const t = std.mem.trim(u8, raw, " \n");
    std.debug.print("[{s}]\n", .{t});
    std.debug.print("[{s}]\n", .{std.mem.trimStart(u8, raw, " ")});
    std.debug.print("[{s}]\n", .{std.mem.trimEnd(u8, raw, " \n")});
}
[hire Kai mekwarrior]
[hire Kai mekwarrior  
]
[   hire Kai mekwarrior]

Trimming returns a smaller slice of the same memory; nothing is copied. trimStart and trimEnd do one side only.

To take a line apart into words there are two iterators, and the difference between them matters:

tokenize.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const line = "hire   Kai  mekwarrior";

    var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, line, ' ');
    while (it.next()) |word| {
        std.debug.print("[{s}] ", .{word});
    }
    std.debug.print("\n", .{});

    var sp = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, line, ' ');
    while (sp.next()) |piece| {
        std.debug.print("[{s}] ", .{piece});
    }
    std.debug.print("\n", .{});

    // A fixed record: two commas, so always three fields.
    var csv = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, "3025,7,14", ',');
    const year = csv.next().?;
    const month = csv.next().?;
    const day = csv.next().?;
    std.debug.print("year={s} month={s} day={s}\n", .{ year, month, day });

    // The same record with the month left blank. The field is still there.
    var blank = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, "3025,,14", ',');
    const b_year = blank.next().?;
    const b_month = blank.next().?;
    const b_day = blank.next().?;
    std.debug.print("year={s} month=[{s}] day={s}\n", .{ b_year, b_month, b_day });
}
[hire] [Kai] [mekwarrior] 
[hire] [] [] [Kai] [] [mekwarrior] 
year=3025 month=7 day=14
year=3025 month=[] day=14

tokenizeScalar treats any run of the delimiter as a single break and never yields an empty piece, so "hire Kai mekwarrior" gives three words however many spaces sit between them.

splitScalar breaks at every delimiter separately. Count the delimiters in that line. There are five spaces, and the second output row has six pieces. The empty ones are the gaps between two adjacent spaces, which are real pieces with no bytes in them. The rule is that n delimiters always produce n+1 pieces, empties included, so a three-field record split on commas gives you three fields whatever they contain.

That rule is what tells you which of the two to reach for. Use tokenizeScalar when a person typed the line, where a run of spaces is just loose typing and only the words matter. Use splitScalar when the format is fixed and a field's position carries its meaning. In the last output row above the month is blank, and splitScalar still reports three fields with the day in its proper place. tokenizeScalar on "3025,,14" would hand back only [3025] and [14], sliding the day silently into the month.

Both are driven by while (it.next()) |piece|, the same loop shape you will use for every iterator in the standard library.

The .? needs an explanation of its own, because it is the first thing on this page that is not about strings. next() does not return a slice. It returns ?[]const u8, an optional slice, meaning either a slice or nothing at all. That is how an iterator reports that it has run out, and it is what while (it.next()) |piece| has been quietly doing in every loop above: the capture |piece| runs the body only while there is a value, and ends the loop the first time there is not.

Calling next() outside a loop hands you that "or nothing" to deal with yourself. The .? operator is the blunt way to do that. It unwraps the optional and asserts that a value is there. When the assertion is wrong the program stops and says so.

unwrap.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var csv = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, "3025", ',');
    _ = csv.next().?; // fine, there is one field
    const second = csv.next().?; // nothing left
    std.debug.print("never reached: {s}\n", .{second});
}
thread 7484770 panic: attempt to use null value
ch11/unwrap.zig:6:30: in main (unwrap)
    const second = csv.next().?; // nothing left
                             ^

That is a safety check, not undefined behaviour: you get the file, line and column of the .? that was wrong. Use it where the value is guaranteed by something you already know, as with the three fields of a record your own code just built. When the text comes from outside the program, handle the nothing instead:

unwrap2.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const input = "3025";  // a record that is missing its month and day
    var csv = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, input, ',');

    const year = csv.next() orelse "????";
    const month = csv.next() orelse "??";
    std.debug.print("year={s} month={s}\n", .{ year, month });

    if (csv.next()) |day| {
        std.debug.print("day={s}\n", .{day});
    } else {
        std.debug.print("no day field in \"{s}\"\n", .{input});
    }
}
year=3025 month=??
no day field in "3025"

orelse supplies a value to use when there is none; if (opt) |v| takes its branch only when there is a value and binds it to v. Chapter 15 covers optionals properly. This is the minimum you need to read the rest of this chapter.

Neither of those is an error path, and that is worth saying plainly. An iterator running out, or a line arriving blank, is an ordinary thing for a program to meet. Handling it needs no error type, no try and no catch. You have in fact been handling it all along, because while (it.next()) |piece| ends the loop on exactly the same null.

When there is no sensible value to substitute, orelse can run a block instead, which is the usual way to leave a function quietly:

blank.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn firstWord(line: []const u8) void {
    var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, line, ' ');
    const verb = it.next() orelse {
        std.debug.print("blank line, nothing to do\n", .{});
        return;
    };
    std.debug.print("verb={s}\n", .{verb});
}

pub fn main() void {
    firstWord("newlance 1st Recon Lance");
    firstWord("   ");
}
verb=newlance
blank line, nothing to do

So there are three positions to take, and only you can say which fits. .? claims the value is guaranteed. orelse and if treat its absence as normal and deal with it on the spot. Turning it into an error, which the next note describes, is for when the caller rather than this function should decide what happens.

One thing you cannot reach for here is try. It works on errors, not on optionals, and the compiler turns it down:

error: expected error union type, found '?[]const u8'
    const verb = try it.next();
                     ~~~~~~~^~
note: consider omitting 'try'

Zig keeps the two ideas apart on purpose. Nothing found is an ordinary outcome, and an iterator reaching its end is not a failure, so it is an optional. Something went wrong is a different matter, and that is an error. Chapter 16 covers errors, and 16.7 bridges the two with orelse return error.EmptyLine on this very iterator, which is how IRON LEDGER's parser turns a missing argument into a refusal the caller can report.

Two more useful methods:

tokenize2.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, "newlance 1st Recon Lance", ' ');
    const verb = it.next().?;
    const rest = it.rest();
    std.debug.print("verb=[{s}] rest=[{s}]\n", .{ verb, rest });
    var seq = std.mem.tokenizeSequence(u8, "a, b, c", ", ");
    while (seq.next()) |p| std.debug.print("<{s}>", .{p});
    std.debug.print("\n", .{});
}
verb=[newlance] rest=[1st Recon Lance]
<a><b><c>

it.rest() hands you everything not yet consumed, which is how a command parser takes one verb and leaves the rest of the line as a free-form name. tokenizeSequence splits on a multi-byte separator.

11.5 Characters: std.ascii

Because a byte is just a u8, single-character questions are functions on u8, gathered in std.ascii:

ascii.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const c: u8 = 'k';
    std.debug.print("{c} {c}\n", .{ std.ascii.toUpper(c), std.ascii.toLower('K') });
    std.debug.print("{} {} {} {}\n", .{
        std.ascii.isDigit('7'),
        std.ascii.isAlphabetic('7'),
        std.ascii.isWhitespace('\t'),
        std.ascii.isAlphanumeric('_'),
    });
    var buf: [16]u8 = undefined;
    const up = std.ascii.upperString(&buf, "atlas");
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{up});
    std.debug.print("{}\n", .{std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase("Atlas", "ATLAS")});
    std.debug.print("{?}\n", .{std.ascii.indexOfIgnoreCase("Kitty Terminal", "term")});
}
K k
true false true false
ATLAS
true
6

isDigit, isAlphabetic, isWhitespace, isAlphanumeric, toUpper, toLower: the names are what you would guess. upperString writes an upper-cased copy into a buffer you provide, which brings us to the question of where new strings live.

11.6 Building strings into a buffer

Everything so far returned slices of existing text. To make new text you need memory to put it in, and in Zig you say where. The simplest place is an array on the stack, and the simplest tool is std.fmt.bufPrint, which is print aimed at a buffer:

bufprint.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() !void {
    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    const s = try std.fmt.bufPrint(&buf, "order {s} hq:{d}", .{ "advance", 3 });
    std.debug.print("{s} (len {d})\n", .{ s, s.len });
    std.debug.print("{any} {any}\n", .{ @TypeOf(s), @TypeOf(&buf) });

    // Build in steps with a fixed writer.
    var w = std.Io.Writer.fixed(&buf);
    try w.print("{d}", .{3025});
    try w.writeByte('-');
    try w.print("{d:0>2}", .{1});
    try w.writeAll("-01");
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{w.buffered()});
}
order advance hq:3 (len 18)
[]u8 *[64]u8
3025-01-01

bufPrint returns a []u8 slice of the buffer holding exactly what it wrote. The buffer is [64]u8; the result is eighteen bytes long. Keep the buffer alive as long as you use the slice, and remember it is the same rule as in Chapter 10: a slice of a local buffer cannot be returned from the function that owns the buffer. The usual design is for the caller to pass the buffer in, exactly as bufPrint itself does.

For building in several steps, wrap the buffer in a fixed writer. print, writeByte and writeAll append; buffered() gives back the slice written so far. This is the same std.Io.Writer interface as stdout in Chapter 2, pointed at memory instead of a file.

What if the buffer is too small? bufPrint returns an error, which is why the function above is !void and the call has try:

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() !void {
    var buf: [8]u8 = undefined;
    const s = try std.fmt.bufPrint(&buf, "{s} {s}", .{ "hello", "world" });
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{s});
}
error: NoSpaceLeft
<zig>/lib/std/Io/Writer.zig:2321:50: in fixedDrain (bufprint_small)
                if (pattern.len > remaining.len) return error.WriteFailed;

error: NoSpaceLeft. No overflow, no truncation you did not ask for. When you cannot know the size in advance, the answer is an allocator and std.fmt.allocPrint, which returns a string of exactly the right length that you later free. That arrives in Chapter 21 and Chapter 23; until then, buffers.

Replacing a substring uses an output buffer in the same way, but it differs from bufPrint in one way that matters. Ask how large the result will be before you write it:

replace.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const src = "1st Lance / 2nd Lance";
    var out: [64]u8 = undefined;

    const size = std.mem.replacementSize(u8, src, "Lance", "Company");
    if (size > out.len) {
        std.debug.print("need {d} bytes, the buffer has {d}\n", .{ size, out.len });
        return;
    }
    const n = std.mem.replace(u8, src, "Lance", "Company", &out);
    std.debug.print("{d} replacements, {d} bytes: {s}\n", .{ n, size, out[0..size] });
}
2 replacements, 25 bytes: 1st Company / 2nd Company

Nothing in the program computed that 64. It is a round number chosen to sit comfortably above what this input needs, which is an honest description of most fixed buffers. std.mem.replacementSize is how you stop guessing, because it reports the exact length the result will occupy. Here that is 25 bytes: each "Lance" is five bytes and each "Company" is seven, so two replacements grow the 21-byte source by four. Call it before replace rather than after, since its purpose is to tell you whether the buffer can hold the answer.

That check is yours to make. bufPrint returns error.NoSpaceLeft when the text will not fit, so the mistake reaches you as a value you can handle. replace returns only a count and verifies nothing, so a buffer that is too small sends it past the end of your array:

replace_small.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const src = "1st Lance / 2nd Lance";
    var out: [16]u8 = undefined; // too small, and nothing says so
    _ = std.mem.replace(u8, src, "Lance", "Company", &out);
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{out});
}
thread 7517233 panic: index out of bounds: index 16, len 16
<zig>/lib/std/mem.zig:4079:19 in replace (replace_small)
            output[i] = input[slide];
                  ^

Safety caught it, so nothing was corrupted, but the trace starts inside std/mem.zig instead of in your own file, which is an awkward place to begin reading. The if in the first program is what keeps you out of it.

11.7 Literals are read-only; copies are not

A literal lives in the program's read-only data. You cannot write into it:

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const lit = "atlas";
    lit[0] = 'A';
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{lit});
}
mutate_lit.zig:5:8: error: cannot assign to constant
    lit[0] = 'A';
    ~~~^~~
referenced by:
    callMain [inlined]: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:698:59
    callMainWithArgs [inlined]: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:638:20
    main: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:663:28
    1 reference(s) hidden; use '-freference-trace=4' to see all references

To change text, copy it into an array that you own. That takes one line, but three separate things happen in it:

mutate.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const lit = "atlas";
    var copy: [5]u8 = lit.*; // copy the bytes out of the literal
    copy[0] = 'A';
    std.debug.print("{s} {s}\n", .{ lit, &copy });
}
atlas Atlas

First, lit is not the text. A string literal is a pointer, and @TypeOf(lit) reports *const [5:0]u8, a pointer to a constant array of five bytes with a zero after them. The pointer occupies eight bytes on a 64-bit machine, and the letters themselves live elsewhere, in the program's read-only data.

Second, .* is the dereference operator, and it means the value that the pointer refers to. So lit.* is the array itself, of type [5:0]u8, rather than its address. Leave the .* off and the line tries to put a pointer into an array variable, which the compiler refuses:

mutate.zig:5:23: error: expected type '[5]u8', found '*const [5:0]u8'
    var copy: [5]u8 = lit;
                      ^~~

Third, an array in Zig is a value rather than a reference, so assigning one copies every byte. copy is a new array on the stack at its own address, and writing to it cannot reach the literal. That is why the program prints the original and the altered copy side by side.

One detail is easy to miss. The type changes from [5:0]u8 to [5]u8 across the assignment, because the destination does not ask for a sentinel and the trailing zero is dropped. Write var copy: [5:0]u8 = lit.*; instead if you want to keep it, which matters when you pass the result to C (Chapter 35).

This is the same const rule as for slices: a []const u8 may look at bytes, a []u8 may change them, and a literal only ever gives you the former.

11.8 Multi-line literals

Long text uses a line-comment-like syntax. Each line starts with \\, and the newlines between lines are part of the string; the final line has no trailing newline.

multiline.zig

const std = @import("std");

const banner =
    \\IRON LEDGER
    \\  a mercenary company simulator
    \\  "no floats in the ledger"
;

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{banner});
    std.debug.print("{d} bytes, {d} newlines\n", .{ banner.len, std.mem.count(u8, banner, "\n") });
}
IRON LEDGER
  a mercenary company simulator
  "no floats in the ledger"
71 bytes, 2 newlines

Nothing inside a \\ line is escaped, so quotes and backslashes can appear as they are. IRON LEDGER's splash screen and its ASCII-art mek are multi-line literals in src/tui/splash.zig.

11.9 Bytes are not characters

All of the above treats a string as bytes. Text is stored in UTF-8, where ASCII characters are one byte each and everything else is two to four. Zig does not hide this:

utf8.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() !void {
    const word = "Mëk";
    std.debug.print("{s}: {d} bytes\n", .{ word, word.len });
    for (word) |b| std.debug.print("{x} ", .{b});
    std.debug.print("\n", .{});

    const n = try std.unicode.utf8CountCodepoints(word);
    std.debug.print("{d} code points\n", .{n});

    var it = (try std.unicode.Utf8View.init(word)).iterator();
    while (it.nextCodepoint()) |cp| std.debug.print("U+{X:0>4} ", .{cp});
    std.debug.print("\n", .{});

    const cp = try std.unicode.utf8Decode(word[1..3]); // the two bytes of ë
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{cp});
}
Mëk: 4 bytes
4d c3 ab 6b 
3 code points
U+004D U+00EB U+006B 
235

"Mëk" is four bytes and three code points. len counts bytes, always. The ë is the pair c3 ab. To count or walk characters, use std.unicode: utf8CountCodepoints counts, Utf8View iterates one code point at a time, and utf8Decode turns the bytes of one character into its number (235 is U+00EB).

The rule that keeps you safe: byte functions like indexOf and eql are fine on UTF-8, because a valid UTF-8 sequence never appears by accident inside another. What is not fine is slicing at an arbitrary byte offset (you may cut a character in half) and calling std.ascii.toUpper on non-ASCII bytes (it leaves them alone, which is correct but not what you meant). The terminal client in IRON LEDGER reads keys as u21 code points for exactly this reason.

11.10 Parsing numbers

The last everyday string job is turning text into a number, and it can fail:

parse.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() !void {
    const n = try std.fmt.parseInt(u32, "3025", 10);
    const f = try std.fmt.parseFloat(f64, "1.5");
    std.debug.print("{d} {d}\n", .{ n + 1, f * 2 });
    const bad = std.fmt.parseInt(u32, "30x5", 10);
    std.debug.print("{!}\n", .{bad});
}
3026 3
error.InvalidCharacter

parseInt takes the target type, the text and the base. Invalid text is an error, not zero and not a crash; {!} prints either the value or the error name. Chapter 16 shows how to handle these errors properly; Chapter 23 covers the rest of std.fmt.

11.11 The string toolkit at a glance

Everything in this chapter, gathered for reference. Each of these takes []const u8 and returns a slice, a count, a bool or an optional, because there is no string type to return.

CallGives youNotesSection
std.mem.eql(u8, a, b)boolexact, byte for byte11.2
std.mem.order(u8, a, b).lt, .eq, .gtfor sorting11.2
std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase(a, b)boolASCII only11.2
std.mem.startsWith(u8, hay, needle)bool11.3
std.mem.endsWith(u8, hay, needle)bool11.3

Two of these allocate nothing and yet hand you text: trim and it.rest() both return a slice pointing into the string you passed in. That slice stays valid only as long as the original bytes do, which is the rule Chapter 10 set out and the one worth carrying into the rest of the book.

In IRON LEDGER. The command-line parser is nothing but this chapter's functions applied in order. A line becomes a token iterator, the first token is compared against known verbs with std.mem.eql, the rest is parsed or trimmed: 
// src/sim/cli.zig
pub fn parseCommand(verb: []const u8, tokens: *std.mem.TokenIterator(u8, .scalar)) ParseError!?Command {
    const eq = std.mem.eql;
    if (eq(u8, verb, "admit")) return .{ .admit = @enumFromInt(try num(u32, tokens.next())) };
    if (eq(u8, verb, "shares")) return .{ .set_shares_pct = try num(u8, tokens.next()) };
    if (eq(u8, verb, "newlance")) {
        const site = try parseSite(try need(tokens.next()));
        var name = std.mem.trim(u8, tokens.rest(), " ");
        // ...
    }
    return null; // not a verb we know
}

Three things in that signature belong to later chapters, and you can read past them for now. The * makes tokens a pointer, so that parseCommand advances the caller's iterator instead of a copy of it, which is what lets it consume the arguments the caller has not read yet (Chapter 18). The .scalar names the kind of delimiter the iterator splits on, and it is part of the type rather than a value in a field, so an iterator from tokenizeAny would not fit this parameter (Chapter 26). The return type ParseError!?Command stacks two wrappers on Command and gives the function three outcomes: a command, null for a word that is not a verb at all, or a parse error for a known verb with bad arguments (Chapter 15 and Chapter 16). Keeping the unknown word separate from the error is deliberate, because the caller can offer help for one and must report the other.

const eq = std.mem.eql; is a small trick to shorten a function you call twenty times in a row. Elsewhere, std.mem.startsWith(u8, token, "hq:") recognises references like hq:3 (src/main.zig), and the terminal-detection code uses std.ascii.indexOfIgnoreCase to spot "iterm" in an environment variable regardless of case (src/tui/emblem.zig). Every one of those functions takes a []const u8 and returns a slice or an optional index; there is no string object anywhere in the 31,000 lines.

Exercises

Exercise 11.1 · String predicates warm-up

Write isQuit (trim, then case-insensitive match against three words), isNumber (all digits, at least one) and isHqRef (the form hq:<digits>). Name the file: exercises/11-strings/ex1_predicates.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 11, exercise 1: string predicates.
//! Run with:  zig test ex1_predicates.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// True when the command is one of the quit words, ignoring case and
/// surrounding whitespace.
fn isQuit(cmd: []const u8) bool {
    const t = std.mem.trim(u8, cmd, " \t\r\n");
    return std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase(t, "quit") or std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase(t, "q") or
        std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase(t, "exit");
}

/// True when every byte is a decimal digit and there is at least one.
fn isNumber(s: []const u8) bool {
    if (s.len == 0) return false;
    for (s) |c| {
        if (!std.ascii.isDigit(c)) return false;
    }
    return true;
}

/// True when `s` looks like "hq:<digits>".
fn isHqRef(s: []const u8) bool {
    return std.mem.startsWith(u8, s, "hq:") and isNumber(s["hq:".len..]);
}

test "isQuit" {
    try std.testing.expect(isQuit("quit"));
    try std.testing.expect(isQuit("  Q\n"));
    try std.testing.expect(isQuit("EXIT"));
    try std.testing.expect(!isQuit("quit now"));
    try std.testing.expect(!isQuit(""));
}

test "isNumber" {
    try std.testing.expect(isNumber("3025"));
    try std.testing.expect(isNumber("0"));
    try std.testing.expect(!isNumber(""));
    try std.testing.expect(!isNumber("30x5"));
    try std.testing.expect(!isNumber("-1"));
}

test "isHqRef" {
    try std.testing.expect(isHqRef("hq:1"));
    try std.testing.expect(isHqRef("hq:42"));
    try std.testing.expect(!isHqRef("hq:"));
    try std.testing.expect(!isHqRef("co:1"));
    try std.testing.expect(!isHqRef("hq"));
}

s["hq:".len..] slices past the prefix using the literal's own length, so the two cannot drift apart. isNumber rejects the empty string explicitly; without that check an empty input would loop zero times and return true.

Exercise 11.2 · Taking a command line apart practice

Using the tokenizer and splitter, write verb, wordCount, args (the rest of the line after the verb, trimmed) and parseDate, which turns "3025-1-1" into three numbers and rejects the wrong number of pieces. Name the file: exercises/11-strings/ex2_tokens.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 11, exercise 2: taking a command line apart.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_tokens.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// The first whitespace-separated word, or "" when there is none.
fn verb(line: []const u8) []const u8 {
    var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, line, ' ');
    return it.next() orelse "";
}

/// Number of whitespace-separated words.
fn wordCount(line: []const u8) usize {
    var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, line, ' ');
    var n: usize = 0;
    while (it.next()) |_| n += 1;
    return n;
}

/// Everything after the first word, trimmed. "" if there is nothing.
fn args(line: []const u8) []const u8 {
    var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, line, ' ');
    _ = it.next();
    return std.mem.trim(u8, it.rest(), " ");
}

/// Parse "YYYY-MM-DD" into three numbers. Any other shape is an error.
fn parseDate(s: []const u8) ![3]u16 {
    var it = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, s, '-');
    var out: [3]u16 = undefined;
    for (&out) |*slot| {
        const piece = it.next() orelse return error.BadDate;
        slot.* = try std.fmt.parseInt(u16, piece, 10);
    }
    if (it.next() != null) return error.BadDate;
    return out;
}

test "verb" {
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("hire", verb("hire Kai mekwarrior"));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("day", verb("   day"));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("", verb("   "));
}

test "wordCount" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 3), wordCount("hire Kai mekwarrior"));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 3), wordCount("  hire   Kai  mekwarrior "));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 0), wordCount(""));
}

test "args" {
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Kai mekwarrior", args("hire Kai mekwarrior"));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("1st Recon Lance", args("newlance   1st Recon Lance  "));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("", args("day"));
}

test "parseDate" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual([3]u16{ 3025, 1, 1 }, try parseDate("3025-1-1"));
    try std.testing.expectEqual([3]u16{ 3026, 12, 31 }, try parseDate("3026-12-31"));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.BadDate, parseDate("3025-1"));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.BadDate, parseDate("3025-1-1-1"));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.InvalidCharacter, parseDate("3025-x-1"));
}

it.next() orelse "" turns "no token" into the empty string. parseDate uses splitScalar, not tokenizeScalar, because a missing field should be an error rather than silently skipped; after three pieces it checks that nothing is left.

Exercise 11.3 · Building strings into a buffer practice

Write fullName with one bufPrint, shoutWords with a fixed writer (normalising spaces and upper-casing), and money, which inserts thousands separators. Every function takes the output buffer as a parameter and returns a slice of it. Name the file: exercises/11-strings/ex3_build.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 11, exercise 3: building strings into a buffer.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_build.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// "Last, First" into buf.
fn fullName(buf: []u8, first: []const u8, last: []const u8) ![]const u8 {
    return std.fmt.bufPrint(buf, "{s}, {s}", .{ last, first });
}

/// The words of `line` joined by a single space, upper-cased, into buf.
fn shoutWords(buf: []u8, line: []const u8) ![]const u8 {
    var w = std.Io.Writer.fixed(buf);
    var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, line, ' ');
    var first = true;
    while (it.next()) |word| {
        if (!first) try w.writeByte(' ');
        first = false;
        for (word) |c| try w.writeByte(std.ascii.toUpper(c));
    }
    return w.buffered();
}

/// A C-bills amount with thousands separators: 1234567 -> "1,234,567".
fn money(buf: []u8, amount: u64) ![]const u8 {
    var digits: [20]u8 = undefined;
    const d = try std.fmt.bufPrint(&digits, "{d}", .{amount});
    var w = std.Io.Writer.fixed(buf);
    for (d, 0..) |c, i| {
        const remaining = d.len - i;
        if (i != 0 and remaining % 3 == 0) try w.writeByte(',');
        try w.writeByte(c);
    }
    return w.buffered();
}

test "fullName" {
    var buf: [32]u8 = undefined;
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Allard, Kai", try fullName(&buf, "Kai", "Allard"));
}

test "fullName refuses a too-small buffer" {
    var buf: [4]u8 = undefined;
    try std.testing.expectError(error.NoSpaceLeft, fullName(&buf, "Kai", "Allard"));
}

test "shoutWords" {
    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("HIRE KAI NOW", try shoutWords(&buf, "  hire   kai now "));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("", try shoutWords(&buf, ""));
}

test "money" {
    var buf: [32]u8 = undefined;
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("0", try money(&buf, 0));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("999", try money(&buf, 999));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("1,000", try money(&buf, 1000));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("1,234,567", try money(&buf, 1234567));
}

money first prints the digits into a small scratch array, then copies them out one at a time, inserting a comma whenever the number of digits still to come is a multiple of three. The second fullName test shows the buffer-too-small case turning into error.NoSpaceLeft, which expectError checks for.

Exercise 11.4 · Bytes are not characters challenge

Write charCount (code points, not bytes), takeChars (the first n code points as a slice, never cutting a character), and reverseAscii, which refuses non-ASCII input rather than scrambling it. Name the file: exercises/11-strings/ex4_utf8.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 11, exercise 4: bytes are not characters (challenge).
//! Run with:  zig test ex4_utf8.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Number of code points, or error.Utf8InvalidStartByte for malformed input.
fn charCount(s: []const u8) !usize {
    return std.unicode.utf8CountCodepoints(s);
}

/// The first `n` code points of `s` (fewer if s is shorter), as a slice of s.
/// Never cuts a multi-byte character in half.
fn takeChars(s: []const u8, n: usize) ![]const u8 {
    var view = try std.unicode.Utf8View.init(s);
    var it = view.iterator();
    var taken: usize = 0;
    while (taken < n) : (taken += 1) {
        if (it.nextCodepointSlice() == null) break;
    }
    return s[0..it.i];
}

/// Reverse a string byte-by-byte into buf. Only valid for ASCII input,
/// so refuse anything with a byte >= 0x80.
fn reverseAscii(buf: []u8, s: []const u8) ![]const u8 {
    for (s) |c| {
        if (c >= 0x80) return error.NotAscii;
    }
    for (s, 0..) |c, i| buf[s.len - 1 - i] = c;
    return buf[0..s.len];
}

test "charCount" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 3), try charCount("Mëk"));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 4), "Mëk".len);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 0), try charCount(""));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.Utf8InvalidStartByte, charCount("\xff"));
}

test "takeChars" {
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Më", try takeChars("Mëk", 2));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Mëk", try takeChars("Mëk", 10));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("", try takeChars("Mëk", 0));
}

test "reverseAscii" {
    var buf: [16]u8 = undefined;
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("salta", try reverseAscii(&buf, "atlas"));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.NotAscii, reverseAscii(&buf, "Mëk"));
}

Utf8View.iterator() keeps a byte offset in its i field; after stepping n code points, s[0..it.i] is a slice that ends on a character boundary. The test also documents that "Mëk".len is 4 while the character count is 3.

Check your understanding

  1. What is the type of a string literal, and what does it coerce to?
    Answer*const [N:0]u8, a pointer to a zero-terminated constant byte array. It coerces to []const u8, and to [:0]const u8 if you want to keep the sentinel.
  2. How do you compare two strings for equality?
    Answerstd.mem.eql(u8, a, b). == is a compile error ("cannot compare strings with ==").
  3. What is the difference between tokenizeScalar and splitScalar on "a,,b" with ','?
    AnswertokenizeScalar yields a and b; splitScalar yields a, an empty string, and b.
  4. What does std.mem.indexOf return when the needle is absent?
    Answernull. Its return type is ?usize, an optional index.
  5. Why can a function not return the result of bufPrint into a local buffer?
    AnswerThe result is a slice of the local array, which ceases to exist when the function returns. Let the caller pass the buffer in, or allocate.
  6. What is "Mëk".len?
    Answer4. len counts bytes; ë takes two bytes in UTF-8. std.unicode.utf8CountCodepoints gives 3.
  7. Does std.mem.trim copy the string?
    AnswerNo. It returns a shorter slice into the same bytes.
What you learned.
  • There is no string type. A string is []const u8; a literal is *const [N:0]u8 and coerces to it.
  • Compare with std.mem.eql or std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase; order with std.mem.order.
  • Search with startsWith, endsWith, indexOf, indexOfScalar, lastIndexOfScalar, count; positions come back as ?usize.
  • Trim with std.mem.trim; split with tokenizeScalar (collapses runs) or splitScalar (exact fields); rest() gives the remainder.
  • std.ascii has the per-byte helpers; upperString and friends write into a buffer you provide.
  • Build new text with std.fmt.bufPrint or a fixed std.Io.Writer into a caller-owned buffer; too small is error.NoSpaceLeft. allocPrint comes with allocators.
  • Literals are read-only; copy with lit.* to modify. Multi-line literals use \\.
  • len counts bytes. Use std.unicode when characters matter.

12. Structs and methods

In this chapter you will group related values into a struct, give fields default values, attach functions to the type and call them with dot syntax, and learn the one decision that matters most about a method: whether it takes self by value or by pointer. You will also nest structs, compare them, meet tuples, and teach a struct how to print itself.

12.1 Grouping values

A pilot has a name and two skill numbers. Passing those around as three separate values gets old fast; a struct bundles them under one name.

basics.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Pilot = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    gunnery: u8,
    piloting: u8,
};

pub fn main() void {
    const kai = Pilot{ .name = "Kai Allard", .gunnery = 2, .piloting = 3 };
    std.debug.print("{s}: {d}/{d}\n", .{ kai.name, kai.gunnery, kai.piloting });

    var rookie: Pilot = .{ .name = "Rookie", .gunnery = 5, .piloting = 6 };
    rookie.gunnery -= 1; // fields of a var struct can change
    std.debug.print("{s}: {d}/{d}\n", .{ rookie.name, rookie.gunnery, rookie.piloting });
}
Kai Allard: 2/3
Rookie: 4/6

The declaration const Pilot = struct { ... }; makes a new type. Each line inside is a field: a name, a colon, a type. Zig types are values, so a type is declared with const like anything else, and by convention type names are capitalised.

To make a value, write the type name followed by braces and every field with a leading dot: Pilot{ .name = ..., .gunnery = ..., .piloting = ... }. You read fields with a dot, kai.name, and if the variable is a var you can assign to them.

The second value uses the form you will see most: a type on the left of the colon and an anonymous literal .{ ... } on the right. The dot-brace literal has no type of its own; it takes whatever type the context expects. You have been using it since Chapter 2, where the arguments to print are a .{ ... } that becomes a tuple.

Every field must be given a value. Leave one out and the compiler tells you which:

const std = @import("std");

const Pilot = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    gunnery: u8,
    piloting: u8,
};

pub fn main() void {
    const kai = Pilot{ .name = "Kai Allard", .gunnery = 2 };
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{kai.name});
}
missing.zig:10:22: error: missing struct field: piloting
    const kai = Pilot{ .name = "Kai Allard", .gunnery = 2 };
                ~~~~~^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
missing.zig:3:15: note: struct declared here
const Pilot = struct {
              ^~~~~~
referenced by:
    callMain [inlined]: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:698:59
    callMainWithArgs [inlined]: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:638:20
    main: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:663:28
    1 reference(s) hidden; use '-freference-trace=4' to see all references

This is different from C, where a forgotten field is silently garbage, and from JavaScript, where it is silently undefined. If you truly want to leave a field uninitialised for now, say .field = undefined explicitly.

12.2 Default values

A field can carry a default, written after = in the declaration. Then it may be omitted from the literal.

defaults.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Pilot = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    gunnery: u8 = 4, // the "green" defaults
    piloting: u8 = 5,
    injured: bool = false,
};

pub fn main() void {
    const a = Pilot{ .name = "Kai" };
    const b = Pilot{ .name = "Nat", .gunnery = 2 };
    std.debug.print("{s}: {d}/{d} injured={}\n", .{ a.name, a.gunnery, a.piloting, a.injured });
    std.debug.print("{s}: {d}/{d} injured={}\n", .{ b.name, b.gunnery, b.piloting, b.injured });
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{a});
}
Kai: 4/5 injured=false
Nat: 2/5 injured=false
.{ .name = { 75, 97, 105 }, .gunnery = 4, .piloting = 5, .injured = false }

name has no default and must be supplied; the other three are optional in the literal. When every field has a default, Pilot{} is a complete value. IRON LEDGER's GameState has about forty fields, most with defaults, so that init only has to set the few that depend on the configuration.

The last line prints the whole struct with {any}. Handy for debugging, with one surprise: the name came out as { 75, 97, 105 }. A []const u8 is a slice of bytes, and {any} does not know it is text. Section 12.9 fixes that.

12.3 Methods

A struct can contain functions as well as fields. A function whose first parameter is the struct type can be called with dot syntax, and that is all a "method" is in Zig: a namespaced function with a convenient call form.

methods.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Pilot = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    gunnery: u8 = 4,
    piloting: u8 = 5,
    xp: u32 = 0,

    /// Reads only: self is a copy.
    pub fn skillTotal(self: Pilot) u8 {
        return self.gunnery + self.piloting;
    }

    /// Mutates: self is a pointer to the caller's value.
    pub fn train(self: *Pilot, points: u32) void {
        self.xp += points;
        if (self.xp >= 10 and self.gunnery > 0) {
            self.gunnery -= 1;
            self.xp -= 10;
        }
    }
};

pub fn main() void {
    var kai = Pilot{ .name = "Kai", .gunnery = 3 };
    std.debug.print("total {d}\n", .{kai.skillTotal()});
    kai.train(6);
    kai.train(6);
    std.debug.print("gunnery {d}, xp {d}\n", .{ kai.gunnery, kai.xp });
    std.debug.print("total {d}\n", .{Pilot.skillTotal(kai)}); // the same call, spelled out
}
total 8
gunnery 2, xp 2
total 7

Two methods, two different first parameters, and the difference is the heart of this chapter.

skillTotal(self: Pilot) takes the struct by value. self is a copy of kai. The function can read it, and it could even modify its copy (after copying into a var), but the caller's kai is untouched. This is the right choice for anything that only reads.

train(self: *Pilot, ...) takes a pointer to the struct. self is the address of kai, and self.xp += points writes into the caller's value. Zig lets you write self.xp rather than self.*.xp; field access through a pointer follows the pointer automatically (there is no -> as in C).

The last line shows there is no magic: kai.skillTotal() is exactly Pilot.skillTotal(kai). The dot form passes the thing before the dot as the first argument. For kai.train(6) Zig passes &kai, because the parameter is a pointer.

The compiler enforces the distinction in both directions. A pointer method on a const value is refused, because the method might write:

const std = @import("std");

const Pilot = struct {
    xp: u32 = 0,
    pub fn train(self: *Pilot, points: u32) void {
        self.xp += points;
    }
};

pub fn main() void {
    const kai = Pilot{};
    kai.train(5);
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{kai.xp});
}
method_const.zig:12:8: error: expected type '*method_const.Pilot', found '*const method_const.Pilot'
    kai.train(5);
    ~~~^~~~~~
method_const.zig:12:8: note: cast discards const qualifier
method_const.zig:5:24: note: parameter type declared here
    pub fn train(self: *Pilot, points: u32) void {
                       ^~~~~~
referenced by:
    callMain [inlined]: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:698:59
    callMainWithArgs [inlined]: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:638:20
    main: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:663:28
    1 reference(s) hidden; use '-freference-trace=4' to see all references

And a by-value method cannot write, because parameters are immutable:

const std = @import("std");

const Pilot = struct {
    xp: u32 = 0,
    pub fn train(self: Pilot, points: u32) void {
        self.xp += points;
    }
};

pub fn main() void {
    var kai = Pilot{};
    kai.train(5);
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{kai.xp});
}
method_value.zig:6:13: error: cannot assign to constant
        self.xp += points;
        ~~~~^~~
referenced by:
    main: method_value.zig:12:14
    callMain [inlined]: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:698:59
    callMainWithArgs [inlined]: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:638:20
    main: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:663:28
    1 reference(s) hidden; use '-freference-trace=5' to see all references
Choosing self. Take self: T when the method only reads and the struct is small. Take self: *T when it modifies anything. Take self: *const T when it only reads but the struct is large enough that copying it would be wasteful, or when it returns a slice or pointer into the struct (a copy would vanish when the method returned, as Chapter 10 warned). Whatever you choose, call it self; the language does not require the name, but every Zig programmer expects it.

12.4 @This() and namespaced declarations

Besides fields and methods, a struct can hold constants and plain functions. They live in the struct's namespace and are reached with Type.name.

this.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Money = struct {
    cbills: i64,

    const Self = @This();

    pub const zero: Self = .{ .cbills = 0 };
    pub const bp_scale: i64 = 10_000;

    pub fn fromThousands(k: i64) Self {
        return .{ .cbills = k * 1000 };
    }

    pub fn applyBp(self: Self, bp: i64) Self {
        return .{ .cbills = @divTrunc(self.cbills * bp, bp_scale) };
    }

    pub fn add(self: *Self, other: Self) void {
        self.cbills += other.cbills;
    }
};

pub fn main() void {
    var funds = Money.fromThousands(500);
    funds.add(Money.zero);
    funds.add(.{ .cbills = 250 });
    const with_bonus = funds.applyBp(12_500); // times 1.25
    std.debug.print("{d} -> {d}\n", .{ funds.cbills, with_bonus.cbills });
}
500250 -> 625312

@This() returns the type currently being defined. Writing const Self = @This(); at the top of a struct lets the methods say Self instead of repeating the type's name, which pays off when the name is long or when the struct is anonymous or generated (Chapter 26). Money.zero is a constant of the type stored inside the type. fromThousands has no self; it is a plain function that happens to live in Money, and it plays the role a constructor plays elsewhere. Note the call funds.add(.{ .cbills = 250 }): the anonymous literal becomes a Money because that is the parameter type.

The @divTrunc is Zig insisting you say which kind of integer division you mean (Chapter 4); IRON LEDGER's applyBp in src/domain/types.zig is this exact function.

12.5 Nested structs

A field's type can be another struct, named or written inline:

nested.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Date = struct { year: u16, month: u8, day: u8 };

const Contract = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    start: Date,
    end: Date,
    pay: struct { advance: i64, monthly: i64 }, // an inline anonymous struct type
};

pub fn main() void {
    const c = Contract{
        .name = "Garrison duty",
        .start = .{ .year = 3025, .month = 1, .day = 1 },
        .end = .{ .year = 3025, .month = 7, .day = 1 },
        .pay = .{ .advance = 100_000, .monthly = 45_000 },
    };
    std.debug.print("{s}: {d}/{d} to {d}/{d}, {d}/month\n", .{
        c.name, c.start.month, c.start.year, c.end.month, c.end.year, c.pay.monthly,
    });
}
Garrison duty: 1/3025 to 7/3025, 45000/month

Nested literals stay anonymous: .start = .{ .year = 3025, ... } becomes a Date because the field is a Date. The pay field uses an inline struct type, which is fine for a one-off grouping; give it a name the moment a second place needs it. Access chains with dots: c.pay.monthly.

12.6 Structs are values; pointers reach in

Like arrays, structs copy on assignment:

copy.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Pilot = struct { name: []const u8, hp: u8 };

pub fn main() void {
