    const a = Pilot{ .name = "Kai", .hp = 10 };
    var b = a; // a copy of both fields
    b.hp = 0;
    std.debug.print("a.hp={d} b.hp={d}\n", .{ a.hp, b.hp });
}
a.hp=10 b.hp=0

Note that copying the struct copied the slice name, not the bytes it points at; both values still point at the same "Kai". A struct holding slices or pointers is a shallow copy, the same as in C or Go.

To share a struct rather than copy it, pass a pointer, and read fields through it without any extra syntax:

ptr_access.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Pilot = struct { name: []const u8, hp: u8 };

fn wound(p: *Pilot, dmg: u8) void {
    p.hp -|= dmg; // no arrow, no explicit deref: Zig follows the pointer for you
    std.debug.print("{s} now at {d}\n", .{ p.name, p.hp });
}

pub fn main() void {
    var kai = Pilot{ .name = "Kai", .hp = 10 };
    const ptr = &kai;
    wound(ptr, 3);
    wound(&kai, 30);
    std.debug.print("{d} {d}\n", .{ kai.hp, ptr.*.hp }); // ptr.*.hp is the long form
}
Kai now at 7
Kai now at 0
0 0

p.hp on a *Pilot reads the caller's hp; ptr.*.hp is the same thing spelled out. -|= is saturating subtraction so the second wound stops at zero instead of panicking on underflow.

12.7 Comparing structs

By now you can guess: no ==.

const std = @import("std");

const Date = struct { year: u16, month: u8, day: u8 };

pub fn main() void {
    const a = Date{ .year = 3025, .month = 1, .day = 1 };
    const b = Date{ .year = 3025, .month = 1, .day = 1 };
    std.debug.print("{}\n", .{a == b});
}
equality_op.zig:8:33: error: operator == not allowed for type 'equality_op.Date'
    std.debug.print("{}\n", .{a == b});
                              ~~^~~~
equality_op.zig:3:14: note: struct declared here
const Date = struct { year: u16, month: u8, day: u8 };
             ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
referenced by:
    callMain [inlined]: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:698:59
    callMainWithArgs [inlined]: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:638:20
    main: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:663:28
    1 reference(s) hidden; use '-freference-trace=4' to see all references

Use std.meta.eql, which compares field by field (and recurses into nested structs and arrays), or write the comparison yourself when only some fields matter:

equality.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Date = struct { year: u16, month: u8, day: u8 };

pub fn main() void {
    const a = Date{ .year = 3025, .month = 1, .day = 1 };
    const b = Date{ .year = 3025, .month = 1, .day = 1 };
    std.debug.print("{}\n", .{std.meta.eql(a, b)});
    std.debug.print("{}\n", .{a.year == b.year and a.month == b.month and a.day == b.day});
}
true
true

In tests, expectEqual compares structs field by field too, which is why IRON LEDGER can write expectEqual(Date{ .year = 3024, .month = 2, .day = 29 }, d). One caution: for a field that is a slice, std.meta.eql compares the pointer and length, not the bytes, the same rule as expectEqual in Chapter 8.

12.8 Tuples, briefly

A tuple is a struct whose fields are numbered instead of named. You have been making them all along: .{ 1, "x" } is a tuple literal. They are the natural way to return two values.

tuples.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn minMax(xs: []const i32) struct { i32, i32 } {
    var lo = xs[0];
    var hi = xs[0];
    for (xs) |x| {
        if (x < lo) lo = x;
        if (x > hi) hi = x;
    }
    return .{ lo, hi };
}

pub fn main() void {
    const pair = minMax(&[_]i32{ 4, -2, 9, 0 });
    std.debug.print("min {d}, max {d}\n", .{ pair[0], pair[1] });
    const lo, const hi = minMax(&[_]i32{ 7, 3 }); // destructuring
    std.debug.print("{d} {d}\n", .{ lo, hi });
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{pair});
}
min -2, max 9
3 7
.{ -2, 9 }

struct { i32, i32 } declares a tuple type with two i32 fields; you index it with [0] and [1], and you can pull it apart into two names in one const lo, const hi = ... statement. If the two values have different meanings, prefer a named struct: struct { lo: i32, hi: i32 } costs nothing more and reads better six months later.

12.9 Printing a struct: {any} and a format method

{any} prints every field, which is fine for debugging and wrong for users. A struct can define how it prints by providing a method named format. In Zig 0.16 the signature is fixed:

pub fn format(self: T, w: *std.Io.Writer) std.Io.Writer.Error!void

It receives a writer, the same interface as stdout and fixed buffers, and prints whatever it likes to it. You then ask for it with the {f} specifier:

format.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Date = struct {
    year: u16,
    month: u8,
    day: u8,

    pub fn format(self: Date, w: *std.Io.Writer) std.Io.Writer.Error!void {
        try w.print("{d:0>4}-{d:0>2}-{d:0>2}", .{ self.year, self.month, self.day });
    }
};

const Plain = struct { year: u16, month: u8, day: u8 };

pub fn main() !void {
    const d = Date{ .year = 3025, .month = 3, .day = 7 };
    const p = Plain{ .year = 3025, .month = 3, .day = 7 };
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{p});
    std.debug.print("{f}\n", .{d});
    var buf: [32]u8 = undefined;
    const s = try std.fmt.bufPrint(&buf, "start {f}", .{d});
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{s});
}
.{ .year = 3025, .month = 3, .day = 7 }
3025-03-07
start 3025-03-07

{f} works anywhere a format string does: std.debug.print, bufPrint, a file writer. This is how a Date can print as 3025-03-07 in one place and be a plain three-field struct everywhere else.

{any} ignores your format. In 0.16, {any} (and a bare {}) always print the raw fields, even when the type has a format method: 
const std = @import("std");

const Date = struct {
    year: u16,
    month: u8,
    day: u8,
    pub fn format(self: Date, w: *std.Io.Writer) std.Io.Writer.Error!void {
        try w.print("{d}-{d}-{d}", .{ self.year, self.month, self.day });
    }
};

pub fn main() void {
    const d = Date{ .year = 3025, .month = 3, .day = 7 };
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{d});
}
.{ .year = 3025, .month = 3, .day = 7 }

Only {f} calls your method. Older Zig picked the method up automatically, so older code and tutorials write {} and expect the custom output; in 0.16 that prints fields. If your nicely formatted struct comes out as .{ .year = ... }, change the specifier to {f}.

In IRON LEDGER. The campaign calendar is a small, complete struct: fields, a namespaced constant, plain functions, a by-value method that returns a new value, and a predicate. It is the shape you should copy for your own small value types: 
// src/sim/clock.zig
pub const Date = struct {
    year: u16,
    month: u8, // 1-12
    day: u8, // 1-31

    pub const campaign_default: Date = .{ .year = 3025, .month = 1, .day = 1 };

    pub fn isLeapYear(year: u16) bool {
        return (year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0) or year % 400 == 0;
    }

    pub fn next(self: Date) Date {
        var d = self;
        d.day += 1;
        if (d.day > daysInMonth(d.year, d.month)) {
            d.day = 1;
            d.month += 1;
            if (d.month > 12) {
                d.month = 1;
                d.year += 1;
            }
        }
        return d;
    }

    pub fn isPayday(self: Date) bool {
        return self.day == 1;
    }
};

next copies self into a var, changes the copy and returns it; nothing is mutated in place, by choice. The other style lives in src/sim/state.zig, where GameState has forty-odd fields, most with defaults, and every method takes self: *GameState because a game state is far too large to copy and is meant to change. Both are correct; the size and the intent decide.

Exercises

Exercise 12.1 · A Date with methods warm-up

Complete IRON LEDGER's Date: isLeapYear, daysInMonth, a by-value next and a by-pointer advance that reuses it. The tests are the game's own, plus one for advance. Name the file: exercises/12-structs/ex1_date.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 12, exercise 1: a Date struct with methods.
//! Run with:  zig test ex1_date.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Date = struct {
    year: u16,
    month: u8, // 1..12
    day: u8, // 1..31

    pub const campaign_default: Date = .{ .year = 3025, .month = 1, .day = 1 };

    pub fn isLeapYear(year: u16) bool {
        return (year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0) or year % 400 == 0;
    }

    pub fn daysInMonth(year: u16, month: u8) u8 {
        return switch (month) {
            1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12 => 31,
            4, 6, 9, 11 => 30,
            2 => if (isLeapYear(year)) @as(u8, 29) else 28,
            else => unreachable,
        };
    }

    /// The day after self, as a new value.
    pub fn next(self: Date) Date {
        var d = self;
        d.day += 1;
        if (d.day > daysInMonth(d.year, d.month)) {
            d.day = 1;
            d.month += 1;
            if (d.month > 12) {
                d.month = 1;
                d.year += 1;
            }
        }
        return d;
    }

    /// Advance self in place by n days.
    pub fn advance(self: *Date, n: u32) void {
        var i: u32 = 0;
        while (i < n) : (i += 1) self.* = self.next();
    }

    pub fn isPayday(self: Date) bool {
        return self.day == 1;
    }
};

test "leap years" {
    try std.testing.expect(Date.isLeapYear(3024));
    try std.testing.expect(!Date.isLeapYear(3025));
    try std.testing.expect(!Date.isLeapYear(3100));
    try std.testing.expect(Date.isLeapYear(3200));
}

test "next rolls over months and years" {
    var d: Date = .{ .year = 3024, .month = 2, .day = 28 };
    d = d.next();
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Date{ .year = 3024, .month = 2, .day = 29 }, d);
    d = .{ .year = 3025, .month = 12, .day = 31 };
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Date{ .year = 3026, .month = 1, .day = 1 }, d.next());
}

test "advance mutates in place" {
    var d = Date.campaign_default;
    d.advance(31);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Date{ .year = 3025, .month = 2, .day = 1 }, d);
    try std.testing.expect(d.isPayday());
    d.advance(1);
    try std.testing.expect(!d.isPayday());
}

advance shows the two styles cooperating: it takes *Date so it can change the caller's value, and does so by assigning self.* = self.next(), the by-value method's result. The @as(u8, 29) inside the switch gives the if expression a concrete type so that both branches agree.

Exercise 12.2 · Defaults, nesting and format practice

Add three defaulted fields to Unit (an Armor struct, an optional pilot name, a destroyed flag), implement totalArmor and hitFront, and write a format method that prints Atlas (100t, 47/14) piloted by Kai [DESTROYED] style output, checked through bufPrint with {f}. Name the file: exercises/12-structs/ex2_unit.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 12, exercise 2: defaults, nesting and a format method.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_unit.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Armor = struct { front: u16, rear: u16 };

const Unit = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    tons: u8,
    armor: Armor = .{ .front = 0, .rear = 0 },
    pilot: ?[]const u8 = null,
    destroyed: bool = false,

    pub fn totalArmor(self: Unit) u32 {
        return @as(u32, self.armor.front) + self.armor.rear;
    }

    /// Apply damage to the front armor; anything left over destroys the unit.
    pub fn hitFront(self: *Unit, dmg: u16) void {
        if (dmg >= self.armor.front) {
            self.armor.front = 0;
            self.destroyed = true;
        } else {
            self.armor.front -= dmg;
        }
    }

    pub fn format(self: Unit, w: *std.Io.Writer) std.Io.Writer.Error!void {
        const a = self.armor;
        try w.print("{s} ({d}t, {d}/{d})", .{ self.name, self.tons, a.front, a.rear });
        if (self.pilot) |p| try w.print(" piloted by {s}", .{p});
        if (self.destroyed) try w.writeAll(" [DESTROYED]");
    }
};

test "defaults" {
    const u = Unit{ .name = "Locust", .tons = 20 };
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 0), u.totalArmor());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?[]const u8, null), u.pilot);
    try std.testing.expect(!u.destroyed);
}

test "damage" {
    var u = Unit{ .name = "Atlas", .tons = 100, .armor = .{ .front = 47, .rear = 14 } };
    u.hitFront(10);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 51), u.totalArmor());
    try std.testing.expect(!u.destroyed);
    u.hitFront(40);
    try std.testing.expect(u.destroyed);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u16, 0), u.armor.front);
}

test "format" {
    var buf: [96]u8 = undefined;
    var u = Unit{
        .name = "Atlas",
        .tons = 100,
        .armor = .{ .front = 47, .rear = 14 },
        .pilot = "Kai",
    };
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings(
        "Atlas (100t, 47/14) piloted by Kai",
        try std.fmt.bufPrint(&buf, "{f}", .{u}),
    );
    u.hitFront(99);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings(
        "Atlas (100t, 0/14) piloted by Kai [DESTROYED]",
        try std.fmt.bufPrint(&buf, "{f}", .{u}),
    );
}

totalArmor widens to u32 before adding, since two u16 can overflow a u16. The optional pilot is unwrapped with if (self.pilot) |p|, a preview of Chapter 15. The format method uses w.print and w.writeAll, the same calls as any writer.

Exercise 12.3 · A lance of meks practice

A Lance holds a [4]Mek. Implement tonnage, readyCount, a pointer-receiver damage that marks one mek by name, and heaviestReady, which returns a pointer into the lance or null. Name the file: exercises/12-structs/ex3_lance.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 12, exercise 3: a struct that holds an array of structs.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_lance.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Mek = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    tons: u8,
    ready: bool = true,
};

const Lance = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    meks: [4]Mek,

    const Self = @This();

    pub fn tonnage(self: Self) u32 {
        var t: u32 = 0;
        for (self.meks) |m| t += m.tons;
        return t;
    }

    pub fn readyCount(self: Self) usize {
        var n: usize = 0;
        for (self.meks) |m| {
            if (m.ready) n += 1;
        }
        return n;
    }

    /// Mark the mek called `name` as not ready. Returns false if no such mek.
    pub fn damage(self: *Self, name: []const u8) bool {
        for (&self.meks) |*m| {
            if (std.mem.eql(u8, m.name, name)) {
                m.ready = false;
                return true;
            }
        }
        return false;
    }

    /// The heaviest ready mek, or null if none is ready.
    pub fn heaviestReady(self: *const Self) ?*const Mek {
        var best: ?*const Mek = null;
        for (&self.meks) |*m| {
            if (!m.ready) continue;
            if (best == null or m.tons > best.?.tons) best = m;
        }
        return best;
    }
};

fn sampleLance() Lance {
    return .{
        .name = "Alpha",
        .meks = .{
            .{ .name = "Atlas", .tons = 100 },
            .{ .name = "Locust", .tons = 20 },
            .{ .name = "Marauder", .tons = 75 },
            .{ .name = "Shadow Hawk", .tons = 55 },
        },
    };
}

test "tonnage and readiness" {
    const l = sampleLance();
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 250), l.tonnage());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 4), l.readyCount());
}

test "damage through a pointer" {
    var l = sampleLance();
    try std.testing.expect(l.damage("Atlas"));
    try std.testing.expect(!l.damage("Urbanmech"));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 3), l.readyCount());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 250), l.tonnage()); // tonnage unchanged
}

test "heaviest ready" {
    var l = sampleLance();
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Atlas", l.heaviestReady().?.name);
    _ = l.damage("Atlas");
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Marauder", l.heaviestReady().?.name);
    for (&l.meks) |*m| m.ready = false;
    try std.testing.expect(l.heaviestReady() == null);
}

damage loops over &self.meks with |*m| so the write to m.ready lands in the struct, not in a copy. heaviestReady takes *const Self because it returns a pointer into the struct; with a by-value self the pointer would refer to a copy that no longer exists.

Exercise 12.4 · A tiny ledger challenge

A Ledger keeps up to eight Entry values in a fixed array with a len counter. Implement post (returning error.Full when out of room), balance, balanceOn(day) and biggestExpense. Only entries[0..len] are meaningful; the rest is undefined. Name the file: exercises/12-structs/ex4_ledger.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 12, exercise 4: a tiny ledger (challenge).
//! Run with:  zig test ex4_ledger.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Entry = struct {
    day: u32,
    label: []const u8,
    amount: i64, // positive = income, negative = expense
};

const Ledger = struct {
    entries: [8]Entry = undefined,
    len: usize = 0,
    opening: i64,

    const Self = @This();

    /// Record an entry. Returns error.Full when the fixed array is used up.
    pub fn post(self: *Self, day: u32, label: []const u8, amount: i64) !void {
        if (self.len == self.entries.len) return error.Full;
        self.entries[self.len] = .{ .day = day, .label = label, .amount = amount };
        self.len += 1;
    }

    pub fn balance(self: Self) i64 {
        var b = self.opening;
        for (self.entries[0..self.len]) |e| b += e.amount;
        return b;
    }

    /// Balance as it stood at the end of `day`.
    pub fn balanceOn(self: Self, day: u32) i64 {
        var b = self.opening;
        for (self.entries[0..self.len]) |e| {
            if (e.day <= day) b += e.amount;
        }
        return b;
    }

    /// The largest single expense (most negative amount), or null.
    pub fn biggestExpense(self: *const Self) ?Entry {
        var best: ?Entry = null;
        for (self.entries[0..self.len]) |e| {
            if (e.amount >= 0) continue;
            if (best == null or e.amount < best.?.amount) best = e;
        }
        return best;
    }
};

test "post and balance" {
    var l = Ledger{ .opening = 1_000_000 };
    try l.post(1, "contract advance", 250_000);
    try l.post(1, "salaries", -60_000);
    try l.post(15, "spare parts", -12_500);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 1_177_500), l.balance());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 1_190_000), l.balanceOn(1));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 1_000_000), l.balanceOn(0));
}

test "biggest expense" {
    var l = Ledger{ .opening = 0 };
    try std.testing.expect(l.biggestExpense() == null);
    try l.post(1, "income", 500);
    try l.post(2, "salaries", -60_000);
    try l.post(3, "repairs", -75_000);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("repairs", l.biggestExpense().?.label);
}

test "full ledger" {
    var l = Ledger{ .opening = 0 };
    var i: u32 = 0;
    while (i < 8) : (i += 1) try l.post(i, "x", 1);
    try std.testing.expectError(error.Full, l.post(9, "one too many", 1));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 8), l.balance());
}

Every reader slices self.entries[0..self.len] so it never looks at the undefined tail. This array-plus-length pattern is what ArrayList does for you with a growable buffer in Chapter 21; building it by hand once makes the real thing obvious.

Check your understanding

  1. What happens if you omit a field without a default from a struct literal?
    AnswerA compile error naming the missing field. Zig never leaves a field silently uninitialised; write .f = undefined if that is what you mean.
  2. What is the difference between fn f(self: T) and fn f(self: *T)?
    AnswerBy value, self is a copy and the method cannot change the caller's struct. By pointer, it can. Calling a pointer method on a const value is a compile error.
  3. Is kai.train(6) different from Pilot.train(&kai, 6)?
    AnswerNo. Method-call syntax passes the value before the dot (or its address, for pointer parameters) as the first argument.
  4. How do you read a field through a pointer to a struct?
    AnswerWith a plain dot: p.hp. Zig follows the pointer; p.*.hp is the explicit form and there is no ->.
  5. How do you compare two structs for equality?
    Answerstd.meta.eql(a, b), or field by field. == is not defined for structs. Slice fields are compared by pointer and length.
  6. What does @This() return?
    AnswerThe type being defined at that point, usually stored as const Self = @This();. At file scope it is the file's own struct type.
  7. You wrote a format method and print("{}", .{d}) still shows raw fields. Why?
    AnswerIn 0.16 only the {f} specifier calls a type's format method; {} and {any} print the fields.
What you learned.
  • const T = struct { field: Type, ... }; declares a type; T{ .field = v } or a typed .{ ... } builds a value. Every non-defaulted field is required.
  • Defaults (field: Type = value) make fields optional in literals.
  • Methods are functions in the struct whose first parameter is the type; v.method() is T.method(v).
  • self: T reads a copy; self: *T mutates the original; self: *const T reads without copying.
  • Field access through a pointer needs no special syntax. Structs copy on assignment (shallowly).
  • @This() names the current type; constants and plain functions can live inside a struct.
  • Compare with std.meta.eql. Tuples are structs with numbered fields.
  • pub fn format(self: T, w: *std.Io.Writer) std.Io.Writer.Error!void plus the {f} specifier gives custom printing; {any} shows raw fields.

13. Enums

In this chapter you will define closed sets of named values, switch over them with the compiler checking that you forgot nothing, give them methods and explicit integer representations, convert between enums and integers and strings, and learn the trick IRON LEDGER uses for every entity ID: the non-exhaustive enum. By the end you should reach for an enum whenever you catch yourself about to use a string or a magic number to mean "which kind".

13.1 A closed set of names

A person in the company has a role: pilot, technician, doctor, administrator. You could store that as a string, but then "Tech", "tech" and "tehc" are all valid and only one is what you meant. An enum lists the allowed values once and makes anything else a compile error.

basics.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Role = enum {
    mekwarrior,
    tech,
    doctor,
    admin,
};

pub fn main() void {
    const r = Role.mekwarrior;
    const t: Role = .tech; // shorthand when the type is known
    std.debug.print("{any} {any}\n", .{ r, t });
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{@tagName(t)});
    std.debug.print("{}\n", .{r == .mekwarrior});
    std.debug.print("{}\n", .{r == t});
}
.mekwarrior .tech
tech
true
false

Role.mekwarrior is the full spelling. When the type is already known, from a declared variable type, a parameter, or a comparison against an existing enum value, you write just the dot and the name: .tech. That shorthand is used far more than the full form; the guide calls it the leading-dot style and you will see it in every switch and every function call that takes an enum.

Enums compare with == and !=; that is one of the reasons to prefer them over strings. @tagName gives you the name as a string, which is how {s} printed tech. {any} prints the leading-dot form.

13.2 Methods and switch

Like a struct, an enum can contain functions, and a function taking the enum as its first parameter is a method. Inside them, switch is the natural tool:

switch.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Role = enum {
    mekwarrior,
    tech,
    doctor,
    admin,

    /// Monthly salary in C-bills.
    pub fn baseSalary(self: Role) i64 {
        return switch (self) {
            .mekwarrior => 1_500,
            .tech => 800,
            .doctor => 1_500,
            .admin => 500,
        };
    }

    pub fn isCombat(self: Role) bool {
        return self == .mekwarrior;
    }
};

pub fn main() void {
    const roster = [_]Role{ .mekwarrior, .mekwarrior, .tech, .doctor, .admin };
    var payroll: i64 = 0;
    for (roster) |r| {
        payroll += r.baseSalary();
        std.debug.print("{s:<10} {d} combat={}\n", .{ @tagName(r), r.baseSalary(), r.isCombat() });
    }
    std.debug.print("payroll {d}\n", .{payroll});
}
mekwarrior 1500 combat=true
mekwarrior 1500 combat=true
tech       800 combat=false
doctor     1500 combat=false
admin      500 combat=false
payroll 5800

switch is an expression here: each arm produces a value and the whole thing is returned. The arms name enum values with the leading dot. And every value is named, which brings us to the property that makes enums worth using.

13.3 The compiler checks exhaustiveness

Add a role and forget to update the salary table:

missing.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Role = enum { mekwarrior, tech, doctor, admin, medic };

fn baseSalary(r: Role) i64 {
    return switch (r) {
        .mekwarrior => 1_500,
        .tech => 800,
        .doctor => 1_500,
        .admin => 500,
    };
}

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{baseSalary(.medic)});
}
missing.zig:6:12: error: switch must handle all possibilities
    return switch (r) {
           ^~~~~~
missing.zig:3:54: note: unhandled enumeration value: 'medic'
const Role = enum { mekwarrior, tech, doctor, admin, medic };
                                                     ^~~~~
missing.zig:3:14: note: enum 'missing.Role' declared here
const Role = enum { mekwarrior, tech, doctor, admin, medic };
             ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
referenced by:
    main: missing.zig:15:42
    callMain [inlined]: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:698:59
    callMainWithArgs [inlined]: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:638:20
    main: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:663:28
    1 reference(s) hidden; use '-freference-trace=5' to see all references

switch must handle all possibilities, and the note tells you which value is unhandled and where the enum is declared. This is the reason IRON LEDGER uses enums for roles, phases, contract states, unit conditions and everything else with a fixed set of kinds: add a variant and the compiler lists every switch in 31,000 lines that needs a decision. A string-based design would fail at runtime, in the one code path nobody tested.

Several values can share an arm, separated by commas, and else catches everything not named:

grouped.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Role = enum { mekwarrior, aero_pilot, tech_mek, tech_aero, astech, doctor, medic, admin };

fn baseSalary(r: Role) i64 {
    return switch (r) {
        .mekwarrior, .aero_pilot => 1_500,
        .tech_mek, .tech_aero => 800,
        .astech => 400,
        .doctor => 1_500,
        .medic => 400,
        else => 500, // everything not named above
    };
}

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{d} {d} {d}\n", .{
        baseSalary(.aero_pilot), baseSalary(.medic), baseSalary(.admin),
    });
}
1500 400 500
else switches off the safety net. The moment a switch has an else arm, adding a new enum value no longer produces an error there; it silently falls into else. Use else when "everything else" genuinely means the same thing, as a default salary might. When each value deserves its own thought, name them all and let the compiler nag you.

13.4 Explicit tag types and integer conversion

Every enum is stored as an integer. By default Zig picks the smallest that fits; you can choose it yourself with enum(u8), and you can assign the values:

tagtype.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Quality = enum(u8) {
    f = 0,
    d = 1,
    c = 2,
    b = 3,
    a = 4,
};

const Phase = enum(u8) { travel, supply, events, battle, finances }; // 0, 1, 2, ...

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{d} bytes\n", .{@sizeOf(Quality)});
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{@intFromEnum(Quality.b)});
    const q: Quality = @enumFromInt(4);
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{@tagName(q)});
    std.debug.print("{d} {d}\n", .{ @intFromEnum(Phase.travel), @intFromEnum(Phase.finances) });
    std.debug.print("{}\n", .{@intFromEnum(Phase.travel) < @intFromEnum(Phase.battle)});

    var counts = [_]u32{0} ** 5;
    for ([_]Quality{ .a, .c, .a, .f }) |x| counts[@intFromEnum(x)] += 1;
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{counts});
}
1 bytes
3
a
0 4
true
{ 1, 0, 1, 0, 2 }

@intFromEnum goes from enum to integer; @enumFromInt goes back, taking its target type from context. With no explicit values, they count up from zero in declaration order, which makes @intFromEnum(a) < @intFromEnum(b) a test of declaration order; IRON LEDGER's clock.zig has a test that checks its day phases are in the right order exactly this way. The last lines show the most common use of the integer: indexing an array of counters by enum value.

Going from an integer to an enum is checked. If the number matches no value, Debug builds panic:

const std = @import("std");

const Quality = enum(u8) { f, d, c, b, a };

pub fn main() void {
    var n: u8 = 4;
    n += 3;
    const q: Quality = @enumFromInt(n);
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{@tagName(q)});
}
thread 6011123 panic: invalid enum value
ch13/badint.zig:8:24: in main (badint)
    const q: Quality = @enumFromInt(n);
                       ^
<zig>/lib/std/start.zig:698:59: in callMain (badint)
    if (fn_info.params.len == 0) return wrapMain(root.main());
                                                          ^
???:?:?: in start (/usr/lib/dyld)

So @enumFromInt is safe to use on trusted numbers (an index you computed from a valid enum) and should be guarded on untrusted ones (a byte from a file). Section 13.5 shows the enum kind that accepts any integer on purpose.

13.5 Non-exhaustive enums and typed IDs

An enum whose last member is _ is non-exhaustive: it declares that any value of the tag type is valid, not only the named ones. It must have an explicit tag type. IRON LEDGER uses this for every entity ID:

nonexh.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub const PersonId = enum(u32) { none = 0, _ };
pub const UnitId = enum(u32) { none = 0, _ };

fn describe(id: PersonId) void {
    switch (id) {
        .none => std.debug.print("nobody\n", .{}),
        _ => std.debug.print("person #{d}\n", .{@intFromEnum(id)}),
    }
}

pub fn main() void {
    const kai: PersonId = @enumFromInt(7);
    describe(kai);
    describe(.none);
    std.debug.print("{}\n", .{kai == .none});
    std.debug.print("{d} bytes, same as u32\n", .{@sizeOf(PersonId)});
}
person #7
nobody
false
4 bytes, same as u32

Read enum(u32) { none = 0, _ } as "a u32 with one named value, none, and every other number allowed". At runtime a PersonId is four bytes, exactly a u32; it costs nothing. But it is a distinct type. Its purpose is the error below:

const std = @import("std");

pub const PersonId = enum(u32) { none = 0, _ };
pub const UnitId = enum(u32) { none = 0, _ };

fn fire(id: PersonId) void {
    std.debug.print("fired #{d}\n", .{@intFromEnum(id)});
}

pub fn main() void {
    const atlas: UnitId = @enumFromInt(3);
    fire(atlas);
}
nonexh_err.zig:12:10: error: expected type 'nonexh_err.PersonId', found 'nonexh_err.UnitId'
    fire(atlas);
         ^~~~~
nonexh_err.zig:4:20: note: enum declared here
pub const UnitId = enum(u32) { none = 0, _ };
                   ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
nonexh_err.zig:3:22: note: enum declared here
pub const PersonId = enum(u32) { none = 0, _ };
                     ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
nonexh_err.zig:6:13: note: parameter type declared here
fn fire(id: PersonId) void {
            ^~~~~~~~
referenced by:
    callMain [inlined]: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:698:59
    callMainWithArgs [inlined]: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:638:20
    main: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:663:28
    1 reference(s) hidden; use '-freference-trace=4' to see all references

A function that wants a person's ID will not accept a unit's ID, even though both are 32-bit numbers underneath. With plain u32 IDs this bug compiles and corrupts a save file; with typed IDs it does not compile. And .none gives a spelled-out "no one" value instead of a magic zero.

A switch on a non-exhaustive enum uses _ as its catch-all arm for the unnamed values, as describe shows. It is different from else: else would also cover any named values you left out, while _ covers only the unnamed ones, so the exhaustiveness check still protects the names.

The whole pattern, as the game writes it. 
// src/domain/types.zig
pub const PersonId = enum(u32) { none = 0, _ };
pub const UnitId = enum(u32) { none = 0, _ };
pub const ForceId = enum(u32) { none = 0, _ };
pub const ContractId = enum(u32) { none = 0, _ };
Converting is explicit and rare: @enumFromInt(n) where a user typed a number, @intFromEnum(id) where the ID is written to a file or printed. Everywhere in between, the ID is opaque.

13.6 From strings to enums

User input arrives as text. std.meta.stringToEnum looks a name up and returns an optional:

stringto.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Role = enum { mekwarrior, tech, doctor, admin };

pub fn main() void {
    const inputs = [_][]const u8{ "tech", "doctor", "pilot", "Tech" };
    for (inputs) |s| {
        if (std.meta.stringToEnum(Role, s)) |r| {
            std.debug.print("{s} -> {any}\n", .{ s, r });
        } else {
            std.debug.print("{s} -> not a role\n", .{s});
        }
    }
}
tech -> .tech
doctor -> .doctor
pilot -> not a role
Tech -> not a role

The match is exact and case-sensitive, so "Tech" is rejected; lower-case the input first if you want to be lenient. Together with @tagName this gives you a free, always-in-sync parser and printer for any enum: the names in the source are the names in the file format.

To iterate over every value, std.enums.values returns them in declaration order, and @typeInfo can count them:

fields.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Role = enum { mekwarrior, tech, doctor, admin };

pub fn main() void {
    // Walk every value of an enum.
    for (std.enums.values(Role)) |r| {
        std.debug.print("{d}: {s}\n", .{ @intFromEnum(r), @tagName(r) });
    }
    std.debug.print("{d} roles\n", .{@typeInfo(Role).@"enum".fields.len});
}
0: mekwarrior
1: tech
2: doctor
3: admin
4 roles

13.7 Enum literals

What is .tech on its own, before it meets a type? Zig calls it an enum literal. It is a compile-time value that becomes whichever enum the context asks for:

literal.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Role = enum { mekwarrior, tech };
const Status = enum { active, tech };

fn roleName(r: Role) []const u8 {
    return @tagName(r);
}

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{roleName(.tech)}); // .tech becomes Role.tech
    const s: Status = .tech; // the same literal, a different enum
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{@tagName(s)});
    const lit = .tech; // no context: an enum literal, not yet any enum
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{@TypeOf(lit)});
}
tech
tech
@EnumLiteral()

The same literal .tech became a Role in the call and a Status in the declaration, because both enums have a member with that name. Assigned to a plain const with no type, it stays an enum literal (@EnumLiteral()) and can be used later wherever an enum with that member is expected. You will see enum literals as lightweight options in the standard library, for example the .real in std.Io.Clock.now(.real, io) and the .scalar in std.mem.TokenIterator(u8, .scalar).

13.8 When to reach for an enum

A few habits will serve you well. If a value can only ever be one of a fixed list of things, it is an enum, even when there are only two of them: enum { attacker, defender } reads better than a bool called is_attacker, and it can grow to three sides without a rewrite. If you find a u8 whose comment says "0 = green, 1 = regular, 2 = veteran", it is an enum with an explicit tag type, and the comment becomes the member names. If a function takes a string and immediately compares it against a handful of known words, parse it once with stringToEnum at the edge and pass the enum inward, so the rest of the program never sees the text.

The one thing an enum cannot do is carry data with each alternative. A key press is enter or escape or a character, and which character; a command is advance_day or hire, and whom. For that you need the enum's bigger sibling, the tagged union, which is the subject of Chapter 14. Everything you learned here, the leading-dot literals, exhaustive switch, @tagName, carries over unchanged.

In IRON LEDGER. The roles enum is the largest in the domain layer, and its salary method is the canonical exhaustive switch: 
// src/domain/person.zig
pub const Role = enum {
    mekwarrior, vehicle_crew, aero_pilot, ba_trooper, infantry,
    tech_mek, tech_mechanic, tech_aero, tech_ba, astech,
    doctor, medic,
    admin_command, admin_logistics, admin_transport, admin_hr, admin_finance,
    dropship_crew, jumpship_crew,

    /// CamOps base monthly salary in C-bills (MekHQ defaults).
    pub fn baseSalary(self: Role) types.CBills {
        return switch (self) {
            .mekwarrior, .aero_pilot => 1_500,
            .vehicle_crew => 900,
            .tech_mek, .tech_aero, .tech_ba => 800,
            .astech => 400,
            .doctor => 1_500,
            .medic => 400,
            .admin_command, .admin_logistics, .admin_transport, .admin_hr, .admin_finance => 500,
            .dropship_crew, .jumpship_crew => 750,
            // ...
        };
    }
};

Elsewhere the same ideas recur: src/main.zig prints @tagName(c.status) and @intFromEnum(c.id) in its reports; src/sim/clock.zig tests that @intFromEnum(DayPhase.travel) < @intFromEnum(DayPhase.supply_consumption); and the typed IDs in src/domain/types.zig keep a PersonId from ever being handed to a function that wanted a UnitId.

Exercises

Exercise 13.1 · An enum with methods warm-up

Give Role three methods: an exhaustive baseSalary with grouped arms, isCombat, and supervisor, which returns an optional Role. The last test walks every value with std.enums.values. Name the file: exercises/13-enums/ex1_roles.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 13, exercise 1: an enum with methods.
//! Run with:  zig test ex1_roles.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Role = enum {
    mekwarrior,
    aero_pilot,
    tech,
    astech,
    doctor,
    medic,
    admin,

    pub fn baseSalary(self: Role) i64 {
        return switch (self) {
            .mekwarrior, .aero_pilot, .doctor => 1_500,
            .tech => 800,
            .astech, .medic => 400,
            .admin => 500,
        };
    }

    pub fn isCombat(self: Role) bool {
        return switch (self) {
            .mekwarrior, .aero_pilot => true,
            else => false,
        };
    }

    /// The role that supervises this one, or null at the top.
    pub fn supervisor(self: Role) ?Role {
        return switch (self) {
            .astech => .tech,
            .medic => .doctor,
            .mekwarrior, .aero_pilot, .tech, .doctor => .admin,
            .admin => null,
        };
    }
};

test "salaries" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 1_500), Role.mekwarrior.baseSalary());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 400), Role.medic.baseSalary());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 500), Role.admin.baseSalary());
}

test "combat" {
    try std.testing.expect(Role.aero_pilot.isCombat());
    try std.testing.expect(!Role.tech.isCombat());
}

test "supervisor chain" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?Role, .tech), Role.astech.supervisor());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?Role, .admin), Role.tech.supervisor());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?Role, null), Role.admin.supervisor());
}

test "payroll over every role" {
    var total: i64 = 0;
    for (std.enums.values(Role)) |r| total += r.baseSalary();
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 6_600), total);
}

baseSalary and supervisor name every value so that adding a role forces a decision in both. isCombat uses else deliberately: a new role is non-combat until someone says otherwise, and that default is safe.

Exercise 13.2 · Explicit tags and conversions practice

Quality is an enum(u8) with values 0 to 4. Implement improve and degrade (stepping through the integer, clamped at the ends), parse from a letter, and letter for display. Name the file: exercises/13-enums/ex2_quality.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 13, exercise 2: explicit tag types and conversions.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_quality.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Unit quality grades, worst to best. The integer is the index into tables.
const Quality = enum(u8) {
    f = 0,
    d = 1,
    c = 2,
    b = 3,
    a = 4,

    /// One grade better, capped at a.
    pub fn improve(self: Quality) Quality {
        if (self == .a) return .a;
        return @enumFromInt(@intFromEnum(self) + 1);
    }

    /// One grade worse, capped at f.
    pub fn degrade(self: Quality) Quality {
        if (self == .f) return .f;
        return @enumFromInt(@intFromEnum(self) - 1);
    }

    /// Parse a single letter, either case. Anything else is null.
    pub fn parse(c: u8) ?Quality {
        return switch (std.ascii.toLower(c)) {
            'f' => .f,
            'd' => .d,
            'c' => .c,
            'b' => .b,
            'a' => .a,
            else => null,
        };
    }

    /// Upper-case letter for display.
    pub fn letter(self: Quality) u8 {
        return std.ascii.toUpper(@tagName(self)[0]);
    }
};

test "size and values" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 1), @sizeOf(Quality));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 3), @intFromEnum(Quality.b));
}

test "improve and degrade clamp" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Quality.d, Quality.f.improve());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Quality.a, Quality.a.improve());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Quality.f, Quality.f.degrade());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Quality.c, Quality.b.degrade());
}

test "parse and letter" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?Quality, .b), Quality.parse('b'));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?Quality, .b), Quality.parse('B'));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?Quality, null), Quality.parse('x'));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 'A'), Quality.a.letter());
}

test "histogram indexed by the tag" {
    var counts = [_]u32{0} ** 5;
    for ([_]Quality{ .a, .c, .a, .f }) |q| counts[@intFromEnum(q)] += 1;
    try std.testing.expectEqual([5]u32{ 1, 0, 1, 0, 2 }, counts);
}

The clamp checks come first so that @enumFromInt is only ever given 0 to 4; without them, .a.improve() would build the value 5 and panic. letter leans on @tagName so the display letter can never disagree with the source.

Exercise 13.3 · Typed IDs practice

Declare PersonId and UnitId exactly as IRON LEDGER does, then write a generator that hands out fresh IDs, a Pilot whose unit defaults to .none, and a parser from text. Name the file: exercises/13-enums/ex3_ids.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 13, exercise 3: typed IDs with non-exhaustive enums.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_ids.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

pub const PersonId = enum(u32) { none = 0, _ };
pub const UnitId = enum(u32) { none = 0, _ };

/// Hands out fresh PersonIds, starting at 1.
const IdGen = struct {
    next: u32 = 1,

    pub fn newPerson(self: *IdGen) PersonId {
        const id: PersonId = @enumFromInt(self.next);
        self.next += 1;
        return id;
    }
};

/// A pilot may or may not be assigned to a unit.
const Pilot = struct {
    id: PersonId,
    unit: UnitId = .none,

    pub fn isAssigned(self: Pilot) bool {
        return self.unit != .none;
    }
};

/// Parse text like "7" into a PersonId. "0" or garbage is null.
fn parsePersonId(s: []const u8) ?PersonId {
    const n = std.fmt.parseInt(u32, s, 10) catch return null;
    if (n == 0) return null;
    return @enumFromInt(n);
}

test "ids are distinct values" {
    var gen = IdGen{};
    const a = gen.newPerson();
    const b = gen.newPerson();
    try std.testing.expect(a != b);
    try std.testing.expect(a != .none);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 1), @intFromEnum(a));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 2), @intFromEnum(b));
}

test "assignment uses .none as absent" {
    var gen = IdGen{};
    var p = Pilot{ .id = gen.newPerson() };
    try std.testing.expect(!p.isAssigned());
    p.unit = @enumFromInt(42);
    try std.testing.expect(p.isAssigned());
}

test "parsing" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?PersonId, @enumFromInt(7)), parsePersonId("7"));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?PersonId, null), parsePersonId("0"));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?PersonId, null), parsePersonId("seven"));
}

test "ids cost nothing" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@sizeOf(u32), @sizeOf(PersonId));
}

The last test is the point of the exercise: @sizeOf(PersonId) == @sizeOf(u32). Type safety here is free at runtime. The parser refuses zero so that .none can only be produced on purpose, never by a user typing 0.

Exercise 13.4 · A day-phase state machine challenge

The phases of a campaign day are an ordered enum. Implement next (using std.enums.values), before, a label that capitalises the tag name into a buffer, and runDay, which steps from a starting phase to the end. Name the file: exercises/13-enums/ex4_phases.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 13, exercise 4: a day-phase state machine (challenge).
//! Run with:  zig test ex4_phases.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// The phases of one campaign day, in order.
const Phase = enum(u8) {
    travel,
    supply,
    events,
    battle,
    finances,
    decisions,

    /// The next phase, or null after the last one.
    pub fn next(self: Phase) ?Phase {
        const all = std.enums.values(Phase);
        const i = @intFromEnum(self);
        if (i + 1 >= all.len) return null;
        return all[i + 1];
    }

    /// True when `self` happens before `other`.
    pub fn before(self: Phase, other: Phase) bool {
        return @intFromEnum(self) < @intFromEnum(other);
    }

    /// Human label: the tag name with the first letter upper-cased, into buf.
    pub fn label(self: Phase, buf: []u8) []const u8 {
        const name = @tagName(self);
        @memcpy(buf[0..name.len], name);
        buf[0] = std.ascii.toUpper(buf[0]);
        return buf[0..name.len];
    }
};

/// Run every phase from `start` to the end, writing the names visited into `out`.
/// Returns how many phases ran.
fn runDay(start: Phase, out: []Phase) usize {
    var n: usize = 0;
    var p: ?Phase = start;
    while (p) |cur| : (p = cur.next()) {
        out[n] = cur;
        n += 1;
    }
    return n;
}

test "next walks in declaration order" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?Phase, .supply), Phase.travel.next());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?Phase, .decisions), Phase.finances.next());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?Phase, null), Phase.decisions.next());
}

test "ordering" {
    try std.testing.expect(Phase.travel.before(.battle));
    try std.testing.expect(!Phase.battle.before(.travel));
    try std.testing.expect(!Phase.battle.before(.battle));
}

test "labels" {
    var buf: [16]u8 = undefined;
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Finances", Phase.finances.label(&buf));
}

test "runDay" {
    var out: [8]Phase = undefined;
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 6), runDay(.travel, &out));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Phase.travel, out[0]);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Phase.decisions, out[5]);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 2), runDay(.finances, &out));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Phase.finances, out[0]);
}

runDay uses while (p) |cur| : (p = cur.next()): loop while the optional holds a value, and after each pass replace it with the next phase, which becomes null after the last one. That loop shape returns in Chapter 15. IRON LEDGER's daily tick (Chapter 43) walks its DayPhase enum in the same spirit.

Check your understanding

  1. When can you write .tech instead of Role.tech?
    AnswerWhenever the expected type is known from context: a typed declaration, a parameter, a switch arm, a comparison with an existing Role.
  2. What happens when a switch over an enum leaves a value out?
    AnswerA compile error, switch must handle all possibilities, naming the unhandled value. Unless the switch has an else arm, which absorbs it silently.
  3. What do @intFromEnum and @enumFromInt do, and which one can panic?
    AnswerThey convert between an enum and its integer tag. @enumFromInt panics in safe builds if the integer matches no named value of an exhaustive enum.
  4. What does the _ at the end of enum(u32) { none = 0, _ } mean?
    AnswerThe enum is non-exhaustive: every u32 is a valid value, not only the named ones. It needs an explicit tag type.
  5. Why does IRON LEDGER use PersonId instead of u32?
    AnswerSame size, same cost, but a distinct type: passing a UnitId where a PersonId is expected is a compile error rather than a silent bug, and .none is a named absent value.
  6. How do you turn the string "doctor" into Role.doctor?
    Answerstd.meta.stringToEnum(Role, "doctor"), which returns ?Role: null if the name does not match exactly.
  7. What is the difference between else and _ as a switch arm?
    Answerelse matches every value not listed, named or not, and disables the exhaustiveness check. _ matches only the unnamed values of a non-exhaustive enum; named values must still all be handled.
What you learned.
  • const E = enum { a, b, c }; declares a closed set; write values as E.a or, with context, .a. Enums compare with ==.
  • Enums hold methods and constants like structs. switch over an enum must be exhaustive unless it has else; grouped arms use commas.
  • enum(u8) fixes the tag type; values may be assigned explicitly. @intFromEnum and @enumFromInt convert; the latter is checked.
  • enum(u32) { none = 0, _ } is a non-exhaustive enum: a typed integer with a named "none". IRON LEDGER uses it for every ID. Switch on it with _.
  • @tagName gives the name; std.meta.stringToEnum parses one; std.enums.values lists them all.
  • A bare .name is an enum literal that becomes whatever enum the context needs.

14. Unions and tagged unions

In this chapter you will learn the type that IRON LEDGER is built around: the tagged union, a value that is exactly one of several alternatives, each with its own data, and always knows which. You will build them, switch over them with payload captures, modify payloads in place, give them methods, and use them as commands, messages and machine states, ending with a small interpreter. If you know Rust enums, Swift enums with associated values, or Haskell sum types, this is Zig's version.

14.1 Bare unions, briefly

A plain union is a piece of memory that can hold one of several fields, one at a time. It is as big as its largest field, and it does not remember which field you stored.

bare.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Number = union {
    int: i64,
    float: f64,
};

pub fn main() void {
    const n = Number{ .int = 42 };
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{n.int});
    std.debug.print("{d} bytes\n", .{@sizeOf(Number)});
}
42
16 bytes

Sixteen bytes, not eight, because safe builds quietly add a hidden tag so they can catch the following mistake:

const std = @import("std");

const Number = union {
    int: i64,
    float: f64,
};

pub fn main() void {
    const n = Number{ .int = 42 };
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{n.float});
}
bare_wrong.zig:10:33: error: access of union field 'float' while field 'int' is active
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{n.float});
                               ~^~~~~~
bare_wrong.zig:3:16: note: union declared here
const Number = union {
               ^~~~~
referenced by:
    callMain [inlined]: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:698:59
    callMainWithArgs [inlined]: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:638:20
    main: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:663:28
    1 reference(s) hidden; use '-freference-trace=4' to see all references

Here the compiler could see the active field; when it cannot, Debug builds panic at runtime instead. Bare unions are for the rare cases where you are reinterpreting memory on purpose, usually at a C boundary (Chapter 35). For everything else, you want the union to carry its tag, so you can ask it which field is active. That is the tagged union.

14.2 union(enum)

Write union(enum) and Zig generates an enum with one member per field, stores its value alongside the data, and keeps it in sync. Here is IRON LEDGER's terminal key type, trimmed:

tagged.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Key = union(enum) {
    char: u21, // a typed character, with its code point
    f: u8, // F1..F12, with the number
    ctrl: u8, // ctrl + a letter
    enter, // no payload: like an enum member
    escape,
    none,
};

pub fn main() void {
    const keys = [_]Key{
        .{ .char = 'q' },
        .{ .f = 3 },
        .{ .ctrl = 'c' },
        .enter,
        .none,
    };
    for (keys) |k| {
        std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{k});
    }
    std.debug.print("{d} bytes\n", .{@sizeOf(Key)});
}
.{ .char = 113 }
.{ .f = 3 }
.{ .ctrl = 99 }
.{ .enter = void }
.{ .none = void }
8 bytes

Three things to read off this. First, the fields: char: u21 has a payload (which character), f: u8 has a payload (which function key), and enter has none, which makes it behave like a plain enum member. A union can mix both freely; void is the implied payload type of a bare name.

Second, the literals. A field with a payload is built as .{ .char = 'q' }, the same anonymous-literal shape as a struct with one field. A field without one is written like an enum value: .enter. Both coerce to Key from context.

Third, the size: eight bytes, which is a u21 rounded up to four bytes, plus the tag, plus padding. Compared with the bare union's hidden tag, this one is yours to inspect.

Key.enter is not a Key. Writing the type name and a payload-less field, Shape.point, gives you the tag enum's value, not a union value. It looks right and then fails with no field or member function named 'scale' in '@typeInfo(Shape).@"union".tag_type.?' the first time you call a method on it. 
const std = @import("std");

const Shape = union(enum) { circle: f64, point };

pub fn main() void {
    const a = Shape.point; // careful: this is the TAG enum value, not a Shape
    const b: Shape = .point; // this is a Shape
    std.debug.print("{any}\n{any}\n", .{ @TypeOf(a), @TypeOf(b) });
}
@typeInfo(tagenum.Shape).@"union".tag_type.?
tagenum.Shape

Always write union values with an expected type in view: const p: Shape = .point;, or .point directly in an argument or array literal.

14.3 Switching with payload captures

The tag makes switch possible, and the payload comes along in a capture:

switch.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Key = union(enum) {
    char: u21,
    f: u8,
    ctrl: u8,
    enter,
    escape,
    none,
};

fn describe(k: Key) void {
    switch (k) {
        .char => |c| std.debug.print("typed '{u}'\n", .{c}),
        .f => |n| std.debug.print("function key F{d}\n", .{n}),
        .ctrl => |c| std.debug.print("ctrl-{c}\n", .{c}),
        .enter => std.debug.print("enter\n", .{}),
        .escape, .none => std.debug.print("nothing useful\n", .{}),
    }
}

pub fn main() void {
    describe(.{ .char = 'q' });
    describe(.{ .f = 3 });
    describe(.{ .ctrl = 'c' });
    describe(.enter);
    describe(.escape);
}
typed 'q'
function key F3
ctrl-c
enter
nothing useful

Each arm names a tag with the leading dot, and |c| binds the payload of that field, typed correctly: c is a u21 in the .char arm and a u8 in the .ctrl arm. Payload-less arms have no capture. Arms can be grouped with commas as long as they do not try to capture different payload types. ({u} prints a code point as its UTF-8 character.)

Exhaustiveness works exactly as it does for enums, and it is the reason the game uses this type for its commands:

const std = @import("std");

const Key = union(enum) { char: u21, f: u8, enter, escape };

fn describe(k: Key) void {
    switch (k) {
        .char => |c| std.debug.print("typed '{u}'\n", .{c}),
        .enter => std.debug.print("enter\n", .{}),
        .escape => std.debug.print("escape\n", .{}),
    }
}

pub fn main() void {
    describe(.enter);
}
missing.zig:6:5: error: switch must handle all possibilities
    switch (k) {
    ^~~~~~
missing.zig:3:38: note: unhandled enumeration value: 'f'
const Key = union(enum) { char: u21, f: u8, enter, escape };
                                     ^
missing.zig:3:13: note: enum '@typeInfo(missing.Key).@"union".tag_type.?' declared here
const Key = union(enum) { char: u21, f: u8, enter, escape };
            ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
referenced by:
    main: missing.zig:14:13
    callMain [inlined]: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:698:59
    callMainWithArgs [inlined]: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:638:20
    main: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:663:28
    1 reference(s) hidden; use '-freference-trace=5' to see all references

Add a variant, and every switch that forgot it stops compiling. The compiler even tells you it is checking the union's tag type, that tag_type.? in the note.

Direct field access is allowed, and checked:

const std = @import("std");

const Key = union(enum) { char: u21, f: u8, enter };

pub fn main() void {
    const k = Key{ .char = 'q' };
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{k.f});
}
wrongfield.zig:7:33: error: access of union field 'f' while field 'char' is active
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{k.f});
                               ~^~
wrongfield.zig:3:13: note: union declared here
const Key = union(enum) { char: u21, f: u8, enter };
            ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
referenced by:
    callMain [inlined]: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:698:59
    callMainWithArgs [inlined]: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:638:20
    main: <zig>/lib/std/start.zig:663:28
    1 reference(s) hidden; use '-freference-trace=4' to see all references

Reading k.f when k holds a .char is a compile error here and a panic at runtime when the compiler cannot see which is active. That is why the normal way to read a payload is a switch or an if on the tag, never a bare field access on a value you have not checked.

14.4 Asking for the tag

Sometimes you only need to know which alternative is active, not what it holds:

tagquery.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Key = union(enum) { char: u21, f: u8, enter };

pub fn main() void {
    const k = Key{ .f = 5 };
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{std.meta.activeTag(k)});
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{@tagName(k)});
    std.debug.print("{}\n", .{k == .f}); // compare the tag only
    std.debug.print("{}\n", .{std.meta.activeTag(k) == .char});
    if (k == .f) std.debug.print("F{d}\n", .{k.f}); // safe: we checked
    const Tag = std.meta.Tag(Key); // the enum behind the union
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{@typeInfo(Tag).@"enum".fields.len});
}
.f
f
true
false
F5
3

std.meta.activeTag(k) returns the tag as an enum value. @tagName works directly on the union. And most conveniently, a tagged union compares with == against an enum literal, comparing only the tag: k == .f is true whatever the F-number is. That is the idiom for a quick check before touching a payload, as the if (k == .f) line does. std.meta.Tag(Key) names the generated enum type when you need to store or pass tags around.

14.5 Modifying a payload in place

A capture with |v| is a copy of the payload. To change the payload inside the union, switch on a pointer to the union and capture with |*v|:

mutate.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Damage = union(enum) {
    armor: u16, // points of armor left
    internal: u16, // structure points left
    destroyed,
};

fn hit(d: *Damage, amount: u16) void {
    switch (d.*) {
        .armor => |*left| {
            if (amount < left.*) {
                left.* -= amount; // modify the payload in place
            } else {
                d.* = .{ .internal = 10 }; // replace the whole value
            }
        },
        .internal => |*left| {
            if (amount < left.*) left.* -= amount else d.* = .destroyed;
        },
        .destroyed => {},
    }
}

pub fn main() void {
    var d = Damage{ .armor = 12 };
    for ([_]u16{ 5, 5, 5, 5, 20 }) |amt| {
        hit(&d, amt);
        std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{d});
    }
}
.{ .armor = 7 }
.{ .armor = 2 }
.{ .internal = 10 }
.{ .internal = 5 }
.{ .destroyed = void }

Two kinds of change appear here. left.* -= amount changes the number stored in the active field without changing which field is active. d.* = .{ .internal = 10 } replaces the whole union, tag and all, which is how a value moves from one state to the next. Note that the switch is on d.*, the union itself, and the pointer capture then refers into it; the same shape works on self.* inside a method.

14.6 Methods on unions

Like structs and enums, unions can hold functions. A method that only reads takes the union by value and switches on it; one that modifies takes a pointer:

methods.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Shape = union(enum) {
    circle: f64, // radius
    rect: struct { w: f64, h: f64 },
    point,

    pub fn area(self: Shape) f64 {
        return switch (self) {
            .circle => |r| std.math.pi * r * r,
            .rect => |r| r.w * r.h,
            .point => 0,
        };
    }

    pub fn scale(self: *Shape, k: f64) void {
        switch (self.*) {
            .circle => |*r| r.* *= k,
            .rect => |*r| {
                r.w *= k;
                r.h *= k;
            },
            .point => {},
        }
    }
};

pub fn main() void {
    var shapes = [_]Shape{ .{ .circle = 1 }, .{ .rect = .{ .w = 2, .h = 3 } }, .point };
    for (&shapes) |*s| {
        s.scale(2);
        std.debug.print("{s}: {d:.2}\n", .{ @tagName(s.*), s.area() });
    }
}
circle: 12.57
rect: 24.00
point: 0.00

rect carries an inline struct as its payload, so |r| gives you something with .w and .h. A union with methods that switch on self is Zig's answer to a class hierarchy with a virtual method: one type, every alternative listed, every case handled in one place, no allocation and no pointers. The trade-off is the same one enums make: adding an alternative touches every switch, and the compiler tells you where.

A union may also name an existing enum as its tag, union(Kind), when you want control over the tag's integer values or want to share the enum elsewhere. A tagged union then coerces to that enum:

explicit_tag.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Kind = enum(u8) { text = 1, number = 2, nothing = 3 };

const Value = union(Kind) {
    text: []const u8,
    number: i64,
    nothing,
};

pub fn main() void {
    const v = Value{ .number = 7 };
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{@intFromEnum(std.meta.activeTag(v))});
    const k: Kind = v; // a tagged union coerces to its tag enum
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{k});
}
2
.number

14.7 Commands, messages and state machines

The most useful thing to do with a tagged union is to make the set of things that can happen into a type. Here is a tiny version of IRON LEDGER's command loop:

commands.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Command = union(enum) {
    advance_day,
    advance_days: u32,
    hire: struct { name: []const u8, salary: i64 },
    fire: u32,
    rename: []const u8,
};

const State = struct {
    day: u32 = 1,
    name: []const u8 = "Unnamed Company",
    staff: u32 = 0,
    funds: i64 = 1_000_000,
};

fn execute(s: *State, cmd: Command) void {
    switch (cmd) {
        .advance_day => s.day += 1,
        .advance_days => |n| s.day += n,
        .hire => |h| {
            s.staff += 1;
            s.funds -= h.salary;
            std.debug.print("hired {s}\n", .{h.name});
        },
        .fire => |id| {
            s.staff -= 1;
            std.debug.print("fired #{d}\n", .{id});
        },
        .rename => |new_name| s.name = new_name,
    }
}

pub fn main() void {
    var s = State{};
    const script = [_]Command{
        .{ .rename = "Grey Death Legion" },
        .{ .hire = .{ .name = "Kai", .salary = 1_500 } },
        .{ .hire = .{ .name = "Nat", .salary = 800 } },
        .advance_day,
        .{ .advance_days = 30 },
        .{ .fire = 2 },
    };
    for (script) |cmd| execute(&s, cmd);
    std.debug.print("{s}: day {d}, {d} staff, {d} C-bills\n", .{
        s.name, s.day, s.staff, s.funds,
    });
}
hired Kai
hired Nat
fired #2
Grey Death Legion: day 32, 1 staff, 997700 C-bills

Every possible request is a Command; the state is only ever changed inside execute; and the script is plain data, an array of commands, that can be built by a parser, read from a file, or written by a test. That separation, where the union is the only way in, is the architecture of the whole game (Chapter 42), and you have now seen all of the language it takes.

The same trick describes a value that changes state over time. Damage in 14.5 was a state machine: armor, then internal, then destroyed, each state carrying only the data that state needs. Compare that with a struct holding an armor field, an internal field and a destroyed flag, where nothing stops destroyed = true alongside armor = 12.

Unions can also refer to themselves through pointers, which is how tree-shaped data is built. An arithmetic expression is a number, or a negation of an expression, or a sum or product of two:

expr.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Expr = union(enum) {
    num: i64,
    neg: *const Expr,
    add: struct { l: *const Expr, r: *const Expr },
    mul: struct { l: *const Expr, r: *const Expr },

    pub fn eval(self: Expr) i64 {
        return switch (self) {
            .num => |n| n,
            .neg => |e| -e.eval(),
            .add => |p| p.l.eval() + p.r.eval(),
            .mul => |p| p.l.eval() * p.r.eval(),
        };
    }
};

pub fn main() void {
    // (2 + 3) * -4
    const two = Expr{ .num = 2 };
    const three = Expr{ .num = 3 };
    const four = Expr{ .num = 4 };
    const sum = Expr{ .add = .{ .l = &two, .r = &three } };
    const neg4 = Expr{ .neg = &four };
    const prod = Expr{ .mul = .{ .l = &sum, .r = &neg4 } };
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{prod.eval()});
}
-20

The payloads hold *const Expr, pointers to other expressions, because a union cannot contain itself by value (it would be infinitely large). The nodes here are locals whose addresses are taken; a real interpreter would allocate them (Chapter 19). eval is a method that recurses through the switch, four lines for a whole evaluator.

14.8 Coming from other languages

You knowIn Zig
Rust enum Key { Char(char), F(u8), Enter }union(enum) { char: u21, f: u8, enter }; match is switch with |v| captures
Swift enum with associated valuessame idea; if case becomes if (k == .f) then k.f, or a switch
C struct { int tag; union { ... } u; }the tag is generated and kept in sync for you; wrong-field reads are caught
TypeScript discriminated union { kind: "f", n: number } | ...same shape, but checked at compile time and stored in a fixed number of bytes
Java/Python class hierarchy with a virtual methodone union with a method that switches on self; no heap, all cases visible in one place
In IRON LEDGER. The game is driven by a single tagged union. Every action a player or a script can take is a variant, and the only function that changes a GameState is the switch over it: 
// src/sim/commands.zig
pub const Command = union(enum) {
    /// End the turn: advance one day.
    advance_day,
    advance_days: u32,
    hire: struct {
        first: []const u8,
        last: []const u8,
        role: person_mod.Role,
    },
    /// Hire a randomly generated candidate (experience rolled on 2d6).
    recruit: person_mod.Role,
    fire: types.PersonId,
    new_company: []const u8,
    rename_force: struct { force: types.ForceId, name: []const u8 },
    // ... about forty more
};

pub fn execute(gs: *GameState, cmd: Command) Error!Result {
    switch (cmd) {
        .advance_day => return advance(gs, 1),
        .advance_days => |n| return advance(gs, n),
        .hire => |h| {
            const id = try gs.hirePerson(h.first, h.last, h.role);
            return .{ .hired = id };
        },
        .recruit => |role| {
            const id = try gs.recruitGenerated(role);
            return .{ .hired = id };
        },
        // ...
    }
}

|n| binds the u32 of advance_days; |h| binds the inline struct so h.first works. Add a variant to Command and this switch fails to compile until you handle it. The same shape at a smaller scale is Key in src/tui/term.zig, whose readKey turns raw bytes into .enter, .{ .ctrl = 'a' + b - 1 } and .{ .f = 3 } with a switch over integer ranges, which exercise 14.2 has you rebuild.

Exercises

Exercise 14.1 · Shapes with methods warm-up

Give Shape four methods: area, perimeter, an in-place scale using |*v| captures, and simplify, which turns an equal-sided rect into a square. Name the file: exercises/14-unions/ex1_shapes.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 14, exercise 1: a tagged union with methods.
//! Run with:  zig test ex1_shapes.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Shape = union(enum) {
    circle: f64, // radius
    rect: struct { w: f64, h: f64 },
    square: f64, // side
    point,

    pub fn area(self: Shape) f64 {
        return switch (self) {
            .circle => |r| std.math.pi * r * r,
            .rect => |r| r.w * r.h,
            .square => |s| s * s,
            .point => 0,
        };
    }

    pub fn perimeter(self: Shape) f64 {
        return switch (self) {
            .circle => |r| 2 * std.math.pi * r,
            .rect => |r| 2 * (r.w + r.h),
            .square => |s| 4 * s,
            .point => 0,
        };
    }

    /// Scale every dimension by k, in place.
    pub fn scale(self: *Shape, k: f64) void {
        switch (self.*) {
            .circle => |*r| r.* *= k,
            .rect => |*r| {
                r.w *= k;
                r.h *= k;
            },
            .square => |*s| s.* *= k,
            .point => {},
        }
    }

    /// A rect whose sides are equal is really a square; normalise it.
    pub fn simplify(self: Shape) Shape {
        return switch (self) {
            .rect => |r| if (r.w == r.h) Shape{ .square = r.w } else self,
            else => self,
        };
    }
};

test "area and perimeter" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(f64, 6), (Shape{ .rect = .{ .w = 2, .h = 3 } }).area());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(f64, 10), (Shape{ .rect = .{ .w = 2, .h = 3 } }).perimeter());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(f64, 9), (Shape{ .square = 3 }).area());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(f64, 0), (Shape{ .point = {} }).area());
    try std.testing.expectApproxEqAbs(@as(f64, 3.14159), (Shape{ .circle = 1 }).area(), 0.001);
}

test "scale in place" {
    var s = Shape{ .rect = .{ .w = 2, .h = 3 } };
    s.scale(2);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(f64, 24), s.area());
    var p: Shape = .point;
    p.scale(100);
    try std.testing.expect(p == .point);
}

test "simplify" {
    const sq = (Shape{ .rect = .{ .w = 2, .h = 2 } }).simplify();
    try std.testing.expect(sq == .square);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(f64, 2), sq.square);
    const r = (Shape{ .rect = .{ .w = 2, .h = 3 } }).simplify();
    try std.testing.expect(r == .rect);
}

scale switches on self.* and captures pointers so the multiplication lands inside the union. simplify uses else => self: only rect needs thought, and returning the value unchanged is the correct default for every future variant. Note var p: Shape = .point; in the test, not Shape.point, for the reason in 14.2.

Exercise 14.2 · Decoding keys practice

Rebuild the byte-to-key decoder from src/tui/term.zig: a switch over a u8 with ranges and lists producing Key values; a describe that prints a key into a buffer; and countChars, which compares tags. Name the file: exercises/14-unions/ex2_keys.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 14, exercise 2: decoding bytes into keys.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_keys.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// IRON LEDGER's terminal key type, trimmed.
const Key = union(enum) {
    char: u21,
    enter,
    escape,
    tab,
    backspace,
    ctrl: u8, // 'a'..'z'
    none,
};

/// Decode one raw byte the way src/tui/term.zig does.
fn decode(b: u8) Key {
    return switch (b) {
        0x1b => .escape,
        '\r', '\n' => .enter,
        '\t' => .tab,
        0x7f, 0x08 => .backspace,
        1...7, 11, 12, 14...26 => .{ .ctrl = 'a' + b - 1 },
        else => .{ .char = b },
    };
}

/// A short human name for a key, into buf.
fn describe(k: Key, buf: []u8) ![]const u8 {
    return switch (k) {
        .char => |c| std.fmt.bufPrint(buf, "'{u}'", .{c}),
        .ctrl => |c| std.fmt.bufPrint(buf, "ctrl-{c}", .{c}),
        .enter, .escape, .tab, .backspace, .none => @tagName(k),
    };
}

/// Count how many of the keys are printable characters.
fn countChars(keys: []const Key) usize {
    var n: usize = 0;
    for (keys) |k| {
        if (k == .char) n += 1;
    }
    return n;
}

test "decode" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Key.escape, decode(0x1b));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Key.enter, decode('\n'));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Key.backspace, decode(0x7f));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Key{ .ctrl = 'c' }, decode(3));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Key{ .ctrl = 'z' }, decode(26));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Key{ .char = 'q' }, decode('q'));
}

test "describe" {
    var buf: [16]u8 = undefined;
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("'q'", try describe(.{ .char = 'q' }, &buf));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("ctrl-c", try describe(.{ .ctrl = 'c' }, &buf));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("escape", try describe(.escape, &buf));
}

test "countChars" {
    const keys = [_]Key{ .{ .char = 'a' }, .enter, .{ .char = 'b' }, .{ .ctrl = 'c' }, .none };
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 2), countChars(&keys));
}

1...7, 11, 12, 14...26 is the game's own arm: the control characters that are not tab, newline or carriage return. The describe switch mixes arms that return a formatted slice with arms that return @tagName(k); both are []const u8, so the switch has one type.

Exercise 14.3 · Commands practice

A Command union drives a small State. Implement execute (one exhaustive switch, returning errors for impossible requests) and parse, which turns a line of text into a command or null. The last test runs a script of six lines through both. Name the file: exercises/14-unions/ex3_commands.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 14, exercise 3: commands as a tagged union.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_commands.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Command = union(enum) {
    advance_day,
    advance_days: u32,
    hire: struct { name: []const u8, salary: i64 },
    fire: u32, // staff index
    deposit: i64,
};

const Error = error{ NoSuchPerson, InsufficientFunds, TooManyStaff };

const State = struct {
    day: u32 = 1,
    funds: i64 = 10_000,
    staff: [4]?[]const u8 = .{ null, null, null, null },

    fn headcount(self: State) usize {
        var n: usize = 0;
        for (self.staff) |s| {
            if (s != null) n += 1;
        }
        return n;
    }
};

fn execute(s: *State, cmd: Command) Error!void {
    switch (cmd) {
        .advance_day => s.day += 1,
        .advance_days => |n| s.day += n,
        .hire => |h| {
            if (h.salary > s.funds) return error.InsufficientFunds;
            for (&s.staff) |*slot| {
                if (slot.* == null) {
                    slot.* = h.name;
                    s.funds -= h.salary;
                    return;
                }
            }
            return error.TooManyStaff;
        },
        .fire => |i| {
            if (i >= s.staff.len or s.staff[i] == null) return error.NoSuchPerson;
            s.staff[i] = null;
        },
        .deposit => |amt| s.funds += amt,
    }
}

/// Parse an optional token as a number; a missing token is an error too.
fn num(comptime T: type, tok: ?[]const u8) !T {
    return std.fmt.parseInt(T, tok orelse "", 10);
}

/// Parse one line of text into a command, or null for an unknown verb.
fn parse(line: []const u8) !?Command {
    var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, line, ' ');
    const verb = it.next() orelse return null;
    const eq = std.mem.eql;
    if (eq(u8, verb, "day")) return .advance_day;
    if (eq(u8, verb, "days")) return .{ .advance_days = try num(u32, it.next()) };
    if (eq(u8, verb, "fire")) return .{ .fire = try num(u32, it.next()) };
    if (eq(u8, verb, "deposit")) return .{ .deposit = try num(i64, it.next()) };
    if (eq(u8, verb, "hire")) {
        const name = it.next() orelse return error.InvalidCharacter;
        const salary = try num(i64, it.next());
        return .{ .hire = .{ .name = name, .salary = salary } };
    }
    return null;
}

test "execute" {
    var s = State{};
    try execute(&s, .{ .hire = .{ .name = "Kai", .salary = 1_500 } });
    try execute(&s, .{ .advance_days = 10 });
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 11), s.day);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 8_500), s.funds);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 1), s.headcount());
    try execute(&s, .{ .fire = 0 });
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 0), s.headcount());
}

test "errors" {
    var s = State{ .funds = 100 };
    const kai: Command = .{ .hire = .{ .name = "Kai", .salary = 1_500 } };
    try std.testing.expectError(error.InsufficientFunds, execute(&s, kai));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.NoSuchPerson, execute(&s, .{ .fire = 2 }));
    s.funds = 1_000_000;
    for ([_][]const u8{ "a", "b", "c", "d" }) |n| {
        try execute(&s, .{ .hire = .{ .name = n, .salary = 1 } });
    }
    const one_more: Command = .{ .hire = .{ .name = "e", .salary = 1 } };
    try std.testing.expectError(error.TooManyStaff, execute(&s, one_more));
}

test "parse" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?Command, .advance_day), try parse("day"));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?Command, .{ .advance_days = 30 }), try parse("days 30"));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?Command, null), try parse("dance"));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.InvalidCharacter, parse("days thirty"));
    const h = (try parse("hire Kai 1500")).?;
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Kai", h.hire.name);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 1500), h.hire.salary);
}

test "a script" {
    var s = State{};
    const lines = [_][]const u8{
        "hire Kai 1500", "hire Nat 800", "deposit 5000", "days 30", "fire 1", "day",
    };
    for (lines) |l| {
        const cmd = (try parse(l)) orelse continue;
        try execute(&s, cmd);
    }
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 32), s.day);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 12_700), s.funds);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 1), s.headcount());
}

This is the guide's parseCommand in miniature, down to the const eq = std.mem.eql; shortcut and the !?Command return type: an error for a malformed number, null for an unknown verb, a command otherwise. expectEqual compares tagged unions by tag and payload, so .{ .advance_days = 30 } can be checked directly.

Exercise 14.4 · A stack-machine interpreter challenge

Op is an instruction set: push, arithmetic, dup, swap, a conditional jump and halt. Write the switch inside Machine.run. The tests include a countdown loop, so the jump must work, and a step limit turns an endless program into error.NoHalt. Name the file: exercises/14-unions/ex4_interpreter.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 14, exercise 4: a tiny stack-machine interpreter (challenge).
//! Run with:  zig test ex4_interpreter.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// One instruction for a stack machine.
const Op = union(enum) {
    push: i64,
    add,
    sub,
    mul,
    dup,
    swap,
    jump_if_zero: usize, // pop; if zero, jump to this instruction index
