    halt,
};

const Error = error{ StackUnderflow, StackOverflow, BadJump, NoHalt };

const Machine = struct {
    stack: [16]i64 = undefined,
    sp: usize = 0, // number of values on the stack
    pc: usize = 0, // index of the next instruction
    steps: usize = 0,

    fn push(self: *Machine, v: i64) Error!void {
        if (self.sp == self.stack.len) return error.StackOverflow;
        self.stack[self.sp] = v;
        self.sp += 1;
    }

    fn pop(self: *Machine) Error!i64 {
        if (self.sp == 0) return error.StackUnderflow;
        self.sp -= 1;
        return self.stack[self.sp];
    }

    /// Run until halt. Returns the top of the stack (or 0 if empty).
    fn run(self: *Machine, program: []const Op) Error!i64 {
        while (self.pc < program.len) {
            const op = program[self.pc];
            self.pc += 1;
            self.steps += 1;
            if (self.steps > 10_000) return error.NoHalt;
            switch (op) {
                .push => |v| try self.push(v),
                .add => try self.push(try self.pop() + try self.pop()),
                .mul => try self.push(try self.pop() * try self.pop()),
                .sub => {
                    const b = try self.pop();
                    const a = try self.pop();
                    try self.push(a - b);
                },
                .dup => {
                    const a = try self.pop();
                    try self.push(a);
                    try self.push(a);
                },
                .swap => {
                    const b = try self.pop();
                    const a = try self.pop();
                    try self.push(b);
                    try self.push(a);
                },
                .jump_if_zero => |target| {
                    if (target > program.len) return error.BadJump;
                    if ((try self.pop()) == 0) self.pc = target;
                },
                .halt => return if (self.sp == 0) 0 else self.stack[self.sp - 1],
            }
        }
        return error.NoHalt;
    }
};

fn runProgram(program: []const Op) Error!i64 {
    var m = Machine{};
    return m.run(program);
}

test "arithmetic" {
    // (2 + 3) * 4 - 1
    const prog = [_]Op{
        .{ .push = 2 }, .{ .push = 3 }, .add, .{ .push = 4 }, .mul, .{ .push = 1 }, .sub, .halt,
    };
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 19), try runProgram(&prog));
}

test "dup and swap" {
    const prog = [_]Op{ .{ .push = 7 }, .dup, .mul, .{ .push = 100 }, .swap, .sub, .halt };
    // swap turns [49, 100] into [100, 49], so sub computes 100 - 49
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 100 - 49), try runProgram(&prog));
}

test "errors" {
    try std.testing.expectError(error.StackUnderflow, runProgram(&[_]Op{ .add, .halt }));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.NoHalt, runProgram(&[_]Op{.{ .push = 1 }}));
    const bad = [_]Op{ .{ .push = 0 }, .{ .jump_if_zero = 99 }, .halt };
    try std.testing.expectError(error.BadJump, runProgram(&bad));
}

test "countdown loop" {
    // n = 5; while (n != 0) n -= 1; leaves 0 on the stack.
    const prog = [_]Op{
        .{ .push = 5 }, // 0
        .dup, // 1: copy n so the test does not consume it
        .{ .jump_if_zero = 7 }, // 2: if n == 0 go to halt
        .{ .push = 1 }, // 3
        .sub, // 4: n = n - 1
        .{ .push = 0 }, // 5
        .{ .jump_if_zero = 1 }, // 6: always jumps (0 is zero)
        .halt, // 7
    };
    var m = Machine{};
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 0), try m.run(&prog));
    try std.testing.expect(m.steps < 100);
}

Every instruction is one arm. sub and swap pop in the right order (b first, since it was pushed last), which the dup and swap test checks: 100 - 49, not 49 - 100. halt is the only arm that returns a value; every other path returns an error, so the function's result type is Error!i64 and the tests use try and expectError as usual.

Check your understanding

  1. What does a tagged union store that a bare union does not?
    AnswerAn enum tag saying which field is active, kept in sync automatically and available to switch, == against a literal, @tagName and std.meta.activeTag.
  2. How do you build a Key holding ctrl-c, and one holding enter?
    Answer.{ .ctrl = 'c' } and .enter, both with a Key expected from context (a typed variable, a parameter, an array element).
  3. What is the difference between |v| and |*v| in a switch arm?
    Answer|v| copies the payload; |*v| gives a pointer to it, which requires switching on a pointer's target (switch (p.*)) and lets you modify the payload in place.
  4. What does k == .f compare?
    AnswerOnly the tag. It is true for any Key whose active field is f, regardless of payload.
  5. Why does reading k.f when k holds .char not silently return garbage?
    AnswerSafe builds check the tag on every field access: a compile error when the active field is known, a panic otherwise.
  6. Why is Shape.point a trap?
    AnswerIt names the generated tag enum's value, not a Shape. Use const p: Shape = .point; so the union type is expected.
  7. Why must a self-referential union hold *const Expr rather than Expr?
    AnswerA value containing itself would have infinite size. A pointer has a fixed size and can refer to another node stored elsewhere.
What you learned.
  • A bare union is one-of-several without a remembered tag; use it only for deliberate memory reinterpretation.
  • union(enum) { a: T, b: U, c } generates and stores a tag; payload-less fields act like enum members.
  • Build with .{ .a = value } or .c where the union type is expected; Type.c is the tag enum, not the union.
  • switch is exhaustive and captures payloads with |v|; |*v| on switch (p.*) modifies in place; assigning a new literal changes state.
  • k == .tag, @tagName(k), std.meta.activeTag(k) and std.meta.Tag(T) work with the tag alone.
  • Unions take methods like structs; union(SomeEnum) uses an explicit tag type and coerces to it.
  • Commands, messages, states and expression trees are all tagged unions; IRON LEDGER's Command is the only way into its game state.

15. Optionals

In this chapter you will learn how Zig represents "a value that might not be there". You will write the optional type ?T, unwrap it with orelse, if, while and .?, and see why an optional pointer costs nothing. By the end you will read a chain like if (gs.person(id)) |p| if (p.born_day) |born| without slowing down.

15.1 The problem with "nothing"

Every program has values that are sometimes missing. A pilot may have no birthday on record. A lookup by name may find nobody. A parser may reach the end of the input. Most languages you have used answer this with a special value: None in Python, null or undefined in JavaScript, NULL in C. The trouble is that in those languages any variable can hold the special value, so any line of code might be the one that trips over it. "Cannot read property of undefined" is the most common runtime error in JavaScript for exactly this reason.

Zig takes a different position. A plain u32 is always a number. A plain *Pilot always points at a pilot. If a value may be absent, its type says so, and the compiler refuses to let you use it as if it were present until you have checked. The type is written with a question mark in front: ?u32 is "maybe a u32", ?*Pilot is "maybe a pointer to a Pilot", ?[]const u8 is "maybe a string".

The absent value is spelled null. It is only ever a valid value for an optional type. You cannot put null into a u32, and the compiler will tell you so.

15.2 Declaring and printing an optional

Here is the smallest program that uses one.

opt1.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var maybe_age: ?u32 = null;
    std.debug.print("start: {?}\n", .{maybe_age});

    maybe_age = 27;
    std.debug.print("later: {?}\n", .{maybe_age});

    const shown: u32 = maybe_age orelse 0;
    std.debug.print("shown: {d}\n", .{shown});

    const nothing: ?u32 = null;
    std.debug.print("fallback: {d}\n", .{nothing orelse 0});
}
start: null
later: 27
shown: 27
fallback: 0

Four things to notice. First, the variable is declared as ?u32 and starts out as null. Second, assigning a plain 27 to it works without ceremony: a u32 coerces into a ?u32 automatically, because "definitely 27" is a fine answer to "maybe a number". The coercion never goes the other way. Third, the format specifier {?} prints an optional, showing either the value or the word null. Fourth, orelse turns the optional back into a plain value by supplying what to use when it is null.

What happens if you try to use a ?u32 where a u32 is required, without unwrapping it?

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const age: ?u32 = 27;
    const n: u32 = age; // error: cannot assign ?u32 to u32
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{n});
}
opt2.zig:5:20: error: expected type 'u32', found '?u32'
    const n: u32 = age; // error: cannot assign ?u32 to u32
                   ^~~
opt2.zig:5:20: note: cannot convert optional to payload type
opt2.zig:5:20: note: consider using '.?', 'orelse', or 'if'
…

Read that error message slowly, because you will see it often in your first weeks: "cannot convert optional to payload type", followed by a helpful list of the three ways to fix it. The payload is the value inside the optional. The rest of this chapter is those three ways.

15.3 Functions that return optionals

The most common place an optional appears is as the return type of a search. Here is a roster and a function that finds a name's position in it.

opt3.zig

const std = @import("std");

const pilots = [_][]const u8{ "Kerensky", "Steiner", "Liao" };

/// Position of a pilot in the roster, or null if not there.
fn indexOfPilot(name: []const u8) ?usize {
    for (pilots, 0..) |p, i| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, p, name)) return i;
    }
    return null;
}

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("Steiner -> {?}\n", .{indexOfPilot("Steiner")});
    std.debug.print("Davion  -> {?}\n", .{indexOfPilot("Davion")});
}
Steiner -> 1
Davion  -> null

The function's return type is ?usize. Inside it, return i returns a plain usize, which coerces to the optional. return null is the "not found" answer. In Python you might return -1 or raise an exception; in C you would return -1 or SIZE_MAX and hope every caller remembers to check. Here, every caller must deal with the possibility of null, because a ?usize cannot be used as an index until it is unwrapped.

15.4 orelse: a fallback, or an early exit

You have already seen x orelse 0: if x is present, use its value; otherwise use 0. The right-hand side of orelse can be any expression of the payload type. But it can also be something that does not produce a value at all: a return, a break, a continue, or unreachable. This is the form you will see the most in real code.

opt4.zig

const std = @import("std");

const pilots = [_][]const u8{ "Kerensky", "Steiner", "Liao" };

fn indexOfPilot(name: []const u8) ?usize {
    for (pilots, 0..) |p, i| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, p, name)) return i;
    }
    return null;
}

/// The pilot after `name` in the roster, or null if `name` is unknown
/// or is the last one. `orelse return null` ends the function early.
fn nextPilot(name: []const u8) ?[]const u8 {
    const i = indexOfPilot(name) orelse return null;
    if (i + 1 >= pilots.len) return null;
    return pilots[i + 1];
}

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("after Kerensky: {?s}\n", .{nextPilot("Kerensky")});
    std.debug.print("after Liao:     {?s}\n", .{nextPilot("Liao")});
    std.debug.print("after Davion:   {?s}\n", .{nextPilot("Davion")});

    // We *know* Steiner is in the roster, so null is impossible here.
    const i = indexOfPilot("Steiner") orelse unreachable;
    std.debug.print("Steiner sits at {d}\n", .{i});
}
after Kerensky: Steiner
after Liao:     null
after Davion:   null
Steiner sits at 1

Look at the first line of nextPilot: const i = indexOfPilot(name) orelse return null;. If the lookup finds nothing, the function returns right there and the rest of the body never runs. If it finds something, i is a plain usize, not an optional, and the code after it is free to use it as an index. This one line replaces a whole if (x == null) return null; block, and it is why Zig functions that do several lookups in a row stay flat instead of nesting.

The last form, orelse unreachable, says "I know this is never null". In a Debug build, if you are wrong, the program panics with a clear message. In a release build with safety off, it is undefined behaviour. Use it only when the surrounding code has already guaranteed the value is there, as in the example: we looked up a name that is literally in the array.

The format specifier {?s} is worth remembering: it prints an optional string, showing null when absent. In general, ? followed by the specifier you would use for the payload works for any optional.

15.5 if (x) |v|: run code only when present

When you want to do something with the value if it is there and something else if it is not, use if with a capture. The bars around v introduce a new constant holding the unwrapped payload, visible only inside the following block.

opt5.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn describe(slot: ?u8) void {
    if (slot) |n| {
        std.debug.print("slot holds {d}\n", .{n});
    } else {
        std.debug.print("slot is empty\n", .{});
    }
}

pub fn main() void {
    describe(4);
    describe(null);

    // if/else as an expression, choosing a value
    const a: ?u8 = 4;
    const b: ?u8 = null;
    const tonnage_a: u8 = if (a) |v| v * 10 else 50;
    const tonnage_b: u8 = if (b) |v| v * 10 else 50;
    std.debug.print("{d} {d}\n", .{ tonnage_a, tonnage_b });

    // comparing with null directly, no unwrap needed
    std.debug.print("a == null? {}\n", .{a == null});
    std.debug.print("b == null? {}\n", .{b == null});
    std.debug.print("a == 4?    {}\n", .{a == 4});
}
slot holds 4
slot is empty
40 50
a == null? false
b == null? true
a == 4?    true

Three forms in one file. The statement form, if (slot) |n| { … } else { … }, is what you reach for most of the time. The expression form, if (a) |v| v * 10 else 50, produces a value and is handy for computing a field from an optional lookup. IRON LEDGER uses exactly this shape to get a unit's tonnage from a catalogue entry that might be missing: const tonnage: u8 = if (chassis_mod.find(u.chassis_key)) |d| d.tonnage else 50;.

The third form is comparison. You may compare an optional to null directly with == and !=, and you may even compare it to a plain value: a == 4 is true when a holds 4 and false when it is null or holds something else. This is a common way to write a guard clause: if (p.leave_until_day != null) ….

Reading the bars. Once you have seen |v| after an if, a while, a for or a catch, you have seen the whole idea: the thing between the bars is the unwrapped value for the block that follows. It is always a fresh constant. If you need to modify the payload in place, capture a pointer to it with |*v|, which works when the optional itself is a variable you can address, as in if (self.gs) |*g| g.deinit(); from the game's terminal client.

15.6 .?: assert it is present

The third unwrapping form is the shortest. Putting .? after an optional gives you the payload, and if the optional is null the program panics.

opt6.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const present: ?u32 = 42;
    const absent: ?u32 = null;

    std.debug.print("present.? = {d}\n", .{present.?});
    std.debug.print("about to unwrap absent...\n", .{});
    std.debug.print("absent.? = {d}\n", .{absent.?});
}
present.? = 42
about to unwrap absent...
thread 12345 panic: attempt to use null value
ch15/opt6.zig:9:49: 0x… in main (opt6)
    std.debug.print("absent.? = {d}\n", .{absent.?});
                                                ^
<zig>/lib/std/start.zig:698:59: 0x… in callMain (opt6)
    if (fn_info.params.len == 0) return wrapMain(root.main());
…

That is a real panic with a real stack trace pointing at the exact expression that failed. .? is the same as orelse unreachable, spelled more briefly. Use it when nullness would be a bug in your program, not a normal outcome. A lookup by a key you just inserted, a value you checked two lines earlier, an ID handed to you by code that only produces valid IDs: those are .? situations. User input is never a .? situation.

Trap. Beginners sprinkle .? everywhere to make the compiler stop complaining. That converts a compile-time check into a run-time crash, which is exactly what optionals exist to prevent. If you find yourself typing .?, ask "what should happen if this is null?" If the honest answer is "that would be a bug", keep it. If the answer is "then skip it" or "then use a default", you want if or orelse instead.

15.7 while (it.next()) |v|: iterators

Combine an optional-returning function with a while capture and you have Zig's iterator protocol. There is no interface to implement and no special syntax to learn: any function that returns ?T can drive a loop, and the loop stops the first time it returns null.

opt7.zig

const std = @import("std");

/// Counts down from `n` to 1, then is exhausted.
const Countdown = struct {
    n: u32,

    fn next(self: *Countdown) ?u32 {
        if (self.n == 0) return null;
        const v = self.n;
        self.n -= 1;
        return v;
    }
};

pub fn main() void {
    var cd = Countdown{ .n = 3 };
    while (cd.next()) |v| {
        std.debug.print("t-minus {d}\n", .{v});
    }

    var words = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, "hire  pilot  Steiner", ' ');
    while (words.next()) |w| {
        std.debug.print("word: {s}\n", .{w});
    }
}
t-minus 3
t-minus 2
t-minus 1
word: hire
word: pilot
word: Steiner

The standard library's tokenizers, splitters, directory walkers and hash-map iterators all work this way. You saw std.mem.tokenizeScalar in Chapter 11; the while (words.next()) |w| line here is why its next returns ?[]const u8. Writing your own iterator, as Countdown does, is a matter of keeping some state in a struct and writing one next method that returns null when done.

15.8 What an optional costs

An optional needs somewhere to record "present or not". For most types that means an extra byte, padded up to the type's alignment. For pointers it costs nothing at all, because a pointer is never allowed to be zero in Zig, so the value zero is free to mean null. This is called the null pointer optimisation, and it means ?*T is exactly as cheap as the raw nullable pointer a C programmer would use, with the compiler doing the checking the C programmer had to do by hand.

opt8.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("u32:    {d} bytes\n", .{@sizeOf(u32)});
    std.debug.print("?u32:   {d} bytes\n", .{@sizeOf(?u32)});
    std.debug.print("*u32:   {d} bytes\n", .{@sizeOf(*u32)});
    std.debug.print("?*u32:  {d} bytes\n", .{@sizeOf(?*u32)});
    std.debug.print("[]u8:   {d} bytes\n", .{@sizeOf([]u8)});
    std.debug.print("?[]u8:  {d} bytes\n", .{@sizeOf(?[]u8)});
}
u32:    4 bytes
?u32:   8 bytes
*u32:   8 bytes
?*u32:  8 bytes
[]u8:   16 bytes
?[]u8:  16 bytes

?u32 doubles in size because of alignment. ?*u32 and ?[]u8 do not grow at all: a slice is a pointer plus a length, and the pointer part carries the null. So when you design a function that "finds a thing or not", returning an optional pointer, ?*const Chassis, is not a compromise. It is the natural shape.

15.9 Optional fields and chains

Optionals are how a struct expresses "not yet" or "not applicable". A person hired by a test might have no birthday. A pilot on leave has a day the leave ends; a pilot not on leave has none. Rather than a magic number like 0 or -1, the field is an optional with a default of null.

opt9.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Person = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    born_day: ?i32 = null,
    leave_until_day: ?u32 = null,

    fn isAvailable(self: Person, day: u32) bool {
        if (self.leave_until_day) |until| return day > until;
        return true;
    }
};

const Unit = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    pilot: ?*const Person = null,
};

pub fn main() void {
    const ada = Person{ .name = "Ada", .born_day = 5 };
    const bo = Person{ .name = "Bo", .leave_until_day = 30 };
    const day: u32 = 20;

    const units = [_]Unit{
        .{ .name = "Locust", .pilot = &ada },
        .{ .name = "Marauder", .pilot = &bo },
        .{ .name = "Atlas" },
    };

    for (units) |u| {
        if (u.pilot) |p| {
            if (p.born_day) |born| {
                const age_days = @as(i64, day) - @as(i64, born);
                std.debug.print("{s}: pilot {s}, age {d} days\n", .{ u.name, p.name, age_days });
            } else {
                std.debug.print("{s}: pilot {s}, birthday unknown\n", .{ u.name, p.name });
            }
            if (!p.isAvailable(day)) std.debug.print("  ({s} is on leave)\n", .{p.name});
        } else {
            std.debug.print("{s}: no pilot assigned\n", .{u.name});
        }
    }

    // A chain: only runs when every link is present.
    for (units) |u| if (u.pilot) |p| if (p.isAvailable(day)) {
        std.debug.print("ready: {s} in the {s}\n", .{ p.name, u.name });
    };
}
Locust: pilot Ada, age 15 days
Marauder: pilot Bo, birthday unknown
  (Bo is on leave)
Atlas: no pilot assigned
ready: Ada in the Locust

Two optionals are nested here: a unit may have no pilot, and a pilot may have no birthday. Each if … |x| peels one layer. The last loop shows the compact chain form, if (u.pilot) |p| if (p.isAvailable(day)) { … }: an if whose body is another if, with no braces between them. It reads as "if there is a pilot, and the pilot is available". You will see this idiom throughout IRON LEDGER, and once you have written it a few times it stops looking odd. Note the semicolon after the closing brace: because the whole thing is the body of a brace-less for, it is a single statement and needs one.

Inside isAvailable, the pattern if (self.leave_until_day) |until| return day > until; followed by return true; is the optional version of a guard clause. It is often clearer than one long boolean expression.

15.10 An optional of an optional

Because ?T is a type like any other, ??T is legal, and it is not the same as ?T. "Present, but holding null" and "absent" are different values. You will rarely want this, but it comes up when a generic container stores optionals, and it explains why orelse only removes one layer at a time.

opt10.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const inner: ?u8 = null;
    const outer: ??u8 = inner;
    std.debug.print("outer == null? {}\n", .{outer == null});
    if (outer) |i| {
        std.debug.print("outer present, inner == null? {}\n", .{i == null});
    }
}
outer == null? false
outer present, inner == null? true

15.11 Why no null by default

Step back and look at what the type system has bought you. Every place a value might be missing is marked in the type. Every place that marking is removed is visible in the code: an orelse, an if capture, a .?. The compiler will not let you forget a check, and when you deliberately assert with .?, a Debug build tells you the exact line if you were wrong. Compare this to hunting for the origin of a null that surfaced three modules away from where it was created.

The price is a little typing. In practice, most Zig programs have far fewer optionals than JavaScript programs have undefined checks, because most values simply are never absent, and their types say so.

In IRON LEDGER. The simulation looks things up by typed ID constantly, and every lookup returns an optional pointer. GameState.person in game/src/sim/state.zig is one line, return self.people.getPtr(id);, with return type ?*person_mod.Person. Callers pick the unwrapping form that fits: a command handler writes const p = gs.person(id) orelse return Error.UnknownPerson; because an unknown ID is a user mistake to report; a query writes if (gs.person(u.pilot)) |pilot| if (pilot.isAvailable(day)) … because a unit with no pilot is simply skipped; and code that has just created a unit writes gs.unit(seat).? because failure there would be a bug. Optional fields carry "not yet" state on the domain structs: leave_until_day: ?u32 = null, wound_heal_day: ?u32 = null, born_day: ?i32 = null. And the catalogue lookup in game/src/domain/chassis.zig is the shape from section 15.8: 
pub fn find(key: []const u8) ?*const Chassis {
    for (catalog) |*c| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, c.key, key)) return c;
    }
    return null;
}

Exercises

Exercise 15.1 · A lookup that may find nothing warm-up

Implement find, which returns the index of a name in a fixed roster or null, and after, which returns the following name using orelse return null. File: exercises/15-optionals/ex1_lookup.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 15, exercise 1: a lookup that may find nothing.
//! Run with:  zig test ex1_lookup.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const roster = [_][]const u8{ "Kerensky", "Steiner", "Liao", "Davion" };

/// Return the index of `name` in the roster, or null when it is not there.
fn find(name: []const u8) ?usize {
    for (roster, 0..) |entry, i| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, entry, name)) return i;
    }
    return null;
}

/// Return the name that follows `name`, or null when `name` is unknown
/// or already the last one. Use `orelse return null`.
fn after(name: []const u8) ?[]const u8 {
    const i = find(name) orelse return null;
    if (i + 1 >= roster.len) return null;
    return roster[i + 1];
}

test "find present and absent" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?usize, 1), find("Steiner"));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?usize, 3), find("Davion"));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?usize, null), find("Marik"));
}

test "after" {
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Liao", after("Steiner").?);
    try std.testing.expect(after("Davion") == null);
    try std.testing.expect(after("Marik") == null);
}

find returns a plain usize from inside the loop and null after it; both coerce to ?usize. In after, the orelse return null makes i a plain index for the rest of the function.

Exercise 15.2 · Defaults and first-present practice

Write four small functions: a default with orelse, a chain of orelse that picks the first present of three, a sum over a slice of ?u32 using if captures, and a count of the null entries using == null. File: exercises/15-optionals/ex2_orelse.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 15, exercise 2: defaults and first-present.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_orelse.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// The tonnage of a unit, or 50 when the catalogue had no entry.
fn tonnageOr50(found: ?u8) u8 {
    return found orelse 50;
}

/// The first of three optionals that is present, or null if none is.
fn firstPresent(a: ?u32, b: ?u32, c: ?u32) ?u32 {
    return a orelse b orelse c;
}

/// Sum of the present values only. Use `if (x) |v|`.
fn sumPresent(values: []const ?u32) u32 {
    var total: u32 = 0;
    for (values) |maybe| {
        if (maybe) |v| total += v;
    }
    return total;
}

/// How many are null? Use `== null`.
fn countMissing(values: []const ?u32) usize {
    var n: usize = 0;
    for (values) |maybe| {
        if (maybe == null) n += 1;
    }
    return n;
}

test "tonnageOr50" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 75), tonnageOr50(75));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 50), tonnageOr50(null));
}

test "firstPresent" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u32, 2), firstPresent(null, 2, 3));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u32, 3), firstPresent(null, null, 3));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u32, null), firstPresent(null, null, null));
}

test "sumPresent and countMissing" {
    const vals = [_]?u32{ 1, null, 4, null, 10 };
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 15), sumPresent(&vals));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 2), countMissing(&vals));
}

a orelse b orelse c works because orelse is right-associative: a orelse (b orelse c). Its right-hand side is a ?u32, so the whole expression is still an optional, which is what the test expects.

Exercise 15.3 · Write your own iterator practice

Give Range a next method that returns ?u32, then write sum as a while (it.next()) |v| loop. File: exercises/15-optionals/ex3_iterator.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 15, exercise 3: write your own iterator.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_iterator.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Yields `start`, `start + step`, ... while the value is below `end`.
const Range = struct {
    next_value: u32,
    end: u32,
    step: u32,

    fn init(start: u32, end: u32, step: u32) Range {
        return .{ .next_value = start, .end = end, .step = step };
    }

    /// Return the next value, or null once the range is exhausted.
    fn next(self: *Range) ?u32 {
        if (self.next_value >= self.end) return null;
        const v = self.next_value;
        self.next_value += self.step;
        return v;
    }
};

/// Drain an iterator with `while (it.next()) |v|` and add up the values.
fn sum(it: *Range) u32 {
    var total: u32 = 0;
    while (it.next()) |v| total += v;
    return total;
}

test "range yields then stops" {
    var r = Range.init(0, 10, 3);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u32, 0), r.next());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u32, 3), r.next());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u32, 6), r.next());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u32, 9), r.next());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u32, null), r.next());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u32, null), r.next());
}

test "sum drains it" {
    var r = Range.init(1, 5, 1);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 10), sum(&r));
    var empty = Range.init(5, 5, 1);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 0), sum(&empty));
}

next takes *Range because it must change the stored counter. Once exhausted it keeps returning null, which is the polite behaviour for an iterator and is what the last two assertions check.

Exercise 15.4 · Optional fields and optional pointers challenge

Complete isAvailable (a guard on an optional field), oldest (returns ?*const Person, skipping people with no birthday) and firstAvailable. File: exercises/15-optionals/ex4_fields.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 15, exercise 4: optional fields and optional pointers.
//! Run with:  zig test ex4_fields.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Person = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    born_day: ?i32 = null,
    leave_until_day: ?u32 = null,

    /// Available unless on leave that has not yet ended.
    fn isAvailable(self: Person, day: u32) bool {
        if (self.leave_until_day) |until| return day > until;
        return true;
    }
};

/// Pointer to the person with the smallest known birthday, or null if
/// nobody has a birthday on record.
fn oldest(people: []const Person) ?*const Person {
    var best: ?*const Person = null;
    for (people) |*p| {
        const born = p.born_day orelse continue;
        if (best) |b| {
            if (born < b.born_day.?) best = p;
        } else {
            best = p;
        }
    }
    return best;
}

/// Pointer to the first available person, or null.
fn firstAvailable(people: []const Person, day: u32) ?*const Person {
    for (people) |*p| if (p.isAvailable(day)) return p;
    return null;
}

const crew = [_]Person{
    .{ .name = "Ada", .born_day = 200, .leave_until_day = 40 },
    .{ .name = "Bo" },
    .{ .name = "Cy", .born_day = 120 },
};

test "isAvailable" {
    try std.testing.expect(!crew[0].isAvailable(30));
    try std.testing.expect(crew[0].isAvailable(41));
    try std.testing.expect(crew[1].isAvailable(0));
}

test "oldest skips unknown birthdays" {
    const o = oldest(&crew) orelse return error.TestUnexpectedResult;
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Cy", o.name);
    const nobody = [_]Person{ .{ .name = "X" }, .{ .name = "Y" } };
    try std.testing.expect(oldest(&nobody) == null);
}

test "firstAvailable" {
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Bo", firstAvailable(&crew, 10).?.name);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Ada", firstAvailable(&crew, 50).?.name);
    const all_away = [_]Person{.{ .name = "Z", .leave_until_day = 99 }};
    try std.testing.expect(firstAvailable(&all_away, 10) == null);
}

In oldest, orelse continue skips a person with no birthday in one line. The running best is itself an optional pointer, so the body uses an if … |b| … else to distinguish "no candidate yet" from "compare with the candidate". The b.born_day.? is safe because we only ever store people whose birthday is present.

Check your understanding

  1. What does the compiler say if you assign a ?u32 to a u32?
    Answer"expected type 'u32', found '?u32'", with a note that you cannot convert an optional to its payload type, and a hint to use .?, orelse or if.
  2. What is the difference between x orelse 0 and x orelse return?
    AnswerThe first substitutes 0 when x is null and continues. The second leaves the function when x is null; the variable being assigned only exists on the present path.
  3. When is .? appropriate?
    AnswerWhen null would be a bug, not a normal outcome: the value was produced or checked by code you control. It panics in Debug if it is wrong. Never use it on user input.
  4. How many bytes does ?*u32 take on a 64-bit machine, and why?
    Answer8, the same as *u32. Pointers cannot be zero, so the zero bit pattern represents null with no extra storage.
  5. How does a while loop know when an iterator is finished?
    Answerwhile (it.next()) |v| stops the first time next returns null. Any function returning ?T can be an iterator.
  6. Is if (a) |v| if (v.b) |w| … legal, and what does it mean?
    AnswerYes. The body of the outer if is another if. It runs the innermost block only when both a and a.b are present.
  7. Can an optional be compared with ==?
    AnswerYes, both to null and to a plain value of the payload type. a == 4 is false when a is null.
What you learned.
  • ?T is a type that holds either a T or null; a T coerces into it, never the other way.
  • Unwrap with orelse (a fallback value, or return/break/continue/unreachable), with if (x) |v| … else …, or with .?, which panics on null.
  • while (it.next()) |v| is the iterator protocol; any ?T-returning function drives it.
  • ?*T and ?[]T cost nothing extra; ?u32 costs padding.
  • Optional fields with = null defaults express "not yet"; chains of captures peel one layer each.
  • The point is that every possible absence is in the type, and every place you remove it is visible in the code.

16. Errors

In this chapter you will learn how Zig functions report failure: not by throwing, not by returning -1, but by returning a value from an error set. You will write error sets, error unions and the four verbs try, catch, switch and errdefer (the last one gets its own chapter next). You will read a real error return trace and learn what an error escaping from main does to your program's exit code.

16.1 Errors are values

If you come from Python or JavaScript, failure means an exception: control jumps out of the current function, and out of its caller, and its caller's caller, until something catches it. Nothing in the source text of the intermediate functions shows that this can happen. If you come from C, failure means a return code that every caller must remember to check, and many do not.

Zig sits between the two. A function that can fail says so in its return type, and callers must do something with the failure: pass it up, handle it, or explicitly assert it cannot happen. But there is no jumping. An error is an ordinary value, returned with an ordinary return, and the code that passes it up is visible in the text as a try.

The values come from an error set, which looks like an enum of failure names:

const HireError = error{
    InsufficientTreasury,
    NoBerth,
    UnknownPerson,
};

A single error value is written error.NoBerth. A function that either succeeds with a u32 or fails with a HireError has the return type HireError!u32, read as "HireError or u32". This is an error union. Here is a complete program.

err1.zig

const std = @import("std");

const HireError = error{
    InsufficientTreasury,
    NoBerth,
    UnknownPerson,
};

fn hire(treasury: u32, cost: u32, free_berths: u32) HireError!u32 {
    if (free_berths == 0) return error.NoBerth;
    if (cost > treasury) return error.InsufficientTreasury;
    return treasury - cost;
}

pub fn main() !void {
    const left = try hire(10_000, 2_500, 3);
    std.debug.print("hired, {d} c-bills left\n", .{left});

    const left2 = try hire(1_000, 2_500, 3);
    std.debug.print("hired again, {d} c-bills left\n", .{left2});
}
$ zig run err1.zig
hired, 7500 c-bills left
error: InsufficientTreasury
ch16/err1.zig:11:26: 0x… in hire (err1)
    if (cost > treasury) return error.InsufficientTreasury;
                         ^
ch16/err1.zig:19:19: 0x… in main (err1)
    const left2 = try hire(1_000, 2_500, 3);
                  ^
$ echo $?
1

There is a lot in that transcript. The first hire succeeds and prints. The second fails: hire returns error.InsufficientTreasury, the try in main sees an error and returns it from main, and because main is declared as !void, the runtime prints the error's name, prints an error return trace, and exits with status 1. The trace is not a stack trace of where the program was; it is a list of every return error… and every try the error passed through on its way out, innermost first. In Debug builds this is free and always on, and it is the single most useful thing Zig gives you for debugging failures.

The exit code matters when your program is run from a script. echo $? after a successful run prints 0. After an error escapes main, it prints 1. You do not have to write any of this yourself.

16.2 try: pass it up

try expr means: evaluate expr; if it is an error, return that error from the current function right now; otherwise unwrap the success value. It is exactly this expansion:

const left = hire(10_000, 2_500, 3) catch |err| return err;

Nine out of ten error sites in real Zig code are a try. The failure path exists, is handled, and takes one syllable. Because try returns from the current function, the current function must itself be able to return errors. If it is not, you get a compile error, and it is one of the first you will meet:

const std = @import("std");

fn mightFail(n: u32) !u32 {
    if (n == 0) return error.Zero;
    return n * 2;
}

pub fn main() void {
    const v = try mightFail(3);
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{v});
}
err6.zig:9:15: error: expected type 'void', found '@typeInfo(@typeInfo(@TypeOf(err6.mightFail)).@"fn".return_type.?).error_union.error_set'
    const v = try mightFail(3);
              ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
err6.zig:8:15: note: function cannot return an error
pub fn main() void {
…

The fix is to change main's return type to !void, or to handle the error on the spot with catch. That type name in the message looks alarming; it is just the compiler spelling out "the error set of mightFail" without a short name for it.

Here is a chain of three functions each using try, so you can see how the trace grows one line per hop.

err9.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn step3(n: u32) !u32 {
    if (n > 2) return error.TooDeep;
    return n;
}
fn step2(n: u32) !u32 {
    return try step3(n + 1);
}
fn step1(n: u32) !u32 {
    return try step2(n + 1);
}

pub fn main() !void {
    std.debug.print("step1(0) = {d}\n", .{try step1(0)});
    std.debug.print("step1(1) = {d}\n", .{try step1(1)});
}
step1(0) = 2
error: TooDeep
ch16/err9.zig:4:16: 0x… in step3 (err9)
    if (n > 2) return error.TooDeep;
               ^
ch16/err9.zig:8:12: 0x… in step2 (err9)
    return try step3(n + 1);
           ^
ch16/err9.zig:11:12: 0x… in step1 (err9)
    return try step2(n + 1);
           ^
ch16/err9.zig:16:43: 0x… in main (err9)
    std.debug.print("step1(1) = {d}\n", .{try step1(1)});
                                          ^

16.3 Inferred error sets: !T

Writing error{…}!u32 on every function gets old. If you write just !u32, the compiler infers the error set from the body: every return error.X and every try contributes its errors. step1, step2 and step3 above all use this. Most functions you write should too. Name the set explicitly when it is part of an interface other people will program against (IRON LEDGER names commands.Error because the UI switches on it), or when you want the compiler to reject an error that should not be possible.

16.4 catch: handle it here

When you do not want to pass an error up, catch handles it in place. It has four shapes, and you will use all of them.

err2.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn parseTonnage(text: []const u8) !u8 {
    return std.fmt.parseInt(u8, text, 10);
}

pub fn main() void {
    // 1. catch with a fallback value
    const a = parseTonnage("55") catch 50;
    const b = parseTonnage("heavy") catch 50;
    std.debug.print("a={d} b={d}\n", .{ a, b });

    // 2. catch and look at the error
    const c = parseTonnage("999") catch |err| blk: {
        std.debug.print("could not parse: {s}\n", .{@errorName(err)});
        break :blk 0;
    };
    std.debug.print("c={d}\n", .{c});

    // 3. catch {} : swallow it (rare, do it on purpose)
    _ = parseTonnage("x") catch {};

    // 4. catch unreachable: "this cannot fail", checked in Debug
    const d = parseTonnage("75") catch unreachable;
    std.debug.print("d={d}\n", .{d});
}
a=55 b=50
could not parse: Overflow
c=0
d=75
  • expr catch value: if it fails, use value instead. It is the most common shape after try.
  • expr catch |err| { … }: capture the error and run a block. If the block must produce a value for the surrounding expression, use a labelled block with break :blk value, as in the third example. If the block returns or continues, no value is needed.
  • expr catch {}: swallow it. Legal, occasionally right, and always worth a comment. The game uses it for "if even the rollback fails there is nothing more to do".
  • expr catch unreachable: assert it cannot fail. Debug builds panic if you are wrong. Reach for it when the input is a compile-time constant you can see is valid, like divCeil(u32, n, 30) catch unreachable where the divisor is literally 30.

Note that "999" failed with Overflow, not with some generic "bad input": parseInt into a u8 reports a number that is too large separately from a string that is not a number. Its error set has several members, and @errorName turns any of them into its name as a string.

16.5 Switching on an error

Inside a catch |err| block, err is a value of the function's error set, and you can switch on it like an enum. The switch must be exhaustive: name every member of the set, or add an else.

err3.zig

const std = @import("std");

const ParseError = error{ Empty, NotANumber, TooBig };

fn parsePercent(text: []const u8) ParseError!u8 {
    if (text.len == 0) return error.Empty;
    const n = std.fmt.parseInt(u32, text, 10) catch return error.NotANumber;
    if (n > 100) return error.TooBig;
    return @intCast(n);
}

fn describe(text: []const u8) void {
    const pct = parsePercent(text) catch |err| {
        const msg = switch (err) {
            error.Empty => "you gave me nothing",
            error.NotANumber => "that is not a number",
            error.TooBig => "a percentage between 0 and 100",
        };
        std.debug.print("'{s}': {s}\n", .{ text, msg });
        return;
    };
    std.debug.print("'{s}': {d}%\n", .{ text, pct });
}

pub fn main() void {
    describe("40");
    describe("");
    describe("forty");
    describe("140");
}
'40': 40%
'': you gave me nothing
'forty': that is not a number
'140': a percentage between 0 and 100

This is the pattern for turning errors into sentences at the edge of a program. Note how parsePercent itself converts the standard library's parse error into its own vocabulary with catch return error.NotANumber. The caller never sees Overflow or InvalidCharacter; it sees the three cases the function promised. Because the set is explicit, forgetting one is a compile error:

const std = @import("std");

const ParseError = error{ Empty, NotANumber };

fn parsePercent(text: []const u8) ParseError!u8 {
    if (text.len == 0) return error.Empty;
    return std.fmt.parseInt(u8, text, 10) catch error.NotANumber;
}

pub fn main() void {
    _ = parsePercent("5") catch |err| switch (err) {
        error.Empty => std.debug.print("empty\n", .{}),
        // forgot NotANumber
    };
}
err4.zig:11:39: error: switch must handle all possibilities
    _ = parsePercent("5") catch |err| switch (err) {
                                      ^~~~~~
err4.zig:11:39: note: unhandled error value: 'error.NotANumber'
…

Add a case to the error set and every switch that forgot it lights up. This is the same exhaustiveness guarantee you met with enums in Chapter 13, and it is why explicit error sets are worth their extra typing at module boundaries.

16.6 Merging sets, anyerror and @errorName

Error sets combine with ||. If load can fail in the file layer or the format layer, its set is the union of both, and any function that calls it with try inherits the union.

err5.zig

const std = @import("std");

const FileError = error{ NotFound, PermissionDenied };
const ParseError = error{ BadSyntax, TooLong };
const LoadError = FileError || ParseError;

fn load(name: []const u8) LoadError!u32 {
    if (name.len == 0) return error.NotFound;
    if (name.len > 8) return error.TooLong;
    if (name[0] == '!') return error.BadSyntax;
    return @intCast(name.len);
}

fn report(err: anyerror) void {
    std.debug.print("failed with {s}\n", .{@errorName(err)});
}

pub fn main() void {
    const names = [_][]const u8{ "save1", "", "!bad", "far_too_long" };
    for (names) |n| {
        const v = load(n) catch |err| {
            report(err);
            continue;
        };
        std.debug.print("loaded {s}: {d}\n", .{ n, v });
    }

    // an error set is a type; its members are values you can compare
    const e: LoadError = error.TooLong;
    std.debug.print("e == error.TooLong? {}\n", .{e == error.TooLong});
    std.debug.print("the whole union: {}\n", .{LoadError});
}
loaded save1: 5
failed with NotFound
failed with BadSyntax
failed with TooLong
e == error.TooLong? true
the whole union: error{BadSyntax,NotFound,PermissionDenied,TooLong}

anyerror is the set of every error in the whole program. A function taking anyerror accepts any error value at all, which is what you want for a generic "print this failure" helper like report. Any specific set coerces to anyerror; the reverse needs an explicit check. Printing an error set type with {} shows its members, sorted, as the last line demonstrates.

Two more shapes you will meet in signatures. std.mem.Allocator.Error!T says "this can only fail with OutOfMemory". And error{}!T uses the empty set: the function cannot fail, but has the error-union shape so that try on it compiles. It appears in generic code that wants one calling convention whether or not the underlying operation can fail.

const std = @import("std");

/// `error{}` is the empty set: this function promises it cannot fail,
/// but still has the error-union shape so `try` works on it.
fn cannotFail(x: u32) error{}!u32 {
    return x + 1;
}

fn onlyOom(a: std.mem.Allocator) std.mem.Allocator.Error![]u8 {
    return a.alloc(u8, 4);
}

pub fn main() !void {
    const v = try cannotFail(1);
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{v});
    const buf = try onlyOom(std.heap.page_allocator);
    defer std.heap.page_allocator.free(buf);
    std.debug.print("{d} bytes\n", .{buf.len});
}
2
4 bytes

16.7 An error union around an optional

Because ?T is a type, E!?T is a type: "either an error, or maybe a T". The two mean different things and both are useful. A command parser is the classic case: a malformed line is an error, an unrecognised verb is simply no command.

err7.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Command = union(enum) {
    hire: []const u8,
    fire: []const u8,
    quit,
};

const ParseError = error{ MissingName, EmptyLine };

/// Can fail (bad syntax), and on success may still be "not a command".
fn parseCommand(line: []const u8) ParseError!?Command {
    var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, line, ' ');
    const verb = it.next() orelse return error.EmptyLine;
    if (std.mem.eql(u8, verb, "quit")) return .quit;
    if (std.mem.eql(u8, verb, "hire")) return .{ .hire = it.next() orelse return error.MissingName };
    if (std.mem.eql(u8, verb, "fire")) return .{ .fire = it.next() orelse return error.MissingName };
    return null; // not a verb we know
}

pub fn main() void {
    const lines = [_][]const u8{ "hire Steiner", "dance", "hire", "", "quit" };
    for (lines) |line| {
        const maybe = parseCommand(line) catch |err| {
            std.debug.print("'{s}': error {s}\n", .{ line, @errorName(err) });
            continue;
        };
        if (maybe) |cmd| {
            std.debug.print("'{s}': {s}\n", .{ line, @tagName(cmd) });
        } else {
            std.debug.print("'{s}': unknown verb, ignored\n", .{line});
        }
    }
}
'hire Steiner': hire
'dance': unknown verb, ignored
'hire': error MissingName
'': error EmptyLine
'quit': quit

Read the type inside-out: an optional Command, wrapped in a possible ParseError. Unwrap it in the same order: catch or try first to remove the error, then if … |cmd| or orelse to remove the optional. Inside the parser, it.next() orelse return error.MissingName converts a missing token (an optional) into an error in one expression. Keep the two ideas distinct in your own designs: an optional is for "absent, and that is normal"; an error is for "something went wrong and the caller should know why".

16.8 Testing errors

std.testing.expectError asserts that an expression fails with a specific error. Combined with try on the success path, it lets a test cover both outcomes without any if.

err8.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Bank = struct {
    funds: u32,

    const WithdrawError = error{Insufficient};

    fn withdraw(self: *Bank, amount: u32) WithdrawError!void {
        if (amount > self.funds) return error.Insufficient;
        self.funds -= amount;
    }
};

test "withdraw succeeds when funds allow" {
    var b = Bank{ .funds = 100 };
    try b.withdraw(40);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 60), b.funds);
}

test "withdraw fails when short" {
    var b = Bank{ .funds = 10 };
    try std.testing.expectError(error.Insufficient, b.withdraw(40));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 10), b.funds);
}
1/2 err8.test.withdraw succeeds when funds allow...OK
2/2 err8.test.withdraw fails when short...OK
All 2 tests passed.

Note that test blocks themselves return !void, which is why try works inside them. A test that returns an error fails.

16.9 Why this design

Exceptions hide control flow: any call might not return. Return codes hide failures: any caller might not check. Zig's error unions make the failure part of the type and the propagation part of the text, so both are visible, and the compiler enforces that neither is forgotten. The cost is a try on most lines that call something fallible. In exchange you get exhaustive handling at the edges, a return trace that names every hop, and functions whose signatures tell you everything that can go wrong.

One thing errors deliberately cannot do is carry data. error.UnknownPerson has no field for which person. If the caller needs details, put them somewhere the caller can read (a field on the struct, an out-parameter, a log), or return a tagged union instead. This keeps errors as cheap as an integer, which is what makes returning them on every hop free.

In IRON LEDGER. The command layer names its error set explicitly in game/src/sim/commands.zig, about sixty members merged with the allocator's, and every command goes through one function with that set in its signature: 
pub const Error = error{
    UnknownPerson,
    UnknownForce,
    UnknownUnit,
    InsufficientTreasury,
    CompanyDeployed,
    NoBerth,
    BadPercent,
    BadYear,
    // … about sixty
} || std.mem.Allocator.Error;   // merged with OutOfMemory

pub fn execute(gs: *GameState, cmd: Command) Error!Result { // … }
The errors travel up unchanged until the user interface, where errorText in game/src/sim/cli.zig takes an anyerror and switches it into sentences, with else => @errorName(err) as the fallback so an unexpected error still shows its name. The terminal client's key loop is a single catch: self.handleKey(key) catch |err| self.say(.crit, "error: {s}", .{@errorName(err)});, so no keypress can crash the game, and the REPL parser returns ParseError!?Command, exactly the nesting from section 16.7.

Exercises

Exercise 16.1 · An error set and a function that uses it warm-up

Implement parsePercent returning ParseError!u8, converting the standard library's parse failure into error.NotANumber, and sumPercent which propagates with try. File: exercises/16-errors/ex1_parse.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 16, exercise 1: an error set and a function that uses it.
//! Run with:  zig test ex1_parse.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const ParseError = error{ Empty, NotANumber, TooBig };

/// "40" -> 40. "" -> Empty. "forty" -> NotANumber. "140" -> TooBig.
fn parsePercent(text: []const u8) ParseError!u8 {
    if (text.len == 0) return error.Empty;
    const n = std.fmt.parseInt(u32, text, 10) catch return error.NotANumber;
    if (n > 100) return error.TooBig;
    return @intCast(n);
}

/// Parse two percentages and add them; propagate any error with `try`.
fn sumPercent(a: []const u8, b: []const u8) ParseError!u32 {
    const x = try parsePercent(a);
    const y = try parsePercent(b);
    return @as(u32, x) + y;
}

test "good input" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 40), try parsePercent("40"));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 100), try parsePercent("100"));
}

test "bad input" {
    try std.testing.expectError(error.Empty, parsePercent(""));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.NotANumber, parsePercent("forty"));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.TooBig, parsePercent("140"));
}

test "try propagates" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 70), try sumPercent("30", "40"));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.TooBig, sumPercent("30", "400"));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.Empty, sumPercent("", "400"));
}

The catch return error.NotANumber is the translation step: callers only ever see the three errors in ParseError. Parsing into a u32 first and checking > 100 afterwards keeps "140" a TooBig rather than an overflow.

Exercise 16.2 · catch, and switching on an error practice

Write parseOr with a one-line catch, an exhaustive errorText switch, and describe, which returns a tagged union of value or message. File: exercises/16-errors/ex2_catch.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 16, exercise 2: catch, and switching on an error.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_catch.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const ParseError = error{ Empty, NotANumber, TooBig };

fn parsePercent(text: []const u8) ParseError!u8 {
    if (text.len == 0) return error.Empty;
    const n = std.fmt.parseInt(u32, text, 10) catch return error.NotANumber;
    if (n > 100) return error.TooBig;
    return @intCast(n);
}

/// Parse, or fall back to `default`. One line with `catch`.
fn parseOr(text: []const u8, default: u8) u8 {
    return parsePercent(text) catch default;
}

/// A sentence for each error. The switch must be exhaustive.
fn errorText(err: ParseError) []const u8 {
    return switch (err) {
        error.Empty => "you gave me nothing",
        error.NotANumber => "that is not a number",
        error.TooBig => "a percentage between 0 and 100",
    };
}

/// Parse and, on failure, return the sentence instead of the number.
/// Return type: a tagged union so the caller can tell which happened.
const Outcome = union(enum) { value: u8, message: []const u8 };

fn describe(text: []const u8) Outcome {
    const v = parsePercent(text) catch |err| return .{ .message = errorText(err) };
    return .{ .value = v };
}

test "parseOr" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 40), parseOr("40", 5));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 5), parseOr("", 5));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 5), parseOr("x", 5));
}

test "errorText" {
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("you gave me nothing", errorText(error.Empty));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("a percentage between 0 and 100", errorText(error.TooBig));
}

test "describe" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 12), describe("12").value);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("that is not a number", describe("twelve").message);
}

describe shows catch |err| return …: the catch block leaves the function, so no value is needed for v on that path. Try deleting one arm of errorText's switch to see the exhaustiveness error.

Exercise 16.3 · Merging sets, anyerror and @errorName practice

Define LoadError as the merge of two sets and Allocator.Error, implement load, and write an errorText(anyerror) with an else that falls back to @errorName. File: exercises/16-errors/ex3_merge.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 16, exercise 3: merging error sets, anyerror and @errorName.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_merge.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const FileError = error{ NotFound, PermissionDenied };
const FormatError = error{ BadSyntax, TooLong };

/// Everything `load` can fail with: both sets merged, plus OutOfMemory.
const LoadError = FileError || FormatError || std.mem.Allocator.Error;

/// Pretend loader. Returns a copy of `name` (caller frees) or an error:
///   ""        -> NotFound
///   "locked"  -> PermissionDenied
///   starts '!' -> BadSyntax
///   > 8 chars -> TooLong
fn load(a: std.mem.Allocator, name: []const u8) LoadError![]u8 {
    if (name.len == 0) return error.NotFound;
    if (std.mem.eql(u8, name, "locked")) return error.PermissionDenied;
    if (name[0] == '!') return error.BadSyntax;
    if (name.len > 8) return error.TooLong;
    return a.dupe(u8, name);
}

/// A message for any error at all. Unknown ones fall back to @errorName.
fn errorText(err: anyerror) []const u8 {
    return switch (err) {
        error.NotFound => "no such save",
        error.PermissionDenied => "that save is locked",
        error.OutOfMemory => "out of memory",
        else => @errorName(err),
    };
}

test "load ok" {
    const s = try load(std.testing.allocator, "save1");
    defer std.testing.allocator.free(s);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("save1", s);
}

test "load errors" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    try std.testing.expectError(error.NotFound, load(a, ""));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.PermissionDenied, load(a, "locked"));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.BadSyntax, load(a, "!x"));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.TooLong, load(a, "far_too_long"));
}

test "errorText" {
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("no such save", errorText(error.NotFound));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("TooLong", errorText(error.TooLong));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Whatever", errorText(error.Whatever));
}

The last assertion passes error.Whatever, an error that appears nowhere else in the program. It is still a valid anyerror, and the else arm prints its name. Also note the first test frees what load returned: an error union around an owned slice is the usual shape for "allocate or fail".

Exercise 16.4 · An error union around an optional challenge

Implement parseCommand returning ParseError!?Command: errors for malformed lines, null for unknown verbs, a command otherwise. File: exercises/16-errors/ex4_nested.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 16, exercise 4: an error union around an optional (E!?T).
//! Run with:  zig test ex4_nested.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Command = union(enum) {
    hire: []const u8,
    fire: []const u8,
    advance: u32,
    quit,
};

const ParseError = error{ EmptyLine, MissingArgument, BadNumber };

/// Parse one line of the REPL.
///   error  -> the line was malformed
///   null   -> well-formed but not a verb we know
///   value  -> a command
fn parseCommand(line: []const u8) ParseError!?Command {
    var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, line, ' ');
    const verb = it.next() orelse return error.EmptyLine;
    if (std.mem.eql(u8, verb, "quit")) return .quit;
    if (std.mem.eql(u8, verb, "hire")) return .{ .hire = it.next() orelse return error.MissingArgument };
    if (std.mem.eql(u8, verb, "fire")) return .{ .fire = it.next() orelse return error.MissingArgument };
    if (std.mem.eql(u8, verb, "advance")) {
        const arg = it.next() orelse return error.MissingArgument;
        const n = std.fmt.parseInt(u32, arg, 10) catch return error.BadNumber;
        return .{ .advance = n };
    }
    return null;
}

test "commands" {
    const h = (try parseCommand("hire Steiner")).?;
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Steiner", h.hire);
    const adv = (try parseCommand("advance 7")).?;
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 7), adv.advance);
    try std.testing.expect((try parseCommand("quit")).? == .quit);
}

test "unknown verb is null, not an error" {
    try std.testing.expect((try parseCommand("dance wildly")) == null);
}

test "malformed lines are errors" {
    try std.testing.expectError(error.EmptyLine, parseCommand("   "));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.MissingArgument, parseCommand("hire"));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.BadNumber, parseCommand("advance soon"));
}

Every missing token becomes an error through orelse return error.…, and the number parse becomes BadNumber through catch return. The tests unwrap in the right order: (try parseCommand(…)).? removes the error first, then the optional.

Check your understanding

  1. What does try f() expand to?
    Answerf() catch |err| return err: on failure, return the error from the current function; on success, the unwrapped value.
  2. Why does try inside a function returning void fail to compile?
    AnswerBecause try may return an error, and the function's return type says it returns none. Make it !void or handle the error with catch.
  3. What happens when an error escapes main?
    AnswerThe runtime prints error: Name, an error return trace in Debug builds, and the process exits with status 1.
  4. What is the difference between an error return trace and a stack trace?
    AnswerA stack trace shows where the program is now. An error return trace lists every return error and try the error passed through on its way up, innermost first.
  5. When would you use catch unreachable?
    AnswerWhen you can see from the inputs that failure is impossible, such as dividing by a literal constant. Debug builds panic if you are wrong.
  6. What does A || B mean for error sets?
    AnswerThe merged set containing every member of both. A function that trys calls from both layers has the merged set as its inferred error set.
  7. What is the difference between returning null and returning an error from a parser?
    Answernull means "nothing here, and that is normal" (unknown verb). An error means "something went wrong and the caller should know why" (missing argument).
  8. Can an error carry a payload, like a message or an ID?
    AnswerNo. Errors are bare names, as cheap as an integer. Put the details somewhere else, or return a tagged union.
What you learned.
  • An error set is a list of names; error.Name is a value; E!T is "error or value"; !T lets the compiler infer E.
  • try passes an error up and is only legal in a function that can return errors.
  • catch value, catch |err| {…}, catch {} and catch unreachable handle errors in place.
  • A switch on an error must be exhaustive; explicit sets make forgotten cases compile errors.
  • A || B merges sets; anyerror accepts all; @errorName gives the name as text.
  • An error escaping main prints a return trace and exits with status 1.
  • E!?T nests an optional inside an error union; unwrap the error first, then the optional.

17. defer, errdefer and cleanup

In this chapter you will learn Zig's answer to "make sure this gets cleaned up": the defer statement, which runs when the enclosing block ends, and its sibling errdefer, which runs only when the block ends with an error. You will see the exact order they run in, the classic resource pairs they protect, and the two things a defer is not allowed to do.

17.1 The cleanup problem

Almost every resource comes in a pair. You open a file and must close it. You allocate memory and must free it. You lock a mutex and must unlock it. You begin a database transaction and must commit or roll it back. The first half is easy: it happens where you need the resource. The second half is where bugs live, because a function can leave in more ways than one. An early return, a try that fails, a break out of a loop: each is a path that has to remember the cleanup.

Languages solve this differently. Python has with, Java has try-with-resources, C++ runs destructors when a variable goes out of scope, Go has defer. Zig has defer too, but scoped to the block rather than the function, and it comes with a variant that only fires on failure. Together they let you write the cleanup on the line right after the setup, where you cannot forget it, and then stop thinking about it.

17.2 defer runs at the end of the block

def1.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("open the hangar\n", .{});
    defer std.debug.print("close the hangar\n", .{});

    std.debug.print("power up the mech\n", .{});
    defer std.debug.print("power down the mech\n", .{});

    std.debug.print("run the mission\n", .{});
}
open the hangar
power up the mech
run the mission
power down the mech
close the hangar

defer statement; means "do not run this now; run it when the surrounding block is about to end". The block here is main's body, so both deferred prints run after "run the mission". Notice the order: the mech powers down before the hangar closes. Deferred statements run in reverse order of registration, last in, first out. That is not an accident. If setup happens in the order A then B, cleanup should happen B then A, because B may depend on A still being there. The mech needs the hangar around it to power down inside; the file needs the directory open to be closed. You get the right order for free by writing each cleanup directly after its setup.

def2.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    defer std.debug.print("1st defer registered, runs last\n", .{});
    defer std.debug.print("2nd defer registered, runs second\n", .{});
    defer std.debug.print("3rd defer registered, runs first\n", .{});
    std.debug.print("body done\n", .{});
}
body done
3rd defer registered, runs first
2nd defer registered, runs second
1st defer registered, runs last

One more detail worth seeing once: a deferred statement is evaluated when it runs, not when it is registered. If it mentions a variable, it sees the variable's final value.

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var x: u32 = 1;
    defer std.debug.print("defer sees x = {d}\n", .{x});
    x = 2;
    std.debug.print("body sets x = {d}\n", .{x});
}
body sets x = 2
defer sees x = 2

17.3 The scope is the block, not the function

This is the point where Zig differs from Go, and the one to get right early. A defer belongs to the innermost block it appears in: a function body, but also a bare { … } block, an if body, or a loop body. It runs when that block exits.

def3.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("start of main\n", .{});
    {
        defer std.debug.print("  leaving the inner block\n", .{});
        std.debug.print("  inside the inner block\n", .{});
    }
    std.debug.print("back in main, block already cleaned up\n", .{});

    var i: u32 = 0;
    while (i < 3) : (i += 1) {
        defer std.debug.print("  end of iteration {d}\n", .{i});
        std.debug.print("  iteration {d}\n", .{i});
    }
    std.debug.print("end of main\n", .{});
}
start of main
  inside the inner block
  leaving the inner block
back in main, block already cleaned up
  iteration 0
  end of iteration 0
  iteration 1
  end of iteration 1
  iteration 2
  end of iteration 2
end of main

The defer inside the bare block ran before "back in main". The defer inside the loop body ran at the end of every iteration, not once at the end of main. This is nearly always what you want: if you open a file per iteration, you want it closed per iteration. It is also the source of the one real trap with defer, in section 17.7.

17.4 errdefer: only on the failure path

Sometimes cleanup should happen only if things went wrong. You began a transaction: on success you commit and keep the changes; on failure you roll back. You allocated a struct and are filling it in: on success you hand it to the caller, who now owns it; on failure you must free it yourself, because the caller will never see it. errdefer registers a statement that runs only when the block exits by returning an error.

def4.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn work(fail: bool) !void {
    std.debug.print("  BEGIN\n", .{});
    errdefer std.debug.print("  ROLLBACK (errdefer)\n", .{});
    defer std.debug.print("  cleanup (defer, always)\n", .{});

    if (fail) return error.Boom;
    std.debug.print("  COMMIT\n", .{});
}

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("success path:\n", .{});
    work(false) catch {};
    std.debug.print("failure path:\n", .{});
    work(true) catch |err| std.debug.print("  caller saw {s}\n", .{@errorName(err)});
}
success path:
  BEGIN
  COMMIT
  cleanup (defer, always)
failure path:
  BEGIN
  cleanup (defer, always)
  ROLLBACK (errdefer)
  caller saw Boom

Read the failure path carefully. Both deferred statements were registered, errdefer first and defer second. On the way out they run in reverse: the defer cleanup, then the errdefer rollback. On the success path the errdefer is silently skipped. "Exits with an error" means specifically that the block's function returns an error value: a return error.X, or a try that fails. A normal return, even of a value the caller might consider bad, does not trigger it.

You can capture the error that is escaping, which is useful for logging:

def5.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn load(name: []const u8) !u32 {
    errdefer |err| std.debug.print("load('{s}') failed: {s}\n", .{ name, @errorName(err) });
    if (name.len == 0) return error.EmptyName;
    if (name[0] == '#') return error.BadName;
    return @intCast(name.len);
}

pub fn main() void {
    _ = load("alpha") catch {};
    _ = load("") catch {};
    _ = load("#x") catch {};
}
load('') failed: EmptyName
load('#x') failed: BadName

The successful call to load("alpha") printed nothing, because its errdefer never ran.

17.5 The constructor pattern

The most important use of errdefer is in functions that build something out of several allocations. Suppose the first allocation succeeds and the second fails. The function returns an error; the caller receives nothing and so cannot free anything. Unless the function itself frees the first allocation on the way out, it leaks. The rule is: after each step that acquires something, add an errdefer that releases it. Then any later failure unwinds everything acquired so far, in reverse order, and the success path hands the whole thing to the caller intact.

def6.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Pilot = struct { name: []const u8, skill: u8 };

/// Builds a pilot on the heap. If anything after the allocation fails,
/// the errdefer gives the memory back so the caller has nothing to clean.
fn makePilot(a: std.mem.Allocator, name: []const u8, skill: u8) !*Pilot {
    const p = try a.create(Pilot);
    errdefer a.destroy(p);

    if (skill > 8) return error.SkillOutOfRange;
    p.* = .{ .name = name, .skill = skill };
    return p;
}

test "makePilot cleans up after itself on failure" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;

    const ok = try makePilot(a, "Ada", 4);
    defer a.destroy(ok);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Ada", ok.name);

    // No leak here: errdefer destroyed the half-built pilot.
    try std.testing.expectError(error.SkillOutOfRange, makePilot(a, "Bo", 9));
}
1/1 def6.test.makePilot cleans up after itself on failure...OK
All 1 tests passed.

The test uses std.testing.allocator, which fails the test if any allocation is not freed by the end. Remove the errdefer line and run it again: the second call leaks the half-built pilot and the test reports it. (Chapter 19 shows that report in full.) Here is a slightly harder version, where a loop acquires several things and the errdefer has to release however many were done:

def7.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn buildRoster(a: std.mem.Allocator, count: usize) ![][]u8 {
    const roster = try a.alloc([]u8, count);
    errdefer a.free(roster);

    var built: usize = 0;
    errdefer for (roster[0..built]) |name| a.free(name);

    for (roster, 0..) |*slot, i| {
        if (i == 3) return error.Simulated; // fail part way through
        slot.* = try std.fmt.allocPrint(a, "pilot-{d}", .{i});
        built += 1;
    }
    return roster;
}

test "partial failure frees everything built so far" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    try std.testing.expectError(error.Simulated, buildRoster(a, 5));

    const r = try buildRoster(a, 2);
    defer {
        for (r) |name| a.free(name);
        a.free(r);
    }
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("pilot-1", r[1]);
}
1/1 def7.test.partial failure frees everything built so far...OK
All 1 tests passed.

The counter built is read by the errdefer at the moment it runs, not when it was registered, so it sees how far the loop got. This is the same "evaluated late" behaviour from section 17.2, doing useful work. Also notice the order: the errdefer that frees the names was registered second, so it runs first, before the one that frees the outer slice it reads from.

17.6 The classic pairs

Once you see resources as pairs, defer becomes a habit: write the acquire, immediately write defer release, and move on. Here are three real pairs in one program, using the 0.16 standard library.

def10.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    const a = init.gpa;

    // Pair 1: alloc / free
    const buf = try a.alloc(u8, 16);
    defer a.free(buf);

    // Pair 2: lock / unlock
    var mutex: std.Io.Mutex = .init;
    try mutex.lock(io);
    defer mutex.unlock(io);

    // Pair 3: open / close, on a real file
    var dir = std.Io.Dir.cwd();
    var file = try dir.createFile(io, "def10_out.txt", .{});
    defer file.close(io);

    @memset(buf, '=');
    var wb: [64]u8 = undefined;
    var w = file.writer(io, &wb);
    try w.interface.print("{s}\n", .{buf});
    try w.interface.flush();
    std.debug.print("wrote {d} bytes, all three pairs unwind now\n", .{buf.len + 1});
}
wrote 17 bytes, all three pairs unwind now

Three pairs, three defers, each on the line after its acquire, and the function body below them never mentions cleanup again. When main ends they run in reverse: the file closes, the mutex unlocks, the buffer is freed. The fourth classic pair, begin and rollback or commit, is a job for errdefer, and you will see the game's real one in the IRON LEDGER box below.

AcquireReleaseUsual form
a.alloc(T, n) / a.create(T)a.free(s) / a.destroy(p)defer in the owner, errdefer in a constructor
dir.openFile(io, …) / createFilefile.close(io)defer
mutex.lock(io)mutex.unlock(io)defer
db.exec("BEGIN")db.exec("ROLLBACK")errdefer, with COMMIT as the last statement
list.init / .emptylist.deinit(a)defer
ArenaAllocator.init(gpa)arena.deinit()defer

A note on the mutex: in Zig 0.16 the general mutex is std.Io.Mutex, its lock takes an io and can return an error (cancellation), and unlock also takes io. Older tutorials show std.Thread.Mutex, which no longer exists. Chapter 36 covers threads properly.

17.7 Traps

Trap: defer in a loop. Because a loop body is a block, a defer inside it runs every iteration. That is right for per-iteration resources. It is wrong if you meant "clean up once, after the loop". If you write defer list.deinit(a) inside a loop that appends to list, the list is destroyed at the end of the first iteration and you are using freed memory on the second. Put the defer where the resource was created: if the list was created before the loop, the defer goes before the loop. Exercise 17.4 makes you do this right.
Trap: a defer cannot return or try. A deferred statement runs while the block is already leaving; there is no function left to return from, and no way to route an error. Both are compile errors: 
const std = @import("std");

fn f() !void {
    defer return error.Nope;
}

pub fn main() !void {
    try f();
}
def8.zig:4:11: error: cannot return from defer expression
    defer return error.Nope;
          ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
def8.zig:4:5: note: defer expression here
    defer return error.Nope;
    ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
const std = @import("std");

fn f() !void {
    defer {
        try std.fmt.parseInt(u8, "x", 10);
    }
}

pub fn main() !void {
    try f();
}
def9.zig:5:9: error: 'try' not allowed inside defer expression
        try std.fmt.parseInt(u8, "x", 10);
        ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
def9.zig:4:5: note: defer expression here
    defer {
    ^~~~~
If a cleanup can fail, decide what to do with the failure right there: defer file.close(io); is fine because close cannot fail; errdefer db.exec("ROLLBACK") catch {}; is how the game says "if the rollback itself fails, there is nothing more we can do". The catch {} is deliberate and commented.
Not a trap, but a surprise: no destructors. Zig will not run cleanup for you when a variable goes out of scope. A struct with a deinit method does nothing when it dies; you must write defer thing.deinit() yourself. This is on purpose. Nothing in Zig happens that you did not write, so there is never a hidden call at the end of a block. The trade is one line of defer per resource, which the compiler helps you remember for memory (the testing allocator) and which review makes easy to check, since setup and cleanup are adjacent.
In IRON LEDGER. The save store's opener in game/src/persist/store.zig has every idea from this chapter in twelve lines: a transaction begun, an errdefer that rolls it back with its own failure swallowed, a series of trys that each might trigger it, and a COMMIT that stands only if all of them passed. 
pub fn fromDb(db: sqlite.Db) !Store {
    try db.exec(ddl);
    const store: Store = .{ .db = db };
    const stored: u32 = @intCast(@max(1, store.getSetting("schema_version", 1)));
    if (stored > schema_version) return error.StoreNewerThanGame;
    try db.exec("BEGIN");
    errdefer db.exec("ROLLBACK") catch {};
    for (migrations) |m| {
        if (m.version <= stored) continue;
        if (!try hasColumnRt(db, m.table, m.column)) try db.exec(m.sql);
    }
    try store.setSetting("schema_version", schema_version);
    try db.exec("COMMIT");
    return store;
}
The constructor pattern appears in game/src/tui/emblem.zig, where Emblem.load decodes a PNG, registers errdefer { var i = img; i.deinit(gpa); }, and only then duplicates the bytes; if the dupe fails, the decoded image is released.
