And the wizard's generateCampaign in game/src/tui/app.zig builds a GameState, writes errdefer gs.deinit();, then runs three commands through try: any failure tears down the half-made campaign instead of leaking it into the app.

Exercises

Exercise 17.1 · Predict the order warm-up

Before running the program, write down the order of its eight output lines. Then run it and compare. File: exercises/17-defer/ex1_order.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 17, exercise 1: predict the order.
//! Run with:  zig run ex1_order.zig
//! Goal: before running, write down the order of the lines. Then run it.
//! Expected output:
//!   enter mission
//!     enter hangar
//!     leave hangar
//!   mission step 1
//!   mission step 2
//!   mission step 3
//!   leave mission (second defer)
//!   leave mission (first defer)
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("enter mission\n", .{});
    defer std.debug.print("leave mission (first defer)\n", .{});
    defer std.debug.print("leave mission (second defer)\n", .{});
    {
        std.debug.print("  enter hangar\n", .{});
        defer std.debug.print("  leave hangar\n", .{});
    }
    var i: u32 = 1;
    while (i <= 3) : (i += 1) {
        std.debug.print("mission step {d}\n", .{i});
    }
}

The hangar's defer belongs to the inner block, so it fires before the loop. The two mission defers belong to main and fire at the very end, in reverse order of registration.

Exercise 17.2 · errdefer keeps a failing constructor leak-free practice

Implement Squad.create, which makes two allocations and validates in between. A bad size must return error.BadSize without leaking. The testing allocator will tell you if you got it wrong. File: exercises/17-defer/ex2_errdefer.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 17, exercise 2: errdefer keeps a failing constructor leak-free.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_errdefer.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests. The testing
//! allocator fails the test if anything leaks.
const std = @import("std");

const Squad = struct {
    name: []u8,
    skills: []u8,

    /// Allocates a copy of `name` and a skills array. If `size` is 0 or
    /// more than 12, fails with error.BadSize, leaking nothing.
    fn create(a: std.mem.Allocator, name: []const u8, size: usize) !Squad {
        const name_copy = try a.dupe(u8, name);
        errdefer a.free(name_copy);

        if (size == 0 or size > 12) return error.BadSize;

        const skills = try a.alloc(u8, size);
        errdefer a.free(skills);
        @memset(skills, 4);

        return .{ .name = name_copy, .skills = skills };
    }

    fn deinit(self: *Squad, a: std.mem.Allocator) void {
        a.free(self.skills);
        a.free(self.name);
    }
};

test "good squad" {
    var s = try Squad.create(std.testing.allocator, "Alpha", 4);
    defer s.deinit(std.testing.allocator);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Alpha", s.name);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 4), s.skills.len);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 4), s.skills[3]);
}

test "bad size leaks nothing" {
    try std.testing.expectError(error.BadSize, Squad.create(std.testing.allocator, "Beta", 0));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.BadSize, Squad.create(std.testing.allocator, "Gamma", 13));
}

Each allocation is followed by its own errdefer. The second one is technically unnecessary as written, since nothing after it can fail, but adding it costs nothing and protects you when someone later adds a step. Try removing the first errdefer and read the leak report.

Exercise 17.3 · begin / commit / rollback practice

Implement Ledger.payAll so that a list of bills is paid atomically: begin a transaction, roll back with errdefer if any debit fails, commit at the end. File: exercises/17-defer/ex3_transaction.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 17, exercise 3: begin / commit / rollback with errdefer.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_transaction.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Ledger = struct {
    funds: i64,
    snapshot: i64 = 0,
    in_transaction: bool = false,
    rollbacks: u32 = 0,

    fn begin(self: *Ledger) void {
        self.snapshot = self.funds;
        self.in_transaction = true;
    }
    fn commit(self: *Ledger) void {
        self.in_transaction = false;
    }
    fn rollback(self: *Ledger) void {
        self.funds = self.snapshot;
        self.in_transaction = false;
        self.rollbacks += 1;
    }

    fn debit(self: *Ledger, amount: i64) !void {
        if (amount > self.funds) return error.InsufficientTreasury;
        self.funds -= amount;
    }

    /// Pay every bill in `bills` as one transaction: either all of them
    /// are paid, or none are. Use begin, errdefer rollback, commit.
    fn payAll(self: *Ledger, bills: []const i64) !void {
        self.begin();
        errdefer self.rollback();
        for (bills) |b| try self.debit(b);
        self.commit();
    }
};

test "all bills paid" {
    var l = Ledger{ .funds = 100 };
    try l.payAll(&.{ 10, 20, 30 });
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 40), l.funds);
    try std.testing.expect(!l.in_transaction);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 0), l.rollbacks);
}

test "one bad bill rolls back the rest" {
    var l = Ledger{ .funds = 100 };
    try std.testing.expectError(error.InsufficientTreasury, l.payAll(&.{ 10, 20, 500, 5 }));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 100), l.funds);
    try std.testing.expect(!l.in_transaction);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 1), l.rollbacks);
}

Four lines, and the same shape as the game's fromDb. The second test checks that after the failure the funds are back to 100, the transaction flag is clear, and exactly one rollback happened.

Exercise 17.4 · defer inside a loop challenge

Implement processAll, which opens and closes one fake file per iteration. The tests require that at most one file is open at a time, that every open is matched by a close, and that an error part way through still closes the current file. File: exercises/17-defer/ex4_loop.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 17, exercise 4: defer inside a loop runs every iteration.
//! Run with:  zig test ex4_loop.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// A fake file handle that counts opens and closes on a shared tally.
const Tally = struct { opens: u32 = 0, closes: u32 = 0, max_open: u32 = 0, open_now: u32 = 0 };

fn open(t: *Tally) void {
    t.opens += 1;
    t.open_now += 1;
    if (t.open_now > t.max_open) t.max_open = t.open_now;
}
fn close(t: *Tally) void {
    t.closes += 1;
    t.open_now -= 1;
}

/// Process `n` files one after another. Each must be closed before the
/// next is opened, and every file must be closed even when `fail_at`
/// makes the function return early with an error.
fn processAll(t: *Tally, n: u32, fail_at: ?u32) !void {
    var i: u32 = 0;
    while (i < n) : (i += 1) {
        open(t);
        defer close(t);
        if (fail_at) |f| if (i == f) return error.Corrupt;
    }
}

test "every open is matched by a close, one at a time" {
    var t = Tally{};
    try processAll(&t, 5, null);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 5), t.opens);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 5), t.closes);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 1), t.max_open);
}

test "an early error still closes the current file" {
    var t = Tally{};
    try std.testing.expectError(error.Corrupt, processAll(&t, 5, 2));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 3), t.opens);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 3), t.closes);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 0), t.open_now);
}

Because the defer close(t) is inside the loop body, it runs at the end of every iteration, which keeps max_open at 1. When the return error.Corrupt fires on iteration 2, the block still unwinds, so the third open gets its close.

Check your understanding

  1. In what order do three defers in the same block run?
    AnswerReverse order of registration: the last one written runs first.
  2. When does a defer inside a while body run?
    AnswerAt the end of every iteration, because the loop body is a block.
  3. What triggers an errdefer?
    AnswerThe block's function returning an error: a return error.X or a failing try. A normal return, even of an unhappy value, does not.
  4. Why does a constructor need errdefer after each allocation?
    AnswerIf a later step fails, the caller receives an error and no object, so it cannot free the earlier allocations. Only the constructor can, and errdefer does it on the error path alone.
  5. Can you try inside a defer?
    AnswerNo. The block is already leaving; there is nowhere for the error to go. Handle it there, for example with catch {}.
  6. Does a deferred expression see the value of a variable at registration time or at run time?
    AnswerAt run time. It is evaluated when it runs, which is how a loop counter can tell the errdefer how much to undo.
  7. Why does Zig not run deinit automatically when a struct goes out of scope?
    AnswerNo hidden control flow: nothing runs that you did not write. You add defer x.deinit() yourself, right after creating x.
What you learned.
  • defer stmt; runs stmt when the enclosing block ends, however it ends, in reverse order of registration.
  • The scope is the block: a bare {}, an if body or a loop body, not just the function.
  • errdefer runs only when the block exits with an error; errdefer |err| captures which one.
  • After each acquire in a constructor, write an errdefer release; the success path hands everything to the caller.
  • Write the release on the line after the acquire: alloc/free, open/close, lock/unlock, begin/rollback.
  • A deferred statement cannot return or try; handle cleanup failures in place.

18. Pointers

In this chapter you will learn what a pointer is, how to take one with & and follow it with .*, and why a function that needs to change its argument takes a pointer. You will meet the four pointer shapes Zig distinguishes, the difference between a constant pointer and a pointer to a constant, function pointers, and the two classic pointer bugs, one of which the 0.16 compiler now catches for you.

18.1 A pointer is an address

Every variable lives somewhere in memory, at a numbered location called its address. A pointer is a value that holds such an address. Instead of holding a morale score, it holds "where the morale score is". Through the pointer you can read the score, and, if the pointer allows it, change it. That indirection is the whole idea; everything else in this chapter is about the rules Zig puts around it so that it stays safe.

If you come from Python or JavaScript you have used pointers without the name: when you pass a list to a function and the function appends to it, the caller sees the change, because the "list" you passed was really a reference to the list. Zig makes that reference explicit and gives it a type. If you come from C, Zig's pointers are C's pointers with the dangerous operations removed: no arithmetic on single-item pointers, no implicit null, no silent casts.

ptr1.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var morale: u8 = 50;
    const p: *u8 = &morale; // p holds the address of morale

    std.debug.print("morale = {d}\n", .{morale});
    std.debug.print("p.*    = {d}\n", .{p.*});

    p.* += 10; // write through the pointer
    std.debug.print("after p.* += 10, morale = {d}\n", .{morale});

    morale = 5; // write to the variable directly
    std.debug.print("after morale = 5, p.* = {d}\n", .{p.*});

    std.debug.print("type of p: {s}\n", .{@typeName(@TypeOf(p))});
}
morale = 50
p.*    = 50
after p.* += 10, morale = 60
after morale = 5, p.* = 5
type of p: *u8

Three pieces of syntax. *u8 is the type "pointer to a u8". &morale takes the address of morale, producing a value of that type. p.* follows the pointer, and can appear on either side of an assignment: p.* += 10 writes through it, p.* in a print reads through it. Because p and morale name the same byte of memory, changing one changes what you see through the other.

Note that p itself is declared const. That is because the pointer value never changes: it always points at morale. What it points at changes freely, because the type is *u8, a pointer to a mutable byte. Section 18.6 comes back to this distinction.

18.2 *const T: look but do not touch

A pointer type can promise not to write. *const u8 is a pointer through which you may only read. Trying to assign through it is a compile error.

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var morale: u8 = 50;
    const view: *const u8 = &morale; // may read, may not write
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{view.*});
    view.* = 60;
}
ptr2.zig:7:9: error: cannot assign to constant
    view.* = 60;
    ~~~~^~
referenced by:
…

A *T coerces to a *const T automatically (giving up the right to write is always safe), never the reverse. This is why so many function parameters in Zig are *const Something: the function is saying "I need to see the whole thing without copying it, and I promise not to change it". Taking the address of a const variable gives you a *const pointer; you cannot get a mutable pointer to something that was declared constant.

18.3 Passing a pointer to mutate

Function arguments in Zig are passed by value: the function gets its own copy and changes to the copy are invisible to the caller. To let a function change the caller's variable, pass a pointer to it. This is the same rule you saw for self in Chapter 12: methods that mutate take self: *T, methods that only read take self: T or self: *const T.

ptr3.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Pilot = struct { name: []const u8, morale: u8, missions: u32 };

// Takes a copy. Changes stay inside this function.
fn cheerCopy(p: Pilot) void {
    var local = p;
    local.morale += 10;
}

// Takes a pointer. Changes reach the caller's variable.
fn cheer(p: *Pilot) void {
    p.morale += 10; // no arrow, no (*p).morale: field access auto-derefs
    p.missions += 1;
}

fn describe(p: *const Pilot) void {
    std.debug.print("{s}: morale {d}, {d} missions\n", .{ p.name, p.morale, p.missions });
}

pub fn main() void {
    var ada = Pilot{ .name = "Ada", .morale = 50, .missions = 0 };
    cheerCopy(ada);
    describe(&ada);
    cheer(&ada);
    describe(&ada);
    cheer(&ada);
    describe(&ada);
}
Ada: morale 50, 0 missions
Ada: morale 60, 1 missions
Ada: morale 70, 2 missions

cheerCopy did nothing visible: it cheered a copy and the copy was thrown away. cheer took *Pilot and its changes stuck. Two conveniences make pointer code read cleanly. First, field access through a pointer needs no arrow: p.morale works whether p is a Pilot or a *Pilot; the compiler inserts the dereference. Second, when you call a method on a variable, Zig takes the address for you: ada.cheer() would work as well as cheer(&ada). You only write & explicitly when passing the pointer as an ordinary argument, as here.

When to take a pointer, and when not to. Take *T when you must mutate. Take *const T when the struct is large and you only read it. Take a plain T for small structs you only read; the compiler is free to pass them however is cheapest. Do not take a pointer "for speed" on a two-field struct; it makes the call site noisier for nothing.

18.4 Pointers to elements, to whole arrays, and to many items

Zig has four pointer shapes, and the type spells out which one you have.

TypePoints atCan index?Knows its length?
*Texactly one Tnon/a
*[N]Tan array of N itemsyesyes, at compile time
[]T (slice)len itemsyesyes, at run time
[*]Tsome unknown number of itemsyesno

ptr4.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var hp = [_]u8{ 10, 20, 30, 40 };

    // pointer to one element
    const second: *u8 = &hp[1];
    second.* = 25;

    // iterate by pointer to modify in place
    for (&hp) |*h| h.* += 1;

    // pointer to the whole array, and coercion to a slice
    const whole: *[4]u8 = &hp;
    const sl: []u8 = whole; // *[N]T coerces to []T
    std.debug.print("{any} len {d}\n", .{ sl, sl.len });
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{@typeName(@TypeOf(&hp))});

    // many-item pointer: no length, indexable, used at C boundaries
    const many: [*]u8 = &hp;
    std.debug.print("many[0] = {d}, many[3] = {d}\n", .{ many[0], many[3] });
    std.debug.print("back to a slice: {any}\n", .{many[0..4]});
}
{ 11, 26, 31, 41 } len 4
*[4]u8
many[0] = 11, many[3] = 41
back to a slice: { 11, 26, 31, 41 }

&hp[1] is a single-item pointer to the second element. for (&hp) |*h| iterates the array by pointer, so h.* += 1 changes each element in place; you met this in Chapter 9. &hp on the whole array is a *[4]u8, a pointer to an array, and it coerces to a slice []u8 whenever a slice is wanted, which is why you can pass &array to any function that takes a slice. This coercion is the most common way slices come into existence.

The many-item pointer [*]T is the odd one out: it can be indexed, but carries no length, so nothing stops you indexing past the end. Zig keeps it for one reason: it is what a C pointer is. You will see [*]u8 and its zero-terminated cousin [*:0]const u8 at the boundary with C libraries and almost nowhere else. Whenever you get one, turn it back into a slice as soon as you know the length, as the last line does with many[0..4].

18.5 Alignment, *anyopaque and @ptrCast

Every type has an alignment: an address it may live at must be a multiple of that number. A u32 lives at a multiple of 4, a u64 at a multiple of 8. Structs take the largest alignment of their fields. You rarely think about this, because the compiler and allocators handle it, but the numbers are visible and pointer types carry them.

ptr5.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Unit = struct { tonnage: u8, armour: u16 };

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("u8   size {d} align {d}\n", .{ @sizeOf(u8), @alignOf(u8) });
    std.debug.print("u16  size {d} align {d}\n", .{ @sizeOf(u16), @alignOf(u16) });
    std.debug.print("u32  size {d} align {d}\n", .{ @sizeOf(u32), @alignOf(u32) });
    std.debug.print("u64  size {d} align {d}\n", .{ @sizeOf(u64), @alignOf(u64) });
    std.debug.print("Unit size {d} align {d}\n", .{ @sizeOf(Unit), @alignOf(Unit) });

    var u = Unit{ .tonnage = 55, .armour = 120 };

    // Erase the type: any pointer can become *anyopaque.
    const opaque_ptr: *anyopaque = &u;

    // Recover it: @ptrCast changes the pointee type, @alignCast asserts alignment.
    const back: *Unit = @ptrCast(@alignCast(opaque_ptr));
    back.armour += 1;
    std.debug.print("armour via round trip: {d}\n", .{u.armour});
}
u8   size 1 align 1
u16  size 2 align 2
u32  size 4 align 4
u64  size 8 align 8
Unit size 4 align 2
armour via round trip: 121

*anyopaque is the pointer that has forgotten its type: "an address, of something". It is Zig's spelling of C's void*. Any single-item pointer coerces to it. To get the type back you use @ptrCast, and because *anyopaque has an alignment of 1 while *Unit requires 2, you also need @alignCast, which asserts (checked in Debug) that the address really is suitably aligned. The pair @ptrCast(@alignCast(p)) is the standard incantation, and the destination type is taken from the declared type of the variable you assign to. This is exactly how the allocator interface works: std.mem.Allocator stores a *anyopaque to "whatever the concrete allocator is" and each implementation casts it back to itself. You will write that cast yourself in Chapter 20.

18.6 Constant pointer versus pointer to constant

Two different things can be constant: the pointer, or what it points at. They are independent.

ptr7.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var a: u8 = 1;
    var b: u8 = 2;

    // A pointer to a mutable value; the variable p itself can be re-pointed.
    var p: *u8 = &a;
    p.* = 10;
    p = &b;
    p.* = 20;

    // A constant pointer to a mutable value: q always points at a,
    // but a may still be changed through it.
    const q: *u8 = &a;
    q.* += 1;

    // A pointer to a constant: r may be re-pointed, but never written through.
    var r: *const u8 = &a;
    r = &b;

    std.debug.print("a={d} b={d} r.*={d}\n", .{ a, b, r.* });
}
a=11 b=20 r.*=20
  • var p: *u8: both may change. You can re-point p and write through it.
  • const q: *u8: the pointer is fixed, the target is writable. This is the common case for a local you take once.
  • var r: *const u8: the pointer may be re-pointed, but never written through.
  • const s: *const u8: neither, the fully read-only view.

Read the type from right to left: *const u8 is "pointer to (const u8)". The const or var at the front of the declaration is about the variable holding the pointer, as for any other variable.

18.7 Optional pointers

Chapter 15 promised that ?*T is free, and it is the shape every "find or fail" function returns. Combine it with a capture and you can mutate what you found.

ptr8.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Pilot = struct { name: []const u8, skill: u8 };

var roster = [_]Pilot{
    .{ .name = "Ada", .skill = 4 },
    .{ .name = "Bo", .skill = 6 },
};

fn find(name: []const u8) ?*Pilot {
    for (&roster) |*p| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, p.name, name)) return p;
    }
    return null;
}

pub fn main() void {
    if (find("Bo")) |p| {
        p.skill -= 1; // train: lower is better in this ruleset
        std.debug.print("{s} now skill {d}\n", .{ p.name, p.skill });
    }
    const missing = find("Cy");
    std.debug.print("Cy found? {}\n", .{missing != null});
    std.debug.print("?*Pilot is {d} bytes, same as *Pilot ({d})\n", .{ @sizeOf(?*Pilot), @sizeOf(*Pilot) });
}
Bo now skill 5
Cy found? false
?*Pilot is 8 bytes, same as *Pilot (8)

A plain pointer in Zig can never be null; that is what allows the optimisation and what makes p.* always safe on a *T. The compiler is strict about it even at the lowest level:

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const p: *u32 = @ptrFromInt(0x0);
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{p.*});
}
ptr11.zig:4:33: error: pointer type '*u32' does not allow address zero
    const p: *u32 = @ptrFromInt(0x0);
                                ^~~
…

18.8 Function pointers

Functions have addresses too, so you can store one in a variable and call it later. The type is *const fn (Args) Ret, and a plain function name coerces to it. A table of function pointers is how you build a dispatcher, a pipeline, or a callback.

ptr6.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn double(x: i32) i32 {
    return x * 2;
}
fn negate(x: i32) i32 {
    return -x;
}

const Op = *const fn (i32) i32;

fn applyAll(ops: []const Op, start: i32) i32 {
    var v = start;
    for (ops) |op| v = op(v);
    return v;
}

pub fn main() void {
    const f: Op = double;
    std.debug.print("double(21) = {d}\n", .{f(21)});

    const pipeline = [_]Op{ double, negate, double };
    std.debug.print("pipeline(3) = {d}\n", .{applyAll(&pipeline, 3)});
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{@typeName(Op)});
}
double(21) = 42
pipeline(3) = -12
*const fn (i32) i32

The const in *const fn is required: you cannot write through a pointer into code. Calling through a function pointer looks exactly like calling a function, op(v). In the standard library, this is how sorting takes its comparison function and how the allocator's vtable holds its four operations.

18.9 The two classic pointer bugs

A pointer is only as good as the memory behind it. Two mistakes produce a pointer to memory that is no longer what you think it is. Both are called dangling pointers, and using one is undefined behaviour: the program might crash, might print garbage, or might appear to work until the day it does not.

Bug 1: a pointer to a local that has ended. Local variables live in the function's stack frame, which is discarded when the function returns. A pointer to one of them is meaningless afterwards. In C this compiles silently. In Zig 0.16, the simple case is a compile error:

const std = @import("std");

// DO NOT DO THIS. `n` lives in makeCounter's stack frame, which is gone
// the moment the function returns. The pointer now points at garbage.
fn makeCounter() *u32 {
    var n: u32 = 0;
    return &n;
}

pub fn main() void {
    const c = makeCounter();
    c.* += 1;
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{c.*});
}
ptr9.zig:7:13: error: returning address of expired local variable 'n'
    return &n;
            ^
ptr9.zig:6:9: note: declared runtime-known here
    var n: u32 = 0;
…

The compiler cannot catch every variation, for instance storing &local into a struct that outlives the function, so keep the rule in your head: never let a pointer to a local escape the block the local was declared in. If a value must outlive the function that made it, put it on the heap (Chapter 19) or return it by value and let the caller store it.

Bug 2: a pointer into a container that grew. A growable list keeps its items in one buffer. When it runs out of room, it allocates a bigger buffer, copies the items across, and frees the old one. Any pointer you took into the old buffer now points at freed memory. This one the compiler cannot see, because whether the buffer moves depends on run-time sizes.

ptr10.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const a = init.gpa;
    var list: std.ArrayList(u32) = .empty;
    defer list.deinit(a);

    try list.append(a, 7);
    const first: *u32 = &list.items[0]; // pointer into the list's buffer
    std.debug.print("before growth, first -> {d}\n", .{first.*});

    // Grow the list a lot. Sooner or later it must move its buffer.
    var i: u32 = 0;
    while (i < 10_000) : (i += 1) try list.append(a, i);

    const still_same = (first == &list.items[0]);
    std.debug.print("buffer still at the old address? {}\n", .{still_same});
    std.debug.print("safe way: re-fetch, items[0] = {d}\n", .{list.items[0]});
    // Reading first.* here would be use-after-free. We do not.
}
before growth, first -> 7
buffer still at the old address? false
safe way: re-fetch, items[0] = 7

The program compares addresses rather than reading through the stale pointer, because reading it would be undefined behaviour and no output from it could be trusted. The comparison shows the buffer moved. The rule that follows: do not hold a pointer into a list or map across an operation that can grow it. Hold an index or a key instead, and re-fetch the pointer after the insert. The IRON LEDGER box has the game's own version of this lesson.

Trap. The dangerous thing about dangling pointers is that they often work. The old buffer's bytes may still be there for a while, so a test passes, and the bug appears weeks later when an allocator reuses that memory. In Debug builds the DebugAllocator helps, because it never hands freed memory back out and unmaps it where it can, so a stale read usually crashes immediately with a trace. Run your tests in Debug.
In IRON LEDGER. Every command handler is a function on gs: *GameState, and every lookup returns an optional pointer into the state's maps: gs.person(id), gs.unit(id), gs.force(id) are all ?*T. The RNG bag in game/src/sim/rng.zig seeds its array of generators by iterating with pointers so it can assign through them: 
for (&self.prngs, 0..) |*prng, i| {
    prng.* = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(seed ^ (0x9E3779B97F4A7C15 *% (i + 1)));
}
The stale-pointer bug from section 18.9 is one the project hit for real. From the original guide: "If you hold *Force from a hash map and then insert into that map, the map may reallocate and your pointer now points at freed memory. The fix is to re-fetch after any insert." That is why you will see gs.force(id) called again a few lines after a createForce, rather than a pointer kept across it, and why the domain code passes typed IDs around instead of pointers wherever a value must survive a tick.

Exercises

Exercise 18.1 · Swap through pointers warm-up

Write swap(a: *i32, b: *i32), bump(p: *u32, by: u32) and twice(p: *const u32) u32. File: exercises/18-pointers/ex1_swap.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 18, exercise 1: swap through pointers.
//! Run with:  zig test ex1_swap.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Exchange the values behind the two pointers.
fn swap(a: *i32, b: *i32) void {
    const tmp = a.*;
    a.* = b.*;
    b.* = tmp;
}

/// Add `by` to the value behind `p`.
fn bump(p: *u32, by: u32) void {
    p.* += by;
}

/// Read-only: a pointer to const may be read but never written through.
fn twice(p: *const u32) u32 {
    return p.* * 2;
}

test "swap" {
    var x: i32 = 1;
    var y: i32 = 2;
    swap(&x, &y);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, 2), x);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, 1), y);
}

test "bump and twice" {
    var n: u32 = 5;
    bump(&n, 3);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 8), n);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 16), twice(&n));
    const frozen: u32 = 21;
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 42), twice(&frozen));
}

twice takes *const u32, which is why the test can pass &frozen, the address of a constant. Try changing its parameter to *u32 and see the compile error.

Exercise 18.2 · Mutate a struct through a pointer practice

Implement survive(p: *Pilot), which updates fields in place, rating(p: *const Pilot), and surviveAll(pilots: []Pilot), which iterates by pointer. File: exercises/18-pointers/ex2_mutate.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 18, exercise 2: mutate a struct through a pointer.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_mutate.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Pilot = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    gunnery: u8,
    piloting: u8,
    missions: u32 = 0,
};

/// One mission survived: missions + 1; every 3rd mission improves
/// gunnery by one (lower is better, minimum 0).
fn survive(p: *Pilot) void {
    p.missions += 1;
    if (p.missions % 3 == 0 and p.gunnery > 0) p.gunnery -= 1;
}

/// Sum of both skills. Takes a pointer to const: it only reads.
fn rating(p: *const Pilot) u8 {
    return p.gunnery + p.piloting;
}

/// Apply `survive` to every pilot in the slice, in place.
fn surviveAll(pilots: []Pilot) void {
    for (pilots) |*p| survive(p);
}

test "survive mutates the caller's pilot" {
    var ada = Pilot{ .name = "Ada", .gunnery = 4, .piloting = 5 };
    survive(&ada);
    survive(&ada);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 2), ada.missions);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 4), ada.gunnery);
    survive(&ada);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 3), ada.gunnery);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 8), rating(&ada));
}

test "surviveAll" {
    var lance = [_]Pilot{
        .{ .name = "A", .gunnery = 4, .piloting = 5, .missions = 2 },
        .{ .name = "B", .gunnery = 0, .piloting = 5, .missions = 2 },
    };
    surviveAll(&lance);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 3), lance[0].gunnery);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 0), lance[1].gunnery);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 3), lance[1].missions);
}

Inside surviveAll, for (pilots) |*p| gives a *Pilot for each element, which is exactly what survive wants. Without the star you would get copies and the array would not change.

Exercise 18.3 · Arrays, elements and many items practice

Four functions, one per pointer shape: a slice to double in place, a *[4]u8 to fill, a ?*u32 pointing at the largest element, and a [*]const u32 summed with an explicit length. File: exercises/18-pointers/ex3_arrays.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 18, exercise 3: pointers to arrays, elements and many items.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_arrays.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Double every element in place.
fn doubleAll(items: []u32) void {
    for (items) |*x| x.* *= 2;
}

/// Pointer to a fixed-size array: set every element to `v`.
fn fill4(arr: *[4]u8, v: u8) void {
    for (arr) |*x| x.* = v;
}

/// Pointer to the largest element, or null for an empty slice.
fn largest(items: []u32) ?*u32 {
    if (items.len == 0) return null;
    var best: *u32 = &items[0];
    for (items[1..]) |*x| if (x.* > best.*) {
        best = x;
    };
    return best;
}

/// A many-item pointer has no length, so the caller passes one.
fn sumMany(p: [*]const u32, n: usize) u32 {
    var total: u32 = 0;
    var i: usize = 0;
    while (i < n) : (i += 1) total += p[i];
    return total;
}

test "doubleAll" {
    var hp = [_]u32{ 1, 2, 3 };
    doubleAll(&hp); // *[3]u32 coerces to []u32
    try std.testing.expectEqualSlices(u32, &.{ 2, 4, 6 }, &hp);
}

test "fill4" {
    var buf: [4]u8 = undefined;
    fill4(&buf, 'x');
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("xxxx", &buf);
}

test "largest points into the slice" {
    var hp = [_]u32{ 5, 9, 2 };
    const p = largest(&hp).?;
    p.* = 0; // writing through the pointer changes the array
    try std.testing.expectEqualSlices(u32, &.{ 5, 0, 2 }, &hp);
    var none = [_]u32{};
    try std.testing.expect(largest(&none) == null);
}

test "sumMany" {
    const hp = [_]u32{ 1, 2, 3, 4 };
    const many: [*]const u32 = &hp;
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 10), sumMany(many, 4));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 3), sumMany(many, 2));
}

largest returns a pointer into the caller's slice, and the test proves it by writing zero through the pointer and checking the array. sumMany has to be told the length; that is the price of a many-item pointer, and why you convert to a slice as soon as you can.

Exercise 18.4 · A dispatch table of function pointers challenge

Build a table mapping names to *const fn (i32) i32, a lookup returning ?Op, an apply that combines lookup and call, and a pipeline. File: exercises/18-pointers/ex4_fnptr.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 18, exercise 4: a dispatch table of function pointers.
//! Run with:  zig test ex4_fnptr.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Op = *const fn (i32) i32;

fn double(x: i32) i32 {
    return x * 2;
}
fn negate(x: i32) i32 {
    return -x;
}
fn square(x: i32) i32 {
    return x * x;
}

const Entry = struct { name: []const u8, op: Op };

const table = [_]Entry{
    .{ .name = "double", .op = double },
    .{ .name = "negate", .op = negate },
    .{ .name = "square", .op = square },
};

/// Look up the operation by name, or null if unknown.
fn lookup(name: []const u8) ?Op {
    for (table) |e| if (std.mem.eql(u8, e.name, name)) return e.op;
    return null;
}

/// Apply the named operation, or return null if the name is unknown.
fn apply(name: []const u8, x: i32) ?i32 {
    const op = lookup(name) orelse return null;
    return op(x);
}

/// Run every op in `ops` left to right, starting from `start`.
fn pipeline(ops: []const Op, start: i32) i32 {
    var v = start;
    for (ops) |op| v = op(v);
    return v;
}

test "apply by name" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?i32, 10), apply("double", 5));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?i32, -5), apply("negate", 5));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?i32, 25), apply("square", 5));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?i32, null), apply("cube", 5));
}

test "pipeline" {
    const ops = [_]Op{ double, square, negate };
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, -36), pipeline(&ops, 3));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, 7), pipeline(&.{}, 7));
}

Function names coerce to the pointer type when placed in the table. apply uses orelse return null so that an unknown name becomes a null result rather than a crash.

Exercise 18.5 · Do not keep a pointer across a growth challenge

Implement recruit, which appends a pilot to an ArrayList and then links the new pilot and the previous one as wingmen. The list grows five thousand times in the test, so any pointer taken before the append is unsafe afterwards. Use indices. File: exercises/18-pointers/ex5_stale.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 18, exercise 5: do not keep a pointer across a growth.
//! Run with:  zig test ex5_stale.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests. `recruit`
//! must never read through a pointer that may have gone stale.
const std = @import("std");

const Pilot = struct { name: []const u8, wingman: ?usize = null };

/// Add `name`, then pair the new pilot with the previous one as wingmen.
/// Returns the index of the new pilot. Hold INDICES, not pointers,
/// across the append: appending may move the whole buffer.
fn recruit(a: std.mem.Allocator, list: *std.ArrayList(Pilot), name: []const u8) !usize {
    const new_index = list.items.len;
    try list.append(a, .{ .name = name });
    if (new_index > 0) {
        const prev = new_index - 1;
        list.items[new_index].wingman = prev;
        list.items[prev].wingman = new_index;
    }
    return new_index;
}

test "pairing survives many reallocations" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    var list: std.ArrayList(Pilot) = .empty;
    defer list.deinit(a);

    var i: usize = 0;
    while (i < 5000) : (i += 1) {
        const idx = try recruit(a, &list, "pilot");
        try std.testing.expectEqual(i, idx);
    }
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?usize, 1), list.items[0].wingman);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?usize, 2), list.items[1].wingman);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?usize, 4999), list.items[4998].wingman);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?usize, 4998), list.items[4999].wingman);
}

The tempting wrong version takes const prev = &list.items[len - 1]; before the append and writes prev.wingman after it. It may even pass a small test. Indices survive reallocation because they are re-resolved against list.items every time.

Check your understanding

  1. What do &x and p.* do?
    Answer&x produces a pointer to x; p.* follows a pointer to read or write the value it points at.
  2. Why must a function that changes its argument take a pointer?
    AnswerArguments are passed by value, so the function gets a copy. A pointer lets it reach the caller's original.
  3. What is the difference between *[4]u8, []u8 and [*]u8?
    AnswerPointer to an array of exactly 4 (length known at compile time); slice (pointer plus run-time length); many-item pointer (no length at all, for C boundaries).
  4. Is const p: *u8 = &x; a pointer you can write through?
    AnswerYes. const fixes the pointer variable; the type *u8 allows writing through it. *const u8 would not.
  5. What does @ptrCast(@alignCast(p)) do to a *anyopaque?
    Answer@alignCast asserts the address has the alignment the target type needs; @ptrCast changes the pointee type to the one being assigned to.
  6. Why is returning &local from a function wrong, and what does Zig 0.16 do about it?
    AnswerThe local's stack frame is gone after return, so the pointer dangles. The compiler rejects the direct case with "returning address of expired local variable".
  7. You take a pointer to an element of an ArrayList, then append. What should you assume?
    AnswerThat the pointer is invalid. The buffer may have moved. Keep an index and re-fetch after the append.
What you learned.
  • *T holds an address; &x makes one; p.* follows it; field access through a pointer needs no arrow.
  • *const T may only be read through; *T coerces to it, not the reverse.
  • Pass *T to mutate, *const T to read a large struct, plain T for small read-only values.
  • Four shapes: *T, *[N]T (coerces to a slice), []T, [*]T (C boundary only).
  • *anyopaque is the untyped pointer; recover the type with @ptrCast(@alignCast(p)).
  • Pointers can be null only as ?*T; function pointers are *const fn (…) R.
  • Never let a pointer to a local escape, and never hold a pointer into a container across a growth.

19. Memory: stack, heap and allocators

In this chapter you will learn where your program's bytes live, why some values need the heap, and how Zig hands out heap memory: not with a hidden new, but through an allocator you pass around like any other value. You will allocate and free, watch the testing allocator catch a leak, and learn the ownership conventions that tell you, for any slice, whether you must free it.

19.1 Two places to keep a value

Every value your program makes has to live somewhere. Zig gives you two places, and it matters which one you choose.

The stack is a region of memory that grows and shrinks as functions are called and return. When a function starts, it gets a frame on the stack, and every local variable lives in that frame. When the function returns, the frame is discarded, all at once, for free. That is why locals are so cheap and why Chapter 18 warned you never to return a pointer to one: the memory is reclaimed the instant the function ends. Stack frames are also small; a few kilobytes each, a few megabytes in total.

The heap is everything else: a large pool of memory from which you can request a block of any size, keep it as long as you like, across as many function calls as you like, and give it back when you are done. The price is that you have to give it back. Nothing does it for you.

mem2.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn stackBuffer() void {
    var buf: [8]u8 = undefined; // lives in this function's frame
    @memset(&buf, 'z');
    std.debug.print("stack: {s}\n", .{buf});
} // buf is gone here, for free

fn heapBuffer(a: std.mem.Allocator) ![]u8 {
    const buf = try a.alloc(u8, 8); // lives until someone frees it
    @memset(buf, 'h');
    return buf; // fine: the memory outlives this function
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    stackBuffer();
    const b = try heapBuffer(init.gpa);
    defer init.gpa.free(b);
    std.debug.print("heap:  {s}\n", .{b});
}
stack: zzzzzzzz
heap:  hhhhhhhh

stackBuffer's array is created and destroyed inside the function. heapBuffer's slice comes from an allocator, is returned to the caller, and the caller frees it. The rule of thumb: use the stack when the size is known at compile time and the value does not need to outlive the function. Use the heap when the size depends on run-time data (a list of pilots read from a file), when the value must outlive the function that made it, or when it is too big for a frame.

19.2 Why Zig has no new

In most languages, heap allocation is invisible. Python makes a list and you never think about where it went. C++ has new and Go has make, but the standard library allocates behind your back all the time. Zig's rule is that nothing allocates unless you hand it an allocator. There is no global heap function. If a function needs heap memory, it takes a parameter of type std.mem.Allocator, and every call site shows it.

This buys three things. You can always see which lines might allocate (and therefore might fail with OutOfMemory, which is an ordinary error you handle with try). You can choose a different strategy for different parts of the program, because the allocator is just a value; Chapter 20 is about that choice. And a library you use can never surprise you with allocation, because it has nowhere to get memory except from you.

The allocator is small, two pointers:

mem9.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("Allocator is {d} bytes: a data pointer and a vtable pointer\n", .{@sizeOf(std.mem.Allocator)});
    inline for (@typeInfo(std.mem.Allocator).@"struct".fields) |f| {
        std.debug.print("  field {s}: {s}\n", .{ f.name, @typeName(f.type) });
    }
}
Allocator is 16 bytes: a data pointer and a vtable pointer
  field ptr: *anyopaque
  field vtable: *const mem.Allocator.VTable

ptr is the concrete allocator's own state, as an untyped pointer. vtable points at its four functions (allocate, resize, remap, free). Every allocator in the standard library, and any you write, is something that can produce this two-pointer value. Passing it by value is cheap, so you pass it everywhere.

19.3 alloc, free, create, destroy, dupe

The allocator interface has a handful of methods you will use constantly. Where does the allocator itself come from? For now, from the init parameter of main: init.gpa is a general-purpose allocator the runtime prepares for you, leak-checked in Debug builds. Section 19.6 shows how to make your own.

mem1.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const a = init.gpa; // std.mem.Allocator

    // alloc: n values of T, returned as a slice you own
    const hp = try a.alloc(u16, 4);
    defer a.free(hp);
    @memset(hp, 100);
    hp[2] = 37;
    std.debug.print("hp = {any}\n", .{hp});

    // create: one T on the heap, returned as *T
    const Pilot = struct { name: []const u8, skill: u8 };
    const p = try a.create(Pilot);
    defer a.destroy(p);
    p.* = .{ .name = "Ada", .skill = 4 };
    std.debug.print("{s} skill {d}\n", .{ p.name, p.skill });

    // dupe: copy a slice into fresh memory you own
    const greeting = try a.dupe(u8, "hello, commander");
    defer a.free(greeting);
    greeting[0] = 'H';
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{greeting});
}
hp = { 100, 100, 37, 100 }
Ada skill 4
Hello, commander
  • a.alloc(T, n) gives you n values of T as a slice []T. The bytes are uninitialised; write before you read. Release with a.free(slice).
  • a.create(T) gives you one T as a pointer *T. Release with a.destroy(ptr).
  • a.dupe(T, slice) allocates a copy of a slice. Release with a.free. This is the way to make a string you own from one you were only lent.

Every one of them can fail with error.OutOfMemory, so every call has a try. And every one of them is paired with a defer on the next line, as Chapter 17 taught. Free with the same allocator you allocated from; mixing allocators is a bug the DebugAllocator will catch loudly.

Free takes the slice, not just the pointer. a.free(hp) receives the whole slice, pointer and length. That is how the allocator knows how much to release without keeping its own size table. Consequently you must free exactly the slice you were given, not a sub-slice of it.

19.4 The testing allocator catches leaks

Forgetting a free is the classic manual-memory bug, and Zig's answer is to make the tests find it. std.testing.allocator is a debug allocator that records every allocation with the stack trace of where it happened; at the end of each test, anything not freed fails the test and prints where it came from. Here is a function that leaks, and the report.

mem3.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn makeGreeting(a: std.mem.Allocator, name: []const u8) ![]u8 {
    return std.fmt.allocPrint(a, "welcome, {s}", .{name});
}

test "greeting" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    const g = try makeGreeting(a, "commander");
    // oops: no free
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("welcome, commander", g);
}
1/1 mem3.test.greeting...OK
[DebugAllocator] (err): memory address 0x… leaked: 
<zig>/lib/std/fmt.zig:636:27: 0x… in allocPrint__anon_36363 (test)
    return aw.toOwnedSlice();
                          ^
ch19/mem3.zig:4:30: 0x… in makeGreeting (test)
    return std.fmt.allocPrint(a, "welcome, {s}", .{name});
                             ^
ch19/mem3.zig:9:31: 0x… in test.greeting (test)
    const g = try makeGreeting(a, "commander");
                              ^
<zig>/lib/compiler/test_runner.zig:291:25: 0x… in mainTerminal (test)
        if (test_fn.func()) |_| {
                        ^
<zig>/lib/compiler/test_runner.zig:73:28: 0x… in main (test)
        return mainTerminal(init);
                           ^
<zig>/lib/std/start.zig:699:88: 0x… in callMain (test)
    if (fn_info.params[0].type.? == std.process.Init.Minimal) return wrapMain(root.main(.{
                                                                                       ^
???:?:?: 0x… in start (/usr/lib/dyld)

…

Read it from the top. The test's assertions all passed ("OK"), and then the allocator spoke: one block was never freed, allocated inside allocPrint, called from makeGreeting, called from the test. That is the exact call chain of the leaked allocation. The final lines say the test run failed. The fix is one line: defer a.free(g); after the call. Use the testing allocator in every test that allocates; it is free insurance.

19.5 Ownership: who frees this?

When a function returns a slice, a question arises that never comes up in Python: does the caller now have to free it? Zig has no runtime answer; the answer is a convention, written in the function's doc comment and followed by everyone. Two conventions cover nearly everything.

Caller owns. The function allocates the result with the allocator it was given, and the caller must free it with the same allocator. Any function that takes an Allocator and returns a slice or pointer is almost certainly this. allocPrint, dupe, readFileAlloc: all caller-owns.

Borrowed. The function returns a slice into memory the caller already has. Nothing was allocated; there is nothing to free; the result is only valid as long as the original is. Any function that takes no allocator and returns a slice is this. std.mem.trim, tokenizer.next(), slicing with s[a..b]: all borrowed.

mem6.zig

const std = @import("std");

/// Caller owns the returned slice and must free it with `a`.
fn upperCopy(a: std.mem.Allocator, s: []const u8) ![]u8 {
    const out = try a.alloc(u8, s.len);
    for (s, out) |c, *o| o.* = std.ascii.toUpper(c);
    return out;
}

/// Borrows `s`: returns a slice INTO the caller's memory. Nothing to free.
fn firstWord(s: []const u8) []const u8 {
    const end = std.mem.indexOfScalar(u8, s, ' ') orelse s.len;
    return s[0..end];
}

test "owned vs borrowed" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    const line = "hire steiner now";

    const w = firstWord(line); // borrowed: points into `line`
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("hire", w);

    const up = try upperCopy(a, line); // owned: we must free
    defer a.free(up);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("HIRE STEINER NOW", up);
}
1/1 mem6.test.owned vs borrowed...OK
All 1 tests passed.

A useful habit: if a function returns a slice and takes an allocator, expect to defer free the result. If it does not take an allocator, it could not have allocated, so do not. When you write your own, say which it is in the doc comment; IRON LEDGER's are full of "caller owns" and "borrows from the arena".

Trap: storing a borrowed slice. A borrowed slice is a pointer into someone else's buffer. If you keep it in a struct that outlives that buffer, you have a dangling pointer. When a function receives a []const u8 and needs to keep it, it should dupe it and own the copy. The next example shows the idiom.

mem8.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Roster = struct {
    names: std.ArrayList([]u8),
    a: std.mem.Allocator,

    fn init(a: std.mem.Allocator) Roster {
        return .{ .names = .empty, .a = a };
    }

    fn deinit(self: *Roster) void {
        for (self.names.items) |n| self.a.free(n);
        self.names.deinit(self.a);
    }

    /// Copies `name`, so the caller may reuse its buffer afterwards.
    fn add(self: *Roster, name: []const u8) !void {
        const copy = try self.a.dupe(u8, name);
        errdefer self.a.free(copy);
        try self.names.append(self.a, copy);
    }
};

test "roster owns copies of the names" {
    var r = Roster.init(std.testing.allocator);
    defer r.deinit();

    var scratch: [16]u8 = undefined;
    const n1 = try std.fmt.bufPrint(&scratch, "pilot-{d}", .{1});
    try r.add(n1);
    const n2 = try std.fmt.bufPrint(&scratch, "pilot-{d}", .{2}); // overwrites scratch
    try r.add(n2);

    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("pilot-1", r.names.items[0]);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("pilot-2", r.names.items[1]);
}
1/1 mem8.test.roster owns copies of the names...OK
All 1 tests passed.

The test deliberately reuses one scratch buffer for both names. If add had stored the slice it was handed instead of a copy, the first name would have been overwritten by the second, and the test would fail. Because add owns copies, deinit must free each one and then the list, which is why Roster remembers its allocator.

19.6 Making an allocator: DebugAllocator

init.gpa is convenient, but you should see what is behind it. std.heap.DebugAllocator is the general-purpose allocator for development. You create one as a variable, ask it for an Allocator value, and call deinit() at the end, which returns .ok or .leak.

mem4.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var gpa_state: std.heap.DebugAllocator(.{}) = .init;
    defer {
        const check = gpa_state.deinit();
        std.debug.print("allocator says: {s}\n", .{@tagName(check)});
    }
    const a = gpa_state.allocator();

    const kept = a.alloc(u8, 32) catch return;
    _ = kept; // never freed on purpose, to see the report
    const freed = a.alloc(u8, 8) catch return;
    a.free(freed);
}
error(DebugAllocator): memory address 0x… leaked: 
ch19/mem4.zig:11:25: 0x… in main (mem4)
    const kept = a.alloc(u8, 32) catch return;
                        ^
<zig>/lib/std/start.zig:698:59: 0x… in callMain (mem4)
    if (fn_info.params.len == 0) return wrapMain(root.main());
                                                          ^
???:?:?: 0x… in start (/usr/lib/dyld)

allocator says: leak

The three-line pattern is worth memorising, because you will type it at the top of most main functions that do not use init.gpa:

var gpa_state: std.heap.DebugAllocator(.{}) = .init;
defer _ = gpa_state.deinit();
const a = gpa_state.allocator();

The .{} is a configuration struct with defaults. .init is the initial state. deinit() returns the check result, and _ = discards it when you only want the printed report. The testing allocator is a DebugAllocator underneath; so is init.gpa, which in Debug builds prints the same report if your program exits with something unfreed:

mem10.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const names = try init.gpa.alloc([]const u8, 3);
    names[0] = "Ada";
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{names[0]});
    // forgot: init.gpa.free(names)
}
Ada
error(DebugAllocator): memory address 0x… leaked: 
ch19/mem10.zig:4:37: 0x… in main (mem10)
    const names = try init.gpa.alloc([]const u8, 3);
                                    ^
<zig>/lib/std/start.zig:737:30: 0x… in callMain (mem10)
…

In a release build, init.gpa switches to a fast allocator with no checking, so the leak reports cost you nothing in production while catching bugs in development.

19.7 toOwnedSlice and errdefer free

The common way to build a result of unknown length is to append to an ArrayList and then hand the buffer to the caller with toOwnedSlice. The list gives up its buffer, becomes empty, and the caller owns a plain slice. On the failure path, errdefer frees whatever was built so far. Chapter 21 covers ArrayList in depth; here is the ownership shape.

mem7.zig

const std = @import("std");

/// Builds a list of lines and hands the buffer to the caller.
/// Caller owns the result: free each line, then the slice.
fn summary(a: std.mem.Allocator, funds: u32, pilots: u32) ![][]const u8 {
    var out: std.ArrayList([]const u8) = .empty;
    errdefer {
        for (out.items) |line| a.free(line);
        out.deinit(a);
    }
    try out.append(a, try std.fmt.allocPrint(a, "  {d} c-bills in the treasury", .{funds}));
    try out.append(a, try std.fmt.allocPrint(a, "  {d} pilots on the roster", .{pilots}));
    return out.toOwnedSlice(a);
}

test "toOwnedSlice hands over ownership" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    const lines = try summary(a, 12_000, 4);
    defer {
        for (lines) |line| a.free(line);
        a.free(lines);
    }
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 2), lines.len);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("  4 pilots on the roster", lines[1]);
}
1/1 mem7.test.toOwnedSlice hands over ownership...OK
All 1 tests passed.

Notice the two levels of ownership: the outer slice, and each string inside it. The caller must free both, inner first. That is a lot of bookkeeping for the caller, which is exactly why the next chapter introduces the arena: with an arena, the caller frees everything with one call and the inner loop disappears.

In IRON LEDGER. main in game/src/main.zig takes init.gpa and hands it down: var gs = game.state.GameState.init(init.gpa, .{ .seed = 3025 }); followed by defer gs.deinit();. Nothing in the 31,000 lines below allocates from anywhere else; every function that needs memory has an alloc or a parameter. The query layer's convention is "caller owns", implemented with toOwnedSlice, as in dataProvenance in game/src/root.zig: 
pub fn dataProvenance(alloc: std.mem.Allocator) ![]const u8 {
    if (build_info.data_dir) |dir| {
        var out: std.ArrayListUnmanaged(u8) = .empty;
        try out.appendSlice(alloc, try std.fmt.allocPrint(alloc, "mod {s}: {d} file{s} overlaid", .{ … }));
        // …
        return out.toOwnedSlice(alloc);
    }
    // …
}
The errdefer-free idiom is in the PNG decoder, game/src/tui/png.zig: const rgb = try alloc.alloc(u8, …); errdefer alloc.free(rgb);, followed by a dozen trys that would otherwise leak it. And every test in the project that allocates uses std.testing.allocator, which is how the test suite doubles as a leak detector for the whole game.

Exercises

Exercise 19.1 · Allocate, fill, hand over, free warm-up

Write squares(a, n), which allocates and fills a []u32 the caller owns, and shout(a, s), which returns an upper-cased copy via dupe. File: exercises/19-memory/ex1_alloc.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 19, exercise 1: allocate, fill, hand over, free.
//! Run with:  zig test ex1_alloc.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests. The testing
//! allocator fails the test if you leak.
const std = @import("std");

/// The first `n` square numbers. Caller owns the result and frees it with `a`.
fn squares(a: std.mem.Allocator, n: usize) ![]u32 {
    const out = try a.alloc(u32, n);
    for (out, 0..) |*x, i| x.* = @intCast(i * i);
    return out;
}

/// A fresh, upper-cased copy of `s`. Caller owns it.
fn shout(a: std.mem.Allocator, s: []const u8) ![]u8 {
    const out = try a.dupe(u8, s);
    for (out) |*c| c.* = std.ascii.toUpper(c.*);
    return out;
}

test "squares" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    const sq = try squares(a, 5);
    defer a.free(sq);
    try std.testing.expectEqualSlices(u32, &.{ 0, 1, 4, 9, 16 }, sq);
}

test "shout" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    const s = try shout(a, "contract signed");
    defer a.free(s);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("CONTRACT SIGNED", s);
}

Both functions take an allocator and return a slice, so both are "caller owns", and the tests defer a.free each result. Delete one of those defers to see the leak report.

Exercise 19.2 · One struct on the heap practice

Implement Pilot.create, which uses a.create and then dupes the name, and Pilot.destroy, which frees both. The second test uses a failing allocator to make the dupe fail, so the struct must be released by an errdefer. File: exercises/19-memory/ex2_create.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 19, exercise 2: one struct on the heap with create/destroy.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_create.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Pilot = struct {
    name: []u8,
    skill: u8,

    /// Heap-allocate a Pilot that owns a copy of `name`.
    fn create(a: std.mem.Allocator, name: []const u8, skill: u8) !*Pilot {
        const p = try a.create(Pilot);
        errdefer a.destroy(p);
        p.* = .{ .name = try a.dupe(u8, name), .skill = skill };
        return p;
    }

    /// Free the name, then the struct itself.
    fn destroy(self: *Pilot, a: std.mem.Allocator) void {
        a.free(self.name);
        a.destroy(self);
    }
};

test "create and destroy" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    const p = try Pilot.create(a, "Ada", 4);
    defer p.destroy(a);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Ada", p.name);
    p.skill -= 1;
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 3), p.skill);
}

test "a failing allocator leaks nothing" {
    // failing_allocator fails the 2nd allocation: the dupe. The errdefer
    // must destroy the already-created struct.
    var failing = std.testing.FailingAllocator.init(std.testing.allocator, .{ .fail_index = 1 });
    try std.testing.expectError(error.OutOfMemory, Pilot.create(failing.allocator(), "Bo", 5));
}

std.testing.FailingAllocator wraps another allocator and fails the allocation at a chosen index. With fail_index = 1, the create succeeds and the dupe fails, exercising exactly the path the errdefer protects. Free in reverse order in destroy: the name, then the struct holding it.

Exercise 19.3 · Find and fix the leak practice

The starter's parseEntry leaks on one error path. Run the tests, read the report, and add the one missing line. File: exercises/19-memory/ex3_leak.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 19, exercise 3: find and fix the leak.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_leak.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests. In the
//! starter, one error path forgets to free; the testing allocator
//! reports it.
const std = @import("std");

/// Reads "name:skill" into a heap copy of the name and a number.
const Entry = struct { name: []u8, skill: u8 };

fn parseEntry(a: std.mem.Allocator, text: []const u8) !Entry {
    const colon = std.mem.indexOfScalar(u8, text, ':') orelse return error.NoColon;
    const name = try a.dupe(u8, text[0..colon]);
    errdefer a.free(name); // the fix: without this, a bad number leaks `name`
    const skill = try std.fmt.parseInt(u8, text[colon + 1 ..], 10);
    return .{ .name = name, .skill = skill };
}

test "good entry" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    const e = try parseEntry(a, "Ada:4");
    defer a.free(e.name);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Ada", e.name);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 4), e.skill);
}

test "bad entries leak nothing" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    try std.testing.expectError(error.NoColon, parseEntry(a, "Ada"));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.InvalidCharacter, parseEntry(a, "Ada:four"));
}

The name is duplicated before the number is parsed; if the parse fails, the function returns an error and the caller never sees the name. The errdefer a.free(name) right after the dupe fixes it. This is the constructor pattern from Chapter 17 in its smallest form.

Exercise 19.4 · An owned list of borrowed slices challenge

Write lines(a, text), which returns a caller-owned slice of slices that each borrow from text, using an ArrayList and toOwnedSlice. File: exercises/19-memory/ex4_owned.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 19, exercise 4: an owned list of borrowed slices.
//! Run with:  zig test ex4_owned.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Split `text` on newlines. The outer slice is OWNED by the caller
/// (free it with `a`); each inner slice BORROWS from `text`, so there
/// is nothing else to free. Empty lines are skipped.
fn lines(a: std.mem.Allocator, text: []const u8) ![][]const u8 {
    var out: std.ArrayList([]const u8) = .empty;
    errdefer out.deinit(a);
    var it = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, text, '\n');
    while (it.next()) |line| {
        if (line.len == 0) continue;
        try out.append(a, line);
    }
    return out.toOwnedSlice(a);
}

/// Total length of all lines. Borrows everything, allocates nothing.
fn totalLen(ls: []const []const u8) usize {
    var n: usize = 0;
    for (ls) |l| n += l.len;
    return n;
}

test "lines" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    const text = "hire Ada\n\nadvance 3\nquit\n";
    const ls = try lines(a, text);
    defer a.free(ls);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 3), ls.len);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("advance 3", ls[1]);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 21), totalLen(ls));
    // borrowed: the line points into `text`
    try std.testing.expect(ls[0].ptr == text.ptr);
}

test "empty text" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    const ls = try lines(a, "");
    defer a.free(ls);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 0), ls.len);
}

Only the outer slice is allocated; the test proves the inner slices are borrowed by checking that ls[0].ptr == text.ptr. The caller frees one thing. Contrast with summary in section 19.7, where the inner strings were owned too and needed a loop to free.

Check your understanding

  1. When must a value go on the heap rather than the stack?
    AnswerWhen its size is only known at run time, when it must outlive the function that creates it, or when it is too large for a stack frame.
  2. Why does Zig have no global new or malloc?
    AnswerSo that every allocation is visible at the call site (it needs an allocator argument), can fail with an ordinary error, and can use whatever strategy the caller chose.
  3. What does a.free need, and why?
    AnswerThe whole slice, pointer and length, so it knows how much to release. Free exactly what alloc returned, with the same allocator.
  4. How do you know whether to free a slice a function returned?
    AnswerBy convention: if the function took an allocator, the caller owns the result and frees it; if not, the result borrows existing memory and must not be freed.
  5. What does std.testing.allocator do at the end of a test?
    AnswerReports every allocation that was not freed, with the stack trace of where it was allocated, and fails the test.
  6. What does DebugAllocator.deinit() return?
    Answer.ok if everything was freed, .leak otherwise, having printed a report for each leaked block.
  7. What does list.toOwnedSlice(a) do?
    AnswerHands the list's buffer to the caller as a plain slice the caller now owns and must free; the list becomes empty.
What you learned.
  • Stack memory is per function frame, automatic and short-lived; heap memory is requested and must be returned.
  • Nothing allocates without a std.mem.Allocator parameter; the allocator is two pointers passed by value.
  • alloc/free for slices, create/destroy for single values, dupe to own a copy; all can fail with OutOfMemory.
  • std.testing.allocator fails a test that leaks and shows where the leak was allocated.
  • DebugAllocator(.{}) is .init, .allocator(), .deinit() returning .ok or .leak; init.gpa is one, ready made.
  • "Caller owns" when a function takes an allocator and returns a slice; "borrowed" when it does not. dupe what you need to keep.
  • toOwnedSlice transfers a list's buffer to the caller; errdefer frees partial work on failure.

20. Choosing an allocator

In this chapter you will meet the allocators the standard library ships, learn what each one is for, and see the one pattern that does most of the work in real Zig programs: an arena per lifetime. You will run out of memory on purpose, watch a use-after-free crash cleanly, write an allocator of your own that counts what passes through it, and finish with a table to choose from.

20.1 The allocator is a decision

Chapter 19 showed that a std.mem.Allocator is a small value that any function can take. Because it is a value, the caller decides which one to pass, and different choices have very different behaviour. One allocator checks every free and reports leaks. One never frees anything individually and releases everything at once. One hands out memory from a fixed array and refuses when it is full. They all present the same interface, so the code that uses them does not change; only the line that creates the allocator does.

This is the part of Zig that newcomers find strangest, and the part that experienced Zig programmers like most. Instead of one heap with one policy for the whole program, you match the allocator to the lifetime of the data. Memory that lives for one frame gets a frame allocator. Memory that lives for one campaign gets a campaign allocator. The program becomes easier to reason about because the question "when is this freed?" has a structural answer.

20.2 DebugAllocator: the one for development

You met it in Chapter 19. std.heap.DebugAllocator(.{}) is a general-purpose allocator that tracks every block, detects leaks, double frees and, where the operating system allows, use-after-free. It is slower than a production allocator, which is fine, because its job is to be in your Debug builds and tests. Here is what a use-after-free looks like under it.

al8.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var gpa: std.heap.DebugAllocator(.{}) = .init;
    defer _ = gpa.deinit();
    const a = gpa.allocator();

    const buf = a.alloc(u8, 4) catch return;
    a.free(buf);
    buf[0] = 1; // use after free
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{buf[0]});
}
Segmentation fault at address 0x…
ch20/al8.zig:10:8: 0x… in main (al8)
    buf[0] = 1; // use after free
       ^
…

The crash is immediate and points at the offending line, because the DebugAllocator unmaps freed pages rather than reusing them. The same bug under a production allocator would silently write into memory that something else may now own. This is why you run tests in Debug.

init.gpa in main is a DebugAllocator in Debug builds. In release builds the runtime swaps it for std.heap.c_allocator if you linked libc and std.heap.smp_allocator otherwise, both fast and unchecked. Your code does not change.

20.3 page_allocator: straight from the operating system

std.heap.page_allocator asks the operating system for memory directly, one page at a time. It needs no setup and no deinit, and it is thread-safe. It is also the most expensive way to get a small block, because a page is the smallest thing the OS will give you, and a system call is the slowest thing your program does.

al4.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() !void {
    const a = std.heap.page_allocator;
    const small = try a.alloc(u8, 1);
    defer a.free(small);
    const big = try a.alloc(u8, 10_000);
    defer a.free(big);
    std.debug.print("page size on this machine: {d}\n", .{std.heap.pageSize()});
    std.debug.print("1-byte alloc at {*}\n", .{small.ptr});
    std.debug.print("10000-byte alloc at {*}\n", .{big.ptr});
}
page size on this machine: 16384
1-byte alloc at u8@100d8c000
10000-byte alloc at u8@100d90000

Asking for one byte cost a whole 16-kilobyte page. Use the page allocator as the backing for other allocators (it is what DebugAllocator and ArenaAllocator get their big chunks from) and for a few large, long-lived buffers. Do not use it for thousands of small strings.

20.4 ArenaAllocator: free everything at once

An arena takes a backing allocator, grabs chunks from it, and hands out pieces of those chunks by bumping a pointer. Allocation is nearly free. Individual free calls do nothing. When you are done with everything the arena gave out, you call arena.deinit() and all of it goes back at once.

al1.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var arena = std.heap.ArenaAllocator.init(init.gpa);
    defer arena.deinit(); // one call frees every allocation below
    const a = arena.allocator();

    var total: usize = 0;
    var i: u32 = 0;
    while (i < 1000) : (i += 1) {
        const line = try std.fmt.allocPrint(a, "log line {d}: contract signed", .{i});
        total += line.len;
        // no free. Ever. The arena remembers.
    }
    std.debug.print("built 1000 strings, {d} bytes, zero frees written\n", .{total});
    std.debug.print("arena holds about {d} bytes\n", .{arena.queryCapacity()});
}
built 1000 strings, 28890 bytes, zero frees written
arena holds about 56886 bytes

A thousand strings, no frees, no leak report: the single defer arena.deinit() covers them all. The arena is the right tool whenever a group of allocations share one lifetime: everything built while answering one request, drawing one frame, running one test, or loading one file. The code that does the work can allocate freely and never think about cleanup, because the boundary of the lifetime is where the arena is destroyed.

The cost is that memory only grows until the arena is reset. If one thing inside the group needs to be freed early, an arena will not do it. And you must not hand an arena's memory to something that outlives the arena. If a value must escape, dupe it into a longer-lived allocator first.

Arenas can also be reset instead of destroyed. arena.reset(.retain_capacity) forgets every allocation but keeps the chunks, so the next round of allocations reuses them without touching the backing allocator. This is the frame pattern:

al2.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn drawFrame(a: std.mem.Allocator, frame_no: u32) !void {
    // Every frame formats a handful of strings and forgets them.
    var rows: std.ArrayList([]const u8) = .empty;
    var i: u32 = 0;
    while (i < 3) : (i += 1) {
        try rows.append(a, try std.fmt.allocPrint(a, "frame {d} row {d}", .{ frame_no, i }));
    }
    std.debug.print("{s} ... {d} rows\n", .{ rows.items[0], rows.items.len });
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var frame = std.heap.ArenaAllocator.init(init.gpa);
    defer frame.deinit();

    var frame_no: u32 = 0;
    while (frame_no < 3) : (frame_no += 1) {
        _ = frame.reset(.retain_capacity); // wipe last frame, keep the pages
        try drawFrame(frame.allocator(), frame_no);
        std.debug.print("  capacity after frame {d}: {d}\n", .{ frame_no, frame.queryCapacity() });
    }
}
frame 0 row 0 ... 3 rows
  capacity after frame 0: 424
frame 1 row 0 ... 3 rows
  capacity after frame 1: 424
frame 2 row 0 ... 3 rows
  capacity after frame 2: 424

After the first frame, capacity stops changing: the arena has learned how much a frame needs and simply reuses it. Three reset modes exist: .free_all releases the chunks too, .retain_capacity keeps them all, and .retain_with_limit = n keeps up to n bytes, a good choice when one unusual frame might otherwise pin a large buffer forever. reset returns a bool saying whether it could satisfy the request, which is why the examples write _ = arena.reset(…).

20.5 FixedBufferAllocator: a heap inside an array

Sometimes you want allocation without a heap at all: in a tiny embedded program, in a hot loop where a system call is unacceptable, or just because you know an upper bound and want to be told if you were wrong. FixedBufferAllocator hands out slices of an array you give it, and returns OutOfMemory when the array is full.

al3.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() !void {
    var buffer: [64]u8 = undefined; // the whole heap, on the stack
    var fba = std.heap.FixedBufferAllocator.init(&buffer);
    const a = fba.allocator();

    const first = try a.alloc(u8, 40);
    std.debug.print("got {d} bytes, used {d} of {d}\n", .{ first.len, fba.end_index, buffer.len });

    const second = a.alloc(u8, 40) catch |err| {
        std.debug.print("second alloc failed: {s}\n", .{@errorName(err)});
        return;
    };
    _ = second;
}
got 40 bytes, used 40 of 64
second alloc failed: OutOfMemory

The buffer here is a local array, so the "heap" lives on the stack and vanishes with the function. There is no deinit. free only reclaims the most recent allocation (it is a bump allocator, like the arena), so treat it as an arena with a hard limit. The end_index field tells you how much is used, which is handy in tests.

20.6 stackFallback: small on the stack, big on the heap

A common shape is "this is usually small, but occasionally huge". std.heap.stackFallback(N, fallback) gives you an allocator that serves requests from an N-byte buffer on the stack until it runs out, then transparently switches to the fallback allocator. Small cases never touch the heap; large cases still work.

al6.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn join(a: std.mem.Allocator, parts: []const []const u8) ![]u8 {
    return std.mem.join(a, ", ", parts);
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    // Up to 256 bytes come from the stack; anything bigger goes to init.gpa.
    var sfa = std.heap.stackFallback(256, init.gpa);
    const a = sfa.get();

    const short = try join(a, &.{ "Ada", "Bo" });
    defer a.free(short);
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{short});

    const parts = [_][]const u8{"a-fairly-long-name"} ** 30;
    const long = try join(a, &parts);
    defer a.free(long);
    std.debug.print("{d} bytes, spilled to the fallback\n", .{long.len});
}
Ada, Bo
598 bytes, spilled to the fallback

Note the sfa.get() rather than .allocator(): the stack-fallback allocator must be a var and get takes its address, because the buffer lives inside it. Free through the same allocator as always; it knows which memory came from where.

20.7 c_allocator: libc's malloc

If your program links the C library, std.heap.c_allocator wraps malloc and free. It is fast, thread-safe and the natural choice when you are also handing memory to C code that will free it. It needs libc, so build with -lc (on macOS libc is always present, so it works either way; on Linux without -lc the link fails).

al5.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() !void {
    const a = std.heap.c_allocator; // needs: zig run -lc al5.zig
    const s = try a.dupe(u8, "malloc says hi");
    defer a.free(s);
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{s});
}
malloc says hi

For pure-Zig programs that need a fast general-purpose allocator in release builds, std.heap.smp_allocator does the same job with no libc dependency. As noted above, init.gpa already makes this choice for you.

20.8 The pattern: one arena per lifetime

Put the pieces together and you get the structure IRON LEDGER uses, and that most substantial Zig programs converge on. There are three lifetimes, and each gets an allocator that matches it.

LifetimeAllocatorWhat lives thereFreed when
The processinit.gpa (DebugAllocator in Debug)The app struct, the terminal, the save store, the backing for every arenamain returns; leaks reported
The campaignAn ArenaAllocator owned by GameStateEvery person, unit, log line and ledger rowgs.deinit(): one call
One frame, one request, one testA per-frame arena, reset each frame; a per-test arenaQuery results: rows of formatted text drawn onceframe.reset(.retain_capacity) before the next frame

The arena is why the simulation core can be relaxed about strings. A query builds hundreds of small strings with allocPrint and never frees one; the caller resets the arena after drawing. The game state does the same at campaign scale: there is no per-object destructor anywhere in the domain, because gs.deinit() is the destructor for everything. The trade is stated plainly in the source: memory grows monotonically over a campaign (a long game holds every log line it ever wrote), in exchange for never having a use-after-free and never forgetting a free.

The habit to take from this: when you write a function that allocates, do not decide the lifetime inside it. Take an allocator, use it, and let the caller decide by choosing what to pass. The same summary(a, &gs) function serves a test with a throwaway arena, a TUI with a frame arena, and a CLI with init.gpa and explicit frees, and it does not know which.

20.9 Writing an allocator: a counting wrapper

An allocator is a struct pointer plus a vtable of four functions, so writing one is not magic. The most useful custom allocator is a wrapper that forwards to another allocator and measures. Here is one that counts.

al7.zig

const std = @import("std");

/// An allocator that wraps another and counts what passes through.
const Counting = struct {
    child: std.mem.Allocator,
    allocs: usize = 0,
    frees: usize = 0,
    bytes: usize = 0,

    fn allocator(self: *Counting) std.mem.Allocator {
        return .{ .ptr = self, .vtable = &vtable };
    }

    const vtable: std.mem.Allocator.VTable = .{
        .alloc = alloc,
        .resize = resize,
        .remap = remap,
        .free = free,
    };

    fn alloc(ctx: *anyopaque, len: usize, alignment: std.mem.Alignment, ret_addr: usize) ?[*]u8 {
        const self: *Counting = @ptrCast(@alignCast(ctx));
        const result = self.child.rawAlloc(len, alignment, ret_addr);
