        if (result != null) {
            self.allocs += 1;
            self.bytes += len;
        }
        return result;
    }

    fn resize(ctx: *anyopaque, memory: []u8, alignment: std.mem.Alignment, new_len: usize, ret_addr: usize) bool {
        const self: *Counting = @ptrCast(@alignCast(ctx));
        return self.child.rawResize(memory, alignment, new_len, ret_addr);
    }

    fn remap(ctx: *anyopaque, memory: []u8, alignment: std.mem.Alignment, new_len: usize, ret_addr: usize) ?[*]u8 {
        const self: *Counting = @ptrCast(@alignCast(ctx));
        return self.child.rawRemap(memory, alignment, new_len, ret_addr);
    }

    fn free(ctx: *anyopaque, memory: []u8, alignment: std.mem.Alignment, ret_addr: usize) void {
        const self: *Counting = @ptrCast(@alignCast(ctx));
        self.frees += 1;
        self.child.rawFree(memory, alignment, ret_addr);
    }
};

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var counting = Counting{ .child = init.gpa };
    const a = counting.allocator();

    var list: std.ArrayList(u32) = .empty;
    defer list.deinit(a);
    var i: u32 = 0;
    while (i < 1000) : (i += 1) try list.append(a, i);

    const s = try std.fmt.allocPrint(a, "{d} items", .{list.items.len});
    defer a.free(s);
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{s});
    std.debug.print("allocs={d} frees={d} bytes requested={d}\n", .{ counting.allocs, counting.frees, counting.bytes });
}
1000 items
allocs=9 frees=7 bytes requested=9380

The four vtable functions take the state as *anyopaque and cast it back with @ptrCast(@alignCast(ctx)), exactly as Chapter 18 described. Each forwards to the child's raw method and updates a tally. The alignment parameter's type is std.mem.Alignment and the ret_addr is for debug traces; you pass both straight through. With the wrapper in place you can see that appending a thousand items to an ArrayList took nine allocations (the buffer doubles as it grows) and that the seven frees plus the two defers still pending at print time will balance. Exercise 20.4 has you write this yourself and assert the balance in a test.

20.10 The comparison table

AllocatorSetupIndividual freeThread-safeUse it for
DebugAllocator(.{}).init, deinit() returns .ok/.leakyes, checkedyes by defaultDebug builds and tests; init.gpa, std.testing.allocator
smp_allocatornoneyesyesRelease builds without libc
c_allocatornone, needs -lcyesyesPrograms that link libc or share memory with C
page_allocatornoneyes, whole pagesyesBacking other allocators; a few large buffers
ArenaAllocatorinit(backing), deinit(), reset(mode)no (no-op)noA group of allocations with one lifetime: a request, frame, test, campaign
FixedBufferAllocatorinit(&buffer)only the lastnoBounded scratch space with no heap
stackFallback(N, fallback)var sfa = …; sfa.get()yesnoUsually-small, occasionally-large temporaries
If in doubt. Start with init.gpa for the program and std.testing.allocator for tests. The moment you find yourself writing a loop to free the parts of a result, ask whether those parts share a lifetime; if they do, that is an arena. Reach for the others when you have a specific reason.
In IRON LEDGER. The three lifetimes are three fields and three lines. GameState in game/src/sim/state.zig owns the campaign arena and exposes it as the only allocator the domain ever sees: 
arena: std.heap.ArenaAllocator,
// …
pub fn init(gpa: std.mem.Allocator, config: Config) GameState {
    return .{
        .arena = std.heap.ArenaAllocator.init(gpa),
        .rng = rng_mod.Rng.init(config.seed),
        // …
    };
}

pub fn deinit(self: *GameState) void {
    self.arena.deinit();
}

/// All campaign-lifetime allocations come from here.
pub fn allocator(self: *GameState) std.mem.Allocator {
    return self.arena.allocator();
}
The terminal client in game/src/tui/app.zig keeps two more arenas, frame and lobby, both created with std.heap.ArenaAllocator.init(gpa), and the first line of draw is _ = self.frame.reset(.retain_capacity);. Every row of text the screen shows is allocated from self.frame.allocator() and forgotten. And every test that calls a query begins with the three lines from the original guide: var arena = std.heap.ArenaAllocator.init(std.testing.allocator); defer arena.deinit(); const a = arena.allocator();, which means the testing allocator still sees the arena's chunks and still reports a leak if the arena itself is forgotten.

Exercises

Exercise 20.1 · An arena for a pile of short-lived strings warm-up

Write report(a, n), which builds n formatted lines into an owned slice. The first test runs it through an arena and frees with one deinit; the second runs it through the testing allocator and frees piece by piece. Same function, both must pass. File: exercises/20-allocators/ex1_arena.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 20, exercise 1: an arena for a pile of short-lived strings.
//! Run with:  zig test ex1_arena.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Build a report of `n` lines using `a` and return the lines. The
/// caller decides how to free (with an arena: one deinit).
fn report(a: std.mem.Allocator, n: u32) ![][]const u8 {
    var out: std.ArrayList([]const u8) = .empty;
    var i: u32 = 0;
    while (i < n) : (i += 1) {
        try out.append(a, try std.fmt.allocPrint(a, "day {d}: nothing to report", .{i + 1}));
    }
    return out.toOwnedSlice(a);
}

test "arena frees everything at once" {
    var arena = std.heap.ArenaAllocator.init(std.testing.allocator);
    defer arena.deinit(); // this is the ONLY free in the test
    const a = arena.allocator();

    const lines = try report(a, 50);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 50), lines.len);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("day 50: nothing to report", lines[49]);
}

test "the same function works with a plain allocator, if you free" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    const lines = try report(a, 3);
    defer {
        for (lines) |l| a.free(l);
        a.free(lines);
    }
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("day 2: nothing to report", lines[1]);
}

The function does not know or care which allocator it was given. That is the whole point of taking it as a parameter: the caller chooses the lifetime.

Exercise 20.2 · A fixed buffer runs out practice

Implement countUntilFull, which allocates labels from a FixedBufferAllocator over a size-byte array until it fails, and returns how many fit. File: exercises/20-allocators/ex2_fba.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 20, exercise 2: a fixed buffer runs out.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_fba.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Format `n` into memory taken from `a`. Caller frees.
fn label(a: std.mem.Allocator, n: u32) ![]u8 {
    return std.fmt.allocPrint(a, "unit-{d}", .{n});
}

/// How many labels fit in a buffer of `size` bytes before OutOfMemory?
fn countUntilFull(comptime size: usize) usize {
    var buffer: [size]u8 = undefined;
    var fba = std.heap.FixedBufferAllocator.init(&buffer);
    const a = fba.allocator();
    var n: usize = 0;
    while (true) : (n += 1) {
        _ = label(a, 100) catch break;
    }
    return n;
}

test "labels come out of the buffer" {
    var buffer: [32]u8 = undefined;
    var fba = std.heap.FixedBufferAllocator.init(&buffer);
    const a = fba.allocator();
    const l = try label(a, 7);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("unit-7", l);
    try std.testing.expect(fba.end_index >= 6);
}

test "a full buffer fails cleanly with OutOfMemory" {
    var buffer: [16]u8 = undefined;
    var fba = std.heap.FixedBufferAllocator.init(&buffer);
    const a = fba.allocator();
    _ = try label(a, 1);
    _ = try label(a, 2);
    try std.testing.expectError(error.OutOfMemory, label(a, 3));
}

test "bigger buffer, more labels" {
    try std.testing.expect(countUntilFull(64) < countUntilFull(256));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 0), countUntilFull(4));
}

size is comptime because it is the length of an array type. The loop stops on the first OutOfMemory, which the catch break turns into ordinary control flow. There is no cleanup: the buffer is a local.

Exercise 20.3 · One arena per frame practice

Implement runFrames, which draws frames frames through one arena, resetting with .retain_capacity between them, and returns the final capacity. The test asserts that 200 frames use no more capacity than one. File: exercises/20-allocators/ex3_frame.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 20, exercise 3: one arena per frame, reset between frames.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_frame.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// One frame's worth of work: a few formatted rows, never freed one by one.
fn drawFrame(a: std.mem.Allocator, frame_no: u32) !usize {
    var bytes: usize = 0;
    var i: u32 = 0;
    while (i < 20) : (i += 1) {
        const row = try std.fmt.allocPrint(a, "frame {d} row {d}", .{ frame_no, i });
        bytes += row.len;
    }
    return bytes;
}

/// Run `frames` frames through one arena, resetting it between frames
/// so that its capacity stops growing after the first frame.
/// Returns the arena's capacity after the last frame.
fn runFrames(gpa: std.mem.Allocator, frames: u32) !usize {
    var arena = std.heap.ArenaAllocator.init(gpa);
    defer arena.deinit();
    var f: u32 = 0;
    while (f < frames) : (f += 1) {
        _ = arena.reset(.retain_capacity);
        _ = try drawFrame(arena.allocator(), f);
    }
    return arena.queryCapacity();
}

test "capacity does not grow with the number of frames" {
    const one = try runFrames(std.testing.allocator, 1);
    const many = try runFrames(std.testing.allocator, 200);
    try std.testing.expect(one > 0);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(one, many);
}

Change the reset mode to .free_all and the test still passes (capacity after the last frame is the same), but the arena now goes back to the backing allocator every frame. Remove the reset entirely and the assertion fails, because the arena keeps growing.

Exercise 20.4 · An allocator that counts challenge

Fill in the four vtable functions of Counting so that it forwards to its child and tallies allocations, frees and bytes requested. The second test checks that an ArrayList frees exactly as many times as it allocates. File: exercises/20-allocators/ex4_counting.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 20, exercise 4: an allocator that counts.
//! Run with:  zig test ex4_counting.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests. Implement the
//! four vtable functions by forwarding to `child` and keeping the tallies.
const std = @import("std");

const Counting = struct {
    child: std.mem.Allocator,
    allocs: usize = 0,
    frees: usize = 0,
    bytes_requested: usize = 0,

    fn allocator(self: *Counting) std.mem.Allocator {
        return .{ .ptr = self, .vtable = &vtable };
    }

    const vtable: std.mem.Allocator.VTable = .{
        .alloc = alloc,
        .resize = resize,
        .remap = remap,
        .free = free,
    };

    fn alloc(ctx: *anyopaque, len: usize, alignment: std.mem.Alignment, ret_addr: usize) ?[*]u8 {
        const self: *Counting = @ptrCast(@alignCast(ctx));
        const p = self.child.rawAlloc(len, alignment, ret_addr);
        if (p != null) {
            self.allocs += 1;
            self.bytes_requested += len;
        }
        return p;
    }

    fn resize(ctx: *anyopaque, memory: []u8, alignment: std.mem.Alignment, new_len: usize, ret_addr: usize) bool {
        const self: *Counting = @ptrCast(@alignCast(ctx));
        return self.child.rawResize(memory, alignment, new_len, ret_addr);
    }

    fn remap(ctx: *anyopaque, memory: []u8, alignment: std.mem.Alignment, new_len: usize, ret_addr: usize) ?[*]u8 {
        const self: *Counting = @ptrCast(@alignCast(ctx));
        return self.child.rawRemap(memory, alignment, new_len, ret_addr);
    }

    fn free(ctx: *anyopaque, memory: []u8, alignment: std.mem.Alignment, ret_addr: usize) void {
        const self: *Counting = @ptrCast(@alignCast(ctx));
        self.frees += 1;
        self.child.rawFree(memory, alignment, ret_addr);
    }
};

test "counts allocs, frees and bytes" {
    var c = Counting{ .child = std.testing.allocator };
    const a = c.allocator();

    const x = try a.alloc(u8, 10);
    const y = try a.alloc(u32, 4);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 2), c.allocs);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 26), c.bytes_requested);
    a.free(x);
    a.free(y);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 2), c.frees);
}

test "a list balances its allocations" {
    var c = Counting{ .child = std.testing.allocator };
    const a = c.allocator();
    {
        var list: std.ArrayList(u64) = .empty;
        defer list.deinit(a);
        var i: u64 = 0;
        while (i < 500) : (i += 1) try list.append(a, i);
    }
    try std.testing.expect(c.allocs > 0);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(c.allocs, c.frees);
}

Only successful allocations are counted, which is why alloc checks the result before incrementing. The child's rawAlloc, rawResize, rawRemap and rawFree are the vtable calls without the type-safe wrapping, which is what a forwarding allocator wants.

Check your understanding

  1. What happens when you call free on memory from an ArenaAllocator?
    AnswerNothing. Arena memory is released all at once by deinit() or reset().
  2. When is an arena the wrong choice?
    AnswerWhen parts of the data need to be freed at different times, when memory must not grow unboundedly, or when a value must outlive the arena (then dupe it elsewhere).
  3. What does reset(.retain_capacity) do differently from deinit()?
    AnswerBoth forget every allocation; reset keeps the chunks so the next round reuses them without going back to the backing allocator, and the arena stays usable.
  4. Why is page_allocator a poor choice for many small strings?
    AnswerEvery allocation is at least one page (16 KiB here) and costs a system call.
  5. What does FixedBufferAllocator do when its buffer is full?
    AnswerReturns error.OutOfMemory, an ordinary error you handle with try or catch.
  6. What is init.gpa in a Debug build, and in a release build?
    AnswerA DebugAllocator with leak checking in Debug; c_allocator if libc is linked or smp_allocator otherwise in release.
  7. What are the four functions in an allocator's vtable?
    Answeralloc, resize, remap and free, each receiving the allocator's state as *anyopaque.
  8. A function takes an allocator and builds a result out of many pieces. Who decides how long the pieces live?
    AnswerThe caller, by choosing which allocator to pass: an arena for "all together", a general-purpose allocator for piece-by-piece freeing.
What you learned.
  • The allocator is chosen by the caller and should match the lifetime of the data.
  • DebugAllocator for development: leaks, double frees and use-after-free are reported with traces. init.gpa is one in Debug.
  • page_allocator is the raw OS source, good as a backing allocator; c_allocator and smp_allocator are the fast general-purpose choices for release.
  • ArenaAllocator frees everything at once; reset(.retain_capacity) makes it a reusable per-frame or per-request allocator.
  • FixedBufferAllocator allocates from an array and fails cleanly when full; stackFallback uses the stack first and a fallback after.
  • One arena per lifetime, process / campaign / frame, is how IRON LEDGER never writes a per-object free.
  • An allocator is a pointer plus four vtable functions; a counting wrapper is thirty lines.

21. Growable lists: ArrayList

In this chapter you will meet std.ArrayList, the standard library's growable array, and learn its 0.16 shape: an unmanaged struct that starts as .empty and takes an allocator on every call that might grow it. You will append, insert, remove, iterate by pointer, build strings with it, hand its buffer to a caller with toOwnedSlice, and learn the one trap that bites everyone: a pointer into the list that goes stale when the list regrows.

21.1 Why arrays are not enough

An array in Zig has a length that is part of its type. [4]u32 is four integers, always, forever. A slice is a view of memory somebody else owns. Neither can grow. But most real programs collect things whose count they do not know in advance: lines of a file, units in a hangar, people who answered a recruiting ad. For that you need a buffer on the heap that can be replaced with a bigger one when it fills up. That is exactly what std.ArrayList(T) is: a slice called items, a capacity that says how big the underlying buffer really is, and a handful of methods that keep the two in step.

If you come from Python this is a list; from JavaScript, an array; from C++, a std::vector. The difference is that Zig's version will not allocate behind your back. Every method that might need more room takes the allocator as its first argument, so the call site shows you where memory can be requested and where it can fail.

21.2 The smallest list

a_basic.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() !void {
    var gpa_state: std.heap.DebugAllocator(.{}) = .init;
    defer _ = gpa_state.deinit();
    const gpa = gpa_state.allocator();

    var list: std.ArrayList(u32) = .empty;
    defer list.deinit(gpa);

    try list.append(gpa, 10);
    try list.append(gpa, 20);
    try list.append(gpa, 30);

    std.debug.print("items: {any}\n", .{list.items});
    std.debug.print("len: {d}, capacity: {d}\n", .{ list.items.len, list.capacity });
    std.debug.print("second: {d}\n", .{list.items[1]});
}
items: { 10, 20, 30 }
len: 3, capacity: 33
second: 20

Four things to notice. First, the type is std.ArrayList(u32): a function that takes a type and returns a struct type, which is how all generic containers work in Zig (you will write your own in Chapter 26). Second, the starting value is .empty, a constant on the type meaning "no buffer, length zero, capacity zero". No allocator is stored in the list. Third, append takes gpa because it might need to grow, and it returns an error union because growing can fail, hence try. Fourth, deinit takes the allocator too, since it has to know whom to give the buffer back to, and we put it in a defer right after the declaration so it cannot be forgotten.

list.items is an ordinary slice, []u32. Anything you learned about slices in Chapter 10 works on it: index it, take its .len, loop over it, pass it to a function that wants a slice. The capacity (33 here, on this platform and this element size) is larger than the length because the list grows in jumps so that appending is cheap on average. The exact number is an implementation detail and you should never rely on it.

In Zig 0.16 there is only one ArrayList and it is unmanaged. Older tutorials show std.ArrayList(u32).init(allocator) and calls like list.append(5) with no allocator. Those forms no longer exist. The name std.ArrayListUnmanaged still works as an alias and IRON LEDGER uses it throughout, but it means exactly the same type as std.ArrayList.

21.3 Watching it grow

Let's print the capacity every time it changes while we append two hundred bytes.

b_growth.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() !void {
    var gpa_state: std.heap.DebugAllocator(.{}) = .init;
    defer _ = gpa_state.deinit();
    const gpa = gpa_state.allocator();

    var list: std.ArrayList(u8) = .empty;
    defer list.deinit(gpa);

    var last_cap: usize = 0;
    for (0..200) |i| {
        try list.append(gpa, @intCast(i));
        if (list.capacity != last_cap) {
            std.debug.print("len {d: >3} -> capacity {d}\n", .{ list.items.len, list.capacity });
            last_cap = list.capacity;
        }
    }
}
len   1 -> capacity 129
len 130 -> capacity 323

Two hundred appends, two allocations. When the buffer is full, the list asks the allocator for a bigger one (here about two and a half times the size), copies the old contents across, frees the old buffer and carries on. Most appends therefore touch no allocator at all; they just write one element and bump items.len. This is why append is described as "amortised constant time": expensive once in a while, free the rest of the time.

If you already know how many elements you will add, say so with ensureTotalCapacity and then use appendAssumeCapacity, which cannot fail and takes no allocator. You will see that in 21.8.

21.4 Adding and removing

Here is the full toolkit for changing a list, on a list of strings so the effect is easy to see. The show helper exists because {s} prints one string, not a slice of strings.

c_remove.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn show(label: []const u8, items: []const []const u8) void {
    std.debug.print("{s: <22}", .{label});
    for (items) |s| std.debug.print("{s} ", .{s});
    std.debug.print("\n", .{});
}

pub fn main() !void {
    var gpa_state: std.heap.DebugAllocator(.{}) = .init;
    defer _ = gpa_state.deinit();
    const gpa = gpa_state.allocator();

    var list: std.ArrayList([]const u8) = .empty;
    defer list.deinit(gpa);
    try list.appendSlice(gpa, &.{ "alpha", "bravo", "charlie", "delta", "echo" });
    show("start:", list.items);

    try list.insert(gpa, 1, "NEW");
    show("insert(1, NEW):", list.items);

    const gone = list.orderedRemove(1);
    show("orderedRemove(1):", list.items);
    std.debug.print("  (removed {s})\n", .{gone});

    const swapped = list.swapRemove(0);
    show("swapRemove(0):", list.items);
    std.debug.print("  (removed {s})\n", .{swapped});

    const top = list.pop();
    show("pop():", list.items);
    std.debug.print("  (popped {?s})\n", .{top});

    list.clearRetainingCapacity();
    std.debug.print("cleared: len {d}, capacity {d}\n", .{ list.items.len, list.capacity });
    std.debug.print("pop on empty: {?s}\n", .{list.pop()});
}
start:                alpha bravo charlie delta echo 
insert(1, NEW):       alpha NEW bravo charlie delta echo 
orderedRemove(1):     alpha bravo charlie delta echo 
  (removed NEW)
swapRemove(0):        echo bravo charlie delta 
  (removed alpha)
pop():                echo bravo charlie 
  (popped delta)
cleared: len 0, capacity 15
pop on empty: null

Read the transcript against the calls:

  • appendSlice(gpa, slice) appends many at once. The argument &.{ ... } is a pointer to an anonymous array, which coerces to a slice.
  • insert(gpa, i, item) shifts everything from i onward one place right. It takes the allocator because it may grow.
  • orderedRemove(i) removes element i and shifts the rest left, preserving order. It returns the removed element. No allocator: removing never allocates.
  • swapRemove(i) removes element i by moving the last element into its slot. It is constant time, but the order changes: echo jumped to the front.
  • pop() removes and returns the last element as an optional. On an empty list it returns null instead of crashing, which is why the last line prints null.
  • clearRetainingCapacity() sets the length to zero but keeps the buffer, so refilling the list will not allocate again. Its sibling clearAndFree(gpa) gives the buffer back too.

Choose swapRemove when you do not care about order and the list is long; choose orderedRemove when order matters. Removing from the front of a long list with orderedRemove in a loop is quadratic, so if you find yourself doing that, ask whether you want a different data structure.

21.5 Iterating: by value or by pointer

A for loop over list.items gives you each element by value, which means a copy. If the element is a struct and you want to change it in place, you need a pointer, and the syntax is the same one you met for arrays and slices in Chapter 18: put a * in front of the capture name.

d_pointers.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Merc = struct { name: []const u8, wounds: u8 };

pub fn main() !void {
    var gpa_state: std.heap.DebugAllocator(.{}) = .init;
    defer _ = gpa_state.deinit();
    const gpa = gpa_state.allocator();

    var roster: std.ArrayList(Merc) = .empty;
    defer roster.deinit(gpa);
    try roster.append(gpa, .{ .name = "Kell", .wounds = 0 });
    try roster.append(gpa, .{ .name = "Natasha", .wounds = 1 });

    // By value: `m` is a copy. Changing it changes nothing in the list.
    for (roster.items) |m| {
        var copy = m;
        copy.wounds += 10;
    }
    std.debug.print("after by-value loop: {d} {d}\n", .{ roster.items[0].wounds, roster.items[1].wounds });

    // By pointer: `m` points into the list's buffer.
    for (roster.items) |*m| m.wounds += 1;
    std.debug.print("after by-pointer loop: {d} {d}\n", .{ roster.items[0].wounds, roster.items[1].wounds });

    // Or index straight in.
    roster.items[0].name = "Morgan Kell";
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{roster.items[0].name});
}
after by-value loop: 0 1
after by-pointer loop: 1 2
Morgan Kell

The first loop copies each Merc into m, then into copy, and adds ten to the copy. The list is untouched. (The extra copy variable is there because the compiler rejects assigning to a by-value capture; it knows that would be a silent no-op.) The second loop captures *m, a *Merc pointing into the list's buffer, and m.wounds += 1 writes through it. Zig auto-dereferences field access on pointers, so you write m.wounds, not m.*.wounds.

21.6 The stale-pointer trap

There is a trap here. Because the list's buffer can move when it grows, a pointer into items is only valid until the next call that might grow the list.

e_stale.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() !void {
    var gpa_state: std.heap.DebugAllocator(.{}) = .init;
    defer _ = gpa_state.deinit();
    const gpa = gpa_state.allocator();

    var list: std.ArrayList(u32) = .empty;
    defer list.deinit(gpa);
    try list.append(gpa, 10);

    const first = &list.items[0]; // a pointer into the buffer
    std.debug.print("capacity {d}, first lives at {*}\n", .{ list.capacity, first });

    for (0..100) |i| try list.append(gpa, @intCast(i)); // forces a regrow
    std.debug.print("capacity {d}, first now at {*}\n", .{ list.capacity, &list.items[0] });

    std.debug.print("through the old pointer: {d}\n", .{first.*}); // BUG
}
capacity 33, first lives at u32@1074a0000
capacity 158, first now at u32@1074e0000
Segmentation fault at address 0x1074a0000
e_stale.zig:18:20: 0x102a19bd0 in main (e_stale)
    std.debug.print("through the old pointer: {d}\n", .{first.*}); // BUG

The list started with room for 33 elements. The 101 appends forced a regrow, the buffer moved to a new address, and the old one was returned to the allocator. first still points at the old address. In Debug mode the DebugAllocator unmaps freed pages, so reading through first crashes immediately with a stack trace. That is the good outcome. In ReleaseFast, the same read might silently return stale data, or whatever the allocator has since put there.

Rule. Never keep a pointer (or a slice) into list.items across a call to append, appendSlice, insert, ensureTotalCapacity, or anything else that takes the allocator. Keep the index instead and re-derive the pointer when you need it: &list.items[i]. The same rule applies to every growable container in this Part, including the hash maps of Chapter 22.

This is also why for (list.items) |*m| is safe: the loop does not append. If you ever need to append while iterating, iterate by index and expect the loop bound to change.

21.7 A string builder

A string is bytes, so std.ArrayList(u8) is a growable string. It even has a print method that formats straight into the buffer, so you do not need allocPrint and a temporary.

f_builder.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() !void {
    var gpa_state: std.heap.DebugAllocator(.{}) = .init;
    defer _ = gpa_state.deinit();
    const gpa = gpa_state.allocator();

    var sb: std.ArrayList(u8) = .empty;
    defer sb.deinit(gpa);

    try sb.appendSlice(gpa, "Lance: ");
    const pilots = [_][]const u8{ "Kell", "Natasha", "Grayson" };
    for (pilots, 0..) |p, i| {
        if (i > 0) try sb.appendSlice(gpa, ", ");
        try sb.appendSlice(gpa, p);
    }
    try sb.append(gpa, '\n');
    try sb.print(gpa, "{d} pilots, {d} bytes so far", .{ pilots.len, sb.items.len });

    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{sb.items});

    const owned = try sb.toOwnedSlice(gpa); // sb is now empty; we own `owned`
    defer gpa.free(owned);
    std.debug.print("owned len {d}, list len {d}\n", .{ owned.len, sb.items.len });
}
Lance: Kell, Natasha, Grayson
3 pilots, 30 bytes so far
owned len 55, list len 0

toOwnedSlice(gpa) is the handshake at the end. It shrinks the buffer to exactly the length used, returns it as a plain []u8, and resets the list to .empty. The caller now owns that slice and must free it with the same allocator; the list owns nothing, so its deinit in the defer is harmless. This is how functions return "a list of things" in Zig: build with an ArrayList, return a slice.

Sometimes you want a real *std.Io.Writer (the thing print and writeAll live on, which you met when printing to stdout in Chapter 2) that grows a heap buffer. That is std.Io.Writer.Allocating. It is the right choice when you want to pass "somewhere to write" to a function that should not know or care whether it is writing to a file, a fixed buffer or memory.

g_allocating.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn describe(w: *std.Io.Writer, name: []const u8, tons: u32) !void {
    try w.print("{s} ({d} tons)", .{ name, tons });
}

pub fn main() !void {
    var gpa_state: std.heap.DebugAllocator(.{}) = .init;
    defer _ = gpa_state.deinit();
    const gpa = gpa_state.allocator();

    var aw: std.Io.Writer.Allocating = .init(gpa);
    defer aw.deinit();

    try describe(&aw.writer, "Atlas", 100);
    try aw.writer.writeAll(" / ");
    try describe(&aw.writer, "Locust", 20);

    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{aw.written()});

    const text = try aw.toOwnedSlice();
    defer gpa.free(text);
    std.debug.print("{d} bytes\n", .{text.len});
}
Atlas (100 tons) / Locust (20 tons)
35 bytes

aw.writer is the generic writer, aw.written() is the bytes so far, and aw.toOwnedSlice() hands you the buffer exactly like the list did. Internally it is an ArrayList(u8) with a writer interface on top.

21.8 A list of structs, returned as a slice

The pattern IRON LEDGER uses in every query: build a list of small structs inside a function, hand the buffer to the caller.

h_structs.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Unit = struct { name: []const u8, tons: u32, bv: u32 };

fn heaviest(units: []const Unit) ?Unit {
    if (units.len == 0) return null;
    var best = units[0];
    for (units[1..]) |u| if (u.tons > best.tons) {
        best = u;
    };
    return best;
}

fn buildLance(gpa: std.mem.Allocator) ![]Unit {
    var list: std.ArrayList(Unit) = .empty;
    errdefer list.deinit(gpa);
    try list.ensureTotalCapacity(gpa, 4); // one allocation, not four
    list.appendAssumeCapacity(.{ .name = "Atlas", .tons = 100, .bv = 1897 });
    list.appendAssumeCapacity(.{ .name = "Marauder", .tons = 75, .bv = 1363 });
    list.appendAssumeCapacity(.{ .name = "Locust", .tons = 20, .bv = 432 });
    return list.toOwnedSlice(gpa);
}

pub fn main() !void {
    var gpa_state: std.heap.DebugAllocator(.{}) = .init;
    defer _ = gpa_state.deinit();
    const gpa = gpa_state.allocator();

    const lance = try buildLance(gpa);
    defer gpa.free(lance);

    var total: u32 = 0;
    for (lance) |u| total += u.tons;
    std.debug.print("{d} units, {d} tons\n", .{ lance.len, total });
    if (heaviest(lance)) |h| std.debug.print("heaviest: {s}\n", .{h.name});
}
3 units, 195 tons
heaviest: Atlas

Three details worth copying. errdefer list.deinit(gpa) rather than defer: if toOwnedSlice succeeds, the list is empty and the caller owns the buffer, so we only want to clean up on the error path. ensureTotalCapacity followed by appendAssumeCapacity turns three possible allocations into one. And heaviest takes a plain []const Unit, not the list: functions that only read should accept slices, so they work on arrays, lists and anything else.

21.9 Method reference

CallAllocator?What it does
.emptynoStarting value: no buffer.
append(gpa, x)yesAdd one to the end.
appendSlice(gpa, xs)yesAdd many to the end.
appendNTimes(gpa, x, n)yesAdd x repeated n times.
insert(gpa, i, x)yesInsert at index, shifting right.
print(gpa, fmt, args)yesFormat into the list (u8 only).
ensureTotalCapacity(gpa, n)yesGrow the buffer once, ahead of time.
appendAssumeCapacity(x)noAppend into reserved room; cannot fail.
pop()noRemove and return last as ?T.
getLast()noLast element; panics if empty.
orderedRemove(i)noRemove keeping order; returns it.
swapRemove(i)noRemove by swapping in the last; returns it.
clearRetainingCapacity()noLength to zero, keep buffer.
toOwnedSlice(gpa)yesHand the buffer to the caller; list becomes empty.
deinit(gpa)yesFree the buffer.

There is one more form worth knowing: std.ArrayList(T).initBuffer(&array) makes a list that lives inside a fixed array you provide and never allocates; use appendBounded on it, which returns error.OutOfMemory when the array is full. This replaced the old std.BoundedArray, which no longer exists in 0.16. Chapter 24 shows it.

In IRON LEDGER. The pattern of 21.8 is the skeleton of every query in game/src/sim/queries.zig. The People screen builds its rows like this (trimmed): 
pub fn people(alloc: Alloc, gs: *GameState, filter: HallFilter) !People {
    var rows: std.ArrayListUnmanaged(PersonRow) = .empty;
    var it = gs.people.iterator();
    while (it.next()) |e| {
        const p = e.value_ptr;
        // ... filter ...
        try rows.append(alloc, .{ .id = p.id, .text = try std.fmt.allocPrint(alloc, "...", .{ ... }) });
    }
    return .{ .header = "id   name ...", .rows = try rows.toOwnedSlice(alloc), .total = total };
}
The allocator passed in is a per-frame arena, so nobody ever frees the rows or the strings; the whole arena is reset after the screen is drawn. And money, the c-bill formatter in the same file, is a string builder exactly like 21.7: it prints the digits with bufPrint, walks them appending a comma every third digit into an ArrayListUnmanaged(u8), and returns out.toOwnedSlice(alloc).

Exercises

Exercise 21.1 · Squares warm-up

Write fn squaresUpTo(gpa: std.mem.Allocator, n: u32) ![]u32 that returns the squares of 0 to n-1 as a slice the caller owns. Reserve the capacity up front so there is exactly one allocation. Name the file: exercises/21-arraylist/ex1_squares.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 21, exercise 1: build a list, hand it back as a slice.
//! Run with:  zig test ex1_squares.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Return the squares 0*0, 1*1, ... (n-1)*(n-1) as a slice the caller owns.
fn squaresUpTo(gpa: std.mem.Allocator, n: u32) ![]u32 {
    var list: std.ArrayList(u32) = .empty;
    errdefer list.deinit(gpa);
    try list.ensureTotalCapacity(gpa, n);
    for (0..n) |i| {
        const v: u32 = @intCast(i);
        list.appendAssumeCapacity(v * v);
    }
    return list.toOwnedSlice(gpa);
}

test "five squares" {
    const s = try squaresUpTo(std.testing.allocator, 5);
    defer std.testing.allocator.free(s);
    try std.testing.expectEqualSlices(u32, &.{ 0, 1, 4, 9, 16 }, s);
}

test "zero squares is an empty slice, not an error" {
    const s = try squaresUpTo(std.testing.allocator, 0);
    defer std.testing.allocator.free(s);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 0), s.len);
}

errdefer list.deinit(gpa) covers the case where ensureTotalCapacity succeeds and toOwnedSlice fails; on success the list is already empty. For n = 0 the result is an empty slice and free on it is fine.

Exercise 21.2 · Remove all, two ways practice

Write removeAllOrdered, which removes every element equal to a value and keeps order, and removeAllFast, which may reorder. Both return the count removed. Think carefully about what happens to your loop index after each removal. Name the file: exercises/21-arraylist/ex2_remove_all.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 21, exercise 2: remove every matching element, two ways.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_remove_all.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Remove every element equal to `value`, keeping the order of the rest.
/// Returns how many were removed.
fn removeAllOrdered(list: *std.ArrayList(i32), value: i32) usize {
    var removed: usize = 0;
    var i: usize = 0;
    while (i < list.items.len) {
        if (list.items[i] == value) {
            _ = list.orderedRemove(i);
            removed += 1;
        } else {
            i += 1;
        }
    }
    return removed;
}

/// Same, but order does not matter, so use the cheaper swapRemove.
/// Walking backwards means a swap never moves an element we still need to look at.
fn removeAllFast(list: *std.ArrayList(i32), value: i32) usize {
    var removed: usize = 0;
    var i = list.items.len;
    while (i > 0) {
        i -= 1;
        if (list.items[i] == value) {
            _ = list.swapRemove(i);
            removed += 1;
        }
    }
    return removed;
}

test "ordered removal keeps order" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    var list: std.ArrayList(i32) = .empty;
    defer list.deinit(a);
    try list.appendSlice(a, &.{ 7, 1, 7, 2, 7, 3, 7 });
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 4), removeAllOrdered(&list, 7));
    try std.testing.expectEqualSlices(i32, &.{ 1, 2, 3 }, list.items);
}

test "fast removal keeps the right elements" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    var list: std.ArrayList(i32) = .empty;
    defer list.deinit(a);
    try list.appendSlice(a, &.{ 7, 1, 7, 2, 7, 3, 7 });
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 4), removeAllFast(&list, 7));
    std.mem.sort(i32, list.items, {}, std.sort.asc(i32));
    try std.testing.expectEqualSlices(i32, &.{ 1, 2, 3 }, list.items);
}

test "nothing to remove" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    var list: std.ArrayList(i32) = .empty;
    defer list.deinit(a);
    try list.appendSlice(a, &.{ 1, 2 });
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 0), removeAllFast(&list, 9));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 2), list.items.len);
}

In the ordered version, after removing at i the next element has slid into slot i, so do not increment. The fast version walks backwards: swapRemove(i) moves the last element into i, and since everything after i has already been examined, nothing is skipped.

Exercise 21.3 · Join practice

Write joinWith(gpa, parts, sep) using an ArrayList(u8) as a string builder, then describeLance which produces "2 units: Atlas, Locust" (and "1 unit: Atlas" for one). Use the list's print method for the count. Name the file: exercises/21-arraylist/ex3_join.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 21, exercise 3: a string builder.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_join.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Join `parts` with `sep` between them. The caller owns the result.
fn joinWith(gpa: std.mem.Allocator, parts: []const []const u8, sep: []const u8) ![]u8 {
    var sb: std.ArrayList(u8) = .empty;
    errdefer sb.deinit(gpa);
    for (parts, 0..) |p, i| {
        if (i > 0) try sb.appendSlice(gpa, sep);
        try sb.appendSlice(gpa, p);
    }
    return sb.toOwnedSlice(gpa);
}

/// "3 units: Atlas, Locust, Marauder"
fn describeLance(gpa: std.mem.Allocator, names: []const []const u8) ![]u8 {
    var sb: std.ArrayList(u8) = .empty;
    errdefer sb.deinit(gpa);
    try sb.print(gpa, "{d} unit{s}: ", .{ names.len, if (names.len == 1) "" else "s" });
    const joined = try joinWith(gpa, names, ", ");
    defer gpa.free(joined);
    try sb.appendSlice(gpa, joined);
    return sb.toOwnedSlice(gpa);
}

test "join three" {
    const s = try joinWith(std.testing.allocator, &.{ "a", "b", "c" }, ", ");
    defer std.testing.allocator.free(s);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("a, b, c", s);
}

test "join one and none" {
    const one = try joinWith(std.testing.allocator, &.{"solo"}, "-");
    defer std.testing.allocator.free(one);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("solo", one);
    const none = try joinWith(std.testing.allocator, &.{}, "-");
    defer std.testing.allocator.free(none);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("", none);
}

test "describe" {
    const s = try describeLance(std.testing.allocator, &.{ "Atlas", "Locust" });
    defer std.testing.allocator.free(s);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("2 units: Atlas, Locust", s);
    const t = try describeLance(std.testing.allocator, &.{"Atlas"});
    defer std.testing.allocator.free(t);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("1 unit: Atlas", t);
}

The standard library has std.mem.join that does the first function for you; writing it once by hand is the point. Notice the defer gpa.free(joined) for the temporary: describeLance owns it until it has been copied into the builder.

Exercise 21.4 · Roster challenge

Build a Roster struct wrapping an ArrayList(Merc) with hire, battle (every merc takes one wound, in place), releaseWorseThan(limit) (ordered removal, returns count) and best() which returns a pointer to the merc with the lowest gunnery, or null. The tests write through that pointer. Name the file: exercises/21-arraylist/ex4_roster.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 21, exercise 4: a roster of structs.
//! Run with:  zig test ex4_roster.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Merc = struct { name: []const u8, gunnery: u8, wounds: u8 };

const Roster = struct {
    mercs: std.ArrayList(Merc) = .empty,

    fn deinit(self: *Roster, gpa: std.mem.Allocator) void {
        self.mercs.deinit(gpa);
    }

    fn hire(self: *Roster, gpa: std.mem.Allocator, name: []const u8, gunnery: u8) !void {
        try self.mercs.append(gpa, .{ .name = name, .gunnery = gunnery, .wounds = 0 });
    }

    /// Every merc takes one wound. Must mutate in place.
    fn battle(self: *Roster) void {
        for (self.mercs.items) |*m| m.wounds += 1;
    }

    /// Release every merc whose gunnery is worse (higher) than `limit`, keeping order.
    fn releaseWorseThan(self: *Roster, limit: u8) usize {
        var released: usize = 0;
        var i: usize = 0;
        while (i < self.mercs.items.len) {
            if (self.mercs.items[i].gunnery > limit) {
                _ = self.mercs.orderedRemove(i);
                released += 1;
            } else i += 1;
        }
        return released;
    }

    /// Pointer to the best shot (lowest gunnery), or null if empty.
    fn best(self: *Roster) ?*Merc {
        if (self.mercs.items.len == 0) return null;
        var b = &self.mercs.items[0];
        for (self.mercs.items[1..]) |*m| if (m.gunnery < b.gunnery) {
            b = m;
        };
        return b;
    }
};

test "hire, fight, release" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    var r: Roster = .{};
    defer r.deinit(a);
    try r.hire(a, "Kell", 2);
    try r.hire(a, "Rookie", 6);
    try r.hire(a, "Natasha", 1);
    r.battle();
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 1), r.mercs.items[1].wounds);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 1), r.releaseWorseThan(4));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Kell", r.mercs.items[0].name);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Natasha", r.mercs.items[1].name);
}

test "best is a live pointer" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    var r: Roster = .{};
    defer r.deinit(a);
    try std.testing.expect(r.best() == null);
    try r.hire(a, "Kell", 2);
    try r.hire(a, "Natasha", 1);
    r.best().?.wounds = 9; // writes through to the list
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 9), r.mercs.items[1].wounds);
}

best returns a pointer into the list, which is fine as long as the caller uses it before the next hire. The test does exactly that. If you wanted a safer API you would return the index instead.

Exercise 21.5 · Run-length encoding challenge

Write encode(gpa, bytes) ![]Run where Run is struct { byte: u8, count: u32 }, and decode(gpa, runs) ![]u8 that reverses it (look at appendNTimes). Name the file: exercises/21-arraylist/ex5_rle.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 21, exercise 5: run-length encoding into a list of structs.
//! Run with:  zig test ex5_rle.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Run = struct { byte: u8, count: u32 };

fn encode(gpa: std.mem.Allocator, input: []const u8) ![]Run {
    var runs: std.ArrayList(Run) = .empty;
    errdefer runs.deinit(gpa);
    for (input) |c| {
        if (runs.items.len > 0 and runs.items[runs.items.len - 1].byte == c) {
            runs.items[runs.items.len - 1].count += 1;
        } else {
            try runs.append(gpa, .{ .byte = c, .count = 1 });
        }
    }
    return runs.toOwnedSlice(gpa);
}

fn decode(gpa: std.mem.Allocator, runs: []const Run) ![]u8 {
    var out: std.ArrayList(u8) = .empty;
    errdefer out.deinit(gpa);
    for (runs) |r| try out.appendNTimes(gpa, r.byte, r.count);
    return out.toOwnedSlice(gpa);
}

test "encode" {
    const runs = try encode(std.testing.allocator, "aaabccdddd");
    defer std.testing.allocator.free(runs);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 4), runs.len);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Run{ .byte = 'a', .count = 3 }, runs[0]);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Run{ .byte = 'd', .count = 4 }, runs[3]);
}

test "round trip" {
    const text = "mmmmeeeeccchhh warrior";
    const runs = try encode(std.testing.allocator, text);
    defer std.testing.allocator.free(runs);
    const back = try decode(std.testing.allocator, runs);
    defer std.testing.allocator.free(back);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings(text, back);
}

test "empty" {
    const runs = try encode(std.testing.allocator, "");
    defer std.testing.allocator.free(runs);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 0), runs.len);
}

The encoder peeks at the last run through runs.items[runs.items.len - 1] and mutates it in place; that expression is re-evaluated each time, so it is never stale even though append happens between iterations.

Check your understanding

  1. Why does append take an allocator but pop does not?
    Answerappend may need to grow the buffer, which means asking an allocator for memory (and possibly failing). pop only decrements the length; it never allocates, so it needs neither the allocator nor an error return.
  2. What is the difference between items.len and capacity?
    Answeritems.len is how many elements are in use; capacity is how many the underlying buffer could hold before the next regrow. Capacity is always at least the length.
  3. After const p = &list.items[2]; try list.append(gpa, x);, is p safe to use?
    AnswerNo. The append may have moved the buffer, leaving p pointing at freed memory. Keep the index and take the pointer again afterwards.
  4. What does swapRemove(0) do to a list [a, b, c, d]?
    AnswerIt returns a and moves the last element into slot 0: the list becomes [d, b, c]. Order is not preserved.
  5. After const s = try list.toOwnedSlice(gpa);, who must free what?
    AnswerThe caller must gpa.free(s). The list is now .empty, so its deinit frees nothing (but is still harmless to call).
  6. How do you change a struct element inside a list during a for loop?
    AnswerCapture by pointer: for (list.items) |*item| item.field = ...;. A plain capture gives you a copy.
  7. You want to build a string by calling a function that takes a *std.Io.Writer. Which type do you use?
    Answerstd.Io.Writer.Allocating, initialised with .init(gpa); pass &aw.writer and read back aw.written() or toOwnedSlice().
What you learned.
  • std.ArrayList(T) is unmanaged in 0.16: start it as .empty, pass the allocator to every growing call, and deinit(gpa) it.
  • items is a normal slice; capacity is the buffer size; growth happens in jumps so appends are cheap on average.
  • append, appendSlice, insert grow; pop (optional), orderedRemove, swapRemove, clearRetainingCapacity do not.
  • Iterate with |*item| to mutate in place; never hold a pointer into the list across a growing call.
  • ArrayList(u8) plus print is a string builder; std.Io.Writer.Allocating is the same idea behind a writer interface.
  • Build inside a function, return toOwnedSlice(gpa), use errdefer for cleanup on the failure path.

22. Hash maps

In this chapter you will use Zig's hash maps to look things up by key: AutoHashMapUnmanaged for integers and structs, StringHashMapUnmanaged for strings, and the ArrayHashMap family that remembers insertion order. You will learn put, get, getPtr, getOrPut, remove and the iterators, why string keys must outlive the map, which key types work automatically and which do not, and why IRON LEDGER keeps every entity in an ordered map.

22.1 Lookup by key

An ArrayList answers "what is the fifth element". A hash map answers "what is the value for this key", where the key can be a number, a string or a small struct. Python calls it a dict, JavaScript a Map or object, C++ an unordered_map. Internally the map computes a hash of the key, uses it to pick a slot in a table, and stores the key and value there. Lookups take about the same time whether the map holds ten entries or ten million.

Like ArrayList, Zig's maps are unmanaged in 0.16. They start as .empty, every call that might allocate takes the allocator, and deinit(gpa) frees the table. The map stores its keys and values by value, in its own table. What it does not own is anything those values point to, which is the whole subject of 22.5.

22.2 AutoHashMapUnmanaged: integers in, values out

a_auto.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() !void {
    var gpa_state: std.heap.DebugAllocator(.{}) = .init;
    defer _ = gpa_state.deinit();
    const gpa = gpa_state.allocator();

    // key: unit id, value: tonnage
    var tons: std.AutoHashMapUnmanaged(u32, u32) = .empty;
    defer tons.deinit(gpa);

    try tons.put(gpa, 7, 100); // Atlas
    try tons.put(gpa, 3, 20); // Locust
    try tons.put(gpa, 12, 75); // Marauder

    std.debug.print("count: {d}\n", .{tons.count()});
    std.debug.print("unit 7 weighs {?d}\n", .{tons.get(7)});
    std.debug.print("unit 99 weighs {?d}\n", .{tons.get(99)});
    std.debug.print("has 3? {}  has 4? {}\n", .{ tons.contains(3), tons.contains(4) });

    try tons.put(gpa, 3, 25); // put on an existing key overwrites
    std.debug.print("unit 3 now {?d}\n", .{tons.get(3)});

    const removed = tons.remove(12);
    const removed_again = tons.remove(12);
    std.debug.print("removed: {} then {}, count {d}\n", .{ removed, removed_again, tons.count() });
}
count: 3
unit 7 weighs 100
unit 99 weighs null
has 3? true  has 4? false
unit 3 now 25
removed: true then false, count 2

The name AutoHashMapUnmanaged(K, V) means "a hash map whose hashing and equality for K are worked out automatically". The five calls you will use most:

  • put(gpa, key, value) inserts, or overwrites if the key is already there. It takes the allocator because the table may need to grow.
  • get(key) returns ?V: a copy of the value, or null. Because it is an optional you print it with {?d} and unwrap it with if, orelse or .?, as in Chapter 15.
  • contains(key) is a bool, for when you do not need the value.
  • remove(key) deletes the entry and returns whether there was one. It never allocates.
  • count() is the number of entries.

The map does not preserve any order, and you must not assume one. We will make this visible in 22.4.

22.3 getPtr and getOrPut: changing what is inside

Because get hands back a copy, changing that copy does nothing to the map. To modify a stored value in place you ask for a pointer.

b_getptr.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Unit = struct { name: []const u8, armor: u32 };

pub fn main() !void {
    var gpa_state: std.heap.DebugAllocator(.{}) = .init;
    defer _ = gpa_state.deinit();
    const gpa = gpa_state.allocator();

    var units: std.AutoHashMapUnmanaged(u32, Unit) = .empty;
    defer units.deinit(gpa);
    try units.put(gpa, 1, .{ .name = "Atlas", .armor = 300 });

    // get() returns a COPY of the value.
    if (units.get(1)) |u| {
        var copy = u;
        copy.armor -= 50;
    }
    std.debug.print("after get:    {d}\n", .{units.get(1).?.armor});

    // getPtr() returns a pointer to the value inside the map.
    if (units.getPtr(1)) |u| u.armor -= 50;
    std.debug.print("after getPtr: {d}\n", .{units.get(1).?.armor});

    // getOrPut: one lookup, insert if missing.
    const gop = try units.getOrPut(gpa, 2);
    if (!gop.found_existing) gop.value_ptr.* = .{ .name = "Locust", .armor = 64 };
    gop.value_ptr.armor += 1;
    std.debug.print("unit 2: {s} {d} (existed before? {})\n", .{ gop.value_ptr.name, gop.value_ptr.armor, gop.found_existing });

    const again = try units.getOrPut(gpa, 2);
    std.debug.print("second getOrPut found_existing = {}\n", .{again.found_existing});
}
after get:    300
after getPtr: 250
unit 2: Locust 65 (existed before? false)
second getOrPut found_existing = true

getPtr(key) returns ?*V, a pointer into the table. Write through it and the map changes. The same warning as for lists applies: the pointer is valid only until the next put or getOrPut, because those can rehash and move every entry.

getOrPut(gpa, key) is the workhorse for "insert if missing, then update". It does one hash lookup and returns a small struct with found_existing: bool, key_ptr and value_ptr. If the key was not there, the slot has been reserved but the value is undefined: you must write to value_ptr.* before reading it, which is what the if (!gop.found_existing) line does. Compare the alternative, if (map.get(k)) |v| put(k, v+1) else put(k, 1): two lookups and twice the code. Every counter, tally and index you build will use getOrPut.

22.4 Iterating, and why order matters

There are three iterators, and one important difference between the two map families. Let's put the same five people into an AutoHashMapUnmanaged and an AutoArrayHashMapUnmanaged.

c_iter.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() !void {
    var gpa_state: std.heap.DebugAllocator(.{}) = .init;
    defer _ = gpa_state.deinit();
    const gpa = gpa_state.allocator();

    var hashed: std.AutoHashMapUnmanaged(u32, []const u8) = .empty;
    defer hashed.deinit(gpa);
    var ordered: std.AutoArrayHashMapUnmanaged(u32, []const u8) = .empty;
    defer ordered.deinit(gpa);

    const names = [_][]const u8{ "Kell", "Natasha", "Grayson", "Morgan", "Jaime" };
    for (names, 0..) |n, i| {
        const id: u32 = @intCast(100 + i * 37);
        try hashed.put(gpa, id, n);
        try ordered.put(gpa, id, n);
    }

    std.debug.print("AutoHashMap iterator:      ", .{});
    var it = hashed.iterator();
    while (it.next()) |e| std.debug.print("{d}={s} ", .{ e.key_ptr.*, e.value_ptr.* });
    std.debug.print("\n", .{});

    std.debug.print("AutoArrayHashMap iterator: ", .{});
    var oit = ordered.iterator();
    while (oit.next()) |e| std.debug.print("{d}={s} ", .{ e.key_ptr.*, e.value_ptr.* });
    std.debug.print("\n", .{});

    std.debug.print("keys() slice:              {any}\n", .{ordered.keys()});
    std.debug.print("keyIterator on hashed:     ", .{});
    var kit = hashed.keyIterator();
    while (kit.next()) |k| std.debug.print("{d} ", .{k.*});
    std.debug.print("\nvalueIterator on hashed:   ", .{});
    var vit = hashed.valueIterator();
    while (vit.next()) |v| std.debug.print("{s} ", .{v.*});
    std.debug.print("\n", .{});
}
AutoHashMap iterator:      211=Morgan 174=Grayson 248=Jaime 137=Natasha 100=Kell 
AutoArrayHashMap iterator: 100=Kell 137=Natasha 174=Grayson 211=Morgan 248=Jaime 
keys() slice:              { 100, 137, 174, 211, 248 }
keyIterator on hashed:     211 174 248 137 100 
valueIterator on hashed:   Morgan Grayson Jaime Natasha Kell

iterator() yields entries with key_ptr and value_ptr (pointers, so dereference with .* or write through them). keyIterator() and valueIterator() yield pointers to just one side. All three work the same on both map types.

Now look at the order. The plain hash map walked the entries in the order of their hash slots, which looks random and will change when the table grows or when the standard library changes its hash function. The array hash map walked them in the order we inserted them. That is its defining feature: it keeps keys and values in two dense arrays, with a hash index on the side pointing into them. Because of that it also offers keys() and values() as plain slices, which you can loop over directly, sort, or hand to any function that takes a slice.

Use AutoArrayHashMapUnmanaged (or the string flavour, StringArrayHashMapUnmanaged) whenever the order of iteration can affect output, and reach for the plain AutoHashMapUnmanaged only when you know you will never iterate, or genuinely do not care. The ordered map costs a little more memory and its remove is slower, but "a program whose output depends on the hash function" is a bug factory. This is not a stylistic preference in IRON LEDGER; the whole determinism story of the game rests on it.

Removing from an array hash map comes in two flavours that mirror the list: swapRemove(key) is fast and moves the last entry into the hole; orderedRemove(key) shifts everything down and keeps the order. There is also orderedRemoveAt(index) when you already have the position, for instance while walking values().

22.5 String keys and who owns them

StringHashMapUnmanaged(V) is a map whose keys are []const u8, hashed by content. The map stores the slice (a pointer and a length), not a copy of the characters. If the bytes the slice points at change or disappear, the map's key silently changes or becomes garbage, and lookups start failing in ways that are very hard to debug.

d_strkeys.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() !void {
    var gpa_state: std.heap.DebugAllocator(.{}) = .init;
    defer _ = gpa_state.deinit();
    const gpa = gpa_state.allocator();

    var stock: std.StringHashMapUnmanaged(u32) = .empty;
    defer stock.deinit(gpa);

    // Literal keys live in the binary forever: safe to use directly.
    try stock.put(gpa, "medium laser", 4);
    try stock.put(gpa, "LRM-10 ammo", 2);

    // Keys built at runtime must outlive the map. This one is on the stack...
    var buf: [32]u8 = undefined;
    const temp = try std.fmt.bufPrint(&buf, "{s} {d}", .{ "SRM", 6 });
    // ...so we copy it to the heap and let the MAP own the copy.
    try stock.put(gpa, try gpa.dupe(u8, temp), 9);
    @memset(&buf, 'x'); // scribble on the stack buffer; the map does not care

    std.debug.print("SRM 6: {?d}\n", .{stock.get("SRM 6")});
    std.debug.print("medium laser: {?d}\n", .{stock.get("medium laser")});

    // Free the keys we duped before the map goes away.
    var kit = stock.keyIterator();
    while (kit.next()) |k| {
        if (std.mem.startsWith(u8, k.*, "SRM")) gpa.free(k.*);
    }
}
SRM 6: 9
medium laser: 4

The literal keys are fine: string literals live in the executable for the whole run. The third key was built into a stack buffer with bufPrint, and that buffer is reused and overwritten a few lines later. Had we stored temp directly, the key would now read "xxxxx". Instead we store gpa.dupe(u8, temp), a heap copy that lives until we free it, and since the map is now the only thing that knows about that copy, we free it by walking the keys before deinit.

Rule. A string key must outlive the map. Three safe sources: a string literal; a slice into a buffer that you know lives longer than the map (a file's contents you read once, for example); or a copy made with allocator.dupe that you free when the entry goes. When in doubt, dupe, and use an arena so the frees take care of themselves.

The same rule applies to string values, and to any pointer or slice inside a value struct. The map copies the struct; it does not copy what the struct points at.

22.6 Which keys work automatically

"Auto" hashing looks at the bytes of the key. That works for integers, enums, bools and for structs and arrays built from those, so a coordinate struct is a fine key:

e_structkey.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Hex = struct { q: i16, r: i16 };

pub fn main() !void {
    var gpa_state: std.heap.DebugAllocator(.{}) = .init;
    defer _ = gpa_state.deinit();
    const gpa = gpa_state.allocator();

    var terrain: std.AutoHashMapUnmanaged(Hex, []const u8) = .empty;
    defer terrain.deinit(gpa);

    try terrain.put(gpa, .{ .q = 0, .r = 0 }, "clear");
    try terrain.put(gpa, .{ .q = 1, .r = -1 }, "woods");

    std.debug.print("{?s} {?s} {?s}\n", .{
        terrain.get(.{ .q = 1, .r = -1 }),
        terrain.get(.{ .q = 0, .r = 0 }),
        terrain.get(.{ .q = 5, .r = 5 }),
    });
}
woods clear null

What it refuses is a key that contains a slice. Hashing a slice by its bytes would hash the pointer and length, not the contents, so two equal strings at different addresses would be different keys. Rather than guess, the compiler stops you:

e_slicekey.zig

const std = @import("std");
pub fn main() !void {
    var m: std.AutoHashMapUnmanaged([]const u8, u32) = .empty;
    try m.put(std.heap.page_allocator, "atlas", 100);
}
<zig>/std/hash_map.zig:15:13: error: std.hash.autoHash does not allow slices here ([]const u8) because the intent is unclear. Consider using std.StringHashMap for hashing the contents of []const u8. Alternatively, consider using std.hash.autoHashStrat or providing your own hash function instead.
            @compileError("std.hash.autoHash does not allow slices here (" ++
            ^~~~~~~~~~~~~
<zig>/std/hash_map.zig:56:39: note: called at comptime here
        pub const hash = getAutoHashFn(K, @This());

The message tells you the fix: for []const u8 keys use StringHashMapUnmanaged. For anything more exotic (a struct with a string inside it, case-insensitive matching, floats) you write your own context type with hash and eql functions and use std.HashMapUnmanaged(K, V, Context, load_percentage) directly. You will rarely need that; in IRON LEDGER, every key is either an integer-backed enum ID or a string.

22.7 An ID to entity registry

Here is the pattern that the whole game is built on: entities live in an ordered map keyed by a typed ID (a non-exhaustive enum, from Chapter 13), and every other part of the program refers to them by ID, never by pointer.

f_registry.zig

const std = @import("std");

const UnitId = enum(u32) { _ };
const Unit = struct { name: []const u8, armor: u32, destroyed: bool = false };

const Hangar = struct {
    units: std.AutoArrayHashMapUnmanaged(UnitId, Unit) = .empty,
    next_id: u32 = 1,

    fn deinit(self: *Hangar, gpa: std.mem.Allocator) void {
        self.units.deinit(gpa);
    }

    fn add(self: *Hangar, gpa: std.mem.Allocator, name: []const u8, armor: u32) !UnitId {
        const id: UnitId = @enumFromInt(self.next_id);
        self.next_id += 1;
        try self.units.putNoClobber(gpa, id, .{ .name = name, .armor = armor });
        return id;
    }

    fn unit(self: *Hangar, id: UnitId) ?*Unit {
        return self.units.getPtr(id);
    }

    fn scrap(self: *Hangar, id: UnitId) bool {
        return self.units.orderedRemove(id);
    }
};

pub fn main() !void {
    var gpa_state: std.heap.DebugAllocator(.{}) = .init;
    defer _ = gpa_state.deinit();
    const gpa = gpa_state.allocator();

    var h: Hangar = .{};
    defer h.deinit(gpa);

    const atlas = try h.add(gpa, "Atlas", 300);
    const locust = try h.add(gpa, "Locust", 64);
    _ = try h.add(gpa, "Marauder", 230);

    if (h.unit(locust)) |u| u.armor = 0;
    if (h.unit(locust)) |u| u.destroyed = u.armor == 0;
    std.debug.print("scrapped locust? {}\n", .{h.scrap(locust)});
    std.debug.print("scrapped again?  {}\n", .{h.scrap(locust)});
    std.debug.print("atlas still there? {}\n", .{h.unit(atlas) != null});

    // Deterministic order: insertion order, minus what was removed.
    for (h.units.keys(), h.units.values()) |id, u| {
        std.debug.print("  #{d} {s: <9} armor {d}\n", .{ @intFromEnum(id), u.name, u.armor });
    }
}
scrapped locust? true
scrapped again?  false
atlas still there? true
  #1 Atlas     armor 300
  #3 Marauder  armor 230

Why IDs rather than pointers? Because the map can move its entries. Store a *Unit somewhere and it is stale after the next add. Store a UnitId and you can always ask the hangar for a fresh pointer with unit(id), use it briefly, and let it go. The ?*Unit return type also handles the case where the unit has been scrapped: you get null, not a crash. putNoClobber is put that asserts the key is new, which documents the intent that IDs are never reused.

The final loop uses keys() and values() together in one for: both are slices of the same length, so the multi-object for from Chapter 6 walks them in lockstep. That only works because this is an array hash map.

22.8 Method reference

CallReturnsNotes
put(gpa, k, v)!voidInsert or overwrite.
putNoClobber(gpa, k, v)!voidInsert; asserts k is new.
get(k)?VA copy.
getPtr(k)?*VValid until the next insert.
getOrPut(gpa, k)!GetOrPutResultfound_existing, key_ptr, value_ptr; value undefined if new.
contains(k)bool
remove(k)boolHash map. Array map: swapRemove / orderedRemove.
fetchRemove(k)?KVRemove and get the old pair back.
count()usize
iterator()entrieskey_ptr, value_ptr
keyIterator(), valueIterator()pointers
keys(), values()slicesArray map only.
clearRetainingCapacity()Empty it, keep the table.
deinit(gpa)Free the table (not what keys/values point to).
In IRON LEDGER. GameState in game/src/sim/state.zig is mostly a set of registries exactly like 22.7: 
people: std.AutoArrayHashMapUnmanaged(types.PersonId, person_mod.Person) = .empty,
units: std.AutoArrayHashMapUnmanaged(types.UnitId, unit_mod.Unit) = .empty,
forces: std.AutoArrayHashMapUnmanaged(types.ForceId, force_mod.Force) = .empty,
hqs: std.AutoArrayHashMapUnmanaged(types.HqId, hq_mod.Hq) = .empty,
contracts: std.AutoArrayHashMapUnmanaged(types.ContractId, contract_mod.Contract) = .empty,
They are all array hash maps because the daily tick iterates them, and two campaigns with the same seed must produce identical logs; a plain hash map would make the order of events depend on hash slots. String-keyed stock uses the ordered string flavour, and the console prints it with the entry iterator (game/src/main.zig): 
fn printStockLines(stock: *const std.StringArrayHashMapUnmanaged(u32)) void {
    var it = stock.iterator();
    while (it.next()) |entry| {
        if (entry.value_ptr.* == 0) continue;
        std.debug.print("    {s:<18} x{d:<4} ({d}t)\n", .{
            entry.key_ptr.*, entry.value_ptr.*, entry.value_ptr.* * game.part.tons(entry.key_ptr.*),
        });
    }
}
And the maintenance pass in game/src/sim/maintenance.zig is a textbook getOrPut: a tech's remaining hours are computed lazily the first time that tech is looked up, then decremented in place through entry.value_ptr.

Exercises

Exercise 22.1 · Inventory warm-up

Complete an Inventory wrapping AutoHashMapUnmanaged(u32, u32): stock adds (creating the entry with getOrPut), take removes if there is enough and deletes the key when the count reaches zero, onHand returns zero for unknown parts. Name the file: exercises/22-hashmaps/ex1_inventory.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 22, exercise 1: a parts inventory keyed by part number.
//! Run with:  zig test ex1_inventory.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Inventory = struct {
    parts: std.AutoHashMapUnmanaged(u32, u32) = .empty,

    fn deinit(self: *Inventory, gpa: std.mem.Allocator) void {
        self.parts.deinit(gpa);
    }

    /// Add `n` of part `id` (creating the entry if needed).
    fn stock(self: *Inventory, gpa: std.mem.Allocator, id: u32, n: u32) !void {
        const gop = try self.parts.getOrPut(gpa, id);
        if (!gop.found_existing) gop.value_ptr.* = 0;
        gop.value_ptr.* += n;
    }

    /// Take `n` of part `id`. Returns false (and changes nothing) if there are not enough.
    /// When the count hits zero the entry is removed.
    fn take(self: *Inventory, id: u32, n: u32) bool {
        const p = self.parts.getPtr(id) orelse return false;
        if (p.* < n) return false;
        p.* -= n;
        if (p.* == 0) _ = self.parts.remove(id);
        return true;
    }

    fn onHand(self: Inventory, id: u32) u32 {
        return self.parts.get(id) orelse 0;
    }
};

test "stock and take" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    var inv: Inventory = .{};
    defer inv.deinit(a);
    try inv.stock(a, 100, 3);
    try inv.stock(a, 100, 2);
    try inv.stock(a, 200, 1);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 5), inv.onHand(100));
    try std.testing.expect(inv.take(100, 4));
    try std.testing.expect(!inv.take(100, 4));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 1), inv.onHand(100));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 0), inv.onHand(999));
}

test "taking the last one removes the key" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    var inv: Inventory = .{};
    defer inv.deinit(a);
    try inv.stock(a, 7, 1);
    try std.testing.expect(inv.take(7, 1));
    try std.testing.expect(!inv.parts.contains(7));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 0), inv.parts.count());
}

take uses getPtr so it can decrement in place, and orelse return false handles the missing key. Note onHand takes self by value: it only reads, and get does not need a pointer to the map.

Exercise 22.2 · Word count practice

Write wordCounts(gpa, text): tokenize on spaces, tabs and newlines, count each word in a StringHashMapUnmanaged(u32), then return an owned slice of { word, n } sorted by count descending and word ascending. The words are slices into text, so no duping is needed here; say in a comment why that is safe. Name the file: exercises/22-hashmaps/ex2_wordcount.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 22, exercise 2: count words.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_wordcount.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Count = struct { word: []const u8, n: u32 };

/// Count each whitespace-separated word in `text`. The words are slices into `text`,
/// so the returned array is valid as long as `text` is.
/// Results are sorted by count descending, then word ascending.
fn wordCounts(gpa: std.mem.Allocator, text: []const u8) ![]Count {
    var map: std.StringHashMapUnmanaged(u32) = .empty;
    defer map.deinit(gpa);

    var it = std.mem.tokenizeAny(u8, text, " \t\n");
    while (it.next()) |w| {
        const gop = try map.getOrPut(gpa, w);
        if (!gop.found_existing) gop.value_ptr.* = 0;
        gop.value_ptr.* += 1;
    }

    var out: std.ArrayList(Count) = .empty;
    errdefer out.deinit(gpa);
    var mit = map.iterator();
    while (mit.next()) |e| try out.append(gpa, .{ .word = e.key_ptr.*, .n = e.value_ptr.* });

    std.mem.sort(Count, out.items, {}, struct {
        fn lt(_: void, a: Count, b: Count) bool {
            if (a.n != b.n) return a.n > b.n;
            return std.mem.lessThan(u8, a.word, b.word);
        }
    }.lt);
    return out.toOwnedSlice(gpa);
}

test "counts" {
    const text = "the mech the pilot the lance\nmech pilot";
    const counts = try wordCounts(std.testing.allocator, text);
    defer std.testing.allocator.free(counts);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 4), counts.len);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("the", counts[0].word);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 3), counts[0].n);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("mech", counts[1].word);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("pilot", counts[2].word);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("lance", counts[3].word);
}

test "empty text" {
    const counts = try wordCounts(std.testing.allocator, "   \n ");
    defer std.testing.allocator.free(counts);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 0), counts.len);
}

The keys point into text, which the caller keeps alive, so the map never owns anything and a plain deinit is enough. The map is only a scratch structure; the ordered result comes from copying into a list and sorting with a custom lessThan, which Chapter 24 covers in depth.

Exercise 22.3 · Invert practice

Given an AutoArrayHashMapUnmanaged(u32, []const u8) from pilot ID to callsign, build the reverse StringArrayHashMapUnmanaged(u32). Return error.Duplicate if two pilots share a callsign, without leaking. Name the file: exercises/22-hashmaps/ex3_invert.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 22, exercise 3: invert a map.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_invert.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Callsigns = std.AutoArrayHashMapUnmanaged(u32, []const u8); // pilot id -> callsign
const ByCallsign = std.StringArrayHashMapUnmanaged(u32); // callsign -> pilot id

/// Build the reverse map. If two pilots share a callsign, return error.Duplicate.
/// The callsign strings are shared with the input map, not copied.
fn invert(gpa: std.mem.Allocator, in: Callsigns) !ByCallsign {
    var out: ByCallsign = .empty;
    errdefer out.deinit(gpa);
    var it = in.iterator();
    while (it.next()) |e| {
        const gop = try out.getOrPut(gpa, e.value_ptr.*);
        if (gop.found_existing) return error.Duplicate;
        gop.value_ptr.* = e.key_ptr.*;
    }
    return out;
}

test "invert" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    var cs: Callsigns = .empty;
    defer cs.deinit(a);
    try cs.put(a, 1, "Widowmaker");
    try cs.put(a, 2, "Phantom");
    try cs.put(a, 3, "Grey");
    var by = try invert(a, cs);
    defer by.deinit(a);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u32, 2), by.get("Phantom"));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u32, null), by.get("Nobody"));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 3), by.count());
    // ArrayHashMap keeps the order we inserted in.
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Widowmaker", by.keys()[0]);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Grey", by.keys()[2]);
}

test "duplicate callsign is an error and leaks nothing" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    var cs: Callsigns = .empty;
    defer cs.deinit(a);
    try cs.put(a, 1, "Ace");
    try cs.put(a, 2, "Ace");
    try std.testing.expectError(error.Duplicate, invert(a, cs));
}

The errdefer out.deinit(gpa) is what makes the duplicate test pass under std.testing.allocator, which fails the test on a leak. The callsign strings are shared with the input map, so nothing needs duping.

Exercise 22.4 · Registry challenge

Build a Registry like the game's: AutoArrayHashMapUnmanaged(PersonId, Person) with hire (fresh ID, putNoClobber), person(id) ?*Person, mission() which increments every active person's mission count in place, and bury() which removes every kia entry while keeping the order of the rest. Name the file: exercises/22-hashmaps/ex4_registry.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 22, exercise 4: an ID -> entity registry, like GameState.people.
//! Run with:  zig test ex4_registry.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const PersonId = enum(u32) { _ };
const Status = enum { active, wounded, kia };
const Person = struct { name: []const u8, status: Status = .active, missions: u32 = 0 };

const Registry = struct {
    people: std.AutoArrayHashMapUnmanaged(PersonId, Person) = .empty,
    next: u32 = 1,

    fn deinit(self: *Registry, gpa: std.mem.Allocator) void {
        self.people.deinit(gpa);
    }

    fn hire(self: *Registry, gpa: std.mem.Allocator, name: []const u8) !PersonId {
        const id: PersonId = @enumFromInt(self.next);
        self.next += 1;
        try self.people.putNoClobber(gpa, id, .{ .name = name });
        return id;
    }

    fn person(self: *Registry, id: PersonId) ?*Person {
        return self.people.getPtr(id);
    }

    /// Every active person flies one mission. Returns how many flew.
    fn mission(self: *Registry) u32 {
        var flew: u32 = 0;
        for (self.people.values()) |*p| {
            if (p.status != .active) continue;
            p.missions += 1;
            flew += 1;
        }
        return flew;
    }

    /// Remove everyone with status kia, keeping the order of the rest.
    /// Returns how many were removed.
    fn bury(self: *Registry) u32 {
        var removed: u32 = 0;
        var i: usize = 0;
        while (i < self.people.count()) {
            if (self.people.values()[i].status == .kia) {
                self.people.orderedRemoveAt(i);
                removed += 1;
            } else i += 1;
        }
        return removed;
    }
};

test "hire, look up, mutate" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    var r: Registry = .{};
    defer r.deinit(a);
    const kell = try r.hire(a, "Kell");
    const nat = try r.hire(a, "Natasha");
    try std.testing.expect(r.person(kell) != null);
    try std.testing.expect(r.person(@enumFromInt(999)) == null);
    r.person(nat).?.status = .wounded;
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 1), r.mission());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 1), r.person(kell).?.missions);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 0), r.person(nat).?.missions);
}

test "bury keeps order and ids stay valid" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    var r: Registry = .{};
    defer r.deinit(a);
    const p1 = try r.hire(a, "one");
    const p2 = try r.hire(a, "two");
    const p3 = try r.hire(a, "three");
    const p4 = try r.hire(a, "four");
    r.person(p1).?.status = .kia;
    r.person(p3).?.status = .kia;
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 2), r.bury());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 2), r.people.count());
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("two", r.people.values()[0].name);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("four", r.people.values()[1].name);
    try std.testing.expect(r.person(p2) != null);
    try std.testing.expect(r.person(p4) != null);
    try std.testing.expect(r.person(p1) == null);
}

mission walks values() by pointer, which is only possible on an array map. bury uses the same "do not advance after removing" loop as Exercise 21.2, with orderedRemoveAt(i).

Exercise 22.5 · Group by, owning the keys challenge

Build Groups: a StringArrayHashMapUnmanaged from role to an ArrayList([]const u8) of names. The role passed to add is a temporary buffer that will be overwritten, so the map must dupe the key on first insert and free every key and list in deinit. Name the file: exercises/22-hashmaps/ex5_groupby.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 22, exercise 5: group names by role, owning the keys.
//! Run with:  zig test ex5_groupby.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Groups = struct {
    map: std.StringArrayHashMapUnmanaged(std.ArrayList([]const u8)) = .empty,

    /// Free every duped key and every list, then the map.
    fn deinit(self: *Groups, gpa: std.mem.Allocator) void {
        for (self.map.keys(), self.map.values()) |k, *list| {
            gpa.free(k);
            list.deinit(gpa);
        }
        self.map.deinit(gpa);
    }

    /// `role` may be a temporary; the map must own its own copy of the key.
    fn add(self: *Groups, gpa: std.mem.Allocator, role: []const u8, name: []const u8) !void {
        const gop = try self.map.getOrPut(gpa, role);
        if (!gop.found_existing) {
            gop.key_ptr.* = try gpa.dupe(u8, role);
            gop.value_ptr.* = .empty;
        }
        try gop.value_ptr.append(gpa, name);
    }

    fn members(self: Groups, role: []const u8) []const []const u8 {
        const list = self.map.get(role) orelse return &.{};
        return list.items;
    }
};

test "group by role with temporary keys" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    var g: Groups = .{};
    defer g.deinit(a);

    var buf: [16]u8 = undefined;
    const rows = [_]struct { role: []const u8, name: []const u8 }{
        .{ .role = "pilot", .name = "Kell" },
        .{ .role = "tech", .name = "Sato" },
        .{ .role = "pilot", .name = "Natasha" },
    };
    for (rows) |r| {
        // Build the key in a reused buffer so it is definitely temporary.
