        const key = try std.fmt.bufPrint(&buf, "{s}", .{r.role});
        try g.add(a, key, r.name);
        @memset(&buf, 0);
    }
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 2), g.members("pilot").len);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Natasha", g.members("pilot")[1]);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 1), g.members("tech").len);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 0), g.members("medic").len);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("pilot", g.map.keys()[0]);
}

The trick is gop.key_ptr.* = try gpa.dupe(u8, role): getOrPut looked the key up using the temporary, and now we replace the stored key with a copy we own. The test scribbles over the buffer after each insert to prove the map is not looking at it any more.

Check your understanding

  1. What does get return, and what does that mean for changing the value?
    Answer?V, a copy of the value or null. Changing the copy does not change the map; use getPtr for that.
  2. After const gop = try map.getOrPut(gpa, k); with found_existing == false, what is in gop.value_ptr.*?
    AnswerUndefined memory. You must assign to it before reading it.
  3. When would you pick AutoArrayHashMapUnmanaged over AutoHashMapUnmanaged?
    AnswerWhenever you iterate and the order can affect anything observable (output, event order, determinism), or when you want keys()/values() as slices. The plain map is for pure lookup tables.
  4. Why can't AutoHashMapUnmanaged([]const u8, V) compile?
    AnswerAuto hashing works on the key's bytes, and for a slice that is the pointer and length, not the characters. The compiler rejects it and points you to StringHashMapUnmanaged, which hashes contents.
  5. You build a key with bufPrint into a stack buffer and put it into a string map that outlives the function. What goes wrong and how do you fix it?
    AnswerThe map stores a slice pointing at the stack buffer, which is gone (or reused) after the function returns; lookups become garbage. Fix: gpa.dupe(u8, key) and free the copies when the entries go (or use an arena).
  6. Is a pointer from getPtr still valid after a put of a different key?
    AnswerNot necessarily. The insert may grow and rehash the table, moving every entry. Re-fetch the pointer after any insert.
  7. Why does IRON LEDGER pass around PersonId values instead of *Person?
    AnswerEntries in the map can move when it grows and can be removed; an ID is always safe to hold and can be turned into a fresh ?*Person on demand, with null when the person is gone.
What you learned.
  • Maps are unmanaged: .empty, allocator on every inserting call, deinit(gpa) frees the table only.
  • put, get (copy, optional), getPtr (pointer, optional), getOrPut (one lookup, found_existing, undefined value when new), remove, contains, count.
  • iterator, keyIterator, valueIterator give pointers; array maps also give keys() and values() slices and iterate in insertion order.
  • Plain hash maps iterate in an order you must not rely on; use the array flavour whenever order matters.
  • String keys are slices: they must outlive the map, so dupe anything temporary and free it yourself.
  • Auto hashing handles integers, enums and plain structs; slices need StringHashMapUnmanaged or a custom context.
  • Keep entities in a map keyed by a typed ID, and hand out IDs, not pointers.

23. Formatting and parsing text

In this chapter you will learn the whole of Zig's format-string grammar: every specifier, width, alignment, fill and precision, positional and named arguments, and how to escape braces. You will see where formatted text can go (the heap, a buffer, a writer, or the compiler itself), how to turn text back into numbers with parseInt and parseFloat and handle their errors, and how to give your own types a format method.

23.1 The grammar

You have been writing {d} and {s} since Chapter 2. Here is the full shape of a placeholder:

{[argument]specifier:[fill][alignment][width][.precision]}

Everything except the braces is optional. argument is a position (0, 1) or a field name in square brackets. specifier is a short letter code saying how to render the value. After a colon come the layout options: a fill character, an alignment (< left, ^ centre, > right), a width in characters and a .precision for floats. Format strings are checked at compile time against the argument tuple: a missing argument, an extra one, or a specifier that does not fit the type is a compile error, never a runtime surprise.

23.2 Every specifier

a_specs.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const n: u32 = 42;
    const neg: i32 = -7;
    const f: f64 = 3.14159;
    const s: []const u8 = "Atlas";
    const c: u8 = 'K';
    const opt: ?u32 = null;
    const eu: anyerror!u32 = error.NoFuel;

    std.debug.print("{{d}}   -> {d}  {d}\n", .{ n, neg });
    std.debug.print("{{x}}   -> {x}    {{X}} -> {X}\n", .{ n, n });
    std.debug.print("{{b}}   -> {b}  {{o}} -> {o}\n", .{ n, n });
    std.debug.print("{{c}}   -> {c}   {{u}} -> {u}\n", .{ c, @as(u21, 0x2694) });
    std.debug.print("{{s}}   -> {s}\n", .{s});
    std.debug.print("{{d}}   -> {d}   {{e}} -> {e}\n", .{ f, f });
    std.debug.print("{{?}}   -> {?}  {{?d}} -> {?d}\n", .{ opt, @as(?u32, 5) });
    std.debug.print("{{!}}   -> {!}  {{!d}} -> {!d}\n", .{ eu, @as(anyerror!u32, 9) });
    std.debug.print("{{any}} -> {any}\n", .{[_]u8{ 1, 2, 3 }});
    std.debug.print("{{*}}   -> {*}\n", .{&n});
    std.debug.print("{{}}    -> {}  {}\n", .{ true, n });
}
{d}   -> 42  -7
{x}   -> 2a    {X} -> 2A
{b}   -> 101010  {o} -> 52
{c}   -> K   {u} -> ⚔
{s}   -> Atlas
{d}   -> 3.14159   {e} -> 3.14159e0
{?}   -> null  {?d} -> 5
{!}   -> error.NoFuel  {!d} -> 9
{any} -> { 1, 2, 3 }
{*}   -> u32@102a234c0
{}    -> true  42
SpecWorks onOutput
{d}integers, floatsDecimal.
{x} {X}integers, byte slicesHex, lower or upper case.
{b} {o}integersBinary, octal.
{c}u8One ASCII character.
{u}u21One Unicode code point, UTF-8 encoded.
{s}[]const u8, [*:0]const u8The bytes as text.
{e}floatsScientific notation.
{?} {?d}optionalsnull or the payload with the spec after ?.
{!} {!d}error unionserror.Name or the payload with the spec after !.
{any}anythingA debug rendering: arrays, structs, enums, whatever.
{*}pointersType and address.
{f}types with a format methodCalls it (23.8).
{t}enums, error setsThe tag name, like @tagName.
{}bools, integersDefault rendering. Not allowed on slices, which must say {s}, {x} or {any}.

The ? and ! prefixes compose: {?d} is "an optional integer, print the integer in decimal if present". They save you an if when debugging. Slices are the one place Zig refuses a bare {}: a []const u8 might be text or bytes, so you have to say which with {s} or {x}.

23.3 Width, alignment, fill and precision

b_width.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const name: []const u8 = "Locust";
    const tons: u32 = 20;
    const f: f64 = 2.0 / 3.0;

    std.debug.print("[{s: <10}] left in 10\n", .{name});
    std.debug.print("[{s: >10}] right in 10\n", .{name});
    std.debug.print("[{s:^10}] centred in 10\n", .{name});
    std.debug.print("[{s:.^10}] centred, fill '.'\n", .{name});
    std.debug.print("[{d: >6}] right in 6\n", .{tons});
    std.debug.print("[{d:0>6}] zero-padded to 6\n", .{tons});
    std.debug.print("[{d:<6}] left in 6 (default fill is space)\n", .{tons});
    std.debug.print("[{d:.2}] two decimals\n", .{f});
    std.debug.print("[{d:8.3}] width 8, three decimals\n", .{f});
    std.debug.print("[{x:0>8}] hex, zero-padded to 8\n", .{@as(u32, 0xBEEF)});

    // A table: the format string is the layout.
    const rows = [_]struct { n: []const u8, t: u32, bv: u32 }{
        .{ .n = "Atlas", .t = 100, .bv = 1897 },
        .{ .n = "Marauder", .t = 75, .bv = 1363 },
        .{ .n = "Locust", .t = 20, .bv = 432 },
    };
    std.debug.print("{s: <10} {s: >5} {s: >6}\n", .{ "name", "tons", "bv" });
    for (rows) |r| std.debug.print("{s: <10} {d: >5} {d: >6}\n", .{ r.n, r.t, r.bv });
}
[Locust    ] left in 10
[    Locust] right in 10
[  Locust  ] centred in 10
[..Locust..] centred, fill '.'
[    20] right in 6
[000020] zero-padded to 6
[20    ] left in 6 (default fill is space)
[0.67] two decimals
[   0.667] width 8, three decimals
[0000beef] hex, zero-padded to 8
name        tons     bv
Atlas        100   1897
Marauder      75   1363
Locust        20    432

Read {s: <10} as: specifier s, then after the colon a fill character (space), an alignment (<), a width (10). The fill is any single character, and it is only recognised if an alignment character follows it, which is why {d:0>6} means "fill with zeros, right-align, width 6" and not "width 06". Numbers align right by default and text aligns... also right, which surprises people; put an explicit < on string columns. Precision for floats is .N and rounds; width and precision combine as {d:8.3}.

The table at the end is the whole trick of text user interfaces: pick a format string once, use it for the header and every row, and the columns line up. IRON LEDGER's screens are hundreds of lines exactly like it.

A 0.16 surprise: signed integers grow a plus sign when given a width.

c_sign.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const unsigned: u32 = 42;
    const signed: i32 = 42;
    std.debug.print("[{d}] [{d}]      no width: same\n", .{ unsigned, signed });
    std.debug.print("[{d: >5}] [{d: >5}]  with width: signed gets a '+'\n", .{ unsigned, signed });
    std.debug.print("[{d: >5}]          negative is what you expect\n", .{@as(i32, -42)});
}
[42] [42]      no width: same
[   42] [  +42]  with width: signed gets a '+'
[  -42]          negative is what you expect
The rule inside the standard library is: for a signed type with a non-zero width, print the sign always. With no width, positive numbers print bare. If you want 42 from an i32, cast to unsigned first when you know it is not negative (@as(u32, @intCast(v))), or format the number into a small buffer with {d} and then align that string with {s: >5}.

23.4 Positional and named arguments, and literal braces

d_positional.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    // Positional: {0} is the first argument, {1} the second.
    std.debug.print("{1s} weighs {0d} tons; yes, {0d}.\n", .{ 100, "Atlas" });

    // Named: the argument is a struct, and {[field]} picks a field.
    std.debug.print("{[name]s}: gunnery {[gun]d}, piloting {[pil]d}\n", .{
        .name = "Natasha", .gun = 1, .pil = 2,
    });

    // Literal braces are doubled.
    std.debug.print("markup looks like {{g}}{s}{{/}}\n", .{"active"});
}
Atlas weighs 100 tons; yes, 100.
Natasha: gunnery 1, piloting 2
markup looks like {g}active{/}

Positional indices let you reuse an argument or reorder them. Named placeholders take a struct instead of a tuple, and {[name]s} reads the field name. Both are rare in everyday code but useful for message templates. The doubled brace is essential: {{ prints {. You will see this constantly in the game, because its colour markup uses braces.

23.5 Where the text goes

std.debug.print sends formatted text to stderr. The same format engine can send it to the heap, to a buffer you own, to any writer, or run at compile time.

e_targets.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() !void {
    var gpa_state: std.heap.DebugAllocator(.{}) = .init;
    defer _ = gpa_state.deinit();
    const gpa = gpa_state.allocator();

    // 1. allocPrint: heap string, caller frees.
    const heap = try std.fmt.allocPrint(gpa, "unit-{d:0>3}", .{7});
    defer gpa.free(heap);
    std.debug.print("allocPrint: {s}\n", .{heap});

    // 2. bufPrint: into a buffer you provide; returns the slice actually used.
    var buf: [16]u8 = undefined;
    const fixed = try std.fmt.bufPrint(&buf, "{d}%", .{95});
    std.debug.print("bufPrint:   {s} ({d} of {d} bytes)\n", .{ fixed, fixed.len, buf.len });

    // 3. bufPrint fails, it does not truncate.
    const too_long = std.fmt.bufPrint(buf[0..4], "{d}", .{123456});
    std.debug.print("too long:   {!s}\n", .{too_long});

    // 4. bufPrintZ: same, with a trailing zero byte for C.
    const z = try std.fmt.bufPrintZ(&buf, "{s}", .{"cstr"});
    std.debug.print("bufPrintZ:  {s} len {d}, byte after is {d}\n", .{ z, z.len, z[z.len] });

    // 5. A fixed Writer: many prints into one buffer.
    var w = std.Io.Writer.fixed(&buf);
    try w.print("{d}", .{1});
    try w.print("+{d}", .{2});
    try w.writeAll("=3");
    std.debug.print("fixed:      {s}\n", .{w.buffered()});

    // 6. comptimePrint: the string is built by the compiler.
    const version = std.fmt.comptimePrint("zig {d}.{d}", .{ 0, 16 });
    std.debug.print("comptime:   {s} ({s})\n", .{ version, @typeName(@TypeOf(version)) });

    // 7. count: how many bytes would it take?
    std.debug.print("count:      {d}\n", .{std.fmt.count("{d}-{s}", .{ 12, "ab" })});
}
allocPrint: unit-007
bufPrint:   95% (3 of 16 bytes)
too long:   error.NoSpaceLeft
bufPrintZ:  cstr len 4, byte after is 0
fixed:      1+2=3
comptime:   zig 0.16 (*const [8:0]u8)
count:      5
  • allocPrint(gpa, fmt, args) returns a []u8 you must free. It is the most common in IRON LEDGER (over five hundred calls), always with an arena so the frees are one deinit.
  • bufPrint(buf, fmt, args) writes into your buffer and returns the slice that was written. If the result does not fit, it returns error.NoSpaceLeft and writes nothing useful. It never truncates silently, which is a deliberate contrast with C's snprintf.
  • bufPrintZ is the same with a zero byte appended, returning [:0]u8, for handing to C (Chapter 35).
  • std.Io.Writer.fixed(&buf) makes a writer backed by your buffer; you can print to it repeatedly and read back buffered(). This is how you build a line from several pieces without an allocator. The growable version is std.Io.Writer.Allocating from Chapter 21.
  • comptimePrint produces the string at compile time. The result's type, *const [8:0]u8, tells you it is a pointer to a constant array baked into the binary. Use it for building names, error messages and @compileError text in generic code.
  • count tells you how long the output would be, useful to size a buffer.

23.6 Parsing numbers

Going the other way, from text to a value, is std.fmt.parseInt(T, text, base), parseUnsigned and parseFloat. They return error unions, and the errors are specific.

f_parse.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{!d}\n", .{std.fmt.parseInt(i32, "-12", 10)});
    std.debug.print("{!d}\n", .{std.fmt.parseInt(u8, "ff", 16)});
    std.debug.print("{!d}\n", .{std.fmt.parseInt(u8, "1010", 2)});
    std.debug.print("{!d}  (base 0: prefix decides)\n", .{std.fmt.parseInt(i32, "0x1F", 0)});
    std.debug.print("{!d}  (underscores allowed)\n", .{std.fmt.parseInt(i32, "1_000", 10)});
    std.debug.print("{!d}  (256 does not fit u8)\n", .{std.fmt.parseInt(u8, "256", 10)});
    std.debug.print("{!d}  (trailing junk)\n", .{std.fmt.parseInt(u8, "12a", 10)});
    std.debug.print("{!d}  (empty)\n", .{std.fmt.parseInt(i32, "", 10)});
    std.debug.print("{!d}  (spaces are junk too)\n", .{std.fmt.parseInt(i32, " 5", 10)});
    std.debug.print("{!d}  (parseUnsigned rejects a sign)\n", .{std.fmt.parseUnsigned(u16, "-1", 10)});
    std.debug.print("{!d}\n", .{std.fmt.parseFloat(f64, "1.5")});
    std.debug.print("{!d}\n", .{std.fmt.parseFloat(f64, "1e3")});
    std.debug.print("{!d}\n", .{std.fmt.parseFloat(f64, "inf")});
    std.debug.print("{!d}\n", .{std.fmt.parseFloat(f32, "abc")});
}
-12
255
10
31  (base 0: prefix decides)
1000  (underscores allowed)
error.Overflow  (256 does not fit u8)
error.InvalidCharacter  (trailing junk)
error.InvalidCharacter  (empty)
error.InvalidCharacter  (spaces are junk too)
error.InvalidCharacter  (parseUnsigned rejects a sign)
1.5
1000
inf
error.InvalidCharacter

The rules: the whole string must be a number (no leading or trailing spaces, no trailing junk); an optional sign is accepted by parseInt but not parseUnsigned; underscores between digits are fine; base 0 means "look at the prefix" (0x, 0o, 0b, or decimal). The value must fit in T or you get error.Overflow. Everything else is error.InvalidCharacter. parseFloat understands exponents, inf and nan.

Because the error set of parseInt is exactly { Overflow, InvalidCharacter }, you can switch on it exhaustively and give the user a precise message:

g_handle.zig

const std = @import("std");

/// Parse "name=value" into a number, explaining any problem.
fn readSetting(line: []const u8) ?i32 {
    const eq = std.mem.indexOfScalar(u8, line, '=') orelse {
        std.debug.print("  no '=' in {s}\n", .{line});
        return null;
    };
    const text = std.mem.trim(u8, line[eq + 1 ..], " ");
    return std.fmt.parseInt(i32, text, 10) catch |err| switch (err) {
        error.InvalidCharacter => {
            std.debug.print("  '{s}' is not a number\n", .{text});
            return null;
        },
        error.Overflow => {
            std.debug.print("  '{s}' does not fit in an i32\n", .{text});
            return null;
        },
    };
}

pub fn main() void {
    const lines = [_][]const u8{ "seed = 42", "seed=-1", "seed", "seed = forty", "seed = 99999999999" };
    for (lines) |l| {
        std.debug.print("{s}:\n", .{l});
        if (readSetting(l)) |v| std.debug.print("  -> {d}\n", .{v});
    }
}
seed = 42:
  -> 42
seed=-1:
  -> -1
seed:
  no '=' in seed
seed = forty:
  'forty' is not a number
seed = 99999999999:
  '99999999999' does not fit in an i32

Notice the trim before the parse. Users type spaces; parseInt does not forgive them; so you strip them. This pairs with the tokenizers of Chapter 24, which is how command lines are chopped into words before each word is parsed.

23.7 Bytes as hex

Older Zig had std.fmt.fmtSliceHexLower. In 0.16 it is gone, and the job is done by the plain {x} specifier applied to a byte slice, or by bytesToHex when you want an array back:

i_hex.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const bytes = [_]u8{ 0xDE, 0xAD, 0xBE, 0xEF };
    std.debug.print("{x}\n", .{&bytes}); // a byte slice with {x}: hex, no separators
    std.debug.print("{X}\n", .{&bytes});
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{&std.fmt.bytesToHex(bytes, .lower)}); // comptime-sized array
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{&bytes}); // {any} prints decimal elements
    var out: [4]u8 = undefined;
    const back = std.fmt.hexToBytes(&out, "deadbeef") catch unreachable;
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{back});
}
deadbeef
DEADBEEF
deadbeef
{ 222, 173, 190, 239 }
{ 222, 173, 190, 239 }

bytesToHex takes an array (not a slice) so it can size its result at compile time; hexToBytes reverses it into a buffer you provide.

23.8 Giving your type a format method

Any struct, union or enum can declare a public format method, and the {f} specifier calls it. The 0.16 signature is small: the value, and a pointer to the writer.

h_custom.zig

const std = @import("std");

const CBills = struct {
    amount: i64,

    /// Called for the {f} specifier. Writes to any writer.
    pub fn format(self: CBills, w: *std.Io.Writer) std.Io.Writer.Error!void {
        if (self.amount < 0) try w.writeByte('-');
        var digits: [24]u8 = undefined;
        const raw = std.fmt.bufPrint(&digits, "{d}", .{@abs(self.amount)}) catch unreachable;
        for (raw, 0..) |ch, i| {
            if (i > 0 and (raw.len - i) % 3 == 0) try w.writeByte(',');
            try w.writeByte(ch);
        }
        try w.writeAll(" C-bills");
    }
};

const Hex = struct { q: i16, r: i16 };

pub fn main() !void {
    const pay: CBills = .{ .amount = 1234567 };
    const debt: CBills = .{ .amount = -950 };
    std.debug.print("{f}\n{f}\n", .{ pay, debt });
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{pay}); // {any} ignores format(): prints the fields

    const h: Hex = .{ .q = 2, .r = -1 };
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{h});

    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    const line = try std.fmt.bufPrint(&buf, "balance: {f}", .{pay});
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{line});
}
1,234,567 C-bills
-950 C-bills
.{ .amount = 1234567 }
.{ .q = 2, .r = -1 }
balance: 1,234,567 C-bills

Inside format you have a full *std.Io.Writer: print, writeAll, writeByte. The error type is fixed as std.Io.Writer.Error, so anything that can fail for other reasons (here, bufPrint into a buffer we know is big enough) is handled locally, with catch unreachable. Once written, the type works everywhere the format engine does: debug.print, allocPrint, bufPrint, file writers.

You must write {f}. In 0.16 the plain {} and {any} do not call format; they print the fields:

h_nof.zig

const std = @import("std");
const CBills = struct { amount: i64,
    pub fn format(self: CBills, w: *std.Io.Writer) std.Io.Writer.Error!void { try w.print("{d} C-bills", .{self.amount}); } };
pub fn main() void { std.debug.print("{}\n", .{CBills{ .amount = 5 }}); }
.{ .amount = 5 }
Older code relied on {} calling format with a four-argument signature (fmt, options, writer). That signature is gone. If you port such code, change the method to format(self, w: *std.Io.Writer) std.Io.Writer.Error!void and the call sites to {f}.
In IRON LEDGER. Every screen is a format string. The People query in game/src/sim/queries.zig lays out a row with widths alone: 
"{d: <4} {s: <20} {s: <15} {s: <7} {s: <5} {d: >3} {s} {s} {s: <11} {d: >3} {d: >3} {s: >7}"
The colour markup that the terminal renders, {g}active{/}, has to be written {{g}}active{{/}} inside format strings, which is where most brace confusion in the code base comes from. The money function is Exercise 23.5 almost verbatim: bufPrint the magnitude with {d}, then walk the digits inserting commas. And the console parser in game/src/sim/cli.zig wraps parseInt in a tiny generic helper that turns both of its errors into the command layer's own error.BadNumber: 
pub fn num(comptime T: type, tok: ?[]const u8) ParseError!T {
    return std.fmt.parseInt(T, tok orelse return error.BadArguments, 10) catch return error.BadNumber;
}
The terminal's status line uses bufPrint into a fixed buffer and falls back to the whole buffer on NoSpaceLeft rather than failing a frame (tui/app.zig, say).

Exercises

Exercise 23.1 · Table row and clock warm-up

Write formatRow(buf, name, tons, bv) producing name left in 10, tons right in 5, bv right in 6 with single spaces between, and formatClock(buf, h, m) producing 07:05. Both use bufPrint. Name the file: exercises/23-formatting/ex1_table.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 23, exercise 1: fixed-width table rows.
//! Run with:  zig test ex1_table.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// name left-aligned in 10, tons right-aligned in 5, bv right-aligned in 6, single spaces between.
fn formatRow(buf: []u8, name: []const u8, tons: u32, bv: u32) ![]u8 {
    return std.fmt.bufPrint(buf, "{s: <10} {d: >5} {d: >6}", .{ name, tons, bv });
}

/// "07:05" style, zero padded.
fn formatClock(buf: []u8, hours: u8, minutes: u8) ![]u8 {
    return std.fmt.bufPrint(buf, "{d:0>2}:{d:0>2}", .{ hours, minutes });
}

test "row" {
    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Atlas        100   1897", try formatRow(&buf, "Atlas", 100, 1897));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Locust        20    432", try formatRow(&buf, "Locust", 20, 432));
}

test "clock" {
    var buf: [8]u8 = undefined;
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("07:05", try formatClock(&buf, 7, 5));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("23:59", try formatClock(&buf, 23, 59));
}

test "a buffer that is too small is an error, not a truncation" {
    var tiny: [4]u8 = undefined;
    try std.testing.expectError(error.NoSpaceLeft, formatClock(&tiny, 7, 5));
}

Unsigned arguments, so no stray plus signs. The third test shows that bufPrint refuses rather than truncates.

Exercise 23.2 · Coordinates practice

Parse "3,-2" (spaces allowed around the numbers) into a Hex{ q, r } of i16, with your own error set { MissingComma, BadNumber }. Name the file: exercises/23-formatting/ex2_coords.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 23, exercise 2: parse "q,r" hex coordinates.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_coords.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Hex = struct { q: i16, r: i16 };
const ParseError = error{ MissingComma, BadNumber };

/// "3,-2" -> Hex{ .q = 3, .r = -2 }. Spaces around the numbers are allowed.
fn parseHex(text: []const u8) ParseError!Hex {
    const comma = std.mem.indexOfScalar(u8, text, ',') orelse return error.MissingComma;
    const q_text = std.mem.trim(u8, text[0..comma], " ");
    const r_text = std.mem.trim(u8, text[comma + 1 ..], " ");
    const q = std.fmt.parseInt(i16, q_text, 10) catch return error.BadNumber;
    const r = std.fmt.parseInt(i16, r_text, 10) catch return error.BadNumber;
    return .{ .q = q, .r = r };
}

test "good input" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Hex{ .q = 3, .r = -2 }, try parseHex("3,-2"));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Hex{ .q = 0, .r = 7 }, try parseHex(" 0 , 7 "));
}

test "bad input" {
    try std.testing.expectError(error.MissingComma, parseHex("3 -2"));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.BadNumber, parseHex("3,x"));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.BadNumber, parseHex(",2"));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.BadNumber, parseHex("40000,0")); // overflow of i16
}

indexOfScalar finds the comma, trim removes spaces, and catch return error.BadNumber folds both parse errors into one domain error, the way the game's num helper does.

Exercise 23.3 · Hex colours practice

Write parseColor("#ff8800") using parseUnsigned with base 16 on two-character slices, and formatColor that prints #0a0b0c with zero-padded hex. Name the file: exercises/23-formatting/ex3_color.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 23, exercise 3: parse and print hex colours.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_color.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Rgb = struct { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 };

/// "#ff8800" or "ff8800" -> Rgb. Case-insensitive.
fn parseColor(text: []const u8) !Rgb {
    const hex = if (text.len > 0 and text[0] == '#') text[1..] else text;
    if (hex.len != 6) return error.WrongLength;
    return .{
        .r = try std.fmt.parseUnsigned(u8, hex[0..2], 16),
        .g = try std.fmt.parseUnsigned(u8, hex[2..4], 16),
        .b = try std.fmt.parseUnsigned(u8, hex[4..6], 16),
    };
}

/// Rgb -> "#ff8800", lower case, always six digits.
fn formatColor(buf: []u8, c: Rgb) ![]u8 {
    return std.fmt.bufPrint(buf, "#{x:0>2}{x:0>2}{x:0>2}", .{ c.r, c.g, c.b });
}

test "parse" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Rgb{ .r = 255, .g = 136, .b = 0 }, try parseColor("#ff8800"));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Rgb{ .r = 255, .g = 136, .b = 0 }, try parseColor("FF8800"));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.WrongLength, parseColor("#fff"));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.InvalidCharacter, parseColor("#gg0000"));
}

test "format round trip" {
    var buf: [8]u8 = undefined;
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("#0a0b0c", try formatColor(&buf, .{ .r = 10, .g = 11, .b = 12 }));
    const c = try parseColor("#12abEF");
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("#12abef", try formatColor(&buf, c));
}

{x:0>2} is fill 0, right-aligned, width 2. The parse error set is inferred (!Rgb) and includes both your WrongLength and parseUnsigned's errors.

Exercise 23.4 · Duration challenge

Give a Duration { seconds: u64 } a format method that renders 2d 3h 4m 5s, dropping leading zero units (2m 5s, 45s, and 0s for zero, but 1h 0m 0s for exactly an hour). Test it through bufPrint and allocPrint with {f}. Name the file: exercises/23-formatting/ex4_duration.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 23, exercise 4: a custom format method.
//! Run with:  zig test ex4_duration.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Duration = struct {
    seconds: u64,

    /// "2d 3h 4m 5s", omitting any leading zero units; "0s" for zero.
    pub fn format(self: Duration, w: *std.Io.Writer) std.Io.Writer.Error!void {
        var rest = self.seconds;
        const days = rest / 86_400;
        rest %= 86_400;
        const hours = rest / 3_600;
        rest %= 3_600;
        const mins = rest / 60;
        rest %= 60;
        var started = false;
        if (days > 0) {
            try w.print("{d}d", .{days});
            started = true;
        }
        if (started or hours > 0) {
            if (started) try w.writeByte(' ');
            try w.print("{d}h", .{hours});
            started = true;
        }
        if (started or mins > 0) {
            if (started) try w.writeByte(' ');
            try w.print("{d}m", .{mins});
            started = true;
        }
        if (started) try w.writeByte(' ');
        try w.print("{d}s", .{rest});
    }
};

fn render(buf: []u8, d: Duration) ![]u8 {
    return std.fmt.bufPrint(buf, "{f}", .{d});
}

test "format" {
    var buf: [32]u8 = undefined;
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("0s", try render(&buf, .{ .seconds = 0 }));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("45s", try render(&buf, .{ .seconds = 45 }));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("2m 5s", try render(&buf, .{ .seconds = 125 }));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("1h 0m 0s", try render(&buf, .{ .seconds = 3600 }));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("2d 3h 4m 5s", try render(&buf, .{ .seconds = 2 * 86400 + 3 * 3600 + 4 * 60 + 5 }));
}

test "works with allocPrint too" {
    const s = try std.fmt.allocPrint(std.testing.allocator, "eta {f}", .{Duration{ .seconds = 90 }});
    defer std.testing.allocator.free(s);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("eta 1m 30s", s);
}

The started flag does the "once a bigger unit has printed, print all the smaller ones" logic. The method takes self by value because the struct is tiny and it does not mutate.

Exercise 23.5 · Money challenge

Write money(gpa, v: i64) ![]u8 that prints thousands separators and a leading minus (-1,234,567), and parseMoney(text) !i64 that accepts the same form (commas optional). The tests round-trip. Name the file: exercises/23-formatting/ex5_money.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 23, exercise 5: money with thousands separators, like IRON LEDGER's.
//! Run with:  zig test ex5_money.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// -1234567 -> "-1,234,567". The caller owns the result.
fn money(gpa: std.mem.Allocator, v: i64) ![]u8 {
    var digits: [24]u8 = undefined;
    const raw = try std.fmt.bufPrint(&digits, "{d}", .{@abs(v)});
    var out: std.ArrayList(u8) = .empty;
    errdefer out.deinit(gpa);
    if (v < 0) try out.append(gpa, '-');
    for (raw, 0..) |c, i| {
        if (i > 0 and (raw.len - i) % 3 == 0) try out.append(gpa, ',');
        try out.append(gpa, c);
    }
    return out.toOwnedSlice(gpa);
}

/// "1,234,567" or "-1,234,567" -> i64. Commas are optional; anything else is an error.
fn parseMoney(text: []const u8) !i64 {
    var clean: [32]u8 = undefined;
    var n: usize = 0;
    for (text) |c| {
        if (c == ',') continue;
        if (n == clean.len) return error.Overflow;
        clean[n] = c;
        n += 1;
    }
    return std.fmt.parseInt(i64, clean[0..n], 10);
}

fn check(expected: []const u8, v: i64) !void {
    const s = try money(std.testing.allocator, v);
    defer std.testing.allocator.free(s);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings(expected, s);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(v, try parseMoney(s));
}

test "money" {
    try check("0", 0);
    try check("999", 999);
    try check("1,000", 1000);
    try check("1,234,567", 1234567);
    try check("-950", -950);
    try check("-1,234,567", -1234567);
}

test "parse rejects junk" {
    try std.testing.expectError(error.InvalidCharacter, parseMoney("1,2x3"));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 5000), try parseMoney("5000"));
}

The comma goes before digit i whenever the number of digits remaining, raw.len - i, is a multiple of three. @abs on an i64 gives a u64, which sidesteps the "minus the most negative value" overflow. This is the game's money function.

Check your understanding

  1. What does {d:0>6} mean, character by character?
    AnswerSpecifier d; fill character 0; alignment > (right); width 6. The value 20 prints as 000020.
  2. How do you print a literal {?
    AnswerDouble it: {{. Likewise }} for }.
  3. Why does bufPrint return an error union?
    AnswerThe buffer may be too small; it returns error.NoSpaceLeft rather than truncating.
  4. What is the difference between parseInt(u8, "-1", 10) and parseUnsigned(u8, "-1", 10)?
    AnswerBoth fail, but for different reasons: parseInt reads the minus sign and then finds -1 does not fit u8 (Overflow); parseUnsigned does not accept a sign at all (InvalidCharacter).
  5. What are the two errors parseInt can return?
    Answererror.Overflow (does not fit the type) and error.InvalidCharacter (anything else: junk, empty string, spaces, bad sign).
  6. You gave a struct a format method but {} still prints the fields. Why?
    AnswerIn 0.16 only {f} calls a format method. {} and {any} use the built-in rendering.
  7. Why does {d: >5} print +42 for an i32 but 42 for a u32?
    AnswerThe integer printer adds an explicit sign to signed values whenever a width is given. Unsigned values have no sign to show. Cast, or format then align the string.
  8. What replaced std.fmt.fmtSliceHexLower?
    AnswerThe {x} specifier on a byte slice (and {X} for upper case), or std.fmt.bytesToHex for an array result.
What you learned.
  • A placeholder is {[arg]spec:[fill][align][width][.prec]}; format strings are checked at compile time.
  • Specifiers: d x X b o c u s e any * f t, with ? and ! prefixes for optionals and error unions.
  • Width and alignment build tables; signed integers with a width print a +.
  • {{ escapes a brace; {0} and {[name]} select arguments.
  • Targets: allocPrint (heap), bufPrint/bufPrintZ (buffer, errors rather than truncates), Writer.fixed, comptimePrint.
  • parseInt(T, text, base), parseUnsigned, parseFloat: whole-string, specific errors, base 0 reads prefixes.
  • A pub fn format(self, w: *std.Io.Writer) std.Io.Writer.Error!void method is invoked by {f}.

24. A tour of std.mem, std.sort and friends

In this chapter you will take a guided walk through the parts of the standard library you will reach for every day: searching and slicing with std.mem, chopping text with tokenizers and splitters, sorting and binary search with custom orderings, integer and float helpers in std.math, ASCII and Unicode utilities, the debugging aids in std.debug, reflection helpers in std.meta, and the small containers EnumArray, EnumMap and bit sets. Every function shown here was compiled with Zig 0.16; a few old favourites that no longer exist are called out with their replacements.

24.1 How to read the standard library

Zig ships its standard library as source, and it is the documentation. When you wonder whether std.mem.something exists, open lib/zig/std/mem.zig from your Zig install (zig env prints the lib_dir) and search for pub fn something. The naming is regular: functions that take an element type start with comptime T: type; functions that operate on one value end in Scalar; functions that search for any of several values end in Any; functions that search for a sequence end in Sequence. Once you know the pattern, you can guess most names correctly.

24.2 std.mem: searching and trimming

a_mem_search.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const line = "contract: garrison duty, 90 days, 2,400,000 c-bills";

    std.debug.print("eql:            {}\n", .{std.mem.eql(u8, "atlas", "atlas")});
    std.debug.print("indexOf:        {?d}\n", .{std.mem.indexOf(u8, line, "days")});
    std.debug.print("indexOf (none): {?d}\n", .{std.mem.indexOf(u8, line, "mechs")});
    std.debug.print("indexOfScalar:  {?d}\n", .{std.mem.indexOfScalar(u8, line, ':')});
    std.debug.print("lastIndexOf:    {?d}\n", .{std.mem.lastIndexOf(u8, line, ",")});
    std.debug.print("indexOfAny:     {?d}\n", .{std.mem.indexOfAny(u8, line, "0123456789")});
    std.debug.print("startsWith:     {}\n", .{std.mem.startsWith(u8, line, "contract")});
    std.debug.print("endsWith:       {}\n", .{std.mem.endsWith(u8, line, "bills")});
    std.debug.print("count:          {d}\n", .{std.mem.count(u8, line, ",")});
    std.debug.print("trim:           [{s}]\n", .{std.mem.trim(u8, "  padded  ", " ")});
    std.debug.print("trimStart:      [{s}]\n", .{std.mem.trimStart(u8, "xxhixx", "x")});
    std.debug.print("trimEnd:        [{s}]\n", .{std.mem.trimEnd(u8, "xxhixx", "x")});

    if (std.mem.indexOf(u8, line, ", ")) |i| {
        std.debug.print("before: [{s}]  after: [{s}]\n", .{ line[0..i], line[i + 2 ..] });
    }
}
eql:            true
indexOf:        28
indexOf (none): null
indexOfScalar:  8
lastIndexOf:    39
indexOfAny:     25
startsWith:     true
endsWith:       true
count:          4
trim:           [padded]
trimStart:      [hixx]
trimEnd:        [xxhi]
before: [contract: garrison duty]  after: [90 days, 2,400,000 c-bills]

All of these take the element type first, which is why you keep writing u8: they work on slices of anything, and text is just the common case. The searchers return ?usize, an optional index, so you unwrap with if or orelse. trim and its one-sided siblings take a set of characters to strip, not a single one; " \t\r\n" is the usual argument for whitespace. The last lines show the everyday idiom: find a separator, then slice around it.

24.3 Tokenize and split

The two families look similar and differ in exactly one way, which the transcript makes obvious.

b_split.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    // tokenize: runs of delimiters collapse, empty pieces never appear.
    var t = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, "  hire   pilot  Kell ", ' ');
    std.debug.print("tokenizeScalar: ", .{});
    while (t.next()) |tok| std.debug.print("[{s}] ", .{tok});

    // split: every delimiter produces a piece, even empty ones.
    var s = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, "a,,b,", ',');
    std.debug.print("\nsplitScalar:    ", .{});
    while (s.next()) |piece| std.debug.print("[{s}] ", .{piece});

    // tokenizeAny: any of several delimiter characters.
    var ta = std.mem.tokenizeAny(u8, "one, two;three\tfour", ", ;\t");
    std.debug.print("\ntokenizeAny:    ", .{});
    while (ta.next()) |tok| std.debug.print("[{s}] ", .{tok});

    // splitSequence: a multi-character delimiter.
    var ss = std.mem.splitSequence(u8, "alpha--beta--gamma", "--");
    std.debug.print("\nsplitSequence:  ", .{});
    while (ss.next()) |piece| std.debug.print("[{s}] ", .{piece});

    // Iterators are structs; you can peek and rest.
    var cmd = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, "transfer outfit hq 5000", ' ');
    const verb = cmd.next().?;
    std.debug.print("\nverb={s} rest=[{s}]\n", .{ verb, cmd.rest() });
}
tokenizeScalar: [hire] [pilot] [Kell] 
splitScalar:    [a] [] [b] [] 
tokenizeAny:    [one] [two] [three] [four] 
splitSequence:  [alpha] [beta] [gamma] 
verb=transfer rest=[outfit hq 5000]

Tokenize skips empty pieces: runs of delimiters collapse and leading or trailing ones vanish. That is what you want for words on a command line. Split is exact: every delimiter separates two pieces, and "a,,b," has four of them, two empty. That is what you want for CSV, where an empty field means something. Both come in Scalar (one delimiter byte), Any (any of a set) and Sequence (a multi-byte delimiter) forms.

They are iterators: structs with a next() that returns ?[]const u8, so the standard while (it.next()) |tok| loop drives them. The pieces are slices into the original string, so nothing is copied and nothing needs freeing. rest() gives you everything not yet consumed, which the game uses to pass "the rest of the line" to a sub-parser.

24.4 std.mem: changing things in place

c_mem_mutate.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var arr = [_]i32{ 5, 3, 9, 1, 7 };

    std.mem.reverse(i32, &arr);
    std.debug.print("reverse:  {any}\n", .{arr});
    std.debug.print("min/max:  {d} {d}\n", .{ std.mem.min(i32, &arr), std.mem.max(i32, &arr) });
    std.debug.print("indexOfMax: {d}\n", .{std.mem.indexOfMax(i32, &arr)});

    std.mem.sort(i32, &arr, {}, std.sort.asc(i32));
    std.debug.print("sorted:   {any}\n", .{arr});

    var out: [32]u8 = undefined;
    const needed = std.mem.replacementSize(u8, "a-b-c-d", "-", " + ");
    const n = std.mem.replace(u8, "a-b-c-d", "-", " + ", &out);
    std.debug.print("replace:  {d} replacements, [{s}] ({d} bytes)\n", .{ n, out[0..needed], needed });

    var word = "hello".*; // copy the literal into a mutable array
    std.mem.replaceScalar(u8, &word, 'l', 'L');
    std.debug.print("replaceScalar: {s}\n", .{&word});

    const zeroed = std.mem.zeroes([4]u8);
    std.debug.print("zeroes:   {any}\n", .{zeroed});
}
reverse:  { 7, 1, 9, 3, 5 }
min/max:  1 9
indexOfMax: 2
sorted:   { 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 }
replace:  3 replacements, [a + b + c + d] (13 bytes)
replaceScalar: heLLo
zeroes:   { 0, 0, 0, 0 }

replace writes into an output buffer you provide and returns the number of replacements; replacementSize tells you how big that buffer must be. The line var word = "hello".*; is worth a pause: a string literal is a pointer to constant memory, and .* dereferences it into a fresh, mutable array on the stack that replaceScalar may then edit. std.mem.zeroes(T) gives you an all-zero value of any type, handy for clearing structs.

24.5 std.mem: bytes and integers

When you write a file format or talk to a network, you need to turn integers into bytes and back, in a byte order you choose rather than whatever the CPU prefers.

d_bytes.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const v: u32 = 0x01020304;

    // The same four bytes, viewed as a byte array (native order; little-endian here).
    const bytes = std.mem.asBytes(&v);
    std.debug.print("asBytes:  {any}\n", .{bytes});
    std.debug.print("toBytes:  {any}\n", .{std.mem.toBytes(v)});

    // Explicit byte order for file formats and network protocols.
    var buf: [4]u8 = undefined;
    std.mem.writeInt(u32, &buf, 258, .big);
    std.debug.print("writeInt big:    {any}\n", .{buf});
    std.mem.writeInt(u32, &buf, 258, .little);
    std.debug.print("writeInt little: {any}\n", .{buf});
    std.debug.print("readInt little:  {d}\n", .{std.mem.readInt(u32, &buf, .little)});
    std.debug.print("readInt big:     {d}\n", .{std.mem.readInt(u32, &buf, .big)});

    // Reinterpret a byte slice as a slice of u16.
    const words = std.mem.bytesAsSlice(u16, &buf);
    std.debug.print("bytesAsSlice u16: {any}\n", .{words});
}
asBytes:  { 4, 3, 2, 1 }
toBytes:  { 4, 3, 2, 1 }
writeInt big:    { 0, 0, 1, 2 }
writeInt little: { 2, 1, 0, 0 }
readInt little:  258
readInt big:     33619968
bytesAsSlice u16: { 258, 0 }

This machine is little-endian, so asBytes shows the low byte first. writeInt and readInt take an explicit .big or .little and a pointer to an array of exactly the right size (*[4]u8 for a u32), so a size mismatch is a compile error. bytesAsSlice reinterprets a byte slice as a slice of a wider type without copying; use it only for data that was produced on the same kind of machine.

24.6 std.sort: ordering and searching

e_sort.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Unit = struct { name: []const u8, tons: u32, bv: u32 };

fn byTons(_: void, a: Unit, b: Unit) bool {
    return a.tons < b.tons;
}

fn byBvDesc(_: void, a: Unit, b: Unit) bool {
    if (a.bv != b.bv) return a.bv > b.bv;
    return std.mem.lessThan(u8, a.name, b.name); // tie-break by name
}

fn cmpTons(key: u32, item: Unit) std.math.Order {
    return std.math.order(key, item.tons);
}

pub fn main() void {
    var units = [_]Unit{
        .{ .name = "Marauder", .tons = 75, .bv = 1363 },
        .{ .name = "Atlas", .tons = 100, .bv = 1897 },
        .{ .name = "Locust", .tons = 20, .bv = 432 },
        .{ .name = "Warhammer", .tons = 70, .bv = 1363 },
    };

    std.mem.sort(Unit, &units, {}, byTons);
    std.debug.print("by tons:   ", .{});
    for (units) |u| std.debug.print("{s} ", .{u.name});

    std.debug.print("\nbinarySearch tons=70: {?d}\n", .{std.sort.binarySearch(Unit, &units, @as(u32, 70), cmpTons)});
    std.debug.print("binarySearch tons=71: {?d}\n", .{std.sort.binarySearch(Unit, &units, @as(u32, 71), cmpTons)});
    std.debug.print("lowerBound tons=71:   {d}\n", .{std.sort.lowerBound(Unit, &units, @as(u32, 71), cmpTons)});

    std.mem.sort(Unit, &units, {}, byBvDesc);
    std.debug.print("by bv desc: ", .{});
    for (units) |u| std.debug.print("{s} ", .{u.name});
    std.debug.print("\nisSorted: {}\n", .{std.sort.isSorted(Unit, &units, {}, byBvDesc)});

    var small = [_]u8{ 3, 1, 2 };
    std.sort.insertion(u8, &small, {}, std.sort.desc(u8));
    std.debug.print("insertion desc: {any}\n", .{small});
}
by tons:   Locust Warhammer Marauder Atlas 
binarySearch tons=70: 1
binarySearch tons=71: null
lowerBound tons=71:   2
by bv desc: Atlas Marauder Warhammer Locust 
isSorted: true
insertion desc: { 3, 2, 1 }

std.mem.sort(T, slice, context, lessThan) is a stable sort. lessThan is a plain function fn (context, a: T, b: T) bool; the context is usually {} (void) and only matters when the comparison needs extra data. For the simple cases std.sort.asc(T) and std.sort.desc(T) generate that function for you. Tie-breaking is your job: byBvDesc falls back to name order so the result is fully determined, which matters whenever output must be reproducible.

binarySearch(T, sorted, key, compare) has a shape that changed in 0.16: the key is the context, and compare is fn (key, item) std.math.Order returning .lt, .eq or .gt. It returns ?usize. lowerBound returns the insertion point for a missing key. isSorted is a cheap assertion for tests. std.sort.insertion is the simple algorithm, best for tiny slices; std.mem.sort picks a good general one.

24.7 std.math

f_math.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("maxInt(u8)={d} minInt(i8)={d} maxInt(i64)={d}\n", .{ std.math.maxInt(u8), std.math.minInt(i8), std.math.maxInt(i64) });
    std.debug.print("clamp: {d} {d} {d}\n", .{ std.math.clamp(@as(i32, -5), 0, 10), std.math.clamp(@as(i32, 5), 0, 10), std.math.clamp(@as(i32, 50), 0, 10) });
    std.debug.print("divCeil: {!d}  divFloor: {!d}  divTrunc: {!d}\n", .{ std.math.divCeil(i32, 7, 2), std.math.divFloor(i32, -7, 2), std.math.divTrunc(i32, -7, 2) });
    std.debug.print("divCeil by zero: {!d}\n", .{std.math.divCeil(i32, 7, 0)});
    std.debug.print("pow: {d}  powi: {!d}  sqrt: {d}  sqrt int: {d}\n", .{ std.math.pow(f64, 2, 10), std.math.powi(i32, 3, 4), std.math.sqrt(@as(f64, 2)), std.math.sqrt(@as(u32, 17)) });
    std.debug.print("log2: {d}  log2_int: {d}  log10_int: {d}\n", .{ std.math.log2(@as(f64, 1024)), std.math.log2_int(u32, 1024), std.math.log10_int(@as(u32, 12345)) });
    std.debug.print("@abs: {d} ({s})\n", .{ @abs(@as(i32, -5)), @typeName(@TypeOf(@abs(@as(i32, -5)))) });
    std.debug.print("cast: {?d} {?d}\n", .{ std.math.cast(u8, @as(i32, 300)), std.math.cast(u8, @as(i32, 30)) });
    std.debug.print("add overflow: {!d}  mul ok: {!d}\n", .{ std.math.add(u8, 200, 100), std.math.mul(u8, 20, 10) });
    std.debug.print("isPowerOfTwo: {} {}  ceilPowerOfTwo: {!d}\n", .{ std.math.isPowerOfTwo(@as(u32, 64)), std.math.isPowerOfTwo(@as(u32, 65)), std.math.ceilPowerOfTwo(u32, 65) });
    std.debug.print("floor/ceil/round: {d} {d} {d}\n", .{ std.math.floor(@as(f64, 2.7)), std.math.ceil(@as(f64, 2.2)), std.math.round(@as(f64, 2.5)) });
    std.debug.print("pi: {d:.5}  order: {}\n", .{ std.math.pi, std.math.order(3, 7) });
}
maxInt(u8)=255 minInt(i8)=-128 maxInt(i64)=9223372036854775807
clamp: 0 5 10
divCeil: 4  divFloor: -4  divTrunc: -3
divCeil by zero: error.DivisionByZero
pow: 1024  powi: 81  sqrt: 1.4142135623730951  sqrt int: 4
log2: 10  log2_int: 10  log10_int: 4
@abs: 5 (u32)
cast: null 30
add overflow: error.Overflow  mul ok: 200
isPowerOfTwo: true false  ceilPowerOfTwo: 128
floor/ceil/round: 2 3 3
pi: 3.14159  order: .lt

Notes on the ones that trip people up. maxInt and minInt return comptime_int, so they fit anywhere a literal would. The three divisions differ on negative numbers: divTrunc rounds toward zero, divFloor toward negative infinity, divCeil toward positive infinity; all three return an error on division by zero rather than crashing. sqrt works on integers as well as floats. std.math.cast is the safe narrowing cast: null instead of a panic when the value does not fit. std.math.add and mul are checked arithmetic returning error.Overflow, the error-union cousins of the wrapping and saturating operators from Chapter 4.

Two removals. std.math.absCast is gone: the builtin @abs returns the unsigned type directly (@abs(i32) is a u32), which is what absCast used to do. And the trigonometric and exponential functions are still there (sin, cos, exp, log), but the more common float operations, @sqrt, @floor, @round, @exp, also exist as builtins, which is what the std.math versions call.

24.8 std.ascii and a glance at std.unicode

g_ascii.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("isDigit('7')={} isAlphabetic('x')={} isWhitespace('\\t')={} isUpper('Q')={}\n", .{
        std.ascii.isDigit('7'), std.ascii.isAlphabetic('x'), std.ascii.isWhitespace('\t'), std.ascii.isUpper('Q'),
    });
    std.debug.print("toUpper('a')={c} toLower('Q')={c}\n", .{ std.ascii.toUpper('a'), std.ascii.toLower('Q') });
    var buf: [16]u8 = undefined;
    std.debug.print("upperString: {s}\n", .{std.ascii.upperString(&buf, "shout")});
    std.debug.print("eqlIgnoreCase: {}  startsWithIgnoreCase: {}\n", .{
        std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase("Atlas", "ATLAS"), std.ascii.startsWithIgnoreCase("Atlas AS7-D", "atlas"),
    });
    std.debug.print("indexOfIgnoreCase: {?d}\n", .{std.ascii.indexOfIgnoreCase("Hello World", "world")});

    // Unicode: bytes are not characters.
    const s = "héllo ⚔";
    std.debug.print("bytes={d} codepoints={!d} valid={}\n", .{ s.len, std.unicode.utf8CountCodepoints(s), std.unicode.utf8ValidateSlice(s) });
    var it = (std.unicode.Utf8View.init(s) catch unreachable).iterator();
    while (it.nextCodepoint()) |cp| std.debug.print("U+{X:0>4} ", .{cp});
    std.debug.print("\n", .{});
}
isDigit('7')=true isAlphabetic('x')=true isWhitespace('\t')=true isUpper('Q')=true
toUpper('a')=A toLower('Q')=q
upperString: SHOUT
eqlIgnoreCase: true  startsWithIgnoreCase: true
indexOfIgnoreCase: 6
bytes=10 codepoints=7 valid=true
U+0068 U+00E9 U+006C U+006C U+006F U+0020 U+2694

std.ascii is byte-at-a-time and only knows the 128 ASCII characters; toUpper('é') would do nothing. The case-insensitive comparisons are what you want for user commands and file extensions. The moment you need to count characters or reverse a string, remember that len counts bytes: "héllo ⚔" is 10 bytes and 7 code points. std.unicode.Utf8View walks the code points; the game uses it to pad table columns by visible width rather than by bytes.

24.9 std.debug and std.meta

h_debug_meta.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Role = enum { pilot, tech, medic };
const Event = union(enum) { hired: []const u8, paid: u32 };
const Pos = struct { x: i32, y: i32 };

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.assert(2 + 2 == 4); // no-op when true; panics with a trace when false in Debug

    std.debug.print("stringToEnum: {?} {?}\n", .{ std.meta.stringToEnum(Role, "tech"), std.meta.stringToEnum(Role, "cook") });
    std.debug.print("activeTag:    {}\n", .{std.meta.activeTag(Event{ .paid = 5 })});
    std.debug.print("Tag type:     {s}\n", .{@typeName(std.meta.Tag(Event))});
    std.debug.print("meta.eql:     {} {}\n", .{
        std.meta.eql(Pos{ .x = 1, .y = 2 }, Pos{ .x = 1, .y = 2 }),
        std.meta.eql(Pos{ .x = 1, .y = 2 }, Pos{ .x = 1, .y = 3 }),
    });
    std.debug.print("fieldNames:   ", .{});
    for (std.meta.fieldNames(Role)) |n| std.debug.print("{s} ", .{n});
    std.debug.print("\ntags:         {any}\n", .{std.meta.tags(Role)});
}
stringToEnum: .tech null
activeTag:    .paid
Tag type:     @typeInfo(h_debug_meta.Event).@"union".tag_type.?
meta.eql:     true false
fieldNames:   pilot tech medic 
tags:         { .pilot, .tech, .medic }

std.debug.assert(cond) panics with a stack trace in Debug and ReleaseSafe builds and is removed entirely in ReleaseFast, so never put a side effect inside one. stringToEnum is the inverse of @tagName and returns an optional. activeTag gives the tag of a tagged union and Tag its enum type. meta.eql compares structs field by field (and arrays element by element), which == does not do for structs. And dumpCurrentStackTrace prints where you are, which is the fastest way to answer "who called this?":

k_trace.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn inner(depth: u32) void {
    if (depth == 0) {
        std.debug.print("where am I?\n", .{});
        std.debug.dumpCurrentStackTrace(.{});
        return;
    }
    inner(depth - 1);
}

pub fn main() void {
    inner(2);
}
where am I?
k_trace.zig:6:40: 0x102e19de3 in inner (k_trace)
        std.debug.dumpCurrentStackTrace(.{});
                                       ^
k_trace.zig:9:10: 0x102e19e07 in inner (k_trace)
    inner(depth - 1);
         ^
k_trace.zig:9:10: 0x102e19e07 in inner (k_trace)
    inner(depth - 1);
         ^
k_trace.zig:13:10: 0x102e19c17 in main (k_trace)
    inner(2);

24.10 EnumArray, EnumMap, EnumSet and bit sets

i_enums_bits.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Role = enum { pilot, tech, medic };

pub fn main() void {
    // EnumArray: a value for EVERY enum member, indexed by the enum.
    var pay = std.enums.EnumArray(Role, u32).initFill(0);
    pay.set(.pilot, 1500);
    pay.getPtr(.tech).* += 900;
    std.debug.print("EnumArray: pilot={d} tech={d} medic={d}  all={any}\n", .{ pay.get(.pilot), pay.get(.tech), pay.get(.medic), pay.values });

    // EnumMap: optional value per member (absent until put).
    var lead = std.enums.EnumMap(Role, []const u8).init(.{ .pilot = "Kell" });
    lead.put(.medic, "Sato");
    std.debug.print("EnumMap: pilot={?s} tech={?s} count={d}\n", .{ lead.get(.pilot), lead.get(.tech), lead.count() });

    // EnumSet: a set of members, stored as bits.
    var present = std.enums.EnumSet(Role).initEmpty();
    present.insert(.pilot);
    present.insert(.tech);
    std.debug.print("EnumSet: tech? {} medic? {} count={d}\n", .{ present.contains(.tech), present.contains(.medic), present.count() });

    // Bit sets: N bits, set/unset/toggle/count/iterate.
    var slots = std.bit_set.IntegerBitSet(16).initEmpty();
    slots.set(3);
    slots.set(9);
    slots.toggle(0);
    std.debug.print("bits: isSet(3)={} isSet(4)={} count={d} first={?d} set: ", .{ slots.isSet(3), slots.isSet(4), slots.count(), slots.findFirstSet() });
    var it = slots.iterator(.{});
    while (it.next()) |i| std.debug.print("{d} ", .{i});

    var big = std.bit_set.StaticBitSet(200).initFull();
    big.unset(100);
    std.debug.print("\nStaticBitSet(200): count={d}, type={s}\n", .{ big.count(), @typeName(@TypeOf(big)) });
}
EnumArray: pilot=1500 tech=900 medic=0  all={ 1500, 900, 0 }
EnumMap: pilot=Kell tech=null count=2
EnumSet: tech? true medic? false count=2
bits: isSet(3)=true isSet(4)=false count=3 first=0 set: 0 3 9 
StaticBitSet(200): count=199, type=bit_set.ArrayBitSet(usize,200)

EnumArray(E, V) is an array with one slot per enum member, indexed by the enum rather than by an integer. It cannot be out of bounds and it cannot forget a member; adding a variant to Role automatically adds a slot. Use it for "a value for every kind of thing". EnumMap is the same but each slot may be absent, and EnumSet is a set of members packed into bits. Bit sets proper come in IntegerBitSet(N) (fits in one integer) and ArrayBitSet (larger); StaticBitSet(N) picks for you, as the printed type name shows. They support set, unset, toggle, count, find-first and iteration, plus set algebra (setUnion, setIntersection, complement).

24.11 A fixed-capacity list

Older Zig had std.BoundedArray, a list that lived inside a fixed array and needed no allocator. It is gone in 0.16, and its job is done by ArrayList itself, pointed at a buffer you own:

j_bounded.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    // A list that lives entirely inside a fixed array: no allocator, cannot exceed 4.
    var storage: [4]u32 = undefined;
    var list: std.ArrayList(u32) = .initBuffer(&storage);

    list.appendBounded(10) catch unreachable;
    list.appendBounded(20) catch unreachable;
    list.appendSliceBounded(&.{ 30, 40 }) catch unreachable;
    std.debug.print("{any} len={d} cap={d}\n", .{ list.items, list.items.len, list.capacity });

    const full = list.appendBounded(50);
    std.debug.print("fifth append: {!}\n", .{full});
    std.debug.print("pop: {?d}\n", .{list.pop()});
}
{ 10, 20, 30, 40 } len=4 cap=4
fifth append: error.OutOfMemory
pop: 40

initBuffer(&storage) makes a list whose capacity is the array's length and which can never grow; the Bounded methods return error.OutOfMemory when it is full instead of allocating. Everything that does not allocate (pop, items, orderedRemove, iteration) works as before.

24.12 Gone in 0.16

OldNow
std.BoundedArray(T, n)std.ArrayList(T).initBuffer(&buf) with appendBounded
std.math.absCast(x)@abs(x)
std.mem.tokenize(u8, s, " ")std.mem.tokenizeAny / tokenizeScalar / tokenizeSequence
std.mem.split(u8, s, ",")std.mem.splitScalar / splitAny / splitSequence
std.mem.trimLeft / trimRightstd.mem.trimStart / trimEnd
std.sort.sort(...)std.mem.sort(...)
binarySearch(T, key, items, ctx, cmp)binarySearch(T, items, key, cmp) with cmp: fn (key, item) Order
In IRON LEDGER. A count of the calls in game/src tells you what matters: std.mem.eql appears over two hundred times, std.mem.indexOf and startsWith dozens of times, tokenizeScalar seventeen, std.math.clamp and divCeil sixteen each. The console REPL in game/src/main.zig is 24.3 in one line: var tokens = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, line, ' '); followed by parseInt on each token. Sorting with a tie-break, as in 24.6, is how the hangar screen orders units (game/src/sim/queries.zig): 
std.mem.sort(HangarRow, out.items, {}, struct {
    fn lt(_: void, a: HangarRow, b: HangarRow) bool {
        if (a.cost_index != b.cost_index) return a.cost_index > b.cost_index;
        return a.bill > b.bill;
    }
}.lt);
The comparison is an anonymous struct with one function, declared right where it is used; you will see that idiom often. And std.ascii.endsWithIgnoreCase(e.name, ".png") is how the emblem loader (tui/emblem.zig) filters a directory listing.

Exercises

Exercise 24.1 · Command line warm-up

Write parseCommand(line) that tokenizes on spaces and tabs, matches the first word case-insensitively against an enum of verbs (lower-case it into a small buffer, then stringToEnum), and reports the argument count and the first argument. Name the file: exercises/24-std-tour/ex1_command.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 24, exercise 1: chop a command line into a verb and arguments.
//! Run with:  zig test ex1_command.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Verb = enum { hire, fire, transfer, unknown };
const Command = struct { verb: Verb, arg_count: usize, first_arg: ?[]const u8 };

/// "  hire   pilot Kell " -> verb hire, 2 args, first arg "pilot".
/// The verb is matched case-insensitively.
fn parseCommand(line: []const u8) Command {
    var it = std.mem.tokenizeAny(u8, line, " \t");
    const word = it.next() orelse return .{ .verb = .unknown, .arg_count = 0, .first_arg = null };
    var lower_buf: [16]u8 = undefined;
    const verb: Verb = if (word.len > lower_buf.len)
        .unknown
    else
        std.meta.stringToEnum(Verb, std.ascii.lowerString(&lower_buf, word)) orelse .unknown;
    const first = it.next();
    var count: usize = if (first != null) 1 else 0;
    while (it.next()) |_| count += 1;
    return .{ .verb = verb, .arg_count = count, .first_arg = first };
}

test "hire" {
    const c = parseCommand("  hire   pilot Kell ");
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Verb.hire, c.verb);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 2), c.arg_count);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("pilot", c.first_arg.?);
}

test "case and tabs" {
    const c = parseCommand("TRANSFER\toutfit\thq\t5000");
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Verb.transfer, c.verb);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 3), c.arg_count);
}

test "unknown and empty" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Verb.unknown, parseCommand("dance").verb);
    const e = parseCommand("   ");
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Verb.unknown, e.verb);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 0), e.arg_count);
    try std.testing.expect(e.first_arg == null);
}

lowerString writes into a buffer you own and returns the slice it used, so a word longer than the buffer has to be rejected first. orelse .unknown turns the optional from stringToEnum into a definite verb.

Exercise 24.2 · CSV of integers practice

Write parseCsvInts(out, line) using splitScalar (not tokenize: an empty field must be an error), trim and parseInt, filling a caller-provided slice, and stats returning sum, min and max using std.mem.minMax. Name the file: exercises/24-std-tour/ex2_csv.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 24, exercise 2: a CSV line of numbers.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_csv.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Parse "12, 7,3" into `out`, trimming spaces around each field.
/// Returns the slice of `out` that was filled. Empty fields are an error.
fn parseCsvInts(out: []i32, line: []const u8) ![]i32 {
    var n: usize = 0;
    var it = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, line, ',');
    while (it.next()) |raw| {
        const field = std.mem.trim(u8, raw, " \t");
        if (field.len == 0) return error.EmptyField;
        if (n == out.len) return error.TooManyFields;
        out[n] = try std.fmt.parseInt(i32, field, 10);
        n += 1;
    }
    return out[0..n];
}

/// Sum, min and max of a slice in one pass, or null if empty.
fn stats(xs: []const i32) ?struct { sum: i64, min: i32, max: i32 } {
    if (xs.len == 0) return null;
    var sum: i64 = 0;
    for (xs) |x| sum += x;
    const mm = std.mem.minMax(i32, xs);
    return .{ .sum = sum, .min = mm[0], .max = mm[1] };
}

test "parse" {
    var buf: [8]i32 = undefined;
    const got = try parseCsvInts(&buf, "12, 7,3 , -1");
    try std.testing.expectEqualSlices(i32, &.{ 12, 7, 3, -1 }, got);
    const s = stats(got).?;
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 21), s.sum);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, -1), s.min);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, 12), s.max);
}

test "errors" {
    var buf: [2]i32 = undefined;
    try std.testing.expectError(error.EmptyField, parseCsvInts(&buf, "1,,2"));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.TooManyFields, parseCsvInts(&buf, "1,2,3"));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.InvalidCharacter, parseCsvInts(&buf, "1,x"));
    try std.testing.expect(stats(&.{}) == null);
}

Because the function fills a slice it was given, it never allocates; the caller decides how many fields are acceptable by the size of out. The inferred error set carries both your errors and parseInt's.

Exercise 24.3 · Sort and search practice

Sort units heaviest first with names as a tie-break, then sort by name and implement findByName with std.sort.binarySearch and a cmpName(key, item) Order function using std.mem.order. Name the file: exercises/24-std-tour/ex3_sort_search.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 24, exercise 3: sort by several keys, then binary search.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_sort_search.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Unit = struct { name: []const u8, tons: u32, bv: u32 };

/// Heaviest first; equal tonnage sorts by name A to Z.
fn byWeightThenName(_: void, a: Unit, b: Unit) bool {
    if (a.tons != b.tons) return a.tons > b.tons;
    return std.mem.lessThan(u8, a.name, b.name);
}

/// Sort by name only (for searching).
fn byName(_: void, a: Unit, b: Unit) bool {
    return std.mem.lessThan(u8, a.name, b.name);
}

fn cmpName(key: []const u8, item: Unit) std.math.Order {
    return std.mem.order(u8, key, item.name);
}

/// Index of the unit called `name` in a name-sorted slice, or null.
fn findByName(units: []const Unit, name: []const u8) ?usize {
    return std.sort.binarySearch(Unit, units, name, cmpName);
}

fn fixture() [5]Unit {
    return .{
        .{ .name = "Marauder", .tons = 75, .bv = 1363 },
        .{ .name = "Atlas", .tons = 100, .bv = 1897 },
        .{ .name = "Locust", .tons = 20, .bv = 432 },
        .{ .name = "Warhammer", .tons = 70, .bv = 1363 },
        .{ .name = "Archer", .tons = 70, .bv = 1300 },
    };
}

test "weight then name" {
    var units = fixture();
    std.mem.sort(Unit, &units, {}, byWeightThenName);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Atlas", units[0].name);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Marauder", units[1].name);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Archer", units[2].name); // 70 tons, A before W
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Warhammer", units[3].name);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Locust", units[4].name);
}

test "binary search by name" {
    var units = fixture();
    std.mem.sort(Unit, &units, {}, byName);
    try std.testing.expect(std.sort.isSorted(Unit, &units, {}, byName));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?usize, 0), findByName(&units, "Archer"));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?usize, 4), findByName(&units, "Warhammer"));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?usize, null), findByName(&units, "Rifleman"));
}

std.mem.order(u8, a, b) is the three-way comparison for slices, the exact shape binarySearch wants. A binary search on a slice that is not sorted by the same key returns nonsense, which is why the test asserts isSorted first.

Exercise 24.4 · Payroll and days off practice

Use an EnumArray(Role, u64) to total salaries per role, an IntegerBitSet(7) to record which weekdays anyone is off, and set algebra to find the first day everyone is present. Name the file: exercises/24-std-tour/ex4_payroll.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 24, exercise 4: EnumArray and a bit set.
//! Run with:  zig test ex4_payroll.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const Role = enum { pilot, tech, medic, admin };
const Person = struct { role: Role, salary: u32, day_off: u3 }; // day 0..6

/// Total salary per role.
fn payroll(people: []const Person) std.enums.EnumArray(Role, u64) {
    var totals = std.enums.EnumArray(Role, u64).initFill(0);
    for (people) |p| totals.getPtr(p.role).* += p.salary;
    return totals;
}

/// Which days of the week (0..6) is at least one person off?
fn daysOff(people: []const Person) std.bit_set.IntegerBitSet(7) {
    var days = std.bit_set.IntegerBitSet(7).initEmpty();
    for (people) |p| days.set(p.day_off);
    return days;
}

/// First day nobody is off, or null if every day has someone away.
fn firstFullStrengthDay(people: []const Person) ?u3 {
    const off = daysOff(people);
    var all = std.bit_set.IntegerBitSet(7).initFull();
    all.setIntersection(off.complement());
    const first = all.findFirstSet() orelse return null;
    return @intCast(first);
}

const crew = [_]Person{
    .{ .role = .pilot, .salary = 1500, .day_off = 0 },
    .{ .role = .pilot, .salary = 1200, .day_off = 1 },
    .{ .role = .tech, .salary = 900, .day_off = 1 },
    .{ .role = .medic, .salary = 1100, .day_off = 5 },
};

test "payroll" {
    const t = payroll(&crew);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u64, 2700), t.get(.pilot));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u64, 900), t.get(.tech));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u64, 0), t.get(.admin));
}

test "days" {
    const off = daysOff(&crew);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 3), off.count());
    try std.testing.expect(off.isSet(5));
    try std.testing.expect(!off.isSet(2));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u3, 2), firstFullStrengthDay(&crew));
    const everyone = [_]Person{
        .{ .role = .tech, .salary = 1, .day_off = 0 }, .{ .role = .tech, .salary = 1, .day_off = 1 },
        .{ .role = .tech, .salary = 1, .day_off = 2 }, .{ .role = .tech, .salary = 1, .day_off = 3 },
        .{ .role = .tech, .salary = 1, .day_off = 4 }, .{ .role = .tech, .salary = 1, .day_off = 5 },
        .{ .role = .tech, .salary = 1, .day_off = 6 },
    };
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u3, null), firstFullStrengthDay(&everyone));
}

complement() flips every bit, setIntersection ands in place, and findFirstSet gives the lowest set bit as ?usize. The u3 for a day index is the compiler enforcing 0 to 7 for you.

Exercise 24.5 · A binary record challenge

Define an 8-byte big-endian wire format (u32 id, u16 armor, u8 flags, one zero pad byte) and write encode and decode with writeInt and readInt. Decoding must reject a non-zero pad byte. Name the file: exercises/24-std-tour/ex5_record.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 24, exercise 5: a fixed binary record with explicit byte order.
//! Run with:  zig test ex5_record.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Wire format, 8 bytes, big-endian: id u32, armor u16, flags u8, pad u8 (zero).
const Record = struct { id: u32, armor: u16, flags: u8 };
const size = 8;

fn encode(r: Record, out: *[size]u8) void {
    std.mem.writeInt(u32, out[0..4], r.id, .big);
    std.mem.writeInt(u16, out[4..6], r.armor, .big);
    out[6] = r.flags;
    out[7] = 0;
}

fn decode(in: *const [size]u8) !Record {
    if (in[7] != 0) return error.BadPadding;
    return .{
        .id = std.mem.readInt(u32, in[0..4], .big),
        .armor = std.mem.readInt(u16, in[4..6], .big),
        .flags = in[6],
    };
}

test "known bytes" {
    var buf: [size]u8 = undefined;
    encode(.{ .id = 258, .armor = 0x0102, .flags = 0xAB }, &buf);
    try std.testing.expectEqualSlices(u8, &.{ 0, 0, 1, 2, 1, 2, 0xAB, 0 }, &buf);
}

test "round trip" {
    var buf: [size]u8 = undefined;
    const r: Record = .{ .id = 0xDEADBEEF, .armor = 65535, .flags = 7 };
    encode(r, &buf);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(r, try decode(&buf));
}

test "bad padding" {
    var buf: [size]u8 = .{ 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 9 };
    try std.testing.expectError(error.BadPadding, decode(&buf));
    buf[7] = 0;
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 1), (try decode(&buf)).id);
}

out[0..4] on a pointer-to-array with comptime bounds is itself a *[4]u8, exactly the type writeInt requires; a wrong slice length is a compile error, not a runtime bug.

Check your understanding

  1. What is the difference between tokenizeScalar and splitScalar on "a,,b"?
    AnswerTokenize yields a, b (empty pieces are skipped). Split yields a, an empty string, b.
  2. Why does every std.mem search function take a type as its first argument?
    AnswerThey are generic over the element type: indexOf(u8, ...) searches bytes, indexOf(u32, ...) searches integers. Text is just the common case.
  3. What does std.mem.sort need from you to sort a slice of structs?
    AnswerA lessThan function fn (context, a: T, b: T) bool (with {} as the context when none is needed), ideally with a tie-break so the order is fully determined.
  4. What is the 0.16 signature of the compare function for std.sort.binarySearch?
    Answerfn (key: K, item: T) std.math.Order; the key is passed as the context argument, and the result is ?usize.
  5. How do divTrunc, divFloor and divCeil differ on -7 / 2?
    Answer-3, -4 and -3 respectively: toward zero, toward negative infinity, toward positive infinity.
  6. What replaced std.math.absCast and std.BoundedArray?
    Answer@abs (which returns the unsigned type) and std.ArrayList(T).initBuffer(&buf) with the appendBounded family.
  7. Why is "héllo".len 6 and not 5?
    Answerlen counts bytes and é is two bytes in UTF-8. Use std.unicode.utf8CountCodepoints for characters.
  8. When would you pick EnumArray over a hash map keyed by the enum?
    AnswerWhenever the key is an exhaustive enum: an EnumArray has a slot for every member, never allocates, cannot miss, and is indexed by the enum directly.
What you learned.
  • The standard library source is the reference; names follow patterns (Scalar, Any, Sequence).
  • std.mem: eql, indexOf*, lastIndexOf, startsWith/endsWith, trim*, count, replace, reverse, min/max, zeroes, asBytes, readInt/writeInt.
  • Tokenize skips empty pieces; split keeps them. Both return slices into the input.
  • std.mem.sort with a lessThan; std.sort.asc/desc; binarySearch(T, items, key, cmp) with an Order compare.
  • std.math: maxInt/minInt, clamp, three divisions, pow/sqrt/log2, safe cast, checked add/mul; @abs replaces absCast.
  • std.ascii is byte-wise; std.unicode counts code points.
  • std.debug.assert, dumpCurrentStackTrace; std.meta.stringToEnum, activeTag, eql.
  • EnumArray, EnumMap, EnumSet, IntegerBitSet/StaticBitSet; ArrayList.initBuffer replaces BoundedArray.

25. comptime

In this chapter you will learn the idea that makes Zig different from every language you have used so far: the compiler can run your code. You will see what "known at compile time" means, the comptime keyword on values, blocks and parameters, the special types comptime_int and comptime_float, types as ordinary values, inline for and inline while, compile-time string concatenation, tables computed while compiling, @compileError, @compileLog, the evaluation quota, and why Zig has no macros and no preprocessor.

25.1 Two worlds

Every value in a Zig program lives in one of two worlds. Either the compiler knows it while it is compiling, or it will only exist when the program runs. The literal 12 is in the first world; a number typed by the user is in the second. Most languages keep these worlds far apart: constants on one side, everything else on the other, and a separate macro or template language for anything in between. Zig instead lets ordinary functions run in either world, and gives you one keyword, comptime, to insist on the first.

a_two_worlds.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn square(x: u32) u32 {
    return x * x;
}

pub fn main() void {
    const a = square(12); // the compiler knows 12, so it can run square now
    const b = comptime square(12); // ...and this insists that it does

    var input: u32 = 12;
    input += 1; // now the compiler cannot know the value
    const c = square(input); // so this runs when the program runs

    std.debug.print("{d} {d} {d}\n", .{ a, b, c });
    std.debug.print("{s} {s} {s}\n", .{ @typeName(@TypeOf(a)), @typeName(@TypeOf(b)), @typeName(@TypeOf(c)) });
}
144 144 169
u32 u32 u32

square is a normal function; nothing about it says "compile time". The first call has a constant argument, so the compiler may evaluate it early (and in practice does). The second call is marked comptime, so the compiler must evaluate it, and it would be an error if it could not. The third call has an argument that depends on a mutated variable, so it necessarily happens at run time. All three produce a u32; the world a value comes from does not change its type, only when it was computed.

The rule that decides the world is simple. A value is comptime-known if it is a literal, a const initialised from comptime-known values, the result of calling a function with comptime-known arguments, or anything marked comptime. A var is never comptime-known once it has been mutated at run time, and anything read from outside the program (arguments, files, the clock) is runtime by nature.

25.2 comptime_int and comptime_float

What type does the literal 12 have before you assign it anywhere? Not i32, not u8; in Zig it is comptime_int, an integer of unlimited size that exists only in the compiler.

b_literal_types.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const n = 1 << 40; // no annotation: comptime_int, any size
    const big = 1 << 100; // far bigger than u64; fine, it is not a machine integer
    const f = 2.5; // comptime_float

    std.debug.print("{s} {s} {s}\n", .{ @typeName(@TypeOf(n)), @typeName(@TypeOf(big)), @typeName(@TypeOf(f)) });
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{big});

    const fits: u8 = 200; // comptime_int coerces when it fits
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{fits});
}
comptime_int comptime_int comptime_float
1267650600228229401496703205376
200

1 << 100 is a perfectly good comptime_int: it never has to fit in a register because it never reaches the CPU. When a comptime value is stored into a typed location, it coerces to that type if it fits, which is why const fits: u8 = 200 works with no cast. If it does not fit, the compiler says so:

b_overflow.zig

const std = @import("std");
pub fn main() void {
    const x: u8 = 200 + 100; // both sides known: checked at compile time
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{x});
}
b_overflow.zig:3:23: error: type 'u8' cannot represent integer value '300'
    const x: u8 = 200 + 100; // both sides known: checked at compile time
                  ~~~~^~~~~

This is the same overflow check you met in Chapter 4, but caught before the program exists. The rule to remember: arithmetic on comptime-known values is checked by the compiler; arithmetic on runtime values is checked by the safety mode. Both refuse to let 300 into a u8; they just complain at different moments.

25.3 comptime blocks, comptime var and the quota

c_comptime_var.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn fib(n: u32) u64 {
    return if (n < 2) n else fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
}

pub fn main() void {
    // A comptime block: everything in it runs in the compiler.
    const fib15 = comptime blk: {
        @setEvalBranchQuota(100_000); // recursion needs more than the default 1000 branches
        break :blk fib(15);
    };

    // comptime var: a variable that exists only during compilation.
    comptime var total = 0;
    inline for (.{ 1, 2, 3, 4 }) |v| total += v;

    std.debug.print("fib(15) = {d}, total = {d}\n", .{ fib15, total });
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{@typeName(@TypeOf(total))});
}
fib(15) = 610, total = 10
comptime_int

A comptime block (or a labelled block with break :blk, as here) runs entirely in the compiler; the result is baked into the binary as a constant, so fib(15) costs nothing at run time. A comptime var is a variable that only the compiler can see and change; the loop that adds to total is unrolled and the final value, 10, is what the program contains. Its type stays comptime_int.

The compiler is not an infinitely patient interpreter. To stop a mistaken infinite loop from hanging your build, each compile-time evaluation gets a budget of one thousand "backward branches" (loop iterations and recursive calls). Exceed it and you get this:

c_quota.zig

fn slow() u32 {
    var s: u32 = 0;
    for (0..5000) |i| s +%= @intCast(i);
    return s;
}
pub fn main() void {
    const v = comptime slow();
    @import("std").debug.print("{d}\n", .{v});
}
c_quota.zig:3:5: error: evaluation exceeded 1000 backwards branches
    for (0..5000) |i| s +%= @intCast(i);
    ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
c_quota.zig:3:5: note: use @setEvalBranchQuota() to raise the branch limit from 1000
c_quota.zig:7:28: note: called at comptime here
    const v = comptime slow();
                       ~~~~^~

The fix is what the note says: call @setEvalBranchQuota(n) inside the scope being evaluated, with a number comfortably above what you need. In c_comptime_var.zig the call sits inside the block, before the recursive fib starts. It is not a global setting; it applies to the evaluation it appears in.

25.4 Types are values

At compile time, a type is just another value. It has a type of its own, type, and you can store it in a constant, pick it with an if, put it in an array, or pass it to a function. This single fact is the whole foundation of generics in Zig, which Chapter 26 builds on.

d_types_are_values.zig

const std = @import("std");
