pub fn main() void {
    const T = u16; // a type stored in a constant
    const x: T = 65535;

    const Wide = if (@sizeOf(usize) == 8) u64 else u32; // chosen by an if, at compile time
    const y: Wide = 1;

    const types = [_]type{ u8, i32, f64, bool }; // an array of types
    inline for (types) |Ty| std.debug.print("{s}: {d} bytes\n", .{ @typeName(Ty), @sizeOf(Ty) });

    std.debug.print("{d} {d} {s}\n", .{ x, y, @typeName(Wide) });
}
u8: 1 bytes
i32: 4 bytes
f64: 8 bytes
bool: 1 bytes
65535 1 u64

The one restriction is that a type value only exists at compile time. You cannot make a runtime if choose between two types, and you cannot use a runtime integer as an array length, because the compiler has to lay out memory before the program runs:

d_runtime_type.zig

pub fn main() void {
    var n: u32 = 3;
    n += 1;
    const a = [n]u8{ 0, 0, 0, 0 }; // an array length must be known at compile time
    _ = a;
}
d_runtime_type.zig:4:16: error: unable to resolve comptime value
    const a = [n]u8{ 0, 0, 0, 0 }; // an array length must be known at compile time
               ^
d_runtime_type.zig:4:16: note: types must be comptime-known

The message "types must be comptime-known" is one you will see often while learning. It always means the same thing: something that shapes memory or code (an array length, a type, a field name) depended on a runtime value. The fix is either to make the value comptime (a constant, a comptime parameter) or to use a runtime structure (a slice, an ArrayList) instead.

25.5 inline for and inline while

A normal for loop is one piece of code that runs many times. An inline for is many pieces of code, one per iteration, generated by the compiler; the loop variable is a compile-time constant inside each copy. That is what lets each copy have a different type.

e_inline.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Difficulty = enum { easy, hard };
const Config = struct { seed: u64, days: u32, difficulty: Difficulty, ironman: bool };

pub fn main() void {
    const cfg: Config = .{ .seed = 42, .days = 30, .difficulty = .hard, .ironman = true };

    // Walk the fields of a struct. The loop body is copied once per field,
    // and in each copy `f.name` and `f.type` are constants.
    inline for (@typeInfo(Config).@"struct".fields) |f| {
        std.debug.print("{s: <5} : {s: <12} = {any}\n", .{ f.name, @typeName(f.type), @field(cfg, f.name) });
    }

    // A tuple of mixed types: only an inline loop can handle each element by its own type.
    const mixed = .{ 1, 2.5, "three", false };
    inline for (mixed, 0..) |v, i| std.debug.print("{d}: {s}\n", .{ i, @typeName(@TypeOf(v)) });

    // inline while, with a comptime counter.
    comptime var i = 0;
    inline while (i < 3) : (i += 1) std.debug.print("unrolled {d}\n", .{i});
}
seed  : u64          = 42
days  : u32          = 30
difficulty : e_inline.Difficulty = .hard
ironman : bool         = true
0: comptime_int
1: comptime_float
2: *const [5:0]u8
3: bool
unrolled 0
unrolled 1
unrolled 2

The first loop is the most useful pattern in this chapter. @typeInfo(Config).@"struct".fields is a compile-time array describing the fields; f.name is a string, f.type is a type, and @field(cfg, f.name) reads the field by name. Because the loop is inline, @field gets a constant name each time and the whole thing compiles to four plain field reads. A runtime for could not do this: there is no such thing as a runtime field name. Chapter 27 is entirely about this kind of reflection.

The second loop walks a tuple whose elements have four different types. Only inline for can do that, because each iteration is compiled separately with its own @TypeOf(v). The third shows inline while with a comptime var counter, which is how you unroll a fixed count of iterations.

Use inline loops when you need to, not for speed. Each iteration is a separate copy of the code, so an inline for over a thousand elements produces a thousand copies of the body. The compiler is also perfectly capable of unrolling ordinary loops when that is faster. Reach for inline when the loop variable has to be comptime: field names, types, tuple elements.

25.6 Building strings in the compiler

++ concatenates arrays and slices, and ** repeats them. Both need the operands' lengths to be known at compile time, because the result is a fixed-size array.

f_concat.zig

const std = @import("std");

const prefix = "IRON";
const name = prefix ++ " " ++ "LEDGER"; // concatenation happens in the compiler
const banner = "=" ** name.len; // repetition too

fn withUnit(comptime label: []const u8) []const u8 {
    return label ++ " (tons)"; // label must be comptime for ++ to work
}

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{s}\n{s}\n", .{ name, banner });
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{withUnit("weight")});
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{@typeName(@TypeOf(name))});
}
IRON LEDGER
===========
weight (tons)
*const [11:0]u8

The result type, *const [11:0]u8, tells the story: a pointer to an eleven-byte, zero-terminated array that the compiler wrote into the binary. Nothing happens at run time. The withUnit function only works because its parameter is comptime; drop that keyword and label ++ " (tons)" fails because the compiler no longer knows how long label is. This is the exact device the tuning checker in IRON LEDGER uses to build dotted field paths.

The precise rule is about lengths, not contents. An array with runtime contents can still be concatenated, because its length is part of its type:

f_concat_array.zig

const std = @import("std");
pub fn main() void {
    var user: [8]u8 = "runtime!".*; // an array: its LENGTH is part of the type
    user[0] = 'R'; // its contents are decided at runtime
    const s = "value: " ++ user; // allowed: 7 + 8 bytes, the compiler knows the size
    std.debug.print("{s} ({s})\n", .{ s, @typeName(@TypeOf(s)) });
}
value: Runtime! (*const [15:0]u8)

A slice with a runtime length cannot:

f_concat_bad.zig

const std = @import("std");
pub fn main() void {
    var len: usize = 3;
    len += 1;
    const user: []const u8 = "runtime"[0..len]; // a slice whose length is a runtime value
    const s = "value: " ++ user;
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{s});
}
f_concat_bad.zig:6:28: error: unable to resolve comptime value
    const s = "value: " ++ user;
                           ^~~~
f_concat_bad.zig:6:28: note: slice being concatenated must be comptime-known

For runtime strings you use the tools of Chapter 21 and Chapter 23: an ArrayList(u8), allocPrint or bufPrint. For compile-time strings you use ++ and std.fmt.comptimePrint.

25.7 Tables computed at compile time

Whenever you find yourself writing a table of magic numbers by hand, ask whether the compiler could write it for you. It can, with an ordinary loop inside a block that initialises a constant.

g_table.zig

const std = @import("std");

/// The 2d6 probability table, in tenths of a percent, computed by the compiler.
const two_d6_permille: [13]u16 = blk: {
    var t: [13]u16 = @splat(0);
    for (1..7) |a| {
        for (1..7) |b| t[a + b] += 1;
    }
    for (&t) |*e| e.* = @intCast(@as(u32, e.*) * 1000 / 36);
    break :blk t;
};

/// A CRC-8 lookup table: 256 entries, each needing 8 inner steps.
fn crc8Table() [256]u8 {
    @setEvalBranchQuota(10_000); // 256 * 8 loop iterations exceed the default
    var t: [256]u8 = undefined;
    for (&t, 0..) |*e, i| {
        var c: u8 = @intCast(i);
        for (0..8) |_| c = if (c & 0x80 != 0) (c << 1) ^ 0x07 else c << 1;
        e.* = c;
    }
    return t;
}
const crc_table = crc8Table();

fn crc8(bytes: []const u8) u8 {
    var c: u8 = 0;
    for (bytes) |b| c = crc_table[c ^ b];
    return c;
}

comptime {
    // Sanity checks that run in the compiler. A failure is a build error.
    std.debug.assert(two_d6_permille[7] == 166);
    std.debug.assert(two_d6_permille[2] == two_d6_permille[12]);
    std.debug.assert(crc_table[0] == 0);
}

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("P(7) = {d}.{d}%  P(12) = {d}.{d}%\n", .{
        two_d6_permille[7] / 10, two_d6_permille[7] % 10,
        two_d6_permille[12] / 10, two_d6_permille[12] % 10,
    });
    std.debug.print("crc8(\"123456789\") = 0x{x}\n", .{crc8("123456789")});
}
P(7) = 16.6%  P(12) = 2.7%
crc8("123456789") = 0xf4

Both tables are written into the executable as data; crc8 at run time is a loop with one table lookup per byte. Notice the ordinary for loops and an ordinary var inside the initialiser: because the whole block is evaluated by the compiler, they are compile-time loops and variables without any special keyword. The @setEvalBranchQuota in crc8Table is needed because 256 times 8 iterations is more than a thousand.

The top-level comptime { ... } block is a container-level assertion. Its std.debug.assert calls run during compilation, and a false one is a build error with a location, which is a cheap way to check that a table came out right, that a struct is the size you expect, or that two constants agree.

25.8 @compileError and @compileLog

@compileError("message") stops the build with your message, if the compiler ever reaches it. Put it behind a comptime condition and you have a custom compile-time check with a readable diagnostic.

h_compile_error.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Tuning = struct { max_lance: u8 = 4, repair_hours: u32 = 20 };
const t: Tuning = .{};

comptime {
    if (t.max_lance > 12) @compileError("a lance cannot have more than 12 units");
    if (@sizeOf(Tuning) > 64) @compileError("Tuning grew past a cache line");
}

fn checkedShift(comptime bits: u8, value: u32) u32 {
    if (bits >= 32) @compileError("shift amount " ++ std.fmt.comptimePrint("{d}", .{bits}) ++ " is too large for u32");
    return value << bits;
}

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{checkedShift(4, 1)});
}
16

With bits = 4 the program builds and prints 16. Change the call to checkedShift(40, 1):

h_compile_error_bad.zig

const std = @import("std");
fn checkedShift(comptime bits: u8, value: u32) u32 {
    if (bits >= 32) @compileError("shift amount " ++ std.fmt.comptimePrint("{d}", .{bits}) ++ " is too large for u32");
    return value << bits;
}
pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{checkedShift(40, 1)});
}
h_compile_error_bad.zig:3:21: error: shift amount 40 is too large for u32
    if (bits >= 32) @compileError("shift amount " ++ std.fmt.comptimePrint("{d}", .{bits}) ++ " is too large for u32");
                    ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
    main: h_compile_error_bad.zig:7:44

The message was assembled with ++ and comptimePrint, so it names the actual offending value. This pattern, "a comptime parameter, a check, a @compileError with a helpful message", is how generic code in Chapter 26 says which types it accepts.

@compileLog(values...) is the compile-time print. It prints its arguments during compilation, then deliberately fails the build so you do not ship it by accident:

i_compile_log.zig

const std = @import("std");
const table = blk: {
    var t: [4]u32 = undefined;
    for (&t, 0..) |*e, i| e.* = @intCast(i * i * i);
    break :blk t;
};
pub fn main() void {
    @compileLog("table is", table, @sizeOf(@TypeOf(table)));
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{table});
}
i_compile_log.zig:8:5: error: found compile log statement
    @compileLog("table is", table, @sizeOf(@TypeOf(table)));
    ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Compile Log Output:
@as(*const [8:0]u8, "table is"), @as([4]u32, .{ 0, 1, 8, 27 }), @as(comptime_int, 16)

Use it when you cannot work out what the compiler thinks a comptime value or type is. Remove it when you are done.

25.9 Why there are no macros

C has a preprocessor; C++ has templates; Rust has two macro systems; Lisp has real macros. Zig has none of these, and the reason is everything above. A macro is a program that writes program text. Zig lets you run the language itself while compiling, with the same syntax, the same functions, the same debugger-visible values. There is no second language to learn, no text substitution to reason about, and every error is reported in terms of real code with real types. Conditional compilation is an if on a comptime value. Generics are functions that take types. Lookup tables are loops. Type-dependent behaviour is a switch on @typeInfo. The cost of this design is that comptime code must be pure and finite (hence the quota) and cannot do I/O; the benefit is that "what does this expand to?" is never a question you have to ask.

In IRON LEDGER. The RNG module sizes an array by the number of enum members, so that adding a stream to the enum grows the array (game/src/sim/rng.zig): 
pub const Stream = enum(u8) {
    generation, market, maintenance, acquisition, battle, events, medical, travel,
    const count = @typeInfo(Stream).@"enum".fields.len;
};

pub const Rng = struct {
    prngs: [Stream.count]std.Random.DefaultPrng,
    ...
};
The tuning sanity test in game/src/domain/tuning.zig is 25.5 and 25.6 together: a recursive function with comptime T: type and comptime name: []const u8 parameters walks a nested struct with inline for, building the dotted path of each field with name ++ "." ++ f.name, so that a bad knob is reported as t.person.share_profit_default_bp. Because the type and the name are comptime, the recursion is entirely resolved during compilation; only the integer comparisons survive into the test binary. And the SQLite binding's else => @compileError("unsupported bind type " ++ @typeName(T)) is 25.8: try to bind a type it does not understand and the build stops with the type's name.

Exercises

Exercise 25.1 · Powers of two warm-up

Fill a [64]u64 table of powers of two in a compile-time block, add a container-level comptime assertion on it, and write ceilLog2(n) ?u6 that searches the table at run time. Name the file: exercises/25-comptime/ex1_powers.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 25, exercise 1: a table computed by the compiler.
//! Run with:  zig test ex1_powers.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// powers[i] == 2^i for i in 0..64, filled in at compile time.
const powers: [64]u64 = blk: {
    var t: [64]u64 = undefined;
    for (&t, 0..) |*e, i| e.* = @as(u64, 1) << @intCast(i);
    break :blk t;
};

// Checks that run while compiling; a failure is a build error, not a test failure.
comptime {
    std.debug.assert(powers[0] == 1);
    std.debug.assert(powers[63] == 1 << 63);
}

/// The smallest i such that 2^i >= n, or null if n is 0 or too large.
fn ceilLog2(n: u64) ?u6 {
    if (n == 0) return null;
    for (powers, 0..) |p, i| {
        if (p >= n) return @intCast(i);
    }
    return null;
}

test "table" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u64, 1024), powers[10]);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u64, 1 << 40), powers[40]);
}

test "ceilLog2" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u6, 0), ceilLog2(1));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u6, 3), ceilLog2(8));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u6, 4), ceilLog2(9));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u6, null), ceilLog2(0));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u6, null), ceilLog2(std.math.maxInt(u64)));
}

test "the table is a compile-time constant" {
    // If this were not comptime-known, the array length below would not compile.
    const n = comptime powers[3];
    const arr: [n]u8 = @splat(7);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 8), arr.len);
}

The last test proves the table is a true constant: only a comptime-known value can be an array length. Note that a doc comment (///) may not sit on a comptime block; use a plain // comment.

Exercise 25.2 · Sieve practice

Compute is_prime: [1000]bool with a sieve of Eratosthenes at compile time (you will need @setEvalBranchQuota), write primesBelow(n), and make prime_count a compile-time constant usable as an array length. Name the file: exercises/25-comptime/ex2_sieve.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 25, exercise 2: a sieve of Eratosthenes at compile time.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_sieve.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

const limit = 1000;

/// is_prime[n] is true when n is prime, for n < limit. Built by the compiler.
const is_prime: [limit]bool = blk: {
    @setEvalBranchQuota(20_000); // the nested loops need more than the default
    var t: [limit]bool = @splat(true);
    t[0] = false;
    t[1] = false;
    var i: usize = 2;
    while (i * i < limit) : (i += 1) {
        if (!t[i]) continue;
        var j = i * i;
        while (j < limit) : (j += i) t[j] = false;
    }
    break :blk t;
};

/// How many primes are below `n` (n <= limit)?
fn primesBelow(n: usize) usize {
    var count: usize = 0;
    for (is_prime[0..n]) |p| {
        if (p) count += 1;
    }
    return count;
}

/// Computed once, at compile time, from the table. The loop runs `limit` times,
/// which is over the default quota, so raise it for this evaluation.
const prime_count = blk: {
    @setEvalBranchQuota(2000);
    break :blk primesBelow(limit);
};

test "small primes" {
    try std.testing.expect(is_prime[2]);
    try std.testing.expect(is_prime[97]);
    try std.testing.expect(!is_prime[1]);
    try std.testing.expect(!is_prime[91]); // 7 * 13
}

test "counts" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 25), primesBelow(100));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 168), prime_count);
}

test "prime_count is usable as an array length" {
    const arr: [prime_count]u8 = undefined;
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 168), arr.len);
}

Two quotas: one for the sieve itself and one for the thousand-iteration count. Each is set inside the evaluation it serves. The same primesBelow function runs in the compiler for prime_count and at run time in the first test.

Exercise 25.3 · Walking fields practice

Write sumIntFields(anytype) that adds up every integer field of a struct (remember that fields of an anonymous literal are comptime_int), boolFieldCount(comptime T) that counts bool fields at compile time, and firstFieldOfType(T, Wanted) returning a field name or null. Name the file: exercises/25-comptime/ex3_fields.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 25, exercise 3: inline for over struct fields.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_fields.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Sum every integer field of a struct; skip fields of other types.
/// Fields of an anonymous literal like .{ .a = 1 } have type comptime_int, so accept that too.
fn sumIntFields(value: anytype) i64 {
    const T = @TypeOf(value);
    var total: i64 = 0;
    inline for (@typeInfo(T).@"struct".fields) |f| {
        switch (@typeInfo(f.type)) {
            .int, .comptime_int => total += @field(value, f.name),
            else => {},
        }
    }
    return total;
}

/// How many fields of type `bool` does the struct type T have? Computed at compile time.
fn boolFieldCount(comptime T: type) usize {
    comptime var n: usize = 0;
    inline for (@typeInfo(T).@"struct".fields) |f| {
        if (f.type == bool) n += 1;
    }
    return n;
}

/// The name of the first field whose type is `Wanted`, or null.
fn firstFieldOfType(comptime T: type, comptime Wanted: type) ?[]const u8 {
    inline for (@typeInfo(T).@"struct".fields) |f| {
        if (f.type == Wanted) return f.name;
    }
    return null;
}

const Unit = struct { tons: u32, armor: u16, name: []const u8, destroyed: bool, salvage: bool, bv: i32 };

test "sum" {
    const u: Unit = .{ .tons = 100, .armor = 300, .name = "Atlas", .destroyed = false, .salvage = true, .bv = -5 };
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 395), sumIntFields(u));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 3), sumIntFields(.{ .a = 1, .b = 2 }));
}

test "counts at compile time" {
    const n = comptime boolFieldCount(Unit);
    const flags: [n]bool = @splat(false);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 2), flags.len);
}

test "first field of type" {
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("armor", (comptime firstFieldOfType(Unit, u16)).?);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("destroyed", (comptime firstFieldOfType(Unit, bool)).?);
    try std.testing.expect(comptime firstFieldOfType(Unit, f64) == null);
}

Everything that depends on a field's type or name happens inside inline for, where f is a constant. f.type == bool is a comparison of two type values, which is legal exactly because types are values.

Exercise 25.4 · Labels practice

Write three functions that return compile-time strings: label(name, unit) using ++ and a @compileError for an empty name, header(text, width) that pads with " " ** n, and version(major, minor, patch) using comptimePrint. Name the file: exercises/25-comptime/ex4_labels.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 25, exercise 4: strings built by the compiler.
//! Run with:  zig test ex4_labels.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// "weight (tons)" from ("weight", "tons"); "weight" alone when unit is empty.
/// An empty name is a compile error.
fn label(comptime name: []const u8, comptime unit: []const u8) []const u8 {
    if (name.len == 0) @compileError("label needs a name");
    if (unit.len == 0) return name;
    return name ++ " (" ++ unit ++ ")";
}

/// A column header: the label left-aligned and padded with spaces to `width`,
/// all decided at compile time.
fn header(comptime text: []const u8, comptime width: usize) []const u8 {
    if (text.len >= width) return text;
    return text ++ (" " ** (width - text.len));
}

/// "v0.16.0" from three numbers.
fn version(comptime major: u32, comptime minor: u32, comptime patch: u32) []const u8 {
    return std.fmt.comptimePrint("v{d}.{d}.{d}", .{ major, minor, patch });
}

test "label" {
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("weight (tons)", label("weight", "tons"));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("name", label("name", ""));
}

test "header" {
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("tons      ", header("tons", 10));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("battle value", header("battle value", 5));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 10), header("tons", 10).len);
}

test "version" {
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("v0.16.0", version(0, 16, 0));
    // The result is a compile-time constant, so it can size an array.
    const n = comptime version(1, 2, 3).len;
    const arr: [n]u8 = @splat('x');
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 6), arr.len);
}

All parameters are comptime, so the functions cannot be called with runtime strings, which is the point: the results are constants. In the last test the call is prefixed with comptime so that .len can size an array.

Exercise 25.5 · Enum tables challenge

Write names(comptime E: type) returning an array of every tag name, values(E) returning the matching enum values, longestName(E) for column sizing, and fromName(E, text) that does a runtime lookup through the compile-time tables (it must work for enums with explicit values). Name the file: exercises/25-comptime/ex5_enum_names.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 25, exercise 5: tables derived from an enum at compile time.
//! Run with:  zig test ex5_enum_names.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// An array of every tag name of enum E, in declaration order.
fn names(comptime E: type) [@typeInfo(E).@"enum".fields.len][]const u8 {
    const fields = @typeInfo(E).@"enum".fields;
    var out: [fields.len][]const u8 = undefined;
    inline for (fields, 0..) |f, i| out[i] = f.name;
    return out;
}

/// Every value of E, in declaration order, matching names(E) index for index.
fn values(comptime E: type) [@typeInfo(E).@"enum".fields.len]E {
    const fields = @typeInfo(E).@"enum".fields;
    var out: [fields.len]E = undefined;
    inline for (fields, 0..) |f, i| out[i] = @enumFromInt(f.value);
    return out;
}

/// The length of the longest tag name, for sizing a column.
fn longestName(comptime E: type) usize {
    comptime var best: usize = 0;
    inline for (@typeInfo(E).@"enum".fields) |f| best = @max(best, f.name.len);
    return best;
}

/// Look a value up by name at runtime, using the compile-time table.
fn fromName(comptime E: type, text: []const u8) ?E {
    const table = comptime names(E);
    const vals = comptime values(E);
    for (table, vals) |n, v| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, n, text)) return v;
    }
    return null;
}

const Role = enum { pilot, tech, medic, quartermaster };
const Weather = enum(u8) { clear = 1, rain = 5, storm = 9 };

test "names" {
    const n = names(Role);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 4), n.len);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("pilot", n[0]);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("quartermaster", n[3]);
}

test "longest" {
    const w = comptime longestName(Role);
    const col: [w]u8 = @splat(' ');
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 13), col.len);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 5), comptime longestName(Weather));
}

test "fromName with explicit values" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?Weather, .storm), fromName(Weather, "storm"));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?Weather, null), fromName(Weather, "snow"));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?Role, .medic), fromName(Role, "medic"));
}

The array length in the return type, [@typeInfo(E).@"enum".fields.len][]const u8, is itself a compile-time expression. fromName builds both tables with comptime and then does an ordinary runtime loop over them; you cannot index fields[i] with a runtime i because fields only exists in the compiler. (The standard library has std.meta.stringToEnum for this job.)

Check your understanding

  1. What is the type of the literal 42 before it is assigned anywhere?
    Answercomptime_int: an unbounded integer that exists only in the compiler and coerces to any integer type it fits in.
  2. What does the comptime keyword in front of an expression guarantee?
    AnswerThat the expression is evaluated by the compiler; if it cannot be, compilation fails. The result is a constant baked into the binary.
  3. Why must an array length be comptime-known?
    AnswerThe length is part of the array's type, and the compiler lays out memory and generates code from types before the program runs. For runtime lengths use a slice or an ArrayList.
  4. When do you need inline for rather than for?
    AnswerWhen the loop variable must be comptime-known inside the body: iterating struct fields, types, or tuple elements of different types. Not for performance.
  5. What does "evaluation exceeded 1000 backwards branches" mean and how do you fix it?
    AnswerA compile-time evaluation looped or recursed more than the default quota. Call @setEvalBranchQuota(n) inside that evaluation with a larger n.
  6. Can ++ join a string literal to a slice read from a file at run time?
    AnswerNo; its operands need comptime-known lengths. Use an ArrayList(u8), allocPrint or bufPrint for runtime strings.
  7. What is the difference between @compileError and @compileLog?
    Answer@compileError fails the build with your message when reached; @compileLog prints values during compilation for debugging and also fails the build so it cannot be left in.
  8. Why does Zig not need a preprocessor or a template language?
    AnswerBecause ordinary Zig code can run at compile time, with types as values: conditional compilation is an if, generics are functions returning types, and tables are loops.
What you learned.
  • Values are either comptime-known or runtime; comptime forces the first world, and literals, constants and pure calls on constants already live there.
  • comptime_int and comptime_float are unbounded literal types that coerce when they fit; overflow is a compile error.
  • comptime blocks, comptime var, and @setEvalBranchQuota for evaluations beyond a thousand branches.
  • Types are values of type type; array lengths, types and field names must be comptime-known.
  • inline for and inline while unroll with a comptime loop variable, which is what field walking and mixed tuples need.
  • ++ and ** build strings in the compiler from operands with known lengths; comptimePrint formats there.
  • Tables are loops inside constant initialisers; container-level comptime {} blocks hold build-time assertions.
  • @compileError gives custom diagnostics; @compileLog prints while compiling.

26. Generics: types as values

In this chapter you will write generic code the Zig way: a function that takes a comptime T: type and returns a struct built around it, @This() to name that struct from inside, anytype parameters whose type is inferred per call, duck typing with @hasDecl and @hasField, generic functions like max(comptime T, a, b), a Pair(A, B), generic containers that take an allocator, and how to constrain T with @typeInfo and @compileError. Along the way you will see that std.ArrayList is nothing more than this, and what "monomorphisation" costs.

26.1 A function that returns a type

Chapter 25 established that a type is a value the compiler can hold. Zig's entire generics story follows from one more step: a function can return a type. There is no template keyword, no <T> syntax; a generic container is a function whose parameter is a type and whose result is a struct.

a_stack.zig

const std = @import("std");

/// A function that takes a type and returns a new struct type built around it.
fn Stack(comptime T: type) type {
    return struct {
        const Self = @This(); // "the struct being defined", whatever it ends up being called

        items: std.ArrayList(T) = .empty,

        pub fn push(self: *Self, gpa: std.mem.Allocator, value: T) !void {
            try self.items.append(gpa, value);
        }

        pub fn pop(self: *Self) ?T {
            return self.items.pop();
        }

        pub fn peek(self: Self) ?T {
            if (self.items.items.len == 0) return null;
            return self.items.getLast();
        }

        pub fn len(self: Self) usize {
            return self.items.items.len;
        }

        pub fn deinit(self: *Self, gpa: std.mem.Allocator) void {
            self.items.deinit(gpa);
        }
    };
}

pub fn main() !void {
    var gpa_state: std.heap.DebugAllocator(.{}) = .init;
    defer _ = gpa_state.deinit();
    const gpa = gpa_state.allocator();

    var numbers: Stack(i32) = .{};
    defer numbers.deinit(gpa);
    try numbers.push(gpa, 10);
    try numbers.push(gpa, 20);
    std.debug.print("peek {?d}, pop {?d}, pop {?d}, pop {?d}\n", .{ numbers.peek(), numbers.pop(), numbers.pop(), numbers.pop() });

    var names: Stack([]const u8) = .{};
    defer names.deinit(gpa);
    try names.push(gpa, "Kell");
    try names.push(gpa, "Natasha");
    std.debug.print("{d} names, top is {?s}\n", .{ names.len(), names.peek() });

    std.debug.print("{s}\n{s}\n", .{ @typeName(Stack(i32)), @typeName(Stack([]const u8)) });
}
peek 20, pop 20, pop 10, pop null
2 names, top is Natasha
a_stack.Stack(i32)
a_stack.Stack([]const u8)

Read Stack top to bottom. It takes comptime T: type. It returns a struct { ... } expression: a struct type, defined inline, in which T is used as an ordinary type. The convention of a capitalised function name tells readers "this returns a type". Calling Stack(i32) produces a struct type; calling Stack([]const u8) produces a different one; the printed type names show the argument inside the parentheses.

@This() is the way a struct refers to itself when it has no name of its own. The anonymous struct inside Stack cannot say Stack(T) for its methods without repeating itself, so the idiom is const Self = @This(); as the first line, and then self: *Self in every method. You saw this shape in Chapter 12 for named structs; here it is essential.

The methods are the same methods you would write for a non-generic stack. push takes an allocator because the list underneath can grow; pop returns ?T; and every mention of the element type is just T. Nothing here is "generic syntax". It is ordinary code with a type-valued constant in scope.

26.2 Generic functions

The same trick works for a function that does not build a type but needs one to describe its arguments.

b_max.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn max(comptime T: type, a: T, b: T) T {
    return if (a > b) a else b;
}

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{d} {d} {d}\n", .{ max(i32, 3, 9), max(f64, 2.5, 1.0), max(u8, 200, 100) });
}
9 2.5 200

The caller passes the type explicitly and the compiler checks that a and b both fit it. Get it wrong and the error is in terms of the real types:

b_max_bad.zig

fn max(comptime T: type, a: T, b: T) T {
    return if (a > b) a else b;
}
pub fn main() void {
    _ = max(i32, 3, 2.5);
}
b_max_bad.zig:5:21: error: fractional component prevents float value '2.5' from coercion to type 'i32'
    _ = max(i32, 3, 2.5);
                    ^~~

Passing the type by hand is verbose, but it is also the most explicit form and it is what the standard library does throughout: std.mem.eql(u8, ...), std.mem.sort(T, ...), std.fmt.parseInt(i32, ...) are all this pattern.

26.3 anytype: let the argument decide

When the type can be worked out from the argument itself, write anytype instead. The compiler substitutes the argument's actual type, and you can name it with @TypeOf.

c_anytype.zig

const std = @import("std");

/// The type is inferred from the first argument; the second must match it.
fn maxOf(a: anytype, b: @TypeOf(a)) @TypeOf(a) {
    return if (a > b) a else b;
}

/// Works on arrays, slices, and pointers to arrays: anything a `for` can walk.
fn sum(items: anytype) i64 {
    var total: i64 = 0;
    for (items) |x| total += x;
    return total;
}

/// Reports what it was given, to show that anytype is resolved per call.
fn describe(x: anytype) void {
    std.debug.print("{s: <14} = {any}\n", .{ @typeName(@TypeOf(x)), x });
}

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{d} {d}\n", .{ maxOf(@as(u8, 3), 200), maxOf(@as(f32, 1.5), 0.5) });

    const arr = [_]i32{ 1, 2, 3 };
    const slice: []const i64 = &.{ 10, 20 };
    std.debug.print("{d} {d} {d}\n", .{ sum(arr), sum(&arr), sum(slice) });

    describe(42);
    describe(@as(u8, 42));
    describe("text");
    describe(.{ .x = 1 });
}
200 1.5
6 6 30
comptime_int   = 42
u8             = 42
*const [4:0]u8 = { 116, 101, 120, 116 }
c_anytype.main__struct_27122 = .{ .x = 1 }

maxOf(a: anytype, b: @TypeOf(a)) infers the type from a and then requires b to have the same one, which is why maxOf(@as(u8, 3), 200) works: the literal 200 coerces to u8. Return types may refer to earlier parameters in the same way. sum(items: anytype) accepts anything a for loop can walk: an array by value, a pointer to an array, a slice. And describe shows the important subtlety: anytype takes the argument's type exactly, so a bare 42 arrives as comptime_int, a string literal as a pointer to an array, and an anonymous struct as a type the compiler named for you. If you need a specific type, cast at the call site or convert inside with @as.

Prefer a concrete type over anytype whenever you can name it. fn area(s: Shape) is clearer than fn area(s: anytype), gives better errors, and shows up in documentation. Use anytype for genuinely polymorphic helpers (formatting, sums, "anything iterable") and for the duck typing of the next section.

26.4 Duck typing with @hasDecl and @hasField

Because @TypeOf(x) is a value, you can ask questions about it at compile time. @hasDecl(T, "name") asks whether the type declares a method or constant called name; @hasField(T, "name") asks about a field. Both require T to be a struct, enum, union or opaque, so guard with @typeInfo first if the argument might be a plain integer.

d_duck.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Dog = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    pub fn speak(self: Dog) void {
        std.debug.print("{s} says woof\n", .{self.name});
    }
};
const Mech = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    tons: u32,
};

/// Duck typing: "if it has a speak method, call it; if it has a name, use that".
fn introduce(x: anytype) void {
    const T = @TypeOf(x);
    if (@typeInfo(T) != .@"struct") {
        std.debug.print("a {s}, which is not a struct\n", .{@typeName(T)});
        return;
    }
    if (@hasDecl(T, "speak")) {
        x.speak();
    } else if (@hasField(T, "name")) {
        std.debug.print("{s} is silent\n", .{x.name});
    } else {
        std.debug.print("something anonymous\n", .{});
    }
}

pub fn main() void {
    introduce(Dog{ .name = "Rex" });
    introduce(Mech{ .name = "Atlas", .tons = 100 });
    introduce(@as(u8, 7));
    introduce(.{ .x = 1 });
}
Rex says woof
Atlas is silent
a u8, which is not a struct
something anonymous

Each if here is decided while compiling, so the version of introduce generated for Dog contains only the speak call and the version for Mech contains only the print. This is duck typing without the runtime cost: "if it has a speak, it can speak". What happens if you skip the check and just call the method?

d_duck_bad.zig

fn shout(x: anytype) void {
    x.speak();
}
pub fn main() void {
    shout(@as(u8, 7));
}
d_duck_bad.zig:2:6: error: no field or member function named 'speak' in 'u8'
    x.speak();
    ~^~~~~~
    main: d_duck_bad.zig:5:10

Still a compile error, still pointing at the real type. The difference from a C++ template error is that the message is one line and names your function, not forty lines of library internals. When you write reusable anytype code, do the @hasDecl check yourself and pair it with a @compileError that says what the function needs.

26.5 Pair(A, B) and type identity

e_pair.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn Pair(comptime A: type, comptime B: type) type {
    return struct {
        first: A,
        second: B,

        pub fn swap(self: @This()) Pair(B, A) {
            return .{ .first = self.second, .second = self.first };
        }
    };
}

/// Infer both types from the arguments.
fn pair(a: anytype, b: anytype) Pair(@TypeOf(a), @TypeOf(b)) {
    return .{ .first = a, .second = b };
}

pub fn main() void {
    const p = pair(@as(u32, 7), "seven");
    const q = p.swap();
    std.debug.print("{d} {s} / {s} {d}\n", .{ p.first, p.second, q.first, q.second });
    std.debug.print("{s}\n{s}\n", .{ @typeName(@TypeOf(p)), @typeName(@TypeOf(q)) });

    // Every call with the same arguments yields the SAME type.
    std.debug.print("same: {}  different: {}\n", .{
        Pair(u8, u8) == Pair(u8, u8),
        Pair(u8, u8) == Pair(u8, u16),
    });
    std.debug.print("sizes: {d} {d}\n", .{ @sizeOf(Pair(u8, u8)), @sizeOf(Pair(u8, u64)) });
}
7 seven / seven 7
e_pair.Pair(u32,*const [5:0]u8)
e_pair.Pair(*const [5:0]u8,u32)
same: true  different: false
sizes: 2 16

Two things to take from this one. First, swap returns Pair(B, A): a generic type can mention other instantiations of itself, and the return type expression is evaluated at compile time like any other. The pair helper infers both parameters, which is how you get the convenience of type inference on top of an explicit generic type.

Second, the last lines: calling a type-returning function twice with the same arguments gives the same type, not two look-alike types. The compiler memoises these calls. That is what lets Stack(i32) in one file and Stack(i32) in another be interchangeable, and why @sizeOf(Pair(u8, u64)) is a stable, meaningful number.

26.6 Constraining T

A generic type will happily accept any T until some line inside it fails to compile for that T, at which point the error points into the middle of your struct. Better to check up front and say what you need.

f_constrain.zig

const std = @import("std");

/// Only numeric types are accepted; anything else is a build error with a clear message.
fn Accumulator(comptime T: type) type {
    switch (@typeInfo(T)) {
        .int, .float => {},
        else => @compileError("Accumulator needs an integer or float type, got " ++ @typeName(T)),
    }
    return struct {
        total: T = 0,
        count: u32 = 0,

        pub fn add(self: *@This(), v: T) void {
            self.total += v;
            self.count += 1;
        }

        pub fn mean(self: @This()) T {
            if (self.count == 0) return 0;
            return switch (@typeInfo(T)) {
                .int => @divTrunc(self.total, @as(T, @intCast(self.count))),
                .float => self.total / @as(T, @floatFromInt(self.count)),
                else => unreachable,
            };
        }
    };
}

pub fn main() void {
    var a: Accumulator(i32) = .{};
    a.add(10);
    a.add(15);
    var f: Accumulator(f64) = .{};
    f.add(10);
    f.add(15);
    std.debug.print("int mean {d}, float mean {d}\n", .{ a.mean(), f.mean() });
}
int mean 12, float mean 12.5

The switch on @typeInfo(T) at the top of Accumulator runs when the type is instantiated, before any method exists. A second switch inside mean picks integer or float division; since T is fixed for a given instantiation, only one arm is ever compiled, and the else => unreachable is there to satisfy the compiler that we thought about it. Hand it the wrong type:

f_constrain_bad.zig

fn Accumulator(comptime T: type) type {
    switch (@typeInfo(T)) {
        .int, .float => {},
        else => @compileError("Accumulator needs an integer or float type, got " ++ @typeName(T)),
    }
    return struct { total: T = 0 };
}
pub fn main() void {
    var a: Accumulator([]const u8) = .{};
    _ = &a;
}
f_constrain_bad.zig:4:17: error: Accumulator needs an integer or float type, got []const u8
        else => @compileError("Accumulator needs an integer or float type, got " ++ @typeName(T)),
                ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
f_constrain_bad.zig:9:23: note: called at comptime here
    var a: Accumulator([]const u8) = .{};
           ~~~~~~~~~~~^~~~~~~~~~~~

The message is yours, it names the offending type, and the "called at comptime here" note points at the instantiation. That is as good as generic error messages get in any language. Use it whenever a generic type has a real requirement: numeric, has a certain method, is an enum, is a pointer.

26.7 std.ArrayList is just this

Everything in Chapter 21 was an instance of the pattern in this chapter. Here is a working, if minimal, ArrayList in thirty lines, to make that concrete.

g_list.zig

const std = @import("std");

/// A tiny ArrayList. This is what std.ArrayList(T) is, minus the conveniences.
fn List(comptime T: type) type {
    return struct {
        const Self = @This();

        items: []T = &.{}, // the part in use
        capacity: usize = 0, // the size of the buffer behind items

        pub fn append(self: *Self, gpa: std.mem.Allocator, value: T) !void {
            if (self.items.len == self.capacity) {
                const new_cap = if (self.capacity == 0) 4 else self.capacity * 2;
                const new_buf = try gpa.alloc(T, new_cap);
                @memcpy(new_buf[0..self.items.len], self.items);
                if (self.capacity > 0) gpa.free(self.items.ptr[0..self.capacity]);
                self.items = new_buf[0..self.items.len];
                self.capacity = new_cap;
            }
            self.items.len += 1;
            self.items[self.items.len - 1] = value;
        }

        pub fn deinit(self: *Self, gpa: std.mem.Allocator) void {
            if (self.capacity > 0) gpa.free(self.items.ptr[0..self.capacity]);
            self.* = .{};
        }
    };
}

pub fn main() !void {
    var gpa_state: std.heap.DebugAllocator(.{}) = .init;
    defer _ = gpa_state.deinit();
    const gpa = gpa_state.allocator();

    var list: List(u32) = .{};
    defer list.deinit(gpa);
    for (0..10) |i| {
        try list.append(gpa, @intCast(i * i));
        if (list.capacity == list.items.len) std.debug.print("full at {d}\n", .{list.capacity});
    }
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{list.items});
}
full at 4
full at 8
{ 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81 }

Compare it with std.ArrayList: an items slice, a capacity, an allocator passed to the growing call, doubling when full, and a deinit that frees exactly what was allocated. The real one adds the many convenience methods, a smarter growth curve, and careful handling of alignment and zero-sized types, but its shape is this. When you open lib/zig/std/array_list.zig you will now recognise pub fn Aligned(comptime T: type, comptime alignment: ?mem.Alignment) type as the function that returns the type (std.ArrayList(T) is an alias for Aligned(T, null)), and const Self = @This(); as the first line inside its return struct. The pointer arithmetic in deinit, self.items.ptr[0..self.capacity], rebuilds the full buffer slice from the in-use slice; it is the one line here that needs Chapter 18.

26.8 Monomorphisation and what it costs

Each distinct set of comptime arguments produces a separate copy of the function or type, compiled and optimised on its own. This is called monomorphisation, and it is why Zig generics are as fast as hand-written code: Stack(i32).push is a function that knows it is pushing 4-byte integers, with no boxing and no runtime type checks.

h_mono.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn Box(comptime T: type) type {
    return struct { value: T };
}

fn describe(x: anytype) void {
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{@typeName(@TypeOf(x))});
}

pub fn main() void {
    // Three distinct struct types, each compiled separately.
    describe(Box(u8){ .value = 1 });
    describe(Box(u64){ .value = 1 });
    describe(Box([]const u8){ .value = "s" });
    // The same type, reused: no new code.
    describe(Box(u8){ .value = 2 });
    std.debug.print("{d} {d} {d}\n", .{ @sizeOf(Box(u8)), @sizeOf(Box(u64)), @sizeOf(Box([]const u8)) });
}
h_mono.Box(u8)
h_mono.Box(u64)
h_mono.Box([]const u8)
h_mono.Box(u8)
1 8 16

The cost is compile time and binary size, one copy per instantiation. Three Box types and four describe calls produced three describe functions, not one (the fourth call reused the first). For a small program this is nothing; in a large one, an anytype helper called with fifty distinct types is fifty functions. Two habits keep it under control. First, keep generic functions small and push the type-independent work into non-generic helpers that take a slice or a pointer. Second, do not make things generic that do not need to be; a function over []const u8 is compiled once, a function over anytype is compiled per caller type. The standard library's own comment on printIntAny says exactly this: "prefer printInt to avoid generic explosion".

In IRON LEDGER. The game uses generics sparingly and exactly where they pay: for small helpers that would otherwise be copied per type. The console parser's number reader takes the target type as a parameter so one function serves i64 amounts and u32 IDs (game/src/sim/cli.zig): 
pub fn num(comptime T: type, tok: ?[]const u8) ParseError!T {
    return std.fmt.parseInt(T, tok orelse return error.BadArguments, 10) catch return error.BadNumber;
}
// ... .admit = @enumFromInt(try num(u32, tokens.next())) ...
// ... .amount = try num(i64, tokens.next()) ...
The save loader does the same for typed IDs, turning a database integer into whichever enum the column represents: fn toId(comptime T: type, v: i64) T { return @enumFromInt(@as(u32, @intCast(v))); } in game/src/persist/store.zig. And the SQLite binding's bind(self, idx, value: anytype) is 26.4 and 26.6 in one function: a switch on @typeInfo(@TypeOf(value)) with an arm per kind of value and an else => @compileError(...), so binding a struct by mistake fails the build instead of corrupting a save. The big containers, GameState.people and friends, are instantiations of the standard library's generic maps; the game never needed a generic container of its own.

Exercises

Exercise 26.1 · Pair warm-up

Write Pair(A, B) with swap returning Pair(B, A) and mapFirst(f) that applies a function to the first element and returns a pair whose first type is f's return type. Add a pair(a, b) helper that infers both types. Name the file: exercises/26-generics/ex1_pair.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 26, exercise 1: a generic pair.
//! Run with:  zig test ex1_pair.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

fn Pair(comptime A: type, comptime B: type) type {
    return struct {
        first: A,
        second: B,

        const Self = @This();

        pub fn swap(self: Self) Pair(B, A) {
            return .{ .first = self.second, .second = self.first };
        }

        /// Apply `f` to the first element, producing a pair with a new first type.
        pub fn mapFirst(self: Self, comptime f: anytype) Pair(@TypeOf(f(self.first)), B) {
            return .{ .first = f(self.first), .second = self.second };
        }
    };
}

/// Build a pair with both types inferred from the arguments.
fn pair(a: anytype, b: anytype) Pair(@TypeOf(a), @TypeOf(b)) {
    return .{ .first = a, .second = b };
}

fn double(x: u32) u64 {
    return @as(u64, x) * 2;
}

test "swap" {
    const p = pair(@as(u32, 7), @as([]const u8, "seven"));
    const q = p.swap();
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("seven", q.first);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 7), q.second);
    try std.testing.expect(@TypeOf(q) == Pair([]const u8, u32));
}

test "mapFirst changes the type" {
    const p = pair(@as(u32, 21), true);
    const m = p.mapFirst(double);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u64, 42), m.first);
    try std.testing.expect(m.second);
    try std.testing.expect(@TypeOf(m) == Pair(u64, bool));
}

test "same arguments, same type" {
    try std.testing.expect(Pair(u8, u8) == Pair(u8, u8));
    try std.testing.expect(Pair(u8, u8) != Pair(u8, u16));
}

The return type of mapFirst calls f on the field to discover its result type: @TypeOf(f(self.first)) is evaluated at compile time and never actually runs f. The test that compares types with == works because types are values.

Exercise 26.2 · Ring buffer practice

Write Ring(T, N), a fixed-capacity FIFO queue with no allocator: push returns error.Full, pop returns ?T, and indices wrap with % N. Name the file: exercises/26-generics/ex2_ring.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 26, exercise 2: a fixed-capacity ring buffer queue.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_ring.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// A queue of at most N items of type T, with no allocator at all.
fn Ring(comptime T: type, comptime N: usize) type {
    return struct {
        const Self = @This();

        buf: [N]T = undefined,
        head: usize = 0, // index of the oldest item
        count: usize = 0,

        pub fn push(self: *Self, v: T) error{Full}!void {
            if (self.count == N) return error.Full;
            self.buf[(self.head + self.count) % N] = v;
            self.count += 1;
        }

        pub fn pop(self: *Self) ?T {
            if (self.count == 0) return null;
            const v = self.buf[self.head];
            self.head = (self.head + 1) % N;
            self.count -= 1;
            return v;
        }

        pub fn len(self: Self) usize {
            return self.count;
        }

        pub fn capacity(_: Self) usize {
            return N;
        }
    };
}

test "fifo order" {
    var q: Ring(u8, 3) = .{};
    try q.push(1);
    try q.push(2);
    try q.push(3);
    try std.testing.expectError(error.Full, q.push(4));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u8, 1), q.pop());
    try q.push(4); // wraps around
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u8, 2), q.pop());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u8, 3), q.pop());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u8, 4), q.pop());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u8, null), q.pop());
}

test "size is decided at compile time" {
    var q: Ring([]const u8, 2) = .{};
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 2), q.capacity());
    try q.push("a");
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 1), q.len());
    try std.testing.expect(@sizeOf(Ring(u8, 4)) < @sizeOf(Ring(u8, 64)));
}

Two comptime parameters, one a type and one a number. Because N is comptime the buffer is a plain array inside the struct and its size shows up in @sizeOf, as the last test checks.

Exercise 26.3 · Numeric helpers practice

Write Elem(T) that extracts the element type of an array, slice or pointer-to-array with @typeInfo; sum(items: anytype) that returns that element type; average(comptime T, xs) that refuses non-float T with @compileError; and maxOfAll(args) over a tuple using inline for. Name the file: exercises/26-generics/ex3_numeric.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 26, exercise 3: generic functions with anytype and constraints.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_numeric.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// The element type of an array, slice, or pointer to array.
fn Elem(comptime T: type) type {
    return switch (@typeInfo(T)) {
        .array => |a| a.child,
        .pointer => |p| switch (p.size) {
            .slice => p.child,
            .one => Elem(p.child), // *[N]T -> T
            else => @compileError("unsupported pointer type " ++ @typeName(T)),
        },
        else => @compileError("sum needs an array or slice, got " ++ @typeName(T)),
    };
}

/// Sum of any array or slice, in the element's own type.
fn sum(items: anytype) Elem(@TypeOf(items)) {
    var total: Elem(@TypeOf(items)) = 0;
    for (items) |x| total += x;
    return total;
}

/// Mean of a slice; T must be a float type, checked at compile time.
fn average(comptime T: type, xs: []const T) T {
    if (@typeInfo(T) != .float) @compileError("average needs a float type, got " ++ @typeName(T));
    if (xs.len == 0) return 0;
    return sum(xs) / @as(T, @floatFromInt(xs.len));
}

/// The largest of any number of arguments passed as a tuple.
fn maxOfAll(args: anytype) @TypeOf(args[0]) {
    var best = args[0];
    inline for (args) |a| {
        if (a > best) best = a;
    }
    return best;
}

test "sum keeps the element type" {
    const arr = [_]u8{ 100, 100, 50 };
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 250), sum(arr));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 250), sum(&arr));
    const sl: []const i64 = &.{ -5, 10 };
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 5), sum(sl));
    try std.testing.expect(@TypeOf(sum(sl)) == i64);
}

test "average" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(f64, 2.5), average(f64, &.{ 1, 2, 3, 4 }));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(f32, 0), average(f32, &.{}));
}

test "maxOfAll" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, 9), maxOfAll(.{ @as(i32, 3), 9, -2, 7 }));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(f64, 2.5), maxOfAll(.{ @as(f64, 1), 2.5 }));
}

Elem is a type-level function that takes a type and returns a type, using it in sum's return type. The .pointer arm looks at p.size to tell slices from single-item pointers, and recurses for *[N]T. Chapter 27 covers @typeInfo in full.

Exercise 26.4 · Matrix challenge

Write Matrix(T, rows, cols) with public Rows and Cols constants, identity() (compile error for non-square), and mul(other) whose result type is Matrix(T, rows, @TypeOf(other).Cols) and which rejects a shape mismatch at compile time. Name the file: exercises/26-generics/ex4_matrix.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 26, exercise 4: a matrix type with compile-time dimensions.
//! Run with:  zig test ex4_matrix.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

fn Matrix(comptime T: type, comptime rows: usize, comptime cols: usize) type {
    return struct {
        const Self = @This();
        pub const Rows = rows;
        pub const Cols = cols;

        data: [rows][cols]T = @splat(@splat(0)),

        pub fn identity() Self {
            if (rows != cols) @compileError("identity needs a square matrix");
            var m: Self = .{};
            for (0..rows) |i| m.data[i][i] = 1;
            return m;
        }

        pub fn at(self: Self, r: usize, c: usize) T {
            return self.data[r][c];
        }

        pub fn set(self: *Self, r: usize, c: usize, v: T) void {
            self.data[r][c] = v;
        }

        /// Multiply by a matrix whose row count equals our column count.
        /// The result's shape is known at compile time; a mismatch is a compile error.
        pub fn mul(self: Self, other: anytype) Matrix(T, rows, @TypeOf(other).Cols) {
            const O = @TypeOf(other);
            if (O.Rows != cols) @compileError("shape mismatch: cannot multiply " ++
                @typeName(Self) ++ " by " ++ @typeName(O));
            var out: Matrix(T, rows, O.Cols) = .{};
            for (0..rows) |i| {
                for (0..O.Cols) |j| {
                    var acc: T = 0;
                    for (0..cols) |k| acc += self.data[i][k] * other.data[k][j];
                    out.data[i][j] = acc;
                }
            }
            return out;
        }
    };
}

test "identity" {
    const I = Matrix(i32, 2, 2).identity();
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, 1), I.at(0, 0));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, 0), I.at(0, 1));
}

test "multiply 2x3 by 3x2 gives 2x2" {
    var a: Matrix(i32, 2, 3) = .{};
    var b: Matrix(i32, 3, 2) = .{};
    // a = [1 2 3; 4 5 6], b = [7 8; 9 10; 11 12]
    var v: i32 = 1;
    for (0..2) |r| for (0..3) |c| {
        a.set(r, c, v);
        v += 1;
    };
    for (0..3) |r| for (0..2) |c| {
        b.set(r, c, v);
        v += 1;
    };
    const p = a.mul(b);
    try std.testing.expect(@TypeOf(p) == Matrix(i32, 2, 2));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, 58), p.at(0, 0));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, 64), p.at(0, 1));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, 139), p.at(1, 0));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, 154), p.at(1, 1));
}

test "identity leaves a matrix unchanged" {
    var m: Matrix(f64, 2, 2) = .{};
    m.set(0, 1, 2.5);
    m.set(1, 0, -1);
    const same = m.mul(Matrix(f64, 2, 2).identity());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(f64, 2.5), same.at(0, 1));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(f64, -1), same.at(1, 0));
}

Publishing Rows and Cols as declarations lets other generic code read the shape off the type with @TypeOf(other).Cols. A wrong shape is a compile error with a message built from @typeName, which is far better than a runtime bounds panic in the inner loop.

Exercise 26.5 · Container with allocator and duck typing challenge

Extend Stack(T) with pushAll, a slice() accessor, and map(gpa, f) that returns a Stack of f's return type. Then write total(container: anytype) that works on anything with a slice() method or any plain slice or array, using @hasDecl. Name the file: exercises/26-generics/ex5_container.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 26, exercise 5: a generic container with an allocator, plus duck typing.
//! Run with:  zig test ex5_container.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

fn Stack(comptime T: type) type {
    return struct {
        const Self = @This();
        pub const Item = T;

        items: std.ArrayList(T) = .empty,

        pub fn deinit(self: *Self, gpa: std.mem.Allocator) void {
            self.items.deinit(gpa);
        }

        pub fn push(self: *Self, gpa: std.mem.Allocator, v: T) !void {
            try self.items.append(gpa, v);
        }

        pub fn pushAll(self: *Self, gpa: std.mem.Allocator, vs: []const T) !void {
            try self.items.appendSlice(gpa, vs);
        }

        pub fn pop(self: *Self) ?T {
            return self.items.pop();
        }

        /// A new stack whose items are f(item) for each item, in the same order.
        /// The result type comes from f's return type.
        pub fn map(self: Self, gpa: std.mem.Allocator, comptime f: anytype) !Stack(@TypeOf(f(@as(T, undefined)))) {
            var out: Stack(@TypeOf(f(@as(T, undefined)))) = .{};
            errdefer out.deinit(gpa);
            try out.items.ensureTotalCapacity(gpa, self.items.items.len);
            for (self.items.items) |v| out.items.appendAssumeCapacity(f(v));
            return out;
        }

        pub fn slice(self: Self) []const T {
            return self.items.items;
        }
    };
}

/// Works on anything that has a `slice()` method returning a slice, or is a slice itself.
fn total(container: anytype) i64 {
    const T = @TypeOf(container);
    const items = if (@typeInfo(T) == .@"struct" and @hasDecl(T, "slice")) container.slice() else container;
    var t: i64 = 0;
    for (items) |x| t += x;
    return t;
}

fn square(x: u32) u64 {
    return @as(u64, x) * x;
}

test "push, pushAll, pop" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    var s: Stack(u32) = .{};
    defer s.deinit(a);
    try s.push(a, 1);
    try s.pushAll(a, &.{ 2, 3 });
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u32, 3), s.pop());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 2), s.slice().len);
    try std.testing.expect(Stack(u32).Item == u32);
}

test "map to a different element type" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    var s: Stack(u32) = .{};
    defer s.deinit(a);
    try s.pushAll(a, &.{ 2, 3, 4 });
    var sq = try s.map(a, square);
    defer sq.deinit(a);
    try std.testing.expect(@TypeOf(sq) == Stack(u64));
    try std.testing.expectEqualSlices(u64, &.{ 4, 9, 16 }, sq.slice());
}

test "total is duck typed" {
    const a = std.testing.allocator;
    var s: Stack(u32) = .{};
    defer s.deinit(a);
    try s.pushAll(a, &.{ 10, 20 });
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 30), total(s));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 6), total(@as([]const i32, &.{ 1, 2, 3 })));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 3), total([_]u8{ 1, 2 }));
}

@TypeOf(f(@as(T, undefined))) asks "what would f return for a T?" without running it. In total, the if on @typeInfo and @hasDecl is resolved at compile time, so each instantiation contains only the branch it needs; the guard on .@"struct" is what keeps @hasDecl legal when a slice is passed.

Check your understanding

  1. How do you write a generic struct in Zig?
    AnswerA function with a comptime T: type parameter that returns a struct { ... } using T. Calling it, e.g. Stack(i32), produces the type.
  2. What is @This() for?
    AnswerIt names the enclosing struct from inside it, which an anonymous struct returned from a function otherwise could not do; the idiom is const Self = @This();.
  3. What is the difference between fn f(comptime T: type, x: T) and fn f(x: anytype)?
    AnswerThe first makes the caller name the type and checks x against it; the second infers the type from the argument exactly (so a literal arrives as comptime_int). Use @TypeOf(x) to name the inferred type.
  4. Is Stack(i32) in one function the same type as Stack(i32) in another?
    AnswerYes. Type-returning functions are memoised on their comptime arguments, so identical arguments give the identical type.
  5. How do you reject an unsuitable T with a readable message?
    AnswerCheck @typeInfo(T) (or @hasDecl/@hasField) at the top of the generic function and call @compileError("... " ++ @typeName(T)) in the failing case.
  6. Why must you guard @hasDecl(T, "x") with a @typeInfo check in an anytype function?
    Answer@hasDecl only accepts struct, enum, union and opaque types; passing a u8 or a slice is a compile error, so test the kind of type first.
  7. What does monomorphisation cost, and how do you limit it?
    AnswerOne compiled copy per distinct instantiation, which adds compile time and binary size. Keep generic functions small, move type-independent work into non-generic helpers, and do not use anytype where a concrete type will do.
What you learned.
  • A generic type is a function fn Name(comptime T: type) type returning a struct; const Self = @This(); names it inside.
  • Generic functions take comptime T: type explicitly, or anytype to infer from the argument, with @TypeOf to name it; return types may depend on parameters.
  • @hasDecl and @hasField give compile-time duck typing; guard them with @typeInfo.
  • Instantiations with equal arguments are the same type; Pair(B, A) can appear inside Pair(A, B).
  • Constrain T up front with @typeInfo and @compileError so mistakes are reported at the instantiation.
  • std.ArrayList is a thirty-line idea: items, capacity, allocator on growth.
  • Each instantiation is compiled separately (monomorphisation): fast code, more compile time; keep generic surfaces small.

27. Reflection with @typeInfo

In this chapter you will ask the compiler questions about types: what kind of thing a type is, what fields a struct has, what tags an enum has, and whether a name exists. You will use the answers, at compile time, to write one function that handles many types. By the end you will understand the tuning-table validator that IRON LEDGER runs on every build.

27.1 Types are values, and values have types

In Chapter 26 you passed types into functions as comptime T: type. Reflection is the other direction: given a value or a type, ask the compiler what it is. The first tool is @TypeOf, which takes any expression and returns its type without evaluating it at run time. The second is @typeName, which turns a type into a string you can print.

typeof.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const a = 42;
    const b: u8 = 42;
    const c = 2.5;
    const name = "Shadow Hawk";
    const list = [_]u16{ 1, 2, 3 };

    std.debug.print("a is {s}\n", .{@typeName(@TypeOf(a))});
    std.debug.print("b is {s}\n", .{@typeName(@TypeOf(b))});
    std.debug.print("c is {s}\n", .{@typeName(@TypeOf(c))});
    std.debug.print("name is {s}\n", .{@typeName(@TypeOf(name))});
    std.debug.print("list is {s}\n", .{@typeName(@TypeOf(list))});
    std.debug.print("list[0..] is {s}\n", .{@typeName(@TypeOf(list[0..]))});
    std.debug.print("a + b is {s}\n", .{@typeName(@TypeOf(a + b))});
}
a is comptime_int
b is u8
c is comptime_float
name is *const [11:0]u8
list is [3]u16
list[0..] is *const [3]u16
a + b is u8

Every line here teaches something you already half knew. A bare literal like 42 is a comptime_int, not a u8 or an i32: it has no width until it meets a typed variable. A string literal is a pointer to a constant, sentinel-terminated array of bytes, which is why "Shadow Hawk" shows as *const [11:0]u8. Slicing an array with [0..] gives a pointer to the whole array, not a slice, because the length is still known. And a + b is a u8: the untyped literal adopted the concrete type next to it.

Why this matters. Zig has no auto keyword and no type inference across function boundaries, but inside an expression the compiler always knows the type. @TypeOf lets you name that type in places where you would otherwise repeat it, such as var copy: @TypeOf(original) = original;. It is also how generic functions with anytype parameters discover what they were given.

27.2 @typeInfo: a description of a type

@typeInfo(T) returns a value of type std.builtin.Type, which is a tagged union (Chapter 14). Each tag names a kind of type, and most tags carry a payload struct with the details. Because it is a tagged union, you inspect it with switch, and because the argument is a type, the whole switch happens at compile time.

describe.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn describe(comptime T: type) []const u8 {
    return switch (@typeInfo(T)) {
        .int => |info| if (info.signedness == .signed) "a signed integer" else "an unsigned integer",
        .float => "a float",
        .bool => "a boolean",
        .pointer => "a pointer",
        .array => "an array",
        .optional => "an optional",
        .error_union => "an error union",
        .@"struct" => "a struct",
        .@"enum" => "an enum",
        .@"union" => "a union",
        .@"fn" => "a function",
        else => "something else",
    };
}

const Role = enum { pilot, tech, medic };
const Pilot = struct { name: []const u8, gunnery: u8 };

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("u32:       {s}\n", .{describe(u32)});
    std.debug.print("i8:        {s}\n", .{describe(i8)});
    std.debug.print("f64:       {s}\n", .{describe(f64)});
    std.debug.print("bool:      {s}\n", .{describe(bool)});
    std.debug.print("*u8:       {s}\n", .{describe(*u8)});
    std.debug.print("[]u8:      {s}\n", .{describe([]const u8)});
    std.debug.print("[4]u8:     {s}\n", .{describe([4]u8)});
    std.debug.print("?u8:       {s}\n", .{describe(?u8)});
    std.debug.print("!u8:       {s}\n", .{describe(anyerror!u8)});
    std.debug.print("Pilot:     {s}\n", .{describe(Pilot)});
    std.debug.print("Role:      {s}\n", .{describe(Role)});
    std.debug.print("fn:        {s}\n", .{describe(@TypeOf(describe))});
}
u32:       an unsigned integer
i8:        a signed integer
f64:       a float
bool:      a boolean
*u8:       a pointer
[]u8:      a pointer
[4]u8:     an array
?u8:       an optional
!u8:       an error union
Pilot:     a struct
Role:      an enum
fn:        a function

Two details of the spelling deserve a pause. The tags for struct, enum, union and function are .@"struct", .@"enum", .@"union" and .@"fn": those words are keywords in Zig, and the @"…" syntax lets an identifier be spelled with a keyword. The other tags are plain lower-case words: .int, .float, .bool, .pointer, .array, .optional, .error_union, .vector, .void, .type.

Old tutorials will mislead you. Before 0.14 the tags were capitalised: .Int, .Struct, .Enum. In 0.16 those do not exist. If a snippet on the web writes @typeInfo(T).Struct.fields, translate it to @typeInfo(T).@"struct".fields.

Notice also that a slice ([]const u8) reports as .pointer. A slice is a pointer with a length, and the pointer payload tells you which flavour it is through a size field: .one, .many, .slice or .c.

Here is the full list of tags in std.builtin.Type as shipped with 0.16, so you never have to guess:

TagPayload fields you will use
.intsignedness (.signed / .unsigned), bits
.floatbits
.bool, .void, .type, .comptime_int, .comptime_floatno payload
.pointersize, child, is_const, alignment, sentinel_ptr
.arraylen, child, sentinel_ptr
.optionalchild
.error_unionerror_set, payload
.error_setan optional slice of Error (name)
.@"struct"fields, decls, layout, is_tuple, backing_integer
.@"enum"fields, decls, tag_type, is_exhaustive
.@"union"fields, decls, tag_type (optional), layout
.@"fn"params, return_type, is_generic, calling_convention
.vectorlen, child
.@"opaque", .enum_literal, .null, .undefined, .noreturnrare

27.3 Reading the payload

The tag tells you the kind; the payload tells you the details. You capture it in a switch arm with |info|, or reach for it directly with field syntax when you already know the kind: @typeInfo(i16).int is the Int payload, and it is a compile error if i16 were not an integer.

intinfo.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn bitsOf(comptime T: type) u16 {
    return switch (@typeInfo(T)) {
        .int => |i| i.bits,
        .float => |f| f.bits,
        else => @compileError("bitsOf wants a number type, got " ++ @typeName(T)),
    };
}

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("u8 has {d} bits\n", .{bitsOf(u8)});
    std.debug.print("i64 has {d} bits\n", .{bitsOf(i64)});
    std.debug.print("u3 has {d} bits\n", .{bitsOf(u3)});
    std.debug.print("f32 has {d} bits\n", .{bitsOf(f32)});
    const info = @typeInfo(i16).int;
    std.debug.print("i16: signedness={s} bits={d}\n", .{ @tagName(info.signedness), info.bits });
    const opt = @typeInfo(?u32).optional;
    std.debug.print("?u32 wraps {s}\n", .{@typeName(opt.child)});
    const arr = @typeInfo([5]f32).array;
    std.debug.print("[5]f32: {d} of {s}\n", .{ arr.len, @typeName(arr.child) });
    const ptr = @typeInfo([]const u8).pointer;
    std.debug.print("[]const u8: size={s} const={} child={s}\n", .{ @tagName(ptr.size), ptr.is_const, @typeName(ptr.child) });
}
u8 has 8 bits
i64 has 64 bits
u3 has 3 bits
f32 has 32 bits
i16: signedness=signed bits=16
?u32 wraps u32
[5]f32: 5 of f32
[]const u8: size=slice const=true child=u8

bitsOf shows the standard shape of a reflective function: switch on the info, use the payload in the arms you support, and turn every other kind into a @compileError with a helpful message. The message is built with ++, which concatenates strings at compile time, so it can include @typeName(T). Try calling bitsOf(bool) and read the error: it names your function, your message and the offending type.

Compile errors are the point. A reflective function that quietly does the wrong thing for an unexpected type is worse than one that refuses. Always end the switch with else => @compileError(…) unless "do nothing" is genuinely the right behaviour, as it is in the validator later in this chapter.

27.4 Walking the fields of a struct

The most useful payload is .@"struct".fields: a slice of StructField, each with a name, a type, and whether it has a default. Combined with inline for, which unrolls the loop at compile time, and @field(value, name), which reads a field by a compile-time known name, you can visit every field of any struct without knowing the struct in advance.

walk.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Pilot = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    gunnery: u8,
    piloting: u8,
    salary: u32,
    active: bool,
};

fn printFields(value: anytype) void {
    const T = @TypeOf(value);
    const info = @typeInfo(T).@"struct";
    std.debug.print("{s} has {d} fields:\n", .{ @typeName(T), info.fields.len });
    inline for (info.fields) |f| {
        std.debug.print("  {s}: {s} = {any}\n", .{ f.name, @typeName(f.type), @field(value, f.name) });
    }
}

pub fn main() void {
    const p = Pilot{ .name = "Kell", .gunnery = 3, .piloting = 4, .salary = 1500, .active = true };
    printFields(p);
}
walk.Pilot has 5 fields:
  name: []const u8 = { 75, 101, 108, 108 }
  gunnery: u8 = 3
  piloting: u8 = 4
  salary: u32 = 1500
  active: bool = true

Read printFields slowly. It takes anytype, so it is specialised per argument type. @TypeOf(value) recovers the type. @typeInfo(T).@"struct" would be a compile error for a non-struct, which is fine: that is the contract. Then inline for runs the body once per field, at compile time, with f a different constant each time. Inside, f.name is a string, f.type is a type, and @field(value, f.name) is the actual field value, with its own concrete type.

The one blemish is the name: {any} printed the string as a list of byte values, because to the formatter a []const u8 is just a slice of integers. You already know the fix from Chapter 23: pick the format by type. Reflection lets you do that inside the loop.

walk2.zig

fn printFields(value: anytype) void {
    const T = @TypeOf(value);
    inline for (@typeInfo(T).@"struct".fields) |f| {
        const v = @field(value, f.name);
        switch (@typeInfo(f.type)) {
            .int => std.debug.print("  {s} = {d}\n", .{ f.name, v }),
            .bool => std.debug.print("  {s} = {}\n", .{ f.name, v }),
            .pointer => std.debug.print("  {s} = \"{s}\"\n", .{ f.name, v }),
            else => std.debug.print("  {s} = ?\n", .{f.name}),
        }
    }
}

  name = "Kell"
  gunnery = 3
  piloting = 4
  salary = 1500
  active = true

The inner switch (@typeInfo(f.type)) is resolved at compile time for each field, so the compiled program contains five straight-line print calls and no switch at all. This pattern, an outer inline for over fields and an inner switch on each field's kind, is the heart of every serializer, pretty-printer and validator written in Zig. Exercise 27.2 asks you to grow it into a general toString.

27.5 Writing fields by name

@field works on the left of an assignment too, provided you have a pointer to the struct. This is how a settings screen or a command parser can map a run-time string like "turnover" onto a field, without a hand-written table that goes stale.

setfield.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Tuning = struct { fatigue_tired: u8 = 30, exhausted: u8 = 70, turnover: u8 = 3 };

fn setByName(t: *Tuning, name: []const u8, value: u8) bool {
    inline for (@typeInfo(Tuning).@"struct".fields) |f| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, f.name, name)) {
            @field(t, f.name) = value;
            return true;
        }
    }
    return false;
}

pub fn main() void {
    var t = Tuning{};
    _ = setByName(&t, "turnover", 5);
    const ok = setByName(&t, "nonsense", 1);
    std.debug.print("turnover={d} nonsense-accepted={}\n", .{ t.turnover, ok });
}
turnover=5 nonsense-accepted=false

The inline for is unrolled at compile time, but the std.mem.eql inside runs at run time, once per field, because name is a run-time value. So this compiles to three string comparisons. That is the usual division of labour: the shape is fixed at compile time, the data flows at run time.

All fields must accept the value. The line @field(t, f.name) = value is compiled once per field, so it must type-check for every field. Here every field is a u8, so a u8 value works. If one field were a u32 and another a bool, you would need an inner switch on f.type to convert or skip, exactly as in walk2.zig.

27.6 @hasField, @hasDecl and the decls list

Sometimes you do not need to walk everything; you just want to know whether a name exists. @hasField(T, "name") answers for fields, @hasDecl(T, "name") for declarations (functions and constants inside the struct). Both return a compile-time bool, so they combine naturally with if to select code paths per type.

has.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Mek = struct {
    tonnage: u32,
    pub fn describe(self: Mek) u32 {
        return self.tonnage;
    }
    pub const max_tonnage = 100;
};
const Rock = struct { mass: u32 };

fn weightOf(thing: anytype) u32 {
    const T = @TypeOf(thing);
    if (@hasField(T, "tonnage")) return thing.tonnage;
    if (@hasField(T, "mass")) return thing.mass;
    @compileError(@typeName(T) ++ " has neither tonnage nor mass");
}

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("mek: {d}\n", .{weightOf(Mek{ .tonnage = 55 })});
    std.debug.print("rock: {d}\n", .{weightOf(Rock{ .mass = 3 })});
    std.debug.print("Mek has describe: {}\n", .{@hasDecl(Mek, "describe")});
    std.debug.print("Rock has describe: {}\n", .{@hasDecl(Rock, "describe")});
    inline for (@typeInfo(Mek).@"struct".decls) |d| {
        std.debug.print("Mek decl: {s}\n", .{d.name});
    }
}
mek: 55
rock: 3
Mek has describe: true
Rock has describe: false
Mek decl: describe
Mek decl: max_tonnage

weightOf is a small example of what other languages call duck typing, except that it is checked when the program is compiled rather than when the line runs. Pass a type with neither field and the @compileError fires with the type's name in the message. Note that the if statements are not comptime if in any special syntax: because the condition is a compile-time constant, the compiler simply drops the branches that cannot be taken, including the @compileError when it is unreachable.

The decls list only contains public declarations. Private functions are invisible to reflection from outside, which keeps @hasDecl honest as an interface check: "does this type provide a public describe?"

27.7 Enums under the microscope

Enums (Chapter 13) expose their tags through .@"enum".fields, each an EnumField with a name and an integer value. The payload also tells you the tag integer type and whether the enum is exhaustive. The length of the field list is a compile-time integer, so it can size an array.

enuminfo.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Stream = enum { combat, market, weather, names };

pub fn main() void {
    const info = @typeInfo(Stream).@"enum";
    std.debug.print("tag type {s}, exhaustive={}\n", .{ @typeName(info.tag_type), info.is_exhaustive });
    inline for (info.fields) |f| {
        std.debug.print("  {s} = {d}\n", .{ f.name, f.value });
    }
    var counters = [_]u32{0} ** info.fields.len;
    counters[@intFromEnum(Stream.weather)] += 1;
    std.debug.print("counters has {d} slots\n", .{counters.len});
