    const parsed = std.meta.stringToEnum(Stream, "market");
    std.debug.print("parsed: {?}\n", .{parsed});
}
tag type u2, exhaustive=true
  combat = 0
  market = 1
  weather = 2
  names = 3
counters has 4 slots
parsed: .market

Notice the tag type: the compiler picked u2, the smallest integer that holds four values. The array counters has exactly one slot per tag, and if someone adds a fifth stream to the enum, the array grows with it and no test needs to change. This is precisely how IRON LEDGER sizes its array of random number generators, one per Stream.

std.meta.stringToEnum is the standard library's version of the loop you would write yourself with inline for over the fields and std.mem.eql. Exercise 27.5 has you write it, so you can see there is no magic.

27.8 Making types: @Int and @Enum

Reflection also runs in reverse: you can construct a type from a description. Older Zig had one builtin, @Type, that took a std.builtin.Type value. Zig 0.16 removed it and replaced it with one builtin per kind: @Int(signedness, bits), @Enum(tag_type, mode, names, values), @Struct(…) and so on. You will rarely need these; the standard library wraps the common ones as std.meta.Int. But they are worth seeing once.

attype.zig

const std = @import("std");

const U12 = @Int(.unsigned, 12);

fn Unsigned(comptime bits: u16) type {
    return @Int(.unsigned, bits);
}

const Color = @Enum(u8, .exhaustive, &.{ "red", "green", "blue" }, &.{ 0, 1, 2 });

pub fn main() void {
    const x: U12 = 4095;
    std.debug.print("{s} max = {d}\n", .{ @typeName(U12), x });
    const y: Unsigned(20) = 1_000_000;
    std.debug.print("{s} holds {d}\n", .{ @typeName(@TypeOf(y)), y });
    std.debug.print("Unsigned(12) == u12: {}\n", .{Unsigned(12) == u12});
    std.debug.print("std.meta.Int(.signed, 7) == i7: {}\n", .{std.meta.Int(.signed, 7) == i7});
    const c: Color = .green;
    std.debug.print("Color.green = {d}\n", .{@intFromEnum(c)});
}
u12 max = 4095
u20 holds 1000000
Unsigned(12) == u12: true
std.meta.Int(.signed, 7) == i7: true
Color.green = 1

Two things to take from this. First, types are compared with == and a constructed u12 is the same type as the one you would write by hand; there is only one u12. Second, the arguments to @Enum are ordinary compile-time values (a slice of names, a slice of values), which means a program can compute an enum from a table. That is a deep rabbit hole; for this course, knowing that @Type is gone and @Int exists is enough.

Trap. If you paste code that calls @Type(.{ .int = … }), 0.16 says error: invalid builtin function: '@Type'. Replace it with @Int(.unsigned, bits) or std.meta.Int(.unsigned, bits).

27.9 Worked example: validating a tuning table

Now the pieces come together. IRON LEDGER keeps every balance constant in one nested struct, Tuning, loaded from a data file (the next chapter explains how). The designers wanted a test that checks every unsigned knob is positive and every basis-point knob (a field whose name ends in _bp) is at most 100,000, and they wanted the test to cover new knobs automatically. Here is the whole thing, with a small stand-in table so the file runs on its own.

tuning.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Tuning = struct {
    person: struct { fatigue_tired: u8, exhausted_fatigue: u8, turnover_target: u8 },
    market: struct { fab_cost_bp: u32, fab_days: u32, morale_delta: i8 },
};

const t = Tuning{
    .person = .{ .fatigue_tired = 30, .exhausted_fatigue = 70, .turnover_target = 3 },
    .market = .{ .fab_cost_bp = 12_000, .fab_days = 14, .morale_delta = -2 },
};

fn checkPositive(comptime T: type, value: T, comptime name: []const u8) !void {
    switch (@typeInfo(T)) {
        .int => |info| {
            if (info.signedness == .signed) return;
            if (value <= 0) {
                std.debug.print("tuning field {s} must be positive\n", .{name});
                return error.BadTuning;
            }
            if (std.mem.endsWith(u8, name, "_bp") and value > 100_000) {
                std.debug.print("tuning field {s} is over 100000 basis points\n", .{name});
                return error.BadTuning;
            }
        },
        .@"struct" => |info| inline for (info.fields) |f|
            try checkPositive(f.type, @field(value, f.name), name ++ "." ++ f.name),
        else => {},
    }
}

test "every tuning value is positive and every basis-point knob is sane" {
    try checkPositive(Tuning, t, "t");
}

test "a zero knob is caught" {
    var bad = t;
    bad.market.fab_days = 0;
    try std.testing.expectError(error.BadTuning, checkPositive(Tuning, bad, "bad"));
}

test "a silly basis-point knob is caught" {
    var bad = t;
    bad.market.fab_cost_bp = 5_000_000;
    try std.testing.expectError(error.BadTuning, checkPositive(Tuning, bad, "bad"));
}
$ zig test tuning.zig
1/3 tuning.test.every tuning value is positive and every basis-point knob is sane...OK
2/3 tuning.test.a zero knob is caught...tuning field bad.market.fab_days must be positive
OK
3/3 tuning.test.a silly basis-point knob is caught...tuning field bad.market.fab_cost_bp is over 100000 basis points
OK
All 3 tests passed.

Walk through checkPositive one arm at a time.

  • The .int arm is the only one that does run-time work. Signed integers are skipped entirely (deltas may be negative by design). Unsigned ones are compared against zero, and if the dotted name ends in _bp, against the basis-point ceiling. std.mem.endsWith runs on a comptime string here, so the compiler evaluates it and drops the whole if for fields whose names do not qualify.
  • The .@"struct" arm is pure compile-time recursion. For each field it calls checkPositive again with three arguments: the field's type, the field's value read with @field, and a longer name made with ++. Because T and name are comptime parameters, each call is a distinct specialisation, and by the time the program runs there is no recursion left, only a flat list of integer checks with their names baked into the error messages.
  • The else => {} arm is deliberate. Floats, enums, booleans and strings are not knobs this test cares about, so it passes over them rather than refusing. This is the one place where a silent else is the right design, because the test is about a specific property, not about supporting every type.

The payoff is in the last sentence of the guide's description: add a knob to the table and it is covered by this test with no change to the test. Exercise 27.4 asks you to extend the validator with arrays, optionals and floats.

In IRON LEDGER. The validator above is lifted almost line for line from game/src/domain/tuning.zig, where the real Tuning struct has seven sections and well over a hundred knobs; the test at the bottom of that file is simply try checkPositive(Tuning, t, "t");. The other big use of reflection is the SQLite binding in game/src/persist/sqlite.zig, which binds any value to a prepared statement by switching on its type: 
pub fn bind(self: Stmt, idx: c_int, value: anytype) Error!void {
    const T = @TypeOf(value);
    const rc = switch (@typeInfo(T)) {
        .int, .comptime_int => sqlite3_bind_int64(self.h, idx, @intCast(value)),
        .bool => sqlite3_bind_int64(self.h, idx, @intFromBool(value)),
        .@"enum" => blk: {
            if (@typeInfo(T).@"enum".is_exhaustive) {
                const name = @tagName(value);
                break :blk sqlite3_bind_text(self.h, idx, name.ptr, @intCast(name.len), transient);
            }
            break :blk sqlite3_bind_int64(self.h, idx, @intCast(@intFromEnum(value)));
        },
        .optional => if (value) |v| return self.bind(idx, v) else sqlite3_bind_null(self.h, idx),
        .pointer => blk: {
            const s: []const u8 = value;
            break :blk sqlite3_bind_text(self.h, idx, s.ptr, @intCast(s.len), transient);
        },
        else => @compileError("unsupported bind type " ++ @typeName(T)),
    };
    // …
}
Read the enum arm: exhaustive enums are stored by name so a save file stays readable, while non-exhaustive typed IDs are stored as integers. That policy lives in one place because reflection let it.

Exercises

Exercise 27.1 · Describe a type warm-up

Write describe(comptime T: type) []const u8 returning a short kind name (distinguish slices from other pointers), bitsOf for ints and floats with a compile error otherwise, and fits(T, n) using std.math.minInt / maxInt. File: exercises/27-reflection/ex1_describe.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 27, exercise 1: describe a type.
//! Run with:  zig test ex1_describe.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Return a short human description of T, built only from @typeInfo.
pub fn describe(comptime T: type) []const u8 {
    return switch (@typeInfo(T)) {
        .int => |i| if (i.signedness == .signed) "signed int" else "unsigned int",
        .float => "float",
        .bool => "bool",
        .pointer => |p| if (p.size == .slice) "slice" else "pointer",
        .array => "array",
        .optional => "optional",
        .error_union => "error union",
        .@"struct" => "struct",
        .@"enum" => "enum",
        .@"union" => "union",
        .@"fn" => "function",
        else => "other",
    };
}

/// How many bits an int or float occupies. Compile error for anything else.
pub fn bitsOf(comptime T: type) u16 {
    return switch (@typeInfo(T)) {
        .int => |i| i.bits,
        .float => |f| f.bits,
        else => @compileError("bitsOf: not a number: " ++ @typeName(T)),
    };
}

/// True when T is an integer that can hold `n` without overflow.
pub fn fits(comptime T: type, n: comptime_int) bool {
    return n >= std.math.minInt(T) and n <= std.math.maxInt(T);
}

test "describe" {
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("unsigned int", describe(u8));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("signed int", describe(i32));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("float", describe(f16));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("slice", describe([]const u8));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("pointer", describe(*u8));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("array", describe([3]u8));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("optional", describe(?u8));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("error union", describe(anyerror!void));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("struct", describe(struct { a: u8 }));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("enum", describe(enum { a, b }));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("union", describe(union(enum) { a: u8 }));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("function", describe(@TypeOf(describe)));
}

test "bitsOf" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u16, 8), bitsOf(u8));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u16, 3), bitsOf(u3));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u16, 64), bitsOf(f64));
}

test "fits" {
    try std.testing.expect(fits(u8, 255));
    try std.testing.expect(!fits(u8, 256));
    try std.testing.expect(fits(i8, -128));
    try std.testing.expect(!fits(i8, 128));
}

The pointer arm captures its payload to look at p.size. fits needs no reflection at all: std.math.maxInt(T) is itself implemented with @typeInfo.

Exercise 27.2 · A generic toString practice

Write toString(w: *std.Io.Writer, value: anytype) that prints ints, floats, bools, enum tag names, optionals (null or the payload), []const u8 in quotes, arrays as [a, b] and structs as {field=value, …}, recursively. File: exercises/27-reflection/ex2_tostring.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 27, exercise 2: a generic toString.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_tostring.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Write a readable form of `value` into `w`, choosing the format by type.
/// Structs print as {field=value, ...}, enums as their tag name, optionals
/// as "null" or the payload, []const u8 as quoted text.
pub fn toString(w: *std.Io.Writer, value: anytype) std.Io.Writer.Error!void {
    const T = @TypeOf(value);
    switch (@typeInfo(T)) {
        .int, .comptime_int => try w.print("{d}", .{value}),
        .float, .comptime_float => try w.print("{d:.2}", .{value}),
        .bool => try w.print("{}", .{value}),
        .@"enum" => try w.print("{s}", .{@tagName(value)}),
        .optional => if (value) |v| try toString(w, v) else try w.writeAll("null"),
        .pointer => |p| {
            if (p.size == .slice and p.child == u8) {
                try w.print("\"{s}\"", .{value});
            } else if (p.size == .one) {
                try toString(w, value.*);
            } else {
                @compileError("toString: unsupported pointer " ++ @typeName(T));
            }
        },
        .array => {
            try w.writeAll("[");
            for (value, 0..) |item, i| {
                if (i != 0) try w.writeAll(", ");
                try toString(w, item);
            }
            try w.writeAll("]");
        },
        .@"struct" => |info| {
            try w.writeAll("{");
            inline for (info.fields, 0..) |f, i| {
                if (i != 0) try w.writeAll(", ");
                try w.print("{s}=", .{f.name});
                try toString(w, @field(value, f.name));
            }
            try w.writeAll("}");
        },
        else => @compileError("toString: unsupported type " ++ @typeName(T)),
    }
}

/// Convenience: render into a fixed buffer and return the written slice.
pub fn toBuf(buf: []u8, value: anytype) ![]u8 {
    var w = std.Io.Writer.fixed(buf);
    try toString(&w, value);
    return w.buffered();
}

const Role = enum { pilot, tech };
const Pilot = struct { name: []const u8, role: Role, gunnery: u8, callsign: ?[]const u8 };

test "scalars" {
    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("42", try toBuf(&buf, @as(u8, 42)));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("true", try toBuf(&buf, true));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("tech", try toBuf(&buf, Role.tech));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("null", try toBuf(&buf, @as(?u8, null)));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("7", try toBuf(&buf, @as(?u8, 7)));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("\"hi\"", try toBuf(&buf, @as([]const u8, "hi")));
}

test "arrays and structs" {
    var buf: [128]u8 = undefined;
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("[1, 2, 3]", try toBuf(&buf, [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3 }));
    const p = Pilot{ .name = "Kell", .role = .pilot, .gunnery = 3, .callsign = null };
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings(
        "{name=\"Kell\", role=pilot, gunnery=3, callsign=null}",
        try toBuf(&buf, p),
    );
    const q = Pilot{ .name = "Ana", .role = .tech, .gunnery = 5, .callsign = "Wrench" };
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings(
        "{name=\"Ana\", role=tech, gunnery=5, callsign=\"Wrench\"}",
        try toBuf(&buf, q),
    );
}

test "nested struct" {
    var buf: [128]u8 = undefined;
    const Pos = struct { x: i32, y: i32 };
    const Unit = struct { id: u16, pos: Pos };
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings(
        "{id=9, pos={x=-1, y=4}}",
        try toBuf(&buf, Unit{ .id = 9, .pos = .{ .x = -1, .y = 4 } }),
    );
}

Every arm either prints or recurses. The .pointer arm must decide between "a string" and "a pointer to one thing", which is why it inspects p.size and p.child. The inline for with 0.. gives an index so commas go between fields.

Exercise 27.3 · Generic deep equality practice

Write eql(a: anytype, b: @TypeOf(a)) bool that compares scalars with ==, optionals, arrays and slices element by element (slices by content, not address), structs field by field and tagged unions by tag then payload. File: exercises/27-reflection/ex3_equal.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 27, exercise 3: a generic deep equality.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_equal.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Deep structural equality. Slices compare by content, not by address.
pub fn eql(a: anytype, b: @TypeOf(a)) bool {
    const T = @TypeOf(a);
    switch (@typeInfo(T)) {
        .void => return true,
        .int, .comptime_int, .float, .comptime_float, .bool, .@"enum" => return a == b,
        .optional => {
            if (a == null and b == null) return true;
            if (a == null or b == null) return false;
            return eql(a.?, b.?);
        },
        .array => {
            for (a, b) |x, y| if (!eql(x, y)) return false;
            return true;
        },
        .pointer => |p| switch (p.size) {
            .one => return eql(a.*, b.*),
            .slice => {
                if (a.len != b.len) return false;
                for (a, b) |x, y| if (!eql(x, y)) return false;
                return true;
            },
            else => @compileError("eql: unsupported pointer " ++ @typeName(T)),
        },
        .@"struct" => |info| {
            inline for (info.fields) |f| {
                if (!eql(@field(a, f.name), @field(b, f.name))) return false;
            }
            return true;
        },
        .@"union" => |info| {
            if (info.tag_type == null) @compileError("eql: untagged union " ++ @typeName(T));
            const Tag = info.tag_type.?;
            const ta: Tag = a;
            const tb: Tag = b;
            if (ta != tb) return false;
            inline for (info.fields) |f| {
                if (ta == @field(Tag, f.name)) {
                    return eql(@field(a, f.name), @field(b, f.name));
                }
            }
            unreachable;
        },
        else => @compileError("eql: unsupported type " ++ @typeName(T)),
    }
}

const Pilot = struct { name: []const u8, gunnery: u8, callsign: ?[]const u8 };
const Event = union(enum) { none, wound: u8, promoted: []const u8 };

test "scalars and optionals" {
    try std.testing.expect(eql(@as(u8, 3), 3));
    try std.testing.expect(!eql(@as(u8, 3), 4));
    try std.testing.expect(eql(@as(?u8, null), null));
    try std.testing.expect(!eql(@as(?u8, 1), null));
}

test "slices compare by content" {
    const a: []const u8 = "Kell";
    var storage = [_]u8{ 'K', 'e', 'l', 'l' };
    const b: []const u8 = storage[0..];
    try std.testing.expect(a.ptr != b.ptr);
    try std.testing.expect(eql(a, b));
    try std.testing.expect(!eql(a, @as([]const u8, "Kel")));
}

test "structs with slices and optionals" {
    const p = Pilot{ .name = "Kell", .gunnery = 3, .callsign = "Ace" };
    var q = Pilot{ .name = "Kell", .gunnery = 3, .callsign = "Ace" };
    try std.testing.expect(eql(p, q));
    q.callsign = null;
    try std.testing.expect(!eql(p, q));
    q.callsign = "Ace";
    q.gunnery = 4;
    try std.testing.expect(!eql(p, q));
}

test "tagged unions" {
    try std.testing.expect(eql(Event{ .wound = 2 }, Event{ .wound = 2 }));
    try std.testing.expect(!eql(Event{ .wound = 2 }, Event{ .wound = 3 }));
    try std.testing.expect(!eql(Event{ .wound = 2 }, Event.none));
    try std.testing.expect(eql(Event{ .promoted = "Sgt" }, Event{ .promoted = "Sgt" }));
}

test "arrays of structs" {
    const a = [_]Pilot{ .{ .name = "A", .gunnery = 1, .callsign = null } };
    const b = [_]Pilot{ .{ .name = "A", .gunnery = 1, .callsign = null } };
    try std.testing.expect(eql(a, b));
}

The union arm is the subtle one: coerce both values to the tag type to compare tags, then inline for over the union fields and compare the payload of the matching one. A void payload (like .none) needs its own arm returning true, since == is not defined on void.

Exercise 27.4 · A stronger tuning validator challenge

Extend the worked example: unsigned ints must be positive, _bp names at most 100,000, floats within 0 and 1, optionals checked when present, arrays element by element, structs recursively. Report the dotted path of the bad knob. File: exercises/27-reflection/ex4_validator.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 27, exercise 4: a tuning-table validator.
//! Run with:  zig test ex4_validator.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

pub const Tuning = struct {
    person: struct { fatigue_tired: u8, exhausted_fatigue: u8, morale_delta: i8 },
    market: struct { fab_cost_bp: u32, fab_days: u32, rarity_target: [3]u8 },
    battle: struct { salvage_bp: u32, retreat_chance: ?f32 },
};

pub const stock = Tuning{
    .person = .{ .fatigue_tired = 30, .exhausted_fatigue = 70, .morale_delta = -2 },
    .market = .{ .fab_cost_bp = 12_000, .fab_days = 14, .rarity_target = .{ 5, 3, 1 } },
    .battle = .{ .salvage_bp = 2_500, .retreat_chance = 0.25 },
};

pub const Problem = error{ Zero, TooManyBasisPoints, BadFraction };

/// Walk `value` recursively. Rules:
///  - unsigned ints must be > 0                     (error.Zero)
///  - names ending in _bp must be <= 100_000        (error.TooManyBasisPoints)
///  - floats must be within 0.0 ... 1.0 inclusive   (error.BadFraction)
///  - signed ints are free, optionals check the payload when present,
///    arrays check every element, structs recurse into every field.
/// On failure, print "bad knob: <dotted.path>" to stderr before returning.
pub fn validate(comptime T: type, value: T, comptime path: []const u8) Problem!void {
    switch (@typeInfo(T)) {
        .int => |info| {
            if (info.signedness == .signed) return;
            if (value == 0) return fail(path, error.Zero);
            const is_bp = comptime std.mem.endsWith(u8, path, "_bp");
            if (is_bp and value > 100_000) return fail(path, error.TooManyBasisPoints);
        },
        .float => if (value < 0.0 or value > 1.0) return fail(path, error.BadFraction),
        .optional => |o| if (value) |v| try validate(o.child, v, path),
        .array => |a| for (value) |item| try validate(a.child, item, path ++ "[]"),
        .@"struct" => |info| inline for (info.fields) |f|
            try validate(f.type, @field(value, f.name), path ++ "." ++ f.name),
        else => {},
    }
}

fn fail(path: []const u8, err: Problem) Problem!void {
    std.debug.print("bad knob: {s}\n", .{path});
    return err;
}

test "stock tuning passes" {
    try validate(Tuning, stock, "t");
}

test "zero in a nested struct" {
    var t = stock;
    t.market.fab_days = 0;
    try std.testing.expectError(error.Zero, validate(Tuning, t, "t"));
}

test "basis points too large" {
    var t = stock;
    t.battle.salvage_bp = 200_000;
    try std.testing.expectError(error.TooManyBasisPoints, validate(Tuning, t, "t"));
}

test "zero inside an array element" {
    var t = stock;
    t.market.rarity_target[2] = 0;
    try std.testing.expectError(error.Zero, validate(Tuning, t, "t"));
}

test "optional float out of range, and null is fine" {
    var t = stock;
    t.battle.retreat_chance = 1.5;
    try std.testing.expectError(error.BadFraction, validate(Tuning, t, "t"));
    t.battle.retreat_chance = null;
    try validate(Tuning, t, "t");
}

test "signed ints may be negative" {
    var t = stock;
    t.person.morale_delta = -100;
    try validate(Tuning, t, "t");
}

One trap worth remembering: comptime std.mem.endsWith(…) and value > 100_000 makes the comptime keyword apply to the whole and expression, which fails because value is a run-time value. Bind the compile-time part to a constant first.

Exercise 27.5 · Enum tables without std.meta practice

Write parseEnum(E, text) using only @typeInfo(E).@"enum".fields, names(E) returning a fixed-size array of tag names, and Counter(E), a struct with one u32 per tag. File: exercises/27-reflection/ex5_enumtable.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 27, exercise 5: enum tables from reflection.
//! Run with:  zig test ex5_enumtable.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Parse a tag name into an enum value, using only @typeInfo (no std.meta).
pub fn parseEnum(comptime E: type, text: []const u8) ?E {
    inline for (@typeInfo(E).@"enum".fields) |f| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, f.name, text)) return @enumFromInt(f.value);
    }
    return null;
}

/// All tag names of E, as a comptime array of strings, in declaration order.
pub fn names(comptime E: type) [@typeInfo(E).@"enum".fields.len][]const u8 {
    const fields = @typeInfo(E).@"enum".fields;
    var out: [fields.len][]const u8 = undefined;
    inline for (fields, 0..) |f, i| out[i] = f.name;
    return out;
}

/// A fixed array with one slot per enum tag, indexed by @intFromEnum.
pub fn Counter(comptime E: type) type {
    return struct {
        counts: [@typeInfo(E).@"enum".fields.len]u32 = @splat(0),
        const Self = @This();
        pub fn bump(self: *Self, e: E) void {
            self.counts[@intFromEnum(e)] += 1;
        }
        pub fn get(self: Self, e: E) u32 {
            return self.counts[@intFromEnum(e)];
        }
    };
}

const Role = enum { pilot, tech, medic, admin };

test "parseEnum" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?Role, .medic), parseEnum(Role, "medic"));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?Role, null), parseEnum(Role, "cook"));
}

test "names" {
    const n = names(Role);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 4), n.len);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("pilot", n[0]);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("admin", n[3]);
}

test "Counter" {
    var c = Counter(Role){};
    c.bump(.tech);
    c.bump(.tech);
    c.bump(.admin);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 2), c.get(.tech));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 0), c.get(.pilot));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 4), c.counts.len);
}

The return type of names uses the field count directly in an array type, which is legal because @typeInfo is evaluated at compile time. @splat(0) fills the counter array whatever its length.

Check your understanding

  1. What is @TypeOf(1 + @as(u16, 2))?
    Answeru16. The untyped literal adopts the concrete type of the other operand.
  2. How do you spell the struct tag of @typeInfo in 0.16, and why?
    Answer.@"struct". struct is a keyword, so the identifier must be quoted with @"…". The same applies to .@"enum", .@"union", .@"fn" and .@"opaque".
  3. Which kind does []const u8 report, and how do you tell it apart from *u8?
    AnswerBoth are .pointer. The payload's size field is .slice for the first and .one for the second.
  4. Why must a loop over @typeInfo(T).@"struct".fields be an inline for?
    AnswerEach field has a different type, so the loop body must be compiled separately per field. inline for unrolls the loop at compile time so each iteration sees a constant field descriptor.
  5. What does @field(value, "x") require of its second argument?
    AnswerIt must be known at compile time. A run-time string cannot be used directly; you loop over the fields and compare with std.mem.eql, as setByName does.
  6. Does @hasDecl(T, "helper") see a private fn helper from another file?
    AnswerNo. Reflection over declarations only sees pub declarations, so @hasDecl is effectively an interface check.
  7. What replaced @Type in Zig 0.16?
    AnswerPer-kind builtins: @Int, @Enum, @Struct and friends, wrapped by helpers such as std.meta.Int.
  8. In the tuning validator, how much of the recursion survives into the compiled program?
    AnswerNone. Because the type and the name are comptime, every recursive call is a separate specialisation resolved during compilation; only the integer comparisons remain at run time.
What you learned.
  • @TypeOf gives the type of any expression; @typeName prints it.
  • @typeInfo(T) is a tagged union; switch on it at compile time. Tags are lower-case, with .@"struct", .@"enum", .@"union", .@"fn" quoted.
  • Payloads carry the details: bits and signedness for ints, child for optionals and pointers, fields and decls for structs and enums.
  • inline for over fields plus @field lets one function walk any struct, reading or writing fields by name.
  • @hasField and @hasDecl answer yes-or-no questions; end reflective switches with @compileError unless skipping is intended.
  • Enum field lists size arrays automatically and let you write your own stringToEnum.
  • @Type is gone in 0.16; @Int, @Enum and std.meta.Int build types.
  • Compile-time recursion over a nested struct gives you a validator that covers new fields for free.

28. ZON: data files as code

In this chapter you will move a table of numbers out of your source and into a .zon file, import it with a declared type so the compiler checks every entry, and see exactly what happens when the file is wrong. You will also parse ZON at run time with std.zon.parse, write it back with std.zon.stringify, and read the build.zig.zon that every project carries.

28.1 What ZON is

ZON stands for Zig Object Notation. It is not a new language: it is the subset of Zig you already use to write literals. An anonymous struct literal .{ .a = 1 }, an anonymous list .{ 1, 2, 3 }, numbers, strings, booleans, null, and enum literals such as .common. A ZON file contains exactly one such value and nothing else: no const, no functions, no expressions like 2 + 3, no references to other names. Comments are allowed.

Here is a small table of balance knobs in that form. Save it as tuning.zon.

tuning.zon

// Tuning knobs. Typed against `Tuning` in tuning.zig at compile time.
.{
    .person = .{
        .fatigue_tired = 30,
        .exhausted_fatigue = 70,
        .turnover_target = 3, // 2d6 < 3 + flags
    },
    .market = .{
        .fab_cost_bp = 12_000,
        .fab_days = 14,
    },
}

If you have used JSON, the mapping is direct: braces become .{ }, keys become .name =, and you gain three things JSON lacks: comments, numeric underscores like 12_000, and enum literals. If you have used TOML or YAML, ZON is stricter and smaller; there is one way to write everything, and zig fmt formats it.

28.2 Importing a ZON file with a declared type

The remarkable part is how you load it. You do not open the file at run time. You @import it, the same builtin you use for other source files, and assign the result to a constant with an explicit type. The compiler reads the file while compiling, treats it as a literal, and coerces it to that type.

typed.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub const Tuning = struct {
    person: struct { fatigue_tired: u8, exhausted_fatigue: u8, turnover_target: u8 },
    market: struct { fab_cost_bp: u32, fab_days: u32 },
};

pub const t: Tuning = @import("tuning.zon");

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("tired at {d}, exhausted at {d}\n", .{ t.person.fatigue_tired, t.person.exhausted_fatigue });
    std.debug.print("fab: {d} bp over {d} days\n", .{ t.market.fab_cost_bp, t.market.fab_days });
}
$ zig run typed.zig
tired at 30, exhausted at 70
fab: 12000 bp over 14 days

Yes, that is plain zig run on a single file with the .zon sitting next to it. No build script is needed as long as the data file lives in the same directory as the source, or below it. The constant t is an ordinary Tuning value that exists in the compiled binary; reading t.market.fab_days costs the same as reading any other constant, and there is nothing to parse when the program starts.

The type annotation is what makes it safe. Without : Tuning, the import would still work, but the value would be an anonymous struct and any typo in the file would only surface where a field is used, if at all. With the annotation, the whole file is checked against the whole struct at the point of import, once, for every build.

28.3 What the compiler catches

Let us break the file on purpose. First a misspelled field name (turnover_targt):

$ zig run bad.zig
bad.zon:2:82: error: unexpected field 'turnover_targt'
    .person = .{ .fatigue_tired = 30, .exhausted_fatigue = 70, .turnover_targt = 3 },
                                                                                 ^
bad.zig:8:31: note: imported here
pub const t: Tuning = @import("bad.zon");
                              ^~~~~~~~~

Then a value that does not fit its field (exhausted_fatigue is a u8) and a string where a number belongs:

$ zig run bad2.zig
bad2.zon:2:60: error: type 'u8' cannot represent integer value '300'
    .person = .{ .fatigue_tired = 30, .exhausted_fatigue = 300, .turnover_target = 3 },
                                                           ^~~
bad2.zig:8:31: note: imported here
pub const t: Tuning = @import("bad2.zon");

Each error points at the line and column in the data file, with a note showing which import pulled it in. A missing field without a default is reported the same way. Compare this with a JSON config loaded at start-up: the typo is discovered by a player, perhaps hours into a campaign, when the game reads a field that is not there. Here it is discovered by the person who made the typo, seconds later, before the program even links.

The first error stops the file. The compiler reports the first problem in a ZON file and stops. If your file has three mistakes you will fix them one at a time. That is still far better than finding them one at a time at run time.

28.4 Lists of records, with defaults

Tables are usually lists of rows. In ZON a list is an anonymous tuple, .{ row, row, row }, and it coerces to a slice of the row type. Struct fields with default values need not be written in every row, which keeps a catalogue readable.

designs.zon

.{
    .{ .key = "SHD-2H", .name = "Shadow Hawk", .tonnage = 55, .rarity = .common, .jump_mp = 3 },
    .{ .key = "AS7-D", .name = "Atlas", .tonnage = 100, .rarity = .rare },
    .{ .key = "LCT-1V", .name = "Locust", .tonnage = 20, .rarity = .common, .walk_mp = 8 },
}

designs.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub const Rarity = enum { common, uncommon, rare };
pub const Design = struct {
    key: []const u8,
    name: []const u8,
    tonnage: u32,
    rarity: Rarity,
    walk_mp: u8 = 4,
    jump_mp: u8 = 0,
};

pub const catalog: []const Design = @import("designs.zon");

pub fn find(key: []const u8) ?Design {
    for (catalog) |d| if (std.mem.eql(u8, d.key, key)) return d;
    return null;
}

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{d} designs\n", .{catalog.len});
    for (catalog) |d| {
        std.debug.print("{s:<8} {s:<12} {d:>3}t walk {d} jump {d} {s}\n", .{ d.key, d.name, d.tonnage, d.walk_mp, d.jump_mp, @tagName(d.rarity) });
    }
    if (find("AS7-D")) |atlas| std.debug.print("Atlas weighs {d}\n", .{atlas.tonnage});
}

test "every key is unique" {
    for (catalog, 0..) |a, i| {
        for (catalog[i + 1 ..]) |b| {
            try std.testing.expect(!std.mem.eql(u8, a.key, b.key));
        }
    }
}

test "tonnage is a multiple of 5 between 20 and 100" {
    for (catalog) |d| {
        try std.testing.expect(d.tonnage >= 20 and d.tonnage <= 100 and d.tonnage % 5 == 0);
    }
}
$ zig run designs.zig
3 designs
SHD-2H   Shadow Hawk   55t walk 4 jump 3 common
AS7-D    Atlas        100t walk 4 jump 0 rare
LCT-1V   Locust        20t walk 8 jump 0 common
Atlas weighs 100
$ zig test designs.zig
1/2 designs.test.every key is unique...OK
2/2 designs.test.tonnage is a multiple of 5 between 20 and 100...OK
All 2 tests passed.

The declared type is []const Design, so the tuple of three anonymous structs becomes a slice of three Design values, and the Atlas row gets walk_mp = 4 and jump_mp = 0 from the defaults. The enum literal .rare is checked against Rarity; write .legendary and the build fails.

The two tests show the second half of the pattern. The type system checks shape: field names, field types, enum tags. It cannot check meaning: that keys are unique, that tonnage is in the BattleTech range. So you write tests over the imported table, and because the table is a compile-time constant, those tests run on the real data every time. IRON LEDGER's data tests work this way: every loadout part must exist in the parts catalogue, every random-assignment entry must name a real design.

28.5 Where the file may live

@import resolves paths relative to the importing file, and subdirectories are fine: @import("data/tables/tuning.zon") works with zig run. What does not work is reaching upward. A file outside the directory tree of the root source file is refused:

$ cd inner && zig run outside.zig
outside.zig:8:31: error: import of file outside module path
pub const t: Tuning = @import("../tuning.zon");
                              ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

The rule is the same for .zig files: a module is a directory tree with one root, and imports cannot escape it. Projects that keep data beside the source tree (data/ next to src/, as IRON LEDGER does) solve this in build.zig: addAnonymousImport binds a file anywhere on disk to a name, and the code writes @import("tuning_zon"). Section 28.9 shows the minimum version and Chapter 31 explains the build script in full.

28.6 Parsing ZON at run time

Sometimes the data is not known when you compile: a user's settings file, a save game, a mod dropped into a folder. For that there is std.zon.parse. It takes the target type, an allocator, the text, an optional diagnostics object and an options struct, and returns a value of the type or error.ParseZon.

The text must be sentinel-terminated ([:0]const u8), because the parser is the compiler's own tokenizer and it wants a zero byte at the end. String literals already have one; text read from a file needs allocator.dupeZ. There are two entry points:

  • std.zon.parse.fromSlice(T, gpa, source, diag, options) for types that contain no pointers (plain numbers, enums, booleans, fixed arrays, nested structs of those). The result needs no freeing.
  • std.zon.parse.fromSliceAlloc(T, gpa, source, diag, options) for types with slices or strings. Free the result with std.zon.parse.free(gpa, value), or simpler, parse into an arena and free everything at once.

runtime_nopointer.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Point = struct { x: i32, y: i32 };

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const p = try std.zon.parse.fromSlice(Point, init.gpa, ".{ .x = 3, .y = -4 }", null, .{});
    std.debug.print("({d}, {d})\n", .{ p.x, p.y });
}
$ zig run runtime_nopointer.zig
(3, -4)

runtime.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Config = struct {
    seed: u64 = 3025,
    difficulty: enum { easy, normal, hard } = .normal,
    autosave: bool = true,
    company_name: []const u8 = "Unnamed",
};

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const gpa = init.gpa;
    const source: [:0]const u8 =
        \\.{ .seed = 42, .difficulty = .hard, .company_name = "Kell Hounds" }
    ;
    var diag: std.zon.parse.Diagnostics = .{};
    defer diag.deinit(gpa);
    const cfg = std.zon.parse.fromSliceAlloc(Config, gpa, source, &diag, .{}) catch |err| {
        std.debug.print("could not parse config: {s}\n{f}", .{ @errorName(err), diag });
        return err;
    };
    defer std.zon.parse.free(gpa, cfg);
    std.debug.print("seed={d} difficulty={s} autosave={} name={s}\n", .{ cfg.seed, @tagName(cfg.difficulty), cfg.autosave, cfg.company_name });

    const broken: [:0]const u8 = ".{ .seed = 42, .difficulty = .impossible }";
    var diag2: std.zon.parse.Diagnostics = .{};
    defer diag2.deinit(gpa);
    _ = std.zon.parse.fromSliceAlloc(Config, gpa, broken, &diag2, .{}) catch |err| {
        std.debug.print("second parse failed: {s}\n{f}", .{ @errorName(err), diag2 });
    };
}
$ zig run runtime.zig
seed=42 difficulty=hard autosave=true name=Kell Hounds
second parse failed: ParseZon
1:31: error: unexpected enum literal 'impossible'
1:31: note: supported: 'easy', 'normal', 'hard'

Three things to notice. Defaults in the struct apply to fields the text omits, exactly as with @import. The Diagnostics value, printed with the {f} specifier, produces the same quality of message the compiler gives, including the list of accepted enum tags. And options is a struct with two useful fields: ignore_unknown_fields (default false, so a typo is an error) and free_on_error.

Use an arena for parsed data. A parsed Config whose company_name came from the text owns heap memory, while one that kept the default points at a string literal. std.zon.parse.free knows the difference in practice, but the simplest robust habit is to parse with an ArenaAllocator and deinit the arena when you are done, as Exercise 28.2 does.

28.7 @embedFile: bytes in the binary

Between "checked at compile time" and "parsed at run time" there is a third option. @embedFile("path") reads a file while compiling and gives you its bytes as a constant, sentinel-terminated string. The file is baked into the executable, so nothing needs to exist on disk when the program runs, but the bytes are not interpreted: you parse them yourself.

embed.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Point = struct { x: i32, y: i32 };
const raw = @embedFile("point.zon");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    std.debug.print("embedded {d} bytes: {s}", .{ raw.len, raw });
    const p = try std.zon.parse.fromSlice(Point, init.gpa, raw, null, .{});
    std.debug.print("parsed ({d}, {d})\n", .{ p.x, p.y });
    const typed: Point = @import("point.zon");
    std.debug.print("imported ({d}, {d})\n", .{ typed.x, typed.y });
}
$ zig run embed.zig
embedded 20 bytes: .{ .x = 7, .y = 9 }
parsed (7, 9)
imported (7, 9)

The same file is used both ways so you can see the difference: @embedFile gives raw text that fromSlice then parses (its sentinel makes it directly acceptable), while @import gives a finished value. Use @embedFile for things that are not ZON at all, such as a test image or a shader; IRON LEDGER embeds a small PNG for its decoder's tests.

28.8 Writing ZON

The reverse direction is std.zon.stringify.serialize(value, options, writer). It walks the value with reflection (Chapter 27) and writes valid ZON to any *std.Io.Writer. The default output is formatted the way zig fmt would format it; .{ .whitespace = false } gives one compact line.

stringify.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Save = struct { day: u32, funds: i64, name: []const u8, roster: []const u8 };

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var w = std.Io.File.stdout().writer(init.io, &buf);
    const s = Save{ .day = 12, .funds = -3_500, .name = "Kell Hounds", .roster = "ABC" };
    try std.zon.stringify.serialize(s, .{}, &w.interface);
    try w.interface.writeAll("\n");
    try w.interface.flush();
}
$ zig run stringify.zig
.{
    .day = 12,
    .funds = -3500,
    .name = "Kell Hounds",
    .roster = "ABC",
}

Because the output is a legal ZON literal, it can be read back by std.zon.parse at run time or even by @import if you commit it as a source file. Exercise 28.3 makes a round trip.

28.9 build.zig.zon: the file every project has

You have already met one ZON file without being told: build.zig.zon, which zig init generates beside build.zig. It is the package manifest, and it is parsed by the compiler with a declared type just like your tuning table. Trimmed of its comments, the 0.16 version looks like this:

.{
    .name = .init,
    .version = "0.0.0",
    .fingerprint = 0xc674e47417e230d0, // Changing this has security and trust implications.
    .minimum_zig_version = "0.16.0",
    .dependencies = .{
        // .example = .{ .url = "https://…/foo.tar.gz", .hash = "…" },
        // .local = .{ .path = "foo" },
    },
    .paths = .{
        "build.zig",
        "build.zig.zon",
        "src",
    },
}
  • .name is an enum literal, not a string: the package's identifier.
  • .fingerprint is generated once and never changed; it is how the toolchain recognises a package across versions.
  • .dependencies maps names to either a url plus hash or a local path. zig fetch --save <url> fills entries in for you.
  • .paths lists what belongs to the package when it is fetched by someone else.

Everything you learned about ZON applies: comments are fine, a misspelled key is an error with a line number, and the file is checked before any build step runs.

28.10 Data beside the source: a first look at addAnonymousImport

To import a file from outside the source tree, build.zig can name it. Here is the smallest project that does so. The full meaning of every line waits for Chapter 31; for now, focus on the two lines marked with the import name.

proj/build.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn build(b: *std.Build) void {
    const target = b.standardTargetOptions(.{});
    const optimize = b.standardOptimizeOption(.{});

    // -Ddata=<dir> overlays data/tuning.zon from another directory (a "mod").
    const data_dir = b.option([]const u8, "data", "Directory overlaying data/*.zon");

    const exe = b.addExecutable(.{
        .name = "tables",
        .root_module = b.createModule(.{
            .root_source_file = b.path("src/main.zig"),
            .target = target,
            .optimize = optimize,
        }),
    });

    var tuning_path: std.Build.LazyPath = b.path("data/tuning.zon");
    if (data_dir) |dir| tuning_path = .{ .cwd_relative = b.pathJoin(&.{ dir, "tuning.zon" }) };
    exe.root_module.addAnonymousImport("tuning_zon", .{ .root_source_file = tuning_path });

    b.installArtifact(exe);

    const run_cmd = b.addRunArtifact(exe);
    const run_step = b.step("run", "Run the app");
    run_step.dependOn(&run_cmd.step);

    const tests = b.addTest(.{ .root_module = exe.root_module });
    const test_step = b.step("test", "Run tests");
    test_step.dependOn(&b.addRunArtifact(tests).step);
}

proj/src/main.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub const Tuning = struct {
    person: struct { fatigue_tired: u8, exhausted_fatigue: u8, turnover_target: u8 },
    market: struct { fab_cost_bp: u32, fab_days: u32 },
};

/// The live table: whichever file build.zig bound to the name "tuning_zon".
pub const t: Tuning = @import("tuning_zon");

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("fab_days = {d}\n", .{t.market.fab_days});
}

test "fab days is at least a week" {
    try std.testing.expect(t.market.fab_days >= 7);
}
$ zig build run
fab_days = 14
$ zig build run -Ddata=mymod
fab_days = 7
$ zig build test --summary all
Build Summary: 3/3 steps succeeded; 1/1 tests passed
test success
+- run test 1 pass (1 total) 229ms MaxRSS:2M
   +- compile test Debug native success 979ms MaxRSS:263M

The source file says @import("tuning_zon"), a name with no path and no extension. The build script decides which file that name means: data/tuning.zon normally, or mymod/tuning.zon when the user passes -Ddata=mymod. The simulation code neither knows nor cares. This is the mechanism behind IRON LEDGER's mod support, and it is why the modding guide tells you to run zig build test -Ddata=mymod: the same data tests run against your replacement tables.

28.11 Why compile-time data beats JSON for game tables

It is worth stating the trade-off plainly, because "just use JSON" is the default in most ecosystems.

JSON parsed at start-upZON imported at compile time
Typos found when the field is read, maybe neverTypos found at the import, with a line number
Needs a parser, an allocator and error handling at run timeNo run-time cost at all; the value is a constant
Types are whatever the parser guesses (every number is a double)Types are whatever your struct says (u8, CBills, an enum)
Comments are not allowedComments are allowed
Data can change without rebuildingChanging data means rebuilding
Tests need fixtures that mirror the real fileTests run over the real table

The last row of the left column is the one real advantage of run-time data, and it is exactly why the game keeps both tools: balance tables that ship with the binary are ZON imported at compile time, while player settings and mod overlays that must vary after the build go through std.zon.parse or the build option. Choose by asking "who changes this, and when?"

In IRON LEDGER. Every table the simulation reads is a ZON file under game/data/, bound by name in build.zig and imported with a declared type. The tuning table opens like this (game/data/tables/tuning.zon): 
// Tuning knobs. Typed against domain/tuning.zig `Tuning` at comptime.
.{
    .hq = .{
        .influence_ly = .{ .field = 15, .regional = 60, .brigade = 90 },
        .paperwork_base_days = 21,
        .upgrade_cost_per_level = .{ .mek_bay = 800_000, .warehouse = 400_000, /* … */ },
    },
    .person = .{
        .fatigue_tired = 30,
        .exhausted_fatigue = 70,
        .turnover_target = 3, // 2d6 < 3 + flags
        // …
    },
}
and game/src/domain/tuning.zig gives it a shape and a name: pub const t: Tuning = @import("tuning_zon");. The design catalogue works the same way, one struct per row with defaults so a vehicle need not state mek-only fields; a row of game/data/chassis.zon reads .{ .key = "SHD-2H", .name = "Shadow Hawk", .tonnage = 55, .bv = 1064, .cost = 4_701_800, .rarity = .common, .walk_mp = 5, .jump_mp = 3, … }. The 97 designs, 234 systems and every knob are type-checked on every build, and the data tests in the same files check what types cannot.

Exercises

Exercise 28.1 · A typed design catalogue warm-up

A small project with src/designs.zon next to src/designs.zig. Fill in weightClass, find and countByRarity and make the data tests pass with zig build test inside exercises/28-zon/ex1_designs/. (It is a directory exercise because the checker needs the .zon beside the source.)

Solution

src/designs.zig

//! Chapter 28, exercise 1: a typed design catalogue from a .zon file.
//! Run with:  zig build test   (inside exercises/28-zon/ex1_designs/)
//! Goal: fill in `Design`, import the catalogue, and make every test pass.
const std = @import("std");

pub const Rarity = enum { common, uncommon, rare };

pub const Design = struct {
    key: []const u8,
    name: []const u8,
    tonnage: u32,
    rarity: Rarity,
    walk_mp: u8 = 4,
    jump_mp: u8 = 0,

    pub fn weightClass(self: Design) []const u8 {
        if (self.tonnage <= 35) return "light";
        if (self.tonnage <= 55) return "medium";
        if (self.tonnage <= 75) return "heavy";
        return "assault";
    }
};

pub const catalog: []const Design = @import("designs.zon");

pub fn find(key: []const u8) ?Design {
    for (catalog) |d| if (std.mem.eql(u8, d.key, key)) return d;
    return null;
}

pub fn countByRarity(r: Rarity) usize {
    var n: usize = 0;
    for (catalog) |d| if (d.rarity == r) {
        n += 1;
    };
    return n;
}

test "catalogue has four designs" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 4), catalog.len);
}

test "defaults fill in unspecified fields" {
    const whm = find("WHM-6R").?;
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 4), whm.walk_mp);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 0), whm.jump_mp);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 8), find("LCT-1V").?.walk_mp);
}

test "find and weight classes" {
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("assault", find("AS7-D").?.weightClass());
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("medium", find("SHD-2H").?.weightClass());
    try std.testing.expect(find("nope") == null);
}

test "rarity counts" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 2), countByRarity(.common));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 1), countByRarity(.rare));
}

test "every key is unique and every tonnage is a multiple of 5" {
    for (catalog, 0..) |a, i| {
        try std.testing.expect(a.tonnage % 5 == 0);
        for (catalog[i + 1 ..]) |b| try std.testing.expect(!std.mem.eql(u8, a.key, b.key));
    }
}

The .zon file has rows with and without walk_mp; the defaults in Design fill the gaps, which the second test checks.

Exercise 28.2 · Parse a config at run time practice

Write load(arena, source) that parses a Config with std.zon.parse.fromSliceAlloc, printing diagnostics on failure. File: exercises/28-zon/ex2_runtime.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 28, exercise 2: parse ZON at run time with std.zon.parse.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_runtime.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

pub const Difficulty = enum { easy, normal, hard };

pub const Config = struct {
    seed: u64 = 3025,
    difficulty: Difficulty = .normal,
    autosave: bool = true,
    company_name: []const u8 = "Unnamed Company",
};

/// Parse `source` into a Config. Strings inside the result live in `arena`,
/// so the caller frees everything by resetting the arena. On a parse error,
/// print the diagnostics to stderr and return error.ParseZon.
pub fn load(arena: std.mem.Allocator, source: [:0]const u8) !Config {
    var diag: std.zon.parse.Diagnostics = .{};
    defer diag.deinit(arena);
    return std.zon.parse.fromSliceAlloc(Config, arena, source, &diag, .{}) catch |err| {
        std.debug.print("config error: {f}", .{diag});
        return err;
    };
}

test "full config" {
    var arena = std.heap.ArenaAllocator.init(std.testing.allocator);
    defer arena.deinit();
    const cfg = try load(arena.allocator(),
        \\.{ .seed = 42, .difficulty = .hard, .autosave = false, .company_name = "Kell Hounds" }
    );
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u64, 42), cfg.seed);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Difficulty.hard, cfg.difficulty);
    try std.testing.expect(!cfg.autosave);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Kell Hounds", cfg.company_name);
}

test "defaults apply to missing fields" {
    var arena = std.heap.ArenaAllocator.init(std.testing.allocator);
    defer arena.deinit();
    const cfg = try load(arena.allocator(), ".{ .seed = 7 }");
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u64, 7), cfg.seed);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Difficulty.normal, cfg.difficulty);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Unnamed Company", cfg.company_name);
}

test "bad enum literal is a parse error" {
    var arena = std.heap.ArenaAllocator.init(std.testing.allocator);
    defer arena.deinit();
    try std.testing.expectError(error.ParseZon, load(arena.allocator(), ".{ .difficulty = .brutal }"));
}

test "unknown field is a parse error" {
    var arena = std.heap.ArenaAllocator.init(std.testing.allocator);
    defer arena.deinit();
    try std.testing.expectError(error.ParseZon, load(arena.allocator(), ".{ .sead = 1 }"));
}

Parsing into the arena means the test's defer arena.deinit() frees the strings; no call to std.zon.parse.free is needed.

Exercise 28.3 · Round trip practice

Serialize a Roster with std.zon.stringify.serialize (pretty and compact) and parse it back. File: exercises/28-zon/ex3_roundtrip.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 28, exercise 3: serialize a value to ZON and read it back.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_roundtrip.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

pub const Pilot = struct { name: []const u8, gunnery: u8, piloting: u8 };
pub const Roster = struct { day: u32, funds: i64, pilots: []const Pilot };

/// Render `value` as ZON text into `buf`; return the written slice.
/// `pretty` chooses multi-line Zig style; false gives one compact line.
pub fn toZon(buf: []u8, value: anytype, pretty: bool) ![]u8 {
    var w = std.Io.Writer.fixed(buf);
    try std.zon.stringify.serialize(value, .{ .whitespace = pretty }, &w);
    return w.buffered();
}

/// Parse ZON text back into a Roster, allocating from `arena`.
/// The text must be sentinel-terminated: copy it with allocator.dupeZ first.
pub fn fromZon(arena: std.mem.Allocator, text: []const u8) !Roster {
    const z = try arena.dupeZ(u8, text);
    return std.zon.parse.fromSliceAlloc(Roster, arena, z, null, .{});
}

test "round trip" {
    var arena = std.heap.ArenaAllocator.init(std.testing.allocator);
    defer arena.deinit();
    const pilots = [_]Pilot{
        .{ .name = "Kell", .gunnery = 3, .piloting = 4 },
        .{ .name = "Ana", .gunnery = 5, .piloting = 5 },
    };
    const before = Roster{ .day = 12, .funds = -3_500, .pilots = &pilots };
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    const text = try toZon(&buf, before, true);
    try std.testing.expect(std.mem.indexOf(u8, text, ".name = \"Kell\"") != null);
    const after = try fromZon(arena.allocator(), text);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(before.day, after.day);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(before.funds, after.funds);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 2), after.pilots.len);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Ana", after.pilots[1].name);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 5), after.pilots[1].gunnery);
}

test "pretty and compact forms" {
    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    const p = Pilot{ .name = "X", .gunnery = 1, .piloting = 2 };
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings(
        ".{\n    .name = \"X\",\n    .gunnery = 1,\n    .piloting = 2,\n}",
        try toZon(&buf, p, true),
    );
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings(".{.name=\"X\",.gunnery=1,.piloting=2}", try toZon(&buf, p, false));
}

fromZon has to copy the text with dupeZ because the parser demands a zero terminator, and a slice returned by buffered() has none.

Exercise 28.4 · A mod overlay challenge

Finish build.zig in exercises/28-zon/ex4_overlay/ so that @import("tuning_zon") resolves to data/tuning.zon normally and to <dir>/tuning.zon with -Ddata=<dir>. Verify with zig build run -Ddata=mods/hardcore and zig build test.

Solution

build.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn build(b: *std.Build) void {
    const target = b.standardTargetOptions(.{});
    const optimize = b.standardOptimizeOption(.{});

    // zig build -Ddata=mods/hardcore  overlays data/tuning.zon
    const data_dir = b.option([]const u8, "data", "Directory overlaying data/tuning.zon");

    const mod = b.createModule(.{
        .root_source_file = b.path("src/main.zig"),
        .target = target,
        .optimize = optimize,
    });
    var tuning: std.Build.LazyPath = b.path("data/tuning.zon");
    if (data_dir) |dir| tuning = b.path(b.pathJoin(&.{ dir, "tuning.zon" }));
    mod.addAnonymousImport("tuning_zon", .{ .root_source_file = tuning });

    const exe = b.addExecutable(.{ .name = "overlay", .root_module = mod });
    b.installArtifact(exe);

    const run_step = b.step("run", "Print the live tuning table");
    run_step.dependOn(&b.addRunArtifact(exe).step);

    const tests = b.addTest(.{ .root_module = mod });
    const test_step = b.step("test", "Validate the tuning table");
    test_step.dependOn(&b.addRunArtifact(tests).step);
}
$ zig build run
tired 30 exhausted 70 turnover 3
fab 12000 bp, 14 days
$ zig build run -Ddata=mods/hardcore
tired 20 exhausted 50 turnover 5
fab 20000 bp, 21 days

b.option returns an optional; when it is present we build a different LazyPath and hand it to addAnonymousImport under the same name.

Check your understanding

  1. Can a ZON file contain 2 * 3 or refer to a constant defined elsewhere?
    AnswerNo. ZON is literals only: no expressions, no names, no code.
  2. What does the type annotation in const t: Tuning = @import("tuning.zon"); buy you?
    AnswerThe compiler coerces the literal to Tuning at the import, so unknown fields, missing fields without defaults, and out-of-range values are build errors with line numbers in the data file.
  3. Does plain zig run main.zig support @import("data.zon")?
    AnswerYes, as long as the file is in the same directory as main.zig or below it. Paths that leave the root file's directory are refused.
  4. When do you need fromSliceAlloc rather than fromSlice?
    AnswerWhen the target type contains pointers or slices, such as strings. fromSlice asserts at compile time that no allocation is needed for the result.
  5. Why must the source given to std.zon.parse be [:0]const u8?
    AnswerThe parser reuses the compiler's tokenizer, which expects a zero byte terminator. Use dupeZ for text read from a file; @embedFile and string literals already have one.
  6. What is the difference between @embedFile("x.zon") and @import("x.zon")?
    Answer@embedFile gives the raw bytes as a constant string; @import gives the parsed, type-checked value.
  7. How does a source file import a data file that lives outside its directory tree?
    Answerbuild.zig binds it to a name with module.addAnonymousImport("name", .{ .root_source_file = path }), and the source writes @import("name").
  8. Name one thing types cannot check about a table, and how the game checks it.
    AnswerUniqueness of keys, references between tables, or ranges like "tonnage is a multiple of 5". Tests over the imported constant check those, on the real data, every build.
What you learned.
  • ZON is the literal subset of Zig: anonymous structs and lists, numbers, strings, booleans, null, enum literals, comments.
  • const t: T = @import("file.zon") loads a file at compile time and type-checks it; errors point into the data file.
  • Lists of rows coerce to []const Row, and struct defaults fill omitted fields.
  • Imports may go into subdirectories but never above the root file; addAnonymousImport in build.zig binds outside files to a name.
  • std.zon.parse.fromSlice / fromSliceAlloc parse ZON at run time from a sentinel-terminated string, with optional Diagnostics; parse into an arena.
  • @embedFile bakes raw bytes into the binary; std.zon.stringify.serialize writes ZON back out.
  • build.zig.zon is the package manifest, itself a ZON file with name, version, fingerprint, dependencies and paths.
  • Compile-time data trades "change without rebuilding" for "every mistake is a build error"; game balance tables want the latter.

29. Packed structs, bit casting and vectors

In this chapter you go below the byte. You will use integers of any width, flip individual bits with the bit operators and the counting builtins, lay out a struct so it occupies exactly one byte, reinterpret memory with @bitCast, read big-endian numbers out of a file header, keep a set of flags in std.bit_set, and do arithmetic on several numbers at once with @Vector. Each tool is small; together they are how Zig talks to file formats, hardware and C.

29.1 Integers of any width

You have used u8, i32 and u64. Zig also has u3, u7, i5, u24, in fact uN and iN for any N from 1 to 65535. A u3 holds 0 to 7 and nothing else; overflowing it is the same error as overflowing a u8. In memory it still takes a whole byte (there is no such thing as a 3-bit load), but inside a packed struct it takes exactly three bits.

widths.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const a: u3 = 7;
    const b: u7 = 127;
    const c: i5 = -16;
    std.debug.print("u3 max {d}, u7 max {d}, i5 min {d}\n", .{ a, b, c });
    std.debug.print("u3: size {d} bytes, {d} bits, align {d}\n", .{ @sizeOf(u3), @bitSizeOf(u3), @alignOf(u3) });
    std.debug.print("u7: size {d} bytes, {d} bits\n", .{ @sizeOf(u7), @bitSizeOf(u7) });
    std.debug.print("u24: size {d} bytes, {d} bits, align {d}\n", .{ @sizeOf(u24), @bitSizeOf(u24), @alignOf(u24) });
    std.debug.print("u64: size {d} bytes, align {d}\n", .{ @sizeOf(u64), @alignOf(u64) });
    std.debug.print("bool: size {d} bytes, {d} bits\n", .{ @sizeOf(bool), @bitSizeOf(bool) });
    std.debug.print("maxInt(u3) = {d}, maxInt(u12) = {d}\n", .{ std.math.maxInt(u3), std.math.maxInt(u12) });
}
u3 max 7, u7 max 127, i5 min -16
u3: size 1 bytes, 3 bits, align 1
u7: size 1 bytes, 7 bits
u24: size 4 bytes, 24 bits, align 4
u64: size 8 bytes, align 8
bool: size 1 bytes, 1 bits
maxInt(u3) = 7, maxInt(u12) = 4095

Three builtins measure a type. @sizeOf(T) is the number of bytes a value occupies in memory, rounded up to something the CPU can address, which is why u24 reports 4. @bitSizeOf(T) is the number of bits that carry information. @alignOf(T) is the address multiple the value must sit on. Odd widths are not a curiosity: they are how you say "this field is a 3-bit rank" and have the compiler refuse an 8.

29.2 The bit operators

Six operators work on the individual bits of an integer: & (and), | (or), ^ (exclusive or), ~ (not), << (shift left) and >> (shift right). Alongside them Zig offers builtins that count and rearrange bits. The {b:0>8} format prints an integer in binary, padded with zeros to eight places, which is the best way to see what is happening.

bitops.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const x: u8 = 0b1011_0010;
    const y: u8 = 0b0110_0110;
    std.debug.print("x     = {b:0>8}\n", .{x});
    std.debug.print("y     = {b:0>8}\n", .{y});
    std.debug.print("x & y = {b:0>8}\n", .{x & y});
    std.debug.print("x | y = {b:0>8}\n", .{x | y});
    std.debug.print("x ^ y = {b:0>8}\n", .{x ^ y});
    std.debug.print("~x    = {b:0>8}\n", .{~x});
    std.debug.print("x >> 2 = {b:0>8}\n", .{x >> 2});
    std.debug.print("x << 1 = {b:0>8}  (top bit falls off)\n", .{x << 1});
    std.debug.print("popCount(x) = {d}\n", .{@popCount(x)});
    std.debug.print("clz(x) = {d}, ctz(x) = {d}\n", .{ @clz(x), @ctz(x) });
    std.debug.print("clz(1) = {d}, ctz(0b1000) = {d}\n", .{ @clz(@as(u8, 1)), @ctz(@as(u8, 0b1000)) });
    std.debug.print("byteSwap(0x1234) = 0x{x}\n", .{@byteSwap(@as(u16, 0x1234))});
    std.debug.print("bitReverse(x) = {b:0>8}\n", .{@bitReverse(x)});
    std.debug.print("x as hex {x}, as octal {o}\n", .{ x, x });
    const bit3 = (x >> 3) & 1;
    std.debug.print("bit 3 of x is {d}\n", .{bit3});
    const set = x | (1 << 2);
    const cleared = x & ~@as(u8, 1 << 4);
    std.debug.print("set bit 2: {b:0>8}, clear bit 4: {b:0>8}\n", .{ set, cleared });
}
x     = 10110010
y     = 01100110
x & y = 00100010
x | y = 11110110
x ^ y = 11010100
~x    = 01001101
x >> 2 = 00101100
x << 1 = 01100100  (top bit falls off)
popCount(x) = 4
clz(x) = 0, ctz(x) = 1
clz(1) = 7, ctz(0b1000) = 3
byteSwap(0x1234) = 0x3412
bitReverse(x) = 01001101
x as hex b2, as octal 262
bit 3 of x is 0
set bit 2: 10110110, clear bit 4: 10100010

The three idioms at the bottom are the ones you will write most: test a bit with (x >> n) & 1, set a bit with x | (1 << n), clear a bit with x & ~(1 << n). The counting builtins are @popCount (how many ones), @clz (leading zeros, counted from the top) and @ctz (trailing zeros, from the bottom). @byteSwap reverses the bytes of a multi-byte integer, which section 29.7 will connect to endianness, and @bitReverse reverses all the bits.

Why ~@as(u8, 1 << 4) and not ~(1 << 4)? The literal 1 << 4 is a comptime_int, and "not" of an untyped integer has no defined width. Give it a type first so the compiler knows how many bits to flip.

29.3 Shifts and their rules

Shifting is where Zig's strictness surprises people coming from C. The shift amount for a u8 must be a u3, because shifting an 8-bit value by 8 or more is meaningless; for a u32 it must be a u5. The compiler enforces this at the type level: pass a u8 as the amount and it will not compile.

shift_bad.zig

pub fn main() void {
    const n: u8 = 1;
    var s: u8 = 3;
    s += 1;
    _ = n << s;
}
shift_bad.zig:5:14: error: expected type 'u3', found 'u8'
    _ = n << s;
             ^
shift_bad.zig:5:14: note: unsigned 3-bit int cannot represent all possible unsigned 8-bit values

The fix is @intCast(s) to a u3 (a checked narrowing) or @truncate(s) (keep the low three bits). The second rule concerns bits that fall off the left: a plain << discards them silently, exactly like C, but @shlExact asserts that nothing is lost and @shlWithOverflow reports whether something was.

shifts.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const one: u8 = 1;
    std.debug.print("1 << 7 = {d}\n", .{one << 7});
    std.debug.print("@shlExact(1, 3) = {d}\n", .{@shlExact(one, 3)});
    std.debug.print("@shlWithOverflow(0xF0, 2) = {any}\n", .{@shlWithOverflow(@as(u8, 0xF0), 2)});
    const n: u8 = 200;
    const shift: u3 = 2;
    std.debug.print("200 >> {d} = {d}\n", .{ shift, n >> shift });
    std.debug.print("@shrExact(200, 3) = {d}\n", .{@shrExact(n, 3)});
    const wide: u32 = 1;
    const s: u5 = 31;
    std.debug.print("1 << 31 = {d}\n", .{wide << s});
}
1 << 7 = 128
@shlExact(1, 3) = 8
@shlWithOverflow(0xF0, 2) = .{ 192, 1 }
200 >> 2 = 50
@shrExact(200, 3) = 25
1 << 31 = 2147483648

@shlWithOverflow returns a tuple: the wrapped result and a u1 that is 1 when bits were lost. @shrExact is the right-shift twin: it asserts that no one-bits were shifted out, so it is a way of dividing by a power of two and insisting the division was exact. In Debug and ReleaseSafe a violated @shlExact panics; in ReleaseFast it is undefined behaviour, so use it only where you have already proved the property.

29.4 Packed structs: fields that are bits

A normal struct lets the compiler decide where fields go. A packed struct takes that freedom away: fields are laid out in declaration order, first field in the lowest bits, with no padding, and the whole thing is backed by one integer whose width you write after the keyword. packed struct(u8) must add up to exactly eight bits or it will not compile.

packed1.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Flags = packed struct(u8) {
    armed: bool = false,
    wounded: bool = false,
    veteran: bool = false,
    rank: u3 = 0,
    _pad: u2 = 0,
};

pub fn main() void {
    var f = Flags{ .armed = true, .rank = 5 };
    std.debug.print("size {d} byte(s), bits {d}\n", .{ @sizeOf(Flags), @bitSizeOf(Flags) });
    const byte: u8 = @bitCast(f);
    std.debug.print("as byte: {b:0>8} = 0x{x:0>2}\n", .{ byte, byte });
    f.wounded = true;
    const byte2: u8 = @bitCast(f);
    std.debug.print("after wound: {b:0>8}\n", .{byte2});
    const back: Flags = @bitCast(@as(u8, 0b0010_0110));
    std.debug.print("from 0b00100110: armed={} wounded={} veteran={} rank={d}\n", .{ back.armed, back.wounded, back.veteran, back.rank });
    std.debug.print("offset of rank: {d} bits\n", .{@bitOffsetOf(Flags, "rank")});
}
size 1 byte(s), bits 8
as byte: 00101001 = 0x29
after wound: 00101011
from 0b00100110: armed=false wounded=true veteran=true rank=4
offset of rank: 3 bits

Read the first binary line from the right. Bit 0 is armed (1). Bit 1 is wounded (0). Bit 2 is veteran (0). Bits 3 to 5 are rank, which is 5, or 101. Bits 6 and 7 are padding. Put together, right to left: 00 101 0 0 1, which is 0x29. Field access reads and writes just the right bits; the compiler emits the masks and shifts for you, and a u3 rank cannot be assigned an 8.

Conversion between the struct and its backing integer is @bitCast, in both directions, and it costs nothing: the bits do not move. That is what makes packed structs the natural way to describe a byte of flags in a file format, a hardware register, or a network header.

packed2.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Rgb565 = packed struct(u16) { b: u5, g: u6, r: u5 };
const Ip = packed struct(u32) { d: u8, c: u8, b: u8, a: u8 };

pub fn main() void {
    const c: Rgb565 = .{ .r = 31, .g = 0, .b = 31 };
    std.debug.print("magenta = 0x{x:0>4}\n", .{@as(u16, @bitCast(c))});
    const raw: u16 = 0x07E0;
    const g: Rgb565 = @bitCast(raw);
    std.debug.print("0x07E0 -> r={d} g={d} b={d}\n", .{ g.r, g.g, g.b });
    const ip: Ip = @bitCast(@as(u32, 0xC0A80001));
    std.debug.print("{d}.{d}.{d}.{d}\n", .{ ip.a, ip.b, ip.c, ip.d });
}
magenta = 0xf81f
0x07E0 -> r=0 g=63 b=0
192.168.0.1

RGB565 is a real pixel format (5 bits red, 6 green, 5 blue in 16 bits) and the Ip struct shows a subtlety: because the first field lands in the lowest bits and this machine stores the low byte first, the field order is reversed relative to the dotted notation. Section 29.7 makes that precise.

Packed is not the default, and it is not free of rules. Do not reach for packed for ordinary data; it can make field access slower and forbids some field types. Use it when the bit layout is the specification. For talking to C you want extern, covered next.

29.5 @bitCast: the same bits, another type

@bitCast reinterprets a value as another type of the same size. No conversion happens; the bit pattern is simply relabelled. It is how you look at a float's binary representation, turn a negative number into its two's-complement bytes, or split a word into an array.

bitcast.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const f: f32 = 1.0;
    const bits: u32 = @bitCast(f);
    std.debug.print("1.0f32 is 0x{x:0>8}\n", .{bits});
    const neg: i8 = -1;
    const as_u8: u8 = @bitCast(neg);
    std.debug.print("-1 as u8 is {d}\n", .{as_u8});
    const bytes: [4]u8 = @bitCast(@as(u32, 0x11223344));
    std.debug.print("0x11223344 in memory: {x:0>2} {x:0>2} {x:0>2} {x:0>2}\n", .{ bytes[0], bytes[1], bytes[2], bytes[3] });
    std.debug.print("this machine is {s}-endian\n", .{@tagName(@import("builtin").cpu.arch.endian())});
}
1.0f32 is 0x3f800000
-1 as u8 is 255
0x11223344 in memory: 44 33 22 11
this machine is little-endian

Contrast this with the casts you know. @intCast changes width and checks the value fits; @floatFromInt computes a float with the same mathematical value; @bitCast keeps the bits and changes only the label. The result type must be the same size as the source, and the compiler refuses otherwise. The third line reveals something about your machine: the bytes of 0x11223344 sit in memory lowest byte first. That is little-endian, and it is the subject of section 29.7.

29.6 Three layouts: auto, extern, packed

A struct with no layout keyword is auto: the compiler may reorder fields to reduce padding, and you must not assume where anything is. An extern struct keeps declaration order and uses the C ABI's padding rules, which is what a C library expects. A packed struct has no padding at all. The measuring builtins show the difference, and @offsetOf reports where a field sits in bytes.

layout.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Auto = struct { a: u8, b: u32, c: u8 };
const Extern = extern struct { a: u8, b: u32, c: u8 };
const Reordered = extern struct { b: u32, a: u8, c: u8 };
const Packed = packed struct { a: u8, b: u32, c: u8 };

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("Auto:      size {d} align {d}\n", .{ @sizeOf(Auto), @alignOf(Auto) });
    std.debug.print("Extern:    size {d} align {d}  offsets a={d} b={d} c={d}\n", .{ @sizeOf(Extern), @alignOf(Extern), @offsetOf(Extern, "a"), @offsetOf(Extern, "b"), @offsetOf(Extern, "c") });
    std.debug.print("Reordered: size {d} align {d}\n", .{ @sizeOf(Reordered), @alignOf(Reordered) });
    std.debug.print("Packed:    size {d} bits {d}\n", .{ @sizeOf(Packed), @bitSizeOf(Packed) });
}
Auto:      size 8 align 4
Extern:    size 12 align 4  offsets a=0 b=4 c=8
Reordered: size 8 align 4
Packed:    size 8 bits 48

The same three fields cost 8 bytes as an auto struct (the compiler moved b first), 12 bytes as an extern struct in the written order (three bytes of padding after a and three after c, so the u32 stays 4-aligned), and 8 bytes again when you reorder the extern struct by hand. The packed version holds 48 bits of information but still occupies 8 bytes when stored alone, because its backing integer is rounded up. This table is the whole story of "why is my struct bigger than the sum of its fields", and of why the game's SQLite binding uses extern only where it meets C.

29.7 Endianness: which byte comes first

A u32 is four bytes. When it is written to memory, a file or a network packet, something has to decide whether the most significant byte goes first (big-endian, the convention in most file formats and all of networking) or last (little-endian, the convention of x86 and ARM processors). Your program's memory uses the CPU's order; a file uses whatever its specification says. Getting this wrong does not crash: it silently produces a number like 65536 where you expected 256.

Never convert with arithmetic by hand. std.mem.readInt and std.mem.writeInt take the integer type, a pointer to exactly the right number of bytes, and the endianness, and do the right thing on every machine.

endian.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var buf: [4]u8 = undefined;
    std.mem.writeInt(u32, &buf, 0x01020304, .big);
    std.debug.print("big:    {x:0>2} {x:0>2} {x:0>2} {x:0>2}\n", .{ buf[0], buf[1], buf[2], buf[3] });
    std.mem.writeInt(u32, &buf, 0x01020304, .little);
    std.debug.print("little: {x:0>2} {x:0>2} {x:0>2} {x:0>2}\n", .{ buf[0], buf[1], buf[2], buf[3] });

    const png_ihdr = [_]u8{ 0x00, 0x00, 0x01, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0xC0 };
    const width = std.mem.readInt(u32, png_ihdr[0..4], .big);
    const height = std.mem.readInt(u32, png_ihdr[4..8], .big);
    std.debug.print("PNG {d} x {d}\n", .{ width, height });

    const wrong = std.mem.readInt(u32, png_ihdr[0..4], .little);
    std.debug.print("same bytes read little-endian: {d}\n", .{wrong});
    const n = std.mem.nativeToBig(u16, 0xABCD);
    std.debug.print("nativeToBig(0xABCD) stored as {x}\n", .{n});
}
big:    01 02 03 04
little: 04 03 02 01
PNG 256 x 192
same bytes read little-endian: 65536
nativeToBig(0xABCD) stored as cdab

The PNG example is real: the image header stores width and height as big-endian 32-bit integers, and bytes[0..4] with a comptime-known range gives the *const [4]u8 that readInt wants. Reading the same bytes little-endian gives nonsense, which is the bug you will meet if you ever cast a byte pointer to *u32 the way C code does. std.mem.nativeToBig and its relatives convert a value in a register; @byteSwap from section 29.2 is the primitive under them.

29.8 Bit sets

When you need a set of small integers, "is unit 12 deployed?", a bit per member is the most compact possible representation, and std.bit_set gives it a proper interface so you do not hand-roll masks. IntegerBitSet(N) is backed by one integer for N up to a machine word; StaticBitSet(N) picks the right implementation for any N; DynamicBitSet allocates.

bitset.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var seen = std.bit_set.IntegerBitSet(16).initEmpty();
    seen.set(3);
    seen.set(7);
    seen.set(12);
    std.debug.print("count {d}, has 7? {}, has 8? {}\n", .{ seen.count(), seen.isSet(7), seen.isSet(8) });
    seen.unset(7);
    seen.toggle(0);
    var it = seen.iterator(.{});
    std.debug.print("set bits:", .{});
    while (it.next()) |i| std.debug.print(" {d}", .{i});
    std.debug.print("\nmask = {b:0>16}\n", .{seen.mask});

    var a = std.bit_set.StaticBitSet(200).initEmpty();
    var b = std.bit_set.StaticBitSet(200).initFull();
    a.set(150);
    b.unset(150);
    const both = a.intersectWith(b);
    std.debug.print("200-bit set: a has {d}, b has {d}, a&b has {d}\n", .{ a.count(), b.count(), both.count() });
    std.debug.print("first set in b: {?d}\n", .{b.findFirstSet()});
}
count 3, has 7? true, has 8? false
set bits: 0 3 12
mask = 0001000000001001
200-bit set: a has 1, b has 199, a&b has 0
first set in b: 0

The operations read like a set: set, unset, toggle, isSet, count, findFirstSet, the set algebra unionWith, intersectWith, differenceWith, and an iterator over the members. For the integer-backed version the mask field is the raw integer, which is what you store in a save file. Exercise 29.3 keeps a lance roster this way.

29.9 Vectors: several numbers at once

Modern CPUs can add four or eight numbers in one instruction. Zig exposes that directly: @Vector(4, i32) is a type holding four i32 values, and the ordinary operators +, *, > work on it element by element. Arrays convert to vectors and back by assignment when the lengths match.

vectors.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    const a: @Vector(4, i32) = .{ 1, 2, 3, 4 };
    const b: @Vector(4, i32) = .{ 10, 20, 30, 40 };
    const sum = a + b;
    const prod = a * b;
    std.debug.print("a + b = {any}\n", .{sum});
    std.debug.print("a * b = {any}\n", .{prod});
    std.debug.print("reduce add = {d}, reduce max = {d}\n", .{ @reduce(.Add, prod), @reduce(.Max, prod) });
    const twos: @Vector(4, i32) = @splat(2);
    std.debug.print("a * 2 = {any}\n", .{a * twos});
    const mask = a > twos;
    std.debug.print("a > 2 = {any}\n", .{mask});
    const picked = @select(i32, mask, a, b);
    std.debug.print("select = {any}\n", .{picked});
    const arr: [4]i32 = sum;
    std.debug.print("back to array: {any}, element 2 = {d}\n", .{ arr, sum[2] });
    const f: @Vector(3, f32) = .{ 1.5, 2.5, 3.0 };
    std.debug.print("float sum {d:.1}\n", .{@reduce(.Add, f)});
    const any_big = @reduce(.Or, a > @as(@Vector(4, i32), @splat(3)));
    std.debug.print("any element > 3? {}\n", .{any_big});
}
a + b = { 11, 22, 33, 44 }
a * b = { 10, 40, 90, 160 }
reduce add = 300, reduce max = 160
a * 2 = { 2, 4, 6, 8 }
a > 2 = { false, false, true, true }
