select = { 10, 20, 3, 4 }
back to array: { 11, 22, 33, 44 }, element 2 = 33
float sum 7.0
any element > 3? true

Four builtins complete the toolkit. @splat(x) makes a vector with every lane equal to x (the length comes from the expected type). @reduce(op, v) folds a vector to one value with .Add, .Mul, .Min, .Max, .And, .Or or .Xor. Comparing two vectors gives a vector of bool, and @select(T, mask, a, b) picks lanes from a where the mask is true and from b elsewhere; this is how you write "if" without a branch. Indexing with v[2] reads one lane.

Here is the classic use: summing a long slice eight at a time, with a scalar loop for the tail.

vecsum.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn sumScalar(xs: []const u32) u32 {
    var t: u32 = 0;
    for (xs) |x| t += x;
    return t;
}

fn sumVector(xs: []const u32) u32 {
    const N = 8;
    var acc: @Vector(N, u32) = @splat(0);
    var i: usize = 0;
    while (i + N <= xs.len) : (i += N) {
        const chunk: @Vector(N, u32) = xs[i..][0..N].*;
        acc += chunk;
    }
    var t = @reduce(.Add, acc);
    while (i < xs.len) : (i += 1) t += xs[i];
    return t;
}

test "both sums agree" {
    var data: [1003]u32 = undefined;
    for (&data, 0..) |*d, i| d.* = @intCast(i);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(sumScalar(&data), sumVector(&data));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 1002 * 1003 / 2), sumVector(&data));
}
$ zig test vecsum.zig
1/1 vecsum.test.both sums agree...OK
All 1 tests passed.

The expression xs[i..][0..N].* deserves a look: slicing with a comptime-known length gives a pointer to an array, and .* dereferences it into an array value, which then coerces to the vector. That is the idiom for "load the next N elements".

Should you vectorise? Usually not by hand. Compilers auto-vectorise simple loops in release modes, and a game simulation is rarely bound by arithmetic. Reach for @Vector when you have measured, or when the data is naturally a fixed small tuple: a colour, a position, a set of eight armour locations, as in Exercise 29.4.
In IRON LEDGER. The clearest use of this chapter is the hand-written PNG decoder in game/src/tui/png.zig, which reads emblem images for the terminal client. PNG stores every chunk length and every dimension big-endian, and the decoder walks the chunks exactly as section 29.7 described: 
while (pos + 8 <= bytes.len) {
    const len = std.mem.readInt(u32, bytes[pos..][0..4], .big);
    const kind = bytes[pos + 4 .. pos + 8];
    pos += 8;
    if (pos + len + 4 > bytes.len) return error.Corrupt;
    const data = bytes[pos .. pos + len];
    if (std.mem.eql(u8, kind, "IHDR")) {
        if (len < 13) return error.Corrupt;
        width = std.mem.readInt(u32, data[0..4], .big);
        height = std.mem.readInt(u32, data[4..8], .big);
        depth = data[8];
        color = data[9];
The file's signature check, std.mem.eql(u8, bytes[0..8], "\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n"), is the same test Exercise 29.2 asks you to write, and the decoder's test image is baked in with @embedFile("testdata/rgb4x3.png"). Elsewhere the game deliberately avoids clever bit tricks: money is a plain i64, IDs are enums, and the tuning tables are structs, because the day-to-day code is easier to read that way. Bits are for the edges of the program, where bytes arrive from outside.

Exercises

Exercise 29.1 · A status byte warm-up

Declare Status as a packed struct(u8) with three booleans, a 3-bit rank and a 2-bit morale, plus toByte, fromByte and flagCount (how many of the three booleans are set, via @popCount). File: exercises/29-bits/ex1_flags.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 29, exercise 1: a status byte as a packed struct.
//! Run with:  zig test ex1_flags.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// One byte of pilot status, low bit first. Must fit exactly in a u8.
pub const Status = packed struct(u8) {
    active: bool = false,
    wounded: bool = false,
    veteran: bool = false,
    rank: u3 = 0, // 0..7
    morale: u2 = 1, // 0 = broken, 3 = fanatical

    pub fn toByte(self: Status) u8 {
        return @bitCast(self);
    }
    pub fn fromByte(b: u8) Status {
        return @bitCast(b);
    }
    /// How many of the three boolean flags are set.
    pub fn flagCount(self: Status) u4 {
        const low: u3 = @truncate(self.toByte());
        return @popCount(low);
    }
};

test "layout" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 1), @sizeOf(Status));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 8), @bitSizeOf(Status));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 3), @bitOffsetOf(Status, "rank"));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 6), @bitOffsetOf(Status, "morale"));
}

test "to and from byte" {
    const s = Status{ .active = true, .veteran = true, .rank = 5, .morale = 3 };
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 0b11_101_101), s.toByte());
    const back = Status.fromByte(0b01_010_010);
    try std.testing.expect(!back.active and back.wounded and !back.veteran);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u3, 2), back.rank);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u2, 1), back.morale);
}

test "flag count" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u4, 0), (Status{}).flagCount());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u4, 2), (Status{ .active = true, .wounded = true, .rank = 7 }).flagCount());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u4, 3), Status.fromByte(0xFF).flagCount());
}

flagCount truncates the byte to its low three bits, which are exactly the three booleans, then counts ones. @bitOffsetOf confirms the layout in the tests.

Exercise 29.2 · Parse a PNG header practice

Write parseHeader(bytes): check the 8-byte signature, then the IHDR chunk (length 13, big-endian width and height, depth, colour type, interlace flag). Reject bad input with NotPng, Corrupt or Unsupported. File: exercises/29-bits/ex2_png.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 29, exercise 2: parse a PNG header by hand.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_png.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
//! Compare with the real decoder in game/src/tui/png.zig.
const std = @import("std");

pub const Error = error{ NotPng, Corrupt, Unsupported };

pub const ColorType = enum(u8) { grey = 0, rgb = 2, palette = 3, grey_alpha = 4, rgba = 6 };

pub const Header = struct {
    width: u32,
    height: u32,
    bit_depth: u8,
    color: ColorType,
    interlaced: bool,

    /// Bytes per pixel for 8-bit images.
    pub fn channels(self: Header) u8 {
        return switch (self.color) {
            .grey, .palette => 1,
            .grey_alpha => 2,
            .rgb => 3,
            .rgba => 4,
        };
    }
};

const signature = "\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n";

pub fn isPng(bytes: []const u8) bool {
    return bytes.len >= 8 and std.mem.eql(u8, bytes[0..8], signature);
}

/// Parse the 8-byte signature and the IHDR chunk that must follow it:
///   4 bytes length (big-endian, must be 13)
///   4 bytes type ("IHDR")
///   13 bytes data: width u32, height u32, depth u8, color u8, compression u8,
///                  filter u8, interlace u8
///   4 bytes CRC (ignored here)
pub fn parseHeader(bytes: []const u8) Error!Header {
    if (!isPng(bytes)) return error.NotPng;
    if (bytes.len < 8 + 8 + 13 + 4) return error.Corrupt;
    const len = std.mem.readInt(u32, bytes[8..12], .big);
    if (len != 13) return error.Corrupt;
    if (!std.mem.eql(u8, bytes[12..16], "IHDR")) return error.Corrupt;
    const d = bytes[16..29];
    const color_raw = d[9];
    const color: ColorType = switch (color_raw) {
        0 => .grey,
        2 => .rgb,
        3 => .palette,
        4 => .grey_alpha,
        6 => .rgba,
        else => return error.Corrupt,
    };
    const depth = d[8];
    if (depth != 8) return error.Unsupported;
    if (d[10] != 0 or d[11] != 0) return error.Corrupt;
    return .{
        .width = std.mem.readInt(u32, d[0..4], .big),
        .height = std.mem.readInt(u32, d[4..8], .big),
        .bit_depth = depth,
        .color = color,
        .interlaced = d[12] == 1,
    };
}

/// Build a header blob for tests: signature + IHDR chunk with a fake CRC.
fn makePng(w: u32, h: u32, depth: u8, color: u8, interlace: u8) [33]u8 {
    var out: [33]u8 = undefined;
    @memcpy(out[0..8], signature);
    std.mem.writeInt(u32, out[8..12], 13, .big);
    @memcpy(out[12..16], "IHDR");
    std.mem.writeInt(u32, out[16..20], w, .big);
    std.mem.writeInt(u32, out[20..24], h, .big);
    out[24] = depth;
    out[25] = color;
    out[26] = 0;
    out[27] = 0;
    out[28] = interlace;
    @memset(out[29..33], 0);
    return out;
}

test "a 4x3 RGB image" {
    const png = makePng(4, 3, 8, 2, 0);
    const hdr = try parseHeader(&png);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 4), hdr.width);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 3), hdr.height);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(ColorType.rgb, hdr.color);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 3), hdr.channels());
    try std.testing.expect(!hdr.interlaced);
}

test "big-endian really matters" {
    const png = makePng(256, 1, 8, 6, 1);
    const hdr = try parseHeader(&png);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 256), hdr.width);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 4), hdr.channels());
    try std.testing.expect(hdr.interlaced);
}

test "rejections" {
    try std.testing.expectError(error.NotPng, parseHeader("hello"));
    var bad = makePng(1, 1, 8, 2, 0);
    bad[13] = 'X';
    try std.testing.expectError(error.Corrupt, parseHeader(&bad));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.Unsupported, parseHeader(&makePng(1, 1, 16, 2, 0)));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.Corrupt, parseHeader(&makePng(1, 1, 8, 5, 0)));
}

Every multi-byte number goes through readInt(…, .big). The test helper makePng builds headers with writeInt, so the tests never depend on a file on disk. Note that std.meta.intToEnum no longer exists in 0.16; a switch on the raw byte is clearer anyway.

Exercise 29.3 · A lance roster as a bit set practice

Using std.bit_set.IntegerBitSet(64), write idle(available, deployed), firstIdle, and toBits/fromBits for saving. File: exercises/29-bits/ex3_bitset.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 29, exercise 3: a lance roster as a bit set.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_bitset.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

pub const max_units = 64;
pub const Roster = std.bit_set.IntegerBitSet(max_units);

/// Units that are in `available` but not in `deployed`.
pub fn idle(available: Roster, deployed: Roster) Roster {
    return available.differenceWith(deployed);
}

/// The lowest-numbered idle unit, if any.
pub fn firstIdle(available: Roster, deployed: Roster) ?usize {
    return idle(available, deployed).findFirstSet();
}

/// Pack the roster into a u64 for a save file, and back.
pub fn toBits(r: Roster) u64 {
    return r.mask;
}
pub fn fromBits(bits: u64) Roster {
    return .{ .mask = bits };
}

test "idle units" {
    var avail = Roster.initEmpty();
    avail.setRangeValue(.{ .start = 0, .end = 8 }, true);
    var dep = Roster.initEmpty();
    dep.set(1);
    dep.set(2);
    dep.set(5);
    const free = idle(avail, dep);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 5), free.count());
    try std.testing.expect(free.isSet(0) and !free.isSet(1) and free.isSet(7));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?usize, 0), firstIdle(avail, dep));
    dep.set(0);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?usize, 3), firstIdle(avail, dep));
}

test "nobody idle" {
    const avail = Roster.initFull();
    const dep = Roster.initFull();
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?usize, null), firstIdle(avail, dep));
}

test "round trip through u64" {
    var r = Roster.initEmpty();
    r.set(0);
    r.set(63);
    const bits = toBits(r);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u64, 1) | (@as(u64, 1) << 63), bits);
    try std.testing.expect(fromBits(bits).eql(r));
}

differenceWith is "in a but not in b". The backing mask field is a plain u64, so saving is a field read.

Exercise 29.4 · Armour with @Vector practice

Eight armour locations as @Vector(8, u16). Write applyDamage (never below zero), anyBreached, total and weakest. File: exercises/29-bits/ex4_vector.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 29, exercise 4: damage rolls with @Vector.
//! Run with:  zig test ex4_vector.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

pub const V = @Vector(8, u16);

/// Armor after damage, per location, never below zero.
pub fn applyDamage(armor: V, damage: V) V {
    // `-|` is saturating subtraction and works element-wise on vectors,
    // so no lane can wrap below zero. @select then shows the same idea
    // spelled out with a mask.
    const zero: V = @splat(0);
    const would_break = damage >= armor;
    return @select(u16, would_break, zero, armor -| damage);
}

/// True if any location was reduced to zero.
pub fn anyBreached(armor: V) bool {
    const zero: V = @splat(0);
    return @reduce(.Or, armor == zero);
}

/// Total armor remaining.
pub fn total(armor: V) u32 {
    var t: u32 = 0;
    const arr: [8]u16 = armor;
    for (arr) |a| t += a;
    return t;
}

/// Index of the weakest location (first one on ties).
pub fn weakest(armor: V) usize {
    const min = @reduce(.Min, armor);
    const arr: [8]u16 = armor;
    for (arr, 0..) |a, i| if (a == min) return i;
    unreachable;
}

test "damage saturates at zero" {
    const armor: V = .{ 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10 };
    const dmg: V = .{ 3, 0, 12, 10, 0, 0, 0, 1 };
    const after = applyDamage(armor, dmg);
    const expected: [8]u16 = .{ 7, 10, 0, 0, 10, 10, 10, 9 };
    try std.testing.expectEqual(expected, @as([8]u16, after));
    try std.testing.expect(anyBreached(after));
    try std.testing.expect(!anyBreached(armor));
}

test "totals and weakest" {
    const armor: V = .{ 8, 6, 9, 6, 7, 7, 7, 7 };
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 57), total(armor));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 1), weakest(armor));
}

Plain armor - damage panics in Debug when a lane would go negative, even if @select would discard that lane. The saturating operator -| works lane by lane and solves it; the mask and @select are kept to show the branch-free idiom.

Exercise 29.5 · RGB565 pixels challenge

Pack 8-bit colour channels into 16 bits both with a packed struct and with shifts and masks, unpack them again with the top bits replicated, and store/load pixels little-endian in a byte buffer. File: exercises/29-bits/ex5_rgb.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 29, exercise 5: RGB565 pixels with masks and packed structs.
//! Run with:  zig test ex5_rgb.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

pub const Rgb565 = packed struct(u16) { b: u5, g: u6, r: u5 };

/// Pack 8-bit channels into 16 bits by dropping the low bits.
pub fn pack(r: u8, g: u8, b: u8) u16 {
    const px = Rgb565{ .r = @truncate(r >> 3), .g = @truncate(g >> 2), .b = @truncate(b >> 3) };
    return @bitCast(px);
}

/// Same thing with shifts and masks only, no struct.
pub fn packManual(r: u8, g: u8, b: u8) u16 {
    const r5: u16 = r >> 3;
    const g6: u16 = g >> 2;
    const b5: u16 = b >> 3;
    return (r5 << 11) | (g6 << 5) | b5;
}

/// Expand back to 8-bit channels (top bits replicated so 31 becomes 255).
pub fn unpack(px: u16) [3]u8 {
    const s: Rgb565 = @bitCast(px);
    const r: u8 = (@as(u8, s.r) << 3) | (s.r >> 2);
    const g: u8 = (@as(u8, s.g) << 2) | (s.g >> 4);
    const b: u8 = (@as(u8, s.b) << 3) | (s.b >> 2);
    return .{ r, g, b };
}

/// Write a pixel little-endian into a byte buffer at index i (2 bytes).
pub fn store(buf: []u8, i: usize, px: u16) void {
    std.mem.writeInt(u16, buf[i * 2 ..][0..2], px, .little);
}
pub fn load(buf: []const u8, i: usize) u16 {
    return std.mem.readInt(u16, buf[i * 2 ..][0..2], .little);
}

test "known colours" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u16, 0xF800), pack(255, 0, 0));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u16, 0x07E0), pack(0, 255, 0));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u16, 0x001F), pack(0, 0, 255));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u16, 0xFFFF), pack(255, 255, 255));
}

test "both packers agree" {
    var r: u16 = 0;
    while (r < 256) : (r += 37) {
        const c: u8 = @intCast(r);
        try std.testing.expectEqual(packManual(c, 255 - c, c / 2), pack(c, 255 - c, c / 2));
    }
}

test "unpack expands full scale" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual([3]u8{ 255, 0, 0 }, unpack(0xF800));
    try std.testing.expectEqual([3]u8{ 255, 255, 255 }, unpack(0xFFFF));
    try std.testing.expectEqual([3]u8{ 0, 0, 0 }, unpack(0));
}

test "store and load bytes" {
    var buf: [4]u8 = undefined;
    store(&buf, 0, 0xF800);
    store(&buf, 1, 0x001F);
    try std.testing.expectEqual([4]u8{ 0x00, 0xF8, 0x1F, 0x00 }, buf);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u16, 0x001F), load(&buf, 1));
}

The two packers must agree bit for bit, which is a good test that you understand the packed layout: first field in the lowest bits. Replicating the top bits on unpack is what makes 31 map back to 255 rather than 248.

Check your understanding

  1. What is @sizeOf(u3) and what is @bitSizeOf(u3)?
    Answer1 byte and 3 bits. Stored alone a u3 takes a byte; inside a packed struct it takes three bits.
  2. Why does n << s fail to compile when n is a u8 and s is a u8?
    AnswerThe shift amount for a u8 must be a u3, because shifting by 8 or more is meaningless. Convert with @intCast or @truncate.
  3. In a packed struct(u8), which field occupies bit 0?
    AnswerThe first declared field. Fields fill from the least significant bit upward, with no padding.
  4. What does @bitCast require of its source and destination types?
    AnswerThe same size in bits. It does not convert values; it relabels the bits.
  5. Which layout should a struct passed to a C library use?
    Answerextern struct: declaration order with C padding rules. Auto structs may be reordered and packed structs have no padding.
  6. A PNG width field holds bytes 00 00 01 00. What is the width, and what would readInt(u32, …, .little) give?
    Answer256, because PNG is big-endian. Little-endian reading gives 65536.
  7. What does @reduce(.Or, v > @as(@TypeOf(v), @splat(3))) compute?
    AnswerWhether any lane of v is greater than 3: the comparison yields a vector of booleans and .Or folds them.
  8. Why did armor - damage panic in Exercise 29.4 even though @select discarded the bad lanes?
    AnswerThe subtraction is evaluated for every lane before @select runs, and unsigned underflow is a safety panic. Use saturating -| or wrapping -% when a lane may go out of range.
What you learned.
  • uN/iN exist for any width; @sizeOf, @bitSizeOf and @alignOf measure types.
  • Bit operators plus @popCount, @clz, @ctz, @byteSwap and @bitReverse; print with {b:0>8}.
  • Shift amounts are typed (u3 for a u8); @shlExact asserts nothing is lost, @shlWithOverflow reports it.
  • packed struct(uN) lays fields out bit by bit from the least significant end; @bitCast converts to and from the backing integer for free.
  • Auto structs may be reordered, extern follows C, packed has no padding; @offsetOf shows where fields sit.
  • Use std.mem.readInt/writeInt with an explicit endianness for every multi-byte number that crosses a file or wire.
  • std.bit_set gives sets of small integers with set algebra and iteration.
  • @Vector types support element-wise operators, @splat, @reduce and @select; convert to and from arrays by assignment.

30. Program structure: files, imports, modules

In this chapter you will split a program across several files and directories, learn the one rule of visibility (pub), discover that every file is secretly a struct, and make sure tests in every file actually run. Nothing here needs a build script yet; that comes in Chapter 31.

30.1 Every file is a struct

You have written const std = @import("std"); at the top of every program. It is time to say what that line does. @import takes a path and returns a type: the struct that the file defines. A Zig source file is the body of a struct declaration with the braces left off. Its top-level const, fn and test are that struct's declarations. std is a type, and std.debug.print is a declaration inside a declaration inside it.

Once you see this, importing your own files is obvious: @import("geometry.zig") is the struct defined by geometry.zig, and you use its public declarations with a dot. Here is a program in three files.

app/geometry.zig

//! Tiny geometry helpers for the import demo.
const std = @import("std");

pub const Point = struct { x: i32, y: i32 };

pub fn manhattan(a: Point, b: Point) u32 {
    return @abs(a.x - b.x) + @abs(a.y - b.y);
}

fn secret() u32 {
    return 42;
}

test "manhattan" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 7), manhattan(.{ .x = 0, .y = 0 }, .{ .x = 3, .y = 4 }));
}

app/domain/types.zig

//! Typed IDs shared by the whole program.
pub const PersonId = enum(u32) { _ };
pub const UnitId = enum(u32) { _ };

app/main.zig

const std = @import("std");
const geometry = @import("geometry.zig");
const types = @import("domain/types.zig");

pub fn main() void {
    const a = geometry.Point{ .x = 1, .y = 1 };
    const b = geometry.Point{ .x = 4, .y = 5 };
    std.debug.print("distance {d}\n", .{geometry.manhattan(a, b)});
    const id: types.PersonId = @enumFromInt(7);
    std.debug.print("person {d}\n", .{@intFromEnum(id)});
    std.debug.print("geometry is a {s}\n", .{@typeName(@TypeOf(geometry))});
}
$ cd app && zig run main.zig
distance 7
person 7
geometry is a type

Notice that you ran zig run on main.zig alone and the other two files were found. The path in @import is relative to the importing file, so "domain/types.zig" reaches into a subdirectory. The compiler follows imports from the root file outward and compiles what it finds. There is no list of source files anywhere; the imports are the list.

The last line of output is the proof of the opening claim: @TypeOf(geometry) is type. The value geometry is a type, and geometry.Point is a declaration inside it. This is also why the naming convention is what it is: a file that is used as a namespace gets a lower-case constant (geometry, types), while a file that is used as a type gets a capitalised one (section 30.5).

30.2 pub, and private by default

Zig has one visibility rule. A declaration is private to its file unless it is marked pub. There are no classes with private members, no packages, no friends, no header files. geometry.zig above has a function secret without pub. Try to call it:

priv/main.zig

const geometry = @import("geometry.zig");
pub fn main() void {
    _ = geometry.secret();
}
$ zig run main.zig
main.zig:3:17: error: 'secret' is not marked 'pub'
    _ = geometry.secret();
        ~~~~~~~~^~~~~~~
geometry.zig:10:1: note: declared here
fn secret() u32 {
^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

The same rule applies to constants (pub const), to nested types, and to the fields of a struct only in the sense that fields are always accessible; visibility is about declarations. A file's public surface is therefore easy to read: search for pub. Everything else is an implementation detail that you can rename or delete without looking at other files.

Design advice. Start with nothing pub and add it when another file needs the name. A file with three pub declarations and twenty private helpers is a well-designed file. A file where everything is pub has no boundary, and reflection (Chapter 27) will also see all of it.

30.3 Naming imports

The constant you bind an import to is your choice, and two conventions cover almost every case:

  • Namespace files (functions and types grouped by topic) get a lower-case name matching the file: const geometry = @import("geometry.zig");, const types = @import("domain/types.zig");.
  • When you only want one thing, take it directly: const Point = @import("geometry.zig").Point;. This is common for types used everywhere.
  • Files that are a type (section 30.5) get a capitalised name: const Counter = @import("Counter.zig");.

Imports are cheap to write and it is normal for a file to start with five or ten of them. Unused imports are not an error (they are lazily analysed), but zig fmt and code review will thank you for removing them.

30.4 A root file that re-exports

As a project grows past a handful of files you want one place that names the whole thing. The convention is root.zig: a file whose only job is to import the others and mark them pub. Anyone who imports root.zig, or the module built from it, sees the entire tree through one door.

tests/root.zig

//! Root of a small module. Tests here reference every file we want tested.
const std = @import("std");
pub const money = @import("money.zig");
pub const roster = @import("roster.zig");

test {
    std.testing.refAllDecls(@This());
}

This is exactly the shape of IRON LEDGER's src/root.zig, which the Ledger box below shows. A re-export costs nothing at run time: pub const money = @import("money.zig"); is a compile-time alias. Directory trees follow the same idea in layers: root.zig imports domain/types.zig, sim/state.zig, persist/store.zig, and each directory groups files that change together.

What about the test block at the bottom? Section 30.7 explains it. First, two smaller facts about imports.

30.5 Cyclic imports are fine

In many languages, file A importing file B while B imports A is either an error or a source of subtle bugs. In Zig it simply works, because imports are lazy: @import gives you a type, and the compiler only analyses the declarations you actually reference, when you reference them.

cyc/a.zig

const std = @import("std");
const b = @import("b.zig");
pub fn ping(n: u32) u32 {
    if (n == 0) return 0;
    return 1 + b.pong(n - 1);
}
pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("ping(5) = {d}\n", .{ping(5)});
}

cyc/b.zig

const a = @import("a.zig");
pub fn pong(n: u32) u32 {
    if (n == 0) return 0;
    return 1 + a.ping(n - 1);
}
$ zig run a.zig
ping(5) = 5

The game leans on this: queries.zig imports commands.zig in a test, and commands.zig imports queries.zig for the rating calculation. You should still avoid cycles when a clean layering is possible, because they make the code harder to read, not because the compiler minds.

30.6 @This() and files that are types

If a file is a struct, can it have fields? Yes. Put field declarations at the top level and the file becomes a struct type with those fields, exactly as if you had written const Counter = struct { … }; in another file. Inside such a file you need a way to name the struct you are in, and that is @This().

this/Counter.zig

//! A file that IS a struct: it has fields at the top level.
//! Import it with a capitalised name: `const Counter = @import("Counter.zig");`
count: u32 = 0,
step: u32 = 1,

const Counter = @This();

pub fn bump(self: *Counter) void {
    self.count += self.step;
}

pub fn init(step: u32) Counter {
    return .{ .step = step };
}

this/main.zig

const std = @import("std");
const Counter = @import("Counter.zig");

pub fn main() void {
    var c = Counter.init(5);
    c.bump();
    c.bump();
    std.debug.print("count = {d}\n", .{c.count});
    std.debug.print("size of Counter: {d} bytes\n", .{@sizeOf(Counter)});
}
$ zig run main.zig
count = 10
size of Counter: 8 bytes

@This() returns the innermost struct, enum or union being defined. In a file-as-struct it is the file's type; inside const Stack = struct { … } it is Stack, which is why the idiom const Self = @This(); appears in so many generic types (Chapter 26) where the struct has no name yet. In root.zig above, @This() is the root file itself, handed to refAllDecls.

Fields and top-level code do not mix well. A file with fields cannot have a main that makes sense as a program entry, and its field list comes first by convention. Keep files-as-types small and focused: one type, its methods, its tests.

30.7 Doc comments: //! and ///

Three comment forms exist and they mean different things. // is an ordinary comment. /// directly above a declaration is a doc comment for that declaration; tools and editors pick it up. //! at the very top of a file is a doc comment for the file itself, that is, for the struct the file defines. The Counter.zig file above opens with a //! block, and the contract of this course requires one on every exercise file. A /// that is not followed by a declaration is a compile error, which catches the common mistake of leaving a doc comment on a deleted function.

30.8 Test discovery across files

Here is a trap that catches every new Zig project. Run zig test root_noref.zig on a root file that imports two files full of tests, but never references anything in them:

tests/root_noref.zig

const std = @import("std");
pub const money = @import("money.zig");
pub const roster = @import("roster.zig");
test "root only" {
    try std.testing.expect(true);
}
$ zig test root_noref.zig
1/1 root_noref.test.root only...OK
All 1 tests passed.

One test ran. The tests in money.zig and roster.zig were silently skipped, because of the same laziness that makes cyclic imports work: a file that is imported but never referenced is never analysed, and its tests do not exist. Now the root.zig from section 30.4:

$ zig test root.zig
1/3 root.test_0...OK
2/3 money.test.money...OK
3/3 roster.test.roster...OK
All 3 tests passed.

std.testing.refAllDecls(@This()) is a function that, only while testing, takes the address of every public declaration of the type it is given. Referencing money and roster forces their files to be analysed, and their file-level tests join the run. The anonymous test { … } block gets the name test_0.

But look again at the run: roster.inner.test.inner roster did not appear. refAllDecls goes one level deep; it referenced roster, and roster.zig's own test ran, but a test nested inside the struct inner is only discovered if inner is referenced. Older Zig versions shipped std.testing.refAllDeclsRecursive for this; 0.16 does not. The recursive version is a dozen lines you can keep in your own project:

tests/root_recursive.zig

const std = @import("std");
pub const money = @import("money.zig");
pub const roster = @import("roster.zig");

/// refAllDecls only goes one level deep. This walks nested structs too.
fn refAllDeclsRecursive(comptime T: type) void {
    inline for (comptime std.meta.declarations(T)) |decl| {
        const D = @TypeOf(@field(T, decl.name));
        if (D == type) {
            switch (@typeInfo(@field(T, decl.name))) {
                .@"struct", .@"enum", .@"union", .@"opaque" => refAllDeclsRecursive(@field(T, decl.name)),
                else => {},
            }
        }
        _ = &@field(T, decl.name);
    }
}

test {
    refAllDeclsRecursive(@This());
}
$ zig test root_recursive.zig
1/4 root_recursive.test_0...OK
2/4 money.test.money...OK
3/4 roster.test.roster...OK
4/4 roster.inner.test.inner roster...OK
All 4 tests passed.

It uses std.meta.declarations (reflection again) to visit every public declaration; for those that are types, it recurses. In practice most projects are fine with plain refAllDecls in the root plus a habit of referencing nested namespaces from a file-level test. IRON LEDGER does exactly that, and zig build test reports several hundred tests as a result.

Rule of thumb. If a test you just wrote does not show up in the count, the file it lives in is not referenced. Add it to root.zig, or reference the containing struct from a test that does run.
In IRON LEDGER. The module root game/src/root.zig is a pure table of re-exports, grouped by directory, with the discovery test at the bottom: 
//! Module root for the simulation core. See ARCHITECTURE.md.
//! The core is pure and deterministic: no I/O, no wall clock, no globals.

const std = @import("std");

// domain/ (entities)
pub const types = @import("domain/types.zig");
pub const person = @import("domain/person.zig");
pub const unit = @import("domain/unit.zig");
// …
// sim/ (state, time, randomness, events, battle resolution)
pub const state = @import("sim/state.zig");
pub const tick = @import("sim/tick.zig");
// …
// persist/ (SQLite save files, Stage 11)
pub const sqlite = @import("persist/sqlite.zig");
pub const store = @import("persist/store.zig");

test {
    std.testing.refAllDecls(@This());
}
Every file below it opens with a //! block naming its MekHQ counterpart, a house rule from the project's CLAUDE.md. The executable in game/src/main.zig never imports these files by path; it writes const game = @import("game"); and reaches game.state.GameState, game.commands.execute and so on through the root. The name "game" is not a file: it is a module declared in build.zig, which is where the next chapter begins.

Exercises

Exercise 30.1 · One program, several files warm-up

The tree exercises/30-program-structure/ex1_split/ has main.zig importing domain/types.zig, domain/pilot.zig and roster.zig. Finish roster.zig (add, get, best) so zig build run prints the best pilot and zig build test passes in every file.

Solution

src/roster.zig

//! A fixed-capacity roster indexed by PersonId.
const std = @import("std");
const types = @import("domain/types.zig");
const Pilot = @import("domain/pilot.zig").Pilot;

pub const Roster = struct {
    slots: [16]Pilot = undefined,
    count: usize = 0,

    pub fn add(self: *Roster, p: Pilot) void {
        self.slots[self.count] = p;
        self.count += 1;
    }

    pub fn get(self: *const Roster, id: types.PersonId) ?*const Pilot {
        if (id.index() >= self.count) return null;
        return &self.slots[id.index()];
    }

    pub fn best(self: *const Roster) ?*const Pilot {
        if (self.count == 0) return null;
        var top: usize = 0;
        for (self.slots[0..self.count], 0..) |p, i| {
            if (p.skill() > self.slots[top].skill()) top = i;
        }
        return &self.slots[top];
    }
};

test "roster" {
    var r = Roster{};
    try std.testing.expect(r.best() == null);
    r.add(Pilot.init("A", 4, 4));
    r.add(Pilot.init("B", 2, 2));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("B", r.best().?.name);
    try std.testing.expect(r.get(@enumFromInt(5)) == null);
}

src/main.zig (the test block)

test {
    // Pull every file's tests into this test binary.
    std.testing.refAllDecls(@This());
    _ = types;
    _ = pilot;
    _ = roster;
}

roster.zig imports domain/pilot.zig with a path relative to itself, and takes just the Pilot type. The test block in main.zig references each import so their tests are discovered; _ = types; is enough on its own for a plain import, and refAllDecls is belt and braces.

Exercise 30.2 · A file that is a struct practice

In exercises/30-program-structure/ex2_counter/, src/Ledger.zig has fields at the top level. Finish apply and nextDay and run zig build test.

Solution

src/Ledger.zig

//! Chapter 30, exercise 2: a file that is a struct.
//! This file has fields at the top level, so @import("Ledger.zig") IS the
//! type. By convention such files are named in CapitalCase.
const std = @import("std");

funds: i64,
day: u32 = 1,
log: std.ArrayList(i64) = .empty,

const Ledger = @This();

pub fn init(funds: i64) Ledger {
    return .{ .funds = funds };
}

pub fn deinit(self: *Ledger, gpa: std.mem.Allocator) void {
    self.log.deinit(gpa);
}

pub fn apply(self: *Ledger, gpa: std.mem.Allocator, delta: i64) !void {
    self.funds += delta;
    try self.log.append(gpa, delta);
}

pub fn nextDay(self: *Ledger) void {
    self.day += 1;
}

test "Ledger is the file" {
    try std.testing.expect(@TypeOf(Ledger.init(0)) == Ledger);
}

const Ledger = @This(); names the file's own type so methods can take *Ledger. The test in main.zig ends with _ = Ledger; so the file's own test is discovered.

Exercise 30.3 · Test discovery practice

In exercises/30-program-structure/ex3_discovery/, zig build test --summary all reports too few tests. Change only src/root.zig so that all four run.

Solution

src/root.zig

//! Chapter 30, exercise 3: test discovery across a tree of files.
//! Run with:  zig build test --summary all   (inside ex3_discovery/)
//! Goal: make `zig build test` report 4 tests, without touching the
//!       other files. Hint: tests only run in files that are referenced.
const std = @import("std");

pub const money = @import("sim/money.zig");
pub const clock = @import("sim/clock.zig");

test {
    std.testing.refAllDecls(@This());
}
$ zig build test --summary all
Build Summary: 3/3 steps succeeded; 4/4 tests passed
test success
+- run test 4 pass (4 total) 169ms MaxRSS:2M

The nested test inside Clock is found because clock.zig's own file-level test references Clock; refAllDecls only needed to reach the two files.

Exercise 30.4 · Namespaces inside one file warm-up

A single file: a field-less money struct used as a namespace, a Stack using const Self = @This();, and thisFile() returning the file's own type. File: exercises/30-program-structure/ex4_namespace.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 30, exercise 4: namespaces inside one file.
//! Run with:  zig test ex4_namespace.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// A namespace: a struct with no fields, used only to group declarations.
pub const money = struct {
    pub const CBills = i64;
    pub fn fromCbills(n: i64) CBills {
        return n * 100;
    }
    fn hidden() void {}
};

pub const Stack = struct {
    items: [8]u32 = undefined,
    len: usize = 0,

    const Self = @This();

    pub fn push(self: *Self, v: u32) void {
        self.items[self.len] = v;
        self.len += 1;
    }
    pub fn pop(self: *Self) ?u32 {
        if (self.len == 0) return null;
        self.len -= 1;
        return self.items[self.len];
    }
};

/// The file itself is a struct too. This returns it.
pub fn thisFile() type {
    return @This();
}

test "namespace has no size" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 0), @sizeOf(money));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(money.CBills, 300), money.fromCbills(3));
}

test "Self works like the type name" {
    var s = Stack{};
    s.push(1);
    s.push(2);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u32, 2), s.pop());
    try std.testing.expect(@TypeOf(s) == Stack);
}

test "visibility is per declaration" {
    try std.testing.expect(@hasDecl(money, "fromCbills"));
    try std.testing.expect(@hasDecl(money, "hidden"));
    try std.testing.expect(!@hasDecl(money, "nope"));
}

test "the file is a struct" {
    try std.testing.expect(@typeInfo(thisFile()) == .@"struct");
    try std.testing.expect(@hasDecl(thisFile(), "Stack"));
}

A struct with no fields has size zero and exists only to group names. Note the third test: @hasDecl from inside the same file sees the private hidden, because visibility is about crossing file boundaries.

Check your understanding

  1. What does @import("x.zig") evaluate to?
    AnswerA type: the struct whose declarations are the top-level declarations of x.zig.
  2. How does the compiler know which files belong to a program run with zig run main.zig?
    AnswerIt follows @import from the root file. There is no separate file list.
  3. What is the complete visibility system of Zig?
    Answerpub on a declaration makes it visible to importers; without it the declaration is private to its file.
  4. Is it an error for a.zig to import b.zig while b.zig imports a.zig?
    AnswerNo. Imports are lazy and cycles are allowed, though a clean layering is still easier to read.
  5. When would a file have fields at the top level, and what does @This() return there?
    AnswerWhen the file is one type (conventionally named in CapitalCase). @This() returns that type.
  6. Why did zig test root_noref.zig run only one test?
    AnswerThe imported files were never referenced, so they were never analysed and their tests did not exist. refAllDecls or _ = money; fixes it.
  7. Does std.testing.refAllDeclsRecursive exist in 0.16?
    AnswerNo. Only refAllDecls does; a recursive walk is a few lines with std.meta.declarations.
  8. What is the difference between //! and ///?
    Answer//! documents the file (the struct it defines) and goes at the top; /// documents the declaration immediately below it.
What you learned.
  • A Zig file is a struct; @import returns its type; paths are relative to the importing file and may enter subdirectories.
  • pub is the whole visibility system; everything else is private to its file.
  • Bind namespace imports to lower-case names, type-files to capitalised names, or take a single declaration directly.
  • root.zig re-exports the tree with pub const x = @import("…"); the executable reaches it by module name.
  • Cyclic imports work because analysis is lazy.
  • Files with top-level fields are types; @This() names the enclosing type.
  • //! documents a file, /// a declaration.
  • Tests only run in referenced files: use std.testing.refAllDecls(@This()) in the root, and reference nested namespaces yourself.

31. The build system

In this chapter you will stop typing zig run file.zig and start describing your program in build.zig: a Zig program that builds a graph of steps. You will create a project with zig init, read every line it generates, add modules, options, run and test steps, choose optimisation modes, and finally read IRON LEDGER's real build script from top to bottom.

31.1 zig init

There is one tool, zig. It compiles, tests, formats and runs. For anything bigger than one file it reads build.zig, and the quickest way to get a correct one is to let it write one. In an empty directory:

$ mkdir init && cd init && zig init
info: created build.zig
info: created build.zig.zon
info: created src/main.zig
info: created src/root.zig
info: see `zig build --help` for a menu of options

Four files. build.zig.zon is the package manifest you met in Chapter 28. src/root.zig is a library with one function and a test. src/main.zig is an executable that imports the library. And build.zig is about 150 lines, most of them comments, describing how the two fit together. Trimmed of its comments it is this:

const std = @import("std");

pub fn build(b: *std.Build) void {
    const target = b.standardTargetOptions(.{});
    const optimize = b.standardOptimizeOption(.{});

    const mod = b.addModule("init", .{
        .root_source_file = b.path("src/root.zig"),
        .target = target,
    });

    const exe = b.addExecutable(.{
        .name = "init",
        .root_module = b.createModule(.{
            .root_source_file = b.path("src/main.zig"),
            .target = target,
            .optimize = optimize,
            .imports = &.{
                .{ .name = "init", .module = mod },
            },
        }),
    });
    b.installArtifact(exe);

    const run_step = b.step("run", "Run the app");
    const run_cmd = b.addRunArtifact(exe);
    run_step.dependOn(&run_cmd.step);
    run_cmd.step.dependOn(b.getInstallStep());
    if (b.args) |args| {
        run_cmd.addArgs(args);
    }

    const mod_tests = b.addTest(.{ .root_module = mod });
    const run_mod_tests = b.addRunArtifact(mod_tests);
    const exe_tests = b.addTest(.{ .root_module = exe.root_module });
    const run_exe_tests = b.addRunArtifact(exe_tests);

    const test_step = b.step("test", "Run tests");
    test_step.dependOn(&run_mod_tests.step);
    test_step.dependOn(&run_exe_tests.step);
}

The rest of this chapter explains each of those lines, with a slightly smaller project of our own so the output fits on a page.

31.2 A build script does not build

Read the signature: pub fn build(b: *std.Build) void. When you type zig build, the compiler first compiles this function into a small program called the build runner, runs it, and the function describes the work by adding steps to b. Nothing is compiled while build() executes. Only after it returns does the runner look at the graph, decide which steps the user asked for, work out what is cached, and execute the rest, in parallel where dependencies allow.

That is why the calls are named the way they are: addExecutable, addTest, addRunArtifact. Each adds a node. dependOn adds an edge. b.step("name", …) creates a named entry point the user can type. Everything else is plumbing between nodes.

31.3 Anatomy of build.zig

Here is the project for this chapter: a library module money in lib/, an executable in src/, two options, build-time constants, and run and test steps. Every line is numbered by the comment above it.

ledger/build.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn build(b: *std.Build) void {
    // 1. Options the user can pass on the command line.
    const target = b.standardTargetOptions(.{});
    const optimize = b.standardOptimizeOption(.{});
    const verbose = b.option(bool, "verbose", "Print every transaction") orelse false;
    const company = b.option([]const u8, "company", "Company name baked into the binary") orelse "Unnamed";

    // 2. A library module other code can import as "money".
    const money = b.addModule("money", .{
        .root_source_file = b.path("lib/money.zig"),
        .target = target,
    });

    // 3. Build-time constants, visible in code as @import("build_options").
    const opts = b.addOptions();
    opts.addOption(bool, "verbose", verbose);
    opts.addOption([]const u8, "company", company);

    // 4. The executable: its own root module that imports the library.
    const exe = b.addExecutable(.{
        .name = "ledger",
        .root_module = b.createModule(.{
            .root_source_file = b.path("src/main.zig"),
            .target = target,
            .optimize = optimize,
            .imports = &.{
                .{ .name = "money", .module = money },
                .{ .name = "build_options", .module = opts.createModule() },
            },
        }),
    });
    b.installArtifact(exe);

    // 5. `zig build run -- args`
    const run_cmd = b.addRunArtifact(exe);
    run_cmd.step.dependOn(b.getInstallStep());
    if (b.args) |args| run_cmd.addArgs(args);
    const run_step = b.step("run", "Run the ledger");
    run_step.dependOn(&run_cmd.step);

    // 6. `zig build test`: one test binary per module.
    const lib_tests = b.addTest(.{ .root_module = money });
    const exe_tests = b.addTest(.{ .root_module = exe.root_module });
    const test_step = b.step("test", "Run all tests");
    test_step.dependOn(&b.addRunArtifact(lib_tests).step);
    test_step.dependOn(&b.addRunArtifact(exe_tests).step);
}

ledger/lib/money.zig

//! The "money" module: C-bills as integers, never floats.
const std = @import("std");

pub const CBills = i64;

pub fn fromCbills(n: i64) CBills {
    return n * 100;
}

pub fn format(buf: []u8, amount: CBills) ![]u8 {
    const sign: []const u8 = if (amount < 0) "-" else "";
    const abs: u64 = @abs(amount);
    return std.fmt.bufPrint(buf, "{s}{d}.{d:0>2} C-bills", .{ sign, abs / 100, abs % 100 });
}

test "format" {
    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("12.05 C-bills", try format(&buf, 1205));
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("-0.50 C-bills", try format(&buf, -50));
}

ledger/src/main.zig

const std = @import("std");
const money = @import("money");
const build_options = @import("build_options");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var w = std.Io.File.stdout().writer(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &w.interface;

    var balance: money.CBills = money.fromCbills(1000);
    var it = std.process.Args.Iterator.init(init.minimal.args);
    _ = it.next();
    while (it.next()) |arg| {
        const delta = try std.fmt.parseInt(i64, arg, 10);
        balance += delta;
        if (build_options.verbose) try out.print("  {s:>8} -> {d}\n", .{ arg, balance });
    }
    var fbuf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    try out.print("{s}: {s}\n", .{ build_options.company, try money.format(&fbuf, balance) });
    try out.flush();
}

test "main module compiles and sees the library" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(money.CBills, 200), money.fromCbills(2));
}

1. Options. b.standardTargetOptions registers -Dtarget and -Dcpu, so anyone can cross-compile your project without editing the script. b.standardOptimizeOption registers -Doptimize. b.option(T, name, description) declares your own flag; it returns ?T, null when the user did not pass it, and you supply the default with orelse. Supported Ts include bool, integers, []const u8, enums, and lists of strings.

2. Modules. A module is a tree of source files with one root, plus the settings needed to compile it. b.addModule("money", …) creates one and makes it available under that name to other packages that depend on yours. b.createModule(…) creates one that is private to this build. Both take the same options: root_source_file, target, optimize, and an imports list that says which other modules this one may @import by name.

3. Build options. b.addOptions() creates a step that writes a tiny generated Zig file, and addOption(T, name, value) adds a constant to it. opts.createModule() turns that into a module you can import. In the source, @import("build_options").verbose is then a compile-time bool, and if (build_options.verbose) compiles to nothing at all when it is false.

4. The executable. b.addExecutable takes a name and a root_module. The root module is where main lives, and its imports list is how the source's @import("money") finds the library. b.installArtifact(exe) says "when the user runs the default step, copy this into the install prefix", which is zig-out/bin/ unless changed.

5. Run. b.addRunArtifact(exe) creates a step that executes the built program. Making it depend on the install step means it runs the installed copy. b.args is the optional list of words after -- on the command line, forwarded with addArgs. Finally b.step("run", …) creates the entry point and dependOn wires it to the run step.

6. Tests. b.addTest compiles a module as a test binary. A test binary covers one module, so a project with a library and an executable makes two and runs both under one test step. Steps run in parallel when nothing orders them.

31.4 Running it

$ zig build
$ find zig-out -type f
zig-out/bin/ledger
$ zig build run -- 500 -25
Unnamed: 1004.75 C-bills
$ zig build run -Dverbose -Dcompany="Kell Hounds" -- 500 -25
       500 -> 100500
       -25 -> 100475
Kell Hounds: 1004.75 C-bills
$ zig build test --summary all
Build Summary: 6/6 steps succeeded; 2/2 tests passed
test success
+- run test 1 pass (1 total) 297ms MaxRSS:2M
|  +- compile test Debug native success 1s MaxRSS:272M
+- run test 1 pass (1 total) 164ms MaxRSS:2M
   +- compile test Debug native success 1s MaxRSS:272M
      +- options cached

Three things to notice. A plain zig build prints nothing on success; the artifact appears under zig-out. Words after -- go to the program, words before it (starting with -D) go to the build script. And --summary all shows the step tree, including which steps were served from the cache: the options step did not need to rerun.

The generated help lists your options next to the standard ones, with the description text you wrote:

$ zig build --help
Usage: /opt/homebrew/Cellar/zig/0.16.0_1/bin/zig build [steps] [options]

Steps:
  install (default)            Copy build artifacts to prefix path
  uninstall                    Remove build artifacts from prefix path
  run                          Run the ledger
  test                         Run all tests

Project-Specific Options:
  -Dtarget=[string]            The CPU architecture, OS, and ABI to build for
  -Dcpu=[string]               Target CPU features to add or subtract
  -Dofmt=[string]              Target object format
  -Ddynamic-linker=[string]    Path to interpreter on the target system
  -Doptimize=[enum]            Prioritize performance, safety, or binary size
                                 Supported Values:
                                   Debug
                                   ReleaseSafe
                                   ReleaseFast
                                   ReleaseSmall
  -Dverbose=[bool]             Print every transaction
  -Dcompany=[string]           Company name baked into the binary

zig build -l prints just the steps. A misspelled option is an error, not a silent ignore: zig build -Dnope=1 stops with error: invalid option: -Dnope.

31.5 Optimisation modes

The -Doptimize flag chooses one of four modes, and the choice changes what the language guarantees:

ModeSpeedSafety checksUse it for
Debug (default)slowon: overflow, bounds, null, leak detectiondevelopment, every test run
ReleaseSafefaston: overflow, bounds, null still panicshipping software that must fail loudly
ReleaseFastfastestoff: undefined behaviour on overflowbenchmarks, code you have tested to exhaustion
ReleaseSmallfastoff, plus size over speedembedded, downloads where size matters
$ zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSmall --prefix /tmp/ledger-small
$ zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -p /tmp/ledger-fast
$ ls -l zig-out/bin/ledger /tmp/ledger-small/bin/ledger /tmp/ledger-fast/bin/ledger
2065784 zig-out/bin/ledger
 396936 /tmp/ledger-fast/bin/ledger
 165272 /tmp/ledger-small/bin/ledger

The same program is two megabytes in Debug (full debug info and safety code), 400 KB in ReleaseFast, and 165 KB in ReleaseSmall. --prefix (short form -p) redirects the install from zig-out to any directory, which is how you produce a release tree.

Do not test in ReleaseFast. The safety checks that make Debug and ReleaseSafe catch overflow and out-of-bounds are switched off in ReleaseFast. A bug that panics in Debug may silently corrupt memory there. Develop and test in Debug, ship ReleaseSafe unless you have measured a need for more, and use std.math.add-style checked functions for arithmetic that must be correct in every mode (Exercise 31.4).

31.6 The cache and the output directory

Two directories appear beside build.zig. zig-out/ is the install prefix: bin/ for executables, lib/ for libraries, whatever installDirectory adds. It is yours to ship or delete. .zig-cache/ holds compiled objects keyed by a hash of their inputs, so a second zig build that changes nothing does nothing. There is also a global cache (~/.cache/zig on this machine, see zig env) for the standard library and fetched packages. Both caches are safe to delete; the next build simply takes longer. Add both directories to .gitignore.

31.7 Data files and C libraries

Two more module calls round out the vocabulary. module.addAnonymousImport("name", .{ .root_source_file = path }) binds a file anywhere on disk to an import name; you saw it in Chapter 28 for ZON tables. And for C:

mod.link_libc = true;
mod.linkSystemLibrary("sqlite3", .{});

The first links the C standard library into the module; the second asks the system linker for libsqlite3. Chapter 35 shows what the Zig side of such a binding looks like. Both are set on the module, and any executable or test that uses the module inherits them, which is why IRON LEDGER's tests can open a database without repeating the linker flags.

31.8 Reading IRON LEDGER's build.zig

Now comes the real thing, game/build.zig. It is the zig init template grown up, and you can read it in the order the template used. Comments are trimmed.

pub fn build(b: *std.Build) void {
    const target = b.standardTargetOptions(.{});
    const optimize = b.standardOptimizeOption(.{});

    const mod = b.addModule("game", .{
        .root_source_file = b.path("src/root.zig"),
        .target = target,
    });

The simulation core is a module named game, rooted at the root.zig you read in Chapter 30. Then the data tables:

    const data_dir = b.option([]const u8, "data", "Directory overlaying data/*.zon and data/tables/*.zon (mod support)");
    const DataFile = struct { import_name: []const u8, rel: []const u8 };
    const data_files = [_]DataFile{
        .{ .import_name = "chassis_zon", .rel = "chassis.zon" },
        .{ .import_name = "planets_zon", .rel = "planets.zon" },
        .{ .import_name = "parts_zon", .rel = "parts.zon" },
        .{ .import_name = "tuning_zon", .rel = "tables/tuning.zon" },
        // … nine more
    };
    var overlaid = std.ArrayList([]const u8).empty;
    for (data_files) |f| {
        var path: std.Build.LazyPath = b.path(b.fmt("data/{s}", .{f.rel}));
        if (data_dir) |dir| {
            const candidate = b.pathJoin(&.{ dir, f.rel });
            const exists = if (std.fs.path.isAbsolute(candidate))
                std.Io.Dir.accessAbsolute(b.graph.io, candidate, .{})
            else
                b.build_root.handle.access(b.graph.io, candidate, .{});
            if (exists) |_| {
                path = if (std.fs.path.isAbsolute(candidate)) .{ .cwd_relative = candidate } else b.path(candidate);
                overlaid.append(b.allocator, f.rel) catch @panic("OOM");
            } else |_| {}
        }
        mod.addAnonymousImport(f.import_name, .{ .root_source_file = path });
    }

This is build.zig as a program, not a config file. A table of thirteen data files, a loop, and inside the loop a real file-system check (access through the build's own io) to see whether a mod directory supplies a replacement. Whatever path wins is bound with addAnonymousImport. The list of overlaid files is collected so the binary can report it:

    const build_options = b.addOptions();
    build_options.addOption(?[]const u8, "data_dir", data_dir);
    build_options.addOption([]const []const u8, "data_overlays", overlaid.items);
    mod.addImport("build_options", build_options.createModule());

    mod.link_libc = true;
    mod.linkSystemLibrary("sqlite3", .{});

Options can be optionals and lists of strings; root.zig's dataProvenance function reads them to print "stock tables" or "mod <dir>: 3 files overlaid" on the settings screen. Then SQLite is linked into the module, once. The executable follows the template exactly:

    const exe = b.addExecutable(.{
        .name = "game",
        .root_module = b.createModule(.{
            .root_source_file = b.path("src/main.zig"),
            .target = target,
            .optimize = optimize,
            .imports = &.{ .{ .name = "game", .module = mod } },
        }),
    });
    b.installArtifact(exe);

Packaging adds something the template lacks, installDirectory, with an opt-in for the large soundtrack:

    const bundle_music = b.option(bool, "bundle-music", "Copy data/music into the install prefix (large)") orelse false;
    if (bundle_music) b.installDirectory(.{
        .source_dir = b.path("data/music"),
        .install_dir = .prefix,
        .install_subdir = "share/iron-ledger/music",
    });
    b.installDirectory(.{
        .source_dir = b.path("docs/logos"),
        .install_dir = .prefix,
        .install_subdir = "share/iron-ledger/logos",
        .include_extensions = &.{".png"},
    });

And the run and test steps are the template's, with one addition worth learning from:

    const test_step = b.step("test", "Run tests");
    test_step.dependOn(&run_mod_tests.step);
    test_step.dependOn(&run_exe_tests.step);
    // A green test run must also mean the client builds: the tests compile
    // the TUI as tests, so an exe-only compile error stayed invisible while
    // `zig-out/bin/game` went stale under a passing suite (2026-09-06).
    test_step.dependOn(b.getInstallStep());

A test step that also depends on install means "the tests passed and the binary builds". That line exists because of a real afternoon lost to a green test suite and a stale executable. Build scripts accumulate this kind of knowledge, and because they are ordinary Zig, the comment can sit right next to the fix.

In IRON LEDGER. The commands you will use daily in the game/ directory are zig build (compile and install to zig-out/bin/game), zig build test --summary all (every test block in both modules, plus the install), zig build run -- --tui (build and launch the terminal client), and zig build -Ddata=mymod (overlay tables from a mod directory). Run zig build --help there: the -Ddata and -Dbundle-music options you see are the two b.option calls above, and Zig generated the help text from their descriptions. The whole script is game/build.zig; read it once with this chapter beside you and it will hold no surprises.

Exercises

Exercise 31.1 · Two modules warm-up

In exercises/31-build-system/ex1_two_modules/, expose lib/dice.zig as a module named dice, import it from the executable, and add a test step that runs the tests of both modules. Check with zig build run -- 3025 and zig build test --summary all.

Solution

build.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn build(b: *std.Build) void {
    const target = b.standardTargetOptions(.{});
    const optimize = b.standardOptimizeOption(.{});

    // The library module, importable as "dice".
    const dice = b.addModule("dice", .{
        .root_source_file = b.path("lib/dice.zig"),
        .target = target,
    });

    // The executable imports it.
    const exe = b.addExecutable(.{
        .name = "roll",
        .root_module = b.createModule(.{
            .root_source_file = b.path("src/main.zig"),
            .target = target,
            .optimize = optimize,
            .imports = &.{.{ .name = "dice", .module = dice }},
        }),
    });
    b.installArtifact(exe);

    const run_cmd = b.addRunArtifact(exe);
    if (b.args) |args| run_cmd.addArgs(args);
    b.step("run", "Roll some dice").dependOn(&run_cmd.step);

    const lib_tests = b.addTest(.{ .root_module = dice });
    const exe_tests = b.addTest(.{ .root_module = exe.root_module });
    const test_step = b.step("test", "Run tests in both modules");
    test_step.dependOn(&b.addRunArtifact(lib_tests).step);
    test_step.dependOn(&b.addRunArtifact(exe_tests).step);
}
$ zig build run -- 3025
seed 3025: 4 + 1 = 5
$ zig build test --summary all
Build Summary: 5/5 steps succeeded; 3/3 tests passed
test success

Two addTest calls, one per module, both hanging off the same step. b.step(…) returns the step so .dependOn can be chained directly.

Exercise 31.2 · Options become constants practice

In exercises/31-build-system/ex2_options/, wire -Ddifficulty (an enum), -Dfunds (a u32) and -Dcheats (a bool) through addOptions into @import("build_options"). Try zig build run -Ddifficulty=hard -Dfunds=500000 -Dcheats.

Solution

build.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn build(b: *std.Build) void {
    const target = b.standardTargetOptions(.{});
    const optimize = b.standardOptimizeOption(.{});

    const difficulty = b.option(enum { easy, normal, hard }, "difficulty", "Starting difficulty") orelse .normal;
    const start_funds = b.option(u32, "funds", "Starting C-bills") orelse 1_000_000;
    const cheats = b.option(bool, "cheats", "Enable cheat commands") orelse false;

    const opts = b.addOptions();
    opts.addOption([]const u8, "difficulty", @tagName(difficulty));
    opts.addOption(u32, "start_funds", start_funds);
    opts.addOption(bool, "cheats", cheats);

    const mod = b.createModule(.{
        .root_source_file = b.path("src/main.zig"),
        .target = target,
        .optimize = optimize,
    });
    mod.addOptions("build_options", opts);

    const exe = b.addExecutable(.{ .name = "options", .root_module = mod });
    b.installArtifact(exe);
    b.step("run", "Print the baked-in settings").dependOn(&b.addRunArtifact(exe).step);

    const tests = b.addTest(.{ .root_module = mod });
    b.step("test", "Run tests").dependOn(&b.addRunArtifact(tests).step);
}
$ zig build run
difficulty normal, funds 1000000, cheats false
$ zig build run -Ddifficulty=hard -Dfunds=500000 -Dcheats
difficulty hard, funds 250000, cheats true
cheat commands enabled

An enum option lists its values in --help automatically. The enum is converted to its tag name before being stored, because a build option must be a type the generated file can spell. mod.addOptions("build_options", opts) is a shorthand for adding the options module as an import.

Exercise 31.3 · Custom steps practice

In exercises/31-build-system/ex3_steps/, add a demo step that runs the program with three fixed arguments, a fmt step using b.addFmt with .check = true, and make test depend on the format check. zig build -l should list all of them.

Solution

build.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn build(b: *std.Build) void {
    const target = b.standardTargetOptions(.{});
    const optimize = b.standardOptimizeOption(.{});
    const mod = b.createModule(.{
        .root_source_file = b.path("src/main.zig"),
        .target = target,
        .optimize = optimize,
    });
    const exe = b.addExecutable(.{ .name = "steps", .root_module = mod });
    b.installArtifact(exe);

    // A "run" step that forwards `zig build run -- args`.
    const run_cmd = b.addRunArtifact(exe);
    run_cmd.step.dependOn(b.getInstallStep());
    if (b.args) |args| run_cmd.addArgs(args);
    b.step("run", "Run the program").dependOn(&run_cmd.step);

    // A "demo" step that always runs the program with fixed arguments.
    const demo_cmd = b.addRunArtifact(exe);
    demo_cmd.addArgs(&.{ "alpha", "beta", "gamma" });
    b.step("demo", "Run with three fixed arguments").dependOn(&demo_cmd.step);

    // A "fmt" step: zig fmt --check over src/.
    const fmt = b.addFmt(.{ .paths = &.{"src"}, .check = true });
    b.step("fmt", "Check formatting").dependOn(&fmt.step);

    // "test" depends on tests AND on the format check.
    const tests = b.addTest(.{ .root_module = mod });
    const test_step = b.step("test", "Run tests and the format check");
    test_step.dependOn(&b.addRunArtifact(tests).step);
    test_step.dependOn(&fmt.step);
}
$ zig build -l
  install (default)            Copy build artifacts to prefix path
  uninstall                    Remove build artifacts from prefix path
  run                          Run the program
  demo                         Run with three fixed arguments
  fmt                          Check formatting
  test                         Run tests and the format check
$ zig build demo
3 argument(s)

Two run steps of the same executable are two nodes; each gets its own arguments. A format check that gates the test step is a cheap way to keep a repository tidy.

Exercise 31.4 · Which mode am I in? warm-up

A single file that prints @import("builtin").mode, says whether safety checks are on, and uses std.math.add to detect overflow in a way that works in every mode. Run it with zig run and again with zig run -O ReleaseFast. File: exercises/31-build-system/ex4_mode.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 31, exercise 4: see the optimize mode from inside the program.
//! Run with:  zig run ex4_mode.zig
//! Then try:  zig run -O ReleaseFast ex4_mode.zig
//! Expected output (Debug):
//!   mode: Debug
//!   safety checks: on
//!   overflow check: caught error.Overflow
const std = @import("std");
const builtin = @import("builtin");

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("mode: {s}\n", .{@tagName(builtin.mode)});
    const safe = switch (builtin.mode) {
        .Debug, .ReleaseSafe => true,
        .ReleaseFast, .ReleaseSmall => false,
    };
    std.debug.print("safety checks: {s}\n", .{if (safe) "on" else "off"});
    // Never rely on a panic to catch overflow: use the checked builtin.
    const big: u8 = 250;
    if (std.math.add(u8, big, 10)) |v| {
        std.debug.print("overflow check: {d}\n", .{v});
    } else |err| {
        std.debug.print("overflow check: caught {s}\n", .{@errorName(err)});
    }
}
$ zig run ex4_mode.zig
mode: Debug
safety checks: on
overflow check: caught Overflow
$ zig run -O ReleaseFast ex4_mode.zig
mode: ReleaseFast
safety checks: off
overflow check: caught Overflow

@import("builtin") is a compiler-generated module describing the current build: mode, target, endianness. The checked std.math.add returns an error union, so the overflow is caught in ReleaseFast too, where big + 10 would silently wrap.

Check your understanding

  1. Does build() compile anything while it runs?
    AnswerNo. It adds steps and dependencies to a graph; the build runner executes the graph afterwards.
  2. What is the difference between b.addModule and b.createModule?
    AnswerBoth create a module; addModule also exposes it by name to packages that depend on yours, createModule keeps it private to this build.
  3. How does @import("money") in src/main.zig find lib/money.zig?
    AnswerThrough the executable's root module imports list, which maps the name "money" to the module whose root is lib/money.zig.
  4. Where do words after -- on the zig build run command line go?
    AnswerInto b.args, which the script forwards to the run step with addArgs; the program sees them as its arguments.
  5. What does b.option(bool, "verbose", "…") return when the user passes nothing?
    Answernull; the script supplies a default with orelse.
  6. Which optimisation modes keep safety checks on?
    AnswerDebug and ReleaseSafe. ReleaseFast and ReleaseSmall turn them off.
  7. Why does one project need two addTest calls?
    AnswerA test binary covers one module. A library module and an executable module each need their own.
  8. What does --prefix change, and what is its short form?
    AnswerThe install directory, zig-out by default; -p.
What you learned.
  • zig init writes build.zig, build.zig.zon, src/main.zig and src/root.zig.
  • build() describes a graph of steps; the runner executes it with caching and parallelism.
  • standardTargetOptions, standardOptimizeOption and b.option declare -D flags; zig build --help lists them.
  • addModule/createModule define modules; imports connects them by name; addExecutable takes a root_module.
  • installArtifact, addRunArtifact, b.args, b.step and dependOn build run steps; addTest per module builds test steps.
  • addOptions turns flags into @import("build_options") constants; addAnonymousImport binds data files; link_libc and linkSystemLibrary pull in C.
  • Debug and ReleaseSafe keep safety checks; ReleaseFast and ReleaseSmall drop them. --prefix moves the install; zig-out and .zig-cache are disposable.
  • IRON LEDGER's script is the template plus a data-file loop, build options, SQLite, packaging and a test step that also installs.

32. Command-line programs

In this chapter you will write programs that behave well in a terminal: they read arguments and flags, read standard input line by line or all at once, write results to standard output and complaints to standard error, look at environment variables, and exit with a status that scripts can trust. You will finish with a small read-eval-print loop of the kind IRON LEDGER offers behind --repl.

32.1 What main receives

Since Chapter 1 you have seen two shapes of main: pub fn main() void for programs that only print with std.debug.print, and pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void for everything else. In 0.16 that init parameter is how a program receives everything the operating system gave it. Its fields, from the standard library:

FieldWhat it is
init.iothe std.Io instance every file, clock and process operation needs
init.gpaa general purpose allocator, leak-checked in Debug
init.arenaa pointer to an arena that lives as long as the process; use init.arena.allocator()
init.minimal.argsthe command-line arguments
init.minimal.environthe raw environment block
init.environ_mapthe environment as a map you can query by name
init.preopensfiles handed over by a parent process (mostly WASI)

Nothing is global. A function that wants to read a file must be handed an io; a function that wants the arguments must be handed them. This is the same discipline as allocators, and it has the same benefit: you can see from a signature what a function is able to do.

32.2 Arguments

init.minimal.args is not a slice; it is an opaque handle that works the same on every platform. You either iterate it with std.process.Args.Iterator, or turn it into a slice with toSlice and an allocator. The first entry is always the program itself.

args.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var it = std.process.Args.Iterator.init(init.minimal.args);
    const prog = it.next().?;
    std.debug.print("program: {s}\n", .{prog});
    var n: usize = 0;
    while (it.next()) |arg| : (n += 1) {
        std.debug.print("arg[{d}] = \"{s}\"\n", .{ n, arg });
    }
    std.debug.print("{d} argument(s)\n", .{n});

    // The same list as a slice, allocated once from the process arena.
    const all = try init.minimal.args.toSlice(init.arena.allocator());
    std.debug.print("as a slice: {d} entries, last = {s}\n", .{ all.len, all[all.len - 1] });
}
$ zig run args.zig -- one "two words" 3
program: /Users/john/.cache/zig/o/0550ef7316e5d2796521459761bbf628/args
arg[0] = "one"
arg[1] = "two words"
arg[2] = "3"
3 argument(s)
as a slice: 4 entries, last = 3

Two habits to note. it.next() returns an optional, so the program name comes out with .? (it always exists) and the loop uses while (it.next()) |arg|. And the shell, not Zig, split the command line: "two words" arrived as one argument because of the quotes. The -- after zig run args.zig separates the compiler's arguments from the program's, exactly as zig build run -- does.

The arena allocator is the right choice for toSlice: the argument list is needed for the whole run and freed automatically at exit.

32.3 Parsing flags by hand

Zig's standard library has no flag-parsing framework, and for most programs you do not want one. A loop, std.mem.eql, std.mem.startsWith and an options struct with defaults handle -v, --days 30, --name=Kell and positional arguments in twenty lines, and the result is a plain struct the rest of the program can use.

flags.zig

const std = @import("std");

const Options = struct {
    verbose: bool = false,
    days: u32 = 1,
    name: []const u8 = "campaign",
    files: std.ArrayList([]const u8) = .empty,
};

const usage =
    \\usage: flags [-v] [--days N] [--name NAME] FILE...
    \\
;

fn parse(gpa: std.mem.Allocator, args: std.process.Args) !Options {
    var opts = Options{};
    var it = std.process.Args.Iterator.init(args);
    _ = it.next();
    while (it.next()) |arg| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "-v") or std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "--verbose")) {
            opts.verbose = true;
        } else if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "--days")) {
            const value = it.next() orelse return error.MissingValue;
            opts.days = try std.fmt.parseInt(u32, value, 10);
        } else if (std.mem.startsWith(u8, arg, "--name=")) {
            opts.name = arg["--name=".len..];
        } else if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "--help") or std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "-h")) {
            return error.HelpRequested;
        } else if (std.mem.startsWith(u8, arg, "-")) {
            std.debug.print("unknown flag: {s}\n", .{arg});
            return error.UnknownFlag;
        } else {
            try opts.files.append(gpa, arg);
        }
    }
    if (opts.files.items.len == 0) return error.NoFiles;
    return opts;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) u8 {
    var opts = parse(init.gpa, init.minimal.args) catch |err| switch (err) {
        error.HelpRequested => {
            std.debug.print("{s}", .{usage});
            return 0;
        },
        else => {
            std.debug.print("error: {s}\n{s}", .{ @errorName(err), usage });
            return 2;
        },
    };
    defer opts.files.deinit(init.gpa);
    std.debug.print("verbose={} days={d} name={s} files={d}\n", .{ opts.verbose, opts.days, opts.name, opts.files.items.len });
    for (opts.files.items) |f| std.debug.print("  {s}\n", .{f});
    return 0;
}
$ zig run flags.zig -- -v --days 30 --name=Kell a.txt b.txt
verbose=true days=30 name=Kell files=2
  a.txt
  b.txt
$ zig run flags.zig -- --help
usage: flags [-v] [--days N] [--name NAME] FILE...
$ zig run flags.zig -- --bogus x
unknown flag: --bogus
error: UnknownFlag
usage: flags [-v] [--days N] [--name NAME] FILE...
$ echo $?
2

The structure is worth copying. parse is a pure function from arguments to an Options struct or an error, so it can be tested without a terminal (Exercise 32.3 does exactly that). Values that follow a flag are pulled with another it.next(), and a missing one is an error, not a crash. The usage text is a multi-line string literal with \\, kept in one place. And main is the only function that talks to the user: it maps error.HelpRequested to a clean exit and everything else to a message plus a non-zero status.

32.4 Exit codes

Every process ends with a small integer, and shells, scripts and CI systems read it: zero means success, anything else means failure. Zig gives you three ways to set it.

  • Declare pub fn main(…) u8 and return the code. This is the clearest.
  • Declare main as returning an error union and let an error escape: the runtime prints error: Name with a stack trace and exits with 1.
  • Call std.process.exit(code) from anywhere. It never returns and runs no defers, so use it only for "stop right now" situations.

exit.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) u8 {
    var it = std.process.Args.Iterator.init(init.minimal.args);
    _ = it.next();
    const arg = it.next() orelse {
        std.debug.print("usage: exit <code>\n", .{});
        return 64;
    };
    if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "now")) {
        std.debug.print("leaving immediately\n", .{});
        std.process.exit(3);
    }
    const code = std.fmt.parseInt(u8, arg, 10) catch {
        std.debug.print("not a number: {s}\n", .{arg});
        return 1;
    };
    std.debug.print("returning {d}\n", .{code});
    return code;
}
$ zig build-exe exit.zig
$ ./exit; echo "status $?"
usage: exit <code>
status 64
$ ./exit 7; echo "status $?"
returning 7
status 7
$ ./exit now; echo "status $?"
leaving immediately
status 3
$ ./exit zzz; echo "status $?"
not a number: zzz
status 1

And the error-union version, which is what most of your programs have used so far:

exit_err.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn risky() !void {
    return error.DiskFull;
}

pub fn main() !void {
    try risky();
}
$ ./exit_err; echo "status $?"
error: DiskFull
/…/exit_err.zig:4:5: 0x100b8594b in risky (exit_err)
    return error.DiskFull;
    ^
…
status 1

The stack trace is wonderful while developing and unpleasant for users. Programs meant for other people catch errors in main, print one line, and return a code. The traditional values from sysexits.h are a good vocabulary: 0 success, 1 general failure, 2 bad usage (many tools), 64 usage error, 65 bad input data, 70 internal error, 74 I/O error. Exercise 32.5 uses them.

std.process.exit skips cleanup. Buffered output that has not been flushed is lost, files are not closed by your defers, and the leak checker does not run. Prefer return code; from main, which unwinds normally.

32.5 Reading standard input line by line

Standard input is a file, std.Io.File.stdin(), and like every file in 0.16 you read it through a reader with a buffer you provide. The reader's interface is a *std.Io.Reader, and its takeDelimiter('\n') method returns the next line without the newline, or null at end of input. A line longer than your buffer is error.StreamTooLong, so the buffer size is a real decision.

lines.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var rbuf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var stdin = std.Io.File.stdin().reader(init.io, &rbuf);
    const in = &stdin.interface;

    var wbuf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = std.Io.File.stdout().writer(init.io, &wbuf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;

    var lines: u32 = 0;
    var words: u32 = 0;
    var bytes: u64 = 0;
    while (try in.takeDelimiter('\n')) |line| {
        lines += 1;
        bytes += line.len + 1;
        var it = std.mem.tokenizeAny(u8, line, " \t");
        while (it.next()) |_| words += 1;
        try out.print("{d:>4}: {s}\n", .{ lines, line });
    }
    try out.print("{d} lines, {d} words, {d} bytes\n", .{ lines, words, bytes });
    try out.flush();
}
$ printf 'alpha beta\ngamma\n\ndelta epsilon zeta\n' | zig run lines.zig
   1: alpha beta
   2: gamma
   3:
   4: delta epsilon zeta
4 lines, 6 words, 37 bytes
$ printf 'one\ntwo' | zig run lines.zig
   1: one
   2: two
2 lines, 2 words, 8 bytes
