Two things to check against your intuition. An empty line comes back as an empty slice, not as null; only the true end of input is null. And a final line with no trailing newline is still returned, so "one\ntwo" counts as two lines. The slice you get points into the reader's buffer and is only valid until the next call, so copy it if you need to keep it.

Notice also that the program never blocks waiting for a terminal when its input is a pipe or a file; it simply reads until the end. Run it with no pipe and it waits for you to type, line by line, until you press Ctrl-D.

32.6 Reading all of standard input

When the input is small and you want it whole, allocRemaining reads everything into one allocated slice. The Limit argument is a ceiling that turns a runaway input into error.StreamTooLong rather than an out-of-memory condition.

readall.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var rbuf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdin = std.Io.File.stdin().reader(init.io, &rbuf);
    const text = try stdin.interface.allocRemaining(init.gpa, .limited(1 << 20));
    defer init.gpa.free(text);
    var upper: u32 = 0;
    for (text) |c| if (std.ascii.isUpper(c)) {
        upper += 1;
    };
    std.debug.print("read {d} bytes, {d} upper-case letters\n", .{ text.len, upper });
}
$ printf 'Hello World\nBig Mek\n' | zig run readall.zig
read 20 bytes, 4 upper-case letters

.limited(1 << 20) is one megabyte; .unlimited exists but think twice before using it on input you do not control. The result belongs to you: defer init.gpa.free(text).

32.7 stdout for results, stderr for everything else

A terminal program has two output streams, and the distinction matters as soon as someone pipes your output into another program. Standard output is for the result; standard error is for diagnostics, progress, warnings. Both are files with buffered writers, and both must be flushed. std.debug.print writes to standard error, unbuffered, which is why it has been fine for teaching and is wrong for the main output of a real tool.

streams.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var obuf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = std.Io.File.stdout().writer(init.io, &obuf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;
    var ebuf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var stderr = std.Io.File.stderr().writer(init.io, &ebuf);
    const err = &stderr.interface;

    try out.print("day,funds\n", .{});
    var funds: i64 = 1000;
    for (1..4) |day| {
        funds -= 150;
        try out.print("{d},{d}\n", .{ day, funds });
        if (funds < 700) try err.print("warning: day {d} funds low ({d})\n", .{ day, funds });
    }
    try out.flush();
    try err.flush();
}
$ zig run streams.zig 2>/dev/null
day,funds
1,850
2,700
3,550
$ zig run streams.zig >/dev/null
warning: day 3 funds low (550)

The CSV goes to stdout and survives 2>/dev/null; the warning goes to stderr and survives >/dev/null. Someone can now write streams > report.csv and still see the warning on their screen.

Flush before you block. Output sits in your buffer until flush(). If you print a prompt and then wait for input, flush the prompt first or the user will stare at a blank line. The REPL in section 32.9 does this on every turn.

32.8 Environment variables

init.environ_map is a pointer to a map from names to values, built from the process environment. get returns an optional slice; contains and count do what they say.

env.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const env = init.environ_map;
    const home = env.get("HOME") orelse "(unset)";
    std.debug.print("HOME = {s}\n", .{home});
    const seed_text = env.get("LEDGER_SEED") orelse "3025";
    const seed = try std.fmt.parseInt(u64, seed_text, 10);
    std.debug.print("seed = {d}\n", .{seed});
    std.debug.print("has PATH? {}\n", .{env.contains("PATH")});
    std.debug.print("{d} variables in the environment\n", .{env.count()});
}
$ LEDGER_SEED=99 zig run env.zig
HOME = /Users/john
seed = 99
has PATH? true
59 variables in the environment

The value is a plain []const u8 owned by the map, so it is valid for the life of the program and you do not free it. Parse it as you would any string. The orelse "3025" idiom gives a default without a branch, and is the usual way to let an environment variable override a built-in setting.

32.9 A read-eval-print loop

Everything so far combines into a small interactive shell: print a prompt, flush, read a line, split off the command word, act, repeat, until quit or end of input. This is a miniature of the game's --repl mode, which drives the whole simulation from typed commands.

repl.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var rbuf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdin = std.Io.File.stdin().reader(init.io, &rbuf);
    const in = &stdin.interface;
    var wbuf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = std.Io.File.stdout().writer(init.io, &wbuf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;

    var funds: i64 = 1000;
    var day: u32 = 1;
    try out.print("ledger repl. commands: day, pay N, earn N, status, quit\n", .{});
    while (true) {
        try out.print("day {d}> ", .{day});
        try out.flush();
        const raw = try in.takeDelimiter('\n') orelse break;
        const line = std.mem.trim(u8, raw, " \t\r");
        if (line.len == 0) continue;
        var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, line, ' ');
        const cmd = it.next().?;
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, cmd, "quit")) break;
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, cmd, "day")) {
            day += 1;
            funds -= 50;
        } else if (std.mem.eql(u8, cmd, "pay") or std.mem.eql(u8, cmd, "earn")) {
            const n = std.fmt.parseInt(i64, it.next() orelse "", 10) catch {
                try out.print("  usage: {s} N\n", .{cmd});
                continue;
            };
            funds += if (cmd[0] == 'p') -n else n;
        } else if (std.mem.eql(u8, cmd, "status")) {
            try out.print("  day {d}, {d} C-bills\n", .{ day, funds });
        } else {
            try out.print("  unknown command: {s}\n", .{cmd});
        }
    }
    try out.print("\nbye. final balance {d}\n", .{funds});
    try out.flush();
}
$ printf 'status\nearn 500\nday\nday\npay abc\nfly\nstatus\nquit\n' | zig run repl.zig
ledger repl. commands: day, pay N, earn N, status, quit
day 1>   day 1, 1000 C-bills
day 1> day 1> day 2> day 3>   usage: pay N
day 3>   unknown command: fly
day 3>   day 3, 1400 C-bills
day 3>
bye. final balance 1400

Piping input in shows the prompts jammed together, because the input is not echoed; type the same commands by hand and it reads naturally. The shape to remember: trim the raw line, skip empty lines, tokenizeScalar to get the command and its arguments, parseInt with a catch that prints usage and continues, and orelse break on the read so end of input ends the loop cleanly.

In IRON LEDGER. The executable's entry point, game/src/main.zig, is the flag loop from section 32.3 in the real world: 
pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var gs = game.state.GameState.init(init.gpa, .{ .seed = 3025 });
    defer gs.deinit();

    var args = std.process.Args.Iterator.init(init.minimal.args);
    _ = args.next(); // exe name
    var tui = false;
    var store_path: [:0]const u8 = "campaigns.db";
    while (args.next()) |arg| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "--tui")) tui = true;
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "--store")) store_path = args.next() orelse store_path;
    }
    if (tui) {
        try @import("tui/app.zig").run(init.io, init.gpa, store_path, .{ /* … */ });
    }
    // …
}
--store takes a value with the same args.next() orelse pattern, and init.io is passed down explicitly to the one part of the program that does I/O. The simulation core never receives an io, so it structurally cannot print, read a file or check the clock; the guide calls this "purity as a parameter that is not there". The --repl mode in game/src/sim/cli.zig is the loop from section 32.9 with the game's command set behind it.

Exercises

Exercise 32.1 · echo warm-up

Print the arguments separated by spaces to stdout, with -n suppressing the newline and -u upper-casing. File: exercises/32-cli/ex1_echo.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 32, exercise 1: echo with options.
//! Run with:  zig run ex1_echo.zig -- -n hello world
//! Expected output (for the command above, on stdout):
//!   hello world
//! With no arguments it prints an empty line. `-n` suppresses the newline,
//! `-u` upper-cases every word.
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = std.Io.File.stdout().writer(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;

    var newline = true;
    var upper = false;
    var first = true;
    var it = std.process.Args.Iterator.init(init.minimal.args);
    _ = it.next();
    while (it.next()) |arg| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "-n")) {
            newline = false;
            continue;
        }
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "-u")) {
            upper = true;
            continue;
        }
        if (!first) try out.writeByte(' ');
        first = false;
        if (upper) {
            for (arg) |c| try out.writeByte(std.ascii.toUpper(c));
        } else {
            try out.writeAll(arg);
        }
    }
    if (newline) try out.writeByte('\n');
    try out.flush();
}

Flags are consumed with continue so they never reach the printing code. writeByte and writeAll on the buffered writer avoid formatting when there is nothing to format.

Exercise 32.2 · wc warm-up

Read all of stdin line by line and print N lines, N words, N bytes. File: exercises/32-cli/ex2_wc.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 32, exercise 2: a tiny `wc`.
//! Run with:  printf 'a b\nc\n' | zig run ex2_wc.zig
//! Expected output (for the command above):
//!   2 lines, 3 words, 6 bytes
//! Reads all of stdin line by line; prints one summary line to stdout.
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var rbuf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var stdin = std.Io.File.stdin().reader(init.io, &rbuf);
    const in = &stdin.interface;
    var wbuf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = std.Io.File.stdout().writer(init.io, &wbuf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;

    var lines: u64 = 0;
    var words: u64 = 0;
    var bytes: u64 = 0;
    while (try in.takeDelimiter('\n')) |line| {
        lines += 1;
        bytes += line.len + 1;
        var it = std.mem.tokenizeAny(u8, line, " \t\r");
        while (it.next()) |_| words += 1;
    }
    try out.print("{d} lines, {d} words, {d} bytes\n", .{ lines, words, bytes });
    try out.flush();
}

With no input at all the loop body never runs and the program prints zeros, which is what wc does.

Exercise 32.3 · A testable flag parser practice

Write parse(gpa, args: []const []const u8) !Options supporting -v, --days N, --name NAME, --name=NAME, -h, and a bare -- after which everything is positional. Positionals are returned as an owned slice. File: exercises/32-cli/ex3_flags.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 32, exercise 3: a flag parser you can test.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_flags.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

pub const Options = struct {
    verbose: bool = false,
    days: u32 = 1,
    name: []const u8 = "campaign",
    /// Positional arguments, in order.
    files: []const []const u8 = &.{},
};

pub const ParseError = error{ MissingValue, BadNumber, UnknownFlag, HelpRequested };

/// Parse `args` (WITHOUT the program name). Positionals are copied into a
/// slice allocated from `gpa`; the caller frees `options.files`.
/// Supported: -v / --verbose, --days N, --name NAME, --name=NAME, -h / --help.
/// Everything after a bare "--" is positional even if it starts with "-".
pub fn parse(gpa: std.mem.Allocator, args: []const []const u8) (ParseError || std.mem.Allocator.Error)!Options {
    var opts = Options{};
    var files: std.ArrayList([]const u8) = .empty;
    errdefer files.deinit(gpa);
    var i: usize = 0;
    var only_positional = false;
    while (i < args.len) : (i += 1) {
        const arg = args[i];
        if (only_positional or !std.mem.startsWith(u8, arg, "-")) {
            try files.append(gpa, arg);
        } else if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "--")) {
            only_positional = true;
        } else if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "-v") or std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "--verbose")) {
            opts.verbose = true;
        } else if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "-h") or std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "--help")) {
            return error.HelpRequested;
        } else if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "--days")) {
            i += 1;
            if (i >= args.len) return error.MissingValue;
            opts.days = std.fmt.parseInt(u32, args[i], 10) catch return error.BadNumber;
        } else if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "--name")) {
            i += 1;
            if (i >= args.len) return error.MissingValue;
            opts.name = args[i];
        } else if (std.mem.startsWith(u8, arg, "--name=")) {
            opts.name = arg["--name=".len..];
        } else {
            return error.UnknownFlag;
        }
    }
    opts.files = try files.toOwnedSlice(gpa);
    return opts;
}

test "flags and positionals" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    const o = try parse(gpa, &.{ "-v", "--days", "30", "--name=Kell", "a.txt", "b.txt" });
    defer gpa.free(o.files);
    try std.testing.expect(o.verbose);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 30), o.days);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Kell", o.name);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 2), o.files.len);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("b.txt", o.files[1]);
}

test "defaults" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    const o = try parse(gpa, &.{});
    defer gpa.free(o.files);
    try std.testing.expect(!o.verbose);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 1), o.days);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("campaign", o.name);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 0), o.files.len);
}

test "separate --name value and the -- separator" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    const o = try parse(gpa, &.{ "--name", "Ana", "--", "-not-a-flag" });
    defer gpa.free(o.files);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Ana", o.name);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("-not-a-flag", o.files[0]);
}

test "errors" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    try std.testing.expectError(error.MissingValue, parse(gpa, &.{"--days"}));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.BadNumber, parse(gpa, &.{ "--days", "soon" }));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.UnknownFlag, parse(gpa, &.{"--bogus"}));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.HelpRequested, parse(gpa, &.{ "a", "-h" }));
}

Taking a slice of strings rather than std.process.Args is what makes the parser testable with &.{ "-v", "a" } literals. The errdefer frees the growing list if a later argument is bad.

Exercise 32.4 · A calculator REPL practice

Prompt with > , read A op B lines, print the result or error: Name, stop on quit or end of input. Keep eval pure and test it. File: exercises/32-cli/ex4_repl.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 32, exercise 4: a calculator REPL.
//! Run with:  zig run ex4_repl.zig
//! Then type lines such as  2 + 3  or  10 * 4 , and  quit  to leave.
//! Expected output for  printf '2 + 3\n10 / 4\n7 % 0\nquit\n' | zig run ex4_repl.zig
//!   > 5
//!   > 2
//!   > error: DivisionByZero
//!   > bye
//! Prompt goes to stdout and is flushed before each read. EOF ends the loop
//! exactly like "quit".
const std = @import("std");

const Error = error{ BadSyntax, BadNumber, DivisionByZero, UnknownOperator };

fn eval(line: []const u8) Error!i64 {
    var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, line, ' ');
    const a_text = it.next() orelse return error.BadSyntax;
    const op = it.next() orelse return error.BadSyntax;
    const b_text = it.next() orelse return error.BadSyntax;
    if (it.next() != null) return error.BadSyntax;
    const a = std.fmt.parseInt(i64, a_text, 10) catch return error.BadNumber;
    const b = std.fmt.parseInt(i64, b_text, 10) catch return error.BadNumber;
    if (op.len != 1) return error.UnknownOperator;
    return switch (op[0]) {
        '+' => a + b,
        '-' => a - b,
        '*' => a * b,
        '/' => if (b == 0) error.DivisionByZero else @divTrunc(a, b),
        '%' => if (b == 0) error.DivisionByZero else @rem(a, b),
        else => error.UnknownOperator,
    };
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var rbuf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdin = std.Io.File.stdin().reader(init.io, &rbuf);
    const in = &stdin.interface;
    var wbuf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = std.Io.File.stdout().writer(init.io, &wbuf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;

    while (true) {
        try out.writeAll("> ");
        try out.flush();
        const raw = try in.takeDelimiter('\n') orelse break;
        const line = std.mem.trim(u8, raw, " \t\r");
        if (line.len == 0) continue;
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, line, "quit")) break;
        if (eval(line)) |v| {
            try out.print("{d}\n", .{v});
        } else |err| {
            try out.print("error: {s}\n", .{@errorName(err)});
        }
    }
    try out.writeAll("bye\n");
    try out.flush();
}

test "eval" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 5), try eval("2 + 3"));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, -8), try eval("2 * -4"));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.DivisionByZero, eval("1 / 0"));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.BadSyntax, eval("1 +"));
    try std.testing.expectError(error.UnknownOperator, eval("1 ^ 2"));
}

The file both runs and tests: zig run uses main, zig test runs the eval test and ignores main. Division uses @divTrunc because / on signed integers is a compile error unless the sign is known.

Exercise 32.5 · Exit codes challenge

Sum the arguments and print the total (no arguments prints 0). --help: usage on stderr, status 0. Any other --flag: usage, status 64. A non-number: message, status 65. The word abort: std.process.exit(70) immediately. Output failures: 74. File: exercises/32-cli/ex5_exitcodes.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 32, exercise 5: exit codes that scripts can trust.
//! Run with:  zig run ex5_exitcodes.zig -- 12 30
//! Expected output (stdout): "42" and exit status 0. With no arguments: "0".
//! Rules: --help          -> usage on stderr, status 0;
//!        any other --flag -> usage on stderr, status 64 (EX_USAGE);
//!        a non-number     -> message on stderr, status 65 (EX_DATAERR);
//!        the word "abort" anywhere -> std.process.exit(70) immediately.
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) u8 {
    var obuf: [128]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = std.Io.File.stdout().writer(init.io, &obuf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;

    var it = std.process.Args.Iterator.init(init.minimal.args);
    _ = it.next();
    var sum: i64 = 0;
    while (it.next()) |arg| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "--help")) {
            std.debug.print("usage: exitcodes [--help] N [N...]\n", .{});
            return 0;
        }
        if (std.mem.startsWith(u8, arg, "--")) {
            std.debug.print("unknown flag {s}\nusage: exitcodes [--help] N [N...]\n", .{arg});
            return 64;
        }
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "abort")) {
            std.debug.print("aborting on request\n", .{});
            std.process.exit(70);
        }
        const n = std.fmt.parseInt(i64, arg, 10) catch {
            std.debug.print("not a number: {s}\n", .{arg});
            return 65;
        };
        sum += n;
    }
    out.print("{d}\n", .{sum}) catch return 74;
    out.flush() catch return 74;
    return 0;
}
$ ./ex5_exitcodes 12 30; echo "status $?"
42
status 0
$ ./ex5_exitcodes --bogus; echo "status $?"
unknown flag --bogus
usage: exitcodes [--help] N [N...]
status 64
$ ./ex5_exitcodes 1 x; echo "status $?"
not a number: x
status 65
$ ./ex5_exitcodes 1 abort; echo "status $?"
aborting on request
status 70

Because main returns u8 it cannot use try; every failing call gets an explicit catch return code. That is the price of precise exit codes, and it is a small one.

Check your understanding

  1. How do you get the command-line arguments in 0.16?
    AnswerFrom init.minimal.args, iterated with std.process.Args.Iterator.init(…) or converted with toSlice(allocator). The first entry is the program name.
  2. What are the three ways to set the exit status, and which one skips defer?
    AnswerReturn a u8 from main, let an error escape from main (status 1 with a trace), or call std.process.exit(code), which never returns and runs no defers.
  3. What does takeDelimiter('\n') return for an empty line, and at the end of input?
    AnswerAn empty slice for an empty line; null at end of input. A last line without a newline is still returned.
  4. Why should a program's result go to stdout and its warnings to stderr?
    AnswerSo the result can be piped or redirected into a file without the warnings, and the warnings still reach the terminal.
  5. What happens if you print a prompt and read a line without flushing?
    AnswerThe prompt stays in the buffer; the user sees nothing and the program appears to hang while waiting for input.
  6. How do you read an environment variable with a default?
    Answerinit.environ_map.get("NAME") orelse "default". The returned slice is owned by the map and is not freed by you.
  7. Why is parse in the flag examples written to take a slice of strings instead of reading init directly?
    AnswerSo it can be called from tests with literal argument lists, and so the only code that touches the process is main.
What you learned.
  • std.process.Init carries io, gpa, arena, minimal.args, environ_map; nothing is global.
  • Iterate arguments with std.process.Args.Iterator; parse flags with a loop, std.mem.eql/startsWith, and an options struct.
  • Return u8 from main for exit codes; escaping errors give status 1; std.process.exit is immediate and skips cleanup.
  • Read stdin with std.Io.File.stdin().reader(io, &buf) and takeDelimiter('\n'), or all at once with allocRemaining and a limit.
  • Write results to a buffered stdout writer and diagnostics to stderr; flush both, and flush prompts before reading.
  • Environment variables come from init.environ_map.get.
  • A REPL is prompt, flush, read, trim, tokenize, dispatch, repeat; end of input ends it.

33. Files and directories with std.Io

In this chapter you will create, write, read, append to and delete files, make and list directories, ask for a file's size, handle a missing file gracefully, take paths apart with std.fs.path, and test all of it inside a throw-away directory. Every operation goes through the std.Io interface introduced in Zig 0.16, so this chapter also fixes the habits that older tutorials will try to break.

33.1 The io parameter

In older Zig, std.fs.cwd() was a global you could call from anywhere. In 0.16 the file system, like the clock and the network, is reached through a value of type std.Io that your program receives in main as init.io and passes down explicitly. A directory is std.Io.Dir, a file is std.Io.File, and every method on them takes io as its first argument after the receiver.

The starting point is std.Io.Dir.cwd(), a handle to the current working directory. From it you open, create and delete things by relative path. Absolute paths have their own variants ending in Absolute, such as std.Io.Dir.accessAbsolute(io, "/tmp", .{}). This chapter uses relative paths almost everywhere, because programs that work relative to a directory handle are easier to test.

Do not write these. std.fs.cwd(), std.fs.File, file.writeAll(…) without a writer, std.fs.cwd().readFileAlloc(allocator, path, max) with the old argument order. They are from 0.13 and 0.14 and do not exist now. If a snippet does not mention io, it is not for 0.16.

33.2 Writing a file

There are two ways to write, and you will use both. dir.writeFile(io, .{ .sub_path, .data }) creates (or truncates) a file and writes a slice in one call, ideal for small things that already exist in memory. For anything built up piece by piece, dir.createFile returns a File, file.writer(io, &buf) wraps it in a buffered writer, and you use the familiar print, writeAll and flush on its interface.

write.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    const cwd = std.Io.Dir.cwd();

    // 1. The short way: whole contents in one call.
    try cwd.writeFile(io, .{ .sub_path = "notes.txt", .data = "day 1: founded the company\n" });

    // 2. The streaming way: a file plus a buffered writer.
    var file = try cwd.createFile(io, "ledger.csv", .{});
    defer file.close(io);
    var wbuf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var fw = file.writer(io, &wbuf);
    const w = &fw.interface;
    try w.writeAll("day,funds\n");
    var funds: i64 = 1000;
    for (1..6) |day| {
        funds -= 120;
        try w.print("{d},{d}\n", .{ day, funds });
    }
    try w.flush();
    std.debug.print("wrote notes.txt and ledger.csv\n", .{});
}
$ zig run write.zig
wrote notes.txt and ledger.csv
$ cat notes.txt ledger.csv
day 1: founded the company
day,funds
1,880
2,760
3,640
4,520
5,400

Three details. The defer file.close(io) line comes immediately after the successful open, before anything can fail; that is the habit this chapter is named for. The writer holds a buffer you own, so nothing reaches the disk until flush, and a missing flush is the most common reason for an empty file. And createFile's options struct is empty here, which means "truncate if it exists, create if not, writable".

33.3 Reading a file

Reading mirrors writing. readFileAlloc loads a whole file into memory you own, with a size limit so a surprise gigabyte cannot exhaust memory. openFile plus file.reader(io, &buf) streams it, and takeDelimiter('\n') hands you one line at a time, exactly as it did for standard input in Chapter 32. And readFile fills a buffer you already have, with no allocator at all.

read.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    const cwd = std.Io.Dir.cwd();

    // 1. Whole file into memory. You own the bytes; free them.
    const notes = try cwd.readFileAlloc(io, "notes.txt", init.gpa, .limited(1 << 20));
    defer init.gpa.free(notes);
    std.debug.print("notes.txt ({d} bytes): {s}", .{ notes.len, notes });

    // 2. Line by line through a buffered reader.
    var file = try cwd.openFile(io, "ledger.csv", .{});
    defer file.close(io);
    var rbuf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var fr = file.reader(io, &rbuf);
    const r = &fr.interface;
    var total: i64 = 0;
    var rows: u32 = 0;
    _ = try r.takeDelimiter('\n'); // skip the header
    while (try r.takeDelimiter('\n')) |line| {
        var it = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, line, ',');
        _ = it.next();
        const funds = try std.fmt.parseInt(i64, it.next() orelse "0", 10);
        total += funds;
        rows += 1;
    }
    std.debug.print("{d} rows, average funds {d}\n", .{ rows, @divTrunc(total, rows) });

    // 3. Into a fixed buffer, no allocator at all.
    var small: [64]u8 = undefined;
    const got = try cwd.readFile(io, "notes.txt", &small);
    std.debug.print("readFile gave {d} bytes\n", .{got.len});
}
$ zig run read.zig
notes.txt (27 bytes): day 1: founded the company
5 rows, average funds 640
readFile gave 27 bytes

The argument order of readFileAlloc is (io, path, allocator, limit), and the limit is a std.Io.Limit: .limited(n) or .unlimited. Exceeding it is error.StreamTooLong. The line reader's buffer is also a limit: a line longer than the buffer is error.StreamTooLong too, which Exercise 33.2 turns into a friendlier error.

Which to use? Whole-file for configuration and anything under a few megabytes: simplest code, one allocation, one free. Streaming for logs, large data, or when you want to stop early. Fixed buffer when you know the maximum size and want zero allocation, as in a test or an embedded program.

33.4 Appending

To add to the end of an existing file, open it for writing and position the writer at the current length. The file's length(io) method reports its size, and the File.Writer keeps a pos field that you can set before writing.

append.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    const cwd = std.Io.Dir.cwd();
    var file = try cwd.openFile(io, "notes.txt", .{ .mode = .write_only });
    defer file.close(io);
    const end = try file.length(io);
    var wbuf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var fw = file.writer(io, &wbuf);
    fw.pos = end;
    try fw.interface.print("day 2: hired a tech\n", .{});
    try fw.interface.flush();
    const back = try cwd.readFileAlloc(io, "notes.txt", init.gpa, .limited(4096));
    defer init.gpa.free(back);
    std.debug.print("{s}", .{back});
}
$ zig run append.zig
day 1: founded the company
day 2: hired a tech

openFile's options carry a mode: .read_only is the default, .write_only and .read_write are the others. Opening an existing file for writing does not truncate it; only createFile does.

33.5 When the file is not there

Every open and read returns an error union, and the error you will handle most is error.FileNotFound. A program that loads settings or a save file should treat it as "first run", not as a crash, and a switch on the error makes that policy explicit while letting everything else propagate.

missing.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    const cwd = std.Io.Dir.cwd();
    const data = cwd.readFileAlloc(io, "does-not-exist.txt", init.gpa, .limited(1024)) catch |err| switch (err) {
        error.FileNotFound => {
            std.debug.print("no such file, starting fresh\n", .{});
            return;
        },
        else => return err,
    };
    defer init.gpa.free(data);
    std.debug.print("loaded {d} bytes\n", .{data.len});
}
$ zig run missing.zig
no such file, starting fresh

Other errors you will see: error.AccessDenied (permissions), error.IsDir (you opened a directory as a file), error.PathAlreadyExists (creating a directory that exists, or a file with .exclusive = true), and error.NotDir. All of them are in the error set of the function, so zig build will tell you if a switch is exhaustive.

33.6 Directories

Directories have their own small vocabulary. createDirPath makes a directory and any missing parents (the mkdir -p of Zig; there is no makePath in 0.16). openDir with .iterate = true opens one for listing; without that flag, iteration is illegal. iterate() gives an iterator whose next(io) yields entries with a name and a kind. statFile reports size, kind and timestamps. deleteFile, deleteDir and deleteTree remove things, and access asks whether a path exists.

dirs.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    const cwd = std.Io.Dir.cwd();

    try cwd.createDirPath(io, "saves/campaign-1/backups");
    try cwd.writeFile(io, .{ .sub_path = "saves/campaign-1/day-001.zon", .data = ".{ .day = 1 }\n" });
    try cwd.writeFile(io, .{ .sub_path = "saves/campaign-1/day-002.zon", .data = ".{ .day = 2 }\n" });
    try cwd.writeFile(io, .{ .sub_path = "saves/campaign-1/notes.txt", .data = "hi\n" });

    var dir = try cwd.openDir(io, "saves/campaign-1", .{ .iterate = true });
    defer dir.close(io);
    var it = dir.iterate();
    while (try it.next(io)) |entry| {
        std.debug.print("{s:<10} {s}\n", .{ @tagName(entry.kind), entry.name });
    }

    const st = try dir.statFile(io, "day-002.zon", .{});
    std.debug.print("day-002.zon is {d} bytes, kind {s}\n", .{ st.size, @tagName(st.kind) });

    try dir.deleteFile(io, "notes.txt");
    dir.access(io, "notes.txt", .{}) catch |err| std.debug.print("after delete: {s}\n", .{@errorName(err)});

    // cwd() itself is not iterable; open "." with .iterate to walk it.
    var root = try cwd.openDir(io, ".", .{ .iterate = true });
    defer root.close(io);
    var walker = try root.walk(init.gpa);
    defer walker.deinit();
    var count: u32 = 0;
    while (try walker.next(io)) |e| {
        if (e.kind == .file and std.mem.endsWith(u8, e.basename, ".zon")) count += 1;
    }
    std.debug.print("{d} .zon files below the current directory\n", .{count});
    try cwd.deleteTree(io, "saves");
    std.debug.print("cleaned up\n", .{});
}
$ zig run dirs.zig
file       notes.txt
file       day-001.zon
file       day-002.zon
directory  backups
day-002.zon is 14 bytes, kind file
after delete: FileNotFound
2 .zon files below the current directory
cleaned up

The order of entries is whatever the file system returns, not alphabetical; sort them yourself if it matters (Exercise 33.3). The walk method visits a whole tree recursively, giving each entry's basename, path and kind; it needs an allocator for its stack of open directories, and it must be called on a directory that was opened with .iterate = true. cwd() itself is not iterable, which is why the program opens "." first. Forgetting that produces a confusing failure deep inside the iterator rather than a clear error, so remember: to list or walk, open with .iterate = true.

33.7 Paths

Paths are strings, and std.fs.path has the functions to build and dissect them without hand-written slicing. This namespace is unchanged by the std.Io move because it never touches the disk.

paths.zig

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const p = try std.fs.path.join(init.gpa, &.{ "saves", "campaign-1", "day-002.zon" });
    defer init.gpa.free(p);
    std.debug.print("join:      {s}\n", .{p});
    std.debug.print("basename:  {s}\n", .{std.fs.path.basename(p)});
    std.debug.print("dirname:   {?s}\n", .{std.fs.path.dirname(p)});
    std.debug.print("extension: {s}\n", .{std.fs.path.extension(p)});
    std.debug.print("stem:      {s}\n", .{std.fs.path.stem(p)});
    std.debug.print("absolute?  {}\n", .{std.fs.path.isAbsolute(p)});
    std.debug.print("separator: '{c}'\n", .{std.fs.path.sep});
    std.Io.Dir.accessAbsolute(init.io, "/tmp", .{}) catch |e| std.debug.print("/tmp: {s}\n", .{@errorName(e)});
    std.debug.print("/tmp exists\n", .{});
}
$ zig run paths.zig
join:      saves/campaign-1/day-002.zon
basename:  day-002.zon
dirname:   saves/campaign-1
extension: .zon
stem:      day-002
absolute?  false
separator: '/'
/tmp exists

join allocates, because it builds a new string; everything else returns a slice into the string you passed. dirname is optional (a bare file name has no directory). extension includes the dot, so compare against ".zon". On Windows the separator is a backslash and join uses it; write your paths with join rather than string concatenation and they will work there too.

33.8 Testing file code with tmpDir

File code is easy to test badly: tests that write into the project directory leave litter and fail when run twice. The standard library gives you std.testing.tmpDir(.{}), which creates a uniquely named directory under .zig-cache/tmp, hands you it as tmp.dir, and deletes it in cleanup. Inside tests, the io value is std.testing.io.

tmptest.zig

const std = @import("std");

fn saveScore(dir: std.Io.Dir, io: std.Io, score: u32) !void {
    var buf: [32]u8 = undefined;
    const text = try std.fmt.bufPrint(&buf, "{d}\n", .{score});
    try dir.writeFile(io, .{ .sub_path = "score.txt", .data = text });
}

fn loadScore(dir: std.Io.Dir, io: std.Io) !u32 {
    var buf: [32]u8 = undefined;
    const text = try dir.readFile(io, "score.txt", &buf);
    return std.fmt.parseInt(u32, std.mem.trimEnd(u8, text, "\n"), 10);
}

test "save and load through a temporary directory" {
    const io = std.testing.io;
    var tmp = std.testing.tmpDir(.{});
    defer tmp.cleanup();
    try saveScore(tmp.dir, io, 4242);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 4242), try loadScore(tmp.dir, io));
}

test "missing file is FileNotFound" {
    var tmp = std.testing.tmpDir(.{});
    defer tmp.cleanup();
    try std.testing.expectError(error.FileNotFound, loadScore(tmp.dir, std.testing.io));
}
$ zig test tmptest.zig
1/2 tmptest.test.save and load through a temporary directory...OK
2/2 tmptest.test.missing file is FileNotFound...OK
All 2 tests passed.

The pattern to copy is in the two helper functions: they take a std.Io.Dir and an io as parameters instead of reaching for cwd(). That one design choice is what makes them testable in a temporary directory and, later, usable against a real save directory with no change. IRON LEDGER's persistence layer is written the same way.

33.9 The rest of the toolbox

You now know the dozen calls that cover almost every program. For completeness, here are the other std.Io.Dir and std.Io.File methods you will meet in real code, all taking io in the positions you have seen. None of them introduces a new idea.

CallWhat it does
dir.rename(old, new_dir, new, io)Moves or renames a file or directory; the basis of atomic saves (Exercise 33.4). Note that io comes last here.
dir.copyFile(src, dest_dir, dest, io, .{})Copies a file, creating the destination.
dir.deleteDir(io, path) / dir.deleteTree(io, path)Removes an empty directory, or a whole tree.
dir.createDirPathOpen(io, path, .{})Makes the path and returns it opened, in one call; tmpDir is built on it.
dir.realPathFileAlloc(io, path, allocator)Resolves a relative path to an absolute one.
file.stat(io), file.length(io)Metadata for an open file. Stat has size, kind, permissions, mtime (an Io.Timestamp) and atime (optional, since some systems do not track it).
file.sync(io)Asks the operating system to push the bytes to the physical disk; call it before you tell the user a save is safe.
file.lock(io, .exclusive) / file.unlock(io)Advisory locking, so two copies of a program do not write the same save at once.
file.setTimestampsNow(io)Touches the file.

Two habits close the chapter. First, keep the functions that touch files small and at the edge of the program, taking a Dir and an io, and keep the logic that decides what to save pure; the game's persistence layer is a thin shell around an in-memory GameState for exactly this reason. Second, when something goes wrong, print @errorName(err) and the path; a message like saves/day-002.zon: FileNotFound is worth more than any stack trace to the person reading it.

In IRON LEDGER. The clearest file-system code in the game is the soundtrack scanner in game/src/tui/music.zig, which lists a directory of audio files in exactly the style of section 33.6: 
var dir = std.Io.Dir.cwd().openDir(self.io, dir_path, .{ .iterate = true }) catch return;
defer dir.close(self.io);
var it = dir.iterate();
while (try it.next(self.io)) |e| {
    if (e.kind == .directory) { /* a soundtrack */ continue; }
    if (e.kind != .file or !isAudio(e.name)) continue;
    // …
}
Note the catch return: a missing music directory simply means no music. The io arrives as a field of the client (self.io), threaded in from main. The build script uses the same API at build time, b.build_root.handle.access(b.graph.io, candidate, .{}), to check whether a mod file exists. And the reason none of this appears in game/src/sim/ is the point the guide makes about purity: the simulation never receives an io, so it cannot touch a file, and its determinism is guaranteed by a parameter that is not there. Chapter 47 shows the SQLite save files that sit on top of all this.

Exercises

Exercise 33.1 · Save and load records practice

Write save(dir, io, path, pilots) that writes one name,gunnery,piloting line per pilot, and load that reads it back into an owned slice, treating a missing file as an empty roster and a malformed line as error.BadRecord without leaking. File: exercises/33-files/ex1_records.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 33, exercise 1: save and load a list of records.
//! Run with:  zig test ex1_records.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

pub const Pilot = struct { name: []const u8, gunnery: u8, piloting: u8 };

/// Write one line per pilot: "name,gunnery,piloting\n".
pub fn save(dir: std.Io.Dir, io: std.Io, path: []const u8, pilots: []const Pilot) !void {
    var file = try dir.createFile(io, path, .{});
    defer file.close(io);
    var buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var fw = file.writer(io, &buf);
    const w = &fw.interface;
    for (pilots) |p| try w.print("{s},{d},{d}\n", .{ p.name, p.gunnery, p.piloting });
    try w.flush();
}

/// Read the file back. Names are copied into `gpa`; the caller frees them
/// with `freePilots`. A missing file yields an empty list, not an error.
pub fn load(dir: std.Io.Dir, io: std.Io, gpa: std.mem.Allocator, path: []const u8) ![]Pilot {
    var file = dir.openFile(io, path, .{}) catch |err| switch (err) {
        error.FileNotFound => return try gpa.alloc(Pilot, 0),
        else => return err,
    };
    defer file.close(io);
    var buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var fr = file.reader(io, &buf);
    const r = &fr.interface;
    var out: std.ArrayList(Pilot) = .empty;
    errdefer {
        // On any failure below, give back every name we already copied,
        // then the list itself. One block, so the order is explicit.
        for (out.items) |p| gpa.free(p.name);
        out.deinit(gpa);
    }
    while (try r.takeDelimiter('\n')) |line| {
        if (line.len == 0) continue;
        var it = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, line, ',');
        const name = it.next() orelse return error.BadRecord;
        const g = it.next() orelse return error.BadRecord;
        const p = it.next() orelse return error.BadRecord;
        try out.append(gpa, .{
            .name = try gpa.dupe(u8, name),
            .gunnery = try std.fmt.parseInt(u8, g, 10),
            .piloting = try std.fmt.parseInt(u8, p, 10),
        });
    }
    return out.toOwnedSlice(gpa);
}

pub fn freePilots(gpa: std.mem.Allocator, pilots: []Pilot) void {
    for (pilots) |p| gpa.free(p.name);
    gpa.free(pilots);
}

test "round trip" {
    const io = std.testing.io;
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    var tmp = std.testing.tmpDir(.{});
    defer tmp.cleanup();
    const roster = [_]Pilot{
        .{ .name = "Kell", .gunnery = 3, .piloting = 4 },
        .{ .name = "Ana Ruiz", .gunnery = 5, .piloting = 5 },
    };
    try save(tmp.dir, io, "roster.csv", &roster);
    const back = try load(tmp.dir, io, gpa, "roster.csv");
    defer freePilots(gpa, back);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 2), back.len);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Ana Ruiz", back[1].name);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 3), back[0].gunnery);
}

test "missing file is an empty roster" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    var tmp = std.testing.tmpDir(.{});
    defer tmp.cleanup();
    const back = try load(tmp.dir, std.testing.io, gpa, "nothing.csv");
    defer freePilots(gpa, back);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 0), back.len);
}

test "a broken line is an error and leaks nothing" {
    const io = std.testing.io;
    var tmp = std.testing.tmpDir(.{});
    defer tmp.cleanup();
    try tmp.dir.writeFile(io, .{ .sub_path = "bad.csv", .data = "Kell,3,4\nAna,5\n" });
    try std.testing.expectError(error.BadRecord, load(tmp.dir, io, std.testing.allocator, "bad.csv"));
}

The errdefer block is the subtle part: on failure it must free the names already copied and the list, in that order. Two separate errdefers run in reverse order, which would free the list first and then read freed memory; one block makes the order explicit. This is a preview of Chapter 47, where the same records go to SQLite.

Exercise 33.2 · Word count for files warm-up

Stream a file through a deliberately tiny buffer, counting lines, words and bytes, and turn error.StreamTooLong into error.LineTooLong. File: exercises/33-files/ex2_wordcount.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 33, exercise 2: count lines, words and bytes of a file.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_wordcount.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

pub const Counts = struct { lines: u32 = 0, words: u32 = 0, bytes: u64 = 0 };

/// Stream the file through a small buffer; never load it whole.
pub fn count(dir: std.Io.Dir, io: std.Io, path: []const u8) !Counts {
    var file = try dir.openFile(io, path, .{});
    defer file.close(io);
    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined; // tiny on purpose: lines may be longer
    var fr = file.reader(io, &buf);
    const r = &fr.interface;
    var c = Counts{};
    while (true) {
        const maybe = r.takeDelimiter('\n') catch |err| switch (err) {
            error.StreamTooLong => return error.LineTooLong,
            else => return err,
        };
        const line = maybe orelse break;
        c.lines += 1;
        c.bytes += line.len + 1;
        var it = std.mem.tokenizeAny(u8, line, " \t");
        while (it.next()) |_| c.words += 1;
    }
    return c;
}

test "counts" {
    const io = std.testing.io;
    var tmp = std.testing.tmpDir(.{});
    defer tmp.cleanup();
    try tmp.dir.writeFile(io, .{ .sub_path = "t.txt", .data = "alpha beta\ngamma\n\ndelta epsilon zeta\n" });
    const c = try count(tmp.dir, io, "t.txt");
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 4), c.lines);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 6), c.words);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u64, 37), c.bytes);
}

test "empty file" {
    const io = std.testing.io;
    var tmp = std.testing.tmpDir(.{});
    defer tmp.cleanup();
    try tmp.dir.writeFile(io, .{ .sub_path = "e.txt", .data = "" });
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Counts{}, try count(tmp.dir, io, "e.txt"));
}

test "a line longer than the buffer is reported" {
    const io = std.testing.io;
    var tmp = std.testing.tmpDir(.{});
    defer tmp.cleanup();
    const long = "x" ** 100 ++ "\n";
    try tmp.dir.writeFile(io, .{ .sub_path = "l.txt", .data = long });
    try std.testing.expectError(error.LineTooLong, count(tmp.dir, io, "l.txt"));
}

takeDelimiter returns null at the end, so the loop reads naturally; the catch on the call itself translates the one error you expect.

Exercise 33.3 · List the save files practice

Write listSaves(dir, io, gpa, sub_path, ext) returning the sorted names of regular files with the given extension directly inside sub_path. File: exercises/33-files/ex3_listing.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 33, exercise 3: list save files in a directory.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_listing.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

/// Names of the regular files directly inside `sub_path` whose extension is
/// `ext` (for example ".zon"), sorted, copied into `gpa`.
pub fn listSaves(dir: std.Io.Dir, io: std.Io, gpa: std.mem.Allocator, sub_path: []const u8, ext: []const u8) ![][]u8 {
    var d = try dir.openDir(io, sub_path, .{ .iterate = true });
    defer d.close(io);
    var names: std.ArrayList([]u8) = .empty;
    errdefer freeNames(gpa, names.items);
    errdefer names.deinit(gpa);
    var it = d.iterate();
    while (try it.next(io)) |e| {
        if (e.kind != .file) continue;
        if (!std.mem.eql(u8, std.fs.path.extension(e.name), ext)) continue;
        try names.append(gpa, try gpa.dupe(u8, e.name));
    }
    std.mem.sort([]u8, names.items, {}, lessThan);
    return names.toOwnedSlice(gpa);
}

fn lessThan(_: void, a: []u8, b: []u8) bool {
    return std.mem.lessThan(u8, a, b);
}

pub fn freeNames(gpa: std.mem.Allocator, names: [][]u8) void {
    for (names) |n| gpa.free(n);
    gpa.free(names);
}

test "only .zon files, sorted" {
    const io = std.testing.io;
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    var tmp = std.testing.tmpDir(.{});
    defer tmp.cleanup();
    try tmp.dir.createDirPath(io, "saves/old");
    try tmp.dir.writeFile(io, .{ .sub_path = "saves/day-002.zon", .data = "" });
    try tmp.dir.writeFile(io, .{ .sub_path = "saves/day-001.zon", .data = "" });
    try tmp.dir.writeFile(io, .{ .sub_path = "saves/readme.txt", .data = "" });
    try tmp.dir.writeFile(io, .{ .sub_path = "saves/old/day-000.zon", .data = "" });
    const names = try listSaves(tmp.dir, io, gpa, "saves", ".zon");
    defer freeNames(gpa, names);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 2), names.len);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("day-001.zon", names[0]);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("day-002.zon", names[1]);
}

test "missing directory is FileNotFound" {
    var tmp = std.testing.tmpDir(.{});
    defer tmp.cleanup();
    try std.testing.expectError(error.FileNotFound, listSaves(tmp.dir, std.testing.io, std.testing.allocator, "nope", ".zon"));
}

Entry names are only valid until the next next, so each is copied with dupe before it goes in the list. std.fs.path.extension keeps the comparison honest for names like archive.zon.bak.

Exercise 33.4 · A config file with a default and an atomic rewrite challenge

load returns defaults when config.zon is missing but propagates a parse error; store writes to config.zon.tmp and renames it over the real name so a crash never leaves a half-written file. File: exercises/33-files/ex4_config.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 33, exercise 4: a config file with a default, and a safe rewrite.
//! Run with:  zig test ex4_config.zig
//! Goal: make every test pass without changing the tests.
const std = @import("std");

pub const Config = struct { seed: u64 = 3025, autosave: bool = true };

/// Load "config.zon" from `dir`. If the file does not exist, return the
/// defaults. Any other error (including a bad file) propagates.
pub fn load(dir: std.Io.Dir, io: std.Io, gpa: std.mem.Allocator) !Config {
    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    const text = dir.readFile(io, "config.zon", &buf) catch |err| switch (err) {
        error.FileNotFound => return Config{},
        else => return err,
    };
    const z = try gpa.dupeZ(u8, text);
    defer gpa.free(z);
    return std.zon.parse.fromSlice(Config, gpa, z, null, .{});
}

/// Write "config.zon" atomically: serialize to "config.zon.tmp", then rename
/// over the real name, so a crash mid-write never leaves a half file.
pub fn store(dir: std.Io.Dir, io: std.Io, cfg: Config) !void {
    var file = try dir.createFile(io, "config.zon.tmp", .{});
    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var fw = file.writer(io, &buf);
    try std.zon.stringify.serialize(cfg, .{}, &fw.interface);
    try fw.interface.writeByte('\n');
    try fw.interface.flush();
    file.close(io);
    try dir.rename("config.zon.tmp", dir, "config.zon", io);
}

test "defaults when absent" {
    var tmp = std.testing.tmpDir(.{});
    defer tmp.cleanup();
    const cfg = try load(tmp.dir, std.testing.io, std.testing.allocator);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u64, 3025), cfg.seed);
    try std.testing.expect(cfg.autosave);
}

test "store then load" {
    const io = std.testing.io;
    var tmp = std.testing.tmpDir(.{});
    defer tmp.cleanup();
    try store(tmp.dir, io, .{ .seed = 7, .autosave = false });
    const cfg = try load(tmp.dir, io, std.testing.allocator);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u64, 7), cfg.seed);
    try std.testing.expect(!cfg.autosave);
    try std.testing.expectError(error.FileNotFound, tmp.dir.access(io, "config.zon.tmp", .{}));
}

test "a corrupt file is an error, not a default" {
    const io = std.testing.io;
    var tmp = std.testing.tmpDir(.{});
    defer tmp.cleanup();
    try tmp.dir.writeFile(io, .{ .sub_path = "config.zon", .data = ".{ .seed = \"no\" }" });
    try std.testing.expectError(error.ParseZon, load(tmp.dir, io, std.testing.allocator));
}

The signature of rename in 0.16 is rename(old_dir, old_path, new_dir, new_path, io), with io last. Writing to a temporary name and renaming is the standard way to make a save atomic on every major operating system.

Check your understanding

  1. What replaced std.fs.cwd() in 0.16, and what extra argument do its methods take?
    Answerstd.Io.Dir.cwd(); every operation takes an io: std.Io, which main receives as init.io.
  2. Why might a file you wrote with a writer be empty afterwards?
    AnswerThe writer buffers; without flush() nothing reaches the disk.
  3. What is the argument order of readFileAlloc?
    Answerdir.readFileAlloc(io, path, allocator, limit), where the limit is .limited(n) or .unlimited.
  4. How do you create nested directories in one call?
    Answerdir.createDirPath(io, "a/b/c"). There is no makePath.
  5. What must be true of a directory before you can iterate or walk it?
    AnswerIt must have been opened with .{ .iterate = true }. cwd() is not iterable; open ".".
  6. How should a program react to error.FileNotFound when loading a save?
    AnswerSwitch on the error, treat that case as a fresh start, and propagate everything else.
  7. Where does std.testing.tmpDir put its directory, and which io do tests use?
    AnswerUnder .zig-cache/tmp/ with a random name; tests use std.testing.io. cleanup() deletes it.
  8. Why write file functions to take a Dir parameter instead of calling cwd() inside?
    AnswerSo the same function works in a temporary test directory and in production, and so its signature shows that it touches the file system.
What you learned.
  • All file system access goes through std.Io; start from std.Io.Dir.cwd() and pass io to every call.
  • Write with writeFile for slices, or createFile + file.writer(io, &buf) + flush; always defer file.close(io).
  • Read with readFileAlloc(io, path, allocator, limit), readFile into a buffer, or openFile + reader + takeDelimiter.
  • Append by opening .write_only and setting the writer's pos to file.length(io).
  • Handle error.FileNotFound with a switch; let other errors propagate.
  • createDirPath, openDir(.., .{ .iterate = true }), iterate(), walk(), statFile, deleteFile, deleteTree, access, rename, copyFile, file.sync and file.lock round out the toolbox.
  • std.fs.path.join, basename, dirname, extension, stem, isAbsolute.
  • Test with std.testing.tmpDir(.{}) and std.testing.io; write functions that take a Dir and an io.

34. Time and randomness

In this chapter you will read the wall clock and the monotonic clock through std.Io, measure how long code takes, sleep, and do calendar arithmetic by hand the way IRON LEDGER does. Then you will meet std.Random: seeding a generator, rolling dice, shuffling, and, most importantly, understanding why a simulation wants its randomness to be reproducible.

34.1 Two clocks

Every operating system offers at least two clocks, and it matters which one you ask.

The wall clock tells you what time it is in the world: seconds since midnight on the first of January 1970, UTC, the "Unix epoch". It can jump. A user changes the time zone, NTP corrects a drift, a laptop wakes from sleep; the wall clock moves accordingly, sometimes backwards.

The monotonic clock tells you how long the machine has been running since some arbitrary moment. It never goes backwards. Its absolute value means nothing, but the difference between two readings is a trustworthy duration. That is the clock for "how long did this take".

In Zig 0.16 both live behind std.Io, because reading a clock is talking to the outside world. Just as with files in Chapter 33, you need the io value that main receives. The clock is an enum, std.Io.Clock, and now is a method on it:

s1_wall.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    const now = std.Io.Clock.now(.real, io);
    std.debug.print("nanoseconds since 1970: {d}\n", .{now.nanoseconds});
    std.debug.print("seconds since 1970:     {d}\n", .{now.toSeconds()});
    const days = @divFloor(now.toSeconds(), std.time.s_per_day);
    std.debug.print("days since 1970:        {d}\n", .{days});
}
$ zig run s1_wall.zig
nanoseconds since 1970: 1788964937601115000
seconds since 1970:     1788964937
days since 1970:        20705

Three things to notice. Clock.now returns a plain std.Io.Timestamp, not an error union: reading the clock cannot fail, so there is no try. The timestamp has one field, nanoseconds, of type i96 (wide enough that it will never overflow), and helper methods toSeconds, toMilliseconds and toMicroseconds. And the constants for converting between units live in std.time: ns_per_s, ns_per_ms, s_per_day, ms_per_min and so on. They are comptime integers, so @divFloor(secs, std.time.s_per_day) is ordinary integer arithmetic.

The clock names. The variants of std.Io.Clock in 0.16 are .real (the wall clock), .awake (monotonic, not counting time the machine was suspended), .boot (monotonic, including suspend), .cpu_process and .cpu_thread (CPU time consumed). There is no variant literally called monotonic; when this book says "the monotonic clock" it means .awake. On macOS .awake is CLOCK_UPTIME_RAW, on Linux it is CLOCK_MONOTONIC.
Gone in 0.16. std.time.timestamp(), std.time.milliTimestamp(), std.time.nanoTimestamp() and std.time.Timer no longer exist. Tutorials that use them will not compile. The replacement for all of them is std.Io.Clock.now plus the duration arithmetic below.

34.2 Measuring elapsed time

To time something, read the monotonic clock before and after, and subtract. Zig gives you a method for the subtraction, durationTo, which returns an std.Io.Duration with the same shape as a timestamp: a nanoseconds field and the same toMilliseconds family of helpers.

s2_elapsed.zig
const std = @import("std");

fn slowSum(n: u64) u64 {
    var total: u64 = 0;
    var i: u64 = 0;
    while (i < n) : (i += 1) total +%= i;
    return total;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    const start = std.Io.Clock.now(.awake, io);
    const result = slowSum(50_000_000);
    const stop = std.Io.Clock.now(.awake, io);
    const took = start.durationTo(stop);
    std.debug.print("result {d}\n", .{result});
    std.debug.print("took {d} ns\n", .{took.nanoseconds});
    std.debug.print("took {d} ms\n", .{took.toMilliseconds()});
}
$ zig run s2_elapsed.zig
result 1249999975000000
took 99296500 ns
took 99 ms

This is the whole of what std.time.Timer used to do. If you find yourself timing things often, wrap it in a two-line helper struct that stores the start timestamp and has a read method; that is exactly what the old Timer was.

Two habits make timings honest. First, run the program with -O ReleaseFast when you care about the number; the Debug build above spends much of its 99 ms on overflow checks (the +%= avoids one, but the loop counter still has them). Second, do something with the result (here we print it) so the optimiser cannot delete the work you are measuring.

34.3 Sleeping

Sleeping also goes through io, for the same reason: it is a request to the operating system. The method is io.sleep(duration, clock). The duration is an std.Io.Duration, which you build with .fromMilliseconds, .fromSeconds, or .fromNanoseconds. Because the argument type is known, you can write the shorthand .fromMilliseconds(200) without naming the type.

s3_sleep.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    const before = std.Io.Clock.now(.awake, io);
    try io.sleep(.fromMilliseconds(200), .awake);
    const after = std.Io.Clock.now(.awake, io);
    std.debug.print("asked for 200 ms, slept {d} ms\n", .{before.durationTo(after).toMilliseconds()});
}
$ zig run s3_sleep.zig
asked for 200 ms, slept 206 ms

Sleep can return an error, error.Canceled, because 0.16's I/O layer supports cancelling a blocked operation from another task. In a plain program that never happens, but the type is honest about the possibility, so you write try. And note the 206: sleep promises "at least this long", never "exactly this long". Never build a clock out of repeated sleeps.

34.4 Calendars by hand

The standard library will turn a Unix timestamp into a civil date for you (std.time.epoch has EpochSeconds, getEpochDay, calculateYearDay and calculateMonthDay), and that is the right tool when you need today's real date:

s7_epoch.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const secs = std.Io.Clock.now(.real, init.io).toSeconds();
    const es = std.time.epoch.EpochSeconds{ .secs = @intCast(secs) };
    const yd = es.getEpochDay().calculateYearDay();
    const md = yd.calculateMonthDay();
    const ds = es.getDaySeconds();
    std.debug.print("UTC now: {d}-{d:0>2}-{d:0>2} {d:0>2}:{d:0>2}\n", .{
        yd.year, md.month.numeric(), md.day_index + 1, ds.getHoursIntoDay(), ds.getMinutesIntoHour(),
    });
}
$ zig run s7_epoch.zig
UTC now: 2026-09-09 14:42

But a simulation set in the year 3025 does not want the real date; it wants its own calendar, one it can advance a day at a time, forever, and render as "3025-02-01" when the player asks. This is a small and pleasant piece of code to write yourself, and IRON LEDGER does. There are two representations to keep straight:

  • A day counter: an integer holding the days since the campaign began, which makes arithmetic easy. "Was this person hired more than 90 days ago?" is a subtraction. Every transaction in the game's ledger is stamped with this integer.
  • A civil date: year, month, day. Perfect for humans and for rules that care about the calendar ("payday is the first of the month").

The trick is to store both and advance both together, so you never convert. Advancing a civil date by one day needs only the length of the current month, and that needs only the leap year rule: divisible by 4, except years divisible by 100, except years divisible by 400.

s6_date.zig
const std = @import("std");

const Date = struct {
    year: u16,
    month: u8,
    day: u8,

    fn isLeapYear(year: u16) bool {
        return (year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0) or year % 400 == 0;
    }

    fn daysInMonth(year: u16, month: u8) u8 {
        return switch (month) {
            1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12 => 31,
            4, 6, 9, 11 => 30,
            2 => if (isLeapYear(year)) @as(u8, 29) else 28,
            else => unreachable,
        };
    }

    fn next(self: Date) Date {
        var d = self;
        d.day += 1;
        if (d.day > daysInMonth(d.year, d.month)) {
            d.day = 1;
            d.month += 1;
            if (d.month > 12) {
                d.month = 1;
                d.year += 1;
            }
        }
        return d;
    }
};

pub fn main() void {
    var d: Date = .{ .year = 3024, .month = 2, .day = 27 };
    var day_index: u32 = 0;
    for (0..4) |_| {
        std.debug.print("day {d} = {d}-{d:0>2}-{d:0>2}\n", .{ day_index, d.year, d.month, d.day });
        d = d.next();
        day_index += 1;
    }
}
$ zig run s6_date.zig
day 0 = 3024-02-27
day 1 = 3024-02-28
day 2 = 3024-02-29
day 3 = 3024-03-01

Three details are worth a second look. daysInMonth uses else => unreachable because a month outside 1 to 12 is a bug in the caller, not a runtime condition; in Debug builds the program will stop there with a stack trace if you ever break the rule (Chapter 37 has more on this choice). The @as(u8, 29) in the February arm forces both branches of the if to the same type, because 29 and 28 on their own are comptime_int. And next takes self by value and returns a new Date: no mutation, easy to test.

The format specifier {d:0>2} means "decimal, pad with zeros on the left to width 2", which is how 2 becomes 02. Chapter 23 has the full table.

34.5 Random numbers

Randomness in Zig is a small interface, std.Random, and a handful of generators that implement it. You create a generator with a seed, ask it for a std.Random value, and call methods on that. The generator you want by default is std.Random.DefaultPrng, which is Xoshiro256++: fast, good statistical quality, and 64-bit seeded.

s4_dice.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var prng = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(42);
    const r = prng.random();

    std.debug.print("d6:      {d}\n", .{r.intRangeAtMost(u8, 1, 6)});
    std.debug.print("d6:      {d}\n", .{r.intRangeAtMost(u8, 1, 6)});
    std.debug.print("0..99:   {d}\n", .{r.intRangeLessThan(u32, 0, 100)});
    std.debug.print("any u16: {d}\n", .{r.int(u16)});
    std.debug.print("float:   {d:.3}\n", .{r.float(f64)});
    std.debug.print("coin:    {}\n", .{r.boolean()});

    var deck = [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 };
    r.shuffle(u8, &deck);
    std.debug.print("shuffle: {any}\n", .{deck});

    const weights = [_]u32{ 70, 20, 10 }; // common, uncommon, rare
    std.debug.print("rarity:  {d}\n", .{r.weightedIndex(u32, &weights)});

    const Weather = enum { clear, rain, storm };
    std.debug.print("weather: {s}\n", .{@tagName(r.enumValue(Weather))});
}
$ zig run s4_dice.zig
d6:      4
d6:      4
0..99:   4
any u16: 13752
float:   0.597
coin:    true
shuffle: { 2, 6, 4, 8, 7, 3, 1, 5 }
rarity:  0
weather: rain

The methods you will use most:

CallGives
r.intRangeAtMost(T, lo, hi)an integer in lo..hi, both ends included: a die is (u8, 1, 6)
r.intRangeLessThan(T, lo, hi)an integer in lo..hi, upper end excluded: an index is (usize, 0, len)
r.uintLessThan(T, n)same, starting at 0, unsigned only
r.int(T)any value of the integer type, all bits random
r.float(T)a float in [0, 1)
r.boolean()a fair coin
r.shuffle(T, slice)rearranges the slice in place, every order equally likely
r.weightedIndex(T, weights)an index into weights, chosen proportionally: 70/20/10 above
r.enumValue(E)a random tag of an enum
r.bytes(buf)fills a byte slice

Notice that prng is declared with var: every draw advances the generator's internal state, so random() needs a mutable pointer to it. The std.Random value you get back is a small struct holding that pointer plus a function pointer; it is cheap to pass around by value and you can call prng.random() as often as you like.

Not for secrets. DefaultPrng is predictable by design. For anything security-related (tokens, keys, salts) use the operating system's generator instead: io.random(&buf) fills a buffer from the OS, and std.Random.DefaultCsprng is a cryptographic generator you can seed from it.

34.6 Seeds, and why determinism matters

A pseudo-random generator is a pure function of its seed. Same seed, same sequence, on every machine, forever. That is not a weakness to work around; it is the most useful property a simulation's randomness can have.

s5_seed.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    // Fixed seed: the same three numbers every run.
    var fixed = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(3025);
    std.debug.print("fixed: {d} {d} {d}\n", .{
        fixed.random().intRangeAtMost(u8, 1, 6),
        fixed.random().intRangeAtMost(u8, 1, 6),
        fixed.random().intRangeAtMost(u8, 1, 6),
    });

    // Seed from the operating system: different every run.
    var seed_bytes: [8]u8 = undefined;
    init.io.random(&seed_bytes);
    const seed = std.mem.readInt(u64, &seed_bytes, .little);
    var fresh = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(seed);
    std.debug.print("fresh: {d} {d} {d} (seed {d})\n", .{
        fresh.random().intRangeAtMost(u8, 1, 6),
        fresh.random().intRangeAtMost(u8, 1, 6),
        fresh.random().intRangeAtMost(u8, 1, 6),
        seed,
    });
}
$ zig run s5_seed.zig
fixed: 4 1 1
fresh: 2 4 5 (seed 13483122203582859263)
$ zig run s5_seed.zig
fixed: 4 1 1
fresh: 4 1 5 (seed 10071616139519654204)

The fixed line never changes. The fresh line does, because the seed came from the OS. (You could also seed from the wall clock, @bitCast-ing the nanoseconds into a u64; the OS generator is simpler and better.) The pattern to copy from this program is: print the seed. A game that shows "seed 13483122203582859263" on its title screen can reproduce any bug report exactly.

Determinism buys you three things:

  1. Reproducible bugs. "It crashed on day 212 with seed 42" is a test case. "It crashed sometimes" is a mystery.
  2. Testable rules. A test can seed a generator with 7, run a thousand days, and assert on the exact outcome, because the outcome is a fact about the code and the seed, not about luck.
  3. Save files that replay. If the state after 90 days is a function of (seed, commands), then a save file need not store every dice roll, only the seed and the state.

There is a subtle trap, and IRON LEDGER's answer to it is one of the nicest small designs in the game. Suppose every subsystem shares one generator: the market draws, then a battle draws, then a medical check draws. Now you add one extra weather roll to battles. Every market roll after the first battle shifts by one position; a saved game replays differently after your update; every golden-master test breaks. The fix is to give each subsystem its own stream: a separate generator, derived from the master seed in a stable way. Adding a draw to the battle stream leaves the market stream untouched. Exercise 34.5 has you build exactly this.

In IRON LEDGER. The game's clock is src/sim/clock.zig: a Date struct with isLeapYear, daysInMonth, next and isPayday (the first of the month), wrapped in a Clock that carries both the civil date and day_index, "the canonical timestamp". Everything that records when stores the integer; everything that displays a date renders the struct. Randomness is src/sim/rng.zig: an enum of eight streams (generation, market, maintenance, acquisition, battle, events, medical, travel) and an Rng holding one DefaultPrng per stream, each seeded with seed ^ (0x9E3779B97F4A7C15 *% (i + 1)). Every die in the game is gs.rng.roll2d6(.some_stream). The simulation core never receives an io, so it cannot read the real clock even by accident, and the golden-master test in src/sim/commands.zig (same seed, same script, same hash, twice) guards the whole property on every build. 
pub fn roll2d6(self: *Rng, stream: Stream) u8 {
    const r = self.random(stream);
    return r.intRangeAtMost(u8, 1, 6) + r.intRangeAtMost(u8, 1, 6);
}

Exercises

Exercise 34.1 · Elapsed time warm-up

Time a busy loop at three sizes (one million, ten million, one hundred million iterations) with the monotonic clock, and print each result in milliseconds to stdout. Then run it again with -O ReleaseFast and compare. Name the file: exercises/34-time-random/ex1_elapsed.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 34, exercise 1: measuring elapsed time.
//! Run with:  zig run ex1_elapsed.zig
//! Goal: time three sizes of a busy loop with the monotonic clock and print
//! each duration in milliseconds. Your numbers will differ; the shape
//! (each line roughly ten times the last) should not.
//!
//! Example output:
//!   n=1000000     sum=499999500000        took 1 ms
//!   n=10000000    sum=49999995000000      took 12 ms
//!   n=100000000   sum=4999999950000000    took 121 ms

const std = @import("std");

fn busyLoop(n: u64) u64 {
    var sum: u64 = 0;
    var i: u64 = 0;
    while (i < n) : (i += 1) sum +%= i;
    return sum;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var w = std.Io.File.stdout().writer(io, &buf);
    const out = &w.interface;

    const sizes = [_]u64{ 1_000_000, 10_000_000, 100_000_000 };
    for (sizes) |n| {
        const t0 = std.Io.Clock.now(.awake, io);
        const sum = busyLoop(n);
        const t1 = std.Io.Clock.now(.awake, io);
        const took = t0.durationTo(t1);
        try out.print("n={d:<12} sum={d:<20} took {d} ms\n", .{ n, sum, took.toMilliseconds() });
    }
    try out.flush();
}

Two readings of .awake bracket the work, durationTo subtracts them, and toMilliseconds scales. The {d:<12} specifier left-aligns in a 12-character field so the columns line up. In ReleaseFast the compiler may compute the closed-form sum and every line becomes 0 ms, which is a lesson in its own right.

Exercise 34.2 · A dice roller practice

Write roll(r, count, sides) that returns the total of count dice with sides faces, and roll2d6(r) on top of it. The tests check the range, that 2 and 12 both appear over enough rolls, that the average is near 7, and that two generators with the same seed agree roll for roll. Name the file: exercises/34-time-random/ex2_dice.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 34, exercise 2: a dice roller.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_dice.zig
//! Goal: implement `roll` and `roll2d6`, then make every test pass
//! without changing the tests.

const std = @import("std");

/// Roll `count` dice with `sides` sides each and return the total.
pub fn roll(r: std.Random, count: u8, sides: u8) u32 {
    std.debug.assert(sides >= 1);
    var total: u32 = 0;
    for (0..count) |_| total += r.intRangeAtMost(u8, 1, sides);
    return total;
}

/// The BattleTech die roll.
pub fn roll2d6(r: std.Random) u32 {
    return roll(r, 2, 6);
}

test "one die stays in range" {
    var prng = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(1);
    const r = prng.random();
    for (0..1000) |_| {
        const v = roll(r, 1, 6);
        try std.testing.expect(v >= 1 and v <= 6);
    }
}

test "2d6 stays in range and hits both ends" {
    var prng = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(2);
    const r = prng.random();
    var seen_2 = false;
    var seen_12 = false;
    for (0..5000) |_| {
        const v = roll2d6(r);
        try std.testing.expect(v >= 2 and v <= 12);
        if (v == 2) seen_2 = true;
        if (v == 12) seen_12 = true;
    }
    try std.testing.expect(seen_2 and seen_12);
}

test "2d6 averages close to 7" {
    var prng = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(3);
    const r = prng.random();
    var total: u64 = 0;
    const n = 20_000;
    for (0..n) |_| total += roll2d6(r);
    const avg: f64 = @as(f64, @floatFromInt(total)) / n;
    try std.testing.expect(avg > 6.8 and avg < 7.2);
}

test "same seed, same rolls" {
    var a = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(99);
    var b = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(99);
    for (0..100) |_| {
        try std.testing.expectEqual(roll2d6(a.random()), roll2d6(b.random()));
    }
}

Each die is one intRangeAtMost(u8, 1, sides), summed into a u32 so many dice cannot overflow. The average test converts with @floatFromInt and allows a small tolerance; with 20,000 rolls the sample mean of 2d6 is within 0.2 of 7 essentially always, and because the seed is fixed the test is not flaky at all.

Exercise 34.3 · A seeded shuffle practice

Given a fixed array of six names, write shuffledCopy(seed) that returns a shuffled copy. Tests check that every name survives, that the same seed gives the same order, and that two different seeds give different orders. Name the file: exercises/34-time-random/ex3_shuffle.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 34, exercise 3: a seeded shuffle.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_shuffle.zig
//! Goal: implement `shuffledCopy` so the tests pass. A shuffle must keep
//! every element exactly once, and the same seed must give the same order.

const std = @import("std");

const names = [_][]const u8{ "Grayson", "Lori", "Clay", "Delmar", "Ricol", "Yorinaga" };

/// Return a shuffled copy of `names`, driven by `seed`.
pub fn shuffledCopy(seed: u64) [names.len][]const u8 {
    var copy = names;
    var prng = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(seed);
    prng.random().shuffle([]const u8, &copy);
    return copy;
}

fn contains(haystack: []const []const u8, needle: []const u8) bool {
    for (haystack) |h| if (std.mem.eql(u8, h, needle)) return true;
    return false;
}

test "every name survives the shuffle" {
    const s = shuffledCopy(1);
    for (names) |n| try std.testing.expect(contains(&s, n));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(names.len, s.len);
}

test "same seed gives same order" {
    const a = shuffledCopy(2024);
    const b = shuffledCopy(2024);
    for (a, b) |x, y| try std.testing.expectEqualStrings(x, y);
}

test "different seeds usually differ" {
    const a = shuffledCopy(1);
    const b = shuffledCopy(2);
    var same = true;
    for (a, b) |x, y| if (!std.mem.eql(u8, x, y)) {
        same = false;
    };
    try std.testing.expect(!same);
}

Copying the array (var copy = names;) is what makes the function pure: the original is never touched. shuffle takes the element type and a slice, and &copy is a pointer to the array, which coerces to that slice. Returning the array by value is fine; it is six slices, 96 bytes.

Exercise 34.4 · Calendar arithmetic practice

Complete a Date struct with isLeapYear, daysInMonth, next, addDays(n) and dayOfYear. Tests include the century rules (1900 is not a leap year, 2000 is), month and year rollover, a 45-day jump, and day 366 of 3024. Name the file: exercises/34-time-random/ex4_calendar.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 34, exercise 4: civil calendar arithmetic by hand.
//! Run with:  zig test ex4_calendar.zig
//! Goal: implement `daysInMonth`, `next`, `addDays` and `dayOfYear` so
//! the tests pass. Leap years: divisible by 4, except centuries, except
//! every 400th year.

const std = @import("std");

pub const Date = struct {
    year: u16,
    month: u8, // 1..12
    day: u8, // 1..31

    pub fn isLeapYear(year: u16) bool {
        return (year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0) or year % 400 == 0;
    }

    pub fn daysInMonth(year: u16, month: u8) u8 {
        return switch (month) {
            1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12 => 31,
            4, 6, 9, 11 => 30,
            2 => if (isLeapYear(year)) @as(u8, 29) else 28,
            else => unreachable,
        };
    }

    pub fn next(self: Date) Date {
        var d = self;
        d.day += 1;
        if (d.day > daysInMonth(d.year, d.month)) {
            d.day = 1;
            d.month += 1;
            if (d.month > 12) {
                d.month = 1;
                d.year += 1;
            }
        }
        return d;
    }

    pub fn addDays(self: Date, n: u32) Date {
        var d = self;
        for (0..n) |_| d = d.next();
        return d;
    }

    /// 1 for January 1st, 365 or 366 for December 31st.
    pub fn dayOfYear(self: Date) u16 {
        var total: u16 = self.day;
        var m: u8 = 1;
        while (m < self.month) : (m += 1) total += daysInMonth(self.year, m);
        return total;
    }
};

test "leap year rules" {
    try std.testing.expect(Date.isLeapYear(2024));
    try std.testing.expect(!Date.isLeapYear(2023));
    try std.testing.expect(!Date.isLeapYear(1900));
    try std.testing.expect(Date.isLeapYear(2000));
    try std.testing.expect(Date.isLeapYear(3024));
}

test "february length" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 29), Date.daysInMonth(3024, 2));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 28), Date.daysInMonth(3025, 2));
}

test "month and year rollover" {
    const d: Date = .{ .year = 3025, .month = 12, .day = 31 };
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Date{ .year = 3026, .month = 1, .day = 1 }, d.next());
    const f: Date = .{ .year = 3024, .month = 2, .day = 28 };
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Date{ .year = 3024, .month = 2, .day = 29 }, f.next());
}

test "addDays crosses months" {
    const d: Date = .{ .year = 3025, .month = 1, .day = 1 };
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Date{ .year = 3025, .month = 2, .day = 15 }, d.addDays(45));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Date{ .year = 3026, .month = 1, .day = 1 }, d.addDays(365));
}

test "dayOfYear" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u16, 1), (Date{ .year = 3025, .month = 1, .day = 1 }).dayOfYear());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u16, 365), (Date{ .year = 3025, .month = 12, .day = 31 }).dayOfYear());
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u16, 366), (Date{ .year = 3024, .month = 12, .day = 31 }).dayOfYear());
}

addDays simply calls next in a loop, which is plenty fast for a game that advances a day at a time and avoids a page of tricky arithmetic. dayOfYear adds up the lengths of the months before this one. Notice that expectEqual compares two Date structs field by field.

Exercise 34.5 · Named streams challenge

Build a miniature of IRON LEDGER's Rng: an enum Stream { market, battle, events } and a struct holding one DefaultPrng per stream, all derived from one seed. Write init(seed), random(stream) and roll2d6(stream). The key test draws a thousand times from .market in one instance and then checks that .battle still matches an untouched twin.
