Name the file: exercises/34-time-random/ex5_streams.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 34, exercise 5: named random streams.
//! Run with:  zig test ex5_streams.zig
//! Goal: implement `Rng.init` so every stream gets its own generator
//! derived from the seed, and make the tests pass.

const std = @import("std");

pub const Stream = enum(u8) {
    market,
    battle,
    events,

    const count = @typeInfo(Stream).@"enum".fields.len;
};

pub const Rng = struct {
    prngs: [Stream.count]std.Random.DefaultPrng,

    pub fn init(seed: u64) Rng {
        var self: Rng = undefined;
        for (&self.prngs, 0..) |*prng, i| {
            prng.* = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(seed ^ (0x9E3779B97F4A7C15 *% (i + 1)));
        }
        return self;
    }

    pub fn random(self: *Rng, stream: Stream) std.Random {
        return self.prngs[@intFromEnum(stream)].random();
    }

    pub fn roll2d6(self: *Rng, stream: Stream) u8 {
        const r = self.random(stream);
        return r.intRangeAtMost(u8, 1, 6) + r.intRangeAtMost(u8, 1, 6);
    }
};

test "streams are independent" {
    var a = Rng.init(42);
    var b = Rng.init(42);
    for (0..1000) |_| _ = a.roll2d6(.market);
    for (0..10) |_| try std.testing.expectEqual(b.roll2d6(.battle), a.roll2d6(.battle));
}

test "streams differ from each other" {
    var r = Rng.init(7);
    var same: usize = 0;
    for (0..50) |_| {
        if (r.roll2d6(.market) == r.roll2d6(.events)) same += 1;
    }
    try std.testing.expect(same < 50);
}

test "2d6 stays in range" {
    var r = Rng.init(7);
    for (0..1000) |_| {
        const v = r.roll2d6(.events);
        try std.testing.expect(v >= 2 and v <= 12);
    }
}

Stream.count is computed by reflection so adding a stream to the enum grows the array automatically. The seed for stream i is the master seed XORed with a large odd constant times i + 1 (wrapping multiply, *%), which spreads the seeds far apart; any stable, distinct derivation would do. The struct starts as undefined and every slot is filled in the loop, which is the idiomatic way to build an array of non-default values.

Check your understanding

  1. Which clock do you use to measure how long a function took, and why not the other one?
    AnswerThe monotonic clock, .awake. The wall clock (.real) can jump forwards or backwards when the system time is adjusted, so a difference of two wall-clock readings is not a reliable duration.
  2. Why does std.Io.Clock.now(.real, io) not need try?
    AnswerIt returns a plain Timestamp, not an error union. Reading a clock cannot fail in a way the program could handle. Sleeping, by contrast, returns Cancelable!void because it blocks and can be cancelled.
  3. What happened to std.time.Timer and std.time.timestamp()?
    AnswerThey are gone in 0.16. Use std.Io.Clock.now for both, with durationTo for elapsed time. The unit constants in std.time (ns_per_s and friends) remain.
  4. Is 3000 a leap year? Is 3024?
    Answer3000 is divisible by 100 but not by 400, so it is not a leap year. 3024 is divisible by 4 and not by 100, so it is.
  5. Why does IRON LEDGER store both a day counter and a civil date?
    AnswerThe integer is for arithmetic and for stamping records (a subtraction answers "how many days ago"); the struct is for display and for calendar rules like payday on the 1st. Advancing both together avoids ever converting between them.
  6. What does r.intRangeAtMost(u8, 1, 6) return, and how would you write "a random index into a slice of length n"?
    AnswerAn integer from 1 to 6 inclusive. For an index use r.intRangeLessThan(usize, 0, n) or r.uintLessThan(usize, n), since the upper bound is excluded.
  7. Two runs with the same seed produce different results. Name three possible causes.
    AnswerSomething read the wall clock; a hash map with unordered iteration decided an order; a second generator was created somewhere with a different seed (or a thread interleaved draws). The golden-master test exists to catch all of these.
  8. Why give each subsystem its own random stream?
    AnswerSo that adding or removing a draw in one subsystem does not shift the sequence every other subsystem sees. Saved games and tests stay stable across updates that touch only one area.
What you learned.
  • std.Io.Clock.now(.real, io) gives Unix time; .awake is the monotonic clock. Both return a Timestamp with a nanoseconds field and toSeconds-style helpers.
  • Elapsed time is start.durationTo(stop); sleeping is try io.sleep(.fromMilliseconds(n), .awake). std.time.Timer and std.time.timestamp() are gone.
  • Unit constants live in std.time: ns_per_s, s_per_day, and so on. Real-date conversion is in std.time.epoch.
  • A simulation calendar is a small struct: leap years, days in month, next(). Keep an integer day counter alongside it.
  • std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(seed) then .random() gives an std.Random with intRangeAtMost, float, boolean, shuffle, weightedIndex, enumValue.
  • Seed from io.random for variety, from a constant for reproducibility, and always print the seed. One generator per subsystem keeps saves and tests stable.

35. Calling C

In this chapter you will call functions from the C standard library and from SQLite without writing a line of C: declaring them with extern fn, matching C's types, handling C strings and opaque handles, and turning C's integer return codes into Zig errors. You will also see @cImport, which reads a C header for you, and export fn, which goes the other way.

35.1 Why this is easy in Zig

Most languages need a "foreign function interface": a binding generator, a wrapper library, some glue in a third language. Zig needs none of that, because Zig's types already include every type C has. A C int is c_int. A C pointer is a Zig pointer. A C string is a pointer to bytes with a zero at the end, and Zig has a type for exactly that. So calling C is a matter of declaring the function with Zig types, and the linker does the rest.

Here is the smallest possible example: two functions from libc.

c1_strlen.zig
const std = @import("std");

extern fn strlen(s: [*:0]const u8) usize;
extern fn getpid() c_int;

pub fn main() void {
    const name: [*:0]const u8 = "Grayson Carlyle";
    std.debug.print("strlen = {d}\n", .{strlen(name)});
    std.debug.print("pid    = {d}\n", .{getpid()});
}
$ zig run -lc c1_strlen.zig
strlen = 15
pid    = 36500

extern fn says "this function exists, somewhere in a library I will link; here is its signature". There is no body. The name must match the C symbol exactly. And -lc on the command line tells Zig to link the C library, which is where strlen and getpid live. (On macOS the system library is always linked, so this particular example happens to work without -lc; on Linux it would fail with an undefined symbol. Always pass -lc when you use libc, so your program is portable.)

35.2 C types in Zig

The signature is the whole contract, so it has to be right. Zig provides the C integer types as builtins whose size follows the target platform:

CZigNotes
int, unsignedc_int, c_uint32 bits on every mainstream target
long, unsigned longc_long, c_ulong64 bits on macOS and Linux, 32 on Windows
charc_char (or u8 for bytes)signedness follows the platform
short, long longc_short, c_longlong
size_tusize
int64_t, uint8_ti64, u8fixed-width types are the same in both
double, floatf64, f32
const char * (a string)[*:0]const u8many-item pointer, zero-terminated
char *buf (a buffer)[*]u8many-item pointer, length passed separately
T * (one thing)*T or ?*T? when NULL is a legal value
void *?*anyopaquepointer to "I don't know what"
void returnvoid
a struct handle you never look insideopaque {}see 35.4

The important mental shift is about pointers. In Zig a pointer's type says whether it points to one thing (*T) or to many ([*]T), and whether it can be null (?). C has one pointer type for all of these, so when you declare a C function you are adding information the C header did not have. Choose honestly: if C can hand you NULL, write ?; if it is a string, write the sentinel.

Two more pieces of vocabulary. callconv(.c) on a Zig function says "make this callable the way C expects", which you need whenever C will call your function (a callback). And @cImport/std.c can spare you writing declarations at all; both come later in the chapter.

35.3 A callback: qsort

C's qsort sorts an array of anything, given the element size and a comparison function. It is the classic example of C calling back into your code, and it shows every type from the table at once.

c3_qsort.zig
const std = @import("std");

const Compare = *const fn (?*const anyopaque, ?*const anyopaque) callconv(.c) c_int;
extern fn qsort(base: ?*anyopaque, count: usize, size: usize, cmp: Compare) void;

fn ascending(a: ?*const anyopaque, b: ?*const anyopaque) callconv(.c) c_int {
    const x: *const c_int = @ptrCast(@alignCast(a.?));
    const y: *const c_int = @ptrCast(@alignCast(b.?));
    if (x.* < y.*) return -1;
    if (x.* > y.*) return 1;
    return 0;
}

pub fn main() void {
    var values = [_]c_int{ 1500, 400, 800, 640 };
    qsort(&values, values.len, @sizeOf(c_int), ascending);
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{values});
}
$ zig run -lc c3_qsort.zig
{ 400, 640, 800, 1500 }

Read the comparator slowly. C promises to call it with two const void *, so the parameters are ?*const anyopaque. We know they are really pointers to c_int, so we convert: a.? unwraps the optional (a null here would be a bug in qsort), @alignCast asserts the pointer is aligned well enough for a c_int, and @ptrCast changes the pointee type. Both casts are safety-checked in Debug builds. The callconv(.c) after the parameter list is what makes this function acceptable where C expects a function pointer.

The type *const fn (...) callconv(.c) c_int is a pointer to such a function. We give it a name, Compare, only to keep the qsort declaration readable. And &values, a pointer to an array, coerces to ?*anyopaque automatically, because any pointer can become a void *.

35.4 Strings across the border

A C string is a [*:0]const u8: a pointer to bytes, with the promise that a zero byte marks the end. A Zig string is a []const u8: a pointer and a length, no terminator needed. Crossing from one to the other is a small ceremony in each direction.

Zig to C. String literals are secretly [:0]const u8, a slice that also promises the terminator, and they coerce to [*:0]const u8 without a copy. That is why passing "Grayson Carlyle" to strlen just worked. A runtime slice does not carry that promise: to hand one to C you copy it into a buffer and add the zero yourself (Exercise 35.5), or allocate with allocator.dupeZ(u8, s), which does the same on the heap.

C to Zig. Given a [*:0]const u8, std.mem.span walks to the zero and returns a proper slice with a length. From then on it is an ordinary Zig string.

c4_span.zig
const std = @import("std");

extern fn getenv(name: [*:0]const u8) ?[*:0]const u8;

pub fn main() void {
    const raw = getenv("HOME") orelse {
        std.debug.print("HOME is not set\n", .{});
        return;
    };
    const home: []const u8 = std.mem.span(raw);
    std.debug.print("HOME has {d} bytes and starts with '{c}'\n", .{ home.len, home[0] });

    // Going the other way: a Zig string literal is already sentinel-terminated.
    const lit: [:0]const u8 = "campaigns.db";
    const ptr: [*:0]const u8 = lit; // coerces, no copy
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{ptr});
}
$ zig run -lc c4_span.zig
HOME has 11 bytes and starts with '/'
campaigns.db

getenv returns NULL when the variable is unset, so the return type is ?[*:0]const u8 and we use orelse. The type system made us think about the missing case, which is precisely what C would not have done.

Who owns the bytes? A string C gives you usually points into C's memory. getenv's result lives as long as the environment; SQLite's column text is valid only until the next step. If you need it later, copy it (allocator.dupe). IRON LEDGER's Stmt.text always copies for this reason.

35.5 Opaque handles and return codes

Most C libraries give you a pointer to some struct they never let you see, and every function returns an int that is zero on success. SQLite is the model citizen of this style, and it is installed on this machine, so we can use the real thing. Three declarations get us open, execute and close:

c8_errors.zig
const std = @import("std");

const Handle = opaque {};
extern fn sqlite3_open(filename: [*:0]const u8, db: *?*Handle) c_int;
extern fn sqlite3_close(db: *Handle) c_int;
extern fn sqlite3_exec(db: *Handle, sql: [*:0]const u8, cb: ?*anyopaque, arg: ?*anyopaque, errmsg: ?*?[*:0]u8) c_int;
extern fn sqlite3_free(p: ?*anyopaque) void;
extern fn sqlite3_libversion() [*:0]const u8;

const SQLITE_OK = 0;

const Db = struct {
    h: *Handle,

    fn open(path: [*:0]const u8) error{SqliteError}!Db {
        var h: ?*Handle = null;
        if (sqlite3_open(path, &h) != SQLITE_OK or h == null) return error.SqliteError;
        return .{ .h = h.? };
    }

    fn close(self: Db) void {
        _ = sqlite3_close(self.h);
    }

    fn exec(self: Db, sql: [*:0]const u8) error{SqliteError}!void {
        var msg: ?[*:0]u8 = null;
        if (sqlite3_exec(self.h, sql, null, null, &msg) != SQLITE_OK) {
            if (msg) |m| {
                std.debug.print("sqlite says: {s}\n", .{m});
                sqlite3_free(m);
            }
            return error.SqliteError;
        }
    }
};

pub fn main() !void {
    std.debug.print("SQLite {s}\n", .{sqlite3_libversion()});
    const db = try Db.open(":memory:");
    defer db.close();
    try db.exec("CREATE TABLE person (name TEXT, salary INTEGER)");
    try db.exec("INSERT INTO person VALUES ('Grayson', 1500)");
    std.debug.print("two statements ran\n", .{});
    db.exec("SELEKT * FROM person") catch |e| std.debug.print("caught {s}\n", .{@errorName(e)});
}
$ zig run -lc -lsqlite3 c8_errors.zig
SQLite 3.51.0
two statements ran
sqlite says: near "SELEKT": syntax error
caught SqliteError

Walk through the shapes:

  • const Handle = opaque {}; declares a type with unknown size and contents. You can have a *Handle and pass it around, but you cannot dereference it or make one yourself. That is exactly what SQLite's sqlite3 * is. Because it is a distinct type, you also cannot pass a statement handle where a database handle belongs; C would let you.
  • sqlite3_open takes an out-parameter, a pointer to a pointer: *?*Handle. We declare var h: ?*Handle = null; and pass &h. After the call, if it succeeded, h is non-null and we unwrap it with h.?.
  • sqlite3_exec's error message is another out-parameter, ?*?[*:0]u8: an optional pointer (we may pass NULL to say "I don't want it") to an optional C string (SQLite may leave it NULL). The message is allocated by SQLite, so we must give it back with sqlite3_free.
  • Every return code is compared with SQLITE_OK, and the wrapper turns "not OK" into error.SqliteError. Above the wrapper, nobody sees a c_int again; they see try db.exec(...).

This is the pattern for every C library: raw extern declarations at the bottom of one file, a thin Zig struct with methods above them that speaks errors and slices, and nothing C-shaped leaking out of that file. If you forget to link the library, the error is clear and comes from the linker, not the compiler:

$ zig run -lc c8_errors.zig
error: undefined symbol: _sqlite3_close
    note: referenced by .../c8_errors_zcu.o:_c8_errors.Db.close
error: undefined symbol: _sqlite3_exec
    ...

35.6 @cImport and std.c: letting the compiler read the header

Writing declarations by hand is fine for a dozen functions, and it keeps your dependency on the C library explicit and reviewable. For a large API, Zig can translate the header for you. @cImport takes a block of @cInclude calls and produces a namespace containing every function, type and macro from those headers:

c7_cimport.zig
const std = @import("std");
const c = @cImport({
    @cInclude("stdio.h");
    @cInclude("math.h");
});

pub fn main() void {
    const root = c.sqrt(2.0);
    _ = c.printf("sqrt(2) = %.4f\n", root);
    std.debug.print("c_int is {d} bits, c_long is {d} bits\n", .{ @bitSizeOf(c_int), @bitSizeOf(c_long) });
}
$ zig run -lc c7_cimport.zig
c_int is 32 bits, c_long is 64 bits
sqrt(2) = 1.4142

This works directly from zig run -lc in 0.16; no build.zig configuration is needed for headers that live in the system include path. (In a build script the equivalent is exe.linkLibC() plus, for third-party headers, exe.addIncludePath.) The translated declarations use C's loose pointer types ([*c]u8, a "C pointer" that may be null and may point to one or many), so you will do a little more casting than with hand-written declarations, but you get the entire header for free. Exercise 35.4 wraps strtol this way.

For libc specifically there is a middle path: std.c already contains hand-written declarations for most of POSIX, with good Zig types.

c5_stdc.zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("pid  {d}\n", .{std.c.getpid()});
    std.debug.print("ppid {d}\n", .{std.c.getppid()});
    if (std.c.getenv("SHELL")) |sh| std.debug.print("shell {s}\n", .{sh});
}
$ zig run -lc c5_stdc.zig
pid  36661
ppid 36655
shell /bin/zsh

Not everything is there (strlen is not, for instance, because std.mem covers it), so when a name is missing, declare it yourself. Note also that std.c.getenv is typed to return ?[*:0]u8, and {s} knows how to print a sentinel-terminated pointer.

35.7 The other direction: export

export fn makes a Zig function visible to C under its exact name, with the C calling convention. Compile the file as a library (zig build-lib) and a C program can link against it; or, as here, simply call it from Zig, which is a handy way to test.

c6_export.zig
const std = @import("std");

export fn ledger_apply_bp(amount: i64, bp: i64) i64 {
    return @divTrunc(amount * bp, 10_000);
}

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{ledger_apply_bp(1500, 11_000)});
}
$ zig run c6_export.zig
1650

An exported function's parameters and return type must be C-compatible: integers, floats, pointers, extern structs. A Zig slice or error union would not have a C representation, and the compiler will tell you so. This is how IRON LEDGER could one day expose its simulation to a C or Python front end: an exported function per command, taking integers and C strings.

In IRON LEDGER. The game's whole persistence layer stands on src/persist/sqlite.zig: eleven extern fn declarations against SQLite plus two opaque {} handle types, with no header translation. The file is the pattern of 35.5 at full size. Db.open, Db.exec and Db.prepare wrap return codes; Stmt.bind uses @typeInfo (as in Chapter 27) to choose sqlite3_bind_int64, sqlite3_bind_text or sqlite3_bind_null from the Zig type of the value; Stmt.text copies column bytes into an allocator because SQLite's buffer dies on the next step. The constant transient is SQLite's SQLITE_TRANSIENT, the special destructor pointer (void*)-1, spelled as @ptrFromInt(std.math.maxInt(usize)). The linker finds the symbols because build.zig says linkSystemLibrary("sqlite3"), the build-script form of -lsqlite3. The same discipline holds for the terminal: std.posix.tcsetattr for raw mode and std.c.waitpid for the music player are each confined to one file. 
pub fn open(path: [*:0]const u8) Error!Db {
    var h: ?*Handle = null;
    if (sqlite3_open(path, &h) != SQLITE_OK or h == null) return error.SqliteError;
    return .{ .h = h.? };
}

Exercises

Exercise 35.1 · Three libc functions warm-up

Declare strlen, getpid and toupper with extern fn, using the right Zig types from the table, and print the results. Name the file: exercises/35-c-interop/ex1_libc.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 35, exercise 1: three libc functions by hand.
//! Run with:  zig run -lc ex1_libc.zig
//! Goal: declare strlen, getpid and toupper with `extern fn`, call them,
//! and print the results. Expected output (pid differs):
//!   strlen("Grayson Carlyle") = 15
//!   pid = 12345 (positive: true)
//!   toupper('m') = M

const std = @import("std");

extern fn strlen(s: [*:0]const u8) usize;
extern fn getpid() c_int;
extern fn toupper(ch: c_int) c_int;

pub fn main() void {
    const name: [*:0]const u8 = "Grayson Carlyle";
    std.debug.print("strlen(\"{s}\") = {d}\n", .{ name, strlen(name) });
    const pid = getpid();
    std.debug.print("pid = {d} (positive: {})\n", .{ pid, pid > 0 });
    const up: u8 = @intCast(toupper('m'));
    std.debug.print("toupper('m') = {c}\n", .{up});
}

toupper takes and returns int in C (so it can represent EOF), hence c_int both ways and the @intCast back to a u8 for printing with {c}.

Exercise 35.2 · qsort with your comparator practice

Sort an array of i64 salaries with libc's qsort and a comparator written in Zig. Name the file: exercises/35-c-interop/ex2_qsort.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 35, exercise 2: qsort with a Zig comparator.
//! Run with:  zig run -lc ex2_qsort.zig
//! Goal: sort an array of salaries with libc's qsort, using a comparator
//! written in Zig with callconv(.c). Expected output:
//!   before: { 1500, 400, 800, 640, 1500, 500 }
//!   after:  { 400, 500, 640, 800, 1500, 1500 }

const std = @import("std");

const CompareFn = *const fn (?*const anyopaque, ?*const anyopaque) callconv(.c) c_int;
extern fn qsort(base: ?*anyopaque, nmemb: usize, size: usize, compar: CompareFn) void;

fn byValue(a: ?*const anyopaque, b: ?*const anyopaque) callconv(.c) c_int {
    const x: *const i64 = @ptrCast(@alignCast(a.?));
    const y: *const i64 = @ptrCast(@alignCast(b.?));
    if (x.* < y.*) return -1;
    if (x.* > y.*) return 1;
    return 0;
}

pub fn main() void {
    var salaries = [_]i64{ 1500, 400, 800, 640, 1500, 500 };
    std.debug.print("before: {any}\n", .{salaries});
    qsort(&salaries, salaries.len, @sizeOf(i64), byValue);
    std.debug.print("after:  {any}\n", .{salaries});
}

The element type changed from c_int to i64, so the size argument (@sizeOf(i64)) and the casts inside the comparator changed with it. Get either wrong and qsort will sort garbage; C checks nothing. The @alignCast is what lets Zig check at least the alignment in Debug builds.

Exercise 35.3 · A tiny SQLite binding challenge

Extend the open/exec/close wrapper into a binding with prepared statements: declare sqlite3_prepare_v2, step, finalize, reset, bind_int64, bind_text, column_int64 and column_text, wrap them in Db and Stmt structs that return Zig errors, insert two people and read them back. Name the file: exercises/35-c-interop/ex3_sqlite.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 35, exercise 3: a tiny SQLite binding.
//! Run with:  zig run -lc -lsqlite3 ex3_sqlite.zig
//! Goal: declare the eight SQLite functions needed to open a database,
//! create a table, insert rows with a prepared statement and read them
//! back. Wrap return codes in Zig errors. Expected output:
//!   sqlite 3.51.0
//!   Grayson earns 1500
//!   Clay earns 800
//!   2 rows

const std = @import("std");

const Handle = opaque {};
const StmtHandle = opaque {};

extern fn sqlite3_libversion() [*:0]const u8;
extern fn sqlite3_open(filename: [*:0]const u8, db: *?*Handle) c_int;
extern fn sqlite3_close(db: *Handle) c_int;
extern fn sqlite3_exec(db: *Handle, sql: [*:0]const u8, cb: ?*anyopaque, arg: ?*anyopaque, errmsg: ?*?[*:0]u8) c_int;
extern fn sqlite3_free(p: ?*anyopaque) void;
extern fn sqlite3_prepare_v2(db: *Handle, sql: [*]const u8, nbyte: c_int, stmt: *?*StmtHandle, tail: ?*?[*]const u8) c_int;
extern fn sqlite3_step(stmt: *StmtHandle) c_int;
extern fn sqlite3_finalize(stmt: *StmtHandle) c_int;
extern fn sqlite3_reset(stmt: *StmtHandle) c_int;
extern fn sqlite3_bind_int64(stmt: *StmtHandle, idx: c_int, v: i64) c_int;
extern fn sqlite3_bind_text(stmt: *StmtHandle, idx: c_int, text: [*]const u8, n: c_int, destructor: ?*const anyopaque) c_int;
extern fn sqlite3_column_int64(stmt: *StmtHandle, col: c_int) i64;
extern fn sqlite3_column_text(stmt: *StmtHandle, col: c_int) ?[*:0]const u8;
extern fn sqlite3_errmsg(db: *Handle) [*:0]const u8;

const SQLITE_OK = 0;
const SQLITE_ROW = 100;
const SQLITE_DONE = 101;
const transient: ?*const anyopaque = @ptrFromInt(std.math.maxInt(usize));

pub const Error = error{SqliteError};

pub const Db = struct {
    h: *Handle,

    pub fn open(path: [*:0]const u8) Error!Db {
        var h: ?*Handle = null;
        if (sqlite3_open(path, &h) != SQLITE_OK or h == null) return error.SqliteError;
        return .{ .h = h.? };
    }

    pub fn close(self: Db) void {
        _ = sqlite3_close(self.h);
    }

    pub fn exec(self: Db, sql: [*:0]const u8) Error!void {
        var err: ?[*:0]u8 = null;
        if (sqlite3_exec(self.h, sql, null, null, &err) != SQLITE_OK) {
            if (err) |e| {
                std.debug.print("sqlite: {s}\n", .{e});
                sqlite3_free(e);
            }
            return error.SqliteError;
        }
    }

    pub fn prepare(self: Db, sql: []const u8) Error!Stmt {
        var s: ?*StmtHandle = null;
        const rc = sqlite3_prepare_v2(self.h, sql.ptr, @intCast(sql.len), &s, null);
        if (rc != SQLITE_OK or s == null) {
            std.debug.print("sqlite: {s}\n", .{sqlite3_errmsg(self.h)});
            return error.SqliteError;
        }
        return .{ .h = s.? };
    }
};

pub const Stmt = struct {
    h: *StmtHandle,

    pub fn finalize(self: Stmt) void {
        _ = sqlite3_finalize(self.h);
    }

    pub fn bindInt(self: Stmt, idx: c_int, v: i64) Error!void {
        if (sqlite3_bind_int64(self.h, idx, v) != SQLITE_OK) return error.SqliteError;
    }

    pub fn bindText(self: Stmt, idx: c_int, s: []const u8) Error!void {
        if (sqlite3_bind_text(self.h, idx, s.ptr, @intCast(s.len), transient) != SQLITE_OK)
            return error.SqliteError;
    }

    /// Run an INSERT to completion, then reset so it can be bound again.
    pub fn run(self: Stmt) Error!void {
        const rc = sqlite3_step(self.h);
        if (rc != SQLITE_DONE and rc != SQLITE_ROW) return error.SqliteError;
        _ = sqlite3_reset(self.h);
    }

    /// Advance a SELECT: true while rows remain.
    pub fn next(self: Stmt) Error!bool {
        const rc = sqlite3_step(self.h);
        if (rc == SQLITE_ROW) return true;
        if (rc == SQLITE_DONE) return false;
        return error.SqliteError;
    }

    pub fn int(self: Stmt, col: c_int) i64 {
        return sqlite3_column_int64(self.h, col);
    }

    /// Borrowed: valid only until the next step.
    pub fn text(self: Stmt, col: c_int) []const u8 {
        const p = sqlite3_column_text(self.h, col) orelse return "";
        return std.mem.span(p);
    }
};

pub fn main() !void {
    std.debug.print("sqlite {s}\n", .{sqlite3_libversion()});
    const db = try Db.open(":memory:");
    defer db.close();
    try db.exec("CREATE TABLE person (name TEXT, salary INTEGER)");

    const ins = try db.prepare("INSERT INTO person VALUES (?1, ?2)");
    defer ins.finalize();
    const people = [_]struct { name: []const u8, salary: i64 }{
        .{ .name = "Grayson", .salary = 1500 },
        .{ .name = "Clay", .salary = 800 },
    };
    for (people) |p| {
        try ins.bindText(1, p.name);
        try ins.bindInt(2, p.salary);
        try ins.run();
    }

    const sel = try db.prepare("SELECT name, salary FROM person");
    defer sel.finalize();
    var rows: u32 = 0;
    while (try sel.next()) : (rows += 1) {
        std.debug.print("{s} earns {d}\n", .{ sel.text(0), sel.int(1) });
    }
    std.debug.print("{d} rows\n", .{rows});
}

This is a two-thirds-size copy of the game's binding. The interesting declarations are sqlite3_prepare_v2, which takes the SQL as a pointer plus a byte count (so a Zig slice's .ptr and .len map straight onto it), and sqlite3_bind_text's destructor argument, where transient asks SQLite to copy the bytes. Stmt.next turns the three-valued step (ROW, DONE, or an error) into !bool, which reads naturally in a while (try sel.next()) loop.

Exercise 35.4 · @cImport and strtol practice

Import stdlib.h with @cImport and wrap strtol in a Zig function that returns error.NotANumber when no digits were consumed and error.TrailingGarbage when the string did not end after the number. Name the file: exercises/35-c-interop/ex4_cimport.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 35, exercise 4: @cImport and wrapping a C return code.
//! Run with:  zig run -lc ex4_cimport.zig
//! Goal: import <stdlib.h> and <errno.h> with @cImport, wrap strtol in a
//! Zig function that returns an error instead of a sentinel, and print:
//!   "42" -> 42
//!   "  -7" -> -7
//!   "12abc" -> error.TrailingGarbage
//!   "abc" -> error.NotANumber

const std = @import("std");
const c = @cImport({
    @cInclude("stdlib.h");
    @cInclude("errno.h");
});

const ParseError = error{ NotANumber, TrailingGarbage };

/// strtol reports failure by returning 0 and leaving `end` at the start,
/// or by stopping early. Turn both into Zig errors.
fn parseLong(text: [*:0]const u8) ParseError!c_long {
    var end: [*c]u8 = undefined;
    const v = c.strtol(text, &end, 10);
    if (end == @as([*c]u8, @constCast(text))) return error.NotANumber;
    if (end[0] != 0) return error.TrailingGarbage;
    return v;
}

pub fn main() void {
    const inputs = [_][*:0]const u8{ "42", "  -7", "12abc", "abc" };
    for (inputs) |s| {
        if (parseLong(s)) |v| {
            std.debug.print("\"{s}\" -> {d}\n", .{ s, v });
        } else |e| {
            std.debug.print("\"{s}\" -> {s}\n", .{ s, @errorName(e) });
        }
    }
}

strtol's second argument is a char ** out-parameter that receives where parsing stopped. The translated type is [*c][*c]u8, so the local is a [*c]u8 and we pass its address. "Nothing consumed" is end == text, which needs a @constCast because the C signature drops the const. "Not at the end" is end[0] != 0. Both sentinels become errors, which is the whole point of wrapping.

Exercise 35.5 · Sentinel strings both ways practice

Write toC(buf, s), which copies a Zig slice into a buffer and appends the zero, returning [:0]u8 or error.TooLong; fromC(p), which turns a [*:0]const u8 into a slice; and an exported ledger_bp function. No libc is needed, so this one is a zig test. Name the file: exercises/35-c-interop/ex5_span.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 35, exercise 5: sentinel strings both ways.
//! Run with:  zig test ex5_span.zig
//! Goal: implement `toC` (copy a Zig slice into a sentinel-terminated
//! buffer for C) and `fromC` (turn a C string back into a slice) and
//! export a C-callable `ledger_bp` function. No libc needed.

const std = @import("std");

/// Copy `s` into `buf` and add the terminating zero. Returns the
/// sentinel-terminated slice, or error.TooLong if it does not fit.
pub fn toC(buf: []u8, s: []const u8) error{TooLong}![:0]u8 {
    if (s.len + 1 > buf.len) return error.TooLong;
    @memcpy(buf[0..s.len], s);
    buf[s.len] = 0;
    return buf[0..s.len :0];
}

/// A C string comes back as a many-item pointer; find its length.
pub fn fromC(p: [*:0]const u8) []const u8 {
    return std.mem.span(p);
}

/// Exported so a C caller could use it: apply basis points to an amount.
export fn ledger_bp(amount: i64, bp: i64) i64 {
    return @divTrunc(amount * bp, 10_000);
}

test "toC adds the sentinel" {
    var buf: [16]u8 = undefined;
    const s = try toC(&buf, "Clay");
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 4), s.len);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 0), s[4]);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Clay", s);
}

test "toC refuses when there is no room for the zero" {
    var buf: [4]u8 = undefined;
    try std.testing.expectError(error.TooLong, toC(&buf, "Clay"));
}

test "fromC finds the length" {
    const p: [*:0]const u8 = "Kalmar";
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("Kalmar", fromC(p));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 6), fromC(p).len);
}

test "exported function is callable from Zig too" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 1650), ledger_bp(1500, 11_000));
}

The slice syntax buf[0..s.len :0] produces a sentinel-terminated slice and, in Debug builds, checks that buf[s.len] really is zero. The length test (s.len + 1 > buf.len) is the one C programmers forget; Zig makes you write it because the return type promises the sentinel exists.

Check your understanding

  1. What is the Zig type for a C const char * that is a string, and for a char * that is a byte buffer with a separate length?
    Answer[*:0]const u8 for the string (zero-terminated many-item pointer); [*]u8 for the buffer. If either may be NULL, prefix with ?.
  2. Why declare const Handle = opaque {}; instead of using *anyopaque for SQLite's database pointer?
    AnswerBoth are pointers you cannot look inside, but *Handle and *StmtHandle are distinct types, so the compiler stops you passing a statement where a database belongs. *anyopaque would accept anything.
  3. What does callconv(.c) do and when do you need it?
    AnswerIt makes a Zig function use the C calling convention so C code can call it. You need it on callbacks you pass to C (like a qsort comparator); export fn implies it.
  4. What is the difference between -lc and -lsqlite3, and what happens if you forget the second?
    Answer-lc links the C standard library; -lsqlite3 links SQLite. Without it the compile succeeds but the linker reports undefined symbol: _sqlite3_open and friends.
  5. Does @cImport work from zig run in 0.16?
    AnswerYes, with -lc, for headers on the system include path. In build.zig you call linkLibC() and, for other headers, addIncludePath.
  6. You receive a [*:0]const u8 from C and want to store it in a struct for later. What two steps are needed?
    Answerstd.mem.span to get a slice with a length, then allocator.dupe(u8, slice) to copy it into memory you own, because C's buffer may be freed or reused.
  7. Why does IRON LEDGER wrap every c_int return code inside sqlite.zig instead of returning it?
    AnswerSo the rest of the program uses try and Zig error sets, cannot forget to check a code, and never depends on SQLite's constants. All the C-shaped code stays in one file.
What you learned.
  • extern fn name(args) ret; declares a C function; link its library with -lc, -lsqlite3, or linkSystemLibrary in build.zig.
  • C's types map onto c_int, c_long, usize, [*:0]const u8, [*]u8, ?*T, ?*anyopaque; add ? wherever NULL is possible.
  • opaque {} is a type you can point at but never inspect: the right shape for a library handle. Out-parameters are pointers to optionals, *?*Handle.
  • Callbacks C will call need callconv(.c); export fn publishes a Zig function to C.
  • std.mem.span turns a C string into a slice; string literals already coerce to [*:0]const u8; copy anything C hands you if you keep it.
  • @cImport translates headers (works from zig run -lc); std.c has many POSIX functions pre-declared.
  • Wrap return codes into Zig errors in one file per C library, and let nothing C-shaped escape it.

36. Threads and atomics

In this chapter you will start threads with std.Thread.spawn, wait for them with join, and see exactly what goes wrong when two threads touch the same variable. Then you will fix it three ways: give each thread its own slot, use an atomic, or take a mutex. You will meet std.Io.Group for running a batch of tasks, and learn when a program should not use threads at all.

36.1 Spawn and join

A thread is a second instruction pointer running through your program at the same time as the first, sharing all the same memory. Zig starts one with std.Thread.spawn, which takes a configuration struct (usually empty), a function, and a tuple of arguments for that function. It returns a Thread handle, or an error if the OS refused. join blocks until the thread's function returns.

t1_hello.zig
const std = @import("std");

fn greet(name: []const u8, times: u32) void {
    for (0..times) |i| std.debug.print("{s} {d}\n", .{ name, i });
}

pub fn main() !void {
    const t = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, greet, .{ "worker", 3 });
    greet("main", 3);
    t.join();
    std.debug.print("done\n", .{});
}
$ zig run t1_hello.zig
main 0
main 1
main 2
worker 0
worker 1
worker 2
done

Run it a few times and the lines interleave differently, or not at all, depending on how the operating system schedules the two threads. That is the first lesson: the order in which threads run is not yours to choose. The only ordering guarantee in this program is that done comes after both, because join waits.

The arguments tuple .{ "worker", 3 } is matched to greet's parameters at compile time, so passing the wrong number or type is a compile error rather than a crash. The values are copied into the new thread; to share something, pass a pointer (next section). Every thread you spawn must eventually be joined (or detached if you truly do not care when it ends); forgetting is a resource leak, and a program that returns from main while threads are still running ends them abruptly.

36.2 The data race

Because threads share memory, two of them can write the same variable. Here four threads each add one to a global counter a hundred thousand times.

t2_race.zig
const std = @import("std");

var counter: u64 = 0;

fn bump() void {
    for (0..100_000) |_| counter += 1;
}

pub fn main() !void {
    var threads: [4]std.Thread = undefined;
    for (&threads) |*t| t.* = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, bump, .{});
    for (threads) |t| t.join();
    std.debug.print("counter = {d} (wanted 400000)\n", .{counter});
}
$ zig run t2_race.zig
counter = 103977 (wanted 400000)
$ zig run t2_race.zig
counter = 103684 (wanted 400000)

Not 400,000, and a different wrong number every run. counter += 1 is three steps on the machine: read the value, add one, write it back. If thread A reads 50, thread B reads 50, both add one and both write 51, one increment has vanished. With four threads hammering the same cache line, most of them vanish.

This is undefined behaviour, not just a wrong answer. Zig, like C, defines a program with a data race as having no meaning at all. The numbers above are what happened on this machine today; on another CPU or with -O ReleaseFast the compiler may hoist the load out of the loop and print 100000, or anything else. Do not reason about what a race "usually" does. Remove it.

There are three honest ways to remove it, and the rest of the chapter is those three.

36.3 Fix one: do not share

The best synchronisation is none. If every thread writes to its own slot and only the main thread reads the slots after join, there is nothing to race on. This is how nearly all "split the work in N pieces" programs should look.

t5_parts.zig
const std = @import("std");

fn sumChunk(chunk: []const u64, out: *u64) void {
    var s: u64 = 0;
    for (chunk) |v| s += v;
    out.* = s;
}

pub fn main() !void {
    var data: [1000]u64 = undefined;
    for (&data, 0..) |*d, i| d.* = i;

    var parts: [4]u64 = undefined;
    var threads: [4]std.Thread = undefined;
    for (&threads, 0..) |*t, i| {
        t.* = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, sumChunk, .{ data[i * 250 .. (i + 1) * 250], &parts[i] });
    }
    for (threads) |t| t.join();
    std.debug.print("parts {any}\n", .{parts});
    std.debug.print("total {d}\n", .{parts[0] + parts[1] + parts[2] + parts[3]});
}
$ zig run t5_parts.zig
parts { 31125, 93625, 156125, 218625 }
total 499500

Each thread receives a slice of the input (a view, not a copy) and a pointer to exactly one element of parts. The slices do not overlap and the pointers are distinct, so no two threads ever touch the same byte. join is what makes the main thread's reads of parts safe: joining a thread is a guarantee that everything it wrote is visible afterwards. The pattern generalises: chunk the input, one output slot per chunk, join, reduce.

36.4 Fix two: atomics

Sometimes threads really do need one shared number: a progress counter, a "stop now" flag, an ID generator. For a single machine word, the CPU can do read-modify-write as one indivisible step, and Zig exposes that as std.atomic.Value(T).

t3_atomic.zig
const std = @import("std");

var counter: std.atomic.Value(u64) = .init(0);

fn bump() void {
    for (0..100_000) |_| _ = counter.fetchAdd(1, .monotonic);
}

pub fn main() !void {
    var threads: [4]std.Thread = undefined;
    for (&threads) |*t| t.* = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, bump, .{});
    for (threads) |t| t.join();
    std.debug.print("counter = {d}\n", .{counter.load(.seq_cst)});
}
$ zig run t3_atomic.zig
counter = 400000

Exactly right, every time. fetchAdd(1, .monotonic) adds one atomically and returns the old value (which we discard with _ =). The methods are load, store, swap, fetchAdd, fetchSub, fetchAnd, fetchOr, cmpxchgStrong and cmpxchgWeak, and each takes a memory ordering as its last argument. .init(0) is the initial value.

The ordering argument answers a question you might not know you were asking: "when this thread sees this atomic change, which of the other writes made before it is it guaranteed to see too?" The choices are .monotonic, .acquire, .release, .acq_rel and .seq_cst. For a beginner, two rules cover almost everything:

  • If the atomic is the only thing shared (a pure counter), .monotonic is enough: you want the arithmetic to be atomic and nothing else.
  • If the atomic announces other data ("the buffer is ready", "please stop"), the writer uses .release and the reader uses .acquire. Together they promise the reader sees everything the writer did before the store.

When in doubt, .seq_cst is the strongest and always correct, merely a little slower. Here is the announcement pattern, a stop flag:

t7_flag.zig
const std = @import("std");

var stop: std.atomic.Value(bool) = .init(false);
var ticks: std.atomic.Value(u32) = .init(0);

fn spin() void {
    while (!stop.load(.acquire)) _ = ticks.fetchAdd(1, .monotonic);
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const t = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, spin, .{});
    try init.io.sleep(.fromMilliseconds(20), .awake);
    stop.store(true, .release);
    t.join();
    std.debug.print("worker ticked {d} times before it saw the flag\n", .{ticks.load(.seq_cst)});
}
$ zig run t7_flag.zig
worker ticked 10134572 times before it saw the flag

The worker spins reading the flag with .acquire; main sleeps 20 ms and stores true with .release. Without atomics, the compiler would be entitled to read stop once, see false, and loop forever; the atomic load tells it the value can change under its feet.

36.5 Fix three: a mutex

Atomics cover one word. When the shared thing is bigger (a list, a hash map, two fields that must change together), you need a lock. A mutex ("mutual exclusion") is a token only one thread can hold; while a thread holds it, everyone else who asks waits. In 0.16 the mutex lives in std.Io, because waiting for a lock is a blocking operation the I/O layer wants to know about, so lock and unlock take the io value.

t4_mutex.zig
const std = @import("std");

var mutex: std.Io.Mutex = .init;
var total: u64 = 0;
var names: std.ArrayList([]const u8) = .empty;

fn work(io: std.Io, gpa: std.mem.Allocator, name: []const u8, pay: u64) !void {
    mutex.lockUncancelable(io);
    defer mutex.unlock(io);
    total += pay;
    try names.append(gpa, name);
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    const gpa = init.gpa;
    defer names.deinit(gpa);
    const t1 = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, work, .{ io, gpa, "Grayson", 1500 });
    const t2 = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, work, .{ io, gpa, "Clay", 800 });
    t1.join();
    t2.join();
    std.debug.print("total {d}, {d} names\n", .{ total, names.items.len });
}
$ zig run t4_mutex.zig
total 2300, 2 names

The shape to memorise is the pair: lock immediately followed by defer unlock. Whatever happens between them, including an early return or a try that fails, the lock is released. Everything that touches total or names happens inside that window, so the two threads take turns, and the ArrayList's internal pointer juggling is never interrupted half way.

lockUncancelable is the plain blocking form. There is also try mutex.lock(io), which can return error.Canceled if the task is cancelled while waiting; use it inside code that participates in cancellation, and the uncancelable form everywhere else.

Gone in 0.16. std.Thread.Mutex, std.Thread.Pool and std.Thread.WaitGroup no longer exist. The mutex is std.Io.Mutex (initialised with .init, methods take io), and the pool-and-wait-group job is done by std.Io.Group, next. If you see the old names in a tutorial, translate.

Hold locks briefly, and never call out to unknown code while holding one. The classic mistake is thread A holding lock 1 waiting for lock 2 while thread B holds 2 waiting for 1: a deadlock, and both wait forever. One lock per program, held for a few lines at a time, avoids it entirely.

36.6 A group of tasks: std.Io.Group

Spawning and joining threads by hand is fine for four fixed workers. For "run these N things and wait for all of them", 0.16 offers std.Io.Group. You call group.async(io, function, args) once per task and group.await(io) once at the end. The io implementation decides how to run them: the default Threaded implementation you get from main uses a pool of OS threads sized to the machine.

t6_group.zig
const std = @import("std");

fn sumChunk(chunk: []const u64, out: *u64) void {
    var s: u64 = 0;
    for (chunk) |v| s += v;
    out.* = s;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    var data: [1000]u64 = undefined;
    for (&data, 0..) |*d, i| d.* = i;

    var parts: [4]u64 = undefined;
    var group: std.Io.Group = .init;
    for (0..4) |i| group.async(io, sumChunk, .{ data[i * 250 .. (i + 1) * 250], &parts[i] });
    try group.await(io);
    std.debug.print("total {d}\n", .{parts[0] + parts[1] + parts[2] + parts[3]});
    std.debug.print("this machine has {d} cpus\n", .{try std.Thread.getCpuCount()});
}
$ zig run t6_group.zig
total 499500
this machine has 14 cpus

Same work as 36.3, no thread handles to manage. std.Thread.getCpuCount() tells you how many hardware threads exist, which is the natural upper bound on how many chunks are worth making. await returns error.Canceled if the group was cancelled, hence the try. The functions you hand to a group must return void or an error union that includes error.Canceled; plain void, as here, is simplest.

The async story, in one paragraph. Group.async is one corner of a larger design. std.Io in 0.16 also has io.async and io.concurrent, which return a Future you later await, plus cancellation that propagates through them. The point of putting all of this behind the io value is that the same code can run on a thread pool today (std.Io.Threaded) and on an event loop tomorrow, without changing the call sites. This book stops here; the standard library's Io.zig has the reference, and the language keywords async/await from older Zig versions are gone.

36.7 When not to use threads

Threads make a program faster only when there is enough independent work to keep more than one core busy, and they make every program harder to reason about. Some honest guidance:

  • A turn-based simulation does not need them. IRON LEDGER advances one day in a few microseconds. Adding threads would add nothing but the risk of a data race breaking determinism.
  • I/O-bound work rarely needs them. Waiting for a disk or a socket does not use a core. The std.Io design exists so such waiting can overlap without you managing threads.
  • Small inputs do not need them. Spawning a thread costs tens of microseconds; summing a thousand numbers costs less than one. Exercise 36.4 measures this.
  • Anything touching a random generator or a hash map from two threads is wrong until you add a lock, and once you add the lock the threads mostly wait for each other.

The places threads do pay off: big, chunkable, CPU-heavy work (image processing, batch parsing, running many independent simulations for statistics); and keeping a user interface responsive while something slow happens in the background. If your program is neither, single-threaded is not a compromise, it is the right design.

In IRON LEDGER. The simulation core in src/sim/ is single-threaded on purpose: the golden-master test in src/sim/commands.zig demands that the same seed and script always produce the same state hash, and a second thread drawing from the RNG or appending to a list would break that in ways no test could reliably catch. The one place the game reaches for concurrency is the terminal client, where the soundtrack plays in a separate process, not a thread: src/tui/music.zig starts the player with std.process.spawn(io, ...) and reaps it with std.c.waitpid, so the audio can be killed and restarted without any shared memory at all. That is a good rule of thumb: prefer a process when the two halves share nothing, a thread only when they must share memory, and neither when the work is small.

Exercises

Exercise 36.1 · Spawn and join warm-up

Start four workers, each summing its own quarter of 0..1_000_000 into its own slot, join them, and print the total. Name the file: exercises/36-concurrency/ex1_spawn.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 36, exercise 1: spawn and join.
//! Run with:  zig run ex1_spawn.zig
//! Goal: start four worker threads, each computing the sum of its own
//! range into its own slot, then join them and add the slots. The
//! per-thread lines may appear in any order. Expected output:
//!   worker 0: 0..250000
//!   worker 1: 250000..500000
//!   worker 2: 500000..750000
//!   worker 3: 750000..1000000
//!   total = 499999500000

const std = @import("std");

fn worker(id: usize, lo: u64, hi: u64, out: *u64) void {
    std.debug.print("worker {d}: {d}..{d}\n", .{ id, lo, hi });
    var s: u64 = 0;
    var i = lo;
    while (i < hi) : (i += 1) s += i;
    out.* = s;
}

pub fn main() !void {
    const n_threads = 4;
    const total_n: u64 = 1_000_000;
    var slots: [n_threads]u64 = undefined;
    var threads: [n_threads]std.Thread = undefined;
    const chunk = total_n / n_threads;
    for (&threads, 0..) |*t, i| {
        t.* = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, worker, .{ i, i * chunk, (i + 1) * chunk, &slots[i] });
    }
    for (threads) |t| t.join();
    var total: u64 = 0;
    for (slots) |s| total += s;
    std.debug.print("total = {d}\n", .{total});
}

The per-thread lines come out in scheduler order, so they differ between runs, but the total is always 499999500000 because each slot is written by exactly one thread and read only after join.

Exercise 36.2 · A shared counter, done right practice

Write bumpAtomic, using std.atomic.Value(u64), and bumpMutex, using std.Io.Mutex around a plain u64, so that four threads each adding 100,000 produce exactly 400,000. The test file gets its io from std.testing.io. Name the file: exercises/36-concurrency/ex2_counter.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 36, exercise 2: a shared counter, three ways.
//! Run with:  zig test ex2_counter.zig
//! Goal: fill in the atomic and mutex versions of `bump` so both tests
//! count exactly 4 * 100_000. The plain version is left as a demonstration
//! of a data race and is not tested (its result is not defined).

const std = @import("std");

const per_thread = 100_000;
const n_threads = 4;

var atomic_count: std.atomic.Value(u64) = .init(0);

fn bumpAtomic() void {
    for (0..per_thread) |_| _ = atomic_count.fetchAdd(1, .monotonic);
}

var mutex_count: u64 = 0;
var mutex: std.Io.Mutex = .init;

fn bumpMutex(io: std.Io) void {
    for (0..per_thread) |_| {
        mutex.lockUncancelable(io);
        defer mutex.unlock(io);
        mutex_count += 1;
    }
}

test "atomic counter is exact" {
    var threads: [n_threads]std.Thread = undefined;
    for (&threads) |*t| t.* = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, bumpAtomic, .{});
    for (threads) |t| t.join();
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u64, n_threads * per_thread), atomic_count.load(.seq_cst));
}

test "mutex counter is exact" {
    const io = std.testing.io;
    var threads: [n_threads]std.Thread = undefined;
    for (&threads) |*t| t.* = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, bumpMutex, .{io});
    for (threads) |t| t.join();
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u64, n_threads * per_thread), mutex_count);
}

The atomic version needs no io; the mutex version does, so it is passed as a thread argument. Note std.testing.io: tests are given a working I/O implementation, which is also what you would use to test file code. Try timing both: the mutex version is many times slower, because every increment is a lock and unlock.

Exercise 36.3 · Parallel sum over a slice practice

Write parallelSum(data, n_threads) that splits any slice into n_threads chunks (the last one may be short, and there may be fewer items than threads), sums each on its own thread, and returns the total. Tests compare with a serial sum for 1001 items and 4 or 7 threads, and check a 2-item slice with 8 threads and an empty slice. Name the file: exercises/36-concurrency/ex3_parallel_sum.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 36, exercise 3: a parallel sum over a slice.
//! Run with:  zig test ex3_parallel_sum.zig
//! Goal: implement `parallelSum` so it splits `data` into `n_threads`
//! chunks, sums each chunk on its own thread, and returns the total.
//! Handle a slice shorter than n_threads and a remainder chunk.

const std = @import("std");

fn sumChunk(chunk: []const u32, out: *u64) void {
    var s: u64 = 0;
    for (chunk) |v| s += v;
    out.* = s;
}

pub fn parallelSum(data: []const u32, comptime n_threads: usize) !u64 {
    var partial = [_]u64{0} ** n_threads;
    var threads: [n_threads]?std.Thread = [_]?std.Thread{null} ** n_threads;
    const chunk_len = (data.len + n_threads - 1) / n_threads; // ceil
    for (0..n_threads) |i| {
        const lo = @min(i * chunk_len, data.len);
        const hi = @min(lo + chunk_len, data.len);
        if (lo == hi) break; // fewer items than threads
        threads[i] = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, sumChunk, .{ data[lo..hi], &partial[i] });
    }
    for (threads) |maybe| if (maybe) |t| t.join();
    var total: u64 = 0;
    for (partial) |p| total += p;
    return total;
}

test "matches a serial sum" {
    var data: [1001]u32 = undefined;
    for (&data, 0..) |*d, i| d.* = @intCast(i);
    var serial: u64 = 0;
    for (data) |v| serial += v;
    try std.testing.expectEqual(serial, try parallelSum(&data, 4));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(serial, try parallelSum(&data, 7));
}

test "short slices and empty slices" {
    const two = [_]u32{ 5, 6 };
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u64, 11), try parallelSum(&two, 8));
    const none = [_]u32{};
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u64, 0), try parallelSum(&none, 4));
}

The chunk length is rounded up, so the last chunk absorbs the remainder; @min clamps both bounds to the slice; and an empty chunk means "no more work", so we break and leave the remaining thread handles null. Storing ?std.Thread lets the join loop skip the threads that were never started.

Exercise 36.4 · The same work with Io.Group challenge

Allocate one hundred million u64s, sum them once with eight raw threads and once with an std.Io.Group of eight tasks, and time both with the monotonic clock. Print the CPU count. Then shrink the input to a thousand elements and observe that the timings are dominated by thread start-up. Name the file: exercises/36-concurrency/ex4_group.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 36, exercise 4: the same work with std.Io.Group.
//! Run with:  zig run ex4_group.zig
//! Goal: rewrite the parallel sum with an Io.Group instead of raw
//! threads, and time both. Expected output (timings vary):
//!   threads: 4999999950000000 in 30 ms
//!   group:   4999999950000000 in 30 ms
//!   cpus: 14

const std = @import("std");

fn sumChunk(chunk: []const u64, out: *u64) void {
    var s: u64 = 0;
    for (chunk) |v| s += v;
    out.* = s;
}

const n = 100_000_000;
const n_tasks = 8;

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    const data = try init.gpa.alloc(u64, n);
    defer init.gpa.free(data);
    for (data, 0..) |*d, i| d.* = i;
    var parts: [n_tasks]u64 = undefined;
    const chunk = n / n_tasks;

    var t0 = std.Io.Clock.now(.awake, io);
    var threads: [n_tasks]std.Thread = undefined;
    for (&threads, 0..) |*t, i| {
        t.* = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, sumChunk, .{ data[i * chunk .. (i + 1) * chunk], &parts[i] });
    }
    for (threads) |t| t.join();
    var total: u64 = 0;
    for (parts) |p| total += p;
    var t1 = std.Io.Clock.now(.awake, io);
    std.debug.print("threads: {d} in {d} ms\n", .{ total, t0.durationTo(t1).toMilliseconds() });

    t0 = std.Io.Clock.now(.awake, io);
    var group: std.Io.Group = .init;
    for (0..n_tasks) |i| {
        group.async(io, sumChunk, .{ data[i * chunk .. (i + 1) * chunk], &parts[i] });
    }
    try group.await(io);
    total = 0;
    for (parts) |p| total += p;
    t1 = std.Io.Clock.now(.awake, io);
    std.debug.print("group:   {d} in {d} ms\n", .{ total, t0.durationTo(t1).toMilliseconds() });
    std.debug.print("cpus: {d}\n", .{try std.Thread.getCpuCount()});
}

Both versions take about the same time, because the group is a thread pool underneath. The value of the group is not speed but bookkeeping: no handle array, no join loop, and the pool is already sized to the machine. Compare the code of the two halves and notice which one you would rather maintain.

Check your understanding

  1. Why did the plain counter print 103977 instead of 400000, and why is the exact number meaningless?
    Answercounter += 1 is a read, an add and a write; two threads interleaving those steps lose increments. A program with a data race has undefined behaviour, so the value depends on the CPU, the optimiser and luck.
  2. What does join guarantee besides "the thread has finished"?
    AnswerThat everything the thread wrote is visible to the joining thread afterwards. That is what makes reading the per-thread slots after join safe without any atomics.
  3. When is .monotonic ordering enough, and when do you need .release/.acquire?
    Answer.monotonic suffices when the atomic itself is the only shared data (a counter). When the atomic announces other data ("buffer ready", "stop"), the writer stores with .release and the reader loads with .acquire.
  4. Write the idiomatic mutex pair in 0.16.
    Answermutex.lockUncancelable(io); defer mutex.unlock(io); with var mutex: std.Io.Mutex = .init;. Note that std.Thread.Mutex is gone.
  5. Why must a function given to std.Thread.spawn receive a pointer to write its result, rather than returning it?
    AnswerA spawned function may only return void, !void, u8 or noreturn, and join does not hand the value back. Writing through a pointer to a slot the caller owns is how results come back, and join makes the write visible.
  6. What replaced std.Thread.Pool and WaitGroup?
    Answerstd.Io.Group: group.async(io, fn, args) per task and try group.await(io) to wait for all of them. The default Io.Threaded runs them on a thread pool.
  7. Give two reasons IRON LEDGER's simulation stays single-threaded.
    AnswerA day's work is far too small to benefit, and any second thread touching the RNG, the maps or the lists would destroy the determinism the golden-master test guards.
What you learned.
  • std.Thread.spawn(.{}, f, .{args}) starts a thread; t.join() waits and makes its writes visible. Arguments are copied; share by pointer.
  • Two threads writing one variable without synchronisation is a data race: undefined behaviour, not merely a wrong count.
  • Fix it by not sharing (one slot per thread), with std.atomic.Value(T) (load, store, fetchAdd, orderings .monotonic/.acquire/.release/.seq_cst), or with std.Io.Mutex and lockUncancelable/defer unlock.
  • std.Io.Group runs a batch of tasks on the I/O layer's thread pool; std.Thread.getCpuCount() sizes the batch. std.Thread.Mutex, Pool and WaitGroup are gone in 0.16.
  • Use threads for large, chunkable, CPU-bound work; prefer a process when nothing is shared; stay single-threaded when the work is small or must be deterministic.

37. Style, idioms and reading compile errors

In this chapter you will learn how Zig code is expected to look (the formatter, the naming rules, the order of things in a file, the idioms every library uses), and then spend most of the chapter on the skill that matters most day to day: reading what the compiler and the runtime tell you. Six real compile errors, a panic with a stack trace, an error return trace, and the three build modes that decide which checks stay on.

37.1 zig fmt

Zig has one formatting style and a tool that applies it. There is nothing to configure and no argument to have.

before.zig
const std=@import("std");
pub fn main( ) void{
std.debug.print("x\n",.{});}
$ zig fmt --check before.zig
before.zig
$ echo $status
1
$ zig fmt before.zig
before.zig
$ cat before.zig
const std = @import("std");
pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("x\n", .{});
}

zig fmt file.zig rewrites the file in place; zig fmt --check lists files that would change and exits non-zero, which is the form you put in a pre-commit hook or CI. Run it on a directory to format everything under it. The style is four-space indent, one statement per line, and a rule you will come to rely on: a trailing comma in any list (.{ a, b, }, struct fields, arguments) makes the formatter put one item per line; removing it makes the formatter put them on one line. That comma is the only formatting decision left to you, and it is a good one.

37.2 Names

The conventions are simple and the standard library follows them without exception, so your code will read as native if you do too.

ThingStyleExamples
Types (structs, enums, unions, and functions that return types)TitleCasePerson, PersonId, ArrayList, fn Stack(comptime T: type) type
Functions and methodscamelCasebaseSalary, advanceDay, readFileAlloc
Variables, constants, fields, parameters, enum tags, error names' fieldssnake_casehired_day, max_roster_size, .mekwarrior
Error valuesTitleCaseerror.UnknownPerson, error.OutOfMemory
Filessnake_case.zig, or TitleCase.zig when the file is a structfinance.zig, rng.zig; ArrayList.zig

A useful consequence: you can tell what an identifier is from its shape. Role.baseSalary is a function on a type; role.base_salary would be a field. Acronyms are treated as words: HqId, not HQID; parseJson, not parseJSON.

37.3 Doc comments and the order of a file

Two kinds of comment carry meaning for tools. //! at the top of a file documents the file itself (that is what every exercise header in this book is). /// immediately before a declaration documents that declaration, and zig build-exe -femit-docs or an editor will show it. Ordinary // comments are for humans reading the code right there.

s_style.zig
//! A file-level doc comment: what this file is for.
const std = @import("std");

/// Money in C-bills. Doc comments (three slashes) attach to the next declaration.
pub const CBills = i64;

/// A person's job.
pub const Role = enum {
    mekwarrior,
    tech,

    pub fn baseSalary(self: Role) CBills {
        return switch (self) {
            .mekwarrior => 1_500,
            .tech => 800,
        };
    }
};

pub const Roster = struct {
    people: std.ArrayList(Role) = .empty,

    const Self = @This();

    pub fn deinit(self: *Self, gpa: std.mem.Allocator) void {
        self.people.deinit(gpa);
    }

    pub fn add(self: *Self, gpa: std.mem.Allocator, role: Role) !void {
        try self.people.append(gpa, role);
    }

    pub fn payroll(self: Self) CBills {
        var total: CBills = 0;
        for (self.people.items) |r| total += r.baseSalary();
        return total;
    }
};

const max_roster_size = 12;

test "payroll" {
    var roster: Roster = .{};
    defer roster.deinit(std.testing.allocator);
    try roster.add(std.testing.allocator, .mekwarrior);
    try roster.add(std.testing.allocator, .tech);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(CBills, 2_300), roster.payroll());
    try std.testing.expect(roster.people.items.len <= max_roster_size);
}
$ zig test s_style.zig
All 1 tests passed.
$ zig fmt --check s_style.zig && echo clean
clean

The file also shows the conventional order, top to bottom: the file doc comment; imports; public types; the functions that belong to each type inside it; free functions; private constants near where they are used; tests at the bottom. Within a struct: fields first, then const Self = @This(); if the struct needs to name itself, then init/deinit, then the rest. None of this is enforced, but every file in the standard library follows it and readers expect it.

37.4 The idioms

You have met each of these in an earlier chapter; here they are together, as the checklist a reviewer would apply.

  • init and deinit. A type that owns resources has a function that creates it and a method that releases them, in that order and with those names. deinit takes *Self (it may need to mutate) and, for unmanaged containers, the allocator that was used.
  • The allocator is the first parameter. fn init(gpa: std.mem.Allocator, ...), list.append(gpa, item). Seeing an allocator in a signature is how you know a function may allocate; not seeing one is how you know it cannot.
  • .empty and .init as starting values. var list: std.ArrayList(T) = .empty;, var mutex: std.Io.Mutex = .init;. A declaration with a type and a leading-dot value, and no allocation until the first use.
  • Self. Inside a struct, const Self = @This(); so methods can say self: *Self and the struct can be renamed without touching every method.
  • defer right after acquire, errdefer for partial construction. The line that gets a resource is immediately followed by the line that gives it back (Chapter 17). errdefer undoes the steps already taken when a later step fails.
  • Errors are values; try is the default. Handle an error where you can do something about it; otherwise try and let the caller decide. Never catch unreachable to silence one.
  • Slices in, slices out. Functions take []const u8, not arrays or pointers to arrays; they return slices of memory the caller owns or was told about.
  • Prefer const. The compiler insists: a var that is never mutated is an error.
  • Pure core, I/O at the edges. Functions that compute take values and return values; the io and the allocator are handed in from main and stay near it. IRON LEDGER's simulation never sees an io.

37.5 Reading compile errors

Zig's compiler is strict, and a beginner's first hour is mostly spent being told no. That is the language doing its job: each of these errors is a bug in another language. Every message has the same anatomy: file:line:column: error: what, then the offending line with a caret under the exact spot, then zero or more note: lines that point at the other half of the story. Read the first error only; later ones are often consequences of it. Here are the six you will hit most.

1. Unused constant or variable.

const std = @import("std");
pub fn main() void {
    const unused = 5;
    std.debug.print("hi\n", .{});
}
$ zig run e1.zig
e1.zig:3:11: error: unused local constant
    const unused = 5;
          ^~~~~~

Zig refuses dead values because they are almost always a mistake (you meant to use it) or leftovers (delete it). If you genuinely need to discard something, say so: _ = unused;. The same rule applies to function parameters (_ = param;) and to a var that is never written, which gets its own message, local variable is never mutated, with the note consider using 'const'.

2. Shadowing.

const std = @import("std");
pub fn main() void {
    const count: u32 = 1;
    for (0..3) |count| {
        std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{count});
    }
}
$ zig run e2.zig
e2.zig:4:17: error: capture 'count' shadows local constant from outer scope
    for (0..3) |count| {
                ^~~~~
e2.zig:3:11: note: previous declaration here
    const count: u32 = 1;
          ^~~~~

In Zig a name means one thing within a function. The note tells you where the other count is; rename one of them. This also applies to a local that shadows a top-level declaration (naming a variable std, for instance).

3. Missing switch case.

const std = @import("std");
const Role = enum { mekwarrior, tech, medic };
fn salary(r: Role) i64 {
    return switch (r) {
        .mekwarrior => 1500,
        .tech => 800,
    };
}
pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{salary(.medic)});
}
$ zig run e3.zig
e3.zig:4:12: error: switch must handle all possibilities
    return switch (r) {
           ^~~~~~
e3.zig:2:39: note: unhandled enumeration value: 'medic'
const Role = enum { mekwarrior, tech, medic };
                                      ^~~~~
e3.zig:2:14: note: enum 'e3.Role' declared here

This is the error you want. Add a variant to an enum and the compiler lists every switch that needs a new arm. The fix is an arm for .medic, or, if you truly mean "everything else", an else arm (which silences future additions, so use it sparingly).

4. Type mismatch between branches.

const std = @import("std");
fn describe(funds: i64) i64 {
    const bonus: i64 = 100;
    return if (funds > 0) bonus else "broke";
}
pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{describe(5)});
}
$ zig run e4.zig
e4.zig:4:38: error: expected type 'i64', found '*const [5:0]u8'
    return if (funds > 0) bonus else "broke";
                                     ^~~~~~~

An if used as a value must produce one type from both branches ("peer type resolution"), and here the result is also being returned as i64. The message names the type it wanted and the type it found; *const [5:0]u8 is what a string literal is. When you see an unexpected type in one of these messages, the fix is usually to make both branches the same kind of thing, or to add @as(T, ...) to a literal so the compiler knows what you meant.

5. try in a function that cannot fail.

const std = @import("std");
fn parse(s: []const u8) i32 {
    const n = try std.fmt.parseInt(i32, s, 10);
    return n;
}
pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{parse("12")});
}
$ zig run e5.zig
e5.zig:3:15: error: expected type 'i32', found 'error{InvalidCharacter,Overflow}'
    const n = try std.fmt.parseInt(i32, s, 10);
              ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
e5.zig:2:25: note: function cannot return an error
fn parse(s: []const u8) i32 {
                        ^~~

The message looks like a type mismatch, and it is: try means "return the error to my caller", and this function's return type i32 has no room for an error. The note says it plainly. Change the return type to !i32, or handle the error right there with catch.

6. Integer overflow at compile time.

const std = @import("std");
pub fn main() void {
    const days: u8 = 200 + 100;
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{days});
}
$ zig run e6.zig
e6.zig:3:26: error: type 'u8' cannot represent integer value '300'
    const days: u8 = 200 + 100;
                     ~~~~^~~~~

Both operands are known at compile time, so the sum is computed at compile time, and 300 does not fit in a u8. The compiler refuses rather than wrapping. Widen the type (u16) or reconsider the value. The same computation with runtime values produces the runtime panic in the next section.

37.6 Reading a panic and a stack trace

When a safety check fails at runtime, the program panics: it prints a message, a stack trace, and exits. Here is an index one past the end:

const std = @import("std");
pub fn main() void {
    const items = [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3 };
    var idx: usize = 2;
    idx += 1;
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{items[idx]});
}
$ zig run e9.zig
thread 5965804 panic: index out of bounds: index 3, len 3
/.../e9.zig:6:37: 0x102f7dcd3 in main (e9)
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{items[idx]});
                                    ^
/opt/homebrew/Cellar/zig/0.16.0_1/lib/zig/std/start.zig:698:59: 0x102f7dbb3 in callMain (e9)
    if (fn_info.params.len == 0) return wrapMain(root.main());
                                                          ^
???:?:?: 0x18a24c4e3 in start (/usr/lib/dyld)

Read it top down. The first line is the message, with the numbers you need (index 3, length 3). Then one frame per function on the call stack, innermost first: the panic happened at e9.zig:6:37 in main, which was called by callMain in the standard library's start code, which was called by the dynamic loader. The frames below your own file are scaffolding; the first frame in a file you wrote is where to look, and the caret is under the exact expression. The other messages of this family are integer overflow, attempt to unwrap null (using .? on a null optional), attempt to use null value, division by zero, reached unreachable code, and attempt to cast negative value to unsigned.

An error return trace looks similar but tells a different story: not where the program stopped, but the path an error travelled before nobody handled it.

const std = @import("std");
fn open(name: []const u8) !u32 {
    if (name.len == 0) return error.EmptyName;
    return 1;
}
fn load(name: []const u8) !u32 {
    const h = try open(name);
    return h * 2;
}
pub fn main() !void {
    const v = try load("");
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{v});
}
$ zig run e8.zig
error: EmptyName
/.../e8.zig:3:24: 0x10479199b in open (e8)
    if (name.len == 0) return error.EmptyName;
                       ^
/.../e8.zig:7:15: 0x104791a7f in load (e8)
    const h = try open(name);
              ^
/.../e8.zig:11:15: 0x104791bbf in main (e8)
    const v = try load("");
              ^

The error was created in open, passed through the try in load, passed through the try in main, and main returned it, so the runtime printed it. Each frame is a try or return error.X the error went through. This trace is unique to Zig and costs almost nothing in Debug builds; it is the reason "just try it" is good advice, because when the error finally surfaces you still know where it was born.

37.7 Panicking on purpose: @panic, assert, unreachable

Three tools let you say "this cannot happen", and they mean slightly different things.

@panic("message") stops the program with your message and a stack trace. Use it for a situation the program cannot continue from and that is not the caller's fault to handle: a corrupted data file, an impossible state.

const std = @import("std");

fn withdraw(funds: i64, amount: i64) i64 {
    if (amount > funds) @panic("withdraw: insufficient funds");
    return funds - amount;
}

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{withdraw(100, 30)});
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{withdraw(100, 300)});
}
$ zig run s_panic.zig
70
thread 5998933 panic: withdraw: insufficient funds
/.../s_panic.zig:4:25: 0x102572faf in withdraw (s_panic)
    if (amount > funds) @panic("withdraw: insufficient funds");
                        ^
/.../s_panic.zig:10:40: 0x102571c67 in main (s_panic)

(In real code this particular case should be an error, error.InsufficientFunds, because the caller can do something about it. A panic is for when nobody can.)

std.debug.assert(condition) documents a promise the caller must keep. If the condition is false, it panics with reached unreachable code and a trace pointing at the assert. The point is the documentation: an assert at the top of a function is a precondition anyone can read. IRON LEDGER's daysInMonth could assert month >= 1 and month <= 12.

unreachable is an expression that says "control never gets here". You have seen it as the else arm of a switch over values the type system does not exclude:

const std = @import("std");

fn dayName(d: u8) []const u8 {
    return switch (d) {
        0 => "Mon", 1 => "Tue", 2 => "Wed", 3 => "Thu", 4 => "Fri", 5 => "Sat", 6 => "Sun",
        else => unreachable,
    };
}

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{dayName(2)});
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{dayName(9)});
}
$ zig run s_unreachable.zig
Wed
thread 5998793 panic: reached unreachable code
/.../s_unreachable.zig:6:17: 0x1009222ef in dayName (s_unreachable)
        else => unreachable,
                ^

The rule for choosing: if the bad input can come from the outside world (a user, a file, the network), it is an error and the caller handles it. If it can only come from a bug in your own program, it is an assert or unreachable, and you want the loudest possible failure as close to the bug as possible. Exercise 37.3 practises the distinction.

37.8 Debug, ReleaseSafe, ReleaseFast

Every panic in this chapter came from a safety check the compiler inserted: bounds checks on indexing, overflow checks on arithmetic, null checks on .?, and the check that unreachable really is. Whether those checks exist depends on the build mode.

ModeSafety checksOptimisationUse it for
Debug (default)onnonedevelopment, tests, this whole book
ReleaseSafeonfullshipping software; fast and still panics instead of corrupting
ReleaseFastofffullbenchmarks, code you have tested to exhaustion
ReleaseSmallofffor sizeembedded targets, tiny binaries

The same out-of-bounds program under each mode:

$ zig run e9.zig
thread 5965804 panic: index out of bounds: index 3, len 3
...
$ zig run -O ReleaseSafe e9.zig
thread 5969181 panic: index out of bounds: index 3, len 3
...
$ zig run -O ReleaseFast e9.zig
0

ReleaseFast printed 0: it read whatever byte happened to follow the array. No message, no trace, no guarantee it will do the same tomorrow. That is undefined behaviour, and it is why the default for anything you ship should be ReleaseSafe. Likewise unreachable in ReleaseFast is a promise to the optimiser, which will happily delete the branch and any code it can prove leads there.

To build a standalone executable rather than run one: zig build-exe -O ReleaseFast e7.zig writes e7 next to the source. In a build.zig project the same choice is zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe (Chapter 31). You can also change safety for one block with @setRuntimeSafety(false), which is the right granularity for the rare inner loop that needs it.

In IRON LEDGER. The whole repository is zig fmt clean, and its file layout is 37.3 at scale: src/domain/types.zig begins with a //! comment, then pub const CBills = i64;, then typed IDs, then enums with their methods, then tests. The naming table is visible in one line from src/domain/person.zig: types.applyBp(self.role.baseSalary(), self.experience().salaryMultBp()), three camelCase methods on TitleCase types returning a snake_case-typed Bp. The game's Date.daysInMonth uses else => unreachable exactly as in 37.7, and its commands.zig has an Error set of a dozen names (UnknownPerson, NotACompany, CompanyDeployed) for everything a player could ask for and be refused. One project story from the original guide is worth keeping: a column binding was once lost when the formatter reflowed a long argument list and an edit missed the new shape. The round-trip test caught it. Formatting is not cosmetic; a diff you can read is a bug you can see.

Exercises

Exercise 37.1 · Fix six errors warm-up

The starter contains all six errors from 37.5. Run it, read the first error, fix it, run again, until it prints the five expected lines. Name the file: exercises/37-style/ex1_fix_errors.zig.

Solution 
//! Chapter 37, exercise 1: fix six compile errors.
//! Run with:  zig run ex1_fix_errors.zig
//! Goal: the starter has six errors (unused constant, shadowing, missing
//! switch case, type mismatch, try in a non-error function, comptime
//! overflow). Fix them one at a time, re-running after each. Expected
//! output:
//!   mekwarrior earns 1500
//!   tech earns 800
//!   medic earns 400
//!   parsed 42
//!   days in the year: 365

const std = @import("std");

const Role = enum { mekwarrior, tech, medic };

fn salary(r: Role) i64 {
    return switch (r) {
        .mekwarrior => 1500,
        .tech => 800,
        .medic => 400, // was missing: "switch must handle all possibilities"
    };
}

// was `fn parse(s: []const u8) i32`: try needs an error-union return type
fn parse(s: []const u8) !i32 {
    return try std.fmt.parseInt(i32, s, 10);
}

fn label(funds: i64) []const u8 {
