Notice what the second session shows: the file saved by the first session loads, the log line from day 15 is still there, the events continue from the saved random state, and an unknown verb is an error message rather than a crash. When you get this output from your own file, you have built the thing.

38.8 What you built, and what the game adds

Line up the two programs and the correspondence is one to one. Your Company is the game's GameState: one arena, one dice bag, ordered collections, a clock, a ledger. Your execute is theirs. Your advanceDay with two phases is theirs with fifteen. Your text save file is their SQLite database (forty tables instead of six record kinds, and migrations, but the same delete-and-reinsert-then-hash-must-match idea). Your parseLine is src/sim/cli.zig; your main loop is the non-TUI branch of src/main.zig. Your golden master is theirs.

What the game adds is width, not new shapes: more types (units, forces, contracts, HQs, each with a typed ID), ZON data files for the rule tables (Chapter 28), a query layer that computes screens from state without mutating it, a battle resolver, and a terminal client. Each of those is a chapter in Part 5. You already know how to read them.

In IRON LEDGER. The file to open next to your stage 6 is src/sim/commands.zig. Its Command union starts with the same three variants you wrote (advance_day, advance_days: u32, hire: struct { first, last, role }, fire: types.PersonId), its Error set begins with UnknownPerson, and its execute is a switch (cmd) whose .hire arm is const id = try gs.hirePerson(h.first, h.last, h.role); return .{ .hired = id };. The test at the bottom is your golden master with the game's script: three hires, 45 days, a firing, 45 more days, two hashes, expectEqual. The pure-core rule is enforced by a parameter that is not there: execute takes *GameState and a Command, and nothing in src/sim/ ever receives an io.

Exercises

The six stages are the exercises of this chapter. Each starter in exercises/38-capstone/ contains the tests and the type skeletons with // TODO bodies; the solutions are the complete files shown above. Work them in order.

Exercise 38.5 · Stage 5, events and the golden master challenge

Exercise 38.6 · Stage 6, the REPL with save and load challenge

Add ReplCommand, parseLine, save, load and main. The header comment shows how to pipe a script into it. Then extend it: add a raise ID BP command that adjusts one person's pay through basis points, carrying it through the union, execute, the parser and the save format. Name the file: exercises/38-capstone/ex6_repl.zig.

Solution

See 38.7; complete file solutions/ex6_repl.zig (without the raise extension, which is yours). Adding a command touches four places, and the compiler will point at three of them; the save format is the fourth, and the round-trip test is what catches it.

Check your understanding

  1. Why is money an i64 and a percentage an integer number of basis points?
    AnswerFloats cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, so sums drift. Integer C-bills and integer basis points make every computation exact and identical on every machine, which the golden master depends on.
  2. What does the arena buy the Company, and what does it cost?
    AnswerOne deinit frees everything, there are no per-object destructors, and references between records (a transaction's note pointing at a name) are always valid. The cost is that memory only grows until the company is destroyed.
  3. Why is Command a tagged union rather than a set of methods the REPL calls directly?
    AnswerA union value is data: it can be put in an array (a script), replayed, logged, compared, and run by any front end through one execute. The golden-master test is a script of commands.
  4. State the invariant that postTransaction protects.
    Answerfunds == starting_funds + ledger.balance() at all times, because the balance and the ledger change only together, in that one function.
  5. Why does the company that starts on January 1st not pay on day 0?
    AnswerPayroll runs inside advanceDay after the clock moves, so the first check happens on day 1 (January 2nd). The test "31 days crosses exactly one payday" pins this down.
  6. What kinds of bug does the golden-master test catch, and what does it not catch?
    AnswerIt catches any source of non-determinism: real-clock reads, OS-seeded randomness, unordered iteration, races, uninitialised memory. It does not catch wrong rules that are wrong deterministically; those need the ordinary unit tests.
  7. Why is the random stream state saved to the file?
    AnswerSo that a loaded company continues exactly as the unsaved one would have. Re-seeding from the seed alone would restart the sequence from day 0's position.
  8. Which parts of stage 6 receive an io, and which must never?
    Answermain, save and load take io. Nothing above the "pure core" line does: Company, execute, advanceDay and runEvents cannot touch the outside world because the parameter is not there.
What you learned.
  • Start a program with its vocabulary types, tested alone: integer money, basis points, typed IDs, enums with methods.
  • A state struct owns its memory through one arena; init/deinit/allocator(); copy every string you keep.
  • Commands are a tagged union and execute is the single entry point returning a Result or a named error.
  • Money moves through one function that writes the ledger and the balance together; the invariant is a test.
  • Time moves in advanceDay, a fixed sequence of phases; the calendar is a struct beside an integer day counter.
  • Randomness comes from a seeded, named-stream generator owned by the state; a hash and a golden-master test guard determinism.
  • Parsing, printing, saving and loading live at the edge, hold the io, and turn every failure into a message. Save the RNG state and prove round-trips with a hash.
  • This is IRON LEDGER's architecture at one-sixtieth scale; Part 5 reads the full-size version.

39. The architecture in one picture

In this chapter you meet IRON LEDGER as a whole before you read any of its parts. You will learn the one rule the entire program is built around, see how the source tree enforces that rule, and learn the two doors through which every other part of the program talks to the simulation. By the end you will know where to look for anything.

What you need from earlier chapters. This chapter leans on Chapter 30 (files, imports and modules: every Zig file is a struct, and a module has one root file), Chapter 31 (the build system: addModule, addExecutable, root_module, build options), and Chapter 33 (the std.Io value that all real-world I/O needs in 0.16). If b.addAnonymousImport or init.io look unfamiliar, skim those chapters first. Everything else here is prose and a map.

39.1 What you are about to read

IRON LEDGER is a single-player BattleTech mercenary-company simulator. You are the commander of an outfit, not a pilot: every screen is a roster, a ledger, a map or a report, and battles are resolved by the simulation from the state you prepared beforehand (training, maintenance, supply, morale). The whole thing is about 31,500 lines of Zig 0.16 with no libraries beyond the system's SQLite. It was built in stages over a few weeks by one person and a coding assistant, and its history is visible in the comments: many of them say which stage introduced a rule and why.

That size is the point of Part 5. A 200-line example program cannot show you how a language feels at scale; a 31,000-line one can. Every chapter from here to the end takes one slice of the program, shows you the real code, tells you which functions to open and in what order, and gives you exercises that you carry out inside the repository with the compiler and the test suite as your safety net.

Before you start, run the suite once in a copy of the game so that you know what green looks like:

$ cp -r game /tmp/il && cd /tmp/il
$ zig build test --summary all
Build Summary: 10/10 steps succeeded; 246/247 tests passed (1 skipped)

Work in the copy. The exercises in Part 5 ask you to change the game, and a copy lets you experiment without fear. (The original guide this Part is adapted from was written at an earlier commit with 224 tests; the count has since grown, and a few numbers in the guide's prose have drifted. This book was checked against the source as it stands today, commit 8958001.)

39.2 The source tree

Here is the whole repository at the directory level, with the one distinction that matters marked on the right:

src/
├── domain/     entities and rule tables: person, unit, chassis, contract, hq, tuning …   (pure)
├── sim/        state, the daily tick, commands, queries, battle, medical, personnel …    (pure)
├── econ/       finance, markets, logistics                                               (pure)
├── gen/        company and person generators                                             (pure)
├── persist/    sqlite.zig (C binding) and store.zig (save/load, migrations)              (I/O)
├── tui/        term.zig, screen.zig, app.zig, emblem.zig, png.zig, music.zig, splash.zig, paths.zig  (I/O)
├── root.zig    the `game` module: re-exports everything above except tui/
└── main.zig    the executable: flags, the REPL, the demo, and the hand-off to tui/app.zig
data/
├── chassis.zon  planets.zon  parts.zon
└── tables/      tuning.zon meklab.zon names.zon ranks.zon awards.zon abilities.zon
                 rat.zon factions.zon scenarios.zon terrain.zon difficulty.zon

Four directories are marked pure. That word has a precise meaning here, stated in the game's ARCHITECTURE.md and repeated in CLAUDE.md as a hard rule:

Sim core (src/domain, src/sim, src/econ, src/gen) is pure and deterministic: no I/O, no wall clock, no global mutable state.

Given the same starting seed and the same sequence of player commands, two runs of the simulation produce byte-for-byte identical state. Everything else in the program's design is a consequence of wanting that to be true and wanting it to stay true as the code grows. Keep the rule in mind as you read; each of the next chapters will show you one thing it forces.

39.3 How a directory becomes a promise

A rule in a document is only a wish. What makes this one hold is the module layout in build.zig. Chapter 31 taught you that a Zig program is one or more modules, each a tree of files with a single root. IRON LEDGER has two:

build.zig (trimmed; the real file is heavily commented)
const mod = b.addModule("game", .{
    .root_source_file = b.path("src/root.zig"),
    .target = target,
});
// … the .zon data files are attached to `mod` here (Chapter 40) …
mod.link_libc = true;
mod.linkSystemLibrary("sqlite3", .{});

const exe = b.addExecutable(.{
    .name = "game",
    .root_module = b.createModule(.{
        .root_source_file = b.path("src/main.zig"),
        .target = target,
        .optimize = optimize,
        .imports = &.{
            .{ .name = "game", .module = mod },
        },
    }),
});
b.installArtifact(exe);

The library module game is rooted at src/root.zig, and the executable is rooted at src/main.zig, which imports the library by the name given in the .imports list. Now look at what root.zig re-exports:

src/root.zig (the shape; some lines omitted)
//! Module root for the simulation core. See ARCHITECTURE.md.
//! The core is pure and deterministic: no I/O, no wall clock, no globals.

const std = @import("std");

// domain/ — entities
pub const types = @import("domain/types.zig");
pub const person = @import("domain/person.zig");
pub const unit = @import("domain/unit.zig");
pub const chassis = @import("domain/chassis.zig");
pub const tuning = @import("domain/tuning.zig");
// … fifteen more domain files …

// sim/ — state, time, randomness, events, battle resolution
pub const state = @import("sim/state.zig");
pub const tick = @import("sim/tick.zig");
pub const commands = @import("sim/commands.zig");
pub const queries = @import("sim/queries.zig");
pub const cli = @import("sim/cli.zig");
// …

// persist/ — SQLite save files (Stage 11)
pub const sqlite = @import("persist/sqlite.zig");
pub const store = @import("persist/store.zig");

// econ/, gen/ …

test {
    std.testing.refAllDecls(@This());
}

There is no tui line. The terminal client lives outside the game module entirely; it is part of the executable's module, reached from main.zig with @import("tui/app.zig"). That means the simulation cannot import the client even by accident, because the file is not in its module. The dependency points one way.

The purity rule has a second, quieter enforcement that Chapter 33 prepared you for. In Zig 0.16, anything that touches the outside world needs an std.Io value: opening a file, reading the clock, spawning a process. The executable receives one in main and hands it to the client and to the save store. It never hands one to the simulation. A function in src/sim that wanted to read the time would have no io to read it with. As the original guide put it: purity is not a promise in a comment; it is a parameter that is not there.

Try it. In your copy of the game, run 
$ grep -rlE 'std\.Io|std\.posix|std\.fs\.|Clock\.now|std\.time' src/sim src/domain src/econ src/gen
It prints nothing. Now run the same search over src/tui src/persist src/main.zig and you get eight files. That is the boundary, visible from the shell.

One exception is worth knowing about now so it does not surprise you later: persist/ is inside the game module (so tests can round-trip a campaign through SQLite), but it does I/O. It talks to the C library directly rather than through std.Io, which is why the grep above does not flag it. The store is not part of the simulation; it reads a GameState and writes one, and nothing in sim/ imports it.

39.4 The picture

ARCHITECTURE.md draws the layers like this:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Frontends: CLI (REPL, demo) and the terminal client │
└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                       │ Commands in / Queries out
┌──────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────┐
│  Simulation core (pure, deterministic)              │
│   sim/    clock, daily pipeline, events, autoresolve│
│   domain/ person, unit, part, force, contract, hq   │
│   econ/   finance, markets, logistics network       │
│   gen/    company/person/name generation            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  data/   static game data loaded from .zon files    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  persist/  SQLite save files, schema migrations     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Read the arrow in the middle carefully, because it names the two doors. A frontend changes the simulation by building a Command value (a tagged union, Chapter 14) and passing it to commands.execute. A frontend reads the simulation by calling a function in queries.zig, which returns plain data: formatted strings plus the IDs a key handler will need. There is a third, smaller door shared by both frontends: cli.parseCommand turns a typed line of text into a Command, so a verb added for the REPL works in the terminal client's : line for free.

Here is that hand-off in the executable's main, which is the only place in the program that sees all three layers at once:

src/main.zig
pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var gs = game.state.GameState.init(init.gpa, .{ .seed = 3025 });
    defer gs.deinit();

    var args = std.process.Args.Iterator.init(init.minimal.args);
    _ = args.next(); // exe name
    var repl = false;
    var tui = false;
    var ascii = false;
    var no_splash = false;
    var no_music = false;
    var data_dir: ?[]const u8 = null;
    var store_arg: ?[:0]const u8 = null;
    while (args.next()) |arg| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "--repl")) repl = true;
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "--tui")) tui = true;
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "--ascii")) ascii = true;
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "--no-splash")) no_splash = true;
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "--no-music")) no_music = true;
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "--store")) store_arg = args.next() orelse store_arg;
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "--data")) data_dir = args.next() orelse data_dir;
    }

    // Without --store the save lives beside the binary in a source tree and
    // in the per-user data directory for an installed copy (tui/paths.zig).
    const store_path = store_arg orelse
        try paths.defaultStore(init.io, init.arena.allocator(), init.environ_map);

    if (tui) {
        try @import("tui/app.zig").run(init.io, init.gpa, init.environ_map, store_path,
            .{ .ascii = ascii, .no_splash = no_splash, .no_music = no_music, .data_dir = data_dir });
    } else if (repl) {
        try runRepl(&gs, init.io, init.gpa, store_path);
    } else {
        try runDemo(&gs);
    }
}

Compare this with the main you wrote in Chapter 32: the same std.process.Init, the same argument iterator, the same pattern of flags. What is new is only the scale of what it hands off to. Notice also where init.io goes: into the client and the REPL, both of which need files and a terminal, and not into GameState.init, which gets an allocator and a seed.

39.5 Four consequences of the one rule

Each of the next chapters is, at bottom, a study of one thing the purity rule forces. Here they are in one place so you can see the shape of Part 5:

  • Randomness is a value inside the state. There is no global random generator. GameState carries a bag of seeded generators, one per subsystem, and every dice roll names the stream it draws from. Chapter 41.
  • Time is an integer. The campaign clock is day_index: u32, days since the campaign began. The calendar date exists too, but only so it can be printed and so that "the first of the month" is easy to detect. Nobody reads a wall clock. Chapter 43.
  • Money is an integer. Every amount is a 64-bit count of C-bills, every multiplier is basis points, and there is not one floating-point number in the rules. Two machines produce the same balance to the C-bill. Chapter 45.
  • The state is one tree with one owner. A single arena allocator owns every allocation a campaign makes and frees them all in one call, so the domain code has no destructors and no use-after-free. Chapter 41.

The payoff for all of it is a single test in Chapter 49: two campaigns, same seed, same script, must hash identically. It is cheap, it runs on every build, and it catches a whole class of bugs (an unordered hash map iteration, a stray PRNG, a wall-clock read) that would otherwise surface as "saved games replay differently after an update".

39.6 A note on reading large code

You will not read all 31,000 lines and you should not try. The files are long because the game is detailed, not because the code is dense: queries.zig is four thousand lines mostly because there are many screens, each of which formats many columns. The skill to practise in Part 5 is navigating: opening a file, finding the top-level declarations with a search for pub fn or pub const, reading one function end to end, and following one call into another file when you need to.

Two habits help. First, every file opens with a //! comment saying what it is and, by house rule, which MekHQ class it mirrors; read that before anything else. Second, the test blocks at the bottom of each file are the best documentation of what the code is for; a test named "tier upgrade: refusals keep the money" tells you the rule and the bug it once had in one line.

Guided reading

Open these in order. Each is short; the whole list is twenty minutes.

  1. ARCHITECTURE.md, sections 1 and 4 only (the design pillars and the layer diagram). Note the phrase "pure and deterministic" and the list of player actions as commands.
  2. CLAUDE.md, the "Hard rules" list. These are the rules the exercises in Part 5 will ask you to respect; most of them will make more sense after the chapter that covers them.
  3. build.zig, skipping the long comments on first read. Find addModule("game", the data_files table, linkSystemLibrary("sqlite3", and the test step. Notice that the test step also depends on the install step: a green test run means the client compiled too, and the comment above it records the day that stopped being true by accident.
  4. src/root.zig, top to bottom. Count the re-exports (there are more than forty) and confirm that none of them mentions tui. Read the small dataProvenance function in the middle: it is the first real function of the codebase you meet, and it uses only things you learned in Chapter 21 and Chapter 23.
  5. src/main.zig, the main function and the small test block above it that pulls the tui/ files into the executable's test build. Skim runDemo to see what a scripted campaign looks like: it is nothing but execute calls and prints.

Exercises

Exercise 39.1 · Prove the boundary from the shell warm-up

Without reading any code, use grep to find every file in src/ that mentions std.Io or std.posix, and every file that mentions commands.execute. From the two lists, write one sentence describing which directories do I/O and which directories may change the simulation.

Solution 
$ grep -rlE 'std\.Io|std\.posix' src
src/tui/emblem.zig
src/tui/term.zig
src/tui/music.zig
src/tui/app.zig
src/tui/paths.zig
src/tui/png.zig
src/tui/screen.zig
src/main.zig
$ grep -rl 'commands.execute' src
src/main.zig
src/tui/app.zig
src/persist/store.zig
src/sim/commands.zig
src/sim/queries.zig
src/sim/…  (a handful of sim files, all inside test blocks)

I/O happens only in src/tui and src/main.zig (plus the C calls in src/persist, which are not std.Io). Outside of tests, the simulation is changed only from main.zig and tui/app.zig, and always through commands.execute. Nearly every hit in src/sim and src/persist is inside a test block driving a small campaign, or in a helper those tests share.

Exercise 39.2 · A test that guards the boundary practice

Add a test at the bottom of src/root.zig that uses reflection (Chapter 27) to check two things: the module root has at least forty public declarations, and it has no declaration named tui. Run zig build test.

Solution 
test "the module root re-exports at least forty namespaces" {
    const decls = @typeInfo(@This()).@"struct".decls;
    try std.testing.expect(decls.len >= 40);
    // The client is not one of them: the core cannot reach the terminal.
    try std.testing.expect(!@hasDecl(@This(), "tui"));
}

@This() is the struct that is root.zig itself (every file is a struct, Chapter 30). @typeInfo(...).@"struct".decls lists its public declarations at compile time, so decls.len is a constant. @hasDecl is the direct way to ask about one name. If someone later adds pub const tui = @import("tui/app.zig"); to the root, this test fails and names the reason.

Exercise 39.3 · Trace one command from the shell to the state practice

Starting from runDemo in src/main.zig, follow the very first execute call (.create_commander) as far as you can into the simulation using only "find the definition" jumps. List the files you pass through, in order, and stop when you reach the function that actually creates the commander.

Solution
  1. src/main.zig: runDemo calls game.commands.execute(gs, .{ .create_commander = … }).
  2. src/sim/commands.zig: execute switches on the union; the .create_commander arm refuses a start year outside 3000 to 3060 (Error.BadYear), sets the calendar year, calls gs.createCommander(c.name, c.origin, c.profession), names the outfit after the commander if it still has the placeholder name, and opens the markets.
  3. src/sim/state.zig: GameState.createCommander refuses a second commander, picks the home world with planet_mod.weightedPickByFaction(&self.rng, origin.key()) (a dice roll from the state's own generator bag, Chapter 41), builds a regional HQ with eight starter facilities, recruits its back-office staff with recruitGenerated, and hands it founding capital through transferFunds.
  4. Along the way it reaches into src/domain/commander.zig (the Faction and Profession enums), src/domain/planet.zig (the star map) and src/domain/hq.zig (the HQ struct and its facilities).

The point of the exercise is the shape of the path: an executable file, then the one execute switch, then a method on GameState, then the domain. You will see that same shape for every command in Chapter 42.

Check your understanding

  1. Name the two modules in build.zig and the root file of each.
    AnswerThe library module game, rooted at src/root.zig, and the executable's module, rooted at src/main.zig, which imports game by name.
  2. Why can code in src/sim not open a file, even if a programmer tried?
    AnswerOpening a file in 0.16 requires an std.Io value. main passes init.io only to the client and the REPL; no function in the simulation core receives one, so there is nothing to call openFile with.
  3. What are the two doors between a frontend and the simulation?
    Answercommands.execute(gs, cmd) to change state, and the functions in queries.zig to read it as formatted rows plus IDs. (cli.parseCommand is a helper that produces commands from text; it does not touch state.)
  4. Where does the terminal client live, and why is that placement significant?
    AnswerIn src/tui/, which is not re-exported by root.zig; it belongs to the executable's module. The simulation therefore cannot import it, so the dependency can only point from client to core.
  5. List the four consequences of the determinism rule that later chapters cover.
    AnswerRandomness lives inside the state as named streams; time is an integer day counter; money is integer C-bills with basis-point multipliers; the state is one tree owned by one arena.
  6. Which test summarises the whole architecture, and what does it assert?
    AnswerThe golden-master test in commands.zig: two campaigns with the same seed and the same command script must produce the same gs.hash().
What you learned.
  • IRON LEDGER is organised around one rule: the simulation core is a pure, deterministic function of its seed and its command history.
  • The rule is enforced by the module layout (tui/ is outside the game module) and by the absence of an std.Io parameter anywhere in the core.
  • Frontends change state only through commands.execute and read it only through queries.*; cli.parseCommand is shared by both frontends.
  • Randomness, time, money and memory ownership are each shaped by the rule; the golden-master test guards it.
  • Read large code by navigating, not by scanning: file header comments and test names tell you what things are for.

40. Data: ZON files become typed tables

In this chapter you see how IRON LEDGER keeps its numbers out of its code. Every balance constant, every mek design and every planet lives in a .zon file that the compiler type-checks against a Zig struct at build time. You will read the mechanism end to end, from build.zig to a rules formula, break it on purpose to see what the compiler says, and add a knob of your own.

What you need from earlier chapters. Chapter 28 (ZON: a struct literal in a file, imported with @import and given a type by the declaration that receives it), Chapter 31 (build options with b.option, and addAnonymousImport), Chapter 12 (struct fields with and without defaults), and Chapter 27 for the last section, where a test walks a struct's fields with @typeInfo and inline for. Chapter 15's ?*const T return type appears in the catalogue lookup.

40.1 The problem the data layer solves

A management game is mostly numbers: what a mekwarrior is paid, how far an HQ's influence reaches, how many days paperwork takes, how likely a rare part is to appear on a market. The first version of IRON LEDGER had these as constants scattered through the code with // TUNE comments. That is fine for a prototype and bad for a game, because balancing means changing the numbers often and a modder cannot change them at all.

The obvious fix in most languages is a config file parsed at start-up: JSON, TOML, whatever. That buys flexibility and costs safety. A misspelled key becomes a default silently; a string where a number belongs becomes a crash on turn 40. Zig offers a third option that Chapter 28 introduced: a data file in the language's own literal syntax, imported at compile time, type-checked against a struct. IRON LEDGER uses it for all fourteen of its tables. The rule in CLAUDE.md is blunt: static game data belongs in data/*.zon, not hardcoded.

40.2 One knob, end to end

Take one number and follow it. Here is the top of the tuning table:

data/tables/tuning.zon
// Tuning knobs (Stage 12.17). Typed against domain/tuning.zig `Tuning` at
// comptime. Money in C-bills, multipliers in basis points (10_000 = ×1).
// The formulas live beside their subsystems; this file only holds the
// numbers they were built on, so play-testing edits land here.
.{
    .hq = .{
        .influence_ly = .{ .field = 15, .regional = 60, .brigade = 90 }, // ARCH §9.2
        .influence_per_comms_ly = 10,
        .influence_per_spaceport_ly = 5,
        .paperwork_base_days = 21,
        .paperwork_min_days = 5,
        .paperwork_days_per_admin_level = 3,
        .upgrade_cost_per_level = .{ .mek_bay = 800_000, .warehouse = 400_000, .hospital = 500_000,
            .mess = 150_000, .training_ground = 300_000, .hiring_hall = 200_000,
            .comms = 600_000, .spaceport = 1_200_000 },
        .warehouse_tons_per_level_sq = 200, // 200 / 800 / 1800 / 3200 / 5000
        .upkeep = .{ .field = 10_000, .regional = 25_000, .brigade = 60_000 },
        .founding_funds = 1_000_000,
        .found_field_hq_cost = 500_000,
        .sale_pct = 40,
    },
    .logistics = .{
        .ly_per_jump = 30,
        .recharge_days = 7,
        // …
    },
    // … network, market, person, medical, battle, rating, contract …
}

It is exactly the anonymous struct literal syntax you used for .{ .year = 3025 } in Chapter 12, with nothing around it. Comments are allowed. Underscores in numbers are allowed. Nested literals are allowed. What is not here is any hint of a type; the file does not know what it is describing.

The type is on the Zig side:

src/domain/tuning.zig
//! Tuning tables: every balance constant the sim reads, loaded at comptime
//! from data/tables/tuning.zon (Stage 12.17, closing the "// TUNE" debt).
//! Mirrors MekHQ `campaign/CampaignOptions` — knobs, not rules; the
//! formulas stay legible in the modules that use them. The ZON file is
//! type-checked against `Tuning` at compile time: a missing or misspelled
//! field is a build error, not a silent default.

const std = @import("std");
const types = @import("types.zig");

pub const Tuning = struct {
    hq: struct {
        influence_ly: struct { field: u32, regional: u32, brigade: u32 },
        influence_per_comms_ly: u32,
        influence_per_spaceport_ly: u32,
        paperwork_base_days: u32,
        paperwork_min_days: u32,
        paperwork_days_per_admin_level: u32,
        upgrade_cost_per_level: struct { mek_bay: types.CBills, warehouse: types.CBills, /* … */ },
        warehouse_tons_per_level_sq: u32,
        upkeep: struct { field: types.CBills, regional: types.CBills, brigade: types.CBills },
        founding_funds: types.CBills,
        found_field_hq_cost: types.CBills,
        sale_pct: u32,
    },
    logistics: struct {
        ly_per_jump: u32,
        recharge_days: u32,
        // …
    },
    // …
};

/// The live table.
pub const t: Tuning = @import("tuning_zon");

The last line is the whole mechanism. @import("tuning_zon") returns the file's value; declaring the constant as : Tuning forces the compiler to coerce that anonymous literal to the Tuning struct, field by field, at compile time. A field in the file that the struct does not have is an error. A field the struct has that the file lacks (and that has no default) is an error. A string where a u32 belongs is an error. And they are errors with line numbers in the .zon file, as you will see in a moment.

Then the rules code reads the value as a plain constant. Here is the founding-capital line from GameState.createCommander (Chapter 41), where tuning is @import("../domain/tuning.zig").t:

self.transferFunds(.outfit, .{ .hq = id }, tuning.hq.founding_funds, 0) catch {};

No lookup, no parsing, no getOrDefault. tuning.hq.founding_funds is an i64 known at compile time, so the optimiser treats it exactly like the literal 1_000_000 it replaced.

40.3 What the compiler says when you get it wrong

The claim "a wrong field is a build error" is easy to make and worth checking. In your copy of the game, misspell one field in the ZON file (fatigue_tired to fatigue_tierd, say) and build:

$ zig build test
data/tables/tuning.zon:108:26: error: unexpected field 'fatigue_tierd'
        .fatigue_tierd = 30,
                         ^~
src/domain/tuning.zig:398:31: note: imported here
pub const t: Tuning = @import("tuning_zon");
                              ^~~~~~~~~~~~

Now put a string where a number belongs (.paperwork_base_days = "21"):

data/tables/tuning.zon:10:32: error: expected type 'u32'
        .paperwork_base_days = "21",
                               ^~~~

Both point at the data file, both name the field, and neither lets the game build. Compare with what a runtime config parser would do with the same two mistakes: the first would probably be ignored, the second would crash the first time the value was used. That is the trade the ZON approach makes: the data is baked into the binary (you cannot edit it without rebuilding), and in exchange the binary can never disagree with it.

40.4 How the file gets its name

The string "tuning_zon" is not a path. It is a name that build.zig attaches to the module, and this indirection is what makes mod support cheap:

build.zig
const data_dir = b.option([]const u8, "data", "Directory overlaying data/*.zon and data/tables/*.zon (mod support)");
const DataFile = struct { import_name: []const u8, rel: []const u8 };
const data_files = [_]DataFile{
    .{ .import_name = "chassis_zon", .rel = "chassis.zon" },
    .{ .import_name = "planets_zon", .rel = "planets.zon" },
    .{ .import_name = "parts_zon", .rel = "parts.zon" },
    .{ .import_name = "tuning_zon", .rel = "tables/tuning.zon" },
    .{ .import_name = "meklab_zon", .rel = "tables/meklab.zon" },
    .{ .import_name = "names_zon", .rel = "tables/names.zon" },
    .{ .import_name = "ranks_zon", .rel = "tables/ranks.zon" },
    .{ .import_name = "awards_zon", .rel = "tables/awards.zon" },
    .{ .import_name = "abilities_zon", .rel = "tables/abilities.zon" },
    .{ .import_name = "rat_zon", .rel = "tables/rat.zon" },
    .{ .import_name = "factions_zon", .rel = "tables/factions.zon" },
    .{ .import_name = "scenarios_zon", .rel = "tables/scenarios.zon" },
    .{ .import_name = "terrain_zon", .rel = "tables/terrain.zon" },
    .{ .import_name = "difficulty_zon", .rel = "tables/difficulty.zon" },
};
var overlaid = std.ArrayList([]const u8).empty;
for (data_files) |f| {
    var path: std.Build.LazyPath = b.path(b.fmt("data/{s}", .{f.rel}));
    if (data_dir) |dir| {
        const candidate = b.pathJoin(&.{ dir, f.rel });
        const exists = if (std.fs.path.isAbsolute(candidate))
            std.Io.Dir.accessAbsolute(b.graph.io, candidate, .{})
        else
            b.build_root.handle.access(b.graph.io, candidate, .{});
        if (exists) |_| {
            path = if (std.fs.path.isAbsolute(candidate)) .{ .cwd_relative = candidate } else b.path(candidate);
            overlaid.append(b.allocator, f.rel) catch @panic("OOM");
        } else |_| {}
    }
    mod.addAnonymousImport(f.import_name, .{ .root_source_file = path });
}
// What the binary can say about its data (settings screen, REPL banner).
const build_options = b.addOptions();
build_options.addOption(?[]const u8, "data_dir", data_dir);
build_options.addOption([]const []const u8, "data_overlays", overlaid.items);
mod.addImport("build_options", build_options.createModule());

Read the loop slowly; it is ordinary Zig running inside the build script, which is itself an ordinary Zig program (Chapter 31). For each of the fourteen files it computes a path, defaulting to data/…. If the user passed -Ddata=mymod and a file exists at the same relative path under that directory, the path is swapped. Then addAnonymousImport binds the name to whichever path won. The simulation code says @import("tuning_zon") and never learns which file it got.

Two smaller things to notice. The build script itself uses the 0.16 I/O API (b.graph.io, std.Io.Dir.accessAbsolute) to test for the file, because the build runner is a real program with real I/O. And the last four lines create a second tiny module, build_options, whose contents are values computed here: the data directory and the list of files it overlaid. root.zig imports it as build_info and uses it in dataProvenance to print "mod mymod: 1 file overlaid (tables/tuning.zon)" on the settings screen. That is how a binary can say where its numbers came from.

Try it. Run zig build --help in the game directory and find the two lines 
  -Ddata=[string]              Directory overlaying data/*.zon and data/tables/*.zon (mod support)
  -Dbundle-music=[bool]        Copy data/music into the install prefix (large)
Zig generated that help text from the b.option calls; nobody wrote it twice.

40.5 A catalogue: rows with defaults

The tuning table is one big struct. The design catalogue is a slice of small ones, and it shows the other half of the idea: fields with defaults let a row leave out what does not apply to it.

src/domain/chassis.zig
pub const Chassis = struct {
    key: []const u8, // variant designation, e.g. "SHD-2H"
    name: []const u8, // "Shadow Hawk"
    tonnage: u8,
    bv: u16, // BV2 — autoresolve base strength (ARCH §7)
    cost: types.CBills,
    rarity: types.Rarity, // market appearance tier (ARCH §9.8)
    /// First year the design is in service (12C.16, MekHQ `introYear`);
    /// the market, RATs and salvage only field what exists in the campaign year.
    intro_year: u16 = 2400,
    kind: unit.UnitKind = .mek,
    // Construction facts (Stage 10 MekLab; meks only, defaults for others).
    walk_mp: u8 = 0,
    jump_mp: u8 = 0,
    heat_sinks: u8 = 10,
    armor_half_tons: u16 = 0,
    // Transport facts (Stage 12.15; dropships/jumpships only, TRO:3025).
    mek_bays: u8 = 0,
    asf_bays: u8 = 0,
    vehicle_bays: u8 = 0,
    cargo_tons: u32 = 0,
    collars: u8 = 0,
    loadout: []const LoadoutSlot,

    pub fn engineRating(self: *const Chassis) u32 {
        return @as(u32, self.tonnage) * self.walk_mp;
    }

    pub fn weightClass(self: *const Chassis) WeightClass {
        return switch (self.tonnage) {
            0...35 => .light,
            36...55 => .medium,
            56...75 => .heavy,
            else => .assault,
        };
    }
};

pub const catalog: []const Chassis = @import("chassis_zon");

pub fn find(key: []const u8) ?*const Chassis {
    for (catalog) |*c| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, c.key, key)) return c;
    }
    return null;
}

Six fields have no default and must be present in every row: key, name, tonnage, bv, cost, rarity, plus the loadout slice. Everything else may be omitted, so a vehicle row need not state jump_mp and a mek row need not state collars. Here is one of the 97 rows:

data/chassis.zon (one row)
.{ .key = "SHD-2H", .name = "Shadow Hawk", .tonnage = 55, .bv = 1064, .cost = 4_672_315,
   .rarity = .common, .walk_mp = 5, .jump_mp = 3, .heat_sinks = 12, .armor_half_tons = 19,
   .loadout = .{
    .{ .slot = "lt.ac5.1", .part = "ac5", .class = .weapon },
    .{ .slot = "rt.lrm5.1", .part = "lrm5", .class = .weapon },
    .{ .slot = "ra.mlas.1", .part = "mlas", .class = .weapon },
    .{ .slot = "hd.srm2.1", .part = "srm2", .class = .weapon },
    .{ .slot = "lt.ammo_ac5.1", .part = "ammo_ac5", .class = .ammo },
    .{ .slot = "rt.ammo_lrm.1", .part = "ammo_lrm", .class = .ammo },
    .{ .slot = "ct.ammo_srm.1", .part = "ammo_srm", .class = .ammo },
} },

Note .rarity = .common and .class = .weapon: enum literals in a data file. The compiler resolves them against types.Rarity and unit.SlotClass because the struct says those are the field types, so a typo like .commom is a build error too. (If you compare this row with the original guide, the cost has changed; the catalogue was re-priced from the sourcebooks after the guide was written. The data moved and the code did not need to.)

The lookup function find is the pattern from Chapter 15: it returns ?*const Chassis, a maybe-pointer into the constant table, and null for an unknown key. Callers write chassis.find(u.chassis_key) orelse … or if (chassis.find(key)) |c| …. There is no error type because "not in the catalogue" is an ordinary outcome, not a failure.

40.6 What the type system cannot check, tests do

The compiler checks shape: fields, types, enum names. It cannot check meaning: that the part key "ac5" in a loadout exists in the parts catalogue, that every entry in a house's random assignment table names a mek of the stated weight class, or that a design's tonnage adds up under the construction rules. Those are cross-file facts, and the game checks them with tests that run against the data:

src/domain/part.zig
test "every chassis loadout part resolves in the part catalog" {
    const chassis = @import("chassis.zig");
    for (chassis.catalog) |c| {
        for (c.loadout) |slot| {
            try std.testing.expect(find(slot.part) != null);
        }
    }
    for (component_keys) |k| try std.testing.expect(find(k) != null); // the fabrication guarantee
}
src/domain/rat.zig
test "every RAT entry names a catalogue mek of the right class; every house has all four classes" {
    try std.testing.expect(table.len >= 6);
    for (table) |row| {
        inline for (.{ chassis.WeightClass.light, .medium, .heavy, .assault }) |class| {
            const pool = row.pool(class);
            try std.testing.expect(pool.len > 0);
            for (pool) |key| {
                const c = chassis.find(key) orelse {
                    std.debug.print("RAT {s}: unknown design {s}\n", .{ row.faction, key });
                    return error.TestUnexpectedResult;
                };
                try std.testing.expect(c.kind == .mek);
                if (c.weightClass() != class) {
                    std.debug.print("RAT {s}: {s} is {s}, listed as {s}\n", .{ row.faction, key, @tagName(c.weightClass()), @tagName(class) });
                    return error.TestUnexpectedResult;
                }
            }
        }
    }
    // …
}

Two habits from Chapter 8 appear here. A test that loops over data prints which row failed before returning error.TestUnexpectedResult, because "expect failed" on its own would send you hunting through 97 rows. And the loops are cheap: the whole catalogue is a compile-time constant, so these tests cost microseconds and nobody is tempted to skip them.

This is why docs/modding.md tells a modder to run zig build test -Ddata=mymod rather than just zig build. The build proves the mod has the right shape; the tests prove its rows refer to each other correctly. In the exercises you will see that the tuning table has an even stronger check: a test that visits every field, however deeply nested, without naming any of them.

40.7 The tuning sanity test

You met this function in Chapter 27 as an example of reflection. Now read it as its authors use it:

src/domain/tuning.zig
fn checkPositive(comptime T: type, value: T, comptime name: []const u8) !void {
    switch (@typeInfo(T)) {
        .int => |info| {
            // Signed knobs (deltas, scores) may be zero or negative by design.
            if (info.signedness == .signed) return;
            if (value <= 0) {
                std.debug.print("tuning field {s} must be positive\n", .{name});
                return error.BadTuning;
            }
            if (std.mem.endsWith(u8, name, "_bp") and value > 100_000) {
                std.debug.print("tuning field {s} is over 100000 basis points\n", .{name});
                return error.BadTuning;
            }
        },
        .@"struct" => |info| inline for (info.fields) |f| try checkPositive(f.type, @field(value, f.name), name ++ "." ++ f.name),
        else => {},
    }
}

test "every tuning value is positive and every basis-point knob is sane" {
    try checkPositive(Tuning, t, "t");
}

test "spot checks against the values the formulas were built on" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 60), t.hq.influence_ly.regional);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 6), t.battle.mounts_per_ammo_ton);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(types.Bp, 1_200), t.finance.loan_rate_bp);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(types.CBills, 2_000), t.logistics.freight_per_ly);
}

The recursion is on types, not on values: for a struct it calls itself once per field with the field's type, the field's value (read with @field), and a dotted name built with ++, all at compile time. At runtime what remains is a flat list of integer comparisons, one per unsigned knob. Add a field to Tuning and it is covered with no change to the test, which is exactly what the first exercise asks you to confirm.

The second test is the reverse: four values pinned by hand. It exists so that a mod which changes the numbers the formulas were tuned around fails loudly under zig build test -Ddata=…, and so that an accidental edit to the stock file is noticed.

Guided reading

  1. build.zig: the block from const data_dir = b.option( to mod.addImport("build_options", …). Match each import_name to the Zig file that imports it (grep for _zon" under src/domain and src/gen).
  2. src/domain/tuning.zig: skim the Tuning struct to see how the knobs are grouped by subsystem, then read the three declarations at the bottom: t, checkPositive, and the two tests.
  3. data/tables/tuning.zon next to it. Pick any three knobs and grep the source for their names to find the formula that uses each. You will find that every use is a plain field access.
  4. src/domain/chassis.zig top to bottom (186 lines). Note the four lookup helpers after find (ofWeightClass, ofKind, scoutPool, availableIn) and how each filters the constant slice. Then the tests: the first checks shape facts the compiler cannot (positive BV, unique keys).
  5. src/domain/part.zig, src/domain/rat.zig, src/domain/scenario.zig, src/domain/planet.zig: read only the tests. Each is a cross-file check of the kind described in 40.6.
  6. docs/modding.md: the table of files and the "Rules of the road". It is written for modders, which makes it the clearest statement of what each table holds.

Exercises

Exercise 40.1 · Break it on purpose warm-up

In your copy of the game, make three separate edits to data/tables/tuning.zon, building after each and writing down the first line of the error: (a) misspell a field name; (b) delete a field entirely; (c) change .rarity_target's .common value to "7". Undo each edit before the next.

Solution

(a) error: unexpected field 'fatigue_tierd', pointing at the line in the ZON file. (b) data/tables/tuning.zon:92:16: error: missing field 'fatigue_tired', pointing at the opening .{ of the .person block, with a note saying where the file was imported (src/domain/tuning.zig:398). (c) error: expected type 'u8' (or whatever the field's integer type is), pointing at the string. In all three cases the game does not build, which is the behaviour the design promises. Notice that (b) is reported at the struct literal rather than at the missing line, because there is no missing line to point at.

Exercise 40.2 · Add a knob practice

Add a new tuning knob person.exercise_bonus_xp with the value 5. It needs a field in the Tuning struct and a value in the ZON file. Then write a test in tuning.zig that reads it back. Before running the tests, predict whether checkPositive will cover the new field, and check your prediction by temporarily setting the value to 0.

Solution
src/domain/tuning.zig, inside the person struct
    person: struct {
        weekly_hours: u16,
        exercise_bonus_xp: u32,
        // …
data/tables/tuning.zon, inside .person
    .person = .{
        .weekly_hours = 40,
        .exercise_bonus_xp = 5,
        // …
src/domain/tuning.zig, at the bottom
test "the new knob is on the table" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 5), t.person.exercise_bonus_xp);
}

With the value 0, zig build test prints tuning field t.person.exercise_bonus_xp must be positive and the sanity test fails: checkPositive found the new field through @typeInfo without anyone telling it. The dotted name in the message was built at compile time with ++. Set it back to 5 and everything is green.

Exercise 40.3 · A cross-file check of your own practice

Add a test to src/domain/chassis.zig asserting that every design of kind .mek has at least one loadout slot of class .weapon. Use the pattern from 40.6: loop the constant catalogue, skip rows that do not apply, count, expect.

Solution 
test "every mek carries at least one weapon" {
    for (catalog) |c| {
        if (c.kind != .mek) continue;
        var weapons: u32 = 0;
        for (c.loadout) |slot| if (slot.class == .weapon) {
            weapons += 1;
        };
        try std.testing.expect(weapons > 0);
    }
}

It passes against the stock data. Two details: c.kind is a defaulted field, so rows that omit it read as .mek; and the one-line for … |slot| if (…) { … }; form needs the trailing semicolon because the whole for is a statement whose body is an if expression. If you want the failure message to name the offending design, print c.key before returning error.TestUnexpectedResult, as the RAT test does.

Exercise 40.4 · A mod that changes one number challenge

Create a directory mymod/tables/, copy tuning.zon into it, and change the regional influence radius from 60 to 61 light-years. Build and test with -Ddata=mymod. Which test notices, and why is that the right test to notice? Then run the game's REPL with the same option and find where it reports the overlay.

Solution 
$ mkdir -p mymod/tables && cp data/tables/tuning.zon mymod/tables/
$ sed -i '' 's/.regional = 60, .brigade = 90/.regional = 61, .brigade = 90/' mymod/tables/tuning.zon
$ zig build test -Ddata=mymod
error: 'domain.tuning.test.spot checks against the values the formulas were built on' failed:
       expected 60, found 61
Build Summary: … 1 failed

The spot-check test is the one that notices, and it is the right one: the shape is still valid (so the build succeeds and checkPositive is happy), but a formula somewhere was tuned around 60, and the test exists to say so. A modder who intends the change edits or skips that test; an accidental edit gets caught. The REPL banner prints the result of root.dataProvenance: mod mymod: 1 file overlaid (tables/tuning.zon). The values came from build_options, which the build script computed in the loop you read in 40.4.

Check your understanding

  1. What gives a ZON file its type?
    AnswerThe declaration that receives it: pub const t: Tuning = @import("tuning_zon"); coerces the anonymous literal to Tuning at compile time.
  2. Where is the string "tuning_zon" connected to a real file?
    AnswerIn build.zig, by mod.addAnonymousImport(f.import_name, .{ .root_source_file = path }), where path is either data/tables/tuning.zon or the same relative path under the -Ddata directory.
  3. Which mistakes in a data file does the compiler catch, and which does it not?
    AnswerIt catches shape errors: unknown fields, missing fields without defaults, wrong types, unknown enum literals. It cannot catch cross-file meaning, such as a loadout naming a part that is not in parts.zon; tests do that.
  4. Why can a vehicle row omit jump_mp?
    AnswerBecause Chassis.jump_mp has a default (= 0). Fields with defaults may be omitted from any struct literal, ZON included.
  5. What does find return for an unknown key, and why is that not an error?
    Answernull, because the return type is ?*const Chassis. "Not in the catalogue" is an ordinary outcome the caller handles with orelse or if, not a failure to propagate.
  6. Why does checkPositive take comptime T: type rather than using @TypeOf(value)?
    AnswerBoth would work for the top call, but the recursion needs to pass f.type explicitly for each field, and marking the parameter comptime guarantees the switch (@typeInfo(T)) is resolved while compiling, so only the integer checks survive to runtime.
  7. How does the binary know which files a mod overlaid?
    Answerbuild.zig records them in a generated build_options module (addOptions), which root.zig imports as build_info and formats in dataProvenance.
What you learned.
  • Every table in IRON LEDGER is a .zon struct literal imported by name and coerced to a Zig struct at compile time; the struct is the schema.
  • Shape errors (unknown field, missing field, wrong type, bad enum literal) fail the build with a line number in the data file.
  • build.zig binds each import name to a path, which is how -Ddata=<dir> overlays files without the simulation knowing.
  • Rows with defaulted fields let one struct describe meks, vehicles, fighters and ships.
  • Cross-file facts are checked by tests that loop over the constant data and name the failing row; a reflective test covers every tuning knob automatically.

41. GameState: one arena, one dice bag

In this chapter you open the struct that holds an entire campaign. You will see why every allocation a campaign makes comes from one arena and is freed by one call, why the random number generator is a bag of named streams rather than a single generator, and how a 64-bit hash of the state turns "the simulation is deterministic" from a slogan into a test.

What you need from earlier chapters. Chapter 19 and Chapter 20 (the stack, the heap, and the ArenaAllocator in particular), Chapter 21 and Chapter 22 (unmanaged lists and hash maps: .empty, and an allocator passed to every growing call), Chapter 34 (std.Random.DefaultPrng and seeding), Chapter 18 (pointers into containers going stale), Chapter 13 (non-exhaustive enums as typed IDs) and Chapter 4 (wrapping multiplication, *%).

41.1 The struct

GameState lives in src/sim/state.zig, a file of about two thousand lines of which the struct definition is the first three hundred. Here it is with the fields grouped and most of the comments removed; read the types more than the names:

src/sim/state.zig (abridged)
pub const Config = struct {
    seed: u64 = 3025,
    start_funds: types.CBills = 10_000_000,
    start_date: clock_mod.Date = clock_mod.Date.campaign_default,
};

pub const GameState = struct {
    arena: std.heap.ArenaAllocator,
    rng: rng_mod.Rng,
    clock: clock_mod.Clock,
    funds: types.CBills,
    reputation: i32 = 0,
    outfit_name: []const u8 = "Provisional Mercenary Command",
    commander: ?commander_mod.Commander = null,
    campaign_id: i64 = 0,
    bankrupt: bool = false,
    auto_admit: bool = false,
    share_profit_bp: types.Bp = @import("../domain/tuning.zig").t.person.share_profit_default_bp,
    ledger: finance_mod.Ledger = .{},
    event_queue: events_mod.EventQueue = .{},

    people: std.AutoArrayHashMapUnmanaged(types.PersonId, person_mod.Person) = .empty,
    units: std.AutoArrayHashMapUnmanaged(types.UnitId, unit_mod.Unit) = .empty,
    forces: std.AutoArrayHashMapUnmanaged(types.ForceId, force_mod.Force) = .empty,
    hqs: std.AutoArrayHashMapUnmanaged(types.HqId, hq_mod.Hq) = .empty,
    contracts: std.AutoArrayHashMapUnmanaged(types.ContractId, contract_mod.Contract) = .empty,

    contract_offers: std.ArrayListUnmanaged(contract_mod.Contract) = .empty,
    market_listings: std.ArrayListUnmanaged(market_mod.Listing) = .empty,
    loans: std.ArrayListUnmanaged(finance_mod.Loan) = .empty,
    spare_parts: std.StringArrayHashMapUnmanaged(u32) = .empty,
    part_orders: std.ArrayListUnmanaged(part_mod.AcquisitionOrder) = .empty,
    event_log: std.ArrayListUnmanaged(LogEntry) = .empty,
    fund_couriers: std.ArrayListUnmanaged(FundCourier) = .empty,
    policies: std.ArrayListUnmanaged(StandingPolicy) = .empty,
    supply_policies: std.ArrayListUnmanaged(SupplyPolicy) = .empty,
    stock_policies: std.ArrayListUnmanaged(StockPolicy) = .empty,
    bay_jobs: std.ArrayListUnmanaged(BayJob) = .empty,
    candidates: std.ArrayListUnmanaged(Candidate) = .empty,
    hq_links: std.ArrayListUnmanaged(@import("network.zig").HqLink) = .empty,
    unit_transfers: std.ArrayListUnmanaged(UnitTransfer) = .empty,
    faction_cooling: std.ArrayListUnmanaged(FactionCooling) = .empty,
    faction_standing: std.StringArrayHashMapUnmanaged(i32) = .empty,
    difficulty: difficulty_mod.Level = .regular,
    event_memory: std.AutoArrayHashMapUnmanaged(events_mod.EventKind, EventMemory) = .empty,
    stats: Stats = .{},
    rating_history: std.ArrayListUnmanaged(RatingSnapshot) = .empty,
    refit_plans: std.ArrayListUnmanaged(RefitPlan) = .empty,

    next_person_id: u32 = 1,
    next_unit_id: u32 = 1,
    next_force_id: u32 = 1,
    next_hq_id: u32 = 1,
    next_contract_id: u32 = 1,

    pub fn init(gpa: std.mem.Allocator, config: Config) GameState {
        return .{
            .arena = std.heap.ArenaAllocator.init(gpa),
            .rng = rng_mod.Rng.init(config.seed),
            .clock = .{ .date = config.start_date },
            .funds = config.start_funds,
        };
    }

    pub fn deinit(self: *GameState) void {
        self.arena.deinit();
    }

    pub fn allocator(self: *GameState) std.mem.Allocator {
        return self.arena.allocator();
    }
    // … about a hundred methods …
};

Several things you learned in Parts 1 and 2 are on display at once.

  • Four fields have no default (arena, rng, clock, funds) and init sets exactly those four. Everything else has a default, so init can be a four-line struct literal, and adding a defaulted field never touches init. Exercise 41.2 shows what happens when you add one without a default.
  • Every container is unmanaged and starts as .empty. None of them stores an allocator; the one allocator they all use is the arena, fetched with gs.allocator() at each call site. That is the 0.16 convention from Chapter 21 applied forty times.
  • The five entity maps are AutoArrayHashMapUnmanaged, the ordered kind (Chapter 22). Iterating an ordered map visits entries in insertion order on every machine and every run. An ordinary AutoHashMapUnmanaged would visit them in an order that depends on hash seeds and capacity, and the hash in 41.4 would differ between two identical campaigns. The choice of map type is a determinism decision.
  • Maps are keyed by typed IDs. people is keyed by PersonId, not u32. The non-exhaustive enum trick from Chapter 13 costs nothing at runtime and means gs.people.get(unit_id) is a compile error.
  • The ID counters are plain fields. next_person_id starts at 1 (0 is PersonId.none), and a fresh ID is @enumFromInt(self.next_person_id) followed by an increment. There is no global counter anywhere; it is part of the state and therefore saved, loaded and hashed with it.

What is not in the struct matters too. There is no io and no allocator other than the arena. There is no cache of derived numbers (a company's total battle value, say): those are recomputed by queries when asked. A cache is a second copy of the truth that can drift, and drift is the enemy of a state that must be reproducible.

41.2 The arena: one owner for everything

In Chapter 20 you chose allocators by lifetime. A campaign's lifetime is "from init to deinit", and every string, list, map and log line inside it lives exactly that long. That is the textbook case for an arena, and GameState uses one for everything:

pub fn deinit(self: *GameState) void {
    self.arena.deinit();
}

That one line frees every person, every hull, every ledger row, every formatted log line, and every hash map's backing store. No struct in src/domain needs a destructor that walks its children, and nothing in the simulation ever calls free. (A few domain structs, Person among them, do have a deinit method, but the game state never calls it; it exists for tests that build a Person with the testing allocator on its own.)

The trade, stated in the original guide and worth repeating: memory grows monotonically over a campaign. When a person is fired their record stays in the map with status .resigned; when a log line is written it is never freed; when a list shrinks its buffer is retained. A long campaign holds every log line it ever wrote. In exchange the simulation can never have a use-after-free, never leaks in the sense the testing allocator checks for, and never has to answer "who owns this string?". For a game whose whole state is a few megabytes, that is a good trade.

Look at how the arena shows up at a call site. This is the log method, which every subsystem uses to write a dated line:

src/sim/state.zig
/// Append a tagged, formatted entry (with the campaign date) to the log.
pub fn log(self: *GameState, category: LogCategory, ctx: LogCtx, comptime fmt: []const u8, args: anytype) !void {
    const d = self.clock.date;
    const line = try std.fmt.allocPrint(
        self.allocator(),
        "{d}-{d:0>2}-{d:0>2} " ++ fmt,
        .{ d.year, d.month, d.day } ++ args,
    );
    try self.event_log.append(self.allocator(), .{
        .day = self.clock.day_index,
        .category = category,
        .company = ctx.company,
        .hq = ctx.hq,
        .contract = ctx.contract,
        .text = line,
    });
}

Two compile-time tricks from Chapter 25 make this pleasant. "{d}-{d:0>2}-{d:0>2} " ++ fmt concatenates the caller's format string onto a date prefix at compile time, and .{ … } ++ args concatenates the two argument tuples, so every log line begins with a date and the caller never has to pass one. The formatted string comes from allocPrint on the arena and is stored by reference in the entry. Nobody will ever free it, and nobody needs to.

The LogCtx argument is a small struct of typed IDs with defaults, so a caller with nothing to tag passes .{} and a caller with a company passes .{ .company = id }. The log is queried later by those tags (Chapter 44), which is why the entry stores them as fields rather than baking "Alpha Company" into the text.

Pointers into the maps go stale. gs.people.getPtr(id) returns a *Person that points into the map's storage. If you then insert into gs.people and the map grows, the storage moves and your pointer is dangling. The arena does not save you from this; it is the same rule as Chapter 18's "a pointer into an ArrayList is invalid after append". The codebase's habit is to re-fetch after any insert: gs.force(id) is called again rather than a pointer kept across a createForce. When you write a command in Chapter 42, hire first and look up afterwards.

41.3 The dice bag

The second field of GameState is the random number generator, and it is not one generator:

src/sim/rng.zig (complete apart from the tests)
//! Deterministic RNG with named per-subsystem streams (ARCH §4).
//! Adding a roll in one system must never perturb another, so every
//! subsystem draws from its own stream. All combat/campaign dice are 2d6.

const std = @import("std");

pub const Stream = enum(u8) {
    generation, // company/person/name generation
    market, // contract/personnel/unit market rolls
    maintenance,
    acquisition,
    battle,
    events,
    medical,
    travel,

    const count = @typeInfo(Stream).@"enum".fields.len;
};

pub const Rng = struct {
    prngs: [Stream.count]std.Random.DefaultPrng,

    pub fn init(seed: u64) Rng {
        var self: Rng = undefined;
        for (&self.prngs, 0..) |*prng, i| {
            // Distinct, stable derivation per stream.
            prng.* = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(seed ^ (0x9E3779B97F4A7C15 *% (i + 1)));
        }
        return self;
    }

    pub fn random(self: *Rng, stream: Stream) std.Random {
        return self.prngs[@intFromEnum(stream)].random();
    }

    /// The BattleTech die roll.
    pub fn roll2d6(self: *Rng, stream: Stream) u8 {
        const r = self.random(stream);
        return r.intRangeAtMost(u8, 1, 6) + r.intRangeAtMost(u8, 1, 6);
    }
};

Read init with Chapter 34 in mind. Eight DefaultPrng generators sit in an array sized by the number of enum variants, a trick from Chapter 27: add a stream to the enum and the array grows. Each is seeded from the campaign seed XORed with a large odd constant times the stream index, using wrapping multiplication *% because the product is meant to overflow; plain * would panic in a debug build. The for (&self.prngs, 0..) |*prng, i| form iterates the array by pointer so each element can be assigned through prng.*.

Why eight generators instead of one? The comment at the top says it in a line, and the original guide gave the concrete case: suppose you add a weather roll to battles. With one shared generator, every market roll that happens after the first battle now gets a different number than before, and a saved game replays differently after the update. With named streams, adding a draw to .battle leaves .market exactly where it was. The test below is the rule stated as code:

test "streams are independent and deterministic" {
    var a = Rng.init(42);
    var b = Rng.init(42);

    // Draw heavily from one stream in `a` only; another stream must still
    // match the untouched twin exactly.
    for (0..1000) |_| _ = a.roll2d6(.maintenance);
    for (0..10) |_| {
        try std.testing.expectEqual(b.roll2d6(.battle), a.roll2d6(.battle));
    }
}

Every call site names its stream, and the name is the subsystem: gs.rng.roll2d6(.battle) in the battle resolver, gs.rng.roll2d6(.events) when a monthly event is drawn, gs.rng.roll2d6(.medical) in turnover, &gs.rng with .generation passed to the person generator. The house rule in CLAUDE.md is that no PRNG is ever created anywhere else. If you grep the core for DefaultPrng.init you find exactly the one in rng.zig.

41.4 The hash

The last method to read is the one that makes determinism testable:

src/sim/state.zig
/// Deterministic digest of gameplay-relevant state. Two runs with the
/// same seed and command script must produce the same hash — the
/// regression harness every stage builds on (ARCH §13).
pub fn hash(self: *GameState) u64 {
    var h = std.hash.Wyhash.init(0x42544d43); // "BTMC"
    h.update(std.mem.asBytes(&self.clock.day_index));
    h.update(std.mem.asBytes(&self.funds));
    h.update(std.mem.asBytes(&self.reputation));
    h.update(std.mem.asBytes(&self.share_profit_bp));
    const txn_count: u64 = self.ledger.transactions.items.len;
    h.update(std.mem.asBytes(&txn_count));

    var it = self.people.iterator();
    while (it.next()) |entry| {
        const p = entry.value_ptr;
        h.update(std.mem.asBytes(&p.id));
        h.update(p.first_name);
        h.update(p.last_name);
        h.update(std.mem.asBytes(&p.role));
        h.update(std.mem.asBytes(&p.status));
        h.update(std.mem.asBytes(&p.xp));
        h.update(std.mem.asBytes(&p.fatigue));
        h.update(std.mem.asBytes(&p.morale));
        const injuries: u64 = p.injuries.items.len;
        h.update(std.mem.asBytes(&injuries));
    }
    var uit = self.units.iterator();
    while (uit.next()) |entry| {
        const u = entry.value_ptr;
        h.update(std.mem.asBytes(&u.id));
        h.update(u.chassis_key);
        h.update(std.mem.asBytes(&u.status));
        h.update(std.mem.asBytes(&u.quality));
        h.update(std.mem.asBytes(&u.armor_pct));
        h.update(std.mem.asBytes(&u.force));
        h.update(std.mem.asBytes(&u.pilot));
        h.update(std.mem.asBytes(&u.berth_hq));
    }
    // … forces, contracts, offers, HQs, the commander …
    return h.final();
}

std.hash.Wyhash is a fast non-cryptographic hash from the standard library; you feed it bytes with update and read a u64 with final. std.mem.asBytes(&x) views any value as a byte slice (Chapter 29), which is how integers and enums are fed in; strings are already slices. The function walks the ordered maps in insertion order, which is why the map type matters: an unordered map would feed the same entries in a different order on another run and the digest would differ.

Notice what is hashed and what is not. Names, roles, statuses, fatigue, morale, hull condition: gameplay facts. Not hashed: log text, market listings, the exact RNG state. The digest is meant to say "these two campaigns are the same game", and it is deliberately coarse so that harmless changes (a reworded log line) do not break the golden-master test. The exercises ask you to check that it is nevertheless sensitive to a single C-bill.

41.5 Reading a GameState method

The rest of state.zig is about a hundred methods. They fall into a few kinds, and knowing the kinds makes the file navigable:

  • Lookups that wrap a map's getPtr and return an optional pointer: person(id), unit(id), force(id). Callers write gs.person(id) orelse return Error.UnknownPerson.
  • Creation that mints an ID, builds a struct on the arena and inserts it: hirePerson, hireFromSpec, addUnit, createForce, foundHq, createCommander.
  • Money: postTreasury, treasuryBalance, transferFunds, monthlyPayroll. Chapter 45 is about these.
  • Derived facts that walk the maps and compute a number without caching it: companyOf, companiesAtHq, techHoursFor, siteFreeTons.
  • Stock (physical parts at a site): stockMap, addStock, takeStock, stockCount.

Here is one of the lookups and one of the creators, so you can see the shape:

pub fn person(self: *GameState, id: types.PersonId) ?*person_mod.Person {
    return self.people.getPtr(id);
}

/// Recruit a randomly generated person (AtB-style: experience on 2d6,
/// skills from the band, names from the tables).
pub fn recruitGenerated(self: *GameState, role: person_mod.Role) !types.PersonId {
    const spec = person_gen.generateWithBonus(&self.rng, role, self.recruitBonus());
    return self.hireFromSpec(spec);
}

The creator passes &self.rng to the generator in src/gen, which draws from the .generation stream. Even name generation goes through the dice bag; that is why two campaigns with the same seed hire the same people.

Guided reading

  1. src/sim/rng.zig, all of it. It is sixty lines and you have now seen most of them.
  2. src/sim/clock.zig: Date, Clock (two fields: a date and day_index), and the DayPhase enum that documents the tick order for Chapter 43.
  3. src/sim/state.zig, lines 1 to about 300: the small helper structs (Treasury, FundCourier, StandingPolicy, LogEntry, BayJob, Candidate), then the GameState fields. Every one of those helper structs is something you will meet again on a screen.
  4. Still in state.zig: init, deinit, allocator, postTreasury, treasuryBalance, person, hirePerson, log, stockMap, and finally hash. Use search; they are not adjacent.
  5. src/domain/person.zig: the Person struct fields (about sixty lines). Count how many are optionals with null defaults and note what each "not yet" means.

Exercises

Exercise 41.1 · Seeds diverge warm-up

The existing test shows that two Rng values with the same seed agree. Add a test to src/sim/rng.zig showing that two with different seeds do not: roll .battle fifty times on each and count how often the two rolls coincide. What threshold is safe, and why can you not demand zero coincidences?

Solution 
test "different seeds give different dice" {
    var a = Rng.init(1);
    var b = Rng.init(2);
    var same: u32 = 0;
    for (0..50) |_| {
        if (a.roll2d6(.battle) == b.roll2d6(.battle)) same += 1;
    }
    // Two 2d6 sequences agree by chance on roughly one roll in seven.
    try std.testing.expect(same < 25);
}

Two independent 2d6 rolls are equal with probability about 0.11 (sum over the eleven outcomes of the squared probabilities), so around five or six coincidences in fifty are expected and zero would itself be suspicious. The threshold 25 is far above any plausible run of luck while still catching the bug the test is for: an init that ignored its seed. Because the generator is deterministic, the count for seeds 1 and 2 is in fact a fixed number and the test will never flake; the loose bound just documents the intent.

Exercise 41.2 · Let the compiler find the constructor warm-up

Add a field exercise_marker: u32, (no default) to GameState, right after funds. Build. Read the error, then fix it by giving the field a default rather than by editing init. Which choice would the codebase prefer, and why?

Solution 
src/sim/state.zig:290:17: error: missing struct field: exercise_marker
        return .{
               ~^
src/sim/state.zig:205:23: note: struct declared here
pub const GameState = struct {

There is exactly one place that constructs a GameState from nothing, and the compiler found it. The codebase prefers a default (exercise_marker: u32 = 0,): init then stays a four-line literal, Store.load (which also starts from GameState.init(gpa, .{})) keeps working, and old saves that lack the field load with the default. A field without a default is reserved for things that genuinely have no sensible default, like the arena and the seeded generator.

Exercise 41.3 · Test the log practice

Write a test in src/sim/state.zig that creates a fresh state, calls gs.log(.decision, .{}, "hello {d}", .{7}), and asserts on the single entry: its text, its day and its category. What date prefix do you expect on day zero of a default campaign?

Solution 
test "log lines carry the campaign date and the tags" {
    var gs = GameState.init(std.testing.allocator, .{});
    defer gs.deinit();
    try gs.log(.decision, .{}, "hello {d}", .{7});
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 1), gs.event_log.items.len);
    const e = gs.event_log.items[0];
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("3025-01-01 hello 7", e.text);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 0), e.day);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(LogCategory.decision, e.category);
}

The default Config starts on Date.campaign_default, 1 January 3025, and day_index is 0, so the prefix is 3025-01-01 with the month and day zero-padded by the {d:0>2} specifiers (Chapter 23). The defer gs.deinit() on the second line is not optional: std.testing.allocator reports the arena's memory as a leak without it.

Exercise 41.4 · The hash notices one C-bill practice

Write a test that takes gs.hash() of a fresh state, adds one to gs.funds, and asserts the hash changed; then subtracts one and asserts it is back to the original. Then answer: would the same test pass if you changed a log line's text instead of the funds?

Solution 
test "the hash notices a single c-bill" {
    var gs = GameState.init(std.testing.allocator, .{ .seed = 9 });
    defer gs.deinit();
    const before = gs.hash();
    gs.funds += 1;
    try std.testing.expect(gs.hash() != before);
    gs.funds -= 1;
    try std.testing.expectEqual(before, gs.hash());
}

It passes: funds is one of the first things fed to the hasher. A change to log text would not change the hash, because hash never reads event_log; it is a digest of gameplay-relevant state, and log wording is deliberately left out so that rewording a message does not break the golden-master test.

Check your understanding

  1. Which four fields must GameState.init set, and why those?
    Answerarena, rng, clock and funds: they are the fields without defaults, because each depends on something only the caller knows (the parent allocator, the seed, the start date, the starting money).
  2. What does gs.deinit() do, and what does it not need to do?
    AnswerIt calls arena.deinit(), which frees every allocation the campaign made. It does not need to walk any map or list, because nothing was allocated from anywhere else.
  3. Why are the entity maps AutoArrayHashMapUnmanaged rather than AutoHashMapUnmanaged?
    AnswerThe array variant iterates in insertion order, which is the same on every run and every machine; the hash order of the plain variant is not, and hash() walks the maps.
  4. Why does Rng.init use *%?
    AnswerThe seed derivation multiplies a large constant by the stream index and expects the product to wrap around 64 bits; plain * would be an overflow panic in Debug builds.
  5. What breaks if a new subsystem borrows the .battle stream instead of adding its own?
    AnswerNothing today, but every battle roll after the new subsystem's first draw shifts, so saved campaigns replay differently after the change; a new stream leaves existing streams untouched.
  6. Why is a pointer from gs.people.getPtr unsafe to keep across a hire?
    AnswerHiring inserts into the map; if the map grows it reallocates its storage and the pointer dangles. The arena does not prevent this; re-fetch after inserting.
  7. Name two things the hash includes and two it excludes.
    AnswerIncludes: day_index, funds, each person's fatigue and morale, each unit's status. Excludes: log text, market listings, the internal RNG state.
What you learned.
  • GameState is one struct holding ordered maps of entities keyed by typed IDs, lists of everything else, the clock, the money and two special members: an arena and a dice bag.
  • The arena owns every allocation of a campaign; deinit is one call and the domain has no destructors. Memory grows monotonically in exchange.
  • Rng is eight DefaultPrng generators, one per named stream, seeded from one campaign seed; every roll names its subsystem, so adding rolls to one subsystem never perturbs another.
  • hash() folds gameplay-relevant state into a u64 by walking the ordered maps; it is the instrument the golden-master test reads.
  • Pointers into the maps are invalidated by inserts; look up again after you create.

42. Commands: the only way in

In this chapter you read the one function that is allowed to change a campaign. Every player action is a value of one tagged union, every arm of one switch follows the same three-beat shape, and every refusal is a named error that both frontends turn into a sentence. By the end you will add a command of your own and watch the compiler walk you through every place it must be handled.

What you need from earlier chapters. Chapter 14 (tagged unions, payload captures with |x|, and exhaustive switch), Chapter 16 (error sets, try, catch |err| switch (err), merging sets with ||), Chapter 12 (a result struct whose fields all have defaults), Chapter 11 (tokenising a line with std.mem.tokenizeScalar) and Chapter 8 (expectError).

42.1 One union, one switch

Nothing outside the simulation core mutates GameState except through one function:

pub fn execute(gs: *GameState, cmd: Command) Error!Result

Its argument is a tagged union with 71 variants at the time of writing (the original guide said "about ninety"; the count is easy to check, and Exercise 42.3 pins it). Here is the top of it:

src/sim/commands.zig
pub const Command = union(enum) {
    /// End the turn: advance one day. Turn-based — time only moves here,
    /// and nothing blocks it; decisions wait in the inbox with deadlines.
    advance_day,
    advance_days: u32,
    hire: struct {
        first: []const u8,
        last: []const u8,
        role: person_mod.Role,
    },
    /// Hire a randomly generated candidate (experience rolled on 2d6).
    recruit: person_mod.Role,
    fire: types.PersonId,
    /// Generate a full company: 3 lances of meks with pilots + support tail.
    new_company: []const u8,
    rename_outfit: []const u8,
    rename_force: struct { force: types.ForceId, name: []const u8 },
    /// Attach an emblem image (raw bytes) to a force (ARCH §9.8 identity).
    set_emblem: struct { force: types.ForceId, image: []const u8 },
    /// Character creation: origin picks the starter world (weighted, in the
    /// commander's faction space); profession grants one 2% edge.
    create_commander: struct {
        name: []const u8,
