        origin: commander_mod.Faction,
        profession: commander_mod.Profession,
        /// Campaign start year (12C.16): the market, RATs and salvage field
        /// only what exists by then.
        start_year: u16 = 3025,
    },
    // … sixty more, ending with:
    /// Trim a deployed company's field stores to its field plan …
    trim_stock: types.ForceId,
};

The three payload shapes from Chapter 14 are all here. advance_day carries nothing. fire carries one typed ID. hire carries an inline struct, and create_commander's inline struct even has a defaulted field, so a caller may write .{ .create_commander = .{ .name = "Erik", .origin = .CC, .profession = .quartermaster } } and get the year 3025. A command value is data: it can be built by a key handler, parsed from text, stored in an array for a test script, or (in principle) written to a replay file. That is why a union was chosen over a method per action.

The union's doc comments are worth a moment. They are the specification of the game's rules in the player's terms ("time only moves here, and nothing blocks it"), and they sit exactly where a reader looking for the rule will look.

42.2 The error set and the result

Before the switch, two more types:

pub const Error = error{
    UnknownPerson,
    UnknownForce,
    UnknownUnit,
    UnknownChassis,
    NoSuchEvent,
    NoSuchChoice,
    NotADecision,
    CommanderExists,
    NoHomeWorld,
    NoSuchOffer,
    NotACompany,
    CompanyDeployed,
    UnknownPlanet,
    // … eighty named errors in all, ending with:
    UnknownAbility,
    AlreadyLearned,
    /// That term is already at the best the employer will give.
    TermAtCap,
} || std.mem.Allocator.Error;

pub const Result = struct {
    days_advanced: u32 = 0,
    hired: types.PersonId = .none,
    created_force: types.ForceId = .none,
    /// Tons a `trim_stock` sent home.
    tons_moved: u32 = 0,
    /// The hull a `buy_hull_for` bought, and its delivery time (0 = on hand).
    unit: types.UnitId = .none,
    eta_days: u32 = 0,
    /// People a `crew_company` hired (halls plus the astech/medic pools),
    /// and the manning lines it could not fill because no candidate of
    /// that role walked the boards.
    hired_count: u32 = 0,
    still_open: u32 = 0,
    /// `order_part`: false when logistics failed the sourcing roll.
    sourced: bool = true,
    /// `negotiate`: how the round went.
    negotiation: enum { none, improved, hardened, withdrawn } = .none,
    // …
};

Error is an explicit set merged with std.mem.Allocator.Error (Chapter 16), so try gs.log(…) inside an arm, which can fail with OutOfMemory, needs no conversion. Every other error is a refusal with a name a human can read. There is no Error.Failed; the design rule (from ARCHITECTURE.md) is that command validation returns values the UI can explain, and you will see the explaining in 42.5.

Result is the mirror image: every field has a default, so an arm that has nothing to report returns .{}, and an arm that created something fills one field. A caller that does not care writes _ = try execute(…); a caller that does writes (try execute(gs, .{ .new_company = "Alpha" })).created_force. The doc comments on the fields name the command that fills each, which is how you find your way from a result field back to its arm.

42.3 The shape of an arm

The switch itself is next. The first arms are the simplest, and they show the mechanics of a payload capture:

pub fn execute(gs: *GameState, cmd: Command) Error!Result {
    switch (cmd) {
        .advance_day => return advance(gs, 1),
        .advance_days => |n| return advance(gs, n),
        .hire => |h| {
            const id = try gs.hirePerson(h.first, h.last, h.role);
            return .{ .hired = id };
        },
        .recruit => |role| {
            const id = try gs.recruitGenerated(role);
            return .{ .hired = id };
        },
        .fire => |id| {
            const p = gs.person(id) orelse return Error.UnknownPerson;
            // 12C.2: a firing pays half the departure payout; seats open.
            const paid = try @import("personnel.zig").depart(gs, id, .resigned, tuning.person.fire_severance_bp, "severance (fired)");
            if (paid > 0) try gs.log(.rotation, .{ .company = gs.companyOf(p.assigned_force) }, "[personnel] {s} {s} fired — {d} c-bills severance", .{ p.first_name, p.last_name, paid });
            return .{};
        },
        // …

|n| binds the u32 of advance_days; |h| binds the inline struct so h.first works; |id| binds the typed ID. The .fire arm shows the three beats that every non-trivial arm follows: validate (gs.person(id) orelse return Error.UnknownPerson), mutate (depart), report (a log line, then a Result).

Here is the arm the original guide singled out, because its comment records a real bug:

        .upgrade_tier => |hq_id| {
            // Check everything before a c-bill moves: a refused upgrade used
            // to keep the money.
            const h = gs.hqs.getPtr(hq_id) orelse return Error.UnknownHq;
            if (h.tier != .field) return Error.MaxLevel;
            for (h.projects.items) |p| if (p.kind == .tier_upgrade) return Error.ProjectInProgress;
            if (gs.treasuryBalance(.{ .hq = hq_id }) < hq_ops.tier_upgrade_cost) return Error.InsufficientTreasury;
            hq_ops.startTierUpgrade(gs, hq_id) catch |err| switch (err) {
                error.ProjectInProgress => return Error.ProjectInProgress,
                error.MaxLevel => return Error.MaxLevel,
                error.UnknownHq => return Error.UnknownHq,
                error.OutOfMemory => return Error.OutOfMemory,
            };
            try gs.postTreasury(.{ .hq = hq_id }, .{
                .day = gs.clock.day_index,
                .amount = -hq_ops.tier_upgrade_cost,
                .category = .hq_construction,
                .hq = hq_id,
                .note = "regional upgrade",
            });
            return .{};
        },

Four checks, then two effects, then .{}. An earlier version debited first and checked second, so a refused upgrade kept the money; the discipline "all checks, then all effects" is what prevents that class of bug, and the test "tier upgrade: refusals keep the money; a funded field HQ starts the project and pays once" makes sure it stays prevented.

The middle of the arm shows a pattern from Chapter 16 that you will see throughout the file. hq_ops.startTierUpgrade has its own, smaller error set (it is declared !void, so the compiler infers error{UnknownHq, MaxLevel, ProjectInProgress, OutOfMemory} from its body). The arm translates each case into the command layer's Error explicitly with a catch |err| switch (err). Because a switch on an error set is exhaustive, a new failure mode added to startTierUpgrade shows up here as a compile error ("unhandled error"), which is exactly where you want to be told.

42.4 A longer arm: crewing a company

Most arms are ten to thirty lines. Here is a thirty-line one you will meet again in Chapter 50, where a single keypress runs it:

        .crew_company => |company| {
            const f = gs.force(company) orelse return Error.UnknownForce;
            if (f.echelon != .company) return Error.NotACompany;
            if (gs.deploymentContract(company) != null) return Error.CompanyDeployed;
            const personnel = @import("personnel.zig");
            var hired: u32 = 0;
            var still_open: u32 = 0;
            for (personnel.manningNeeds(gs, company)) |n| {
                var have = personnel.manningHave(gs, company, n.role);
                while (have < n.need) : (have += 1) {
                    if (personnel.isPooledRole(n.role)) {
                        // MekHQ hires astechs and medics to complement on
                        // demand: no market, no signing bonus, salary only.
                        const spec = person_gen.generateWithBonus(&gs.rng, n.role, gs.recruitBonus());
                        const id = try gs.hireFromSpec(spec);
                        gs.person(id).?.assigned_force = company;
                        hired += 1;
                    } else if (try hireRoleFromHall(gs, n.role, company)) {
                        hired += 1;
                    } else {
                        still_open += n.need - have;
                        break;
                    }
                }
            }
            _ = try gs.autoAssign(company);
            try gs.log(.decision, .{ .company = company }, "[raise] {s}: {d} hired to fill the manning table ({d} still open — the halls had nobody)", .{ f.name, hired, still_open });
            return .{ .hired_count = hired, .still_open = still_open };
        },

Three validations, then a loop over the fourteen-row manning table (manningNeeds returns a fixed-size array [14]Need), then autoAssign, then a log line and a two-field result. Notice gs.person(id).?.assigned_force = company;: the person was just created by hireFromSpec, so the lookup cannot fail and .? is the honest way to say so (Chapter 15). Notice also that the code looks the person up after hiring rather than keeping a pointer from before, which is the stale-pointer rule from Chapter 41. And notice hireRoleFromHall calling execute recursively with .hire_candidate: an arm may compose other commands, which keeps the signing-bonus accounting in one place.

42.5 Advancing time is a command too

The two arms at the top of the switch call advance, a private function that is the only place the daily tick (Chapter 43) is invoked from:

fn advance(gs: *GameState, days: u32) Error!Result {
    // Turn-based: each day is a turn; nothing interrupts the advance.
    // Decisions wait in the inbox and default at their deadlines — except
    // money (Stage 12): a negative outfit treasury holds the turn until a
    // loan or a sale covers it, and past all credit the outfit folds.
    var result: Result = .{};
    for (0..days) |_| {
        if (gs.bankrupt) return Error.Bankrupt;
        // Couriers already bound for the outfit count: the turn can end
        // while the money is on the road.
        if (gs.funds + gs.inboundToOutfit() < 0) {
            if (gs.funds + gs.liquidationValue() + gs.creditRemaining() < 0) {
                gs.bankrupt = true;
                try gs.log(.finance, .{}, "[bankrupt] the outfit cannot cover {d}: creditors seize what is left", .{gs.funds});
                return Error.Bankrupt;
            }
            return Error.Insolvent;
        }
        try tick.advanceDay(gs);
        result.days_advanced += 1;
    }
    return result;
}

This is where the game's turn structure lives: a day is a turn, the only thing that can stop the clock is a negative treasury, and days_advanced tells the caller how far it got. It is also a good example of a Zig function that returns an error and has partially done its work: if day three of seven is refused with Error.Insolvent, days one and two happened and the state reflects them. The caller learns this from the error, not from a rollback, because the design says time only moves forward.

42.6 From text to command, and from error to sentence

Both frontends build Command values. The terminal client's keys build them directly (try self.exec(.{ .crew_company = co })). Typed text, whether in the REPL or the client's : line, goes through one parser:

src/sim/cli.zig
pub fn parseCommand(verb: []const u8, tokens: *std.mem.TokenIterator(u8, .scalar)) ParseError!?Command {
    const eq = std.mem.eql;
    if (eq(u8, verb, "transfer")) {
        return .{ .transfer = .{ .from = try parseTreasury(try need(tokens.next())), .to = try parseTreasury(try need(tokens.next())), .amount = try num(i64, tokens.next()) } };
    }
    if (eq(u8, verb, "admit")) return .{ .admit = @enumFromInt(try num(u32, tokens.next())) };
    if (eq(u8, verb, "depot")) return .{ .depot = @enumFromInt(try num(u32, tokens.next())) };
    // …
    if (eq(u8, verb, "shares")) {
        return .{ .set_shares_pct = try num(u8, tokens.next()) };
    }
    // …
    return null; // not a verb we know
}

The return type ParseError!?Command reads inside-out: an optional command (null means "not my verb; maybe the frontend knows it") wrapped in a possible parse error (BadArguments, BadSite, BadNumber). The helpers num and need turn a maybe-token into a number or a required string, and @enumFromInt turns the user's typed number into a typed ID at the edge, which is one of the few places that conversion is legitimate (Chapter 13). A verb also needs a row in the verbs list (for tab completion) and in the usage table (for help), and a test checks that every listed verb has a parser branch, so you cannot add one and forget the others.

When execute refuses, the error travels back up to the frontend, and a shared table turns it into a sentence:

pub fn errorText(err: anyerror) []const u8 {
    return switch (err) {
        error.InsufficientTreasury => "not enough money in that treasury — transfer funds first",
        error.MaxLevel => "already at the top: this HQ is regional (or the facility is maxed)",
        error.ProjectInProgress => "a project is already running here — watch PROJECTS",
        error.BadPercent => "a percentage between 0 and 100",
        error.BadYear => "the campaign starts between 3000 and 3060",
        error.CompanyDeployed => "that company is deployed — hire at an HQ hall and `xfer person <id> co:N` to send people out to it",
        // …
        else => @errorName(err),
    };
}

anyerror accepts any error set, and the else arm falls back to the error's name, so a new error is never silent; it just reads as UnknownAbility until someone writes it a sentence. This is the payoff of Error being a set of names rather than one Failed: the same table serves the REPL's stderr and the client's status line.

42.7 The tests

commands.zig ends with about fifty tests, and their style is the style of the whole suite: build the smallest state that exercises the rule, run one command, assert on state. The refusal test for the arm you read above:

test "tier upgrade: refusals keep the money; a funded field HQ starts the project and pays once" {
    var gs = GameState.init(std.testing.allocator, .{ .seed = 1230 });
    defer gs.deinit();
    _ = try execute(&gs, .{ .create_commander = .{ .name = "T", .origin = .LC, .profession = .paymaster } });
    const home = gs.hqs.keys()[0];
    const home_funds = gs.hqs.getPtr(home).?.funds;
    try std.testing.expectError(Error.MaxLevel, execute(&gs, .{ .upgrade_tier = home })); // already regional
    try std.testing.expectEqual(home_funds, gs.hqs.getPtr(home).?.funds);
    // … found a field HQ, empty its till …
    try std.testing.expectError(Error.InsufficientTreasury, execute(&gs, .{ .upgrade_tier = fb }));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 0), gs.hqs.getPtr(fb).?.projects.items.len);
    // Funded: the project starts and the cost is paid exactly once.
    gs.hqs.getPtr(fb).?.funds = hq_ops.tier_upgrade_cost + 1;
    _ = try execute(&gs, .{ .upgrade_tier = fb });
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(types.CBills, 1), gs.hqs.getPtr(fb).?.funds);
    try std.testing.expectError(Error.ProjectInProgress, execute(&gs, .{ .upgrade_tier = fb }));
}

Every expectError is paired with an expectEqual on the money, which is the actual property: not just "it refused" but "it refused and nothing moved". Tests reach into GameState fields directly (gs.hqs.getPtr(fb).?.funds = …) to set up situations; that is allowed in tests precisely because it is not allowed anywhere else.

Guided reading

  1. src/sim/commands.zig, the Command union, all of it. It is two hundred lines of doc comments and is the best single description of what the game lets you do.
  2. The Error set and Result struct just below it.
  3. execute: read the first ten arms in order, then jump to .upgrade_tier, .crew_company, .set_shares_pct and .trim_stock. Note the three beats in each. Then advance and debitPurchase (a four-line helper that is "check, then post").
  4. src/sim/cli.zig: parseCommand (skim the branches, read newlance fully), errorText, verbs, usage, and the two tests at the bottom.
  5. Back in commands.zig, read three tests: "command validation errors", "tier upgrade: refusals keep the money", and "golden master: same seed + same script". You will return to the last one in Chapter 49.

Exercises

Exercise 42.1 · A command from the union to the REPL challenge

Add a command set_morale_all: u8 that sets the morale of every active person to the given value, refusing values over 100 with Error.BadPercent. Add the variant, the arm, a REPL verb morale <0-100> (verb list, parser branch, usage row), and a test. Do it in that order and read every compile error before fixing it.

Solution

Adding the variant alone makes zig build test fail with error: switch must handle all possibilities at execute's switch and note: unhandled enumeration value: 'set_morale_all'. (The two switch (cmd) in main.zig have else arms and are untouched.) The arm, placed next to .set_shares_pct:

        .set_morale_all => |value| {
            if (value > 100) return Error.BadPercent;
            var it = gs.people.iterator();
            while (it.next()) |entry| {
                const p = entry.value_ptr;
                if (p.status == .active) p.morale = value;
            }
            try gs.log(.decision, .{}, "[exercise] morale set to {d} for everyone on the books", .{value});
            return .{};
        },

In cli.zig: "morale", in the verbs array; .{ "morale", "morale <0-100>" }, in the usage table; and a parser branch if (eq(u8, verb, "morale")) return .{ .set_morale_all = try num(u8, tokens.next()) };. If you forget the usage row, the test "every listed verb parses or fails on arguments" fails with usage(v) != null. The test:

test "set_morale_all touches the active only and refuses over 100" {
    var gs = GameState.init(std.testing.allocator, .{});
    defer gs.deinit();
    const a = try gs.hirePerson("A", "One", .mekwarrior);
    const b = try gs.hirePerson("B", "Two", .tech_mek);
    gs.person(b).?.status = .retired;
    try std.testing.expectError(Error.BadPercent, execute(&gs, .{ .set_morale_all = 101 }));
    _ = try execute(&gs, .{ .set_morale_all = 90 });
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 90), gs.person(a).?.morale);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 50), gs.person(b).?.morale);
}

The retired person keeps the default morale of 50, which checks the .active filter. zig build run -- --repl then accepts morale 75, and so does the terminal client's : line, without either frontend being edited. That is the whole argument for one parser.

Exercise 42.2 · Refusals with expectError warm-up

Write a test proving set_shares_pct refuses 101 with Error.BadPercent and accepts 100, and check what 100 percent becomes in gs.share_profit_bp (read the arm to find the unit).

Solution 
test "shares refuse 101 percent" {
    var gs = GameState.init(std.testing.allocator, .{});
    defer gs.deinit();
    try std.testing.expectError(Error.BadPercent, execute(&gs, .{ .set_shares_pct = 101 }));
    _ = try execute(&gs, .{ .set_shares_pct = 100 });
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(types.Bp, 10_000), gs.share_profit_bp);
}

The arm stores @as(types.Bp, pct) * 100: percent to basis points, the unit Chapter 45 explains. expectError takes the error and the expression, not its result; the call happens inside.

Exercise 42.3 · Count the variants warm-up

Write a one-assertion test that pins the number of Command variants using @typeInfo. First guess the number, then print it with std.debug.print inside the test, then replace the print with an expectEqual.

Solution 
test "the command union is large" {
    const n = @typeInfo(Command).@"union".fields.len;
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 71), n);
}

@typeInfo(Command).@"union".fields is the variant list, available at compile time. The number is 71 today; if you did Exercise 42.1 first it is 72. A pinned count is a mild nuisance for whoever adds the next command, which is the point of the exercise rather than a recommendation: the game does not pin it, and you should think about whether you would.

Exercise 42.4 · Find the three beats practice

Open the .found_hq arm (near .upgrade_tier). It calls debitPurchase before gs.foundHq. Is that a violation of "all checks, then all effects"? Read debitPurchase and foundHq's error set and argue either way in three sentences.

Solution

The arm does its own checks first (planet_mod.find, reachable), so by the time it debits, the only ways foundHq can fail are the ones already ruled out (UnknownPlanet, NotReachable) plus OutOfMemory. debitPurchase itself is "check the balance, then post", so it cannot half-succeed. It is therefore not a violation in practice, but it is fragile: if foundHq gained a new failure mode, the exhaustive catch |err| switch would force someone to add an arm and, one hopes, to notice the money had already left. The .upgrade_tier arm avoids the question by posting last; that ordering is the safer habit.

Check your understanding

  1. Why is a player action a value rather than a method call?
    AnswerA value can be built by a key handler, parsed from text, stored in an array for a test script, or logged; one switch then handles all of them identically, and the compiler checks the switch is complete.
  2. What are the three beats of an arm, and which bug does the order prevent?
    AnswerValidate, mutate, report. Doing every check before any effect prevents a refused command from leaving a partial change behind, such as a debited treasury for an upgrade that never started.
  3. What does catch |err| switch (err) { … } buy over try when calling hq_ops.startTierUpgrade?
    AnswerIt translates the helper's smaller error set into the command layer's set explicitly, and because the switch is exhaustive, a new error in the helper becomes a compile error at the arm.
  4. Why does Result give every field a default?
    AnswerSo most arms can return .{} and only the arms with something to report fill a field; callers read the field they care about.
  5. What does ParseError!?Command mean?
    AnswerParsing may fail (bad number, missing argument); if it succeeds it may still yield null, meaning "not a verb this parser knows", which lets the frontend try its own verbs.
  6. What happens if execute refuses on day 3 of advance_days = 7?
    AnswerDays 1 and 2 have already happened and remain; the error (Insolvent or Bankrupt) is returned and no rollback occurs, because time only moves forward.
  7. Why does errorText take anyerror and end with else => @errorName(err)?
    AnswerSo it can be called with errors from any layer and never fails to produce text; an error without a sentence shows its name until someone writes one.
What you learned.
  • All mutation of a campaign goes through commands.execute, one exhaustive switch over a 71-variant tagged union.
  • Every arm validates, then mutates, then reports; refusals are named errors from one merged set, and results are a struct of defaulted fields.
  • Helpers with smaller error sets are translated with an exhaustive catch |err| switch, so new failure modes surface at compile time.
  • Time advances through the same door, and money is the only thing that can hold a turn.
  • One parser (cli.parseCommand) and one error table (cli.errorText) serve both frontends, so adding a verb is a change in one file.

43. The daily tick

In this chapter you read the function that makes a day happen. It is a fixed list of phases in a fixed order, and the order carries meaning: deliveries land before supplies are eaten, maintenance runs before battles, payroll runs last. You will learn how to read a phase, how the phases are tested in isolation, and how to add one of your own without disturbing the golden master.

What you need from earlier chapters. Chapter 6 (while with a continue expression, index loops that remove items, % for "every seventh day"), Chapter 16 (a function that returns !void and a chain of try calls), Chapter 22 (walking a map with an iterator and mutating through value_ptr), Chapter 12 (the Date struct from clock.zig, which you may remember from the original guide's section on methods) and Chapter 8.

43.1 Two clocks

Time in IRON LEDGER is two numbers that move together:

src/sim/clock.zig
pub const Clock = struct {
    date: Date = Date.campaign_default,
    day_index: u32 = 0, // days since campaign start; the canonical timestamp

    pub fn advance(self: *Clock) void {
        self.date = self.date.next();
        self.day_index += 1;
    }
};

day_index is the timestamp the whole simulation uses: a delivery has an eta_day, a wound has a wound_heal_day, an event has a deadline_day, all as plain u32 days since the campaign began. Comparing two of them is integer comparison. The Date beside it exists for two purposes only: to be printed, and to answer "is it the first of the month?" (isPayday). The house rule is that the calendar is rendered only at the edges. There is no std.Io.Clock.now anywhere in the core, because there is no io to call it with (Chapter 39).

Date.next is the by-value method you may have already read: copy self, bump the day, roll the month and year over, return the copy. Clock.advance takes a pointer and mutates. Both styles appear throughout the codebase and the choice is deliberate each time: a Date is a small value that is pleasant to treat as immutable; a Clock is a field of the state that moves in place.

43.2 The phase list

Here is the whole of a day, exactly as the source has it:

src/sim/tick.zig
pub fn advanceDay(gs: *GameState) !void {
    gs.clock.advance();
    gs.refreshHqStaffing(); // the back office is people (Stage 9C)

    // Phase order per clock.DayPhase — stubs marked with their stage.
    if (gs.clock.day_index % 7 == 0) network.resetWeeklyThroughput(gs); // links' week (Stage 9D)
    try runTravel(gs); // deliveries, couriers, transfers
    try runPolicies(gs); // standing cash top-ups and resupply (Stage 12: daily)
    try runStockPolicies(gs); // warehouse reorder points (Stage 12)
    try hq_ops.runDaily(gs); // bays, fabrication, construction (Stage 9C)
    try runSupplyConsumption(gs); // supply_consumption phase (Stage 9B)
    try medical.runDailyHealing(gs); // medical phase
    try runMarkets(gs); // acquisition_and_markets
    if (gs.clock.day_index % 7 == 0 and gs.clock.day_index > 0) {
        try maintenance.runWeeklyMaintenance(gs); // maintenance phase
        try maintenance.runWeeklyRepairs(gs);
    }
    try medical.runDailyTraining(gs); // training phase
    try runContracts(gs); // contract lifecycle
    try contract_control.runReturns(gs); // companies travelling home arrive
    if (gs.clock.date.day == 1) try contract_events.rollMonthly(gs); // event decks
    if (gs.clock.day_index % 7 == 3) try contract_events.rollWeekly(gs); // weekly happenings (Stage 12)
    try battle.runDaily(gs); // battle_resolution: due engagements resolve
    try contract_control.checkEffectiveness(gs); // the ineffectiveness clock (Stage 9E)
    if (gs.clock.day_index % 7 == 0 and gs.clock.day_index > 0) {
        try medical.runWeeklyRest(gs); // morale_fatigue phase
        runTrainingLances(gs); // lance roles (Stage 12)
    }
    try runFinances(gs);
    try contract_events.expireDue(gs); // decisions phase: deadlines pass
}

Read it as a sentence. The clock ticks. Anything in transit lands (runTravel). Standing orders top up cash and supplies. The HQ's bays and construction crews do a day's work. Deployed companies eat a day's supplies. The wounded heal a day. Markets refresh. Once a week, every hull gets its maintenance check and the repair queue moves. Training programs progress. Contracts start, end, and are scored; companies travelling home arrive. On the first of the month an event is drawn for each contract; on the third day of each week a smaller one. Battles that are due today are resolved. The ineffectiveness clock is checked. Once a week, everyone at home rests and training lances train. Finance runs. Decisions past their deadline default.

Now read it as code. Every phase is a function that takes *GameState and returns !void, called with try, so the first phase to fail stops the day and the error propagates up to advance and out of execute. Weekly phases are gated by day_index % 7 == 0 (with day_index > 0 so that day zero is not a maintenance day) and monthly ones by date.day == 1, which is the one place the calendar participates in a rule. Two phases are called without try because they cannot fail: network.resetWeeklyThroughput and runTrainingLances return void, and the compiler would reject a try on them.

The comments name the stage that introduced each phase. That is not decoration: the enum DayPhase in clock.zig was written at the start of the project as the intended order, and each stage filled in a stub. Reading the two side by side shows how a design sketch became code over time.

43.3 Why the order is the rule

The original guide put it in four sentences worth keeping: deliveries land before consumption so a convoy that arrives today feeds today. Maintenance runs before battles on the same day, so a hull that broke down this week does not fight. Finance runs last so the day's costs are on the books when payroll is counted. When you add a mechanic, the first question is which phase it belongs in and what must already have happened.

There is a fourth example hiding in the list: runReturns (companies arriving home) runs before the weekly runWeeklyRest, so a company that lands on a rest day rests. And a fifth: rollMonthly runs before battle.runDaily, because a monthly event may have spawned the very engagement that resolves today; the doc comment on DayPhase says so explicitly.

None of this is enforced by the compiler. It is enforced by tests that build a state where the order matters and check the outcome, which is the next section.

43.4 Reading a phase

Phases are small and shaped alike. Here is the start of runTravel, the first one:

pub fn runTravel(gs: *GameState) !void {
    // Failed sourcing attempts stay visible for two weeks, then clear.
    var fi: usize = 0;
    while (fi < gs.part_orders.items.len) {
        const o = gs.part_orders.items[fi];
        if (o.status == .failed and o.ordered_day + 14 <= gs.clock.day_index) _ = gs.part_orders.orderedRemove(fi) else fi += 1;
    }
    for (gs.part_orders.items) |*order| {
        if (order.status != .in_transit) continue;
        if (order.eta_day != null and gs.clock.day_index >= order.eta_day.?) {
            order.status = .delivered;
            // Land at the destination site; anything the warehouse or the
            // trucks can't hold is lost on the dock (Stage 9B).
            const dest: types.Site = if (order.dest == .outfit) gs.defaultSite() else order.dest;
            const room = gs.siteFreeTons(dest) / @max(1, part_mod.tons(order.part_key));
            const landed = @min(order.quantity, room);
            try gs.addStock(dest, order.part_key, landed);
            const tags = GameState.treasuryTags(GameState.siteTreasury(dest));
            try gs.log(.delivery, .{ .company = tags.company, .hq = tags.hq }, "[delivery] {s} x{d} received{s}", .{
                order.part_key, landed,
                if (landed < order.quantity) " — NO ROOM for the rest, written off" else "",
            });
        }
    }
    // … couriers, unit transfers …
}

Two loop forms from Chapter 6, chosen for a reason each. The first is an index loop because the body removes items: after orderedRemove(fi) the next item has slid into slot fi, so the index must not advance. The second is a for by pointer (|*order|) because the body mutates the item in place and removes nothing. The "is it due?" test is gs.clock.day_index >= order.eta_day.?, integer against integer, after an explicit null check; this is the pattern for every scheduled thing in the game.

And here is the phase that runs last, runFinances, abridged:

fn runFinances(gs: *GameState) !void {
    if (!gs.clock.date.isPayday()) return;

    var it = gs.people.iterator();
    while (it.next()) |entry| {
        const p = entry.value_ptr;
        if (p.status == .active) p.xp += monthly_service_xp;
    }
    // Seats and experience set ranks before pay is counted (12B.4); service
    // awards come due (12B.5).
    _ = try @import("personnel.zig").refreshRanks(gs);
    _ = @import("personnel.zig").refreshShares(gs);
    // New Year's Day (12C.8): the rating goes in the book.
    if (gs.clock.date.month == 1) {
        // … append a rating snapshot; log the designs entering service this year …
    }
    _ = try @import("personnel.zig").checkAllAwards(gs);
    // Notice is handed in on payday (Stage 12.20); grudges fade (12.21).
    _ = try @import("medical.zig").runMonthlyTurnover(gs);
    @import("contract_control.zig").driftStanding(gs);

    const payroll = gs.monthlyPayroll();
    if (payroll != 0) {
        try gs.postTransaction(.{
            .day = gs.clock.day_index,
            .amount = -payroll,
            .category = .payroll,
            .note = "monthly payroll",
        });
    }
    // … hull upkeep, HQ upkeep, loans, standing policies …
}

The first line is the whole monthly gate: not payday, nothing to do. Then a sequence of sub-phases whose order is again meaning (ranks are refreshed before payroll is summed, because rank scales pay). _ = try f(gs) discards a count the phase returns but a test wants; _ = f(gs) without try is a function that cannot fail. The map walk with entry.value_ptr is how every phase touches every person: a pointer, so the change sticks (Chapter 22).

43.5 Testing a phase on its own

Phases are called from advanceDay, but their tests do not go through it. medical.runMonthlyTurnover is called from runFinances on payday; its test calls it directly on a hand-built state:

src/sim/medical.zig
test "12.20/12.25: the restless hand in notice after a year (an inbox decision), the content stay" {
    var gs = GameState.init(std.testing.allocator, .{ .seed = 1220 });
    defer gs.deinit();
    _ = try gs.createCommander("T", .LC, .paymaster);
    _ = try @import("../gen/company_gen.zig").generateInto(&gs, "Alpha");
    // Content and fresh (and all thirty — age rolls are 12C.4's business):
    // nobody stirs however low the dice.
    gs.clock.day_index = 400;
    var ait = gs.people.iterator();
    while (ait.next()) |e| e.value_ptr.born_day = -30 * 365;
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 0), try runMonthlyTurnover(&gs));
    // Everyone miserable with a year in: notices land in the inbox, nobody has left yet.
    var pit = gs.people.iterator();
    while (pit.next()) |e| {
        e.value_ptr.morale = 5;
        e.value_ptr.fatigue = 90;
    }
    const notices = try runMonthlyTurnover(&gs);
    try std.testing.expect(notices > 0 and notices < gs.people.count());
    // Exhausted and unhappy is one in six a month (2d6 <= 4), not a stampede.
    const pct = notices * 100 / @as(u32, @intCast(gs.people.count()));
    try std.testing.expect(pct >= 6 and pct <= 30);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, notices), gs.event_queue.pending.items.len);
    // …
}

This is the general testing style of the simulation, and it is worth naming its parts. Build the smallest state that exercises the rule (a commander and one generated company). Set the clock and the fields directly, which tests may do. Call the phase. Assert on state, including a statistical bound (pct between 6 and 30) that is safe because the dice are seeded and the number is in fact fixed. The test also documents the rule in its name and comments better than any prose could.

The one test that does go through advanceDay is the payday test at the bottom of tick.zig:

test "payday fires on the 1st and only on the 1st" {
    var gs = GameState.init(std.testing.allocator, .{ .start_funds = 1_000_000 });
    defer gs.deinit();
    _ = try gs.hirePerson("Natasha", "Kerensky", .mekwarrior); // 1500/mo regular → Corporal ×1.1 on payday (12B.4)

    // Jan 1 (day 0) start → advancing 30 days lands on Jan 31: no payroll yet.
    for (0..30) |_| _ = try advanceDay(&gs);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 1_000_000), gs.funds);

    // One more day → Feb 1: payroll posts, a month of service XP lands.
    _ = try advanceDay(&gs);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i64, 998_350), gs.funds);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 1), gs.ledger.transactions.items.len);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, monthly_service_xp), gs.people.values()[0].xp);
}

Thirty-one days on a fresh state with one hire, and an exact number: 1,650 C-bills, which is 1,500 for a regular mekwarrior times 1.1 for the corporal's rank she is promoted to on the same payday, in that order, because refreshRanks runs before monthlyPayroll. If someone reorders those two lines, this number changes and the test says so.

Guided reading

  1. src/sim/clock.zig: Date, DayPhase (read its doc comment about order), Clock, and the leap-year test.
  2. src/sim/tick.zig: advanceDay, then in order runPolicies, runStockPolicies, runTravel, runSupplyConsumption, runMarkets, runContracts, runFinances. Each is under a hundred lines. For each, write down in one line what must already have happened today for it to be correct.
  3. One phase in another file, fully: medical.runDailyHealing in src/sim/medical.zig. Note the same map-walk-and-mutate shape.
  4. battle.runDaily in src/sim/battle.zig: fifteen lines that decide whether today is a battle day for each contract. Chapter 46 follows the call into resolveEngagement.
  5. The tests at the bottom of tick.zig and the turnover test in medical.zig.

Exercises

Exercise 43.1 · The two clocks stay in step warm-up

Write a test in tick.zig that advances a fresh default campaign 365 days and asserts both that day_index is 365 and that the date is 1 January 3026. Is 3025 a leap year? What would the date be if it were?

Solution 
test "the calendar and the day index move in lockstep" {
    var gs = GameState.init(std.testing.allocator, .{});
    defer gs.deinit();
    for (0..365) |_| try advanceDay(&gs);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 365), gs.clock.day_index);
    const clock_mod = @import("clock.zig");
    try std.testing.expectEqual(clock_mod.Date{ .year = 3026, .month = 1, .day = 1 }, gs.clock.date);
}

3025 is not divisible by 4, so it has 365 days and the year rolls over exactly. In a leap year (3024 is one, as the clock test in clock.zig checks) 365 days from 1 January lands on 31 December. expectEqual compares the two Date structs field by field. Note that the full year of ticks, with all phases, runs in well under a second: the phases are cheap when there is nothing to do.

Exercise 43.2 · Add a phase challenge

Add a weekly phase runWeeklyPeace that increments a new counter gs.stats.weeks_at_peace whenever a week ends with no active contract. Decide where in advanceDay it belongs and say why. Write a test on a hand-built state. Then confirm the golden-master test still passes and explain why it was never at risk.

Solution
src/sim/state.zig, in Stats
    people_kia: u32 = 0,
    /// Weeks with no contract under way.
    weeks_at_peace: u32 = 0,
src/sim/tick.zig
    if (gs.clock.day_index % 7 == 0 and gs.clock.day_index > 0) {
        try medical.runWeeklyRest(gs); // morale_fatigue phase
        runTrainingLances(gs); // lance roles (Stage 12)
        runWeeklyPeace(gs);
    }

/// A week with no contract under way is a week of peace.
fn runWeeklyPeace(gs: *GameState) void {
    var it = gs.contracts.iterator();
    while (it.next()) |entry| if (entry.value_ptr.status == .active) return;
    gs.stats.weeks_at_peace += 1;
}

test "peace is counted weekly and only without an active contract" {
    var gs = GameState.init(std.testing.allocator, .{});
    defer gs.deinit();
    for (0..14) |_| try advanceDay(&gs);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 2), gs.stats.weeks_at_peace);
}

It belongs in the existing weekly block after runContracts and runReturns have run, so that a contract that ended today counts as over, and after runWeeklyRest so it reads naturally with the other "end of week" bookkeeping. It returns void and is called without try. Days 7 and 14 are the two weekly ticks in fourteen days, hence 2. The golden master was never at risk because the new phase reads only state and a seeded clock: two campaigns with the same seed still do the same thing. It would have been at risk had the phase read anything outside the state, which is the subject of Chapter 49. (Stats is saved field by field in store.zig, so the new counter is not persisted until you add it there; Chapter 47 shows how.)

Exercise 43.3 · Find the phase practice

Without running anything, answer from the source: (a) which phase turns a wounded person's wound_heal_day into a healed status, and what must be true of medbay_admitted first? (b) Which phase moves money on a standing cash policy, and what stops it from sending twice? (c) If you moved runFinances to the top of advanceDay, name one test that would change its expected number.

Solution

(a) medical.runDailyHealing; a wound only starts healing once the player has admitted the person (medbay_admitted), which is the rule the Person field's comment states and the test "wounded only heal once admitted" in commands.zig checks. (b) runPolicies in tick.zig; it skips an entity whose balance is at or above the floor, whose monthly cap is spent, or that already has a courier in flight (in_flight). (c) Any test that pins a balance after a payday, because costs posted by the day's other phases would no longer be on the books when payroll is counted; the payday test's 998,350 is the obvious one, and the round-trip test in store.zig compares hashes that include funds.

Check your understanding

  1. What is the canonical timestamp, and what is the calendar for?
    Answerday_index: u32, days since campaign start, used for every deadline and comparison; the Date is for rendering and for detecting the first of the month.
  2. Why is there a day_index > 0 in the weekly gate?
    AnswerBecause 0 % 7 == 0: without it, the weekly phases would run on the campaign's first day.
  3. Why are resetWeeklyThroughput and runTrainingLances called without try?
    AnswerThey return void, not an error union; try on a non-error value is a compile error.
  4. Give two orderings in advanceDay that carry meaning.
    AnswerDeliveries (runTravel) before consumption; maintenance before battles; rollMonthly before battle.runDaily; runFinances last; refreshRanks before monthlyPayroll inside finance.
  5. How is a phase like runMonthlyTurnover tested?
    AnswerDirectly, on a hand-built state with fields set to force the situation, asserting on the resulting state (inbox length, statuses), not by advancing the calendar to a payday.
  6. Why does the index loop in runTravel not always increment?
    AnswerAfter orderedRemove(fi) the following item slides into slot fi, so incrementing would skip it.
What you learned.
  • A day is advanceDay: the clock ticks, then a fixed list of phases runs, each a function from *GameState to !void.
  • Weekly and monthly phases are gated by integer arithmetic on day_index and by date.day == 1; nothing reads a wall clock.
  • Order is meaning: what lands, heals, breaks or is paid depends on what ran before it, and tests pin those consequences with exact numbers.
  • Phases are tested in isolation on hand-built states; the whole pipeline is tested by a few end-to-end numbers like the payday test.
  • Adding a mechanic means choosing its phase, writing it as a function over the state, and testing it the same way.

44. Queries: the only way out

In this chapter you read the other door. Frontends never walk GameState to draw a screen; they call a query, which returns rows of formatted text plus the IDs a key handler will need, allocated from an arena the caller throws away after drawing. You will read one query end to end, learn the colour markup that lets one query serve two frontends, meet a bug that taught the project a rule, and extend a query yourself.

What you need from earlier chapters. Chapter 23 (format specifiers, especially width and alignment such as {s: <20} and {d: >3}, and allocPrint), Chapter 21 (ArrayListUnmanaged and toOwnedSlice), Chapter 20 (a per-call arena), Chapter 10 and Chapter 11 (slicing and searching strings), Chapter 13 (an enum with a method, used as a filter) and Chapter 27 (inline for over an enum's fields, in personRecord).

44.1 The contract

Every function in src/sim/queries.zig has the same first two parameters:

pub fn people(alloc: Alloc, gs: *GameState, filter: HallFilter) !People
pub fn hqDetail(alloc: Alloc, gs: *GameState, id: types.HqId) ![]const []const u8
pub fn manning(alloc: Alloc, gs: *GameState, company: types.ForceId) ![]ManningRow
pub fn personRecord(alloc: Alloc, gs: *GameState, id: types.PersonId) ![]const []const u8

An allocator and the state, then whatever selects the view. The allocator is never the state's arena. In the terminal client it is a frame arena that is reset before every draw; in a test it is a small arena created for the call; in the REPL it is a temporary arena around one print. The query allocates freely into it (hundreds of small strings for a busy screen) and frees nothing, and the caller drops the whole arena when the screen has been drawn. This is the third lifetime from Chapter 20: not the process, not the campaign, but one frame.

The return value is plain data with no methods and no pointers back into the state: strings already formatted, and typed IDs next to them. The file is 4,000 lines because there are many screens, not because any query is complicated.

44.2 One query, end to end

The People screen's query is a good first read because it is one loop:

src/sim/queries.zig
pub const PersonRow = struct {
    id: types.PersonId,
    text: []const u8,
    // …
};

pub const People = struct {
    header: []const u8,
    rows: []PersonRow,
    total: usize,
    // …
};

/// Everyone on the payroll (active, wounded, missing), filtered by role group.
pub fn people(alloc: Alloc, gs: *GameState, filter: HallFilter) !People {
    var rows: std.ArrayListUnmanaged(PersonRow) = .empty;
    var total: usize = 0;
    var it = gs.people.iterator();
    while (it.next()) |e| {
        const p = e.value_ptr;
        if (p.status == .kia or p.status == .retired or p.status == .resigned or p.status == .released) continue;
        total += 1;
        if (!filter.matches(p.role)) continue;
        if (filter == .wounded and p.status != .wounded) continue;
        if (filter == .unassigned and !isUnassigned(gs, p)) continue;
        const name = try p.rankedName(alloc);
        try rows.append(alloc, .{ .id = p.id, .text = try std.fmt.allocPrint(alloc, "{d: <4} {s: <20} {s: <15} {s: <7} {s: <5} {d: >3} {s} {s} {s: <11} {d: >3} {d: >3} {s: >7}", .{
            @intFromEnum(p.id),                                                             clip(name, 20),
            @tagName(p.role),                                                               @tagName(p.experience()),
            try skillsText(alloc, p),                                                       p.xp,
            try padMk(alloc, "", try stripMarkup(alloc, try statusText(alloc, gs, p)), 18), try padMk(alloc, "", try stripMarkup(alloc, try assignmentText(alloc, gs, p)), 22),
            clip(locationText(gs, p), 11),                                                  p.fatigue,
            p.morale,                                                                       try money(alloc, p.monthlySalary()),
        }) });
    }
    return .{
        .header = "id   name                 role            exp     skill  XP status             assignment             where       fat mor     pay",
        .rows = try rows.toOwnedSlice(alloc),
        .total = total,
    };
}

Walk it. The map iterator visits people in insertion order (Chapter 41), so the roster is stable from frame to frame. The departed are skipped before total is counted, so the header can say "12 of 30" when a filter is on. Then a row is one allocPrint with a long format string: {d: <4} left-aligns the ID in four columns, {s: <20} left-aligns the name in twenty, {d: >3} right-aligns fatigue in three, {s: >7} right-aligns the money. Everything the format string cannot do (clip a long name, strip colour codes before padding, format money with separators) is a small helper at the top of the file: clip, stripMarkup, padMk, money.

The row carries p.id beside its text. That is the second half of the contract: when the cursor is on row seven and the user presses D to fire, the key handler reads rows[7].id and builds .{ .fire = id }. It never has to work out which person row seven was, because the query told it.

The filter is an enum with a method, the pattern from Chapter 13:

pub const HallFilter = enum {
    all,
    combat, // mekwarriors, vehicle crews, aero pilots
    techs, // tech_mek / tech_mechanic / tech_aero / tech_ba / astech
    medical, // doctors, medics
    admin_command,
    admin_logistics,
    admin_transport,
    admin_hr,
    admin_finance,
    other, // infantry, battle armor, everything else
    unassigned, // personnel screen only: no seat, no HQ posting, no company
    wounded, // personnel screen only: anyone hurt, in the medbay or waiting

    pub fn matches(self: HallFilter, role: person_mod.Role) bool {
        return switch (self) {
            .all, .unassigned, .wounded => true,
            .combat => role == .mekwarrior or role == .vehicle_crew or role == .aero_pilot,
            .techs => role == .tech_mek or role == .tech_mechanic or role == .tech_aero or role == .tech_ba or role == .astech,
            .medical => role == .doctor or role == .medic,
            // …
        };
    }
};

The same enum serves the hiring hall and the people screen, and the client cycles it with a key. Because it is an exhaustive enum with a switch, adding a group is a two-line change and the compiler lists the switch.

44.3 Markup: one query, two frontends

Look at statusText's output being passed through stripMarkup above. Query text carries lightweight colour markup: {g}active{/} means "green until the reset", {c} is critical red, {a} amber, {d} dim, {p} purple, {s} selected. The terminal client's screen renders the codes into styles (Chapter 48); the REPL strips them; and inside a fixed-width column they must be removed before padding, or the invisible codes would count as characters and the columns would drift. That is what stripMarkup is for:

/// Remove `{x}` markup tokens (for fixed-width columns).
pub fn stripMarkup(alloc: Alloc, s: []const u8) ![]const u8 {
    var out: std.ArrayListUnmanaged(u8) = .empty;
    var i: usize = 0;
    while (i < s.len) : (i += 1) {
        if (s[i] == '{' and i + 2 < s.len and s[i + 2] == '}' and std.mem.indexOfScalar(u8, "agcsdtp/", s[i + 1]) != null) {
            i += 2;
            continue;
        }
        try out.append(alloc, s[i]);
    }
    return out.toOwnedSlice(alloc);
}

A hand-written scanner over a byte slice, the Chapter 11 kind. There is a trap here that Chapter 23 warned you about: a literal brace inside a format string must be doubled. So in a plain string literal the markup is "{g}active{/}", but inside an allocPrint format it is "{{g}}{s}{{/}}". You can see both forms in personRecord below. Get it wrong and the compiler complains about an invalid format specifier, which is a kinder failure than most template languages give you.

44.4 A longer query: the person record

The r key on the People screen opens a record, built by personRecord. It is eighty lines of out.append(alloc, try std.fmt.allocPrint(alloc, …)); here are the parts that teach something:

pub fn personRecord(alloc: Alloc, gs: *GameState, id: types.PersonId) ![]const []const u8 {
    var out: std.ArrayListUnmanaged([]const u8) = .empty;
    const p = gs.person(id) orelse return out.toOwnedSlice(alloc);
    const day = gs.clock.day_index;
    try out.append(alloc, try std.fmt.allocPrint(alloc, "{{a}}{s} {s} {s}{{/}}{s}  ·  {s} · {s} · {s}{s}", .{
        p.rank.abbrev(), p.first_name, p.last_name,
        if (p.callsign) |c| try std.fmt.allocPrint(alloc, " \"{s}\"", .{c}) else "",
        @tagName(p.role), @tagName(p.experience()), p.rank.name(),
        if (p.rank_pinned) " (pinned — :promote <id> <rank> unpin lets seats decide)" else "",
    }));
    // … status, assignment, unit …
    try out.append(alloc, "");
    try out.append(alloc, "skill               level   next   XP cost");
    inline for (@typeInfo(types.SkillType).@"enum".fields) |f| {
        const st: types.SkillType = @enumFromInt(f.value);
        if (p.skill(st)) |lvl| {
            const primary = st == p.role.primarySkill();
            if (lvl == 0) {
                try out.append(alloc, try std.fmt.allocPrint(alloc, "{s}{s: <19} {d: >5}   mastered{{/}}", .{ if (primary) "{a}" else "", f.name, lvl }));
            } else {
                const cost = person_mod.improveCost(lvl - 1);
                try out.append(alloc, try std.fmt.allocPrint(alloc, "{s}{s: <19} {d: >5} {d: >6} {d: >8}{s}{{/}}", .{ if (primary) "{a}" else "", f.name, lvl, lvl - 1, cost, if (p.xp >= cost) "  {g}affordable{/}" else "" }));
            }
        }
    }
    // … training, abilities, age, loyalty, shares, record, awards, injuries …
    try out.append(alloc, try std.fmt.allocPrint(alloc, "available   {s}", .{if (p.isAvailable(day)) "{g}yes{/}" else "{c}no{/}"}));
    return out.toOwnedSlice(alloc);
}

Three things. First, an unknown ID returns an empty list rather than an error; a screen with nothing to show is not a failure. Second, the skills table is an inline for over the SkillType enum's fields (Chapter 27): the loop is unrolled at compile time, one iteration per skill, and f.name is the skill's name as a compile-time string, so adding a skill to the enum adds a row here with no edit. Third, the if … else "" idiom inside argument tuples: an optional piece of text is an empty string when absent, which keeps every line a single allocPrint.

44.5 The bug that made a rule

The original guide records a bug worth retelling because its fix is a query. The HQ screen once mapped the cursor row to a facility by position, assuming the facility table started on row one. When the tier section above it grew (a field HQ explains how to become regional; a regional one does not), every row shifted and the u key upgraded the wrong facility. The fix:

/// Which facility a row of `hqDetail` names, or null. The tier section
/// above the facility table varies in length (field HQs explain how to
/// become regional), so the HQ screen's `u` reads the cursor through this
/// rather than by position.
pub fn hqFacilityAtRow(alloc: Alloc, gs: *GameState, id: types.HqId, row: usize) !?@import("../domain/hq.zig").FacilityKind {
    const lines = try hqDetail(alloc, gs, id);
    if (row >= lines.len) return null;
    // The table runs from the "facility" header to the next blank line.
    var header: ?usize = null;
    for (lines, 0..) |l, i| if (std.mem.startsWith(u8, l, "facility ")) {
        header = i;
        break;
    };
    const start = (header orelse return null) + 1;
    if (row < start) return null;
    for (lines[start..row + 1]) |l| if (l.len == 0) return null;
    var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, lines[row], ' ');
    const tag = it.next() orelse return null;
    return std.meta.stringToEnum(@import("../domain/hq.zig").FacilityKind, tag);
}

It reads the rendered rows back, finds the header, checks the row is inside the table, and parses the first word back into the enum with std.meta.stringToEnum. The return type !?FacilityKind is "may fail to allocate; may be no facility". A test builds an HQ, renders it, and checks that every row maps to the facility it names and the header maps to null. The rule of thumb the project took from it: if a key handler needs to know what a row means, ask a query, never count.

44.6 Queries that return structure

Not every query returns lines. When the client needs to act on numbers, the query returns a struct per row and lets the client format the numbers it needs:

pub const ManningRow = struct {
    role: person_mod.Role,
    have: u32,
    need: u32,
    text: []const u8,
};

pub fn manning(alloc: Alloc, gs: *GameState, company: types.ForceId) ![]ManningRow {
    const personnel = @import("personnel.zig");
    const needs = personnel.manningNeeds(gs, company);
    var out: std.ArrayListUnmanaged(ManningRow) = .empty;
    // … tech-hours needed against tech-hours available …
    for (needs) |n| {
        const have = personnel.manningHave(gs, company, n.role);
        const open = n.need -| have;
        const why = /* … */;
        try out.append(alloc, .{ .role = n.role, .have = have, .need = n.need, .text = try std.fmt.allocPrint(alloc,
            "{s: <16} {d: >5} {d: >5} {s}{d: >5}{{/}}   {{d}}{s}{{/}}",
            .{ @tagName(n.role), have, n.need, if (open > 0) "{c}" else "{g}", open, why }) });
    }
    return out.toOwnedSlice(alloc);
}

n.need -| have is saturating subtraction (Chapter 4): zero when the company has more than it needs, never negative. The row carries have and need as numbers as well as in the text, so the raise-a-company wizard can total them without parsing its own output. You will see this query again in Chapter 50, because it is what redraws after the c key crews a company.

Guided reading

  1. src/sim/queries.zig, lines 1 to about 100: the helpers money, padCells, padMk, clip, planetName, personName. Each is a few lines and you will see them in every query.
  2. status and desk (the status strip and the Desk screen), then people, then personRecord.
  3. hqDetail and hqFacilityAtRow, and the test "the HQ screen's facility rows map back to facilities whatever sits above them" at the bottom of the file.
  4. manning, toe and toeFiltered: the structured kind.
  5. summary and rating: two queries that compute rather than list. rating is the game's reputation formula and is also called by the tick (queries.ratingScore in runFinances), an example of a query being pure enough to use as a rule.

Exercises

Exercise 44.1 · One more line on the record practice

Add a line to personRecord showing this person's salary as a percentage of the outfit's monthly payroll (gs.monthlyPayroll()). Only one file changes. Then write a test that hires a 1,500-a-month mekwarrior and a 400-a-month astech and checks the exact line for the mekwarrior.

Solution
src/sim/queries.zig, in personRecord, before the skills header
    {
        const payroll = gs.monthlyPayroll();
        if (payroll > 0) try out.append(alloc, try std.fmt.allocPrint(alloc, "payroll     {d}% of the outfit's monthly payroll", .{@divTrunc(p.monthlySalary() * 100, payroll)}));
    }
test "the record shows the payroll share" {
    var gs = GameState.init(std.testing.allocator, .{});
    defer gs.deinit();
    var arena = std.heap.ArenaAllocator.init(std.testing.allocator);
    defer arena.deinit();
    const a = arena.allocator();
    const id = try gs.hirePerson("Lori", "Kalmar", .mekwarrior);
    _ = try gs.hirePerson("Clay", "Cluny", .astech);
    const rec = try personRecord(a, &gs, id);
    var found: ?[]const u8 = null;
    for (rec) |line| if (std.mem.startsWith(u8, line, "payroll ")) {
        found = line;
    };
    // 1500 of 1900: seventy-eight percent, truncated.
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("payroll     78% of the outfit's monthly payroll", found.?);
}

Integer arithmetic throughout: @divTrunc because CBills is signed (Chapter 45), multiply before dividing to keep the precision, and the payroll > 0 guard because a state with nobody hired would divide by zero. 1500 × 100 / 1900 is 78.94, truncated to 78. Notice the block { … } around the two lines: it scopes payroll so the name cannot collide with anything later in this long function, a habit worth copying in a codebase where shadowing is an error.

Exercise 44.2 · Test a filtered query practice

Write a test for people: hire one mekwarrior and one tech_mek, query with .techs, and assert one row, a total of two, the right id on the row, and that the row text contains the tech's last name. Then query with .all and assert the order matches hiring order.

Solution 
test "the people query filters by role group and keeps ids" {
    var gs = GameState.init(std.testing.allocator, .{});
    defer gs.deinit();
    const pilot = try gs.hirePerson("Grayson", "Carlyle", .mekwarrior);
    const tech = try gs.hirePerson("Clay", "Cluny", .tech_mek);
    var arena = std.heap.ArenaAllocator.init(std.testing.allocator);
    defer arena.deinit();
    const a = arena.allocator();
    const techs = try people(a, &gs, .techs);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 1), techs.rows.len);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 2), techs.total);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(tech, techs.rows[0].id);
    try std.testing.expect(std.mem.indexOf(u8, techs.rows[0].text, "Cluny") != null);
    const everyone = try people(a, &gs, .all);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 2), everyone.rows.len);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(pilot, everyone.rows[0].id);
}

The three-line arena setup is the one the original guide called out as appearing in every query test. total counts before the filter and rows after, which is the property the header relies on. The order assertion holds because gs.people is an ordered map.

Exercise 44.3 · Markup round trip warm-up

Write a test that stripMarkup turns "{g}ok{/} now" into "ok now". Then read stripMarkup again and say what it does with "{x}", which is not a colour, and with a lone "{" at the end of a string.

Solution 
test "markup strips to plain text" {
    var arena = std.heap.ArenaAllocator.init(std.testing.allocator);
    defer arena.deinit();
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("ok now", try stripMarkup(arena.allocator(), "{g}ok{/} now"));
}

"{x}" is copied through unchanged, because 'x' is not in "agcsdtp/"; only the eight known codes are treated as markup. A lone '{' at the end is also copied, because the check i + 2 < s.len fails before any out-of-bounds index is attempted. The function is written so that it can never panic on any input, which matters for text that came from a data file or a player.

Check your understanding

  1. Why does a query take an allocator rather than using gs.allocator()?
    AnswerQuery results live for one frame, not for the campaign; allocating them from the campaign arena would leak a screen's worth of strings on every redraw. The caller passes a frame arena it resets after drawing.
  2. Why does PersonRow carry an id?
    AnswerSo a key handler can act on the highlighted row (fire, admit, assign) by reading the ID beside the text instead of re-deriving which person the row was.
  3. What is {{g}} in a format string, and what is {g} in a plain literal?
    AnswerThe same markup token: braces must be doubled inside a format string because { and } are format syntax, while a plain string literal needs no escaping.
  4. Why must markup be stripped before padding a column?
    AnswerThe tokens are invisible when rendered but count as bytes in {s: <18}, so padding a marked-up string yields columns that are too short by three bytes per token.
  5. What went wrong on the HQ screen, and what is the resulting rule?
    AnswerThe key handler mapped cursor rows to facilities by position; when the section above the table changed length, the mapping was off by the difference. Rule: if a key handler needs to know what a row means, ask a query.
  6. How does personRecord list skills without naming any?
    AnswerWith inline for over @typeInfo(types.SkillType).@"enum".fields, which unrolls one iteration per enum variant at compile time and provides each name as a string.
What you learned.
  • Every query takes an allocator and the state and returns plain data: formatted rows with typed IDs beside them, or small structs of numbers plus text.
  • Callers pass a frame arena and reset it after drawing, so query results cost nothing to free.
  • Row text carries {g}…{/} markup that the terminal renders and the REPL strips; braces are doubled inside format strings.
  • A key handler that needs the meaning of a row asks a query (hqFacilityAtRow) rather than counting rows.
  • Reflection (inline for over an enum) keeps tables in step with the types they display.

45. Money without floats

In this chapter you see how a game whose whole subject is money gets by without a single floating-point number. Every amount is a 64-bit integer, every multiplier is basis points, and money moves in exactly one way: a ledger entry and a treasury balance changing together. You will read that one function, the ledger it feeds, and the summaries built on top, and you will test the rounding rule that makes it all reproducible.

What you need from earlier chapters. Chapter 4 (i64, @divTrunc versus @divFloor, and why signed division must name its rounding), Chapter 5 (why floats are not exact and why that matters for money), Chapter 14 (a small tagged union, Treasury, switched on with payload captures), Chapter 12 (a struct with defaulted fields used as a record), Chapter 21 (a list you only ever append to) and Chapter 27 (an array sized by an enum's variant count).

45.1 Two types and one function

The entire monetary type system of IRON LEDGER is at the top of src/domain/types.zig:

src/domain/types.zig
/// All money is integer C-bills. No floats in the ledger, ever.
pub const CBills = i64;

/// Basis points (1/100 of a percent) for all multiplier math, so payment
/// formulas stay in integer arithmetic. 10_000 bp == ×1.0.
pub const Bp = i64;

pub fn applyBp(amount: CBills, bp: Bp) CBills {
    return @divTrunc(amount * bp, 10_000);
}

test "basis point math stays in integers" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(CBills, 1_500), applyBp(1_500, 10_000));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(CBills, 900), applyBp(1_500, 6_000));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(CBills, 4_800), applyBp(1_500, 32_000));
}

Both are aliases for i64. The aliases buy readability, not safety: the compiler will happily let you add a Bp to a CBills, and the discipline of not doing so is a house rule enforced by review and by the fact that every multiplier goes through applyBp. A 10 percent markup is applyBp(cost, 11_000). A green pilot's 0.6 salary multiplier is 6_000. An elite pilot's 3.2 is 32_000. The test pins those three.

Why not a f64 and cost * 1.1? Chapter 5 gave the general answer: 0.1 is not representable in binary floating point, so a chain of multiplications drifts, and two machines (or two compiler versions) can drift differently. For a game whose determinism test hashes the treasury balance, "differently" is a failing build. With integers, 1_500 * 6_000 / 10_000 is 900 on every machine ever made.

The one subtlety is rounding. amount * bp is exact in i64 for any amount the game will see (a trillion C-bills times a hundred thousand basis points is far inside 63 bits). The division is where a fraction of a C-bill is lost, and Zig makes you say how: @divTrunc rounds toward zero, so applyBp(-1_500, 6_000) is -900 and applyBp(-1, 5_000) is 0, not -1. @divFloor would give -1 for the latter. Neither is wrong; what would be wrong is not choosing, and Zig does not let you write / on signed integers at runtime for exactly that reason (Chapter 4, and appendix A4 shows the error).

45.2 The ledger

Money is recorded in one place, a list of transactions that only ever grows:

src/econ/finance.zig
pub const Category = enum {
    contract_payment,
    advance,
    salvage,
    battle_loss_comp,
    breach_clawback,
    payroll,
    hardship_pay, // remote-deployment payroll bonus (ARCH §9.6)
    maintenance,
    hull_upkeep, // per-hull monthly carry cost, running or not (ARCH §9.8)
    parts,
    supplies,
    local_supplies, // bought beyond the ring at 2–4× (ARCH §9.6)
    freight,
    unit_purchase,
    unit_sale,
    fabrication, // structural parts made at a regional HQ (ARCH §9.8)
    fund_transfer, // outfit treasury ↔ company local funds (ARCH §9.8)
    hq_construction,
    hq_upkeep,
    transport_charter,
    loan_principal,
    loan_interest,
    event,
    misc,
};

pub const Transaction = struct {
    day: u32,
    amount: types.CBills, // signed: income +, expense −
    category: Category,
    /// Cost/profit center; .none = outfit-level overhead.
    company: types.ForceId = .none,
    /// HQ cost center (Stage 9A).
    hq: types.HqId = .none,
    contract: types.ContractId = .none,
    note: []const u8 = "",
};

pub const Ledger = struct {
    transactions: std.ArrayListUnmanaged(Transaction) = .empty,

    pub fn post(self: *Ledger, alloc: std.mem.Allocator, txn: Transaction) !void {
        try self.transactions.append(alloc, txn);
    }

    pub fn balance(self: *const Ledger) types.CBills {
        var total: types.CBills = 0;
        for (self.transactions.items) |t| total += t.amount;
        return total;
    }

    /// Net for one company over [from_day, to_day] — the monthly P&L view.
    pub fn companyNet(self: *const Ledger, company: types.ForceId, from_day: u32, to_day: u32) types.CBills {
        var total: types.CBills = 0;
        for (self.transactions.items) |t| {
            if (t.company == company and t.day >= from_day and t.day <= to_day) total += t.amount;
        }
        return total;
    }
};

A Transaction is a record: a day, a signed amount, a category, and three typed-ID tags that default to .none. The sign convention is in the comment and nowhere else; income is positive, expense negative, and every caller writes .amount = -cost when spending. The tags are what make the ledger a database rather than a log: "the P&L of Alpha Company for March" is companyNet, a filter over the same list, and "what has this contract paid so far" is another filter. There is no second copy of any total anywhere that could disagree with the list.

Ledger stores no allocator; post takes one, and in the game it is always the campaign arena via gs.allocator(). The two finance tests at the bottom of the file use std.testing.allocator and call ledger.deinit(alloc), which is the only reason that method exists.

45.3 The only way money moves

A ledger on its own would let a balance and its history drift apart. The game prevents that by having exactly one function that does both:

src/sim/state.zig
/// Where money lives (Stage 9A, ARCH §11): the outfit's central treasury,
/// an HQ's funds, or a deployed company's operating fund. Spending resolves
/// where the spender stands — the treasury cannot teleport.
pub const Treasury = union(enum) {
    outfit,
    hq: types.HqId,
    company: types.ForceId,
};

/// Post to the outfit's central treasury (the common case).
pub fn postTransaction(self: *GameState, txn: finance_mod.Transaction) !void {
    try self.postTreasury(.outfit, txn);
}

/// The only way money moves: ledger entry + the named treasury's balance,
/// in lockstep. Balances MAY go negative (obligations don't wait);
/// purchases that should refuse instead call `debitOrRefuse` first.
pub fn postTreasury(self: *GameState, treasury: Treasury, txn: finance_mod.Transaction) !void {
    try self.ledger.post(self.allocator(), txn);
    switch (treasury) {
        .outfit => self.funds += txn.amount,
        .hq => |id| if (self.hqs.getPtr(id)) |h| {
            h.funds += txn.amount;
        },
        .company => |id| if (self.forces.getPtr(id)) |f| {
            f.local_funds += txn.amount;
        },
    }
}

pub fn treasuryBalance(self: *GameState, treasury: Treasury) types.CBills {
    return switch (treasury) {
        .outfit => self.funds,
        .hq => |id| if (self.hqs.getPtr(id)) |h| h.funds else 0,
        .company => |id| if (self.forces.getPtr(id)) |f| f.local_funds else 0,
    };
}

Treasury is the small tagged union the guide mentioned: "which till" is a typed value, and a switch over it is exhaustive, so a fourth kind of treasury would have to be handled in both functions before the program compiled. postTreasury appends to the ledger and then adjusts the one named balance, in that order, in one function, with no early return between them. If post fails (out of memory), the balance is untouched and the error propagates. There is no code path in which one happens without the other.

Read the doc comment's second sentence: balances may go negative. Payroll on the first of the month is posted whether or not the outfit can pay it; the consequence is an insolvent turn (Chapter 42's advance), not a skipped payroll. Purchases that should refuse are a separate, four-line function in commands.zig:

fn debitPurchase(gs: *GameState, treasury: state_mod.Treasury, txn: @import("../econ/finance.zig").Transaction) Error!void {
    if (gs.treasuryBalance(treasury) < -txn.amount) return Error.InsufficientTreasury;
    try gs.postTreasury(treasury, txn);
}

Check, then post. Because txn.amount is negative for a purchase, the comparison is against -txn.amount. This is the "all checks, then all effects" discipline of Chapter 42 in its smallest form.

45.4 Sums with different filters

Every report about money is a pass over the list with a filter. The P&L view is the most general:

src/econ/finance.zig
/// Which entity's books to read (Stage 9A).
pub const EntityFilter = union(enum) {
    all,
    company: types.ForceId,
    hq: types.HqId,

    pub fn matches(self: EntityFilter, t: *const Transaction) bool {
        return switch (self) {
            .all => true,
            .company => |id| t.company == id,
            .hq => |id| t.hq == id,
        };
    }
};

pub const Summary = struct {
    income: types.CBills = 0,
    expenses: types.CBills = 0, // stored positive
    by_category: [category_count]types.CBills = @splat(0),

    pub const category_count = @typeInfo(Category).@"enum".fields.len;

    pub fn net(self: *const Summary) types.CBills {
        return self.income - self.expenses;
    }

    pub fn category(self: *const Summary, cat: Category) types.CBills {
        return self.by_category[@intFromEnum(cat)];
    }
};

/// Summarize [from_day, to_day] for the whole outfit or one entity's books.
pub fn summarize(ledger: *const Ledger, from_day: u32, to_day: u32, filter: EntityFilter) Summary {
    var s: Summary = .{};
    for (ledger.transactions.items) |*t| {
        if (t.day < from_day or t.day > to_day) continue;
        if (!filter.matches(t)) continue;
        s.by_category[@intFromEnum(t.category)] += t.amount;
        if (t.amount >= 0) s.income += t.amount else s.expenses -= t.amount;
    }
    return s;
}

Two things from Part 3 are doing quiet work here. by_category is an array sized by @typeInfo(Category).@"enum".fields.len and indexed by @intFromEnum, so adding a category grows the array and the totals with no other change (Exercise 45.3 confirms it). And @splat(0) fills the array with zeros in the default value. The function itself is a filter and two accumulators, kept separate so a statement can show income and expenses rather than one net number, which is what the Ledger screen draws.

The rest of the money code is variations on this: gs.monthlyPayroll() sums monthlySalary() over active people; a person's salary is applyBp(applyBp(role.baseSalary(), experience.salaryMultBp()), rank.payBp()), three integers multiplied in two steps; a contract's monthly net is base pay through a chain of basis-point terms; a rating letter's pay multiplier is a Bp looked up from a table. There is not a float anywhere in src/econ, and a grep for f64 under src/sim and src/domain finds only the star map's coordinates, which are distances, not money.

45.5 Where a C-bill is lost

With integer division, every multiplication that is not by a whole number loses a fraction, and it is worth knowing where. The rule the code follows is: multiply everything first, divide once, truncate toward zero. applyBp(applyBp(x, a), b) truncates twice, which is a design choice the salary formula accepts: a pilot's pay is computed the same way every payday, so the truncation is consistent, and a C-bill a month is not gameplay. What would be gameplay is a truncation that differs between the amount debited and the amount credited, which is why transferFunds moves one computed amount to both sides rather than computing it twice.

The exercise below asks you to pin the truncation direction in a test, so that anyone who later "fixes" @divTrunc to @divFloor learns from the suite that negative amounts round differently.

Guided reading

  1. src/domain/types.zig, the first twenty lines and the two enums with methods (ExperienceLevel.salaryMultBp, Quality.maintenanceModifier). Note that the multiplier table is in basis points.
  2. src/econ/finance.zig, all of it (162 lines). The two tests at the bottom are the clearest specification of the ledger's semantics.
  3. src/sim/state.zig: Treasury, postTransaction, postTreasury, treasuryBalance, treasuryTags, transferFunds, monthlyPayroll.
  4. src/sim/commands.zig: debitPurchase, then the .transfer, .take_loan and .buy_listing arms to see the check-then-post pattern with different treasuries.
  5. src/domain/person.zig: monthlySalary and severance, two formulas that are nothing but applyBp and @divTrunc.
  6. src/sim/queries.zig: ledger and money (the thousands-separator formatter), to see how integers become the text on the Ledger screen.

Exercises

Exercise 45.1 · Pin the rounding warm-up

Add a test to types.zig that fixes the behaviour of applyBp on negative amounts and on fractions below one C-bill: applyBp(-1_500, 6_000), applyBp(-1, 5_000), applyBp(1, 5_000) and a ten percent markup on 1,500. Predict each value before running.

Solution 
test "basis points truncate toward zero on both signs" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(CBills, -900), applyBp(-1_500, 6_000));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(CBills, 0), applyBp(-1, 5_000));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(CBills, 0), applyBp(1, 5_000));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(CBills, 1_650), applyBp(1_500, 11_000));
}

Half a C-bill truncates to zero in both directions, which is the @divTrunc behaviour. Had the function used @divFloor, the second case would be -1 and the test would fail, which is the point: the direction is now a documented decision rather than an accident of which builtin someone reached for.

Exercise 45.2 · One till, not the other practice

Write a test in state.zig that creates a commander (which founds an HQ with its own treasury), posts a 1,000 C-bill expense to that HQ with postTreasury, and asserts three things: the HQ's balance fell by exactly 1,000, the outfit's funds did not change, and the ledger grew by one entry. Then use finance.summarize with an .hq filter and check the expense appears.

Solution 
test "an HQ treasury pays and the outfit's does not" {
    var gs = GameState.init(std.testing.allocator, .{ .seed = 3 });
    defer gs.deinit();
    _ = try gs.createCommander("T", .LC, .paymaster);
    const hq = gs.hqs.keys()[0];
    const outfit_before = gs.funds;
    const hq_before = gs.treasuryBalance(.{ .hq = hq });
    const txns = gs.ledger.transactions.items.len;
    try gs.postTreasury(.{ .hq = hq }, .{
        .day = gs.clock.day_index,
        .amount = -1_000,
        .category = .misc,
        .hq = hq,
        .note = "exercise",
    });
    try std.testing.expectEqual(hq_before - 1_000, gs.treasuryBalance(.{ .hq = hq }));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(outfit_before, gs.funds);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(txns + 1, gs.ledger.transactions.items.len);
    const s = finance_mod.summarize(&gs.ledger, 0, 0, .{ .hq = hq });
    try std.testing.expect(s.expenses >= 1_000);
}

Two details.
