  4. One test of each kind: domain/meklab.zig "12.17: TechManual tables", domain/rat.zig's cross-check, sim/commands.zig "insolvency holds the turn; bankruptcy ends the campaign", persist/store.zig "12.17: a v5 store upgrades in place", tui/app.zig "size tiers follow the documented thresholds".
  5. docs/repl_smoke.sh, all of it (it is short), and the first fifty lines of docs/tui_smoke.py.

Exercises

Exercise 49.1 · Break the golden master practice

Do what 49.2 describes: add a file-level var to tick.zig, use it to change funds in runFinances, and run the suite. Record which tests fail. Then change the global so that it affects something the hash does not read (a log line's text, say) and run again. What do you conclude about the hash's coverage?

Solution

With gs.funds -= paydays_seen, four tests fail: the golden master, the store round trip, and the two payday tests, all with numbers off by a few C-bills. With the global only appended to a log line (try gs.log(.finance, .{}, "payday {d}", .{paydays_seen})), nothing fails, because hash() does not read log text and no test pins that line. Conclusion: the hash is a coarse instrument by design; it guards gameplay state, not every byte. A global that only affected presentation would slip past it, which is acceptable, and a global that affected the dice or the money would not, which is what matters. Remove the global when you are done.

Exercise 49.2 · A second golden master practice

The original test's script never creates a commander, so no HQ, no market and no contract is exercised. Write a second golden-master test whose script is create_commander, new_company and sixty days, and confirm it passes. Why is it worth having both?

Solution 
test "golden master with a commander and a company" {
    const script = [_]Command{
        .{ .create_commander = .{ .name = "Erik Kalmar", .origin = .CC, .profession = .quartermaster } },
        .{ .new_company = "Alpha" },
        .{ .advance_days = 60 },
    };
    var hashes: [2]u64 = undefined;
    for (&hashes) |*out| {
        var gs = GameState.init(std.testing.allocator, .{ .seed = 7 });
        defer gs.deinit();
        for (script) |cmd| _ = try execute(&gs, cmd);
        out.* = gs.hash();
    }
    try std.testing.expectEqual(hashes[0], hashes[1]);
}

It passes. The original script exercises hiring, the tick and firing; this one exercises company generation (hundreds of dice from the .generation stream), the starter HQ, market refreshes and two paydays with a real payroll. A global or an unordered iteration in any of those would show up here and not in the original. Golden masters are cheap; the more of the code a script reaches, the more the property is worth. (The store round-trip test, which plays forty days with a contract, is in effect a third one.)

Exercise 49.3 · Pin the dice warm-up

Write a test in rng.zig that pins the first two .battle rolls for seed 42 to their literal values. Find the values by printing them once. What would cause this test to fail, and would that be a bug?

Solution 
test "the first battle rolls for seed 42 are pinned" {
    var r = Rng.init(42);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 4), r.roll2d6(.battle));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 9), r.roll2d6(.battle));
}

It fails if the seed derivation in Rng.init changes, if the stream order in the Stream enum changes (the index feeds the seed), or if a future Zig release changes DefaultPrng's algorithm. None of those is a bug in the game's logic, but all of them silently change every campaign's dice and make old seeds unreplayable, which is worth knowing about the moment it happens. A pinned-dice test is the cheapest possible alarm for "the random stream moved".

Check your understanding

  1. What does the golden-master test assert, and how long does it take?
    AnswerTwo campaigns with seed 42 and the same six-command script produce equal hash() values after ninety days each; a fraction of a second.
  2. Name three faults it catches.
    AnswerA global mutable counter, a PRNG created outside the dice bag, iteration over an unordered hash map; also a wall-clock read (structurally impossible) and reads of stale memory.
  3. Why did adding a global counter also break the payday tests?
    AnswerThe counter changed the funds those tests pin to exact numbers; they fail on the arithmetic, not on determinism.
  4. What is refAllDecls for?
    AnswerZig compiles only what is referenced; the test references every public declaration so that dead or unreferenced code with a type error still fails the build.
  5. When does a test use an exact number and when a bound?
    AnswerExact for arithmetic (payroll), bounds for dice-driven behaviour (turnover, battles), even though the seed makes both deterministic; the choice states what the test means.
  6. What does "a change is done" mean in this project?
    Answerzig build test --summary all is green (which also builds the client), and both smoke scripts pass.
What you learned.
  • The golden-master test runs the same script twice from the same seed and compares hashes; it is the enforcement of the purity rule.
  • A file-level var that touches state breaks it and several pinned-number tests at once; a change that reads only state and seeded dice does not.
  • The 246 tests are grouped by kind (domain, data, sim, persistence, client, reflective) and live next to their code; two smoke scripts cover the frontends.
  • Seeded dice make every number exact; tests choose exact values for arithmetic and bounds for dice to say what they mean.
  • A bug is reproducible from a seed and a script, and several tests are exactly that.

50. One keypress, end to end

In this chapter you follow a single keypress through every layer you have read: from a byte on a file descriptor, through the client's dispatch, into a command, through validation and mutation, back out as a result, onto the screen through a query, and (not yet) into the save file. Nothing new is introduced; the point is to see the parts you know as one motion, and then to test each layer alone.

What you need from earlier chapters. This chapter is a synthesis of Chapter 42 (the crew_company arm), Chapter 44 (the manning query), Chapter 45 (a signing bonus through postTreasury) and Chapter 48 (readKey, handleKey, draw). If any of those is hazy, this chapter will show you which.

50.1 The setup

Start the client (zig build run -- --tui), load or create a campaign, press F3 for the Forces screen, and put the cursor on a company row. The manning pane on the right (cycle to it with r if it shows damage) lists fourteen roles with have, need and open columns. Some lines are red: the company is short of astechs, or medics, or a mechanic. Press c.

Here is everything that happens, layer by layer, with the source for each.

50.2 Bytes

The loop in App.run is waiting in self.term.readKey(500). The terminal is in raw mode, so the byte 0x63 arrives immediately rather than after Enter. fill polls the file descriptor, reads into the 64-byte pending buffer, and take hands over the first byte:

        return switch (b) {
            0x1b => self.readEscape(),
            '\r', '\n' => .enter,
            '\t' => .tab,
            0x7f, 0x08 => .backspace,
            1...7, 11, 12, 14...26 => .{ .ctrl = 'a' + b - 1 },
            else => self.readUtf8(b),
        };

0x63 is not an escape, not a control byte; readUtf8 sees a one-byte sequence and returns .{ .char = 'c' }. The Key union value goes back to the loop, which resets the frame arena and calls self.handleKey(key).

50.3 Dispatch

Four switches deep. handleKey: no modal is open, so it switches on mode and finds .game. handleGameKey: the key is .char, and 'c' is not one of the global keys (:, n, q, ?, digits), so it falls to screenKey(ch). screenKey switches on self.tab and finds .forces. The Forces arm has already fetched the screen's rows for this frame and computed row, the ToeRow under the cursor, with its force ID:

                    'c' => if (row) |r| {
                        const co = g.companyOf(r.force);
                        if (co != .none) {
                            const res = game.commands.execute(g, .{ .crew_company = co }) catch |err| {
                                self.say(.crit, "{s}", .{game.cli.errorText(err)});
                                return;
                            };
                            self.say(if (res.still_open == 0) .good else .amber, "{s}: {d} hired to fill the manning table · {d} lines still open (no candidates on the boards yet)", .{ q.forceName(g, co), res.hired_count, res.still_open });
                        }
                    },

g.companyOf(r.force) resolves whatever the cursor is on (a lance, a hull inside a lance, the company itself) to its company; a row outside any company yields .none and the key does nothing. Then the client builds the command value .{ .crew_company = co } and calls execute. This arm calls execute directly rather than through self.exec because it wants the Result; the shape of the error handling is the same.

50.4 Validate

Inside execute, the .crew_company arm (Chapter 42) checks three things before touching anything:

            const f = gs.force(company) orelse return Error.UnknownForce;
            if (f.echelon != .company) return Error.NotACompany;
            if (gs.deploymentContract(company) != null) return Error.CompanyDeployed;

The force must exist, must be a company (not a lance or a battalion), and must not be deployed on a contract, because hiring happens at an HQ's hall and a company in the field is light-years away. Any refusal returns a named error, and the client's catch turns it into a red sentence from cli.errorText: "that company is deployed — hire at an HQ hall and xfer person <id> co:N to send people out to it".

50.5 Mutate

With the checks passed, the arm asks personnel.manningNeeds(gs, company) for the fourteen-row table: a role, a need and a reason for each, derived from the company's hulls (a mek wants a mekwarrior and a share of a tech and astechs; a MASH truck wants a doctor and medics). For each row it compares need against manningHave and fills the gap:

            for (personnel.manningNeeds(gs, company)) |n| {
                var have = personnel.manningHave(gs, company, n.role);
                while (have < n.need) : (have += 1) {
                    if (personnel.isPooledRole(n.role)) {
                        // MekHQ hires astechs and medics to complement on
                        // demand: no market, no signing bonus, salary only.
                        const spec = person_gen.generateWithBonus(&gs.rng, n.role, gs.recruitBonus());
                        const id = try gs.hireFromSpec(spec);
                        gs.person(id).?.assigned_force = company;
                        hired += 1;
                    } else if (try hireRoleFromHall(gs, n.role, company)) {
                        hired += 1;
                    } else {
                        still_open += n.need - have;
                        break;
                    }
                }
            }
            _ = try gs.autoAssign(company);
            try gs.log(.decision, .{ .company = company }, "[raise] {s}: {d} hired to fill the manning table ({d} still open — the halls had nobody)", .{ f.name, hired, still_open });

Two paths. Astechs and medics are pooled roles: generated on the spot from the .generation stream (so the same seed produces the same people) and hired by hireFromSpec, which mints a PersonId, builds the Person on the arena and inserts it into the ordered map. Every other role comes from the hiring hall's candidates via hireRoleFromHall, which finds the first candidate of that role and runs the .hire_candidate command, and that arm debits the signing bonus through postTreasury (Chapter 45), one ledger entry and one balance change. When the hall has nobody of a role, the gap is counted in still_open and the loop moves to the next row. Finally autoAssign seats pilots and techs on the company's hulls, and a log line is written with the company tag so the Desk's log can filter it.

Notice what the arm never does: it never allocates from anything but the campaign arena, never reads the clock except through gs.clock, never rolls a die except through gs.rng, and never touches the terminal. It is a pure function of the state and the command, which is the property Chapter 49 tests.

50.6 Report

            return .{ .hired_count = hired, .still_open = still_open };

Two numbers in a Result whose other fields keep their defaults. Back in the client, self.say formats them into one sentence with a style chosen by whether anything is still open: green for "5 hired to fill the manning table · 0 lines still open", amber if the hall could not supply everyone. say writes into a fixed 128-byte buffer with bufPrint (Chapter 23) and stores the style; the status strip draws it on the next frame.

50.7 Redraw

The loop comes round. draw resets the frame arena, clears the grid, and drawForces calls queries.toeFiltered for the tree and queries.manning for the pane:

    for (needs) |n| {
        const have = personnel.manningHave(gs, company, n.role);
        const open = n.need -| have;
        // …
        try out.append(alloc, .{ .role = n.role, .have = have, .need = n.need, .text = try std.fmt.allocPrint(alloc,
            "{s: <16} {d: >5} {d: >5} {s}{d: >5}{{/}}   {{d}}{s}{{/}}",
            .{ @tagName(n.role), have, n.need, if (open > 0) "{c}" else "{g}", open, why }) });
    }

The rows that were red are green, because manningHave recomputed from the people map that now has new entries in it. Nothing was cached and nothing was told to update: the query reads state, the screen draws the query. The tech-hours line above the table changed too, because the new astechs add hours. screen.flush emits the frame, and the terminal shows it.

50.8 Persist

Nothing yet. Saving is its own action (:save, or the save-and-return choice on q), and when it runs, the new people are rows in the person table like any other: one bindAll each, in map order, with ord recording their place (Chapter 47). If the player quits without saving, the arena is freed by gs.deinit() and the hires never happened.

50.9 Every layer alone

The reason to trace a keypress is to see that each layer can be exercised without the others, and the project does:

  • The command has a test with a seeded hall ("12: a raised company is an empty skeleton; hulls bought for it land in a lance …; halls crew it" in commands.zig), which runs .crew_company and asserts on the roster.
  • The query has a test on a generated company ("manning matches the starter generator's ratios" in queries.zig), which checks the fourteen rows against the generator's own numbers.
  • The parser has a test that crew co:1 becomes .{ .crew_company = 1 }, since the same command is reachable by typing.
  • The client is covered by docs/tui_smoke.py, which presses c on the Forces screen and looks for "hired to fill the manning table" in the output.
  • The persistence of the result is covered by the round-trip test, which hires people and compares hashes across a save.

Every layer is visible in the text, and none of them needs the others to be tested. That is what the architecture buys, and it is why the whole program can be read the way you have just read it.

Guided reading

  1. src/tui/term.zig: readKey and readUtf8 once more, with the byte 0x63 in mind.
  2. src/tui/app.zig: run, handleKey, handleGameKey, then the Forces arm of screenKey from where row is computed to the 'c' case. Then say and drawForces.
  3. src/sim/commands.zig: the .crew_company arm, hireRoleFromHall, and the .hire_candidate arm it calls.
  4. src/sim/personnel.zig: Need, isPooledRole, manningNeeds, manningHave.
  5. src/sim/state.zig: hireFromSpec and autoAssign.
  6. src/sim/queries.zig: manning and toeFiltered.

Exercises

Exercise 50.1 · The command alone practice

Write a test in commands.zig that creates a commander and a company, runs crew_company twice, and asserts that the second run hires nobody and reports the same number of open lines as the first. Then assert that crewing ForceId.none is refused, and say which error.

Solution 
test "crewing a company twice hires nobody the second time" {
    var gs = GameState.init(std.testing.allocator, .{ .seed = 11 });
    defer gs.deinit();
    _ = try execute(&gs, .{ .create_commander = .{ .name = "T", .origin = .LC, .profession = .paymaster } });
    const co = (try execute(&gs, .{ .new_company = "Alpha" })).created_force;
    const first = try execute(&gs, .{ .crew_company = co });
    const second = try execute(&gs, .{ .crew_company = co });
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 0), second.hired_count);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(first.still_open, second.still_open);
    try std.testing.expectError(Error.UnknownForce, execute(&gs, .{ .crew_company = .none }));
}

The second run finds have >= need on every row the first run filled, and the same halls empty for the rows it could not, so the counts match. .none fails the first check, gs.force(company) orelse return Error.UnknownForce, before the echelon check can say NotACompany; the order of validations decides which error a caller sees, which is worth knowing when you write errorText entries.

Exercise 50.2 · The parser alone warm-up

Write a test in cli.zig that parses crew co:1 and checks the resulting command's payload is force 1. (If you did Exercise 42.1, add a line for your morale verb.)

Solution 
test "crew parses to the company it names" {
    var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, "co:1", ' ');
    const cmd = (try parseCommand("crew", &it)).?;
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 1), @intFromEnum(cmd.crew_company));
}

parseSite turns co:1 into a Site union and the crew branch takes its company. The .? unwraps the optional (a known verb never returns null) and cmd.crew_company reads the payload, which is a compile error if the tag were something else, since the tag is only checked at runtime; in a test that is fine because a wrong tag panics and fails the test.

Exercise 50.3 · Trace a different key practice

Repeat the seven steps for the A key on the same screen (auto-assign). Which steps are identical, which differ, and which query redraws differently afterwards?

Solution

Bytes (0x41 becomes .{ .char = 'A' }) and dispatch are identical down to the Forces arm. The command is .{ .auto_assign = co }, sent through self.exec because the handler does not need the result. Validation is the arm's own (the force must exist and be a company). Mutation is gs.autoAssign(company) alone: no hiring, no money, so nothing goes through postTreasury. Report is a plain "auto-assigned Alpha" in green. Redraw: the TO&E tree (toeFiltered) changes, because seats now show pilots and techs, while the manning pane's have counts do not change, since assignment moves people between seats rather than onto the payroll. Persist: nothing, as before.

Check your understanding

  1. Why does the byte 0x63 become a key immediately, without Enter?
    AnswerThe terminal is in raw mode (ICANON off), so bytes are delivered as typed rather than line by line.
  2. Where does the client learn which company the cursor is on?
    AnswerFrom the ToeRow the Forces query returned for this frame; its force field is resolved to a company with companyOf. It never counts rows.
  3. Which of the three validations would a deployed company fail, and what does the user see?
    Answergs.deploymentContract(company) != null, returning Error.CompanyDeployed; the status line shows the sentence errorText maps it to.
  4. Where does the signing bonus for a hall hire get debited?
    AnswerNot in the crew_company arm: hireRoleFromHall runs the .hire_candidate command, whose arm posts the bonus through postTreasury.
  5. Why do the manning rows turn green on the next frame?
    AnswerBecause queries.manning recomputes have from the people map every frame; there is no cache to invalidate.
  6. Is anything written to disk by this keypress?
    AnswerNo. Saving is a separate action; until then the hires exist only in the campaign arena.
What you learned.
  • A keypress is: a byte decoded to a Key, four switches of dispatch, a Command value, validate-mutate-report inside execute, a sentence in the status line, and a redraw that recomputes everything from state.
  • Pooled roles are generated from the seeded stream; other roles come from the hall via the hire_candidate command, which is where money moves.
  • Nothing is cached and nothing is written to disk until the player saves.
  • Each layer has its own test: the command, the query, the parser, the client under a pseudo-terminal, and the round trip.

51. Where to go next

In this chapter the book hands you the keys. You have read every layer of IRON LEDGER; now you get a ladder of projects graded from an afternoon to a fortnight, each touching a layer you know, with the tests that will tell you when you are done. Then a reading order for the parts of the source this book did not cover, and a few words about what to read after that.

What you need from earlier chapters. All of Part 5, and the habit from Chapter 37 of letting the compiler and the test suite do the bookkeeping. Every project below is described in terms of the doors and phases you read in Chapter 42 through Chapter 47.

51.1 How to use the ladder

Each rung names a layer, a change, the files it touches, and the test that proves it. Do them in order the first time; each one assumes the muscle memory of the one before. Work in a copy of the game. When a rung says "the compiler lists…", read every error before fixing any; the list is the design checklist. When it says "write the test first", do: the shape of the tests in Chapter 49 (build a small state, run one thing, assert on state) is the shape you want.

Two rules from CLAUDE.md apply to every rung. No new randomness outside rng.zig's streams, and no floats in rules math. If you find yourself wanting either, you have found the wrong design, and the golden master will agree with the book.

51.2 The ladder

Rung 1 · A tuning knob (an hour)

Layer: data. Change: pick a constant in data/tables/tuning.zon (the founding funds, the decision window, a fatigue threshold), change it, and find the test that notices. Then make the same change in a mod directory and build with -Ddata. Files: one ZON file. Done when: you can name the test that pinned the old value and explain whether it should be updated or the change reverted. You did most of this in Chapter 40; the rung is worth repeating with a knob that has a formula behind it, so you follow the grep into the rule.

Rung 2 · A query line (an hour)

Layer: queries. Change: add something to a screen that the state already knows but no query shows. Ideas: a person's age in years on the People list (there is ageYears); the number of days until a contract's next battle on the Contracts screen; a company's total monthly payroll on the Forces detail pane. Files: queries.zig only. Done when: a test on a generated company asserts the exact text of the new line, and the client shows it (run --tui and look). This is Exercise 44.1 with a new subject.

Rung 3 · A command (an afternoon)

Layer: commands and the parser. Change: a new player action with a refusal. Ideas: set_leave_days (put a person on leave for N days, refusing if they are deployed), rename_person, pin_medbay_priority. Files: commands.zig (variant, arm, test), cli.zig (verb, parser branch, usage row, an errorText sentence for any new error). Done when: the compiler has walked you through the switch, the "every listed verb parses" test passes, your own test covers the refusal with expectError and the effect with expectEqual, and the verb works in both the REPL and the client's : line without either frontend being edited. Exercise 42.1 is the model.

Rung 4 · A tick phase (an afternoon)

Layer: the daily tick. Change: a small recurring effect. Ideas: a morale point each week for a company whose mess facility is at level 3 or higher and that is at home; a log line on the first of the month summarising hulls in the depot; a weekly decay of a new counter. Files: tick.zig (the phase and its place in advanceDay), possibly a field in state.zig. Done when: a test on a hand-built state proves the phase fires when it should and not otherwise, you have written one sentence saying why it sits where it does in the phase list, and the golden master still passes. Exercise 43.2 is the model; the harder part of this rung is choosing the phase order and defending it.

Rung 5 · A field that persists (a day)

Layer: persistence. Change: make the field from Rung 4 (or any new Person or Unit field) survive a save. Files: the domain struct, and in store.zig the DDL, a migration, the INSERT and the SELECT. Done when: a round-trip test sets the field, saves to ":memory:", loads, and reads it back; and the "v5 store upgrades in place" test still passes, proving your migration runs on an old file. Exercise 47.1 is the model. If the field is on Stats rather than a person, find how the stats are saved (as key-value rows in meta) and follow that pattern instead.

Rung 6 · An event (a day)

Layer: events. Change: a new entry in one of the decks in contract_events.zig, with options and effects, and if it needs one, a new Effect variant. Files: events.zig (the variant), contract_events.zig (the deck entry, applyEffectsFor), queries.zig (effectsText), and the 12.24 test's classification switch. Done when: the compiler has listed all three switches and you have answered each (how it is shown, what it does, whether it may be automatic), a test rolls the deck at your entry's number and asserts the effect on state, and the "automatic events never move money" test still holds. Exercise 46.1 showed you the checklist.

Rung 7 · A screen (two or three days)

Layer: the client. Change: a new pane on an existing tab, or a new modal. Ideas: a "recent battles" pane on the Contracts tab fed by queries.battleLog; a confirmation modal for trim_stock that shows what will be sent home before sending it. Files: app.zig (a drawX, a key arm, possibly a Modal variant), and a query if the data is not already exposed. Done when: the pane draws at every size tier without overflowing (run with the window at 80 by 24), the smoke script has a new assertion that visits it, and grep still finds no direct writes to g. in app.zig. Chapter 48 is the map; the discipline is to fetch everything through a query and act through exec.

Rung 8 · A subsystem with its own stream (a week)

Layer: all of them. Change: a mechanic that needs its own randomness. Ideas: a weather system that persists per planet and rolls daily (currently weather is rolled per battle); a rumour market that seeds contract offers with partial information; a morale event deck for companies at home. Files: a new Stream variant in rng.zig (the array grows on its own), a new file in src/sim with its own tests, a phase in the tick, one or two commands, a query, persistence for any state it keeps. Done when: the new stream is the only place your code rolls dice, every other stream's rolls are unchanged (write a test in the style of "streams are independent"), the golden master passes, the round trip passes, and a fresh reader can find your subsystem from root.zig and its //! comment. This is the rung at which you are no longer reading IRON LEDGER; you are extending it.

Rung 9 · A second frontend (a fortnight)

Layer: the boundary itself. Change: a new client that uses only the three doors. The natural one is a batch runner: read a script of verbs from a file, execute them through cli.parseCommand and commands.execute, print a query or two, exit with a status. It is the smallest possible frontend, and writing it proves that the boundary is complete: anything you find yourself needing from GameState directly is a missing query, and the fix is to add the query, not to reach past it. Done when: the runner can replay docs/repl_smoke.sh's script and produce the same landmarks, and you have added at least one query that the terminal client did not need but a batch runner does (a machine-readable summary, say).

51.3 What this book did not cover

Part 5 read the spine of the program. These parts of the source were mentioned but not read, and each is a self-contained afternoon:

  • src/gen/company_gen.zig and person_gen.zig. How a starter company is rolled: lances from the house's random assignment table, pilots with skills from an experience band, a support tail sized to the hulls. The heaviest user of the .generation stream, and the reason two campaigns with the same seed have the same people.
  • src/econ/logistics.zig and src/sim/network.zig. The star map's distances, jump counts, freight costs and the HQ link graph. Integer arithmetic on light-years and basis points, with a small graph search.
  • src/econ/market.zig and contract_market.zig. How boards refresh: rarity targets against 2d6, listings that age out, offers scaled by reputation and reach.
  • src/sim/maintenance.zig and hq_ops.zig. Weekly maintenance checks by tech skill against a target number, the repair and fabrication queues, construction projects with paperwork and build days.
  • src/domain/meklab.zig. The construction rules: engine and structure tables, criticals, the refit classes. A pure rules engine over a hull's slots, with tests against TechManual values.
  • src/tui/png.zig and emblem.zig. A PNG decoder with inflate written from the specification, and two terminal graphics protocols. Nothing to do with the game, everything to do with how far "no libraries" can go.

The reading order for the whole source, if you want to go from the top: ARCHITECTURE.md; src/root.zig; src/domain/types.zig; src/sim/rng.zig; src/sim/clock.zig; src/sim/state.zig (skim the fields, read the money and lookup helpers); src/sim/commands.zig (the union and a few arms); src/sim/tick.zig; one query in src/sim/queries.zig; src/persist/sqlite.zig; and finally src/tui/app.zig's run, draw and handleKey. That path is a couple of hours, and after it nothing in the repository will look unfamiliar.

51.4 After IRON LEDGER

You now know Zig as it is used in a program of real size: no hidden allocation, no hidden control flow, errors as values, data checked at compile time, and a test suite that turns design rules into build failures. Three places to take that next.

The standard library. You have used perhaps a tenth of it. It is written in the same style you have been reading and it is on your disk (zig env prints the path). Start with std/array_list.zig and std/hash_map.zig, whose APIs you know, then std/Io/Writer.zig, whose print you have called a thousand times. Reading how {s: <20} is parsed at compile time is a good afternoon.

The build system. Chapter 31 and IRON LEDGER's build.zig showed one module, one executable, one test step and one option. Real projects add dependencies from build.zig.zon, generate files at build time, cross-compile, and ship C libraries built from source. The build runner is ordinary Zig and its source is in the standard library too (std/Build.zig).

Your own program. The capstone in Chapter 38 was a mercenary ledger from scratch; the shape of IRON LEDGER is a way to grow it. A pure core with commands in and queries out, a seeded dice bag, an arena per campaign, integers for money, ZON for data, and a golden-master test from the first commit. None of that is specific to BattleTech. It is a way to make a program you can still reason about at thirty thousand lines, and you have now read the proof that it works.

Exercises

Exercise 51.1 · Plan a rung practice

Choose Rung 3, 4 or 6 and, before writing any code, write the plan as a list: the files you will touch, the switches you expect the compiler to list, the test you will write first, and the phase or arm your change belongs next to. Then do the rung and compare the list with what actually happened.

Solution

There is no single answer, but here is a plan for Rung 3 with set_leave_days that a reader of Part 5 should be able to write: (1) commands.zig: a variant set_leave: struct { person: types.PersonId, days: u32 }; the compiler will list the execute switch and nothing else. (2) The arm: validate the person exists (UnknownPerson), is active, and is not deployed (a new error PersonDeployed, or reuse CompanyDeployed); then set leave_until_day = gs.clock.day_index + days; then log with the company tag; return .{}. (3) cli.zig: verb leave exists already for the medbay modal, so check its parser branch before adding; the usage table and the verbs list. (4) A test: hire, set leave, assert the field; deploy a company and assert the refusal. (5) errorText for any new error. What actually happens: you discover that Person.isAvailable(day) already reads leave_until_day, so no phase needs changing, and that the client's People screen has an L key wired to a leave verb, which tells you the game may already have this command. Reading before planning is the lesson.

Exercise 51.2 · Find the missing query challenge

Begin Rung 9 with a thirty-line program: a new --script <file> flag in main.zig that reads verbs from a file, parses each with cli.parseCommand, executes it, and at the end prints the campaign's day and funds. The first time you reach for a GameState field to print, stop: is there a query for it? If not, add one. Which query did you add?

Solution

The loop is runRepl in main.zig with the prompt removed: tokenise each line with std.mem.tokenizeScalar, take the first token as the verb, call game.cli.parseCommand(verb, &it), and on a command call execute and print errorText on refusal. The day and funds are on queries.status already, so the honest answer for most readers is "none, once I looked". A batch runner that also wants a machine-readable summary (one line per company: name, hulls, people, local funds) finds that queries.summary returns prose, and adds a companiesBrief query returning a slice of small structs. That new query is then available to the terminal client for free, which is the whole argument of Chapter 44.

Check your understanding

  1. Which rung first requires touching more than one layer, and which layers?
    AnswerRung 3: the command layer (commands.zig) and the parser (cli.zig), plus an error sentence.
  2. What proves a migration works on an old save file, given that the round-trip test always starts from fresh DDL?
    AnswerThe "v5 store upgrades in place" test, which inserts hand-written rows in an old schema and opens the store, running every migration.
  3. Why does Rung 8 insist on a new RNG stream?
    AnswerDrawing from an existing stream would shift every later roll in that subsystem, changing saved campaigns' replays; a new stream leaves existing ones untouched.
  4. What does Rung 9 test that no Zig test does?
    AnswerThat the command/query boundary is complete: a second frontend that needs something not exposed reveals a missing query rather than a reason to reach into the state.
  5. Name the six design choices from IRON LEDGER that transfer to any program.
    AnswerA pure core with commands in and queries out; a seeded dice bag with named streams; an arena per campaign or session; integers for money; ZON data checked at compile time; a golden-master test from the start.
What you learned.
  • A nine-rung ladder from a data knob to a second frontend, each naming its layer, its files and the test that proves it.
  • The compiler's switch errors and the suite's pinned numbers are the checklist for every rung; the golden master and the round trip are the safety net.
  • The parts of the source this book skipped, each a self-contained read, and a reading order for the whole tree.
  • The standard library, the build system and your own program are the three places to take the habits you have learned.
  • The design of IRON LEDGER is not about BattleTech: it is a way to keep a large program readable, and you have read the whole proof.

Appendix A1. Builtin functions cheat sheet

This appendix lists every builtin used in the course, grouped by purpose. A builtin is a function whose name starts with @; it is part of the language, not the standard library, and it is documented in the language reference rather than in std. Every row was compiled with Zig 0.16.0 while this appendix was written. "Signature" is a sketch, not the formal grammar: T is a type, x a value, and the result type is often inferred from context (write const n: u8 = @intCast(x) or @as(u8, @intCast(x))).

How result types work. Many casts take no type argument. The result type comes from where the expression is used: a typed const, a function parameter, a struct field, or an explicit @as(T, …). If the compiler says "must have a known result type", wrap the call in @as. This is the biggest difference from tutorials written for Zig 0.10 and earlier, where casts were written @intCast(T, x).

A1.1 Casts and conversions

BuiltinSignature sketchMeaningChapter
@as@as(T, x)Give an expression an explicit type; the one cast that names its type.3
@intCast@intCast(x)Integer to integer of another width or signedness; panics in safe builds if the value does not fit.4
@truncate@truncate(x)Keep only the low bits that fit the narrower result type; never panics.29
@floatFromInt@floatFromInt(x)Integer to float.5
@intFromFloat@intFromFloat(x)Float to integer, truncating toward zero; panics if out of range.5
@floatCast@floatCast(x)Float to float of another width.5
@bitCast@bitCast(x)Reinterpret the bits as another type of the same size (float as int, packed struct as int).29
@enumFromInt@enumFromInt(x)Integer to enum value; the enum type comes from context.13
@intFromEnum@intFromEnum(e)Enum value to its integer tag.13
@intFromBool@intFromBool(b)true to 1, false to 0, as a u1 that widens.5
@ptrCast@ptrCast(p)Pointer to pointer of another pointee type.18
@alignCast@alignCast(p)Assert a pointer has the alignment the result type needs; checked in safe builds.18
@constCast@constCast(p)Remove const from a pointer type. Rare; usually a design smell.18
@intFromPtr@intFromPtr(p)Pointer to its address as usize.18
@ptrFromInt@ptrFromInt(n)Address to pointer. Used in IRON LEDGER for SQLite's -1 sentinel.47
@errorCast@errorCast(e)Narrow an error set or error union to a smaller set; the result type must be known.16
@intFromError, @errorFromInt@intFromError(e)Error value to its global integer code and back. Rare.16

A1.2 Arithmetic

BuiltinSignature sketchMeaningChapter
@divTrunc@divTrunc(a, b)Signed division rounding toward zero. Required for signed integers at runtime.4
@divFloor@divFloor(a, b)Signed division rounding toward negative infinity.4
@divExact@divExact(a, b)Division that asserts there is no remainder.4
@mod, @rem@mod(a, b)Remainder with the sign of the divisor (@mod) or of the dividend (@rem).4
@abs@abs(x)Absolute value; for a signed integer the result is the unsigned type.4
@min, @max@min(a, b, …)Smallest or largest of any numeric arguments; the result type is the narrowest that fits.4
@addWithOverflow, @subWithOverflow, @mulWithOverflow, @shlWithOverflow@addWithOverflow(a, b)Return a tuple { result, overflow_bit } instead of panicking.4
@shlExact, @shrExact@shlExact(x, n)Shifts that assert no bits are lost.29
@clz, @ctz, @popCount@popCount(x)Count leading zeros, trailing zeros, set bits.29
@byteSwap, @bitReverse@byteSwap(x)Reverse the byte order, or every bit.29
@sqrt, @sin, @cos, @tan, @exp, @exp2, @log, @log2, @log10@sqrt(x)Float functions on scalars and vectors.5
@floor, @ceil, @round, @trunc@floor(x)Float rounding; @round rounds half away from zero.5
@mulAdd@mulAdd(T, a, b, c)Fused a * b + c with one rounding.5

Wrapping (+%, *%) and saturating (+|, -|) arithmetic are operators, not builtins; IRON LEDGER uses *% to seed its RNG streams and -| wherever a count must not go below zero (Chapter 41, Chapter 44).

BuiltinSignature sketchMeaningChapter
@memcpy@memcpy(dest, src)Copy a slice or array into another of the same length; regions must not overlap.19

@sizeOf@sizeOf(T)Bytes a value of T occupies in memory, including padding.19

BuiltinSignature sketchMeaningChapter
@TypeOf@TypeOf(x)The type of an expression, without evaluating it at runtime.26

BuiltinSignature sketchMeaningChapter
@atomicLoad, @atomicStore@atomicLoad(T, ptr, .seq_cst)Atomic read or write with a memory ordering.36

Two things that look like builtins but are not: unreachable is a keyword (an expression of type noreturn that asserts the point is never reached), and undefined is a keyword too (a value you promise to overwrite before reading).

Appendix A2. Format specifier reference

This appendix is the complete table of what can go inside {…} in a format string for print, allocPrint, bufPrint and std.debug.print in Zig 0.16. Every example was printed by one program (a2_fmt.zig, compiled and run while writing this page) and the output column is what it printed. If a placeholder is not in this table, it does not exist in 0.16.

A2.1 The grammar

A placeholder is

{[argument][specifier]:[fill][alignment][width].[precision]}
  • argument: nothing (the next argument in order), a number ({0}, {1}), or a field name in square brackets ({[score]}) when the argument tuple is a struct literal with named fields.
  • specifier: one of the letters in A2.2, chosen by the type of the argument.
  • fill: one byte used for padding. If you give a fill you must also give an alignment, or the byte is read as a width.
  • alignment: < left, ^ centre, > right.
  • width: the minimum field width in bytes. Alignment is by bytes, not by displayed characters; it is only right for ASCII.
  • precision: for floats, the number of decimals; for {s}, a maximum length.

A literal brace is doubled: {{ prints { and }} prints }. That matters whenever a format string contains IRON LEDGER's {g}…{/} colour markup (Chapter 44).

A2.2 Specifiers by type

PlaceholderApplies toExampleOutput
{}integers, floats, bools; anything with an unambiguous default{} with -42-42
{d}integers and floats, decimal{d} with -42; with 3.14159-42; 3.14159
{d:.2}floats, fixed decimals{d:.2} with 3.141593.14
{d:.0}floats, no decimals{d:.0} with 2.718283
{e}, {E}floats, scientific{e}; {e:.3} with 3.141593.14159e0; 3.142e0
{x}, {X}integers in hex; also a string as hex bytes{x}, {X} with 255; {x} with "iron"ff; FF; 69726f6e
{b}integers, binary{b} with 5101
{o}integers, octal{o} with 810
{c}an integer of at most 8 bits as an ASCII character{c} with 'A'A
{u}an integer of at most 21 bits as a UTF-8 code point{u} with 0x263A☺
{s}[]const u8, [*:0]const u8, or a pointer to a u8 array{s} with "iron"; with a C string; with &[3]u8{'a','b','c'}iron; zig; abc
{t}enum, tagged union or error: the tag or error name{t} with Color.green; with error.Boom; with a uniongreen; Boom; n
{any}anything: arrays, slices, structs, unions, optionals, in Zig literal syntax{any} with [3]u8{1,2,3}; with a struct; with a union{ 1, 2, 3 }; .{ .x = 1, .y = 2 }; .{ .n = 3 }
{?}, {?d}, {?s}optionals: prints null or the payload with the specifier after ?{?} with null and with 7; {?s} with "maybe"null; 7; maybe
{!}, {!s}error unions: the error name, or the payload with the specifier after !{!} with error.Boom; {!s} with "fine"error.Boom; fine
{f}a struct or union with a pub fn format(self, w: *std.Io.Writer) std.Io.Writer.Error!void method{f} with Point{ .x = 1, .y = 2 }(1, 2)
{B}, {Bi}an integer as a byte size, decimal or binary units{B}, {Bi} with 15361.536kB; 1.5KiB
{b64}a string as standard base64{b64} with "iron"aXJvbg==
{*}a pointer: the pointee type and the address{*} with &ni32@104f837d0 (varies)
{{, }}literal braces{{}}{}
Things that do not work. {} on a slice or string is a compile error ("cannot format slice without a specifier (i.e. {s}, {x}, {b64}, or {any})"): you must say {s} or {any}. {d} on an array or slice of integers is an error too; use {any}. {D} (nanoseconds as a duration) is mentioned in the standard library's doc comment but is rejected for integers in 0.16.0 ("invalid format string 'D' for type 'u64'"); do not use it. And the old format(self, comptime fmt, options, writer: anytype) method signature is no longer called by {}; see A3.

A2.3 Width, alignment, fill and precision

PlaceholderMeaningExampleOutput
{s:<8}left-align in 8with "iron"iron
{s:>8}right-align in 8with "iron" iron
{s:^8}centre in 8with "iron" iron
{s:*^8}centre in 8, fill with *with "iron"**iron**
{d:>6}right-align a number in 6with -42 -42
{d:<6}left-align a number in 6with -42-42
{d:0>6}right-align, fill with zeroswith 42000042
{x:0>8}hex, zero-padded to 8with 255000000ff
{d:>[1]}width taken from argument 1with .{ 7, 5 } 7
{1s} {0s}positional argumentswith .{ "first", "second" }second first
{[b]}{[a]}named argumentswith .{ .a = 1, .b = 2 }21

The IRON LEDGER row format from Chapter 44 uses these with a space after the colon, {d: <4}, which reads as "fill with space, left, width 4"; the space is the fill byte, and it is the same as {d:<4}.

A2.4 The program

For reference, the file that produced every output above. Copy it into your scratch directory and run it with zig run; it is a quick way to check a placeholder before using it.

const std = @import("std");
const Point = struct {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
    pub fn format(self: Point, w: *std.Io.Writer) std.Io.Writer.Error!void {
        try w.print("({d}, {d})", .{ self.x, self.y });
    }
};
const Color = enum { red, green };
pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var w = std.Io.File.stdout().writer(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &w.interface;
    const n: i32 = -42;
    const f: f64 = 3.14159;
    const s: []const u8 = "iron";
    const opt: ?u8 = null;
    const opt2: ?u8 = 7;
    const eu: anyerror!u8 = error.Boom;
    const arr = [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3 };
    const p = Point{ .x = 1, .y = 2 };
    try out.print("{{}}       |{}|\n", .{n});
    try out.print("{{d}}      |{d}|\n", .{n});
    try out.print("{{d}} f    |{d}|\n", .{f});
    try out.print("{{d:.2}}   |{d:.2}|\n", .{f});
    try out.print("{{e}}      |{e}|\n", .{f});
    try out.print("{{x}}      |{x}|\n", .{@as(u32, 255)});
    try out.print("{{x:0>8}}  |{x:0>8}|\n", .{@as(u32, 255)});
    try out.print("{{c}}      |{c}|\n", .{@as(u8, 'A')});
    try out.print("{{u}}      |{u}|\n", .{@as(u21, 0x263A)});
    try out.print("{{s:*^8}}  |{s:*^8}|\n", .{s});
    try out.print("{{any}}    |{any}|\n", .{arr});
    try out.print("{{?}}      |{?}|  |{?}|\n", .{ opt, opt2 });
    try out.print("{{!}}      |{!}|\n", .{eu});
    try out.print("{{t}}      |{t}|\n", .{Color.green});
    try out.print("{{f}}      |{f}|\n", .{p});
    try out.print("{{B}}      |{B}|\n", .{@as(u64, 1536)});
    try out.print("{{b64}}    |{b64}|\n", .{"iron"});
    try out.print("{{1s}} {{0s}} |{1s} {0s}|\n", .{ "first", "second" });
    try out.print("{{[b]}}{{[a]}} |{[b]}{[a]}|\n", .{ .a = 1, .b = 2 });
    try out.print("{{d:>[1]}} |{d:>[1]}|\n", .{ 7, 5 });
    try out.flush();
}
