Appendix A3. Zig 0.16 migration notes

This appendix is for the moment you paste something from a web tutorial and the compiler says a member does not exist. The left column is the form you will find in tutorials and answers written for Zig 0.9 to 0.14; the right column is the 0.16 form. Every right-hand form was compiled with Zig 0.16.0 in one program (a3_new.zig) while writing this page, and the left-hand forms that appear in A4 were confirmed to fail with the messages shown there. Where a chapter covers the topic, it is linked.

The three big changes. First, I/O is explicit: anything that touches the outside world takes an std.Io value, which main receives through std.process.Init (Chapter 33). Second, containers are unmanaged: ArrayList and the hash maps no longer store an allocator, so you pass one to every call that can allocate (Chapter 21). Third, casts infer their result type: @intCast(x), not @intCast(T, x) (Chapter 4). Most rows below are an instance of one of these.

A3.1 Program entry, I/O and the process

Old form (tutorials)Zig 0.16
pub fn main() !void with no way to reach I/O or an allocator except globalspub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void; init.io, init.gpa, init.arena, init.minimal.args, init.environ_map. The old zero-parameter form still compiles for programs that only use std.debug.print.
const out = std.io.getStdOut().writer();var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
var w = std.Io.File.stdout().writer(init.io, &buf);
const out = &w.interface; then try out.print(…) and try out.flush() at the end.
std.io.getStdIn().reader().readUntilDelimiterOrEof(&buf, '\n')var r = std.Io.File.stdin().reader(init.io, &buf);
const line = try r.interface.takeDelimiter('\n'); (returns ?[]u8, null at end of input)
std.io.bufferedWriter(file.writer())Writers are buffered by construction: the buffer is the second argument of .writer(io, &buf). There is no separate wrapper.
std.fs.cwd()std.Io.Dir.cwd(); every Dir and File method takes io first: dir.createFile(io, "x", .{}), dir.openFile(io, …), f.close(io), dir.deleteFile(io, …).
std.fs.cwd().readFileAlloc(alloc, path, max)dir.readFileAlloc(io, path, alloc, .limited(1 << 20)) (the limit is a std.Io.Limit, not an integer)
std.time.timestamp(), std.time.milliTimestamp()const now = std.Io.Clock.now(.real, io); then now.nanoseconds. It is not an error union.
std.time.Timer.start()Gone. Take two readings of std.Io.Clock.now(.awake, io) and subtract the nanoseconds.
std.time.sleep(ns)try std.Io.sleep(io, .{ .nanoseconds = ns }, .awake);
std.process.args(), std.process.argsAlloc(alloc)var it = std.process.Args.Iterator.init(init.minimal.args);
_ = it.next(); // program name
while (it.next()) |arg| { … }
std.os.getenv("HOME"), std.process.getEnvVarOwnedinit.environ_map.get("HOME") (returns ?[]const u8)
std.os.exit(1)std.process.exit(1)
std.ChildProcess.init(argv, alloc) then .spawn()var child = try std.process.spawn(io, .{ .argv = &.{ "echo", "hi" } });
const term = try child.wait(io);

A3.2 Containers and allocators

Old form (tutorials)Zig 0.16
var list = std.ArrayList(u32).init(alloc);
defer list.deinit();
try list.append(1);		var list: std.ArrayList(u32) = .empty;
defer list.deinit(gpa);
try list.append(gpa, 1);. Every growing call takes the allocator; toOwnedSlice(gpa), appendSlice(gpa, …) likewise. (ArrayListUnmanaged is the same type under its older name.)
list.writer() to format into an ArrayList of bytesvar aw: std.Io.Writer.Allocating = .init(gpa);
defer aw.deinit();
try aw.writer.print("{d}", .{1});
aw.written()
std.io.fixedBufferStream(&buf).writer()var fw = std.Io.Writer.fixed(&buf);
try fw.print("{d}", .{42});
fw.buffered()
var m = std.AutoHashMap(u32, u32).init(alloc);var m: std.AutoHashMapUnmanaged(u32, u32) = .empty;
defer m.deinit(gpa);
try m.put(gpa, 1, 2);. Same for StringHashMapUnmanaged and the ArrayHashMap variants.
var gpa = std.heap.GeneralPurposeAllocator(.{}){};var dbg: std.heap.DebugAllocator(.{}) = .init;
defer _ = dbg.deinit();
const a = dbg.allocator();, or simply use init.gpa in main.
std.heap.c_allocator without linking libcUnchanged, but it needs link_libc = true; prefer std.heap.page_allocator or init.gpa.

A3.3 Language and reflection

Old form (tutorials)Zig 0.16
@intCast(u8, x), @floatFromInt(f64, n), @ptrCast(*T, p)const y: u8 = @intCast(x); or @as(u8, @intCast(x)). All casts infer the result type (A1).
@typeInfo(T).Struct.fields, .Enum, .Union, .Int, .Pointer@typeInfo(T).@"struct".fields, .@"enum", .@"union", .int, .pointer, .optional, .error_union, .@"fn": lower-case tags, quoted where they collide with keywords.
usingnamespace other;Gone. Re-export what you need by hand: pub const answer = other.answer;
@Type(.{ .Struct = … })Gone in 0.16 ("invalid builtin function"). Build types with generics (Chapter 26) instead.
for (items) |item, i|for (items, 0..) |item, i| (the index is a second iterable)
async, await, suspendNot in the language. Use threads (Chapter 36) or the std.Io interface.
pub fn format(self: T, comptime fmt: []const u8, options: std.fmt.FormatOptions, writer: anytype) !void, called by {}pub fn format(self: T, w: *std.Io.Writer) std.Io.Writer.Error!void, called by {f}. Plain {} on a struct does not call it.
std.fmt.format(writer, "…", args)try writer.print("…", args) on any *std.Io.Writer
std.testing.expectEqual(5, add(2, 3)) with an untyped literalStill compiles in 0.16 when the literal coerces to the actual value's type. If you see "expected type 'u32', found 'i32'", the two sides have different types; fix with @as(i32, 5) on the expected side.

A3.4 Standard library renames

Old form (tutorials)Zig 0.16
std.rand.DefaultPrng, std.rand.Randomstd.Random.DefaultPrng.init(seed); prng.random() returns a std.Random; r.intRangeAtMost(u8, 1, 6).
std.mem.split(u8, s, ","), std.mem.tokenize(u8, s, " ")std.mem.splitScalar(u8, s, ','), std.mem.splitSequence(u8, s, "::"), std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, s, ' '), tokenizeAny, tokenizeSequence.
std.sort.sort(u8, &arr, {}, comptime std.sort.asc(u8))std.mem.sort(u8, &arr, {}, std.sort.asc(u8))
std.Thread.Mutex{} with .lock() / .unlock()var mtx: std.Io.Mutex = .init;
try mtx.lock(io);
mtx.unlock(io);. std.Thread.Mutex no longer exists; the mutex takes the io because locking can be cancelled.
std.atomic.Atomic(T)std.atomic.Value(T).init(x); .load(.seq_cst), .store(x, .seq_cst), .swap, .cmpxchgStrong.
thread.setName("worker")try thread.setName(io, "worker"). On macOS only a thread may name itself; naming another thread returns error.Unsupported, so write catch {} if the name is cosmetic.
std.Thread.spawn(.{}, f, .{arg})Unchanged; th.join() unchanged.
std.debug.print, std.log.infoUnchanged; both write to stderr without an io. This is why the earliest chapters can print without touching std.Io.

A3.5 build.zig

Old form (tutorials)Zig 0.16
b.addExecutable(.{ .name = "x", .root_source_file = b.path("src/main.zig"), .target = target, .optimize = optimize })b.addExecutable(.{ .name = "x", .root_module = b.createModule(.{ .root_source_file = b.path("src/main.zig"), .target = target, .optimize = optimize, .imports = &.{…} }) }). The executable owns a module; imports are listed on the module.
exe.addModule("game", mod) or exe.root_module.addImport(…) after creationList imports in createModule's .imports, or call mod.addImport("name", other) on a module. b.addModule("game", .{ .root_source_file = …, .target = target }) declares a module others can import.
exe.linkLibC(); exe.linkSystemLibrary("sqlite3")mod.link_libc = true; mod.linkSystemLibrary("sqlite3", .{}); on the module that needs it.
b.addTest(.{ .root_source_file = … })b.addTest(.{ .root_module = mod }); one test executable per module, so a library and an executable need two.
std.fs.cwd() inside build.zigb.build_root.handle.access(b.graph.io, path, .{}), std.Io.Dir.accessAbsolute(b.graph.io, …): the build runner has its own io in b.graph.io.
exe.addAnonymousModule("data", .{ .source_file = … })mod.addAnonymousImport("data_zon", .{ .root_source_file = b.path("data/x.zon") }); then @import("data_zon") in source (Chapter 40).

A3.6 The check program

The right-hand forms above were all compiled in one file. The parts most likely to surprise you are reproduced here so you can paste them into a scratch file and confirm your installed compiler agrees:

const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    const gpa = init.gpa;

    var out_buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var out_w = std.Io.File.stdout().writer(io, &out_buf);
    const out = &out_w.interface;

    var list: std.ArrayList(u32) = .empty;
    defer list.deinit(gpa);
    try list.append(gpa, 1);

    const now = std.Io.Clock.now(.real, io);
    try out.print("ns {d}\n", .{now.nanoseconds});

    var dir = std.Io.Dir.cwd();
    var f = try dir.createFile(io, "a3_out.txt", .{});
    var fb: [128]u8 = undefined;
    var fw = f.writer(io, &fb);
    try fw.interface.print("line {d}\n", .{1});
    try fw.interface.flush();
    f.close(io);
    const data = try dir.readFileAlloc(io, "a3_out.txt", gpa, .limited(1 << 20));
    defer gpa.free(data);
    try dir.deleteFile(io, "a3_out.txt");

    var aw: std.Io.Writer.Allocating = .init(gpa);
    defer aw.deinit();
    try aw.writer.print("{d}-{s}", .{ 1, "x" });
    try out.print("allocating {s}\n", .{aw.written()});

    var mtx: std.Io.Mutex = .init;
    try mtx.lock(io);
    mtx.unlock(io);
    try std.Io.sleep(io, .{ .nanoseconds = 1 }, .awake);

    var child = try std.process.spawn(io, .{ .argv = &.{ "echo", "spawned" } });
    _ = try child.wait(io);

    try out.flush();
}
$ zig run a3_check.zig
spawned
ns 1788967362109410000
allocating 1-x

Appendix A4. Common compile errors, decoded

This appendix collects the compiler messages a beginner meets most often, each reproduced by compiling a tiny file with Zig 0.16.0 while this page was written. For each: the code that triggers it, the message exactly as printed (file names and line numbers will differ), what it means, and the fix. The last section covers the three runtime panics that look like compile errors to a newcomer. Chapter 37 explains how to read a message; this is the lookup table.

Reading a message. The first line is file:line:column: error: … and points at the exact token. Lines beginning note: add context (where a type was declared, which value is unhandled). Lines after referenced by: show the call chain that made the compiler look at this code, which is how a message inside the standard library (as in A4.24) leads back to your own line. Fix the first error and rebuild; later ones are often consequences of it.

A4.1 Unused and misused names

A4.1 unused local constant

pub fn main() void {
    const x: u32 = 5;
}
e01.zig:2:11: error: unused local constant

Meaning. Every local must be used. Fix. Use it, delete it, or discard it on purpose with _ = x;. The same message reads "unused local variable" for a var. (Chapter 3)

A4.2 unused function parameter

fn f(a: u32, b: u32) u32 {
    return a;
}
e02.zig:1:14: error: unused function parameter

Meaning. b is never read. Fix. _ = b; as the first line of the body, or name the parameter _ if it exists only to match a signature. (Chapter 7)

A4.3 local variable is never mutated

pub fn main() void {
    var x: u32 = 5;
    _ = x;
}
e03.zig:2:9: error: local variable is never mutated
e03.zig:2:9: note: consider using 'const'

Meaning. A var that is never assigned after initialisation must be a const. Fix. Do what the note says. This is the error you get most often after deleting code. (Chapter 3)

A4.4 pointless discard of local variable

var x: u8 = 200;
x += 100;
_ = x;
e24.zig:4:9: error: pointless discard of local variable
e24.zig:3:5: note: used here

Meaning. You wrote _ = x; but x is already used. Fix. Remove the discard. (Chapter 3)

A4.5 local constant shadows declaration

const std = @import("std");
pub fn main() void {
    const std = 1;
    _ = std;
}
e04.zig:3:11: error: local constant shadows declaration of 'std'
e04.zig:1:1: note: declared here

Meaning. Zig forbids shadowing entirely; an inner name may not reuse an outer one. Fix. Rename the local. IRON LEDGER's slightly fussy names (uit2, pit2) exist because of this rule. (Chapter 7)

A4.6 unused capture

const items = [_]u8{ 1, 2 };
for (items) |item| {}
e31.zig:3:18: error: unused capture

Meaning. The loop captures item and never reads it. Fix. Write |_| if you only want the iteration count, or use the value. (Chapter 6)

A4.2 Types and coercion

A4.7 expected type 'X', found 'Y'

pub fn main() void {
    const s: []const u8 = 42;
    _ = s;
}
e11.zig:2:27: error: expected type '[]const u8', found 'comptime_int'

Meaning. The value's type cannot coerce to the declared type. Fix. Supply a value of the right type, or convert explicitly. This message has a hundred variants; read both type names carefully, because the difference is often a const, a ?, or a pointer versus a value (see A4.8, A4.9, A4.14). (Chapter 3)

A4.8 unsigned 8-bit int cannot represent all possible signed 64-bit values

pub fn main() void {
    var big: i64 = 300;
    big += 1;
    const small: u8 = big;
    _ = small;
}
e15.zig:4:23: error: expected type 'u8', found 'i64'
e15.zig:4:23: note: unsigned 8-bit int cannot represent all possible signed 64-bit values

Meaning. Integers only coerce implicitly when every value of the source fits the destination. Fix. const small: u8 = @intCast(big);, which checks at runtime, or @truncate if you mean to keep the low bits. (Chapter 4)

A4.9 type 'u8' cannot represent integer value '256'

const x: u8 = 255 + 1;
e08.zig:2:23: error: type 'u8' cannot represent integer value '256'

Meaning. The value is known at compile time and does not fit. Fix. Use a wider type, or if the wrap is intended, wrapping arithmetic (+%) on a runtime value. (Chapter 4)

A4.10 division with 'i32' and 'i32': signed integers must use @divTrunc, @divFloor, or @divExact

var a: i32 = -7;
a -= 1;
const b: i32 = 2;
std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{a / b});
e26.zig:6:34: error: division with 'i32' and 'i32': signed integers must use @divTrunc, @divFloor, or @divExact

Meaning. Truncation and flooring differ on negatives, so Zig makes you choose. Fix. @divTrunc(a, b) for C-style rounding toward zero, as IRON LEDGER's applyBp does. (Chapter 4, Chapter 45)

A4.11 cannot compare strings with ==

const a: []const u8 = "x";
if (a == "x") std.debug.print("same\n", .{});
e16.zig:4:11: error: cannot compare strings with ==

Meaning. Slices compare by pointer and length, not by contents, and the compiler refuses the obvious mistake. Fix. std.mem.eql(u8, a, "x"). (Chapter 11)

A4.12 invalid operands to binary expression: 'optional' and 'comptime_int'

const m: ?u32 = 5;
const n: u32 = m + 1;
e12.zig:3:22: error: invalid operands to binary expression: 'optional' and 'comptime_int'

Meaning. An optional must be unwrapped before use. Fix. (m orelse 0) + 1, if (m) |v| v + 1 else …, or m.? + 1 if you are sure it is not null. (Chapter 15)

A4.13 no field or member function named 'double' in '?P'

const p: ?P = .{ .x = 1 };
_ = p.double();
e30.zig:7:10: error: no field or member function named 'double' in '?e30.P'

Meaning. The same optional trap with a method call: the type is ?P, not P. Fix. Unwrap first. The message also appears, without the ?, when you misspell a method or field name. (Chapter 15)

A4.14 expected type '*u32', found 'u32'

fn bump(n: *u32) void { n.* += 1; }
pub fn main() void {
    var n: u32 = 1;
    bump(n);
}
e34.zig:4:10: error: expected type '*u32', found 'u32'
e34.zig:1:12: note: parameter type declared here

Meaning. The function wants a pointer and you passed a value. Fix. bump(&n);. Method calls take the address for you (gs.deinit()), plain calls do not (execute(&gs, …)). (Chapter 18)

A4.15 cannot assign to constant

const x: u32 = 1;
x = 2;
e14.zig:3:5: error: cannot assign to constant

Meaning. Exactly what it says. The same message appears for p.* = 2 through a *const u32 obtained by &x when x is const. Fix. Declare with var, or take a mutable pointer to a var. (Chapter 3, Chapter 18)

A4.16 slice of non-array type 'u32'

const n: u32 = 5;
const s = n[0..1];
e27.zig:3:16: error: slice of non-array type 'u32'

Meaning. Only arrays, slices and many-item pointers can be sliced. Fix. Slice the container, not the element; if you meant bytes of an integer, use std.mem.asBytes(&n). (Chapter 10)

A4.3 Control flow and completeness

A4.17 switch must handle all possibilities

const Color = enum { red, green, blue };
const n: u8 = switch (c) {
    .red => 1,
    .green => 2,
};
e07.zig:4:19: error: switch must handle all possibilities
e07.zig:1:34: note: unhandled enumeration value: 'blue'
e07.zig:1:15: note: enum 'e07.Color' declared here

Meaning. A switch on an enum, union or error set must name every case or have an else. Fix. Add the arm. This is the error IRON LEDGER relies on when a Command or Effect variant is added (Chapter 42, Chapter 46). For an integer switch the message is the same but with no note listing values; add else. (Chapter 6, Chapter 14)

A4.18 function with non-void return type 'u32' implicitly returns

fn f(a: u32) u32 {
    if (a > 1) return 1;
}
e18.zig:1:14: error: function with non-void return type 'u32' implicitly returns
e18.zig:3:1: note: control flow reaches end of body here

Meaning. Some path reaches the closing brace without returning. Fix. Add the missing return, or make the if an expression with an else. (Chapter 7)

A4.19 unreachable code

pub fn main() void {
    return;
    const x = 1;
    _ = x;
}
e23.zig:3:5: error: unreachable code
e23.zig:2:5: note: control flow is diverted here

Meaning. Code after a return, break, continue or unreachable is an error, not a warning. Fix. Delete it or move the return. (Chapter 6)

A4.20 cannot return from defer expression

defer {
    return;
}
e25.zig:3:9: error: cannot return from defer expression
e25.zig:2:5: note: defer expression here

Meaning. A defer block runs on the way out and may not change where the function returns to or what it returns. Fix. Do the cleanup and nothing else in the block; if the cleanup can fail, catch {} it. (Chapter 17)

A4.4 Errors and try

A4.21 expected type 'void', found '…error_set' / function cannot return an error

fn parse() !u32 { return std.fmt.parseInt(u32, "12", 10); }
pub fn main() void {
    const n = try parse();
    _ = n;
}
e05.zig:4:15: error: expected type 'void', found '@typeInfo(@typeInfo(@TypeOf(e05.parse)).@"fn".return_type.?).error_union.error_set'
e05.zig:3:15: note: function cannot return an error

Meaning. try returns the error from the current function, so the current function must be able to return one; main here returns void. The long type in the message is just "parse's error set". Fix. Change the return type to !void, or handle the error with catch. (Chapter 16)

A4.22 error union is ignored

pub fn main() void {
    parse();
}
e13.zig:4:10: error: error union is ignored
e13.zig:4:10: note: consider using 'try', 'catch', or 'if'

Meaning. A call that can fail must have its result handled. Fix. One of the three in the note, or _ = parse() catch {}; if you truly do not care. (Chapter 16)

A4.23 expectEqual: expected type 'u32', found 'i32'

fn add(a: i32, b: i32) i32 { return a + b; }
test "t" { try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 5), add(2, 3)); }
…/std/testing.zig:83:42: error: expected type 'u32', found 'i32'
…/std/testing.zig:83:42: note: unsigned 32-bit int cannot represent all possible signed 32-bit values
…/std/testing.zig:86:60: note: parameter type declared here
e06.zig:3:39: note: called inline here

Meaning. The expected and actual values have different types and the actual cannot coerce to the expected. The message points into the standard library; the last note is your line. Fix. Make the expected value's type match the function's return type: @as(i32, 5). (An untyped literal, expectEqual(5, add(2, 3)), compiles in 0.16 because the literal coerces.) (Chapter 8)

A4.5 Compile-time and formatting

A4.24 too few arguments (inside Writer.zig)

std.debug.print("{d} {d}\n", .{1});
…/std/Io/Writer.zig:717:13: error: too few arguments
referenced by:
    print__anon_27067: …/std/debug.zig:311:39
    main: e28.zig:3:20

Meaning. Two placeholders, one argument. Format strings are checked at compile time, so the error is inside the formatter with your line in the referenced by chain. Fix. Match the tuple to the placeholders. The sibling message "invalid format string 'd' for type '[]const u8'" means a placeholder does not suit the argument's type; see A2. (Chapter 2, Chapter 23)

A4.25 unable to resolve comptime value / types must be comptime-known

var n: usize = 3;
n += 1;
const arr: [n]u8 = undefined;
e22.zig:5:17: error: unable to resolve comptime value
e22.zig:5:17: note: types must be comptime-known

Meaning. An array length is part of a type, and types are fixed at compile time; n is a runtime value. Fix. Use a slice allocated at runtime (try alloc.alloc(u8, n)), or make n a comptime constant. (Chapter 9, Chapter 25)

A4.26 no field named 'Struct' in union 'builtin.Type'

const n = @typeInfo(P).Struct.fields.len;
e19.zig:4:28: error: no field named 'Struct' in union 'builtin.Type'
…/std/builtin.zig:550:18: note: union declared here

Meaning. The @typeInfo tags were renamed to lower case (.@"struct", .@"enum", .int…). The tutorial you copied from is pre-0.14. Fix. See A3. (Chapter 27)

A4.27 root source file struct 'std' has no member named 'io'

const out = std.io.getStdOut().writer();
e20.zig:3:21: error: root source file struct 'std' has no member named 'io'
…/std/std.zig:1:1: note: struct declared here

Meaning. std.io (lower case) is gone; I/O lives in std.Io and takes an io value. Any "has no member named" against std is a sign of a pre-0.16 tutorial. Fix. A3, first table. (Chapter 2)

A4.28 struct 'array_list.Aligned(u32,null)' has no member named 'init'

var list = std.ArrayList(u32).init(std.heap.page_allocator);
e21.zig:3:34: error: struct 'array_list.Aligned(u32,null)' has no member named 'init'

Meaning. Managed lists are gone; there is no init(alloc). Fix. var list: std.ArrayList(u32) = .empty; and pass the allocator to append, deinit and friends. (Chapter 21)

A4.6 Three runtime panics that are not compile errors

These compile fine and stop the program with a stack trace in Debug and ReleaseSafe builds. The trace names the line; read it the same way.

A4.29 integer overflow

var x: u8 = 200;
x += 100;
thread 6004466 panic: integer overflow
e24.zig:4:7: 0x10109dc53 in main (e24)
    x += 100;
      ^

Meaning. Plain + is checked. Fix. A wider type, +% to wrap, +| to saturate, or @addWithOverflow to inspect. (Chapter 4)

A4.30 index out of bounds

thread 6003567 panic: index out of bounds: index 3, len 3
e32.zig:6:37: 0x104341cd3 in main (e32)

Meaning. Every index into an array or slice is checked against its length. Fix. Check the index, or use if (i < items.len); note that the message gives you both numbers. (Chapter 9)

A4.31 attempt to use null value

thread 6003651 panic: attempt to use null value
e33.zig:5:33: 0x1028d1c97 in main (e33)
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{m.?});
                                ^

Meaning. .? asserted an optional was non-null and it was null. Fix. orelse or if (m) |v|. IRON LEDGER uses .? only where the code just created the value it unwraps (Chapter 42). (Chapter 15)

Appendix A5. Glossary

This appendix defines the terms the course uses, in alphabetical order, with a link to the chapter that introduces each. Zig terms come first in a definition; where IRON LEDGER gives a term a specific meaning, that follows.

allocator
A value of type std.mem.Allocator that hands out and takes back memory. Nothing in Zig allocates without being given one. Chapter 19.
anonymous struct literal
.{ .x = 1 }: a struct value whose type is inferred from where it is used. Also the syntax of ZON files. Chapter 12, Chapter 28.
anytype
A parameter type meaning "whatever the caller passes"; the function is specialised per argument type at compile time. Chapter 26.
arena
std.heap.ArenaAllocator: an allocator that never frees individually and releases everything in one deinit. IRON LEDGER gives each campaign one and each frame another. Chapter 20, Chapter 41.
array
A fixed number of elements known at compile time: [3]u8. Copied by value. Chapter 9.
ArrayList
The standard growable list. In 0.16 it is unmanaged: it starts as .empty and every growing call takes an allocator. Chapter 21.
basis points
Hundredths of a percent; 10,000 is a multiplier of one. IRON LEDGER's Bp type, applied by applyBp in integer arithmetic. Chapter 45.
builtin
A function whose name starts with @, provided by the language rather than the standard library. A1.
build.zig
The build script: an ordinary Zig program that describes modules, executables, tests and options as a graph of steps. Chapter 31.
C-bill
The BattleTech currency. In IRON LEDGER, CBills = i64; there are no floats in money. Chapter 45.
capture
The |x| after if, while, for, catch or a switch arm that binds the unwrapped value, the payload or the error. Chapter 6, Chapter 14.
catch
Handle an error in place: f() catch default, catch |err| { … }, catch unreachable. Chapter 16.
coercion
An implicit conversion the compiler allows because it cannot lose information: u8 to u32, *[3]u8 to []u8, a literal to a typed value. Everything else needs a cast. Chapter 4, Chapter 10.
command
In IRON LEDGER, a value of the Command tagged union; the only way to change a campaign is to pass one to commands.execute. Chapter 42.
comptime
Code and values evaluated while compiling. A comptime parameter must be known at compile time; types are values only at compile time. Chapter 25.
defer
Run a statement when the enclosing block exits by any path. errdefer runs only when it exits with an error. Chapter 17.
determinism
The property that the same inputs produce the same outputs. IRON LEDGER's core is a pure function of a seed and a command history, tested by the golden master. Chapter 39, Chapter 49.
doc comment
/// documents the next declaration; //! documents the file. // is an ordinary comment. Chapter 30.
enum
A closed set of named values, optionally with an integer representation and methods. A non-exhaustive enum (enum(u32) { none = 0, _ }) also accepts every other integer; IRON LEDGER's typed IDs are these. Chapter 13.
error set
A set of error names, error{ A, B }. Sets merge with ||; anyerror is the set of all of them. Chapter 16.
error union
E!T: either an error from E or a T. !T lets the compiler infer E. Chapter 16.
exhaustive switch
A switch that names every case of an enum, union or error set and therefore fails to compile when a case is added. IRON LEDGER uses this as a checklist. Chapter 14, Chapter 46.
extern fn
A declaration of a function defined elsewhere, usually in a C library, with C-shaped parameter types. Chapter 35, Chapter 47.
format string
The first argument of print: literal text with {…} placeholders, checked against the argument tuple at compile time. Chapter 23, A2.
frame arena
In IRON LEDGER's client, the arena reset before each draw and each key; query results live in it. Chapter 44, Chapter 48.
generic
A function that takes a comptime T: type and returns a value or type built from it, such as std.ArrayList(u32). Chapter 26.
golden master
A test that runs a fixed script from a fixed seed twice and compares a hash of the results. Chapter 49.
hash map
std.AutoHashMapUnmanaged(K, V) and relatives. The ArrayHashMap variants keep insertion order, which IRON LEDGER needs for determinism. Chapter 22, Chapter 41.
inline for
A loop unrolled at compile time, one copy of the body per element; required to iterate a tuple or a type's fields. Chapter 27.
io
A value of type std.Io, received in main as init.io, that every file, clock, process and sleep operation takes. Code without one cannot do I/O. Chapter 33, Chapter 39.
labeled block
blk: { … break :blk value; }: a block that yields a value. Chapter 6.
ledger
In IRON LEDGER, the append-only list of tagged transactions from which every balance and report is computed. Chapter 45.
many-item pointer
[*]T: a pointer to an unknown number of elements, with no length. [*:0]const u8 is a C string. Chapter 10, Chapter 35.
markup
In IRON LEDGER's query text, {g}…{/} tokens naming a style, rendered by the terminal client and stripped by the REPL. Chapter 44.
migration
A guarded schema change applied when an old save file is opened; in IRON LEDGER a row in store.migrations. Chapter 47.
module
A tree of source files with one root, declared in build.zig and imported by name. IRON LEDGER has a library module game and an executable module. Chapter 30, Chapter 31.
opaque
opaque {}: a type with unknown contents that can only be pointed to; the type of a C handle. Chapter 35.
optional
?T: a T or null. Unwrapped with orelse, if (x) |v|, or .?. Chapter 15.
orelse
Supply a fallback for a null optional, or exit early: x orelse return error.Missing. Chapter 15.
packed struct
A struct with a specified bit layout, packed struct(u8) { lo: u4, hi: u4 }, convertible to its integer with @bitCast. Chapter 29.
payload
The value carried by a union variant, an optional or an error union; bound by a capture. Chapter 14.
phase
In IRON LEDGER, one function of the daily tick, called in a fixed order from advanceDay. Chapter 43.
pointer
*T is the address of one T; *const T cannot write through; &x takes an address; p.* dereferences. Field access through a pointer needs no arrow. Chapter 18.
PRNG
A pseudo-random number generator: std.Random.DefaultPrng, seeded so its sequence is repeatable. IRON LEDGER keeps eight in a bag with named streams. Chapter 34, Chapter 41.
pub
Makes a declaration visible to importers. Without it, a declaration is private to its file. Chapter 30.
pure
Of a function or module: its result depends only on its inputs, with no I/O, wall clock or global state. IRON LEDGER's src/domain, sim, econ and gen are pure. Chapter 39.
query
In IRON LEDGER, a function in queries.zig that takes an allocator and the state and returns formatted rows with IDs; the only way a frontend reads the simulation. Chapter 44.
refAllDecls
std.testing.refAllDecls(@This()) in a test: references every public declaration so that unreferenced code is still compiled. Chapter 8, Chapter 49.
reflection
Inspecting types at compile time with @typeInfo, @field, @hasDecl and friends. Chapter 27.
REPL
IRON LEDGER's line-oriented console (--repl): reads verbs, parses them with cli.parseCommand, executes, prints. Chapter 39.
result type
The type the compiler infers for an expression from its surroundings; casts like @intCast rely on it. A1.
saturating arithmetic
+|, -|: clamp at the type's bounds instead of overflowing. need -| have is never negative. Chapter 4.
seed
The integer a PRNG starts from; the same seed gives the same sequence. IRON LEDGER's campaign seed is part of Config. Chapter 34.
sentinel
A terminating value in a pointer or slice type: [:0]const u8 is guaranteed to end with a zero byte. Chapter 10, Chapter 35.
shadowing
Reusing an outer name for an inner declaration. A compile error in Zig. Chapter 7, A4.
slice
[]T: a pointer plus a length. Strings are []const u8. Made by slicing an array, arr[a..b]. Chapter 10.
stream (RNG)
In IRON LEDGER, one of eight named generators (.battle, .market, …) so that adding rolls to one subsystem does not disturb another. Chapter 41.
struct
A record of named fields, optionally with defaults and with functions declared inside. Every Zig file is one. Chapter 12, Chapter 30.
tagged union
union(enum) { a: u32, b }: a value that is exactly one of several alternatives and knows which. Consumed by switch with payload captures. Chapter 14.
test block
test "name" { … }, run by zig test or zig build test, using std.testing's assertions and leak-checking allocator. Chapter 8.
tick
In IRON LEDGER, one call of tick.advanceDay: the clock moves one day and every phase runs. Chapter 43.
treasury
In IRON LEDGER, a tagged union naming which balance money moves in: the outfit, an HQ, or a deployed company. Chapter 45.
try
Evaluate an error union; on an error, return it from the current function. Chapter 16.
tuple
An anonymous struct with positional fields, .{ 1, "x" }; the argument list of print. Iterated with inline for. Chapter 23, Chapter 27.
typed ID
In IRON LEDGER, a non-exhaustive enum over u32 (PersonId, UnitId…) so that IDs of different kinds cannot be mixed up at no runtime cost. Chapter 13, Chapter 41.
undefined
A value you promise to write before reading; var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;. Debug builds fill it with 0xAA. Chapter 3.
unmanaged
Of a container: it does not store an allocator, so you pass one to every call that may allocate. The 0.16 default for lists and maps. Chapter 21.
unreachable
An expression asserting that control never gets here; a panic in safe builds, undefined behaviour in fast ones. Chapter 6.
wrapping arithmetic
+%, *%: overflow wraps around instead of panicking. Used where the wrap is intended, as in seeding RNG streams. Chapter 4.
writer
*std.Io.Writer: the interface print, writeAll and flush are called on; obtained from a file with a buffer, from a fixed buffer, or from an allocator. Chapter 2, Chapter 33.
ZON
Zig Object Notation: a data file that is a single Zig literal, imported with @import and type-checked against the declaration that receives it. Chapter 28, Chapter 40.

Assembled 2026-09-20 from the chapter fragments in chapters/. Zig 0.16.0. The original guide this book expands is preserved in reference/original-guide.html.
